{"request_id":"fe211e15633917b1c9260080","rewritten_text":"He could not tell whether the voice belonged to a man or a woman. He could not understand the words, but believed the language was Spanish. This witness described the condition of the room and the bodies as we described it yesterday.

“_Henri Duval_, a neighbor and silversmith, states that he was among the group that first entered the house. He generally confirms Musèt’s testimony. As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which gathered very quickly despite the late hour. This witness believed the shrill voice was that of an Italian. He was certain it was not French. He could not tell whether it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He did not know Italian. He could not make out the words, but was convinced by the speaker’s tone that it was an Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had often spoken with both. He was certain the shrill voice belonged to neither of the dead women.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness offered his testimony voluntarily. Since he did not speak French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He was born in Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the screams began. They continued for several minutes—probably ten. They were long, loud, terrible, and distressing. He was one of those who entered the building. He confirmed the earlier testimony in every respect except one. He was certain the shrill voice belonged to a man—a Frenchman. He could not understand the words. They were loud, rapid, and uneven, apparently spoken in fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh—not truly shrill. He could not describe it as a shrill voice. The rough voice repeatedly said ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu._’

“_Jules Mignaud_, banker with the firm of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She opened an account with his bank in the spring of the year—eight years earlier. She made frequent deposits of small amounts. She wrote no checks until three days before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs. The money was paid in gold, and a clerk accompanied it to her home.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence with the 4000 francs, packed in two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from his hands, while the old woman took the other.”"}

{"request_id":"1a71348d9c85f9de2cf3971b","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologised. He said, “Not at all,” and continued.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, so you may imagine that people considered her a very desirable match. Her half-brother had plenty of money again, but debts and fresh madness soon wasted most of it once more. The differences between him and her were even greater than those between him and their father, and it was suspected that he held a deep and deadly grudge against her because he believed she had turned their father against him. Now I come to the cruel part of the story—pausing only, my dear Handel, to point out that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to force mine into my tumbler, I cannot say at all. I only know that, with persistence better suited to a more worthwhile task, I made the greatest efforts to squeeze it into that small space. Once again I thanked him and apologised, and once again he cheerfully said, “Not at all, I’m sure!” Then he continued.

“There appeared on the scene—at the races, perhaps, or at public balls, or anywhere else you like—a certain man who began courting Miss Havisham. I never saw him, since this happened twenty-five years ago, before you and I were born, Handel, but I heard my father say that he was flashy and exactly the sort of man for the purpose. Still, my father strongly insists that no one should mistake him for a gentleman, unless ignorance or prejudice caused the mistake. My father’s principle is that no man who was not a true gentleman at heart has ever been a true gentleman in manner. He says that no varnish can hide the grain of wood; the more varnish you apply, the more clearly the grain shows. Well! This man pursued Miss Havisham closely and claimed to be devoted to her. I believe she had shown little feeling for anyone before then, but all the feeling she possessed came out at that time, and she loved him passionately. There is no doubt that she worshipped him. He deliberately exploited her love and obtained large sums of money from her. He also persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery—which their father had foolishly left him—for an enormous price, claiming that, once he became her husband, he would have to own and manage the whole business. Your guardian was not yet involved in Miss Havisham’s affairs, and she was too proud and too deeply in love to accept advice from anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"a82cab878c9acdb759d4d432","rewritten_text":"She would be such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed, but added,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, however, is another very pretty and pleasant young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very glad to hear it—but Jane Fairfax is the only one known to be so accomplished and superior!—and she is exactly Emma’s age.”

They discussed this subject very happily, and then moved on to others of similar importance, all passing with the same good feeling. But the evening did not end without a small return of uneasiness. The gruel was brought in, giving them plenty to discuss: much praise and many remarks, firm agreement that it was healthy for every constitution, and rather sharp criticism of the many houses where it was never made properly. Unfortunately, among the failures the daughter mentioned, the most recent and therefore the most memorable was her own temporary cook at South End, a young woman who had never understood what she meant by a basin of smooth, pleasant gruel, thin but not too thin. However often she had asked for it, she had never received anything tolerable. This was a dangerous subject.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern. To Emma, the exclamation meant: “Ah! There is no end to the sad results of your going to South End. It cannot bear discussion.” For a while she hoped he would say no more, and that quietly thinking about it might restore his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After several minutes, however, he began:

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the seaside this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir? I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you had to go to the seaside, you should not have gone to South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was surprised to hear that you had chosen South End.”

“I know many people think that, but it is quite a mistake, sir. We were all perfectly healthy there and never suffered the least inconvenience from the mud. Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely wrong to suppose the place unhealthy, and I am sure he can be trusted, because he thoroughly understands the nature of the air. His own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry once spent a week at Cromer, and he considers it the best of all the seaside resorts.”"}

{"request_id":"206d57b67bfbe0d652ce2d4e","rewritten_text":"“I wrap him in the paper and stuff part of it in his mouth—that was the way.”

“And you think, then, that your master was actually bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him ill?”

“I don’t think anything about it—I know it. Why does he dream about gold so much, if it isn’t because he was bitten by the gold-bug? I’ve heard of those gold-bugs before this.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How do I know? Why, because he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how I know.”

“Well, Jup, perhaps you are right; but to what fortunate circumstance am I to attribute the honor of a visit from you today?”

“What’s the matter, massa?”

“Did you bring any message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I bring this here letter;” and Jupiter handed me a note that read as follows:

“MY DEAR ——Why have I not seen you for so long? I hope you have not been foolish enough to take offense at any slight brusqueness of mine; but no, that is unlikely. Since I saw you, I have had great reason for anxiety. I have something to tell you, yet scarcely know how to tell it, or whether I should tell it at all.

“I have not been entirely well for several days, and poor old Jup annoys me almost beyond endurance with his well-intentioned attentions. Would you believe it?—the other day he prepared a huge stick with which to punish me for eluding him and spending the day alone among the hills on the mainland. I truly believe that my sickly appearance alone saved me from a beating.

“I have added nothing to my collection since we met.

“If you can possibly arrange it, come over with Jupiter. Do come. I wish to see you tonight about a matter of importance. I assure you that it is of the highest importance.

“Ever yours, “WILLIAM LEGRAND”.

There was something in the tone of this note that caused me great uneasiness. Its entire style differed markedly from Legrand’s. What could he be dreaming about? What new obsession had taken hold of his excitable mind? What “business of the highest importance” could he possibly have to conduct? Jupiter’s account of him suggested nothing good. I feared that the continued pressure of misfortune had finally disturbed my friend’s reason. Without the slightest hesitation, therefore, I prepared to accompany the Black man.

When we reached the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat in which we were to cross.

“What does all this mean, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"1af87f8234500fae42e450dc","rewritten_text":"“But when I saw you become the object of another’s love; when I imagined that you might be loved as something other than a sacred image and embodiment of beauty and excellence; or that you might love another with a more ardent affection than the one you felt for me, then the fiend awoke within me. I dismissed your lover, and from that moment I have known no peace. I sought sleep and rest in vain; my eyelids refused to close, and my blood was forever in turmoil. I awoke to a new life as one who dies in hope might awaken in Hell. I will not stain your imagination by recounting my struggles, my anger at myself, and my despair. Let a veil be drawn over the unimaginable sensations of a guilty father; the secrets of so tormented a heart must not be made common. All was uproar, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet still the tenderest love. What first awakened in me the firm resolve to conquer my passion and restore her father to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic sorrow. It was this that brought me here: I thought that if I could awaken again in my heart the grief I had felt at your mother’s loss, and the many associations with her memory that had lain dormant for seventeen years, all love for her child would die. In a moment of heroism I resolved to go alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it was impossible: I had overestimated my strength, or underestimated my love. I should certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. Would that I had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I have been wretchedly mistaken in believing that I could conquer my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields, and woods, which my first love inhabited, seems to have increased it. In my madness I dared say to myself—Diana died to give you birth; her mother’s spirit passed into your body, and you ought to be Diana to me. With every effort to cast it off, this love clings more tightly, this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which withers your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

No time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since I arrived here, I have not for a moment ceased to feel the hell of passion implanted in me, burning until all is cold, rigid, and dead.”"}

{"request_id":"084ac9a0ea06807c5b117181","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had never happened. She believed he had drunk too much of Mr. Weston’s fine wine and was certain he would want to talk nonsense.

To restrain him as much as possible through her own behavior, she immediately prepared to speak with perfect calm and seriousness about the weather and the night. But scarcely had she begun, scarcely had they passed through the gate and joined the other carriage, when she found her subject interrupted—her hand seized, her attention demanded, and Mr. Elton actually declaring his love for her. He took advantage of the precious opportunity, expressing feelings that he thought must already be well known, hoping, fearing, adoring, and ready to die if she refused him. Yet he flattered himself that his ardent attachment, unequalled love, and extraordinary passion could not fail to affect her. In short, he was firmly determined to be accepted as soon as possible. It really was so. Without hesitation, apology, or much visible embarrassment, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s lover, was declaring himself to be her lover. She tried to stop him, but without success; he continued and said everything. Though angry, she decided to control herself when she answered. She felt that half this foolishness must be caused by drink, and therefore hoped it might last only for the moment. So, combining seriousness with playfulness, which she thought best suited his confused state, she replied,

“I am extremely surprised, Mr. Elton. This to me! You have forgotten yourself—you have mistaken me for my friend. I will gladly deliver any message to Miss Smith, but please say no more of this to me.”

“Miss Smith!—A message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean?” He repeated her words with such confident emphasis and exaggerated amazement that she could not help answering sharply:

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behavior! I can explain it in only one way: you are not yourself. Otherwise, you could not speak either to me or about Harriet in this manner. Control yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to raise his spirits, not enough to cloud his judgment. He knew perfectly well what he meant. After warmly protesting that her suspicion was deeply insulting, and briefly mentioning his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—but admitting that he was surprised she had been mentioned at all—he returned to the subject of his own passion and pressed her urgently for a favorable answer."}

content.text: {"request_id":"93091d5a9f90e2f93797aeee","rewritten_text":"I could remember what things had been like during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars a day, valued in gold; in the South, he earned fifty—payable in Confederate shinplasters worth a dollar a bushel. In the North, a pair of overalls cost three dollars—a day’s wages; in the South, they cost seventy-five—which amounted to two days’ wages. Other prices were in the same proportion. Consequently, wages were twice as high in the North as in the South, because one wage had twice the purchasing power of the other.\n\nYes, I made several acquaintances in the hamlet, and one thing that pleased me greatly was finding our new coins in circulation—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, quite a few nickels, and some silver; all of it among the artisans and common people generally. Yes, and even some gold—but that was at the bank, meaning the goldsmith’s. I went in while Marco, Marco’s son, was haggling with a shopkeeper over a quarter pound of salt, and asked for change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They provided it—after chewing the coin, ringing it on the counter, testing it with acid, and asking where I had gotten it, who I was, where I came from, where I was going, when I expected to arrive, and perhaps two hundred other questions. When they ran out of questions, I continued supplying information voluntarily: I told them I owned a dog named Watch, that my first wife was a Free Will Baptist, that her grandfather had been a Prohibitionist, that I had once known a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip, who died hoping for a glorious resurrection, and so on and so on, until even that hungry village inquisitor began to look satisfied—and slightly annoyed. Still, he had to respect a man of my financial standing, so he did not give me any lip. I noticed, however, that he took it out on his subordinates, which was perfectly natural. Yes, they changed my twenty, but I judged that it strained the bank somewhat, as one would expect. It was like walking into a poor village store in the nineteenth century and suddenly asking its owner to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. He might be able to do it, but he would still wonder why a small farmer was carrying so much money in his pocket. That was probably what the goldsmith thought as well, because he followed me to the door and stood there watching me leave with reverent admiration."}

{"request_id":"33fdd8c85da156965989f127","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends, a secret he had cherished since his earliest years. Although he loved his fellow students, he would not trust it to the delicacy or sympathy of any of them. He was in love. He feared they might mock the strength of his passion, and he could not bear for them to insult it by treating as trivial and temporary what he felt was the very life of his life.

A gentleman of modest means lived near his family home and had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty was only one of her qualities. Her mind was clear and strong, and her nature angelically gentle. She and my father had been playmates since infancy. Diana had been a favorite of his mother even as a child, and that affection grew as the beautiful, lively girl grew older. Thus, during his school and college holidays, they were almost always together. Novels, and the many ways in which young people in civilized society learn about passion before truly feeling it, had deeply affected him, for he was unusually open to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his favorite playmate, yet he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older, her upbringing had left her more childish, at least in her understanding and expression of emotion. She received his passionate declarations innocently and returned them without knowing what they meant. She had read no novels and spent time only with her younger sisters; what could she know of the difference between love and friendship? When her growing understanding finally revealed the true nature of their relationship, her heart was already devoted to her friend. She feared only that other attractions or inconstancy might lead him to break the vows he had made as a child.

But their feelings grew more passionate and tender each day. His love had grown with him; it was woven into every ability and feeling, and could end only with his life. No one knew of their love but the two of them. Yet although he feared his companions’ judgment in other matters, and even in this one—because he truly loved someone beneath him in fortune—nothing could for a moment weaken his resolve to marry her as soon as he could gather enough courage to face the difficulties he was determined to overcome.

Diana was entirely worthy of his deepest affection."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a5191c925297d2d09e364483","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was much too broad for his height, making his whole figure absurdly round. His feet could not be seen at all, though a hard, suspicious-looking substance sometimes stuck through a tear in the bottom of the car—or, more accurately, the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair was very gray and tied in a queue behind him. His nose was extremely long, crooked, and red; his eyes were large, bright, and sharp; and his chin and cheeks, though wrinkled with age, were broad, puffy, and doubled. Yet there was no sign of ears anywhere on his head. This strange little gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin coat, with tight matching breeches fastened at the knees by silver buckles. His vest was made of some bright yellow material. A white taffeta cap sat jauntily on one side of his head, and a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped around his throat before falling onto his chest in a fanciful bow of enormous size.\n\nAfter descending, as I said before, to about one hundred feet above the earth, the little old gentleman was suddenly overcome by fear and seemed unwilling to come any closer to the ground. He therefore threw out some sand from a canvas bag, which he lifted with great difficulty, and stopped at once. He then hurriedly and nervously pulled a large morocco wallet from a side pocket of his coat. He weighed it suspiciously in his hand, then stared at it in great surprise, clearly astonished by how heavy it was. At last he opened it and drew out a huge letter sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape. He dropped it directly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent down to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still deeply unsettled and apparently having no further business to keep him in Rotterdam, now began preparing to leave. Since he needed to release ballast in order to rise again, he threw out six bags, one after another, without bothering to empty them. Every bag fell, most unfortunately, onto the burgomaster’s back, rolling him over and over twenty-one times before the eyes of every man in Rotterdam. It cannot be supposed, however, that the great Underduk allowed this insult from the little old man to go unpunished."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7d517e8d15574a94887514a4","rewritten_text":"He chose Friday, August 17, for his appearance, and spent most of the day examining his wardrobe. In the end, he decided on a large, floppy hat with a red feather, a shroud frilled at the wrists and neck, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening, a violent rainstorm broke, and the wind blew so fiercely that every window and door in the old house shook and rattled. It was, in fact, exactly the kind of weather he loved. His plan was as follows. He would make his way quietly to Washington Otis’s room, gibber at him from the foot of the bed, and stab himself three times in the throat to the accompaniment of slow music. He held a particular grudge against Washington, knowing perfectly well that he was the one who regularly removed the famous Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. After reducing the reckless, foolhardy youth to a state of utter terror, he would proceed to the room occupied by the United States Minister and his wife. There he would place a clammy hand on Mrs. Otis’s forehead while hissing the charnel-house’s dreadful secrets into her trembling husband’s ear. As for little Virginia, he had not entirely decided what to do. She had never insulted him, and she was pretty and gentle. A few hollow groans from the wardrobe, he thought, would be quite enough; or, if that failed to wake her, he might claw at the counterpane with fingers twitching as if palsied. Regarding the twins, however, he was firmly resolved to teach them a lesson. First, naturally, he would sit on their chests, creating the suffocating sensation of nightmare. Then, since their beds stood close together, he would position himself between them as a green, ice-cold corpse until fear paralyzed them. Finally, he would throw off the shroud and crawl around the room with bleached white bones and one rolling eyeball, playing ‘Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton,’ a role in which he had produced a powerful effect more than once, and which he considered fully equal to his celebrated part of ‘Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.’\n\nAt half past ten, he heard the family going to bed. For a while, he was distracted by the twins’ wild peals of laughter. With the carefree cheerfulness of schoolboys, they were clearly entertaining themselves before retiring. But at a quarter past eleven, everything was quiet, and when midnight sounded, he set out. An owl struck against the windowpanes, a raven croaked from the old yew tree, and the wind drifted around the house, moaning like a lost soul. The Otis family slept, unaware of their doom, while high above the rain and storm he could hear the United States Minister’s steady snoring."}

content.text: {"request_id":"59edefba0b486a711a300c6b","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself time to think, and scarcely knowing what she felt, Elizabeth, after finishing this letter, immediately seized the other and opened it with the greatest impatience. It read as follows; it had been written a day after the first letter ended.\n\n“By now, my dearest sister, you will have received my hurried letter. I hope this one may be clearer, but although I am not pressed for time, my mind is so confused that I cannot promise to be coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to write, but I have bad news for you, and it cannot wait. Imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate to know that it has taken place, because there is only too much reason to fear that they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, only a few hours after the express. Although Lydia’s brief letter to Mrs. F. led them to believe that they were going to Gretna Green, Denny let something slip, saying that he believed W. had never intended to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was repeated to Colonel F., who immediately became alarmed and set out from B., intending to follow their route. He traced them easily as far as Clapham, but no farther; on entering that place, they changed into a hackney coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All that is known afterward is that they were seen continuing along the London road. I do not know what to think. After making every possible inquiry in that part of London, Colonel F. came on to Hertfordshire, anxiously repeating his questions at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success—no such people had been seen passing through. With the greatest kindness and concern, he came to Longbourn and told us his fears in a way that did him the highest credit. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F.; but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many circumstances might make it preferable for them to marry privately in town rather than follow their original plan; and even if _he_ could form such a scheme against a young woman of Lydia’s connections, which is unlikely, can I imagine her so completely lost to all sense of propriety? Impossible! {"request_id":"6e636d4d1473b85727f407c3","rewritten_text":"Yet despite all this, the boy grew increasingly melancholy, pale, and dejected. She added hot baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges. The boy remained as gloomy as a hearse. She began supporting the water treatment with a sparse oatmeal diet and blister plasters. She measured his capacity as if he were a jug and filled him each day with patent remedies.

By then Tom had become indifferent to persecution. This stage filled the old lady’s heart with alarm. His indifference had to be broken at any cost. Then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a large supply at once. She tasted it and felt profoundly grateful. It was simply fire in liquid form. She abandoned the water treatment and everything else, placing all her faith in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched anxiously for the result. Her troubles immediately vanished and her soul was at peace again, because his “indifference” had been shattered. The boy could not have shown a wilder or more vigorous interest if she had built a fire beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to wake up; this kind of life might be romantic enough in his ruined condition, but it was becoming too lacking in sentiment and too full of distracting variety. He considered several ways to obtain relief and finally decided to pretend that he liked Pain-killer. He asked for it so often that he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have enjoyed the matter without any doubts; but because it was Tom, she secretly watched the bottle. She saw that the medicine really was being used up, but it never occurred to her that the boy was repairing a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One day Tom was pouring medicine into the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat came over, purring, eyeing the teaspoon greedily, and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it clear that he did want it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now that you’ve asked for it, I’ll give it to you, because there’s nothing mean about me; but if you discover that you don’t like it, you must blame no one but yourself.”

Peter agreed. So Tom pried open his mouth and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped several feet into the air, then gave a war whoop and raced around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and creating general havoc."}

{"request_id":"2147b74575f3275c4616e37d","rewritten_text":"Moreover, this is a knot that few people besides sailors can tie, and it is especially associated with the Maltese. I found the ribbon at the foot of the lightning rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead men. Now, even if my conclusion from this ribbon—that the Frenchman was a sailor from a Maltese vessel—is wrong, I can have done no harm by saying what I did in the advertisement. If I am mistaken, he will simply think that some circumstance misled me, and he will not bother to investigate it. But if I am right, we have gained a great advantage. Though innocent of the murder, the Frenchman knows about it, and will naturally hesitate before answering the advertisement and claiming the Ourang-Outang. He will reason in this way: “I am innocent and poor. My Ourang-Outang is extremely valuable—to someone in my position, it is a fortune. Why should I give it up because of vague fears of danger? It is here, within my reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far from the place where the murders occurred. How could anyone suspect that a wild animal committed the crime? The police have failed; they have not found the slightest clue. Even if they trace the animal, they could never prove that I knew about the murder or connect me with it merely because I had that knowledge. Above all, I am known. The person who placed the advertisement identifies me as the animal’s owner. I do not know how much else he may know. If I refuse to claim property of such great value, which everyone knows I possess, I will make the animal itself suspicious. It is not in my interest to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. I will answer the advertisement, recover the Ourang-Outang, and keep it hidden until this affair has passed.””

At that moment, we heard footsteps on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin, “with your pistols, but do not use them or show them until I give you a signal.”

The house’s front door had been left open, so the visitor entered without knocking and climbed several steps. Then he seemed to hesitate. A moment later, we heard him going back down. Dupin was hurrying toward the door when we heard the man coming up again. This time he did not turn back. He climbed firmly and knocked on the door of our room.

“Come in,” said Dupin in a cheerful, welcoming voice.

A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—a tall, broad, muscular man with a bold, reckless expression that was not entirely unpleasant."}

{"request_id":"a7a35af863d5146424f8b8f1","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it and was about to start on the bureau when he was called away to dress for Sunday school.

Mary gave him a tin basin of water and a piece of soap. He carried them outside the door and set the basin on a small bench. Then he dipped the soap in the water, put it down, rolled up his sleeves, gently poured the water onto the ground, and went back into the kitchen. There he began carefully wiping his face with the towel behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said:

“Now aren’t you ashamed, Tom? You mustn’t be so naughty. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was a little unsettled. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a while, gathering his courage. He took a deep breath and began. When he soon came back into the kitchen, both eyes shut and feeling around for the towel, soap and water were dripping honestly from his face. But after he dried himself, he still was not clean enough. The clean part ended at his chin and along his jaws, like a mask; below it, and around the back of his neck, was a wide stretch of untouched dark skin. Mary took charge, and when she finished, he was clean all over, with no difference in color. His wet hair was neatly brushed, its short curls arranged in a delicate, even shape. [In private, he painfully and laboriously smoothed the curls out and plastered his hair flat against his head, because he thought curls were feminine, and his own made him miserable.] Then Mary brought out a suit of clothes he had worn only on Sundays for two years. They were simply called his “other clothes,” which showed how small his wardrobe was. After he dressed, the girl “put him to rights”: she buttoned his tidy roundabout up to his chin, folded his huge shirt collar over his shoulders, brushed him off, and topped him with his speckled straw hat. He now looked much better—and very uncomfortable. He felt just as uncomfortable as he looked, because wearing a complete outfit and being clean made him feel trapped. He hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope failed. As usual, she covered them thoroughly with tallow and brought them out. He lost his temper and said he was always being forced to do everything he did not want to do."}

{"request_id":"7a7995b70ee4d014eaa5b6fc","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse—handsome, clever, and wealthy, with a comfortable home and a cheerful nature—seemed to possess many of life’s finest blessings. She had lived almost twenty-one years with very little to trouble or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters born to a deeply affectionate and indulgent father. After her sister married, Emma had become mistress of his household at a very early age. Her mother had died too long before for Emma to retain more than a vague memory of her caresses, and her place had been filled by an excellent governess whose affection had come close to that of a mother.

Miss Taylor had been part of Mr. Woodhouse’s family for sixteen years, less as a governess than as a friend. She loved both daughters, but Emma especially. Between them, the relationship was more like that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor formally gave up her position as governess, her gentle nature had scarcely allowed her to impose any real discipline; and now that all trace of authority had long disappeared, they had lived together as two mutually devoted friends, with Emma doing exactly as she pleased. She valued Miss Taylor’s judgment highly, but was guided chiefly by her own.

The true disadvantages of Emma’s situation were her ability to have almost everything her own way and her tendency to think rather too highly of herself. These were the flaws that threatened to diminish her many pleasures. Yet the danger was still so unnoticed that she did not regard them as misfortunes at all.

Sorrow came—a gentle sorrow—but not in the form of any unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. It was the loss of Miss Taylor that first brought Emma real grief. On the wedding day of this beloved friend, Emma first sat in prolonged, mournful reflection. Once the wedding was over and the newlyweds had departed, she and her father were left to dine together, with no hope of a third person to brighten the long evening. After dinner, as usual, her father settled himself to sleep, leaving her only to sit and think about what she had lost.

The marriage promised every kind of happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston had an impeccable character, a comfortable fortune, an appropriate age, and agreeable manners. Emma could take some satisfaction in remembering how selflessly and generously she had always wished for and encouraged the match; but it had been a bleak morning for her. Miss Taylor’s absence would be felt every hour of every day. Emma remembered her past kindness—the affection and care of sixteen years—how she had taught and played with her from the age of five, devoted all her abilities to keeping her attached and entertained when she was well, and nursed her through the various illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"5bb6d45ace33160c7a2c9a96","rewritten_text":"In the morning she was found dead in her bed, apparently without having suffered any pain. Sir Mathew Reid was sent for immediately, but naturally there was nothing to be done, and she was to be buried on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death she had made her will, leaving Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, together with all its furniture, personal belongings, and pictures, except for her collection of miniatures, which was to go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to receive. The property was not worth much; but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was extremely anxious that Lord Arthur should return at once, if possible, since there were many bills to settle, and Lady Clementina had never kept proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s affectionate remembrance of him, and felt that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. His love for Sybil, however, outweighed every other feeling, and the knowledge that he had done his duty brought him peace and comfort. When he reached Charing Cross, he felt completely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise that he would never again let anything come between them, and the wedding was set for the 7th of June. Life once more seemed bright and beautiful to him, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, while he was inspecting the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil herself, burning bundles of faded letters and emptying drawers filled with miscellaneous rubbish, the young girl suddenly gave a small cry of delight.

‘What have you found, Sybil?’ Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his work with a smile.

‘This lovely little silver _bonbonnière_, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint and Dutch? Do give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.’

It was the box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint flush rose in his cheek. He had almost completely forgotten what he had done, and it seemed to him a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whose sake he had endured all that terrible anxiety, should be the first to remind him of it.

‘Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clementina myself.’

‘Oh, thank you, Arthur; and may I have the _bonbon_ as well? I had no idea Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.’

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a terrible thought crossed his mind."}

“MY DEAR ——Why have I not seen you for so long? I hope you have not been foolish enough to take offense at any little brusqueness of mine; but no, that is unlikely. Since I saw you, I have had great reason for worry. I have something to tell you, but I hardly know how to tell it, or whether I should tell it at all.

“I have not been well for several days, and poor old Jup annoys me almost beyond endurance with his well-meant attention. Would you believe it? The other day he prepared a huge stick to punish me for slipping away from him and spending the day alone among the hills on the mainland. I truly believe that my sickly appearance alone saved me from a beating.

“I have added nothing to my collection since we met.

“If you can arrange it in any way, come over with Jupiter. Do come. I wish to see you tonight about important business. I assure you that it is of the highest importance.

“Ever yours, “WILLIAM LEGRAND”.

Something in the tone of this note made me very uneasy. Its style was completely unlike Legrand’s. What could he be dreaming about? What new idea had taken hold of his excitable mind? What business of the highest importance could he possibly have to conduct? Jupiter’s description of him suggested nothing good. I feared that his continued misfortunes had finally disturbed my friend’s reason. Without hesitation, therefore, I prepared to go with the Black man.

When we reached the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat in which we were to travel.

“What does all this mean, Jup?”"}

Soon they left again, rising so quickly that their brother was surprised, and hurrying away as if eager to escape Mrs. Bennet’s polite attentions.

The thought of the Netherfield ball pleased every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to believe it was being held as a compliment to her eldest daughter, and she was especially flattered that Mr. Bingley himself had sent the invitation instead of a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening with her two friends and their brother’s attention. Elizabeth looked forward to dancing often with Mr. Wickham and seeing proof of everything she believed in Mr. Darcy’s expression and behavior. Catherine and Lydia’s expected happiness depended less on one event or one person. Although each of them, like Elizabeth, planned to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was far from the only partner who could please them, and a ball was, in any case, a ball. Even Mary assured her family that she had no objection to attending.

“While I can have my mornings to myself,” she said, “that is enough. I do not think it is a sacrifice to take part occasionally in evening activities. Society makes demands on us all, and I consider periods of recreation and amusement desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth was in such high spirits that, although she did not often speak unnecessarily to Mr. Collins, she could not help asking whether he intended to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation and, if so, whether he thought it proper to join the evening’s entertainment. She was rather surprised to learn that he had no hesitation about it and was far from fearing a reprimand, either from the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh, for daring to dance.

“I am certainly not of the opinion,” he said, “that a ball of this kind, given by a respectable young man to respectable people, can have any harmful effect. Far from objecting to dancing myself, I hope to be honored with the hands of all my fair cousins during the evening. I would also like to ask for yours, Miss Elizabeth, especially for the first two dances—a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will understand correctly, and not take as any disrespect toward her.”"}

As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which gathered very quickly despite the late hour. This witness believed the shrill voice was Italian. He could not distinguish the words, but was convinced by the intonation that the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had often spoken with both. He was certain the shrill voice belonged to neither of the deceased.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness came forward voluntarily. Since he did not speak French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He was a native of Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the screams began. They continued for several minutes—probably ten. They were prolonged and loud, extremely terrible and distressing. He was one of those who entered the building. He confirmed the earlier testimony in every respect except one. He was certain the shrill voice was a man’s—that of a Frenchman. He could not distinguish the words. They were loud and rapid, uneven, apparently spoken in fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh—not so much shrill as harsh. He would not call it a shrill voice. The gruff voice repeatedly said ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu._’

“_Jules Mignaud_, banker with the firm of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye possessed some property. She opened an account with his bank in the spring of the year—eight years earlier. She made frequent deposits in small amounts. She had written no checks until three days before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs. The money was paid in gold, and a clerk accompanied her home with it.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence carrying the 4000 francs in two bags. {"request_id":"5e8392a4eb3e2f40366f32a8","rewritten_text":"But my father was beside me, comforting me and driving away bitter memories with bright hopes. I thought it sweet to grieve when he might dry my tears.

Again, he diverted my thoughts from sorrow by comparing it with his despair when he lost my mother. Even then I shuddered at the picture he drew of his passions. He had the imagination of a poet, and when he described the whirlwind that had torn through his feelings, he gave his words such vivid force that I believed him even as I trembled. I wondered how he could ever have returned to the ordinary duties of life after his wild thoughts seemed to have brought him close to the unearthly. As he spoke, the ideas he conveyed were so immense that the human heart seemed far too limited to contain them. His feelings appeared better suited to a spirit whose home was the earthquake and volcano than to one confined within a mortal body and human features. But these were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was all love and gentleness, and when I looked at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips told me that his heart was filled with the tenderest feelings.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me toward deeper studies than those that had occupied me before. My progress delighted him. He was with me throughout my studies and helped with, or took part in, every lesson. We saw a great deal of society, and no day passed without my father trying to brighten it with some new pleasure. The tender affection he felt for me, and the love and reverence I returned, cast a charm over every moment. The hours passed slowly because every minute was occupied; we lived more in one week than many people do in several months, and the variety and novelty of our pleasures gave each one its special delight.

We were constantly making excursions together. Whether we went to admire beautiful scenery, view fine paintings, or sometimes simply seek whatever amusement happened to arise, I was always happy when I was near my father. I regretted whenever a third person joined us, yet if I turned toward my father with a troubled expression, his eyes would meet mine, shining with tenderness, and instantly restore joy to my heart. O, hours of intense delight! Brief as you were, memory has made you seem as long as an entire life, when I look back through the veil of grief that rose immediately afterward, as if to hide you from my sight."}

{"request_id":"dc200414687f56db2d21f036","rewritten_text":"While these events were unfolding in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the same room from which the girl had taken Oliver—brooding over a dull, smoky fire. With his arms folded over them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared absently at the rusty bars.

At a table behind him sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist; the Artful playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The first-named gentleman’s face, always remarkably intelligent, gained still greater interest from his close attention to the game and his careful study of Mr. Chitling’s hand. Whenever the opportunity arose, he cast it a series of serious glances, wisely directing his own play according to what he observed in his neighbour’s cards. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he found it necessary to seek refreshment from a quart pot on the table, already filled with gin and water for the company.

Master Bates was attentive to the game as well; but, being more excitable than his accomplished friend, he applied himself more often to the gin and water and made numerous jokes and irrelevant comments, all thoroughly improper during a serious rubber. Indeed, relying on their close friendship, the Artful more than once took the opportunity to lecture his companion solemnly on these offenses. Master Bates accepted every remonstrance in excellent spirits, merely telling his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with some other neatly phrased joke of the same kind. The cleverness of these replies greatly impressed Mr. Chitling. It was remarkable that he and his partner invariably lost, and that this, far from angering Master Bates, seemed to amuse him intensely; for at the end of every deal he laughed uproariously and declared that he had never seen such a jolly game in all his life.

“That’s two doubles and the rubber,” said Mr. Chitling, looking very miserable as he drew half a crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw such a fellow as you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"ad2830819c41d9385fd09ee0","rewritten_text":"After seeing our friend properly settled in his new office, we turned our attention to Windsor. Its closeness to London made our separation from Raymond and Perdita seem far less painful. We said goodbye to them at the Protectoral Palace. It was amusing to see my sister enter into the spirit of the occasion and try to perform her role with suitable dignity. Her inner pride and modest manner were now more than ever in conflict. Her shyness was not false, but came from a fear that she would not be properly valued, from the slight regard she felt the world paid her—a feeling Raymond also possessed. But Perdita thought more often of others than he did; part of her bashfulness came from a desire to spare those around her any sense of inferiority, a feeling that never entered her own mind. Because of his birth and education, Idris would have been better suited to the formalities of ceremony; but the ease with which Perdita performed such actions, gained through habit, made them tiresome to her. Even with every disadvantage, she clearly enjoyed her position. She was too full of new ideas to suffer much when we left. She said goodbye to us affectionately and promised to visit soon, but she did not regret the events that had brought about our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless. He did not know what to do with his newly acquired power; his head was crowded with plans, though he had chosen none. Still, he promised himself, his friends, and the world that his Protectorate would be marked by some act of extraordinary glory. Talking about them and reflecting on these matters, we returned with our smaller party to Windsor Castle. We were delighted to have escaped political turmoil and sought our solitude with renewed pleasure. We had no shortage of things to occupy us, but my eager nature was now directed only toward intellectual work. I found intense study an excellent remedy for calming the restless excitement that idleness would surely have brought upon me. Perdita had allowed us to take Clara back to Windsor, and she, along with my two lovely infants, provided constant interest and amusement.\n\nThe only thing that disturbed our peace was Adrian’s health. It was clearly worsening, though he showed no symptom that revealed his illness—unless his brighter eyes, lively expression, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption. Yet he felt neither pain nor fear. He devoted himself eagerly to books and rested from his studies in the company he loved best: his sister and me."}

{"request_id":"44b9a7321c597dd50878297b","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I will begin my tale: it is my final task, and I hope I possess strength enough to complete it. I record no crimes; my faults may readily be forgiven, for they arose not from evil intention but from lack of judgement; and I believe few would claim that, through different conduct and greater wisdom, they could have escaped the misfortunes of which I am the victim. My fate was ruled by necessity, a dreadful necessity. It demanded hands stronger than mine—stronger, I believe, than any human power—to break the thick, adamantine chain that bound me, once breathing only joy and filled with warm love and delight in goodness, to misery that could end only, and is now about to end, in death. But I lose myself; my tale remains untold. I will pause for a few moments, wipe my dim eyes, and try to replace the present obscure yet heavy unhappiness with the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank: he had lost his own father early, and was raised by a weak mother who granted him all the indulgence she believed proper for a wealthy nobleman. He was sent to Eton and afterward to college, and from childhood was permitted the free use of large sums of money; thus enjoying from his earliest years the independence that a boy with such advantages always gains at a public school.

Under the influence of these circumstances, his passions found rich soil in which to take root and flourish, as flowers or weeds according to their nature. Having always been allowed to act for himself, his character became strongly and early defined, displaying a varied surface upon which a keen observer might discern the seeds of virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance, which led him to squander immense sums satisfying passing whims—whims whose apparent force he dignified with the name of passions—often revealed itself as boundless generosity. Yet while he occupied himself earnestly with the needs of others, his own desires were indulged to their fullest extent. He gave his money, but sacrificed none of his own wishes to his gifts; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was glad to have awakened in any way.

I do not say that, had his desires been set against those of others, he would have shown excessive selfishness, but that test was never made. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wished to gratify him."}

{"request_id":"e9bc6c94088cf741eede8437","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water to finish the feast. After a while Becky suggested that they move on again. Tom was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“Becky, can you bear it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face went pale, but she thought she could.

“Well, then, Becky, we have to stay here, where there’s water to drink. That small piece is our last candle!”

Becky burst into tears and sobs. Tom tried to comfort her, but it had little effect. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and search for us!”

“Yes, they will! Of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re searching for us now, Tom.”

“Well, I suppose they might be. I hope they are.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I suppose.”

“Tom, it might be dark by then—would they notice that we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

The frightened look on Becky’s face brought Tom to his senses, and he realized he had made a mistake. Becky was not supposed to go home that night! The children fell silent and thoughtful. A moment later, Becky began grieving again, showing Tom that she had understood the same terrible thing: it might be Sunday morning before Mrs. Thatcher discovered that Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children stared at their piece of candle and watched it slowly, mercilessly melt away. They saw the last half inch of wick standing alone; saw the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, pause at its top for a moment, and then—the horror of complete darkness took over!

Neither could say how long afterward it was before Becky slowly realized that she was crying in Tom’s arms. They only knew that, after what seemed like an enormous stretch of time, they both woke from a deep, lifeless sleep and returned to their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday now—perhaps Monday. He tried to make Becky talk, but her sorrow was too heavy, and all her hope was gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and that the search was surely continuing. He would shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried, but the distant echoes sounded so terrible in the darkness that he did not try again.

The hours dragged by, and hunger came to torment the captives once more. Some of Tom’s half of the cake remained; they divided it and ate it. But they seemed even hungrier afterward."}

{"request_id":"2fb5fb4ee79a5d3749faa5ec","rewritten_text":"Having driven a peg with great precision into the ground at the exact place where the beetle had fallen, my friend drew a tape measure from his pocket. He secured one end to that point on the trunk of the tree nearest the peg, unrolled it to the peg, and then continued unrolling it in the direction already fixed by the tree and peg, for fifty feet—Jupiter cutting through the brambles with his scythe. At the place reached, a second peg was driven, and around it, as a centre, a rough circle some four feet across was marked. Legrand then took a spade himself, handed one to Jupiter and another to me, and urged us to begin digging as quickly as we could.

To tell the truth, I had never had any particular taste for such work, and at that moment would gladly have refused it; night was approaching, and I was already greatly wearied by the exercise. Yet I saw no way to escape, and feared that a refusal might upset my poor friend’s composure. Had I been able to rely upon Jupiter’s assistance, I would not have hesitated to try carrying the madman home by force; but I knew the old negro’s character too well to expect him, in any circumstances, to aid me in a physical struggle with his master. I had little doubt that Legrand had fallen prey to one of the countless Southern superstitions concerning buried treasure, and that his fancy had been strengthened by finding the _scarabæus_, or perhaps by Jupiter’s stubborn insistence that it was “a bug of real gold.” A mind inclined toward madness could easily be carried away by such notions—particularly when they agreed with cherished preconceived ideas—and I remembered then the poor fellow’s remark that the beetle was “the index of his fortune.” On the whole, I was deeply troubled and perplexed; but finally I resolved to make a virtue of necessity, dig willingly, and thereby convince the visionary more quickly, through the evidence of his own eyes, that his beliefs were mistaken.

Once the lanterns had been lighted, we all set to work with a zeal better suited to a more sensible purpose; and as the glare shone upon our figures and tools, I could not help reflecting on what a picturesque group we made, and how strange and suspicious our labor must have seemed to any intruder who happened by chance upon our hiding-place.

For two hours we dug with steady persistence."}

{"request_id":"639bf9bbcea84ff26ee4e991","rewritten_text":"Directly before him, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man of dreadful appearance. His eyes glowed like red coals; long grey hair hung over his shoulders in tangled coils; his old-fashioned clothes were dirty and torn, while heavy manacles and rusty fetters dangled from his wrists and ankles.

‘My dear sir,’ said Mr. Otis, ‘I really must ask you to oil those chains, and for that purpose I have brought you a little bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. It is reputed to be entirely effective after one application, and the wrapper bears several testimonials to that effect from some of our most distinguished native divines. I shall leave it here beside the bedroom candles, and will gladly provide more if you need it.’ Saying this, the United States Minister placed the bottle on a marble table, shut his door, and went to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost remained perfectly still in righteous indignation; then he hurled the bottle onto the polished floor, rushed down the corridor with hollow groans, and gave off a dreadful green light. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open, two small figures in white appeared, and a large pillow whizzed past his head! Clearly there was no time to waste, so he hastily employed the Fourth Dimension of Space as an escape route, disappeared through the wainscoting, and left the house completely silent.

When he reached a little secret chamber in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to regain his breath and began trying to comprehend his situation. In all his brilliant, uninterrupted career of three hundred years, he had never suffered such a gross insult. He recalled the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood before the mirror in lace and diamonds; the four housemaids, who had fallen into hysterics when he merely grinned at them through the curtains of a spare bedroom; the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out as he came late one night from the library, and who had remained under Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a complete martyr to nervous disorders; and old Madame de Tremouillac, who, after waking early one morning to see a skeleton sitting in an arm-chair by the fire and reading her diary, had been confined to bed for six weeks with brain fever, and, upon recovering, had reconciled herself to the Church and ended her association with that notorious sceptic, Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"ec6dd06079f8bcfa3f7b5948","rewritten_text":"“Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” said Joe.

“Is there another Miss Havisham down town?” my sister replied.

“She wants this boy to go there and play. And naturally he’s going. He’d better play there, too,” said my sister, shaking her head at me to encourage me to be exceedingly light and playful, “or I’ll work him.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham up town—everyone for miles around had heard of Miss Havisham up town—as an enormously wealthy and grim woman who lived in a great, gloomy house fortified against robbers, and who lived in seclusion.

“Well, to be sure!” said Joe, astonished. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” cried my sister. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Which some person,” Joe politely suggested again, “mentioned that she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? Isn’t it barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook might be one of her tenants, and that he might sometimes—we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, since that would demand too much of you—but sometimes—go there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, always thoughtful and considerate toward us—though you may not believe it, Joseph,” she added in a tone of profound reproach, as though he were the most heartless of nephews, “then mention this boy, standing Prancing here”—which I solemnly swear I was not doing—“to whom I have always been a willing slave?”

“Good again!” cried Uncle Pumblechook. “Well said! Nicely pointed! Very good! Now, Joseph, you understand the case.”

“No, Joseph,” said my sister, still reproachfully, while Joe apologetically rubbed the back of his hand repeatedly across his nose, “you do not yet—though you may not think so—understand the case. You may suppose that you do, but you do _not_, Joseph. For you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that, for all we can tell, this boy’s fortune may be made by his going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, keep him there tonight, and personally take him to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” cried my sister, suddenly throwing off her bonnet in despair, “here I am talking to mere Mooncalfs, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the mare growing cold at the door, and the boy black with soot and dirt from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"1b7685dcd24583f9c0472e32","rewritten_text":"He shuddered and went back, closing the window behind him.

When he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not even look at the murdered man. He felt that the secret was not to acknowledge what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait, the source of all his misery, had vanished from his life. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was a rather unusual Moorish piece, made of dull silver inlaid with arabesques of burnished steel and set with rough turquoise stones. His servant might notice it was missing, and questions might follow. He hesitated briefly, then turned back and took it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the dead thing. How motionless it was! How horribly white the long hands appeared! It looked like a terrible wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he crept quietly downstairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to cry out in pain. Several times he stopped and waited. No: everything was silent. It was only the sound of his own footsteps.

When he reached the library, he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden somewhere. He unlocked a secret cupboard in the paneling, where he kept his own strange disguises, and placed them inside. He could burn them easily later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.

He sat down and began to think. Every year—almost every month—men were hanged in England for what he had done. There had been a murderous madness in the air. Some red star had drawn too near the earth.... And yet, what evidence was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, on the midnight train, as he had planned. Given his peculiar, secretive habits, it would be months before anyone grew suspicious. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before then.

A sudden idea came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went into the hall. There he stopped, hearing the policeman’s slow, heavy footsteps on the pavement outside and seeing the flash of the bull’s-eye reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

After a few moments, he lifted the latch and slipped out, closing the door very gently behind him. Then he began ringing the bell."}

{"request_id":"07b3aec810c2127d077f277d","rewritten_text":"Moreover, this is a knot that few except sailors can tie, and it is peculiar to the Maltese. I picked up the ribbon at the foot of the lightning rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead men. Now, even if my deduction from this ribbon—that the Frenchman was a sailor serving on a Maltese vessel—is wrong, I can have done no harm by saying what I did in the advertisement. If I am mistaken, he will merely assume that some circumstance misled me, and will not trouble himself to investigate it. But if I am right, a great deal is gained. Though aware of the murder and innocent of it, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate to answer the advertisement—to claim the Ourang-Outang. He will reason as follows: ‘I am innocent; I am poor; my Ourang-Outang is extremely valuable—to a man in my circumstances, it is a fortune in itself. Why should I lose it through vague fears of danger? Here it is, within my reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far from the scene of that slaughter. How could anyone suspect that a brute animal committed the deed? The police are mistaken; they have not obtained the slightest clue. Even if they traced the animal, it would be impossible to prove that I knew of the murder, or to implicate me in it because of that knowledge. Above all, I am known. The advertiser identifies me as the animal’s owner. I do not know how far his knowledge may extend. If I avoid claiming property of such great value, which is known to belong to me, I will at least make the animal suspicious. It is not in my interest to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. I will answer the advertisement, recover the Ourang-Outang, and keep it hidden until this affair has blown over.’”

At that moment we heard footsteps on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin, “with your pistols, but do not use them or reveal them until I give a signal.”

The house’s front door had been left open, and the visitor had entered without ringing and climbed several steps. Now, however, he seemed to hesitate. Soon we heard him going back down. Dupin was hurrying toward the door when we heard him coming up again. This time he did not turn back, but climbed decisively and knocked at the door of our room.

“Come in,” said Dupin in a cheerful, welcoming voice.

A man entered. He was plainly a sailor—a tall, broad, muscular-looking man with a certain reckless expression that was not entirely unattractive."}

{"request_id":"61fac217d9f6d1069b013557","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff answered.

“And, translating the word yokel for the ladies’ benefit, I take your meaning to be that this attempt was not made by a countryman?” said Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That’s right, master,” replied Blathers. “This is all concerning the robbery, is it?”

“All of it,” said the doctor.

“Now, what’s this about the boy the servants are talking of?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing whatsoever,” replied the doctor. “One of the terrified servants took it into his head that he had something to do with this attempt to enter the house; but it’s nonsense—sheer absurdity.”

“Very easily settled, if that’s so,” remarked Duff.

“What he says is perfectly correct,” observed Blathers, nodding in confirmation and idly rattling the handcuffs as though they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t fall out of the clouds, did he, master?”

“Of course not,” replied the doctor, casting a nervous look at the two ladies. “I know his entire history; but we can discuss that presently. You would like to see first, I suppose, the place where the thieves attempted to enter?”

“Certainly,” rejoined Mr. Blathers. “We had best inspect the premises first, and question the servants afterwards. That is the customary way of conducting business.”

Lights were procured; and Messrs. Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the native constable, Brittles, Giles, and everybody else, in short, entered the little room at the passage’s end and looked out of the window; then went around by the lawn and looked in through it; after that, they had a candle brought out to examine the shutter; and then a lantern with which to follow the footprints; and finally a pitchfork for poking among the bushes. This completed, amid the breathless interest of every spectator, they returned inside; and Mr. Giles and Brittles were put through a melodramatic enactment of their parts in the previous night’s adventures. They performed it about six times, contradicting one another in no more than one important detail the first time, and in no fewer than a dozen by the last. When this was accomplished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a lengthy conference, which, in secrecy and solemnity, made a consultation of eminent doctors over the most difficult medical question seem mere child’s play.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced the adjoining room in a state of great uneasiness; while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched him with anxious faces.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after a great many very rapid turns, “I scarcely know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"8040bbe161b20042a1153e96","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how mysterious they were! The soul could be animal-like, while the body sometimes seemed spiritual. The senses could become refined, and the intellect could sink into vulgarity. Who could say where physical desire ended and mental desire began? How limited were the neat definitions of ordinary psychologists! And yet how hard it was to choose between the claims of the different schools. Was the soul a shadow sitting in the house of sin? Or was the body truly contained within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Separating spirit from matter was a mystery, and joining spirit to matter was a mystery too.

He began to wonder whether psychology could ever become such an exact science that every small force behind life would be exposed. As things stood, we always misunderstood ourselves and seldom understood anyone else. Experience had no moral value. It was simply the name people gave to their mistakes. Moralists usually treated it as a warning, claiming that it helped shape character, praising it as something that taught us what to pursue and what to avoid. But experience had no power to make us act. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly showed was that our future would resemble our past, and that a sin we had committed once, with disgust, we would commit many times, with pleasure.

It was clear to him that experiment was the only way to reach a scientific understanding of the passions; and Dorian Gray was a subject ready to hand, promising rich and useful results. His sudden, passionate love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological event of great interest. Curiosity and the desire for new experiences had certainly played a large part in it, but it was not a simple passion. It was highly complex. Whatever came from the purely sensual instinct of youth had been reshaped by the imagination into something that seemed, to the boy himself, far removed from the senses—and was therefore more dangerous. The passions whose origins we misunderstood were the ones that ruled us most strongly. Our weakest motives were those whose nature we understood. Often, when we believed we were experimenting on others, we were actually experimenting on ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat thinking about these matters, someone knocked at the door. His valet entered and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"76623a9ccf7908089b7694b6","rewritten_text":"“Stop the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the larboard! Come ahead on the starboard! Stop her! Let your outside turn over slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that head-line out! _Lively_ now! Come—out with your spring-line—what are you about there! Take a turn around that stump with its bight! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Engines done, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (testing the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept whitewashing, paying no heed to the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment, then called: “_Hi-Yi! You’re_ up a stump, ain’t you!”

There was no answer. Tom examined his final stroke with an artist’s eye, then passed his brush over it gently once more and inspected the result as before. Ben came alongside him. Tom’s mouth watered at the apple, but he continued working. Ben said:

“Hello, old fellow, you’ve got to work, hey?”

Tom turned sharply and said:

“Why, it’s you, Ben! I wasn’t noticing.”

“Say—I’m going swimming, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But naturally you’d rather _work_—wouldn’t you? Of course you would!”

Tom studied the boy for a little while, then said:

“What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t _that_ work?”

Tom went back to whitewashing and replied indifferently:

“Well, perhaps it is, and perhaps it isn’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come now, you don’t mean to pretend that you _like_ it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get the chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That made the matter appear differently. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom moved his brush delicately back and forth, stepped away to judge the effect, added a little here and there, and criticized the result again. Ben watched each motion, growing more interested and absorbed all the while. Presently he said:

“Say, Tom, let _me_ whitewash a little.”

Tom thought it over and was about to agree, but changed his mind:

“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t quite do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly is terribly particular about this fence—right here beside the street, you know—but if it were the back fence I wouldn’t care, and _she_ wouldn’t either. Yes, she’s terribly particular about this one; it has to be done very carefully. I reckon there isn’t one boy in a thousand, perhaps two thousand, who can do it as it ought to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh, come now—let me just try. Only a little—I’d let _you_, if you were me, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}
