{"request_id":"b650be68a92bed975f743d65","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and every kind of low vagabond were mixed together in one mass. Drovers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and plunged, sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squealed, hawkers cried out, and shouts, curses, and quarrels rose on every side. Bells rang, and voices roared from every public house. People crowded, pushed, drove, beat, whooped, and yelled; the hideous, discordant din echoed from every corner of the market; and unwashed, unshaven, filthy figures constantly ran back and forth, bursting in and out of the throng. Altogether, it made a stunning and bewildering scene that completely overwhelmed the senses.

Mr. Sikes, dragging Oliver behind him, forced his way through the thickest part of the crowd, paying little attention to the many sights and sounds that astonished the boy. He nodded two or three times to passing acquaintances and refused just as many invitations to have a morning drink, continuing steadily until they had escaped the turmoil and passed through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, looking up at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church. “Nearly seven! You must move faster. Come on, don’t start lagging already, Lazy-legs!”

As he spoke, Mr. Sikes jerked his little companion by the wrist. Oliver quickened his pace into a sort of trot, halfway between walking quickly and running, and kept up with the housebreaker’s long strides as best he could.

They continued at that speed until they had passed Hyde Park Corner and were heading toward Kensington. Then Sikes slowed down until an empty cart, some distance behind them, caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” written on it, he asked the driver, with as much politeness as he could manage, whether he would carry them as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes, he’s my boy,” Sikes replied, staring hard at Oliver and absently putting his hand into the pocket where he kept the pistol.

“Your father walks a little too fast for you, doesn’t he, my lad?” the driver asked, noticing that Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” Sikes interrupted. “He’s used to it. Here, take my hand, Ned. Get in!”

Speaking to Oliver in this way, he helped him into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told him to lie there and rest.

As they passed one milestone after another, Oliver wondered more and more where his companion intended to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford all went by, yet they continued as steadily as though their journey had only just begun."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ffdb7e6f45b8186e08f06d6e","rewritten_text":"With ordinary resources unavailable, the analyst puts himself in his opponent’s place and identifies with him. In this way, he often sees at once the only ways—sometimes absurdly simple ones—to lead him into error or rush him into a wrong calculation.\n\nWhist has long been known for its effect on what is called the calculating faculty. Men of the highest intelligence have taken an apparently inexplicable pleasure in it while dismissing chess as frivolous. Certainly, no similar game puts the power of analysis under such strain. The finest chess player in the world may be little more than a fine chess player; but skill at whist suggests an ability to succeed in any more important undertaking in which one mind contends with another. By skill, I mean perfection in the game, including an understanding of every legitimate source of advantage. These sources are not only numerous but varied, and often lie in areas of thought completely beyond the ordinary mind. Careful observation leads to clear memory, so the focused chess player will do well enough at whist; and Hoyle’s rules, based on the game’s simple mechanics, are generally easy to understand. Thus a strong memory and playing “by the book” are commonly considered the whole of good play. But the analyst’s skill appears in matters beyond mere rules. Silently, he makes countless observations and deductions. His companions may do the same; the difference lies less in the soundness of their deductions than in the quality of their observations. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player limits himself in no way. Because the game is his object, he does not ignore clues outside it. He studies his partner’s face, carefully comparing it with each opponent’s. He considers how the cards are arranged in every hand, often counting trumps and honors by watching the glances their holders give them. As play continues, he notices every change of expression, drawing information from signs of certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered, he judges whether the player who took it can win another in that suit. He recognizes a feint by the manner in which the card is placed on the table. A careless word; the accidental dropping or turning of a card, together with the concern or indifference shown about hiding it; the counting of tricks and their arrangement; embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or fear—all provide his seemingly instinctive perception with clues to the true situation."}

{"request_id":"1dad29634957c7bb8fa12e22","rewritten_text":"“Well,” I said, “I needed the watermelon.” But he said I didn’t need it to help me escape from prison; that was the difference. He said if I had wanted it to hide a knife in and smuggle it to Jim so he could kill the seneschal, then it would have been all right. So I let the matter drop, though I couldn’t see the advantage of pretending to be a prisoner if I had to sit down and think through a lot of fine distinctions like that every time I saw a chance to grab a watermelon.

Well, as I was saying, that morning we waited until everyone had settled down to work and no one was in sight around the yard. Then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood some distance away to keep watch. After a while he came out, and we sat on the woodpile to talk. He said:

“Everything’s all right now except the tools, and that’s easy to fix.”

“Tools?” I said.

“Yes.”

“Tools for what?”

“Why, to dig with. We aren’t going to _gnaw_ him out, are we?”

“Aren’t those old broken picks and things in there good enough to dig a black man out with?” I said.

He turned toward me with such a pitying look that it could make a person cry, and said:

“Huck Finn, have you _ever_ heard of a prisoner having picks and shovels, along with all the modern conveniences, in his wardrobe to dig himself out with? Now I want to ask you—if you have any sense at all—what kind of chance would _that_ give him to be a hero? Why, they might as well lend him the key and be done with it. Picks and shovels—why, they wouldn’t provide them even for a king.”

“Well, then,” I said, “if we don’t want picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of case-knives.”

“To dig out the foundations under that cabin?”

“Yes.”

“Darn it, Tom, that’s foolish.”

“It doesn’t matter how foolish it is; it’s the _right_ way—and the usual way. And there isn’t any _other_ way that I’ve ever heard of, and I’ve read all the books that give information about these things. They always dig out with a case-knife—and not through dirt, mind you; usually it’s through solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever and ever. Why, look at one of those prisoners in the bottom dungeon of the Castle Deef, in the harbor of Marseilles, who dug himself out that way. How long do you suppose _he_ worked at it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don’t know. A month and a half.”"}

{"request_id":"0199dd6d6a2088496cf8df3a","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff replied.

“And, translating the word yokel for the ladies’ benefit, I take your meaning to be that this attempt was not made by a countryman?” Mr. Losberne asked with a smile.

“That’s it, sir,” Blathers replied. “This is all about the robbery, is it?”

“All of it,” said the doctor.

“Now, what’s this about the boy the servants have been talking about?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing at all,” the doctor replied. “One of the frightened servants decided he had something to do with this attempt to break into the house; but it’s nonsense—sheer absurdity.”

“Easily settled, if that’s so,” Duff remarked.

“What he says is quite correct,” Blathers observed, nodding in confirmation and idly playing with the handcuffs as though they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What account does he give of himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t fall out of the clouds, did he, sir?”

“Of course not,” the doctor replied, casting a nervous glance at the two ladies. “I know his entire history; but we can discuss that presently. You would like first to see where the thieves made their attempt, I suppose?”

“Certainly,” Mr. Blathers answered. “We had better inspect the premises first and question the servants afterward. That is the usual way of doing things.”

Lights were then brought; and Messrs. Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and everyone else, went into the little room at the end of the passage and looked out the window. They then went around by way of the lawn and looked in through it; after that, they had a candle passed out so they could inspect the shutter, and then a lantern with which to trace the footprints, and finally a pitchfork for poking through the bushes. This completed, amid the breathless interest of all who watched, they returned inside; and Mr. Giles and Brittles were made to act out their parts in the previous night’s adventures. They performed it some six times over, contradicting each other in no more than one important detail the first time, and in no more than a dozen by the last. Once this was accomplished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a lengthy private council, compared with which a consultation of eminent doctors over the most difficult medical problem would have been child’s play in secrecy and solemnity.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced the adjoining room in a state of great unease, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious faces.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after a great many rapid turns, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"221d1f8240e6117f3eb0af29","rewritten_text":"“These thoughts calmed me, and that afternoon I fell into a deep sleep; but the fever in my blood kept me from peaceful dreams. The terrible scene of the day before played before my eyes again and again: the women fleeing, and the furious Felix dragging me from his father’s feet. I woke exhausted, and, finding that night had come, crept out of my hiding place to search for food.

“When my hunger was satisfied, I followed the familiar path to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crawled into my shelter and waited silently for the usual time when the family rose. That hour passed, and the sun climbed high, but the cottagers did not appear. I trembled violently, fearing that some terrible misfortune had occurred. The cottage was dark inside, and I heard no movement. I cannot describe the agony of waiting.

“Soon two countrymen passed by. They stopped near the cottage and began talking with excited gestures, but I could not understand them, because they spoke the local language, which was different from that of my protectors. Shortly afterward, Felix came toward the cottage with another man. I was surprised, since I knew Felix had not left the cottage that morning, and I waited anxiously to learn from their conversation the reason for these strange events.

“‘Do you understand,’ his companion said, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the produce of your garden? I do not want to take unfair advantage of you, so I ask you to take a few days to consider your decision.’

“‘It is completely useless,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the terrible event I told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their fear. I beg you not to argue with me any longer. Take back your house and let me leave this place.’

“Felix trembled violently as he spoke. He and his companion entered the cottage, where they stayed for a few minutes, and then left. I never saw another member of the De Lacey family again.

“I remained in my shelter for the rest of the day, sunk in complete and senseless despair. My protectors had gone and had broken the only bond connecting me to the world. For the first time, revenge and hatred filled my heart. I did not try to restrain them. Letting myself be carried along by these feelings, I turned my thoughts toward causing harm and death.”"}

{"request_id":"2829fb9bf10c1e3aa82b9156","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”

“A wire fence?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself, two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—the time the Church first tested her strength against us, then decided it was wiser to wait for a more promising season. Well, how have you arranged the fence?”

“I run twelve immensely strong, bare, uninsulated wires from a large dynamo in the cave—a dynamo with no brushes except a positive and a negative one—”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a circle of level ground a hundred yards across; they form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles within circles—and their ends return to the cave.”

“Right; go on.”

“The fences are attached to heavy oak posts only three feet apart, and the posts are sunk five feet into the ground.”

“That is strong enough.”

“Yes. The wires have no ground connection outside the cave. They leave from the dynamo’s positive brush; there is a ground connection through the negative brush; the other ends return to the cave, and each is grounded separately.”

“No, no, that won’t do!”

“Why?”

“It’s too expensive—it wastes power for nothing. You need no ground connection except the one through the negative brush. The other end of every wire must be brought back into the cave and fastened separately, but without any ground connection. Now observe the economy. A cavalry charge throws itself against the fence; you use no power and spend no money, because there is only one ground connection until those horses strike the wire. The instant they touch it, they make a connection with the negative brush through the ground and drop dead. Don’t you see? You use no energy until it is needed; your lightning is waiting, ready like a charge in a gun, but it costs you nothing until you fire it. Yes, the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I don’t know how I missed that. It’s not only cheaper, but more effective than the other arrangement, because if wires break or become tangled, no harm is done.”

“No, especially if we have a warning device in the cave and disconnect the broken wire. Well, go on. The Gatlings?”

“Yes—that’s arranged. In the center of the inner circle, on a spacious platform six feet high, I’ve grouped a battery of thirteen Gatling guns and supplied plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They command every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there will be music. The edge of the precipice above the cave—”

“I’ve put a wire fence there, and a Gatling.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"c344b4f326efa85536637985","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke in the morning, he wondered where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then he remembered. It was the cool gray dawn, and a deep, peaceful calm filled the woods. Not a leaf moved; no sound disturbed Nature’s quiet thoughts. Dewdrops covered the leaves and grass. A white layer of ash covered the fire, and a thin blue thread of smoke rose straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.\n\nFar away in the woods, one bird called, and another answered. Soon the tapping of a woodpecker could be heard. Slowly, the cool, dim gray morning grew lighter, and sounds multiplied as life began to stir. The wonder of Nature waking and going to work unfolded before the thoughtful boy. A little green worm crawled across a wet leaf, raising two-thirds of its body into the air from time to time and “sniffing around,” then moving on again—for Tom said it was measuring. When the worm came near him, Tom sat as still as a stone, his hopes rising and falling as it approached or seemed ready to turn away. At last, after a painful pause with its curved body raised, it came firmly down onto Tom’s leg and began crawling over him. Tom’s heart filled with joy, because this surely meant he would get a new suit of clothes—a bright pirate uniform, without a doubt. Then a line of ants appeared from nowhere and went about their work. One struggled along carrying a dead spider five times its size and dragged it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed the dizzy height of a blade of grass. Tom leaned close and said, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone.” The insect flew off to check, which did not surprise Tom, because he had long known that ladybugs believed easily in fires and had fooled them more than once. Next came a tumblebug, pushing hard against its ball. Tom touched it, and it pulled its legs against its body and pretended to be dead. By then the birds were making a great uproar. A catbird, the Northern mockingbird, landed in a tree above Tom and sang imitations of its neighbors with great delight. Then a sharp-voiced jay flashed down like blue fire and stopped on a twig almost within reach. It tilted its head and stared at the strangers with intense curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large fox squirrel came hurrying by, stopping now and then to sit up, inspect the boys, and chatter at them. The wild creatures had probably never seen a human being before and hardly knew whether they should be afraid."}

{"request_id":"a60d402d18988aa32c7209b1","rewritten_text":"“I regard it as one of the earliest refinements of civilized society.”

“Certainly, sir; and it has the further merit of being fashionable among the world’s less polished societies: every savage can dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. “Your friend dances charmingly,” he continued after a pause, when he saw Bingley join the set; “and I have no doubt that you are yourself skilled in the art, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, certainly, and found no small pleasure in the spectacle. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Do you not think it would be a suitable compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I never offer any place, when I can help it.”

“You have a house in town, I presume?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once had some idea of settling in town myself, being fond of refined society; but I was not entirely convinced that the London air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for a reply; but his companion showed no inclination to give one. At that moment Elizabeth came towards them, and Sir William was seized by the thought of doing something particularly gallant. Calling to her, he said,--

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must permit me to introduce this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot refuse to dance when so much beauty is before you.” Taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy’s, who, though greatly surprised, was not unwilling to accept it, when she immediately withdrew and said, somewhat flustered, to Sir William,--

“Indeed, sir, I have not the slightest intention of dancing. I beg you not to imagine that I came this way to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with solemn courtesy, requested the honour of her hand, but without success. Elizabeth was resolute; nor did Sir William’s efforts to persuade her alter her determination.

“You dance so excellently, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deprive me of the pleasure of watching you; and though this gentleman generally dislikes the amusement, I am sure he can have no objection to oblige us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He is indeed; but given the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot be surprised by his compliance. Who, after all, would object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave him a mischievous look and turned away. Her refusal had not diminished her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was considering her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him,--"}

{"request_id":"38a669b0dad4ab9941f9f7a1","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, one might have said that Nemesis had stolen Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed turned to stone, his face marble in its melancholy. He had lived the delicate, luxurious life of a young man born to wealth and position, a life exquisite in its freedom from sordid cares and its beautiful, boyish insouciance; and now, for the first time, he became aware of Destiny’s terrible mystery, of Doom’s dreadful meaning.

How mad and monstrous it all seemed! Could it be that written on his hand, in characters he could not read but another could decipher, was some fearful secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime? Was there no possible escape? Were we no better than chessmen moved by an unseen power, vessels shaped by the potter’s whim for honour or disgrace? His reason rebelled against it, yet he felt that some tragedy hung over him and that he had suddenly been called upon to bear an intolerable burden. Actors were fortunate. They could choose whether to appear in tragedy or comedy, whether to suffer or celebrate, laugh or weep. But real life was different. Most men and women were forced to play parts for which they had no qualifications. Our Guildensterns played Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets had to jest like Prince Hal. The world was a stage, but the play was badly cast.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers entered the room. When he saw Lord Arthur, he started, and his coarse, fat face turned a greenish yellow. Their eyes met, and for a moment there was silence.

‘The Duchess left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to bring it to her,’ Mr. Podgers said at last. ‘Ah, I see it on the sofa! Good evening.’

‘Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me a straightforward answer to a question I am about to ask.’

‘Another time, Lord Arthur, but the Duchess is anxious. I am afraid I must go.’

‘You shall not go. The Duchess is in no hurry.’

‘Ladies should not be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,’ said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. ‘The fair sex is inclined to be impatient.’

Lord Arthur’s finely shaped lips curled in petulant disdain. The poor Duchess seemed of very little importance to him at that moment. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and held out his hand.

‘Tell me what you saw there,’ he said. ‘Tell me the truth. I must know it. I am not a child.’"}

{"request_id":"89f8dbe720fe972cad690559","rewritten_text":"Her situation was truly one of unusual difficulty and distress. She felt an urgent, burning need to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s past, yet she could not betray the confidence placed in her by the wretched woman she had just spoken with, who had trusted her as a young and innocent girl. The woman’s words and manner had moved Rose Maylie deeply. Alongside her love for Oliver, and almost equal to it in sincerity and strength, was her earnest hope of bringing the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They intended to stay in London for only three days before leaving for several weeks at a distant part of the coast. It was now midnight on the first day. What action could she decide on and carry out within forty-eight hours? And how could she delay their journey without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was staying with them and would remain for the next two days. But Rose knew the good doctor’s impulsive nature too well. She could easily imagine the anger with which, in his first burst of outrage, he would view the person responsible for Oliver’s capture. She could not trust him with the secret while no experienced person was available to support her arguments on the girl’s behalf. For the same reasons, she had to be extremely careful and discreet in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first instinct would certainly be to discuss the matter with the worthy doctor. Seeking legal advice was hardly possible either, even if she had known where to find it. At one point she thought of asking Harry for help; but this brought back the memory of their last parting. It seemed unfair to call him back when—her eyes filled with tears as she followed this thought—he might by now have learned to forget her and might be happier away from her.

Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, leaning first toward one plan and then another, and drawing back from each as new objections arose, Rose spent a sleepless and anxious night. After thinking the matter over again the next day, she reached the painful decision to consult Harry.

“If it hurts him to return here,” she thought, “how much more it will hurt me! But perhaps he will not come. He may write, or he may come in person and carefully avoid seeing me—he did so when he left. I scarcely expected it then; but it was better for both of us.” At this point Rose let the pen fall and turned away, as if even the paper that would carry her message must not see her weep."}

{"request_id":"d37aafa88f602cb214e9e1e7","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a very fine-looking old gentleman and a good-looking younger man with his right arm in a sling. My goodness, how the people yelled and laughed, and kept it up. But I couldn’t see anything funny about it, and I figured the duke and the king would have trouble finding anything funny either. I expected them to turn pale. But no, not a bit did they turn pale. The duke never showed that he suspected anything. He just went around making foolish happy noises, as pleased as a jug bubbling out buttermilk. As for the king, he stared sadly at the newcomers, as if the thought that there could be such frauds and rascals in the world gave him a deep stomachache. Oh, he acted wonderfully. Many of the leading people gathered around him, to show that they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely confused. Soon he began to speak, and I immediately saw that he pronounced words like an Englishman—not in the king’s way, though the king’s imitation was pretty good. I can’t repeat the old gentleman’s exact words or imitate his speech, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting, and I’ll admit, honestly and openly, that I’m not well prepared to face it or answer it. My brother and I have had bad luck. He has broken his arm, and our baggage was mistakenly unloaded at a town upriver sometime last night. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can neither hear nor speak—and can’t even make useful signs now that he has only one hand to use. We are who we claim to be; and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. Until then, I won’t say anything more. I’ll go to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new mute man started off, and the king laughed and blurted out:

“Broken his arm—_very_ likely, _isn’t_ it? And very convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs but hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _excellent_—and very clever—under the _circumstances!_”

Then he laughed again, and everyone else did too, except three or four people, or perhaps half a dozen. One was the doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman carrying an old-fashioned carpetbag made from carpet material. He had just come off the steamboat and was speaking quietly to the doctor, glancing toward the king now and then and nodding. It was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. Another was a big, rough, strong man who had come along, listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was now listening to the king."}

{"request_id":"eb70933e88852b361b83a6e2","rewritten_text":"“He was delivered to you. You see that I know the circumstances?”

“That is certainly true,” said Defarge. His wife had conveyed to him, through an accidental touch of her elbow as she knitted and hummed, that he would do best to answer, but always briefly.

“It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and it was from your care that she took him, accompanied by a neat brown gentleman; what was his name?—in a little wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—and brought him to England.”

“That is true,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much about them now?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In fact,” Madame interrupted, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear about them. We received news of their safe arrival, and perhaps one other letter, or perhaps two; but since then, they have gradually gone their separate ways in life—we ours, they theirs—and we have had no correspondence.”

“Exactly so, madame,” replied the spy. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” Madame echoed. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English are cold, it seems to me.”

“Oh! You know I am English.”

“I can tell by your tongue,” Madame replied; “and I suppose the man is like his tongue.”

He did not take this identification as a compliment, but made the best of it and dismissed it with a laugh. After sipping his cognac to the last drop, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman; to someone who, like herself, was born French. And speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!—it is a curious thing that she is going to marry the nephew of the Marquis for whom Gaspard was raised to that height of so many feet; in other words, the present Marquis. But he lives unknown in England, where he is no Marquis; he is Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge knitted steadily, but the news had a clear effect on her husband. Whatever he did behind the little counter, striking a match and lighting his pipe, he was troubled, and his hand was unsteady. The spy would not have been a spy if he had failed to notice it or record it in his mind.

Having made at least this one discovery, whatever it might prove worth, and with no customers arriving to give him another opportunity, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and left. Before departing, he took the opportunity to say politely that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"623aa83853d82c10e918efce","rewritten_text":"“Oh, bother my hat! I want Virginia!” cried the little Duke, laughing, as they galloped on to the railway station. There Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but he learned nothing. The station-master, however, sent messages up and down the line and assured him that everyone would keep a close watch for her. After buying a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper who was just closing his shop, Mr. Otis rode to Bexley, a village about four miles away. He had been told that it was a favorite place for gypsies, since a large common lay beside it. There they woke the local policeman, but he could give them no information. After riding all over the common, they turned their horses toward home and reached the Chase at about eleven o’clock, exhausted and nearly heartbroken. Washington and the twins were waiting for them at the gatehouse with lanterns, because the avenue was very dark. No trace at all of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley Meadows, but Virginia was not with them. They explained that they had left suddenly because they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and hurried away for fear of being late. They had been deeply upset to hear that Virginia was missing, since they were very grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of them had stayed behind to help search. The carp pond had been dragged, and the entire Chase had been searched, but nothing had been found. It was clear that, at least for that night, Virginia was lost. In the deepest despair, Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, while the groom followed with the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a group of frightened servants. Poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa in the library, almost out of her mind with fear and worry, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a gloomy meal, for hardly anyone spoke. Even the twins were quiet and subdued, as they loved their sister dearly. When they had finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleas, sent them all to bed. He said that nothing more could be done that night and that, in the morning, he would telegraph Scotland Yard and ask for detectives to be sent at once."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d3a01e02cb8c3d1eb071b048","rewritten_text":"He slipped silently out of the wainscoting, wearing an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled mouth, and the moon hid her face behind a cloud as he passed the great oriel window, where his own arms and those of his murdered wife were displayed in blue and gold. On and on he glided like an evil shadow, the darkness itself seeming to hate him as he went. Once he thought he heard something call and stopped; but it was only a dog baying from the Red Farm, so he continued, muttering strange sixteenth-century curses and now and then brandishing the rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the passage leading to luckless Washington’s room. He paused there for a moment, the wind blowing his long grey locks around his head and twisting the nameless horror of the dead man’s shroud into grotesque, fantastic folds. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he felt the moment had come. He chuckled to himself and turned the corner; but no sooner had he done so than, with a pitiful cry of terror, he recoiled and hid his blanched face in his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a horrible spectre, motionless as a carved image and monstrous as a madman’s dream! Its head was bald and shining; its face round, fat, and white; and hideous laughter seemed to have twisted its features into an eternal grin. Scarlet rays streamed from its eyes, its mouth was a wide well of fire, and a hideous garment, like his own, wrapped its silent snows around the Titan form. On its breast hung a placard covered in strange, antique writing, seemingly some scroll of shame, some record of wild sins, some terrible calendar of crime; and in its right hand it held aloft a gleaming steel falchion.\n\nHaving never seen a ghost before, he was naturally terrified, and, after one hurried glance at the dreadful phantom, fled back to his room. As he raced down the corridor, he tripped over his long winding-sheet and finally dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jack-boots, where the butler found it in the morning. Once inside the privacy of his own room, he threw himself onto a small pallet bed and hid his face beneath the blankets. After some time, however, the brave old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to go and speak to the other ghost as soon as daylight came. Accordingly, just as dawn was touching the hills with silver, he returned toward the place where he had first seen the grisly phantom, feeling that, after all, two ghosts were better than one, and that with his new friend’s help he might safely confront the twins."}

{"request_id":"d0054a2cd94779ba54529ad3","rewritten_text":"If not, and you appeal to my patience and to the mercy of those you have deeply harmed, sit down silently in that chair. It has been waiting for you for two full days.”

Monks muttered something unclear, but still hesitated.

“You must act at once,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and the other choice will be lost forever.”

The man continued to hesitate.

“I have no wish to argue,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and since I am defending the most important interests of others, I have no right to do so.”

“Is there—” Monks asked in a faltering voice, “is there—no middle way?”

“None.”

Monks looked anxiously at the old gentleman. But when he saw only severity and determination in his face, he entered the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and come when I ring.”

The men obeyed, leaving the two alone together.

“This is harsh treatment, sir,” said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “It is because the hopes and wishes of our young, happy years were tied to him, and to that beautiful woman of his family who returned to God in her youth and left me here a solitary, lonely man. It is because he knelt with me beside his only sister’s deathbed when he was still a boy, on the morning that would have made her my young wife—if Heaven had not decided otherwise. It is because my wounded heart remained attached to him from that time through all his troubles and mistakes, until he died. It is because old memories and connections filled my heart, and even seeing you brings back thoughts of him. It is because of all these things that I am moved to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to blush at the unworthiness of one who bears his name.”

“What does the name have to do with it?” the other asked, after watching, partly in silence and partly with stubborn wonder, his companion’s agitation. “What does the name mean to me?”

“Nothing,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “Nothing to you. But it was hers, and even now, after all these years, it brings back to me, an old man, the warmth and excitement I once felt simply hearing it spoken by a stranger. I am very glad you have changed it—very, very glad.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks, retaining his assumed name, after a long silence. During it, he had jerked himself back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by one hand."}

{"request_id":"41481eded7a2d0b2c4a86706","rewritten_text":"Then they passed lonely brickfields. The fog was thinner here, and he could see the strange, bottle-shaped kilns with their orange, fanlike tongues of flame. A dog barked as they went by, and far off in the darkness a wandering seagull cried. The horse stumbled in a rut, swerved aside, and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled once more over roughly paved streets. Most of the windows were dark, but now and then fantastic shadows appeared against a lamplit blind. He watched them with curiosity. They moved like monstrous marionettes and gestured like living things. He hated them. A dull rage filled his heart. As they turned a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open doorway, and two men chased the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

It is said that passion makes a person think in circles. Certainly, with hideous repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips formed and re-formed those subtle words concerning soul and sense, until he had found in them what seemed the complete expression of his mood, and had justified through intellectual approval passions that, without such justification, would still have ruled his temper. From cell to cell of his brain crept the single thought; and the wild desire to live, the most terrible of all human appetites, gathered strength in every trembling nerve and fiber. Ugliness, which had once repelled him because it made things real, now became dear to him for that very reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The coarse brawl, the loathsome den, the crude violence of disordered life, even the utter vileness of thief and outcast, were more vivid in their intense immediacy than all the gracious forms of art, all the dreamy shadows of song. They were what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver pulled up sharply at the top of a dark lane. Above the low roofs and jagged chimney stacks rose the black masts of ships. Wreaths of white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere around here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked around. “This will do,” he replied, and after getting out quickly and giving the driver the extra fare he had promised, he walked swiftly toward the quay. Here and there, a lantern gleamed at the stern of some huge merchant ship. Its light trembled and broke apart in the puddles. A red glow came from an outward-bound steamer taking on coal. The slimy pavement looked like a wet raincoat."}

{"request_id":"aace1711ed3106125174ba9a","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, never picked up any book for pleasure except the Baronetage. It gave him something to do in an idle hour and comfort in a troubled one. Reading about the few families with the oldest baronetcy patents filled him with admiration and respect. Any unpleasant feelings caused by family matters naturally turned into pity and contempt as he read through the almost endless new titles created during the previous century. And if nothing else could interest him, he could always read his own history with unfailing pleasure. This was the page where his favourite book always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

That was exactly how the paragraph had come from the printer. But Sir Walter had improved it for his own information and that of his family by adding, after the date of Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset.” He had also carefully added the exact day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

The family’s history and rise followed, written in the usual style: how it had first settled in Cheshire; how it was mentioned by Dugdale; how one of its members had served as high sheriff and represented a borough in three successive parliaments; its loyal service and the dignity of a baronetcy, granted in the first year of Charles II; and all the Marys and Elizabeths whom its members had married. Altogether, it filled two handsome duodecimo pages and ended with the arms and motto: “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset.” Sir Walter’s handwriting appeared once more at the end:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity about his appearance and his position. He had been remarkably handsome when young, and at fifty-four he was still a very fine-looking man. Few women cared more about their appearance than he did, and no valet serving a newly made lord could have been more pleased with his place in society. He believed beauty was a blessing second only to a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, who possessed both, was the constant object of his deepest respect and devotion.

His good looks and rank gave him one reasonable claim to his own admiration, since he must have owed them the wife he had—a woman of far better character than anything he himself deserved."}

{"request_id":"739b136dbd48b16e8d8a8b12","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and courts eventually opened into a broad space, around which stood animal pens and other signs of a cattle-market. Sikes slowed when they arrived there, for the girl could no longer endure the swift pace at which they had been walking. Turning toward Oliver, he harshly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes growled, as Oliver hesitated and glanced about.

They stood in a shadowed corner, well away from the path used by passers-by.

Oliver saw only too clearly that resistance would be useless. He extended his hand, and Nancy gripped it firmly.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, taking Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog raised its head and growled.

“Look here, boy!” said Sikes, placing his other hand around Oliver’s throat; “if he says even the softest word, hold him! Do you understand?”

The dog growled once more; then, licking its lips, watched Oliver as though eager to fasten upon his throat without delay.

“He’s as willing as a Christian, strike me blind if he isn’t!” said Sikes, eyeing the animal with grim, savage approval. “Now you know what to expect, master, so call out as quickly as you please; the dog will soon put a stop to that. Move on, young ’un!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail in response to this unusually affectionate speech and, giving Oliver another warning growl, went ahead.

They were crossing Smithfield, though for all Oliver knew it might have been Grosvenor Square. The night was dark and foggy. The shop lights could scarcely penetrate the dense mist, which grew thicker by the moment and wrapped the streets and houses in gloom. The unfamiliar place seemed stranger still to Oliver, while his uncertainty became more dreary and oppressive.

They had gone only a few hurried steps when a deep church bell struck the hour. At its first stroke, both guides stopped and turned their heads toward the direction from which the sound came.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” said Nancy when the bell fell silent.

“What’s the use of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes answered.

“I wonder whether _they_ can hear it,” said Nancy.

“Of course they can,” replied Sikes. “It was Bartlemy time when I was shopped; and there wasn’t a penny trumpet at the fair whose squeaking I couldn’t hear. After I was locked up for the night, the noise and uproar outside made that thundering old jail so quiet, I could almost have dashed my brains against the iron plates of the door.”"}

I found the ribbon at the foot of the lightning-rod. It could not have belonged to either of the dead men. Now, even if my deduction from this ribbon—that the Frenchman was a sailor serving on a Maltese vessel—should prove mistaken, I can have done no harm by saying what I did in the advertisement. If I am wrong, he will simply assume that some circumstance has misled me, and will not trouble himself to investigate it. But if I am right, much has been accomplished. Though aware of the murder and innocent of it, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate before answering the advertisement—before claiming the Ourang-Outang. He will argue in this fashion:—‘I am innocent; I am poor; my Ourang-Outang is extremely valuable—to a man in my position, a fortune in itself—why should I surrender it because of vague fears of danger? It is here, within my reach. It was discovered in the Bois de Boulogne—far from the place where that slaughter occurred. How could anyone suspect that a mere animal committed the crime? The police are baffled—they have obtained not the smallest clew. Even if they should track down the creature, they could never prove that I knew of the murder, or connect me with the guilt merely because I possessed that knowledge. Above all, _I am known._ The advertiser identifies me as the animal’s owner. I do not know how far his information may go. If I refrain from claiming property of such value, which is known to be mine, I shall at least make the animal appear suspicious. It is not in my interest to draw attention either to myself or to the beast. I will reply to the advertisement, recover the Ourang-Outang, and keep it hidden until this affair has passed.’”

At that instant we heard footsteps on the stairs.

“Be prepared,” said Dupin, “with your pistols, but do not use them or reveal them until I give a signal.”

The house’s front door had been left open, and the visitor entered without ringing, proceeding several steps up the staircase. Then, however, he appeared to pause. Soon we heard him going back down. Dupin was hurrying toward the door when once more we heard him ascending. This time he did not retreat, but came up firmly and knocked at the door of our room.

“Come in,” said Dupin, in a bright and cordial voice.

A man entered. He was plainly a sailor—a tall, broad, powerfully built fellow, with a somewhat reckless expression that was not entirely unattractive."}

{"request_id":"997e3d7de3e9a5a912095216","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is remarkable! I must meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose and paced back and forth through the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is, to me, merely a motive in art. You may see nothing in him. I see everything. He is never more present in my work than when no likeness of him appears. As I have said, he suggests a new manner. I discover him in the curves of certain lines, in the beauty and delicacy of particular colours. That is all.”

“Then why do you refuse to exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I have placed in it some expression of this strange artistic idolatry, which, naturally, I have never wished to mention to him. He knows nothing of it. He must never know anything of it. Yet the world might suspect it, and I will not expose my soul to their shallow, prying eyes. My heart shall never be placed beneath their microscope. There is far too much of myself in the picture, Harry—far too much!”

“Poets are less scrupulous than you. They understand how useful passion can be in print. These days, a broken heart may go through many editions.”

“I despise them for that,” Hallward exclaimed. “An artist ought to make beautiful things, but put none of his own life into them. We live in an age when men regard art as though it were intended to be autobiography. We have lost the abstract feeling for beauty. One day I shall show the world what it is; and for that very reason, the world shall never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I believe you are mistaken, Basil, but I will not debate it with you. Only the intellectually lost ever argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter reflected for several moments. “He likes me,” he replied at last; “I know that he does. Naturally, I flatter him terribly. I take a peculiar pleasure in saying things to him that I know I shall regret saying. Usually he is charming toward me, and we sit in the studio discussing a thousand subjects. At times, however, he is cruelly thoughtless, and appears to enjoy causing me pain. Then I feel, Harry, that I have surrendered my entire soul to someone who treats it as though it were a flower to place in his coat, a small decoration to gratify his vanity, an ornament for a summer day.”"}

{"request_id":"83b3eb35b37271aac84cc752","rewritten_text":"Winters at the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are rarely very harsh, and in autumn it is unusual for anyone to need a fire. Around the middle of October, 18—, however, there came a remarkably cold day. Just before sunset, I made my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, which I had not visited for several weeks. At that time I lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and travel between the two places was far more difficult than it is today. When I reached the hut, I knocked as usual. Receiving no answer, I took the key from its hiding place, unlocked the door, and entered. A bright fire was burning on the hearth. It was unexpected, but very welcome. I removed my overcoat, settled into an armchair beside the crackling logs, and patiently waited for my hosts to return.

They arrived soon after dark and welcomed me warmly. Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, hurried around preparing marsh-hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—what else can I call them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unknown bivalve that formed a new genus. More than that, with Jupiter’s help, he had captured a _scarabæus_ that he believed was entirely new, and he wanted my opinion about it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, warming my hands over the fire and wishing the entire tribe of _scarabæi_ to the devil.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” Legrand said. “But it has been so long since I saw you. How could I have guessed that you would visit me tonight, of all nights? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and foolishly lent him the beetle. So you cannot see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I will send Jup for it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in creation!”

“What? Sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No—the beetle. It is a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and another, slightly longer, at the other. The antennae are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep tellin’ you,” Jupiter interrupted. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, every bit of him, inside and all, ’cept his wing. I never feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"007f8ff12de46d00c4b39c5a","rewritten_text":"Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you see—completely a gentleman, and so was his family. He was well born, as people say, and that matters as much in a man as in a horse, according to the Widow Douglas. No one ever denied that she belonged to the highest class in our town; Pap said it too, though he himself had no more quality than a mudcat. Col. Grangerford was very tall and thin, with a pale, darkish complexion and not a trace of red in it. Every morning he shaved his narrow face clean. He had extremely thin lips and nostrils, a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and the blackest eyes, set so far back that they seemed to look at you from caves. His forehead was high, and his straight black hair fell to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin. Every day he wore a clean shirt and a complete linen suit, white enough to hurt your eyes; on Sundays he wore a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane with a silver handle. There was nothing frivolous about him, and he was never loud. He was as kind as possible—you could feel it, and that gave you confidence. Sometimes he smiled, and it was good to see. But when he stood straight as a liberty pole and lightning began to flash beneath his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree before finding out what was wrong. He never had to tell anyone to behave; everyone had good manners around him. Everyone liked having him there, too. He was usually like sunshine—I mean, he made everything feel like good weather. When he became a cloudbank, it grew terribly dark for half a minute, and that was enough; nothing else went wrong for a week.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs and wished them good morning. No one sat again until they had taken their seats. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held it while they mixed their own, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” The two elders bowed slightly and thanked them, and all three drank. Bob and Tom then poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and the little bit of whisky or apple brandy at the bottom of their tumblers, gave it to me and Buck, and we drank to the old people too."}

{"request_id":"6b40f449e414469054d9a703","rewritten_text":"With great care, my friend drove a peg into the ground at the exact spot where the beetle had fallen. He then took a tape measure from his pocket. He fixed one end to the point on the tree nearest the peg, unrolled it to the peg, and then continued unrolling it in the direction already set by the tree and peg, for fifty feet—while Jupiter cleared the brambles with his scythe. At that point, he drove in a second peg and drew a rough circle about four feet across, using the peg as its center. He took a spade, gave one to Jupiter and one to me, and urged us to begin digging as quickly as possible.

To tell the truth, I had never especially enjoyed such work, and at that moment I would gladly have refused. Night was approaching, and I was already very tired from the exercise. But I could see no way out, and I feared that refusing would upset my poor friend. If I could have relied on Jupiter’s help, I would not have hesitated to take the madman home by force. But I knew the old negro too well to expect him to help me in any physical struggle with his master. I was certain Legrand had been influenced by one of the many Southern superstitions about buried treasure, and that finding the scarabæus had strengthened his belief—or perhaps Jupiter’s stubborn insistence that it was “a bug of real gold” had done so. A mind inclined toward madness could easily be carried away by such ideas, especially when they supported beliefs already held. I also remembered the poor fellow’s claim that the beetle was “the index of his fortune.” In the end, I was deeply troubled and confused, but decided to accept the situation, dig willingly, and so convince the visionary through clear evidence that his beliefs were mistaken.

After the lanterns were lit, we all began working with a zeal better suited to a more sensible purpose. As the light shone on us and our tools, I could not help thinking what a picturesque group we made, and how strange and suspicious our work must have seemed to any stranger who happened to come upon us.

We dug steadily for two hours."}

{"request_id":"2f6961f95eae16f60741ffd2","rewritten_text":"And he always pretended that Peter had written the things to him; but that was false: he had got every single one of them from that young flathead we paddled up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and wept over it. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls; and it left the tanyard (which was doing a good business), together with some other houses and land (worth around seven thousand), and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and said where the six thousand dollars in cash was hidden in the cellar. So the two frauds said they would go bring it up, and make everything fair and above-board; and they told me to come along with a candle. We closed the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag they poured it onto the floor, and it was a beautiful sight, all those yellow-boys. My, how the king’s eyes shone! He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said:

“Oh, _this_ ain’t bully or anything! Oh, no, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, _don’t_ it?”

The duke agreed that it did. They handled the yellow-boys, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle onto the floor; and the king said:

“It ain’t any use talking; being brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs that have been left behind is the line for you and me, Bilge. This here comes from trusting Providence. It’s the best way, in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there ain’t any better way.”

Nearly everybody would have been content with the pile and accepted it on trust; but no, they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. Says the king:

“Dern him, I wonder what he did with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They fretted over it for a while and searched everywhere for it. Then the duke says:

“Well, he was a very sick man, and likely made a mistake—I reckon that’s how it was. The best thing is to let it go, and say nothing about it. We can spare it.”

“Oh, shucks, yes, we can _spare_ it. I don’t care anything about that—it’s the _count_ I’m thinking of. We want to be mighty fair and open and above-board here, you know. We want to carry this here money upstairs and count it before everybody—then there ain’t anything suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"8969c9abfac68869b79ea72f","rewritten_text":"When the wedding took place, about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service most impressively, and everyone agreed that they had never seen a more handsome bride and groom. They were more than handsome, though—they were happy. Lord Arthur never once regretted all he had suffered for Sybil, while she gave him the finest things a woman can give a man: devotion, tenderness, and love. Reality did not destroy their romance. They always felt young.

Several years later, after they had had two beautiful children, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, a lovely old house the Duke had given his son as a wedding present. One afternoon, as she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl dart along the rose walk like flashes of sunlight, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and asked, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, of course I am happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I have no time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last person introduced to me; but usually, as soon as I know people, I grow tired of them.’

‘Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh dear, no! Lions are only useful for one season. Once their manes are cut, they are the dullest creatures alive. Besides, they behave very badly when you are truly kind to them. Do you remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was a terrible fraud. Of course, I did not mind that, and I even forgave him when he asked to borrow money, but I could not tolerate his making love to me. He has made me hate palmistry. I study telepathy now. It is much more entertaining.’

‘You mustn’t say anything against palmistry here, Lady Windermere; it is the only subject Arthur dislikes people joking about. I assure you, he takes it very seriously.’

‘You don’t mean that he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him, Lady Windermere—here he is.’ Lord Arthur came up the garden carrying a large bunch of yellow roses, with his two children dancing around him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You don’t mean that you believe in palmistry?’

‘Of course I do,’ said the young man with a smile.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe it all the happiness of my life,’ he murmured, sinking into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"5d65430b8c9255ca88ca2c70","rewritten_text":"But he had oppressed no one and imprisoned no one. Far from harshly demanding payment of what was owed him, he had voluntarily given it up, cast himself into a world that offered him no favor, secured his own private place there, and earned his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had administered the impoverished and encumbered estate according to written instructions: to spare the people, giving them what little could be given—such fuel as the heavy creditors allowed them in winter, and such produce as could be saved from the same grasp in summer. No doubt he had stated and proved this for his own protection, so that it could not fail to appear now.

This strengthened the desperate resolution Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor in the old story, the winds and currents had carried him within reach of the Loadstone Rock; it was drawing him toward itself, and he had to go. Everything that came before his mind pushed him onward, faster and faster, more steadily, toward that terrible attraction. His hidden uneasiness had been that evil purposes were being carried out in his unhappy country by evil instruments, while he, who could not help knowing that he was better than they, was not there trying to do something to halt the bloodshed and uphold the claims of mercy and humanity. With this uneasiness half suppressed and half accusing him, he had been led to compare himself with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so powerful. That comparison, damaging to himself, had been immediately followed by Monseigneur’s sneers, which had wounded him deeply, and by Stryver’s, which above all were coarse and painful for old reasons. Then had come Gabelle’s letter: an innocent prisoner’s appeal, in danger of death, to his justice, honor, and good name.

His decision was made. He had to go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he had to sail on until he struck it. He knew of no rock and saw scarcely any danger. The purpose behind what he had done, even though he had left it unfinished, presented the act to him in a form that France would gratefully recognize when he appeared to claim it. Then that glorious vision of doing good—which is so often the hopeful mirage of so many good minds—rose before him, and he even saw himself, in that illusion, possessing some influence with which to guide the raging Revolution that was running so terribly wild."}

{"request_id":"979d0fb01ff37e8c8dbd6995","rewritten_text":"He left the room with my nurse, and a moment later my father entered.

Nothing could have pleased me more at that moment than my father’s arrival. I reached out my hand to him and cried,

“Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father reassured me that they were well. He tried to lift my spirits by speaking of matters so dear to me, but he soon saw that a prison could not be a cheerful place. “What a place this is that you live in, my son!” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and miserable room. “You travelled in search of happiness, but some terrible fate seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—”

The name of my unfortunate, murdered friend caused more emotion than my weakened condition could bear, and I began to weep.

“Alas, yes, my father,” I replied. “Some terrible destiny hangs over me, and I must live to complete it. Otherwise, surely, I would have died beside Henry’s coffin.”

We were not permitted to talk for long, because my fragile health made every precaution necessary to preserve my peace. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted that I must not exhaust my strength through too much effort. Yet my father’s presence seemed like that of a good angel, and I slowly regained my health.

As my illness faded, I became consumed by a dark, hopeless melancholy that nothing could relieve. Clerval’s image was always before me, pale and murdered. More than once, the distress caused by these thoughts made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas, why had they preserved such a miserable and hated life? Surely it was so that I might fulfil my destiny, which was now nearing its end. Soon—very soon—death would silence these painful feelings and free me from the great weight of anguish dragging me toward the grave; and, while carrying out the demands of justice, I too would finally rest. Death still seemed far away, though I constantly wished for it. I often sat for hours without moving or speaking, longing for some great upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer beneath its ruins.

The time of the assizes drew near. I had already spent three months in prison, and though I remained weak and constantly at risk of falling ill again, I was forced to travel almost a hundred miles to the country town where the court would meet. Mr. Kirwin took responsibility for gathering the witnesses and preparing my defence."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b20c1c37fffae7fd8792d421","rewritten_text":"The mental qualities described as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely open to analysis. We recognize them only through their effects. Among other things, we know that, when possessed in excessive degree, they are always a source of the keenest pleasure to their owner. As the strong man takes pride in his bodily power, enjoying exercises that set his muscles in motion, so the analyst delights in that mental activity which _disentangles._ He finds pleasure even in the most insignificant occupations that bring his talent into use. He is partial to enigmas, conundrums, and hieroglyphics, displaying in solving each a degree of _acumen_ that seems to ordinary understanding almost supernatural. His conclusions, produced by the very essence of method, have, in fact, every appearance of intuition.\n\nThe faculty of re-solution may perhaps be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, particularly by that highest division of the subject which, unfairly and solely because of its retrograde operations, has been termed, as though _par excellence_, analysis. Yet calculation is not analysis in itself. A chess-player, for instance, performs the former without attempting the latter. It follows that chess is widely misunderstood in its effects upon the mind. I am not composing a treatise now, but merely introducing a somewhat unusual narrative with observations made very much at random; I shall therefore take this opportunity to maintain that the higher and more useful powers of the reflective intellect are exercised more decisively by the quiet game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In the latter game, where the pieces move in different and _bizarre_ ways and possess varied, shifting values, what is merely complicated is mistaken (as often happens) for what is profound. The _attention_ is intensely engaged. If it falters for even a moment, an oversight occurs, bringing injury or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but involute, the opportunities for such oversights increase; and in nine games out of ten, it is the more concentrated rather than the more acute player who wins. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are _unique_ and vary little, the likelihood of inadvertence is reduced, and with mere attention left comparatively idle, whatever advantage either side gains comes from superior _acumen_. To make the point less abstract, imagine a game of draughts in which the pieces have been reduced to four kings, so that, naturally, no oversight need be anticipated. It is clear that here the victory can be determined (assuming the players are otherwise equal) only by some _recherché_ move, arising from a powerful exertion of intellect."}

{"request_id":"7d7fdd30e58d82c217d8deeb","rewritten_text":"After joining in the general expressions of sorrow over the dreadful consequences of the affair, which Elizabeth regarded as nearly certain, while Miss Bennet could not say they were entirely impossible, the former went on: “But tell me everything about it that I have not yet heard. Give me more particulars. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they no suspicion of anything before the elopement? They must have seen them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some partiality, particularly on Lydia’s part, but nothing that caused him alarm. I am so sorry for him. His conduct was as attentive and kind as possible. He was on his way to us, intending to assure us of his concern, before he had any notion that they had not gone to Scotland; when that fear became known, it hastened his journey.”

“And was Denny persuaded that Wickham would not marry? Did he know they meant to run away? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything of their intentions and would not state his true opinion. He did not repeat his belief that they would not marry, and from that I am inclined to hope he may have been misunderstood earlier.”

“And until Colonel Forster came in person, none of you, I suppose, doubted that they were actually married?”

“How could such a thought have entered our minds? I was somewhat uneasy—a little afraid for my sister’s happiness in marrying him, because I knew his behaviour had not always been entirely proper. My father and mother knew nothing of this; they only saw how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then confessed, with very natural satisfaction at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had prepared her for such a step. It seems she had known for many weeks that they were in love.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I believe not.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think poorly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit that he did not speak of Wickham as favourably as he once had. He considered him imprudent and extravagant; and since this unhappy affair occurred, it is said that he left Meryton deeply in debt: though I hope that is untrue.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secretive, if we had told what we knew of him, this could never have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But to reveal a person’s former faults without knowing what their present feelings were seemed unjustifiable.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9e62b624181bb3daeebd3df7","rewritten_text":"Thus I passed two years. Day after day, hundreds upon hundreds slipped by; they brought no outward changes, yet a few slowly worked upon my mind as I moved toward death. I began to study more; to sympathize more with the thoughts of others as expressed in books; to read history, and to lose my individuality among the multitude that had lived before me. Perhaps, as the immediate sensation of suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude also lost some of its appeal: I began once more to long for sympathy—not that I was ever tempted to seek the crowd, but I wished for one friend to love me. You may say that I gradually became fit to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I desired had to be so pure, so free from the influence of outward circumstances, that in the world I could not avoid being thwarted by the coarse materials that constantly mingle even with its finest feelings. Believe me, I was then less suited to any communion with my fellow creatures than before. When I left them, they had tormented me as pain and sickness may torment: something external to the mind that irritated it, and that I wished to cast away. But now I would have desired sympathy; I would have wished to bind my soul to another’s, and would have prepared myself for abundant disappointment and suffering; for I was tender as the sensitive plant, all nerve. I did not desire sympathy and aid in ambition or wisdom, but sweet and mutual affection; smiles to encourage me and gentle words of comfort. I wished for one heart into which I could pour my complaints without restraint, and from the heavenly nature of that soil, blessed fruit might spring from such poor seed. Yet how could I find this? The love that is the soul of friendship is a gentle spirit, seldom found except when two amiable beings are joined from early youth, or bound together by shared suffering and pursuits; it comes to some of the chosen unsought and unrecognized; it descends like gentle dew upon favored places, which, however barren before, become under its benign influence fertile with every sweet plant. But when desired, it flees; it mocks the prayers of those who seek it; it will give itself, but cannot be pursued.\n\nI knew all this and did not go in search of sympathy; yet there, on my solitary heath, beneath my humble roof, where all around was desert, it came to me like a sunbeam in winter, adorning the landscape even as it helped dissolve the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone upon blighted fruit; I did not revive beneath its radiance, for I was too utterly ruined to feel its kindly power."}

{"request_id":"4f0c8623eed7875f92fdfae6","rewritten_text":"The party was divided between two adjoining benches: Anne sat on the front one, and Mr. Elliot had maneuvered so skillfully, with the help of his friend Colonel Wallis, that he secured a seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and the chief object of Colonel Wallis’s attentions, was perfectly satisfied.

Anne’s mind was in an especially favorable state for the evening’s entertainment; it provided just enough occupation. She had feeling for the tender, liveliness for the cheerful, attention for the scientific, and patience for the tedious; and she had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first act. Near its end, during the interval after an Italian song, she explained the song’s words to Mr. Elliot. A concert program lay between them.

“This,” she said, “is nearly the sense—or rather, the meaning—of the words, since one must not speak of the sense of an Italian love song. But it is as close to the meaning as I can make it, for I do not claim to understand the language. I am a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I can see that you are. I see you know nothing about it. You know only enough of the language to translate, at sight, these inverted, rearranged, shortened Italian lines into clear, understandable, elegant English. You need say no more about your ignorance. Here is complete proof.”

“I will not resist such generous politeness; but I should be sorry to be tested by a true expert.”

“I have not had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something of Miss Anne Elliot; and I consider her a woman too modest for the world at large to know half her accomplishments, and too accomplished for modesty to be natural in any other woman.”

“For shame! For shame! That is too much flattery. I have forgotten what comes next,” she said, turning to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot said quietly, “I have known your character longer than you realize.”

“Indeed? How could that be? You can have known it only since I came to Bath, unless you heard me spoken of earlier by my own family.”

“I knew you by reputation long before you came to Bath. I had heard you described by people who knew you intimately. I have known you by character for many years. Your appearance, your disposition, your accomplishments, your manner—all were already present to me.”

Mr. Elliot was not disappointed in the interest he had hoped to arouse. No one can resist the charm of such a mystery."}
