{"request_id":"cd55f53130c8f4e644880665","rewritten_text":"“Stop the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the larboard! Move ahead on the starboard! Stop her! Let your outside paddle turn slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that head-line out! Quickly now! Come on—get out your spring-line—what are you doing there! Wrap its bight around that stump! Stand by that stage, now—let her go! Engines stopped, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (testing the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept whitewashing and paid no attention to the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment, then said, “Hi-Yi! You’re stuck, aren’t you!”

Tom did not answer. He examined his latest stroke like an artist, then gently swept his brush over it again and studied the result as before. Ben came up beside him. Tom’s mouth watered at the apple, but he kept working. Ben said:

“Hello, old fellow. You have to work, huh?”

Tom turned suddenly and said, “Why, it’s you, Ben! I didn’t notice you.”

“Say—I’m going swimming. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather work, wouldn’t you? Of course you would!”

Tom studied the boy for a moment and said, “What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t that work?”

Tom went back to whitewashing and answered casually, “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it isn’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come on. You don’t mean to pretend that you like it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get the chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That made it seem different. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom moved his brush neatly back and forth, stepped back to inspect the effect, added a touch here and there, and examined it again. Ben watched every movement, becoming more interested and absorbed. At last he said:

“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”

Tom thought about it and was about to agree, but then changed his mind.

“No—no—I don’t think that would do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence—it’s right here on the street, you know. If it were the back fence, I wouldn’t mind, and neither would she. Yes, she’s very particular about this fence. It has to be done carefully. I guess there isn’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, who can do it the way it needs to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh, come on—let me try. Just a little. I’d let you if you were me, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest Indian; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him. Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"eba2c80b8fded25475f459d2","rewritten_text":"“April 7th. Rose early, and, to my immense delight, at last saw what there could be no reasonable doubt was the northern Pole itself. It lay there, beyond question, directly beneath my feet; but, alas! I had by then risen to so enormous a height that nothing could be distinguished with precision. Indeed, judging by the sequence of figures marking my several altitudes at different times between six A.M. on April 2nd and twenty minutes before nine A.M. that same day, when the barometer ran down, it might fairly be concluded that, at four o’clock on the morning of April 7th, the balloon had attained an elevation of certainly no less than 7,254 miles above sea level. This height may seem extraordinary, yet the calculation on which it rests almost certainly fell far short of the truth. In any case, I plainly beheld the whole major diameter of the earth; the entire northern hemisphere spread beneath me like an orthographically projected map, while the equator’s great circle itself marked the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies may readily conceive, however, that the restricted tracts within the Arctic circle which had hitherto remained unexplored, though lying immediately below me and thus visible without apparent foreshortening, were nevertheless too small in themselves, and too distant from the point of observation, to permit any very exact inspection. Still, what was visible possessed a singular and thrilling character. Northward from that enormous rim already mentioned—which, with some qualification, may be termed the boundary of human discovery in these parts—one continuous, or nearly continuous, expanse of ice stretched onward. During the first few degrees of its course, the surface became noticeably level; farther on it sank into a plane; and at length, growing considerably concave, it ended at the Pole itself in a sharply marked circular centre. Its apparent diameter, as seen from the balloon, subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its sombre color, varying in intensity, was always darker than any other point on the visible hemisphere, and at times deepened into the most complete and impenetrable blackness. Beyond this, little could be learned. By twelve o’clock the circular centre had greatly diminished in circumference, and by seven P.M. I had lost sight of it altogether; the balloon having passed over the western edge of the ice and rapidly drifted away toward the equator.\n\n“April 8th. Observed a perceptible reduction in the earth’s apparent diameter, together with a considerable change in its general color and aspect."}

{"request_id":"d6306bd51c30140e13702759","rewritten_text":"I ran to her, gathered her into my arms, covered her with kisses, and pleaded:

“Speak, darling, speak! What is it?”

Her head drooped helplessly against my breast, and she breathed, scarcely audibly:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I cried to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopath and tell him to come!”

Within two minutes I was kneeling beside the child’s crib, while Sandy sent servants hurrying in every direction throughout the palace. I understood the case almost at once—membranous croup! Bending over her, I whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart! Hello-Central.”

She opened her gentle eyes languidly and managed to murmur:

“Papa.”

That reassured me. She was not nearly dead yet. I ordered sulphur preparations, and personally brought out the croup-kettle; when Sandy or the child is ill, I do not sit idle waiting for doctors. I knew how to care for both of them, having had practice. This little creature had spent much of its brief life in my arms, and many times I had quieted its troubles and made it laugh through the tears clinging to its lashes when even its mother could not.

Sir Launcelot, clad in his finest armor, came striding down the great hall on his way to the stock-board. He was president of that board and held the Siege Perilous, which he had purchased from Sir Galahad; for the stock-board was made up of the Knights of the Round Table, who now used the Round Table for business. Seats there were worth—well, the amount would never be believed, so there is no point in naming it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, had cornered one of the new lines, and was preparing to squeeze the shorts that day; but what did it matter? He remained the same old Launcelot, and when he glanced through the doorway, discovered that his pet was sick, nothing else mattered. Bulls and bears could battle as they pleased; he would come in and stand by little Hello-Central with all his strength. And so he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute had fitted a fresh wick into the alcohol lamp and was heating the croup-kettle. By then Sandy had made a blanket canopy over the crib, and all was prepared.

Sir Launcelot raised steam. Together we filled the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a little lactic acid, then poured in the water and pushed the steam-spout beneath the canopy. Everything was shipshape, and we sat on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"a63031d2d940ab9b1412b31a","rewritten_text":"And if he asked why I wanted it, and why I believed I had any right to it, I would tell him—though he cared little for such humble dreams—that I had loved Estella deeply and for a long time. Though I had lost her and would have to live with that loss, anything connected with her was still closer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing that Mr. Jaggers remained completely still, silent, and apparently unmoved by my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you have a kind heart. I have seen your pleasant home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful things with which you refresh yourself after your business life. I beg you to say something for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to point out that, considering everything, he ought to be more open with me!”

I have never seen two men look at each other more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this speech. At first, I feared that Wemmick would be dismissed from his job at once. But that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, while Wemmick grew more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father, and you, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the greatest impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” Wemmick replied, growing bolder still. “I think you’re the other one.”

Once again they exchanged their strange looks, each apparently still unsure whether the other was making fun of him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it be so. Now, looking at you, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you were planning and arranging to have a pleasant home of your own one day, when you’ve grown tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams.’ You know more about such things than I do, since you have much fresher experience of them. But now, about this other matter. I’ll give you a case. Remember, I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I fully understood he was expressly admitting nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “suppose this. Suppose a woman, in the circumstances you have described, kept her child hidden and was forced to tell her legal adviser about it because he explained that, for the purposes of preparing her defense, he had to know the truth about the child.”"}

{"request_id":"960bb3a2d207d219644da247","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” Thereupon he shook his head and tapped it, conveying his opinion of Joseph’s shortcomings.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be worn out. Sit down. Here is a chicken had round from the Boar, here is a tongue had round from the Boar, and here are one or two little things had round from the Boar, which I hope you may not disdain. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again the instant after sitting down, “see before me him I once sported with in the happy days of infancy? And may I—_may_ I—?”

By this May I, he meant whether he might shake hands. I gave my consent; he did so warmly, and then sat down once more.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink, Thanks to Fortune, and may she always select her favourites with equal discernment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “see before me One—and also drink to One—without once more expressing—May I—_may_ I—?”

I told him he might, and he shook hands with me again, drained his glass, and turned it upside down. I did likewise; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more straight to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the liver wing and the finest slice of tongue (none of those remote No Thoroughfares of Pork now), while taking, comparatively speaking, scarcely any care of himself. “Ah! poultry, poultry! You little imagined,” said Mr. Pumblechook, apostrophising the fowl in the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what awaited you. You little imagined you were destined to be refreshment beneath this humble roof for one who—ascribe it to weakness, if you please,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? _may_ I—?”

It was becoming needless to repeat the words telling him he might, so he did it immediately. How he managed to do it so often without injuring himself on my knife, I cannot say.

“And your sister,” he continued, after eating steadily for a little while, “who had the honour of bringing you up by hand! It is a sad picter, to think that she is no longer capable of fully appreciating the honour. May—”

I saw he was preparing to approach me again, and stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” said I.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, quite limp with admiration, “that’s the way you know ’em, sir!” (I don’t know who Sir was, but he certainly was not I, and there was no third person present); “that’s the way you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"881d6b2a0d549339972d2cfc","rewritten_text":"“You have not been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy the evening parties here.”

“Oh, no. Their usual character has nothing to offer me. I do not play cards.”

“I know you did not formerly. You used not to like cards; but time brings many changes.”

“I am not yet so greatly changed,” cried Anne, then stopped, afraid he might misunderstand her. After waiting a few moments, he said, as though speaking from a sudden feeling, “It is a long time, indeed! Eight and a half years is a long time.”

Whether he would have said more, Anne could only wonder about later, when she was calmer. While she was still hearing his words, Henrietta distracted her with another subject, eager to use the free time to leave and urging her companions not to delay, in case someone else arrived.

They had to move. Anne said she was quite ready and tried to appear so; but she felt that if Henrietta had known how deeply she regretted and resisted leaving that chair and preparing to leave the room, she would have found, in all her own feelings for her cousin and in the very certainty of Captain Wentworth’s love, enough reason to pity her.

Their preparations were suddenly interrupted. Alarming sounds were heard; other visitors were approaching, and the door opened for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot. Their entrance seemed to chill everyone. Anne immediately felt oppressed, and wherever she looked she saw signs of the same feeling. The room’s comfort, ease, and liveliness disappeared, replaced by cold restraint, deliberate silence, or dull conversation, all to suit the empty elegance of her father and sister. How painful it was to see this happen!

Her jealous attention was satisfied in one respect. Both acknowledged Captain Wentworth again, and Elizabeth did so more warmly than before. She even spoke to him once and looked at him more than once. In fact, Elizabeth was considering an important plan. What followed explained it. After spending a few minutes saying the expected polite remarks, she began to offer the invitation that would settle all remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; nothing formal.” She delivered it very gracefully. The cards she had brought, marked “Miss Elliot at home,” were placed on the table with a courteous, welcoming smile for everyone—and one smile and one card clearly intended for Captain Wentworth. The truth was that Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to understand the value of a man with such an impressive appearance and manner."}

{"request_id":"0e09d8cd51a21fdd96fc9957","rewritten_text":"If she had known that her sister wanted to tear her away from such hopes and realities, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood, for she might have felt almost the same. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was the only thing that comforted her in the sad certainty that her husband never meant to go there himself.

But they knew nothing of what had happened, and their excitement continued, with few breaks, until the very day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now going to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since returning, she had often been in his company, and her agitation had mostly faded; her former partiality had disappeared completely. She had even learned to see, in the very gentleness that had first charmed her, an affected manner and a dull sameness that disgusted and tired her. His present behavior toward her gave her another reason for displeasure. He soon showed an inclination to renew the attentions that had marked the beginning of their acquaintance, but after everything that had happened, this could only annoy her. She no longer cared for him, seeing that he had chosen her as the object of such empty, foolish flirtation. Though she firmly discouraged him, she could not help feeling reproached by his belief that, no matter how long his attentions had been withdrawn or for what reason, renewing them at any time would flatter her vanity and win back her preference.

On the very last day the regiment remained in Meryton, Wickham dined at Longbourn with several other officers. Elizabeth was so unwilling to part from him on friendly terms that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but after a moment’s thought, he smiled again and replied that he had once seen Colonel Fitzwilliam often. After remarking that he was a very gentlemanly man, he asked Elizabeth how she had liked him. Her answer strongly favored the colonel. Soon afterward, with an indifferent air, he added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves with acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with an expression she did not miss. “And may I ask—” But stopping himself, he added in a lighter tone, “Is it in his manner of speaking that he improves?”"}

They gave little attention to the rest of the family; avoiding Mrs. Bennet as much as they could, saying very little to Elizabeth, and nothing whatsoever to the others. They soon departed again, rising with an energy that surprised their brother, and hurrying away as though anxious to escape Mrs. Bennet’s civilities.

The prospect of the Netherfield ball was highly agreeable to every female member of the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to regard it as a compliment to her eldest daughter, and felt especially flattered at receiving the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself rather than a formal card. Jane imagined a delightful evening in the company of her two friends and their brother’s attentions; while Elizabeth looked forward with pleasure to dancing frequently with Mr. Wickham, and to seeing everything confirmed by Mr. Darcy’s expression and conduct. Catherine and Lydia’s expected happiness rested less upon one particular event or person; for although each of them, like Elizabeth, intended to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was certainly not the only partner capable of pleasing them, and a ball was, in any case, a ball. Even Mary could assure her family that she had no objection to attending.

“Provided I may have my mornings to myself,” said she, “it is sufficient. I do not think it any sacrifice to take part occasionally in evening engagements. Society makes demands upon us all; and I count myself among those who regard periods of recreation and amusement as beneficial to everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so elevated by the occasion that, though she seldom addressed Mr. Collins without necessity, she could not refrain from asking whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation, and, if so, whether he considered it proper to participate in the evening’s entertainment. She was somewhat surprised to discover that he had no hesitation on the subject, and was far from fearing a reprimand, either from the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh, for venturing to dance.

“I am by no means of the opinion, I assure you,” said he, “that a ball of this nature, given by a young man of good character for respectable people, can have any harmful tendency; and I am so far from objecting to dancing myself that I hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins during the evening. I take this opportunity, moreover, of requesting yours, Miss Elizabeth, particularly for the first two dances; a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will ascribe to its proper cause, and not to any disrespect toward her.”"}

{"request_id":"d2bbd19b5609ed030127e809","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? That is not much! Many people have fallen out of favor with the Republic and must look out through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am he. Naturally, since I am the last.”

Jarvis Lorry has answered all the earlier questions. Jarvis Lorry has climbed down and now stands with one hand on the coach door, answering a group of officials. They slowly walk around the carriage and slowly climb onto the driver’s seat to inspect the small amount of luggage on the roof. The country people gathered there move closer to the coach doors and stare greedily inside. A small child, carried by its mother, stretches out its short arm to touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, properly countersigned.”

“May one leave, citizen?”

“One may leave. Forward, my postilions! Have a good journey!”

“I salute you, citizens—and the first danger is past!”

Jarvis Lorry says these words again as he clasps his hands and looks upward. Terror fills the carriage; there is crying and the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveler.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can they not be made to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would look like flight, my dear. I must not press them too hard; that would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see whether we are being followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, no one is following us.”

Pairs and groups of houses pass by, along with lonely farms, ruined buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and similar places, then open country and rows of leafless trees. The hard, uneven road lies beneath us, with soft, deep mud on both sides. At times we turn into the mud at the edge to avoid stones that clatter against us and shake us; at other times we get stuck in its ruts and bogs. Our impatience then becomes so painful that, in our panic and haste, we want to get out and run, hide, or do anything rather than stop.

From the open country we pass again among ruined buildings, lonely farms, dye-works, tanneries, and similar places, cottages in pairs and groups, and rows of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and brought us back by another road? Is this not the same place we have passed twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see whether we are being followed! Hush! The posting-house.

Slowly, our four horses are taken out. Slowly, the coach stands in the little street, without horses and with no sign that it will ever move again. Slowly, the new horses appear, one by one. Slowly, the new postilions follow, sucking and braiding the lashes of their whips. Slowly, the old postilions count their money, add it incorrectly, and reach unhappy conclusions."}

{"request_id":"498add3c5ed95042a63b64a6","rewritten_text":"With matters thus amicably and satisfactorily settled, the agreement was solemnly confirmed over another teacup of peppermint mixture, made all the more necessary by the lady’s fluttering and agitated spirits. While she drank it, she informed Mr. Bumble of the old woman’s death.

“Very good,” said that gentleman, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll call at Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send someone tomorrow morning. Was that what frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything in particular, dear,” the lady replied evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble insisted. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” the lady answered. “One of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” exclaimed Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any insolence from one of those male paupers—”

“No, no, love!” the lady interrupted hastily.

“If I thought it was,” continued Mr. Bumble, “if I thought any one of them had dared to raise his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” the lady replied.

“They had better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, parish or otherwise, who would presume to do it; and I can tell him he wouldn’t do it a second time!”

Without the accompanying violence of his gestures, this might not have seemed a very great compliment to the lady’s charms; but as Mr. Bumble delivered the threat with many warlike motions, she was deeply touched by this proof of his devotion and declared, with great admiration, that he was indeed a dove.

The dove then turned up his coat collar and put on his cocked hat; and, after exchanging a long and affectionate embrace with his future partner, once again faced the cold night wind. He paused only a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward, abusing them somewhat, in order to reassure himself that he could perform the duties of workhouse master with the necessary severity. Satisfied of his qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright visions of future advancement, which occupied his thoughts until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out to tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never inclined to undertake more physical exertion than was needed for the convenient performance of eating and drinking. Consequently, the shop remained open, although it was past the usual closing hour. Mr. Bumble tapped several times on the counter with his cane; but, receiving no answer and seeing a light shining through the glass window of the small parlor at the back, he ventured to peer inside and see what was happening. When he saw what was happening, he was considerably surprised."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0036f8c340218aa43fd3a55e","rewritten_text":"“They ought to concern you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You do not wish people to speak of you as something foul and degraded. Naturally, you have your rank, your fortune, and all the rest of it. But rank and fortune are not everything. Believe me, I do not credit these rumours at all. At least, I cannot believe them when I look at you. Sin is something that marks itself upon a man’s face. It cannot be hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices. There are no such things. If a miserable man has a vice, it appears in the lines about his mouth, the heaviness of his eyelids, even in the shape of his hands. Someone—I shall not name him, though you know whom I mean—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never seen him before, and at that time had heard nothing about him, though I have heard plenty since. He offered me an extravagant sum. I refused him. There was something in the form of his fingers that repelled me. I know now that my instinct about him was entirely right. His life is terrible. But you, Dorian, with your clear, radiant, innocent face and your wonderfully untroubled youth—I cannot believe anything against you. And yet I see you so rarely, you never come to the studio now, and when you are away from me, hearing all these dreadful things people whisper about you, I do not know what to think. Why is it, Dorian, that a man such as the Duke of Berwick leaves a club room when you enter? Why is it that so many gentlemen in London will neither visit your house nor ask you to theirs? You were once a friend of Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up in conversation, in connection with the miniatures you have lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that, however artistic your tastes might be, you were a man no pure-minded girl should be permitted to know, and no chaste woman should sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was your friend and asked what he meant. He told me. He said it openly, before everyone. It was dreadful! Why is your friendship so ruinous to young men? There was that unfortunate boy in the Guards who took his own life. You were his closest friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with his name disgraced.”"}

{"request_id":"c164ffc687b8da085f22068a","rewritten_text":"It seemed to be a collection of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, giving the impression of a rather dull retreat. Wemmick’s house was a little wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, with its upper part cut out and painted like a battery fitted with guns.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Looks good, doesn’t it?”

I praised it highly. I think it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the strangest Gothic windows—most of them sham—and a Gothic door almost too small to enter.

“That’s a real flagstaff, you see,” said Wemmick, “and on Sundays I raise a real flag. Now look here. After I’ve crossed this bridge, I hoist it up—like this—and cut off communication.”

The bridge was a plank crossing a chasm about four feet wide and two feet deep. But it was very pleasant to see the pride with which he raised it and secured it, smiling as he did so with genuine enjoyment, not merely out of habit.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There he is, you see! And when you hear him go, I think you’ll say he’s a Stinger.”

The cannon he referred to stood in a separate fortress made of latticework. An ingenious little tarpaulin arrangement, shaped rather like an umbrella, protected it from the weather.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t interfere with the idea of fortifications—for it’s a principle of mine that if you have an idea, you should carry it out and maintain it—I don’t know whether you agree—”

I said I certainly did.

“—At the back, there’s a pig, and there are chickens and rabbits. Then I put together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers; and at supper you’ll judge what sort of salad I can produce. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling again, though seriously too, as he shook his head, “if you can imagine the little place under siege, it would hold out for a devil of a long time as far as provisions are concerned.”

Then he led me to a bower about a dozen yards away. It was reached by such cleverly twisting paths that it took quite a long time to get there, and in this retreat our glasses had already been set out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental lake beside which the bower stood. The water, with an island in the middle that might have supplied the supper salad, was circular, and he had built a fountain in it. When you set a small mill in motion and removed a cork from a pipe, it played with such force that it made the back of your hand quite wet."}

{"request_id":"bfcecf7b436e803bb253731f","rewritten_text":"If she had known that her sister meant to tear her away from prospects and realities such as these, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood her feelings, for she might have felt almost the same. Lydia’s going to Brighton was the only thing that comforted her in the melancholy certainty that her husband never intended to go there himself.

But they knew nothing of what had happened, and their delight continued, with scarcely a pause, until the very day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since her return, she had often been in his company, and her agitation had largely passed; the agitation caused by her former partiality had disappeared entirely. She had even learned to recognize, in the very gentleness that had first charmed her, an affectation and a monotony that disgusted and wearied her. His present conduct toward her gave her another reason for displeasure; for the desire he soon showed to renew the attentions that had marked the beginning of their acquaintance could only, after all that had since occurred, provoke her. She ceased to care for him when she found herself chosen as the object of such idle and frivolous gallantry; and while she firmly restrained it, she could not help feeling the reproach implied by his belief that, however long his attentions had been withdrawn, and for whatever reason, her vanity would be pleased and her preference secured whenever he renewed them.

On the very last day the regiment remained in Meryton, he dined at Longbourn with several other officers. Elizabeth was so little inclined to part from him on friendly terms that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but after a moment’s thought, and with a returning smile, replied that he had often seen him before. After remarking that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked how she had liked him. Her answer warmly favored Colonel Fitzwilliam. Soon afterward, with an air of indifference, he added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves with acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with a look she did not miss. “And may I ask—” But checking himself, he added in a livelier tone, “Is it in his manner that he improves?”"}

Whilst others fight to win the prize, and sail thro’ _blood_ -y seas?

He was considered a marvelous reader. At church “sociables” he was invariably asked to read poetry; and when he had finished, the ladies would raise their hands and drop them helplessly into their laps, and “wall” their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn was sung, the Rev. Mr. Sprague transformed himself into a bulletin-board and read aloud “notices” of meetings, societies, and other matters until it appeared the catalogue might continue to the crack of doom—a strange custom still maintained in America, even in cities, in this age of plentiful newspapers. Often, the less there is to support a traditional custom, the more difficult it becomes to abandon it.

Then the minister prayed. It was a good, liberal prayer, and entered into particulars: it pleaded for the church, and the church’s little children; for the village’s other churches; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the State officers; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the Government’s officers; for poor sailors tossed upon stormy seas; for the oppressed millions groaning beneath European monarchies and Oriental despotisms; for those who possess the light and good tidings, yet have neither eyes to see nor ears to hear; for the heathen on the distant islands of the sea; and ended by asking that the words he was about to utter might find grace and favor, and prove like seed sown in fertile soil, producing in due season a thankful harvest of good. Amen.

There was a rustling of dresses, and the congregation, which had been standing, sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it—if he even did that. He was restless throughout; he unconsciously kept count of the prayer’s details—for he was not listening, but knew the territory well, and the clergyman’s customary path across it—and whenever some small piece of new material was inserted, his ear caught it and his whole nature rebelled; he regarded additions as unfair, and scoundrelly. During the prayer a fly had settled on the back of the pew before him and tormented his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, clasping its head with its arms, and polishing it so vigorously that it seemed almost to separate from the body, leaving a slender thread of neck exposed; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them against its body as though they were coat-tails; performing its entire toilet as peacefully as if it knew itself perfectly secure."}

She would wait—and, sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was settled: Jane was to go. What a surprise to me! I had not the slightest idea! Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her directly that, after considering the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had decided to accept it. I knew nothing about it until everything was settled.”

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us; Mrs. Elton insisted that we come. It was arranged on the hill while we were walking with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend the evening with us,’ she said. ‘I absolutely must have you all come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he refused from the beginning. Although I thought he would come, because Mrs. Elton said she would not excuse him, he did not. But my mother, Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very pleasant evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, must always make one feel welcome, though everyone seemed rather tired after the morning’s party. Even pleasure can be tiring—and I cannot say that any of them seemed to have enjoyed it very much. Still, I shall always consider it a very pleasant party and feel extremely grateful to the kind friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you did not know it, had been making up her mind all day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time comes, it must be unwelcome to her and all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every possible advantage—I mean, in the character and manners of the family.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, it has everything in the world that could make her happy. Except for the Sucklings and Bragges, there is no other nursery position in Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance so generous and elegant. Mrs. Smallridge is a most delightful woman! Her way of living is almost equal to Maple Grove—and as for the children, except for the little Sucklings and little Bragges, there are no such elegant, sweet children anywhere. Jane will be treated with such respect and kindness! It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary! I really cannot bring myself to tell you what her salary is, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"d2eb2a682410749716cc966b","rewritten_text":"It was at Warwick Castle that I encountered the curious stranger I am about to describe. Three things drew me to him: his frank simplicity, his astonishing knowledge of ancient armor, and the ease of his company—for he did all the talking. We fell in together, as quiet people do, at the rear of the group being conducted through, and he immediately began saying things that interested me. As he continued, softly, pleasantly, and smoothly, he seemed gradually to drift out of the present world and age into some distant era and forgotten land; and little by little he cast such a spell over me that I appeared to wander among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mildew of a dim antiquity, conversing with one of its relics! Just as I might speak of my closest friends or enemies, or my most familiar neighbors, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other famous names of the Round Table—and how ancient, impossibly ancient, faded, dry, musty, and old he came to seem as he went on! Presently he turned to me and said, in the same manner one might mention the weather or any ordinary subject—

“You know about transmigration of souls; do you know about transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I said I had never heard of it. He was so unconcerned—just as when people discuss the weather—that he did not seem to notice whether I answered him or not. There was scarcely half a moment of silence before the salaried guide’s droning voice broke in:

“Ancient hauberk, date of the sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole through the chain-mail in the left breast; cannot be explained; supposed to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not with a modern smile, but with one that must have vanished from common use many centuries before—and murmured, apparently to himself:

“Wit ye well, _I saw it done_.” Then, after a pause, he added: “I did it myself.”

Before I had recovered from the electric shock of this statement, he was gone.

That entire evening I sat beside my fire at the Warwick Arms, immersed in a dream of former times, while rain struck the windows and wind bellowed around the eaves and corners. Now and then I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, feasted on its rich abundance of marvels and adventures, inhaled the perfume of its obsolete names, and dreamed once more."}

content.text: {"request_id":"dab2871fbbaffac2f0f8b7c3","rewritten_text":"“The stupor and astonishment caused in my mind by this extraordinary change in the situation was perhaps, after all, the part of the adventure least open to explanation. For the upheaval itself was not only natural and inevitable, but had long been anticipated as something to expect when I reached that precise point in my voyage at which the planet’s attraction would be replaced by that of the satellite—or, more exactly, when the balloon’s gravity toward the earth would become weaker than its gravity toward the moon. Certainly, I had awakened from a deep sleep, all my senses confused, to witness a most startling phenomenon, one that I had expected, though not at that moment. The reversal itself must, of course, have occurred smoothly and gradually, and it is far from certain that, even had I been awake when it happened, I would have detected it through any inward sign of inversion—that is, through any discomfort or disturbance either in my person or in my equipment.\n\n“It is scarcely necessary to say that, once I fully understood my situation and emerged from the terror that had overwhelmed every faculty of my soul, my attention was first directed entirely toward observing the moon’s general physical appearance. It lay beneath me like a map—and although I judged it still to be at a considerable distance, the markings of its surface appeared with a striking and wholly inexplicable clarity. The complete absence of ocean or sea, and indeed of any lake, river, or body of water whatsoever, struck me at first sight as the most extraordinary feature of its geological condition. Yet, strangely, I saw vast level regions of a distinctly alluvial character, while by far the greater part of the visible hemisphere was covered with countless volcanic mountains, conical in form and looking more artificial than naturally formed. The highest of them rises no more than three and three-quarter miles vertically; but a map of the volcanic districts of the Campi Phlegraei would give Your Excellencies a better impression of their general surface than any inadequate description I might attempt. Most of them were plainly erupting, and they made me understand their fury and power with dreadful clarity through the repeated thunder of the so-called meteoric stones, which now shot upward past the balloon with increasingly terrifying frequency.”"}

{"request_id":"40b12da3fcb7af734d9bc690","rewritten_text":"At least, that was what he thought. But who could say? ... No. There had been nothing more. He had spared her out of vanity. He had worn the mask of goodness out of hypocrisy. Out of curiosity, he had tried denying himself. He understood that now.

But this murder—would it pursue him all his life? Was he always to be weighed down by his past? Was he truly going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him. The picture itself—that was evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it for so long? Once, he had taken pleasure in watching it change and grow old. Lately, he had felt no such pleasure. It had kept him awake at night. When he was away, he had been terrified that other eyes might see it. It had cast melancholy over his passions. Even the memory of it had spoiled many moments of joy. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

He looked around and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it many times, until not a stain remained. It was bright and gleaming. As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and everything that work represented. It would kill the past, and once the past was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous life of the soul, and without its hideous warnings, he would be at peace. He seized the knife and drove it into the picture.

A cry rang out, followed by a crash. The cry was so terrible in its agony that the frightened servants woke and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing through the square below stopped and looked up at the great house. They continued on until they met a policeman, then brought him back. The officer rang the bell several times, but no one answered. Except for a light in one of the upper windows, the house was completely dark. After a while, he went away, stood beneath a nearby portico, and watched.

“Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” the policeman replied.

As they walked away, they looked at each other and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed domestics spoke to one another in low whispers. Old Mrs. Leaf was crying and wringing her hands. Francis was pale as death.

After about a quarter of an hour, he took the coachman and one of the footmen and crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"4e547993f20143d258b429d7","rewritten_text":"_P.S._—Do tell me about the bows. Jennings declares they are the fashion.

Lord Arthur looked so grave and miserable over the letter that the Duchess burst into peals of laughter.

‘My dear Arthur,’ she exclaimed, ‘I shall never show you another young lady’s letter! But what am I to say about the clock? I think it is an excellent invention, and I should rather like one myself.’

‘I don’t care much for them,’ said Lord Arthur with a melancholy smile, and, after kissing his mother, he went out of the room.

Once upstairs, he threw himself upon a sofa, and tears came into his eyes. He had done everything he could to commit the murder, yet on both occasions he had failed, through no fault of his own. He had attempted to perform his duty, but it seemed that Destiny herself had betrayed him. He was weighed down by the emptiness of good intentions, by the uselessness of striving to be noble. Perhaps it would be best to end the engagement altogether. Sybil would suffer, certainly, but suffering could not truly spoil a nature as lofty as hers. And as for himself, what difference did it make? There was always some war in which a man might die, some cause for which he could surrender his life; and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny bring about his doom. He would make no effort to assist her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and Lord Arthur was forced to dine with them. Their shallow talk and pointless jokes failed to interest him, and as soon as coffee was served he left, inventing an engagement as an excuse to escape. On leaving the club, the hall-porter gave him a letter. It came from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to call the following evening and inspect an explosive umbrella that discharged itself the moment it was opened. It was the newest invention, and had only just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces. He had resolved to attempt no further experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat beside the river for hours. The moon looked through a mane of tawny clouds like a lion’s eye, while countless stars sprinkled the hollow sky like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. From time to time a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted away with the tide, and the railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as trains went shrieking across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"c9e8af51bc92dcb41de51405","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang instantly leaped through the chamber door, descended the stairs, and then passed through a window, unfortunately left open, into the street.

The Frenchman pursued it in despair; the ape, razor still in its grasp, would sometimes stop to glance back and gesture at its pursuer, until the latter had almost overtaken it. Then it would hurry on again. Thus the chase went forward for a considerable time. The streets were utterly still, since it was close to three in the morning. While going through an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive noticed a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s chamber, on the fourth floor of her house. It rushed to the building, saw the lightning rod, and climbed it with astonishing agility. Seizing the shutter, which stood completely open against the wall, it swung itself by means of it directly onto the bed’s headboard. The entire feat took less than a minute. As the Ourang-Outang entered the room, it kicked the shutter open once more.

Meanwhile, the sailor was at once delighted and troubled. He had good reason to hope that he could now recapture the brute, since it could hardly escape the snare into which it had gone except by the rod, where he might intercept it on its descent. Yet he was also deeply concerned about what it might do inside the house. This thought compelled him to continue after the fugitive. A lightning rod is easy to climb, particularly for a sailor; but when he reached the level of the window, which was well to his left, his progress was halted. The most he could do was lean across far enough to catch a glimpse of the room’s interior. At that glimpse, horror nearly caused him to lose his hold. It was then that the dreadful shrieks rose through the night, awakening the inhabitants of the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, had apparently been arranging papers in the iron chest already described, which had been rolled into the center of the room. It stood open, with its contents scattered on the floor beside it. The victims must have been seated with their backs to the window; and, judging by the interval between the animal’s entrance and the screams, they probably did not notice it at once. The shutter’s slamming shut would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked inside, the enormous animal had seized Madame L’Espanaye by the hair—which hung loose because she had been combing it—and was waving the razor around her face, imitating a barber’s movements."}

{"request_id":"7a4a16a85061ae3c989c7ce5","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often, you’d see one poke his nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she needed things close by to throw at them when she was alone, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot, and said she was generally a good shot with it, but she had strained her arm a day or two before and didn’t know if she could aim straight now. Still, she watched for an opening, and presently let fly at a rat; but she missed him by a wide margin, and cried, “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try the next one. I wanted to get away before the old man returned, but naturally I didn’t show it. I took the thing, and when the first rat poked out his nose, I threw, and if he’d stayed where he was, he would have been a tolerably sick rat. She said that was first-rate, and reckoned I’d hit the next one. She went to fetch the lump of lead and brought it back, along with a hank of yarn she wanted me to help her with. I held up both hands, and she laid the hank over them, continuing to talk about her affairs and her husband’s. But she broke off to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, handy.”

So she dropped the lump into my lap at that very moment, and I clamped my legs together over it while she went on talking. But only for about a minute. Then she removed the hank, looked me straight in the face pleasantly, and said:

“Come now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, mum?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or what is it?”

I reckon I shook like a leaf, and hardly knew what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, mum. If I’m in the way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you, either. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it; and, what’s more, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice, that’s all. It isn’t anything. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been treated badly, and made up your mind to run off. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"f02c37167b3d501d9813c1e0","rewritten_text":"All this, and more—much more—I would gladly explain in detail. But, to be brief, I must have my reward. I long to return to my family and my home; and as the price of any further communication from me—in view of the light I can cast upon many important branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must request, through the influence of your honorable body, a pardon for the crime I committed in causing the creditors’ deaths upon my departure from Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of this paper. Its bearer, an inhabitant of the moon whom I have persuaded and properly instructed to serve as my messenger to Earth, will await your Excellencies’ decision and return to me with the pardon, if it can in any way be obtained.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

After reading this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe on the ground in the height of his astonishment. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and put them in his pocket; then, forgetting both himself and his dignity, he turned three times on his heel in the utmost amazement and admiration. There was no doubt about it—the pardon had to be obtained. So Professor Rub-a-dub swore emphatically, and so the illustrious Von Underduk finally decided as he took his fellow scientist’s arm and, without a word, began making his way home to consider what measures should be taken. When they reached the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor suggested that since the messenger had seen fit to disappear—surely terrified by the savage appearance of Rotterdam’s burghers—the pardon would be useless, since no one but a man from the moon would undertake a journey across so vast a distance. The burgomaster agreed, and the matter therefore ended. The rumors and speculation did not. Once published, the letter produced a variety of gossip and opinions. Some of the excessively wise even made themselves ridiculous by dismissing the whole affair as nothing more than a hoax. But “hoax,” among such people, is, I believe, a general term for anything beyond their understanding. For my part, I cannot imagine what evidence they used to support such an accusation. Let us see what they say:"}

{"request_id":"f7cfc0bd80287585b4435d3c","rewritten_text":"“I must point out, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he put down the newspaper, “that the present situation is very much in our favour. This peace will be sending all our wealthy naval officers ashore. They will all be looking for homes. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, to choose from a number of tenants—very responsible tenants. Many great fortunes were made during the war. If a rich admiral should come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” replied Sir Walter; “that is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would be a prize indeed for him; perhaps the greatest prize of all, however many prizes he may have taken before. Eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he was expected to, at this joke, and then continued—

“I venture to say, Sir Walter, that naval gentlemen are good people to deal with in business. I have had some experience of their methods; and I freely admit that they have very generous ideas, and are as likely to make desirable tenants as any people one could meet. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would suggest is this: if rumours should spread of your intention—which must be considered possible, since we know how difficult it is to keep the actions and plans of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of another—then, although I, John Shepherd, could hide any family matters I wished, because no one would think me worth watching, Sir Walter Elliot has eyes upon him that may be difficult to escape. So I venture to say that, despite all our caution, I shall not be surprised if some report of the truth gets out. In that case, as I was about to observe, applications will certainly follow, and I should consider those from wealthy naval commanders especially worth attention. I should add that I can come over at any time within two hours, to spare you the trouble of replying.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. But soon afterward, standing up and walking about the room, he remarked sarcastically—

“There are few naval gentlemen, I imagine, who would not be surprised to find themselves in a house of this kind.”

“They would look around them, no doubt, and thank their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, who was present. Her father had driven her over, since nothing helped Mrs Clay’s health so much as a drive to Kellynch. “But I quite agree with my father that a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"3a20306e1903cb46fab7e6f2","rewritten_text":"The party was arranged on two adjoining benches: Anne sat among those in front, and Mr Elliot had contrived so successfully, aided by his friend Colonel Wallis, to secure a place beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and receiving the chief of Colonel Wallis’s attentions, was perfectly satisfied.

Anne’s mind was in an especially favourable condition for the evening’s entertainment; it provided just enough occupation. She had feeling for the tender, spirits for the lively, attention for the scientific, and patience for the tedious; and she had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first act. Near its conclusion, in the interval after an Italian song, she explained the song’s words to Mr Elliot. A concert programme lay between them.

“This,” said she, “is almost the sense, or rather the meaning of the words—for certainly the sense of an Italian love-song must not be discussed—but it is as close to the meaning as I can make it; for I do not claim to understand the language. I am a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I see that you are. I see you know nothing about it. You possess only enough knowledge of the language to translate at sight these inverted, transposed, shortened Italian lines into plain, intelligible, graceful English. You need say no more of your ignorance. Here is decisive evidence.”

“I will not resist such courteous kindness; but I should be sorry to be tested by a genuine proficient.”

“I have not had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something of Miss Anne Elliot; and I consider her a person too modest for the world generally to know half her accomplishments, and too accomplished for modesty to be natural in any other woman.”

“For shame! For shame! This is excessive flattery. I forget what comes next,” she said, turning to the programme.

“Perhaps,” said Mr Elliot in a low voice, “I have known your character longer than you suppose.”

“Indeed! How can that be? You could have known it only since I came to Bath, unless you heard me spoken of beforehand by my own family.”

“I knew you by reputation long before you came to Bath. I had heard you described by people who knew you intimately. I have known you by character for many years. Your appearance, your disposition, accomplishments, and manner—all were familiar to me.”

Mr Elliot was not disappointed in the interest he had hoped to awaken. No one can resist the attraction of such a mystery."}

{"request_id":"95f9ff6d4a42f604915172ba","rewritten_text":"This little explanation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma great pleasure. It became one of the pleasant memories of the ball, which she enjoyed as she walked around the lawn the next morning. She was very glad that they now understood each other so well about the Eltons, and that their opinions of both husband and wife were so similar. His praise of Harriet, and his admission that she had been right, pleased her especially. The Eltons’ rudeness, which for a few minutes had threatened to spoil the rest of her evening, had instead brought her some of its greatest pleasures; and she looked forward to another happy result—the end of Harriet’s infatuation. From the way Harriet had spoken of it before they left the ballroom, Emma had strong hopes. It seemed that Harriet’s eyes had suddenly been opened, allowing her to see that Mr. Elton was not the superior person she had believed him to be. The fever was over, and Emma had little fear that harmful politeness would make it return. She trusted the Eltons’ bad feelings to provide all the pointed neglect that might still be needed. Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not too deeply in love, and Mr. Knightley unwilling to quarrel with her—how happy a summer lay ahead of her!

She was not going to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her that he could not give himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, since he had to be home by midday. She did not mind.

Having considered all these matters, examined them carefully, and set them right in her mind, she was turning toward the house, her spirits renewed for the demands of the two little boys and their grandfather, when the large iron gate opened. Two people entered whom she had never expected to see together: Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—Harriet herself! One moment was enough to show her that something unusual had happened. Harriet looked pale and frightened, while he tried to comfort her. The iron gate and the front door were less than twenty yards apart; soon all three were in the hall, and Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted.

A young lady who faints must be brought round; questions must be answered, and surprises explained. Such events are very interesting, but the suspense cannot last long. Within a few minutes Emma knew the whole story.

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also attended the ball, had gone out walking together and taken the Richmond road. Though it seemed public enough to be safe, the road had frightened them. About half a mile beyond Highbury, it made a sudden turn and became deeply shaded by elms on both sides. For quite a distance it was very secluded; and when the young ladies had gone some way along it, they suddenly saw, a short distance ahead, on a wider patch of grass beside the road, a group of gypsies."}

{"request_id":"b921ac61028f7c45741c6731","rewritten_text":"If not, and you rely upon my forbearance and the mercy of those you have grievously wronged, sit down silently in that chair. It has been waiting for you these two entire days.”

Monks muttered several indistinct words, but still remained wavering.

“You will act promptly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and the alternative will be lost forever.”

The man continued to hesitate.

“I have no wish to bargain with you,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and, since I am defending the dearest interests of others, I have no right to do so.”

“Is there—” Monks asked in an unsteady voice—“is there—no course between the two?”

“None.”

Monks glanced anxiously at the old gentleman; but, seeing in his face only sternness and resolve, entered the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

“Lock the door from outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and return when I ring.”

The men complied, leaving the two alone together.

“This is fine treatment, sir,” said Monks, tossing aside his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is precisely because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow; “because the hopes and desires of youthful, happy years were joined with him, and with that lovely creature of his blood and family who returned to her God in youth, leaving me here a solitary and lonely man; because, while still a boy, he knelt beside me at the death-bed of his only sister, on the morning that would—but Heaven decreed otherwise—have made her my young wife; because my scarred heart remained attached to him from that day onward, through all his trials and mistakes, until his death; because old memories and associations filled my heart, and even looking upon you revives old thoughts of him; it is for all these reasons that I am moved to deal gently with you now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to blush for your unworthiness as the bearer of his name.”

“What has the name to do with this?” asked the other, after watching, partly in silence and partly with stubborn wonder, his companion’s agitation. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” answered Mr. Brownlow, “nothing to you. But it was hers, and even after all these years it brings back to me, an old man, the warmth and thrill I once felt merely hearing it spoken by a stranger. I am very glad you have changed it—very—very.”

“This is all very grand,” said Monks (to preserve his assumed name) after a long silence, during which he had jerked himself sullenly back and forth in defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by one hand."}

{"request_id":"0a2704de849ead2f4dad92dd","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No response.

“TOM!”

Still no answer.

“What’s become of that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!”

No answer.

The old woman lowered her spectacles and peered over them around the room; then she raised them and looked beneath them. She hardly ever looked _through_ them for anything as small as a boy; they were her formal pair, the pride of her heart, made for “style” rather than use—she might just as well have looked through two stove-lids. She appeared puzzled for a moment, then said, not angrily, though loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I swear, if I catch you I’ll—”

She left the sentence unfinished, for she was now stooping and jabbing beneath the bed with the broom, and needed her breath to mark each thrust. She brought out nothing except the cat.

“I never saw the equal of that boy!”

She went to the open doorway, stood there, and searched among the tomato vines and “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at an angle meant to carry and called:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind her. She turned just in time to grab a little boy by the loose back of his roundabout and stop his escape.

“There! I might have remembered that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What _is_ that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve told you that if you didn’t leave that jam alone I’d skin you. Give me that switch.”

The switch hung in the air—the danger was extreme—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old woman spun around and snatched her skirts away from danger. At once the boy darted off, scrambled over the tall board fence, and vanished beyond it.

His Aunt Polly remained astonished for a moment, then began to laugh softly.

“Hang that boy, can’t I ever learn? Hasn’t he played me tricks like that often enough for me to watch for him by now? But old fools are the greatest fools there are. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as they say. Yet goodness, he never plays the same one twice, and how can a person know what he’ll try next? He seems to know exactly how long he can torment me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me for a minute or make me laugh, it all settles down again and I can’t strike him once.”"}

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honour ordered me to wake you.”

“Oh! I recollect. Very well, very well.”

After several heavy attempts to fall asleep again, which the man skilfully defeated by keeping the fire stirred for five minutes, he rose, put on his hat, and went out. He entered the Temple, and, having refreshed himself by walking twice along King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings, turned into the Stryver chambers.

The Stryver clerk, who never took part in these meetings, had gone home, and Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose bed-gown, with his throat uncovered for comfort. Around his eyes was that somewhat wild, strained, weathered look seen in all such free livers, from the portrait of Jeffries onward, and traceable, in different artistic disguises, through the portraits of every Drinking Age.

“You are somewhat late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the ordinary hour; perhaps a quarter of an hour afterward.”

They entered a shabby room, its walls covered with books and its floor strewn with papers, where a bright fire burned. A kettle steamed on the hob, while amid the paper chaos a table gleamed, abundantly supplied with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

“You have had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I believe. I dined with the day’s client—or watched him dine; it comes to the same thing!”

“That was an excellent point, Sydney, which you used in establishing the identification. How did you discover it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was a fairly handsome man, and that I should have been much the same kind of man if fortune had favoured me.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his prematurely developed paunch shook.

“You and your fortune, Sydney! Set to work, set to work.”

The jackal, in a sufficiently sullen mood, loosened his clothing, went into the next room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. Dipping the towels in the water and partly wringing them, he arranged them on his head in a dreadful fashion, sat at the table, and said, “Now I am ready!”

“Not much reducing to do tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, as he searched through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two batches.”

“There they are, Sydney. Begin!”

The lion then settled himself on his back upon a sofa at one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own proper table, covered with papers, on the opposite side, the bottles and glasses conveniently within reach."}

{"request_id":"aed9a93456abcc415b74590c","rewritten_text":"He shivered and went back, closing the window behind him.

When he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not even look at the murdered man. He felt that the only way to deal with the whole thing was not to face what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait, the cause of all his misery, was gone from his life. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was a curious Moorish piece, made of dull silver inlaid with polished steel arabesques and set with rough turquoise stones. His servant might notice it was missing, and questions might follow. He hesitated, then went back and took it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the dead body. How still it was! How horribly white the long hands looked! It resembled a terrible wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he crept quietly downstairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to cry out in pain. Several times he stopped and waited. No: everything was silent. It was only the sound of his own footsteps.

When he reached the library, he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden somewhere. He unlocked a secret cupboard in the wood paneling, where he kept his strange disguises, and put them inside. He could burn them later without difficulty. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.

He sat down and began to think. Every year—almost every month—men were hanged in England for what he had done. There had been a murderous madness in the air. Some red star had come too near the earth.... And yet, what proof was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, on the midnight train as he had planned. Because of his secretive habits, it would be months before anyone became suspicious. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before then.

A sudden idea came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went into the hall. There he stopped, hearing the policeman’s slow, heavy footsteps on the pavement outside and seeing the flash of the bull’s-eye reflected in the window. He waited and held his breath.

After a few moments, he lifted the latch and slipped out, closing the door very gently behind him. Then he began ringing the bell."}

{"request_id":"9e3aa5f10dd8f4cc3a3d812f","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”

“A wire fence?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—the first time the Church tested its strength against us, then decided it would be wiser to wait for a more hopeful season. Well, how did you arrange the fence?”

“I ran twelve extremely strong bare wires—not insulated—from a large dynamo in the cave. The dynamo has only two brushes, one positive and one negative.”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a circle of level ground a hundred yards across. They form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles inside one another—and their ends return to the cave.”

“Right. Go on.”

“The fences are attached to heavy oak posts set only three feet apart, and the posts are buried five feet deep.”

“That is strong enough.”

“Yes. Outside the cave, the wires have no connection to the ground. They leave from the dynamo’s positive brush; the negative brush is grounded. The other ends return to the cave, where each is grounded separately.”

“No, no, that won’t do!”

“Why not?”

“It wastes power and costs too much. You need no ground connection except the one through the negative brush. The other end of every wire must return to the cave and be fastened separately, but without being grounded. Now consider how much that saves. A cavalry charge rushes at the fence. You use no power and spend no money, because there is only one ground connection until the horses strike the wire. The instant they touch it, they create a connection with the negative brush through the ground and fall dead. Don’t you see? You use no energy until it is needed. The lightning is waiting there, ready, like a bullet in a gun, but it costs nothing until you fire it. Yes, the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I don’t know how I missed that. It is not only cheaper, but more effective, because if wires break or become tangled, nothing happens.”

“No, especially if we have a warning device in the cave and disconnect any broken wire. Well, go on. The Gatlings?”

“Yes—that is arranged. In the center of the inner circle, on a broad platform six feet high, I have placed a battery of thirteen Gatling guns and supplied plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there will be music. The edge of the precipice above the cave—”

“I’ve put a wire fence there, along with a Gatling.”"}

{"request_id":"517a535fbf9da1b8b6788b57","rewritten_text":"“Yes, it is—and _I_ could have had him if I’d been big enough; I saw him _first_. Who captured him?”

“It was an old man—a stranger—and he sold his claim on him for forty dollars because he has to go up the river and can’t wait. Just think of that! You bet _I’d_ wait, even if it took seven years.”

“That’s me, every time,” I said. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth more than that, if he’ll sell it so cheaply. Maybe something isn’t right about it.”

“But it _is_ right—straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells everything about him exactly—describes him like a picture and names the plantation he came from, below New Orleans. No, sir, there’s no trouble with that deal, you bet. Say, give me a chew of tobacco, will you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t figure anything out. I thought until my head hurt, but I couldn’t see any way out of the trouble. After that long journey, and after everything we had done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing. Everything was ruined because they had the heart to play such a trick on Jim, making him a slave again for the rest of his life, among strangers too, for forty dirty dollars.

At one point I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home with his family, if he had to be a slave, and that I should write Tom Sawyer and tell him to inform Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon abandoned that idea for two reasons: she would be angry and disgusted by his wickedness and ingratitude for leaving her, and would sell him straight down the river again; and even if she didn’t, everyone naturally despises an ungrateful Black man, and they would make Jim feel it constantly, leaving him ashamed and miserable. And then, what about _me_? Word would spread that Huck Finn had helped a Black man escape; and if I ever saw anyone from that town again, I would be so ashamed I’d be ready to kneel down and kiss his boots. That’s how it is: a person does something low and then doesn’t want to face the consequences. He thinks that as long as he can hide it, it isn’t disgraceful. That was exactly my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience tormented me, and the more wicked, low, and miserable I felt."}
