{"request_id":"9916b26ecac056923db184b9","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to relieve you considerably. But what made you react that way? What did you expect we had found?”

Huck was in a tight spot—the questioning eyes were fixed on him. He would have given anything for material for a believable answer, but nothing came to him. The eyes seemed to bore deeper and deeper. A senseless reply suggested itself; there was no time to consider it, so he blurted it out on a chance, weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too troubled to smile, but the old man laughed loudly and happily, shaking every part of his body from head to foot. He ended by saying that such laughter was money in a man’s pocket because it reduced the doctor’s bill enormously. Then he added:

“Poor old fellow, you’re pale and exhausted—you’re not well at all. No wonder you’re a little confused and unsteady. But you’ll recover. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed that he had acted like such a fool and shown such suspicious excitement. He had abandoned the idea that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard the conversation at the widow’s stile. He had only thought it was not the treasure, though—he had not known for certain that it wasn’t—and the suggestion that a bundle had been captured was too much for his self-control. Still, he was glad the little incident had occurred, because now he knew beyond any doubt that that bundle was not the bundle, and his mind was peaceful and completely at ease. Indeed, everything now seemed to be moving in exactly the right direction. The treasure must still be in No. 2; the men would be captured and jailed that day, and he and Tom could take the gold that night without trouble or fear of interruption.

Just as breakfast ended, someone knocked at the door. Huck leaped toward a hiding place, since he had no desire to be connected, even indirectly, with the night’s events. The Welshman admitted several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and noticed groups of citizens climbing the hill to stare at the stile. So the news had spread. The Welshman had to recount the night’s story to the visitors. The widow openly expressed her gratitude for being saved.

“Don’t mention it, madam. There is someone to whom you may owe more than you do to me and my boys, but he won’t let me reveal his name. We would not have been there without him.”"}

{"request_id":"d088be6bf3dab0e3a2cc93d2","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months passed, and winter was well underway. I had been going to school most of the time and could spell, read, and write a little. I could recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five, and I don’t suppose I could ever get beyond that, even if I lived forever. I don’t put much faith in mathematics, anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I got so I could tolerate it. Whenever I became especially tired, I played hooky, and the beating I received the next day did me good and lifted my spirits. So the longer I attended school, the easier it became. I was also getting somewhat used to the widow’s ways, and they didn’t grate on me so much. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed weighed on me pretty heavily most of the time, but before the cold weather came, I used to slip away and sleep in the woods sometimes, and that gave me a rest. I preferred the old ways, but I was beginning to like the new ones a little, too. The widow said I was improving slowly but surely and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning I happened to knock over the saltcellar at breakfast. I reached for some salt as quickly as I could to throw over my left shoulder and ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson got there first and stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; what a mess you’re always making!” The widow spoke up for me, but I knew that wasn’t going to keep the bad luck away. After breakfast I went out feeling anxious and unsteady, wondering where it would strike me and what form it would take. There are ways to ward off some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of them; so I didn’t try to do anything, but simply trudged along, discouraged and watchful.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the high board fence. There was an inch of fresh snow on the ground, and I saw someone’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry, lingered around the stile for a while, and then continued along the garden fence. It was strange that they hadn’t come in after standing there so long. I couldn’t understand it. Somehow, it was very curious. I was about to follow the tracks around, but first I bent down to examine them."}

{"request_id":"dfcc3c00abd3dec689647035","rewritten_text":"On my return, I found this letter from my father:—

“My dear Victor,

“You have likely been waiting impatiently for a letter settling the date of your return to us; at first I was inclined to write only a few lines, simply naming the day on which I expected you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I dare not do so. What would your astonishment be, my son, when, expecting a joyful and happy welcome, you were instead met by tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you of our misfortune? Absence cannot have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows; and how can I bring pain to my son, so long absent? I wish to prepare you for the dreadful news, but I know it cannot be done; even now your eyes hurry across the page, searching for the words that will bring you the terrible tidings.

“William is dead!—that beloved child, whose smiles delighted and warmed my heart, who was so gentle, yet so cheerful! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you; I shall merely relate the circumstances of the event.

“Last Thursday (May 7th), my niece, your two brothers, and I went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, and we extended our walk farther than usual. It was already dusk before we considered returning; then we discovered that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be seen. We therefore sat on a bench until they should come back. Soon Ernest arrived and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said he had been playing with him, that William had run off to hide, and that he had searched for him in vain, then waited a long while, but William had not returned.

“This account caused us some alarm, and we went on looking for him until night came, when Elizabeth supposed that he might have gone back to the house. He was not there. We returned once more with torches; I could not rest, thinking that my dear boy might be lost and exposed to the night’s damp and dew; Elizabeth too endured the greatest anguish. At about five in the morning I found my lovely boy, whom I had seen the previous evening blooming with health and activity, lying on the grass, pale and motionless; the mark of the murderer’s fingers was upon his neck.

“He was carried home, and the grief plainly visible in my face revealed the secret to Elizabeth. She was most anxious to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she persisted, and entering the room where it lay, quickly examined the victim’s neck, then clasped her hands and cried, ‘O God!"}

{"request_id":"aa5eed83e5d7f2e1a7366d8a","rewritten_text":"Directly before him, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man of terrifying appearance. His eyes glowed like red-hot coals; long gray hair hung over his shoulders in tangled coils; his old-fashioned clothes were dirty and torn, and heavy manacles and rusty shackles dangled from his wrists and ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains, and for that purpose I have brought you a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. It is said to be entirely effective after a single application, and the wrapper carries several testimonials to that effect from some of our most distinguished native clergymen. I shall leave it here beside the bedroom candles, and will gladly provide more if you need it.” With these words, the United States Minister placed the bottle on a marble table, closed his door, and went to bed.

For a moment, the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still in righteous indignation. Then he hurled the bottle onto the polished floor and fled down the corridor, uttering hollow groans and giving off a dreadful green light. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open, two small figures in white appeared, and a large pillow whizzed past his head! Clearly there was no time to lose. Quickly adopting the Fourth Dimension of Space as his means of escape, he vanished through the wood paneling, and the house fell silent.

When he reached a small secret chamber in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and began trying to understand his situation. Never, in a brilliant and uninterrupted career lasting three hundred years, had he been so outrageously insulted. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood before the mirror in her lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids, who had gone into hysterics when he merely grinned at them through the curtains of one spare bedroom; of the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out as he came late one night from the library, and who had remained under Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a complete martyr to nervous disorders; and of old Madame de Tremouillac, who, after waking early one morning and seeing a skeleton seated in an armchair by the fire reading her diary, had been confined to bed for six weeks with brain fever. On recovering, she had reconciled herself to the Church and broken off her association with that notorious skeptic, Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"3c426bbd52156d5b6dff0944","rewritten_text":"“I’m not dining at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” said the man, leaving the room.

“Now, Alan, there isn’t a moment to lose. How heavy this chest is! I’ll carry it for you. You bring the other things.” He spoke quickly and with authority. Campbell felt himself being dominated by him. Together they left the room.

When they reached the top landing, Dorian took out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he stopped, and a troubled expression came into his eyes. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he murmured.

“It means nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. As he did, he saw the face of his portrait leering in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that the night before, for the first time in his life, he had forgotten to conceal the fatal canvas, and was about to rush forward when he recoiled with a shudder.

What was that vile red moisture gleaming, wet and shining, on one of the hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood? How horrible it was!—more horrible, it seemed to him at that moment, than the silent thing he knew was stretched across the table, the thing whose grotesquely misshapen shadow on the spotted carpet showed him that it had not moved, but was still there, just as he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, opened the door a little wider, and, with his eyes half closed and his head turned away, walked quickly inside, determined not to look even once at the dead man. Then he bent down, picked up the gold-and-purple hanging, and threw it over the picture.

There he stopped, afraid to turn around, his eyes fixed on the intricate pattern before him. He heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other things he had requested for his dreadful work. He began to wonder whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what they had thought of each other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, only dimly aware that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a glistening yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was long after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale, but completely calm. “I have done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"e53e0a44ee47d0e47129f510","rewritten_text":"They was bringing along a very fine-looking old gentleman, and a good-looking younger one with his right arm in a sling. And, my souls, how the people yelled and laughed, and kept it going. But I couldn’t see any joke in it, and I reckoned it would take some straining for the duke and king to find one either. I figured they’d turn pale. But no, not a shade did they turn. The duke never let on that he suspected anything, but went goo-gooing about, cheerful and contented, like a jug gurgling out buttermilk; and the king just stared sorrowfully down at the newcomers, as if the thought that such frauds and rascals could exist in the world gave him a stomach-ache clear to the heart. Oh, he played it admirable. A lot of the principal people gathered around the king, to show him they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely bewildered. Pretty soon he began to speak, and I saw at once that he pronounced like an Englishman—not in the king’s fashion, though the king’s imitation was pretty good. I can’t give the old gentleman’s exact words, nor imitate him; but he turned to the crowd and said, something like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting; and I’ll admit, plain and frank, that I’m not very well prepared to meet it or answer it; for my brother and I have had misfortunes. He has broken his arm, and our baggage was put off at a town above here last night, during the night, by mistake. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can neither hear nor speak—and can’t even make signs to much purpose, now that he has only one hand to use. We are who we claim to be; and in a day or two, when I get the baggage, I can prove it. But until then I won’t say anything more, but will go to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new dummy started off; and the king laughed and blustered out:

“Broke his arm—_very_ likely, _isn’t_ it?—and very convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _mighty_ good!—and mighty clever—under the _circumstances!_”

Then he laughed again, and everybody else did too, except three or four, or maybe half a dozen. One was the doctor; another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-fashioned carpetbag made of carpet material, who had just come off the steamboat and was speaking to him in a low voice, glancing toward the king now and then and nodding their heads—it was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville; and another was a big, rough, powerful fellow who had come along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

{"request_id":"c2f2293065b64663c1a4d3f0","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but wait a moment. Go on, Joseph. Well done! Go on!”

“What would everyone here say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That miserable hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded again and said with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Press her, Joseph!”

“Then, to finish the matter,” said Joe, happily handing the bag to my sister, “it’s five-and-twenty pounds.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pounds, Mum,” echoed that lowest of swindlers, Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand; “and it’s no more than your merits deserve, as I said when my opinion was asked. I wish you joy of the money!”

If the villain had stopped there, his conduct would have been bad enough. But he made his guilt even worse by taking charge of me, with a sense of authority that made all his earlier crimes seem small.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always finish what they start. This boy must be bound at once. That’s my way. Bound at once.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister, clutching the money, “we’re deeply grateful to you.”

“Never mind me, Mum,” replied that devilish corn merchant. “A pleasure is a pleasure everywhere. But this boy, you know—we must have him bound. I said I would arrange it—to tell you the truth.”

The Justices were sitting nearby in the Town Hall, so we went there at once to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the presence of the magistrates. I say we went, but Pumblechook pushed me along as if I had just picked a pocket or set fire to a haystack. Indeed, everyone in the court seemed to think he had caught me red-handed. As Pumblechook shoved me through the crowd, I heard some people ask, “What has he done?” and others say, “He’s young, too, but he looks bad, doesn’t he?” One mild-looking, kindly person even gave me a religious tract decorated with a woodcut of a wicked young man covered in a complete sausage-shop of chains. It was titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall seemed a strange place to me, with pews higher than those in a church, people leaning over them to watch, and powerful Justices—one with a powdered head—sitting back in chairs with folded arms, taking snuff, falling asleep, writing, or reading newspapers. On the walls hung several shiny black portraits, which my untrained eye saw as a mixture of hard toffee and sticking-plaster."}

{"request_id":"61c817f4aa6cfb5add7f41ea","rewritten_text":"“Shall I ask them? Or Miss Bates? She is nearer still.—And I am not sure that Miss Bates may not understand the inclinations of the other people as well as anyone. I think we do need a larger council. Suppose I go and invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you please,” said Mrs. Weston, somewhat hesitantly, “if you believe she will be of any assistance.”

“You will get nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and gratitude, but she will tell you nothing. She will not even attend to your questions. I see no benefit in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so entertaining, so exceedingly entertaining! I am very fond of listening to Miss Bates talk. And I need not bring the entire family, you know.”

At this point Mr. Weston joined them, and, hearing what was suggested, gave it his firm approval.

“Aye, do, Frank.—Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle the matter at once. She will enjoy the plan, I am certain; and I know no more suitable person to show us how to overcome difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming a little too particular. She is a constant example of how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady—?”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall consider you a great blockhead, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I did not remember at once. Certainly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And off he ran.

Long before he returned, bringing the short, neat, brisk-moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston, like a good wife and sweet-tempered woman, had examined the passage once more and found its difficulties far less than she had first imagined—indeed, very slight; and with that, the question of decision was ended. Everything else, at least in theory, went perfectly smoothly. All the lesser arrangements of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper, arranged themselves; or were left as trifles to be settled later between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes.—Everyone invited was certainly to attend; Frank had already written to Enscombe, suggesting that he remain a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be denied. And it promised to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she most heartily agreed that it must be so. As a counsellor she was unnecessary; but as an approver, a much safer role, she was entirely welcome. Her approval, at once broad and particular, warm and unceasing, could not fail to please; and for another half-hour they all walked back and forth between the various rooms, some proposing, some listening, and everyone happily enjoying the prospect."}

{"request_id":"ddc1d1b5059263313a1df7e4","rewritten_text":"She would be such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed with everything, but added,

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, however, is just as pretty and pleasant a young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very happy to hear it—but only Jane Fairfax is known to be so accomplished and superior!—and exactly Emma’s age.”

They discussed this subject very happily, and others of similar importance followed and ended with the same harmony; but the evening did not pass without a slight return of agitation. The gruel arrived and provided plenty to discuss—much praise and many observations—firm certainty that it was wholesome for every constitution, and rather severe attacks on the many households where it was never prepared properly; but, unfortunately, among the failures her daughter had to mention, the most recent, and therefore most prominent, was her own cook at South End, a young woman hired temporarily, who had never been able to understand what she meant by a basin of good, smooth gruel, thin but not too thin. However often she had wanted and ordered it, she had never managed to obtain anything tolerable. This was a dangerous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern. The exclamation, to Emma’s ear, meant: “Ah! There is no end to the sad consequences of your going to South End. It cannot bear discussion.” For a little while she hoped he would not discuss it, and that silent reflection might be enough to restore his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After several minutes, however, he began:

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir? I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you had to go to the sea, it would have been better not to go to South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was surprised to hear that you had chosen South End.”

“I know many people have that idea, but it is certainly a mistake, sir. We all remained perfectly healthy there and never suffered the least inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely mistaken to suppose the place unhealthy. I am sure he can be trusted, because he thoroughly understands the nature of the air, and his own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry stayed at Cromer for a week once, and considers it the best of all the seaside resorts.”"}

{"request_id":"2ef6fc8ea40f4e32738b48a5","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The neglect had come back upon the sinner; when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no letter of condolence arrived at Kellynch, and there was consequently too much reason to fear that the Dalrymples regarded the relationship as ended. How to put this troubling matter right and be accepted as cousins again was the question; and, in a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot considered it unimportant. “Family connections were always worth preserving, and good society always worth pursuing; Lady Dalrymple had taken a house for three months in Laura Place and would be living in style. She had been in Bath the previous year, and Lady Russell had heard her described as a charming woman. It was very desirable that the connection should be renewed, if it could be done without any sacrifice of propriety on the Elliots’ part.”

Sir Walter, however, would choose his own method, and eventually wrote his distinguished cousin a very fine letter full of explanation, regret, and entreaty. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot admired the letter, but it achieved everything required, producing three lines of scrawl from the Dowager Viscountess: “She was greatly honoured, and would be happy to renew their acquaintance.” The difficult work was finished; the rewards began. They visited at Laura Place, received the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, and placed them wherever they would be most noticeable. “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—were mentioned to everyone.

Anne was ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been especially agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the excitement they caused; but they were nothing of the kind. They possessed no superiority of manner, accomplishment, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the reputation of “a charming woman” because she had a smile and a polite reply for everyone. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and awkward that she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place except for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected better; yet “it was an acquaintance worth having.” When Anne ventured to express her opinion of them to Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but still insisted that, as a family connection, as people of good society, and as those who would gather good society around them, they had value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of intelligent, well-informed people who have a great deal to say; that is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"319ccf928d0666f2db8d6561","rewritten_text":"In my youth, discontent never entered my mind, and if I was ever overcome by ennui, the sight of nature’s beauty or the study of what was excellent and sublime in human creations could always engage my heart and restore elasticity to my spirits. But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has entered my soul; and I felt then that I would live on only to display what I would soon cease to be—a miserable spectacle of ruined humanity, pitiable to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a considerable time at Oxford, wandering through its surroundings and trying to identify every place connected with the most stirring period of English history. Our small voyages of discovery were often extended by the successive sights that appeared before us. We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, my soul rose above its degrading and miserable fears to contemplate the divine ideals of liberty and self-sacrifice that these places commemorated. For an instant, I dared to cast off my chains and look around me with a free and elevated spirit; but the iron had cut into my flesh, and I sank once more, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford reluctantly and went on to Matlock, our next place of rest. The countryside around this village more closely resembled the scenery of Switzerland; but everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the distant white Alps that always crown the pine-covered mountains of my native land. We visited the marvelous cave and the small natural-history cabinets, where the curiosities were arranged in the same way as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name made me tremble whenever Henry spoke it, and I hurried to leave Matlock, now linked in my mind with that terrible scene.

From Derby, continuing northward, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow still lingering on the northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all familiar and beloved sights. Here, too, we made several acquaintances who nearly managed to deceive me into happiness. Clerval’s pleasure was proportionately greater than mine; among talented people, his mind expanded, and he discovered within himself greater abilities and resources than he could have imagined possessing while he kept company with his inferiors."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e8a24f95fd11bc5b59076256","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later, the bell rang for tea, and, when Virginia did not come down, Mrs. Otis sent a footman upstairs to tell her. After a short while he returned and said he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. Since she usually went into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis was not alarmed at first. But when six o’clock struck and Virginia still had not appeared, she became genuinely distressed. She sent the boys out to search for her, while she and Mr. Otis looked through every room in the house. At half past six, the boys returned and said they could find no sign of their sister. They were all now extremely agitated and had no idea what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that, a few days earlier, he had given a band of gypsies permission to camp in the park. He immediately set out for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they were staying, accompanied by his eldest son and two farmhands. The little Duke of Cheshire, frantic with worry, pleaded to be allowed to come as well, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be a struggle. When he reached the place, however, he found that the gypsies had left. Their departure had clearly been sudden: the fire was still burning, and several plates lay on the grass. He sent Washington and the two men to search the surrounding area, then hurried home and telegraphed every police inspector in the county, asking them to watch for a little girl kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then ordered his horse to be brought around and, after insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode off along the Ascot Road with a groom. He had gone scarcely two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Turning, he saw the little Duke riding toward him on his pony, his face flushed and his head bare. “I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy gasped, “but I can’t eat any dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry with me. If you had let us become engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!” The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young scamp, and was deeply moved by his devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted the boy kindly on the shoulders and said, “Well, Cecil, if you won’t go back, I suppose you must come with me. But I’ll have to buy you a hat at Ascot.”"}

{"request_id":"638c32bcb83520ae67ff79ec","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note in the mail. The sight of its outside threw me into great agitation; although I had never seen the handwriting in which it was addressed, I knew whose hand it was. It had no formal opening—Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything—but read as follows:

“I am to come to London the day after tomorrow by the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you should meet me? In any case, Miss Havisham has that impression, and I am writing in obedience to it. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If there had been time, I would probably have ordered several new suits for the occasion; but there was not, and I had to be satisfied with the clothes I already owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I knew neither peace nor rest until the day came. Yet its arrival brought me neither; I was worse than ever, and began haunting the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew perfectly well that it had not, I still felt it unsafe to let the coach office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a time. In this irrational state, I had completed the first half-hour of a four- or five-hour watch when Wemmick ran into me.

“Hello, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I would hardly have expected this to be your usual place.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both thriving, thank you,” said Wemmick, “and especially the Aged. He is in wonderful spirits. He will be eighty-two on his next birthday. I am thinking of firing eighty-two times, if the neighborhood does not object and my cannon can withstand the strain. But this is not London conversation. Where do you think I am going?”

“To the office?” I said, since he was heading that way.

“Almost,” Wemmick replied. “I am going to Newgate. We are dealing with a banker’s-parcel case at present, and I have been down the road to take a look at the scene of the crime. Now I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Good heavens, no,” Wemmick answered very dryly. “But he is accused of it. You or I might be accused of it just as easily. Either of us could be accused, you know.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"7891226556b8efa4fc88eafd","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself time to reflect, and scarcely understanding what she felt, Elizabeth, as soon as she had finished this letter, immediately took up the other and, opening it with the greatest impatience, read as follows: it had been written a day after the first had ended.\n\n“By this time, my dearest sister, you must have received my hurried letter; I hope this will be clearer, but although I am not pressed for time, my mind is so confused that I cannot promise to be coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I scarcely know what to say, but I have bad news for you, and it must not be postponed. Imprudent as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now eager to know that it has actually occurred, for there is only too much cause to fear that they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the previous day, only a few hours after the express. Though Lydia’s brief letter to Mrs. F. led them to believe that they were bound for Gretna Green, Denny let something fall which showed his opinion that W. had never meant to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was repeated to Colonel F., who, immediately alarmed, set out from B., intending to follow their path. He traced them without difficulty as far as Clapham, but no farther; for on reaching that place, they changed into a hackney-coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. The only information afterward is that they were seen proceeding along the London road. I do not know what to think. Having made every possible inquiry in that part of London, Colonel F. came on to Hertfordshire, anxiously repeating his search at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but with no success—no such persons had been seen passing through. With the greatest kindness and concern he continued to Longbourn, and revealed his fears to us in a manner that did the utmost credit to his heart. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F.; but no blame can be laid upon either of them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is extreme. My father and mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many circumstances might make it preferable for them to marry privately in town rather than follow their original plan; and even if _he_ could conceive such a scheme against a young woman of Lydia’s connections, which is unlikely, can I believe her so utterly lost to every principle? Impossible! I am sorry, however, to discover that Colonel F. is unwilling to rely upon their marriage: when I expressed my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared W. was not a man who could be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"389d53cdde30c6db2d3f5384","rewritten_text":"They know what a clever lad he is; he’ll be a lifer. They’ll make the Artful nothing less than a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What’s the point of talking that way to me? Why don’t you speak so I can understand you?”

Fagin was about to translate these mysterious expressions into ordinary language; and, once interpreted, Mr. Bolter would have learned that they meant the phrase “transportation for life,” when the conversation was interrupted by the arrival of Master Bates, his hands in his trouser pockets and his face twisted into an expression of half-comic misery.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” said Charley, after he and his new companion had been introduced to each other.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to identify him; and the Artful’s booked for a passage out,” replied Master Bates. “I’ll need a complete mourning suit, Fagin, and a hatband, to visit him in before he sets out on his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—lively Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad for an ordinary cheap snuffbox! I never thought he’d have done it for less than a gold watch, chain, and seals. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables and go out like a gentleman, instead of as a common thief, without any honour or glory!”

After expressing these feelings for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates sat down on the nearest chair, looking bitter and dejected.

“What do you mean, saying he has neither honour nor glory?” exclaimed Fagin, shooting an angry glance at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best among you all? Is there one of you who could match him or come close to him at any game? Eh?”

“Not one,” replied Master Bates, his voice made hoarse by regret; “not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin answered angrily. “What are you crying for?”

“Because it won’t be on the record, will it?” said Charley, driven into complete defiance of his venerable friend by the force of his grief; “because it won’t appear in the indictment; because no one will ever know half of what he was. How will he appear in the Newgate Calendar? Perhaps he won’t be there at all. Oh, my goodness, what a blow it is!”

“Ha! Ha!” cried Fagin, extending his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter in a fit of laughter that shook him as though he were suffering from palsy. “See how proud they are of their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"0b106be0dcb8ef1620c3bf91","rewritten_text":"“And so I’m the proprietor of some knights,” I said as we rode away. “Who would ever have imagined that I’d live to list assets of that kind? I won’t know what to do with them—unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, sir, and their squires.”

“That’s a good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I didn’t understand you. I’ll tell you presently.” Then she said thoughtfully and softly, turning the words delicately over her tongue: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; yes, that’s it; where do they hang out. Truly, the phrase has a pleasant and charming grace, and is prettily worded as well. I’ll repeat it again and again in my idle moments, so that perhaps I may learn it. Where do they hang out. Exactly! Already it comes trippingly from my tongue, and inasmuch as—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. You remember, a while ago. Figuratively speaking, the game has been called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Go to bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t use so much kindling getting your fire started. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will, and I’ll begin at once. So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I recognized my mistake immediately. I had set her machinery in motion; it was my own fault, and she would take thirty days to reach the facts. She generally began without a preface and ended without a conclusion. If you interrupted her, she would either continue without noticing or answer in a couple of words and then go back and repeat the sentence. So interruptions only made matters worse; yet I had to interrupt, and interrupt fairly often, to save my life. A person would die if he let her monotony drip over him all day long.

“Great Scott!” I said in distress. She went straight back and began again:

“So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, where they were well lodged. In the morning they heard mass in the abbey, and then rode on until they came to a great forest. There Sir Gawaine saw, in a valley beside a turret, twelve fair damsels and two knights armed on great horses, while the damsels went back and forth by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"4cb4c073798a654b71aff113","rewritten_text":"His face, deeply browned by the sun, was more than half concealed by whisker and _mustachio._ He carried a great oaken cudgel, but seemed otherwise unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and wished us “good evening,” in French accents which, though somewhat Neufchatelish, still plainly suggested a Parisian origin.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I presume you have come concerning the Ourang-Outang. Upon my word, I almost envy you the ownership of him; a remarkably fine animal, and doubtless a very valuable one. How old would you say he is?”

The sailor drew a deep breath, like a man relieved of some unbearable weight, and answered confidently:

“I have no means of knowing—but he cannot be more than four or five years old. Have you got him here?”

“Oh no, we had no proper accommodation for keeping him here. He is at a livery stable in the Rue Dubourg, close by. You may collect him in the morning. Naturally, you are ready to identify the property?”

“Certainly, sir.”

“I shall regret giving him up,” said Dupin.

“I do not intend that you should undergo all this trouble for nothing, sir,” said the man. “That would not be expected. I am quite willing to pay a reward for recovering the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” replied my friend, “that is entirely fair, certainly. Let me consider!—what ought I to ask? Ah! I have it. This shall be my reward: you must give me every piece of information within your power concerning the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin uttered the final words very softly and with perfect calm. With equal quietness, he went to the door, locked it, and slipped the key into his pocket. He then took a pistol from his bosom and laid it on the table without the slightest agitation.

The sailor’s face reddened as though he were fighting for breath. He sprang up and seized his cudgel, but an instant later sank back into his chair, shaking violently, his features wearing the look of death itself. He said nothing. I felt the deepest pity for him.

“My friend,” said Dupin gently, “you are needlessly frightening yourself—you truly are. We have no intention of harming you. I give you a gentleman’s, and a Frenchman’s, word that we mean you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. It would not be proper, however, to deny that you are in some degree connected with them.”"}

{"request_id":"ec202db344590e9f1e5a95b4","rewritten_text":"At last, it was decided that we would live together during my stay in the city. Since my financial situation was somewhat better than his, I was allowed to pay for renting and furnishing a house in a style that matched the strange gloom we shared. It was an old, grotesque mansion, long abandoned because of superstitions we never investigated, and close to collapse in a secluded, desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If the world had known how we lived there, it would have considered us madmen—though perhaps harmless ones. We were completely isolated and allowed no visitors. I had carefully kept the location of our retreat secret from my former associates, and Dupin had not known or been known in Paris for many years. We lived entirely within ourselves.

My friend had a strange fondness for the night simply because it was night; and, as with all his other odd habits, I quietly adopted it, giving myself completely to his wild whims. The dark goddess could not always stay with us, but we could imitate her presence. At dawn we shut all the heavy shutters of our old house and lit two strongly scented candles, whose flames gave only the faintest and most ghostly light. By their glow we occupied ourselves with dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the arrival of true Darkness. Then we went out into the streets arm in arm, continuing the day’s discussions or wandering far and wide until late, seeking among the crowded city’s shifting lights and shadows the endless mental excitement that quiet observation can provide.

At such times I could not help noticing and admiring Dupin’s unusual analytical ability, though his rich imagination had prepared me to expect it. He also seemed to take great pleasure in using it, if not exactly in showing it off, and openly admitted how much he enjoyed it. With a soft, chuckling laugh, he would boast that most people, as far as he was concerned, had windows in their chests. He would then support this claim with direct and startling proofs of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. At these moments his manner became cold and distant, his eyes blank. His voice, usually a rich tenor, rose to a treble that might have sounded childish or irritating if not for the care and complete clarity of his speech."}

{"request_id":"9200e040575fbc6ca9814b87","rewritten_text":"He led her to understand that Frank admired her greatly—thought her extremely beautiful and charming; and, with so much to recommend him altogether, she felt she could not judge him too severely. As Mrs. Weston remarked, “all young people would have their little whims.”

There was one person among his new acquaintances in Surrey who was less indulgent. In general, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, he was judged with considerable fairness; generous allowances were made for the minor excesses of so handsome a young man—one who smiled so readily and bowed so gracefully; but there was one spirit among them that censure could not soften, whether by bows or smiles—Mr. Knightley. The matter was told him at Hartfield; for a moment he said nothing, but Emma heard him almost at once afterwards mutter to himself, over the newspaper in his hand, “Hum! just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She was half inclined to resent it; but a moment’s observation persuaded her that it had been said merely to ease his own feelings, and was not intended to provoke her; so she allowed it to pass.

Though in one respect Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit that morning brought unwelcome news, in another it was especially timely. Something happened while they were at Hartfield which made Emma desire their advice; and, still more fortunately, the advice they offered was precisely what she wanted.

The event was this:—The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years, and were very respectable people—friendly, generous, and unassuming; but, on the other hand, they were of humble origin, in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first came into the country, they had lived according to their income, quietly, receiving little company, and spending little on it; but during the last year or two their means had increased considerably—their business in town had produced larger profits, and fortune generally had favoured them. As their wealth grew, so did their ambitions: they wanted a larger house and more society. They enlarged their house, increased their servants, and raised their expenses in every direction; and by this time, in fortune and manner of living, they were second only to the family at Hartfield. Their fondness for company, together with their new dining-room, made everyone expect them to give dinners; and several parties, chiefly for unmarried men, had already been held. Emma could scarcely imagine that the established and finest families would be invited—not Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. Nothing would induce her to attend if they were; and she regretted that her father’s familiar habits would make her refusal seem less significant than she wished."}

{"request_id":"223af4cc2285952626163a7d","rewritten_text":"After supper the whole gang went out onto the bar to search for turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and whenever they found a soft spot, dropped to their knees and dug with their fingers. At times they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. They were perfectly round, white objects, slightly smaller than an English walnut. That evening they enjoyed a grand fried-egg feast, and had another Friday morning.

After breakfast they went whooping and prancing onto the bar, chasing one another in circles and throwing off their clothes as they ran, until they were naked. Then they carried the frolic far up the bar’s shallow water, struggling against the strong current, which repeatedly swept their legs from beneath them and made the sport all the merrier. Every so often they bent together and flung water into one another’s faces with their hands, slowly drawing nearer, their faces turned aside to escape the choking sprays. At last they seized and wrestled until the strongest ducked his neighbor, and then all of them plunged beneath the surface in a tangle of pale arms and legs, rising together, blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for air.

Once thoroughly worn out, they would race ashore and sprawl upon the dry, scorching sand, covering themselves with it. Presently they would dash back into the water and repeat the whole performance. At length they realized that their bare skin made fairly good flesh-colored “tights,” so they marked out a ring in the sand and put on a circus—with three clowns, since none of them would surrender that most honored position to another.

After that they brought out their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until the game lost its charm. Joe and Huck then took another swim, but Tom refused, having discovered that when he kicked off his trousers he had also knocked the string of rattlesnake rattles from his ankle. He wondered how he had avoided cramp for so long without the protection of that mysterious charm. He would not go in again until he found it, and by then the other boys were weary and prepared to rest. Gradually they drifted apart, sank into the “dumps,” and gazed wistfully across the broad river toward the village, which lay dozing in the sunshine. Tom caught himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe. He rubbed it out and scolded himself for being so weak. Yet he wrote it again; he could not resist. He erased it once more, then removed the temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"45667f52c358670fed729c5d","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often reflected on the old philosophy of the Bi-Part Soul, and entertained the notion of a double Dupin—the creative and the analytical.

Let no one suppose, from what I have just said, that I am revealing any mystery or writing a romance. What I have described in the Frenchman was merely the product of an excited, or perhaps diseased, mind. But an example of the nature of his remarks at such times will best convey the idea.

One night we were walking down a long, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Apparently lost in thought, neither of us had spoken a word for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin broke the silence with these words:

“He is a very small fellow, that’s true, and would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_. ”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I replied involuntarily, without at first noticing—so deeply was I absorbed in thought—the extraordinary way in which his words matched my own reflections. A moment later I came to myself, and my astonishment was profound.

“Dupin,” I said gravely, “this is beyond my understanding. I do not hesitate to say that I am amazed and can scarcely trust my senses. How could you know I was thinking of ——?” I stopped, to determine beyond doubt whether he truly knew whom I had in mind.

“—— of Chantilly,” he said. “Why do you stop? You were saying to yourself that his small stature made him unfit for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been thinking. Chantilly had once been a cobbler on the Rue St. Denis who, becoming obsessed with the stage, had attempted the role of Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy of that name and had been notoriously mocked for his efforts.

“Tell me, for Heaven’s sake,” I cried, “the method—if there is a method—by which you have managed to read my mind in this matter.” In truth, I was even more startled than I would have cared to admit.

“It was the fruit seller,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the sole-mender was not tall enough for Xerxes, and all the rest of it.”

“The fruit seller! You astonish me—I know no fruit seller at all.”

“The man who bumped into you as we entered the street—it may have been fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples had indeed nearly knocked me down by accident as we passed from the Rue C—— into the street where we stood. But what this had to do with Chantilly, I could not possibly understand."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c252f078bd615af32ababd57","rewritten_text":"I rose early that morning and once again managed to evade my creditors’ watchfulness. I hurried to the bookseller’s stall and spent what little ready money I had on several volumes of Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. After returning home safely with them, I devoted every spare moment to reading, and soon became, as I believed, sufficiently skilled in such studies to carry out my plan. During this time, I also made every effort to reconcile the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. At last I succeeded—partly by selling enough of my household furniture to satisfy half their claim, and partly by promising to pay the remainder when I completed a small project I told them I had in mind, for which I asked their assistance. By these means—for they were ignorant men—I had little difficulty winning them over to my purpose.\n\n“Once matters were arranged, I secretly and cautiously disposed of the property still remaining to me, with my wife’s help, and borrowed, in small sums and under various pretexts, a considerable amount of ready money, without giving any thought to how I would repay it. With these funds, I gradually obtained very fine cambric muslin, in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a quantity of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and several other articles needed to construct and equip a balloon of extraordinary size. I instructed my wife to assemble it as quickly as possible and gave her all the necessary information about the method to follow. Meanwhile, I made the twine into a net of sufficient dimensions, fitted it with a hoop and the required cords, and purchased a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, an ordinary barometer with important modifications, and two astronomical instruments less commonly known. I also found opportunities to transport by night to a secluded place east of Rotterdam five iron-bound casks, each holding about fifty gallons, along with one larger cask; six tin tubes, three inches in diameter, properly shaped and ten feet long; a quantity of a particular metallic substance, or semimetal, which I will not name; and twelve demijohns of a very common acid. The gas produced from these last materials is one no person but myself has ever generated—or, at least, ever used for a similar purpose. I would have no objection to revealing the secret, except that it rightfully belongs to a citizen of Nantes, France, who communicated it to me conditionally.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cacbfe8efe04fbf31c899530","rewritten_text":"Thus I passed two years. Day after day, hundreds of them, went by. They brought no visible changes, but a few slowly changed my mind as I moved toward death. I began to study more and to understand the thoughts of others as expressed in books. I read history and lost my individuality among the crowds who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the feeling of immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude also lost some of its appeal. I began once more to wish for sympathy—not that I was ever tempted to seek society, but I wished for one friend who would love me. You may say that I was gradually becoming fit to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure, so free from the influence of outward circumstances, that in the world I could only have been disappointed by the coarse things mixed into even its finest feelings. Believe me, I was then less suited to any connection with my fellow creatures than before. When I left them, they had tormented me as pain and sickness might: something outside the mind that irritated it, and that I wished to throw off. But now I would have wanted sympathy. I would have wished to join my soul to another’s, and would have prepared myself for abundant disappointment and suffering; for I was as tender as the sensitive plant, all nerve. I did not want sympathy and help in ambition or wisdom, but gentle and mutual affection: smiles to encourage me and kind words of comfort. I wanted one heart into which I could pour my complaints without restraint, so that, through the heavenly nature of that soil, blessed fruit might grow from such poor seed. Yet how could I find this? The love that gives friendship its soul is a gentle spirit rarely found except when two kind people are joined from childhood, or bound together by shared suffering and pursuits. It comes to some chosen people without being sought or expected; it falls like gentle dew on favored places, which, however barren before, become fertile under its kindly influence. But when desired, it flees; it mocks the prayers of those who seek it. It will give itself, but it will not be pursued.\n\nI knew all this and did not go looking for sympathy. Yet there, on my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof, with desert all around me, it came like winter sunlight, adorning the snowdrifts even as it helped melt them. Alas, the sun shone on blighted fruit. I did not revive beneath its light, for I was too completely ruined to feel its gentle power."}

{"request_id":"508205372fab8d270398e62c","rewritten_text":"She and the children might remain very comfortably.”

“Ah! papa—that is what you have never managed to accomplish, and I do not believe you ever will. Isabella cannot endure staying apart from her husband.”

It was too true to be disputed. Though unwelcome, Mr. Woodhouse could only utter a resigned sigh; and when Emma noticed how much the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband had lowered his spirits, she at once turned the conversation toward a subject more likely to cheer him.

“Harriet must spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I am sure she will enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, are we not, papa? I wonder which she will consider the handsomer, Henry or John?”

“Yes, I wonder which she will. Poor little dears, how delighted they will be to come. They are very fond of visiting Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they are, sir. I am sure I cannot think of anyone who is not.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John resembles his mama very much. Henry is the eldest; he was named for me, rather than for his father. John, the second, bears his father’s name. Some people are surprised, I believe, that the eldest was not, but Isabella wished him to be called Henry, which I thought very kind of her. And he is an exceedingly clever boy. They are all remarkably clever, and have so many charming ways. They come and stand beside my chair, saying, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a piece of string?’ and once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives were made only for grandpapas. I think their father is often too rough with them.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you are so exceptionally gentle yourself; but if you compared him with other papas, you would not call him rough. He wants his boys to be active and hardy; and when they behave badly, he can speak sharply to them now and then. But he is an affectionate father—Mr. John Knightley is certainly an affectionate father. The children are all fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and throws them up to the ceiling in a most alarming manner!”

“But they enjoy it, papa; there is nothing they like better. They take such pleasure in it that, unless their uncle made them take turns, the one who began would never yield to the other.”

“Well, I cannot understand it.”

“That is true of all of us, papa. Half the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other half.”"}

{"request_id":"f03c1d99d0260a3ca7f543c2","rewritten_text":"But that is of little importance.”

“I might as well ask,” she replied, “why, with such an obvious intention of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character. Was that not some excuse for your rudeness, if I _was_ rude? But I have other reasons for resentment. You know I do. If my own feelings had not already decided against you, if they had been indifferent, or even favourable, do you think anything could persuade me to accept the man who has been responsible for destroying, perhaps forever, the happiness of a dearly loved sister?”

As she spoke these words, Mr. Darcy changed colour; but the emotion was brief, and he listened without trying to interrupt her as she continued—

“I have every reason in the world to think badly of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you played _there_. You cannot deny that you were the chief, if not the only, cause of separating them from each other; of exposing one to the world’s censure for caprice and instability, the other to its ridicule for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in the most painful misery.”

She paused and saw, with considerable indignation, that he was listening in a manner proving himself entirely untouched by remorse. He even looked at her with a smile of affected disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did it?” she repeated.

He then replied with assumed calm, “I have no intention of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. Toward _him_ I have been kinder than toward myself.”

Elizabeth refused to appear to notice this courteous remark, but its meaning was not lost on her, nor was it likely to win her over.

“But this is not the only matter,” she continued, “on which my dislike is based. My opinion of you had been formed long before it occurred. Your character was revealed in the account I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. What have you to say about that? In what imaginary act of friendship can you defend yourself here? Or under what false account can you deceive others?”

“You take a keen interest in that gentleman’s affairs,” said Darcy, in a less composed tone, his colour deepening.

“Whoever knows what his misfortunes have been could fail to feel an interest in him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated contemptuously. “Yes, his misfortunes have indeed been great.”

“And caused by you,” Elizabeth cried energetically. “You have reduced him to his present condition of poverty—comparative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"e6f533ba37f6eb3fdbc40099","rewritten_text":"I then went from one shop to another, buying whatever was needed to alter his appearance. That business finished, I turned, for my own purposes, toward Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was seated at his desk, but when he saw me enter, he rose at once and stood in front of the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be cautious.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. For, as I came along, I had carefully considered what I meant to say.

“Don’t implicate yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t implicate anybody else. You understand—anybody. Tell me nothing: I don’t wish to know anything; I am not inquisitive.”

Of course, I perceived that he knew the man had arrived.

“I only wish, Mr. Jaggers,” said I, “to satisfy myself that what I have been told is true. I have no expectation that it is false, but I may at least confirm it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, holding his head to one side, and looking not at me but at the floor, as though listening there. “Told would appear to suggest verbal communication. You cannot have verbal communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say, informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person called Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor who has been unknown to me for so long.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And no one else?” I asked.

“And no one else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you responsible for my errors and mistaken conclusions; but I had always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” returned Mr. Jaggers, turning his cool eyes on me and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that in the least.”

“And yet it seemed so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart cast down.

“Not the smallest particle of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his skirts. “Trust nothing to appearances; trust everything to evidence. There is no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said with a sigh, after remaining silent for a short while. “I have confirmed my information, and that is the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having at last revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout my communications with you, I have kept to the exact line of fact. There has never been the slightest departure from that exact line. You are fully aware of this?”

“Quite, sir.”

“I communicated to Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—the warning that he must never expect me to depart from the exact line of fact.”"}

{"request_id":"41af13b04e09a46182e0bf2d","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. We could all come on donkeys, Jane, Miss Bates, and I—and my caro sposo walking beside us. I really must speak to him about buying one. In country life I imagine it is almost a necessity; for, however many resources a woman may possess, she cannot always be confined at home;—and long walks, you know—in summer there is dust, and in winter mud.”

“You will find neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and at present it is perfectly dry. Come on a donkey, though, if you like. You may borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I should wish everything to suit you as well as possible.”

“That I am certain you would. Indeed, I do you justice, my good friend. Beneath that particular dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are a complete humourist.—Yes, believe me, Knightley, I am fully aware of your attentions to me throughout this whole plan. You have discovered exactly what will please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another motive for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the party; and he knew that having any of them sit outside to eat would inevitably make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not, under the plausible excuse of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell, be lured away to his misery.

He had been invited sincerely. No hidden terrors were waiting to reproach him for his easy trust. He did agree. He had not visited Donwell for two years. “Some very fine morning, he, Emma, and Harriet might go very comfortably; and he could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked around the gardens. He did not imagine they could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He should be extremely pleased to see the old house again, and would be very happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton, and any other neighbours.—He could see no objection whatever to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there some very fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—far cleverer than dining out.—He was not fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was fortunate in receiving everyone’s immediate agreement. The invitation was welcomed so warmly everywhere that it seemed, like Mrs. Elton, they all regarded the plan as a special compliment to themselves.—Emma and Harriet declared that they expected great pleasure from it; and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to bring Frank over to join them if possible, a demonstration of approval and gratitude that might have been spared.—Mr. Knightley was therefore obliged to say that he should be glad to see him; and Mr. Weston undertook to write at once and use every argument to persuade him to come."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0c3a9ff0546c6da9942b646c","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was disproportionately broad, giving his whole figure a remarkably absurd roundness. His feet, naturally, could not be seen at all, though a horny substance of suspicious appearance occasionally protruded through a tear in the bottom of the car—or, more accurately, the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair was very gray and gathered into a queue at the back. His nose was extraordinarily long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes large, bright, and sharp; his chin and cheeks, though creased with age, broad, puffy, and doubled. Yet not the slightest trace of ears, of any sort or shape, could be found anywhere on his head. This strange little gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin surtout, with matching tight breeches fastened at the knees by silver buckles. His vest was made of some vivid yellow fabric; a white taffeta cap sat jauntily to one side of his head; and, completing his outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his throat and descended delicately over his chest in a fantastically oversized bow.\n\nAfter descending, as I have said, to within about one hundred feet of the earth’s surface, the little old gentleman was suddenly overcome by fear and seemed unwilling to come any closer to solid ground. He therefore threw out some sand from a canvas bag, which he lifted with great difficulty, and stopped instantly. He then hurriedly and nervously drew a large morocco pocketbook from a side pocket of his surtout. He weighed it suspiciously in his hand, then stared at it with extreme surprise, plainly astonished by its heaviness. At last he opened it and pulled out a huge letter, sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape, which he dropped directly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still deeply unsettled and apparently having no further business to keep him in Rotterdam, now began making urgent preparations to leave. Since he had to release ballast in order to rise again, the six bags he tossed out one after another, without bothering to empty them, all fell most unfortunately onto the burgomaster’s back and rolled him over and over no fewer than twenty-one times, before the eyes of every man in Rotterdam. It must not be imagined, however, that the great Underduk allowed this insolence from the little old man to go unpunished."}

content.text: {"request_id":"bbbadb3bc19b98e94616120a","rewritten_text":"Colonel Grangerford was a gentleman, you see. He was a gentleman in every way, and so was his family. He was well born, as people say, and that counts for as much in a man as it does in a horse, according to Widow Douglas—and no one ever denied that she belonged to the highest aristocracy in our town. Pap always said it, too, though he had no more quality than a mudcat. Colonel Grangerford was very tall and very thin, with a dark, pale complexion and not a trace of red anywhere. Every morning he shaved his entire thin face clean, and he had the thinnest lips, the narrowest nostrils, a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and the blackest eyes, set so deeply that they seemed to look out at you from caverns, you might say. His forehead was high, and his hair was black, straight, and shoulder-length. His hands were long and thin, and every day of his life he put on a clean shirt and a complete linen suit, from head to foot, so white it hurt your eyes to look at it. On Sundays he wore a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane with a silver head. There was nothing frivolous about him, not the slightest bit, and he was never loud. He was as kind as he could be—you could feel it, you know, and that gave you confidence. Sometimes he smiled, and it was good to see; but when he straightened himself like a liberty pole and lightning began flickering beneath his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and find out what was wrong afterward. He never had to tell anyone to mind their manners—everyone behaved properly when he was there. Everyone loved having him around, too; he was almost always sunshine—I mean, he made it feel like good weather. When he turned into a cloudbank, it grew terribly dark for half a minute, and that was enough; nothing would go wrong again for a week.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs and wished them good morning, and did not sit again until they had sat down. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard, where the decanter stood, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held it while they mixed their own, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” They bowed the slightest bit and said thank you, and all three drank. Then Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and the little bit of whisky or apple brandy at the bottom of their tumblers, gave it to me and Buck, and we drank to the old people too."}

{"request_id":"2ed974fe08f9fb3c2b15fb25","rewritten_text":"He shuddered and returned, shutting the window after him.

When he came to the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not so much as look at the murdered man. He felt that the only way to deal with the whole affair was not to recognize what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait, the source of all his misery, had passed out of his life. That was sufficient.

Then he recalled the lamp. It was a rather unusual Moorish piece, fashioned from dull silver, inlaid with arabesques of burnished steel, and set with rough turquoises. His servant might notice its absence, and questions might follow. He paused briefly, then went back and lifted it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the dead body. How motionless it was! How terribly white the long hands appeared! It resembled a hideous wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he stole quietly down the stairs. The woodwork creaked and seemed to cry out in pain. Several times he stopped and listened. No: all was silent. It was only the noise of his own steps.

On reaching the library, he noticed the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be concealed somewhere. He opened a secret cupboard in the wainscoting, where he kept his own strange disguises, and placed them inside. He could burn them easily later. Then he took out his watch. It was twenty minutes before two.

He sat down and began to reflect. Every year—almost every month—men were hanged in England for what he had done. There had been a murderous madness in the air. Some red star had drawn too near the earth.... And yet, what proof existed against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed.... Paris! Yes. Basil had gone to Paris, on the midnight train, as he had planned. With his peculiar, secretive habits, it would be months before suspicion arose. Months! Everything could be destroyed well before then.

A sudden idea came to him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went into the hall. There he stopped, hearing the policeman’s slow, heavy footsteps on the pavement outside and seeing the bull’s-eye flash reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

After a few moments, he lifted the latch and slipped out, closing the door very softly behind him. Then he began to ring the bell."}

{"request_id":"70904253249905a3d65961ad","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, one might have thought that Nemesis had taken Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed turned to stone, and his face was as pale and sorrowful as marble. He had lived the refined, luxurious life of a young man born to wealth, free from ugly worries and full of carefree charm. Now, for the first time, he understood the terrible mystery of Destiny and the dreadful meaning of Doom.

How insane and monstrous it all seemed! Could it be that his hand carried, in letters he could not read but another person could interpret, some terrible secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime? Was there truly no escape? Were people no more than chess pieces moved by an unseen power, or clay vessels shaped by a potter for honour or disgrace? His reason rebelled against the idea, yet he felt that some tragedy hung over him and that he had suddenly been forced to carry an unbearable burden. Actors were fortunate. They could choose whether to appear in tragedy or comedy, whether to suffer or celebrate, laugh or cry. Real life was different. Most men and women had to play roles for which they were not suited. Our Guildensterns played Hamlet for us, while our Hamlets had to joke like Prince Hal. The world was a stage, but the play was badly cast.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers entered the room. When he saw Lord Arthur, he started, and his coarse, heavy face turned a greenish yellow. Their eyes met, and for a moment neither man spoke.

‘The Duchess left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to bring it to her,’ Mr. Podgers said at last. ‘Ah, I see it on the sofa! Good evening.’

‘Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me a direct answer to a question I am about to ask you.’

‘Another time, Lord Arthur. The Duchess is anxious, and I am afraid I must go.’

‘You will not go. The Duchess is in no hurry.’

‘Ladies should not be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,’ said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. ‘The fair sex can be impatient.’

Lord Arthur’s finely shaped lips curled with irritated disdain. At that moment, the poor Duchess seemed almost unimportant to him. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and held out his hand.

‘Tell me what you saw there,’ he said. ‘Tell me the truth. I must know. I am not a child.’"}
