{"request_id":"852869b6db2f235057acd8af","rewritten_text":"I was sorry to hear Jim say that; it made him seem so diminished. My conscience began tormenting me more fiercely than ever, until at last I said to it, “Leave me alone—it isn’t too late yet. I’ll paddle ashore at first light and tell.” At once I felt easy, happy, and light as a feather. All my troubles were gone. I began watching carefully for a light and half singing to myself. Before long, one appeared. Jim called out:

“We’re safe, Huck, we’re safe! Jump up and click your heels! That’s old Cairo at last, I just know it!”

I said:

“I’ll take the canoe and go see, Jim. It might not be, you know.”

He jumped up, prepared the canoe, put his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. As I pushed off, he said:

“Pretty soon I’ll be shouting for joy, and I’ll say it’s all because of Huck. I’m a free man, and I could never have been free if it hadn’t been for Huck. Huck did it. Jim will never forget you, Huck; you’re the best friend Jim’s ever had, and you’re the only friend old Jim has now.”

I paddled away, sweating to betray him; but when he said that, it seemed to drain all the strength from me. I went on slowly then, and I wasn’t entirely sure whether I was glad I had started or not. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called:

“There you go, the old true Huck—the only white gentleman who ever kept his promise to old Jim.”

I felt sick. But I told myself, I have to do it—I can’t get out of it. Just then a skiff came along with two men carrying guns, and they stopped, so I stopped too. One of them said:

“What’s that over there?”

“A piece of a raft,” I said.

“Do you belong on it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men on it?”

“Only one, sir.”

“Well, five escaped slaves ran off tonight up there, above the head of the bend. Is your man white or black?”

I didn’t answer promptly. I tried, but the words wouldn’t come. For a second or two I tried to gather my courage and say it, but I wasn’t man enough—I didn’t have the nerve of a rabbit. I saw I was weakening, so I gave up trying and said:

“He’s white.”

“I suppose we’ll go see for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I said, “because it’s my father who’s there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft ashore where the light is.”"}

{"request_id":"1cffd7a3cc118ddf60add4c1","rewritten_text":"But if it had not been for me, he never would have escaped. Morgan le Fay hated him with all her heart, and she never would have relented toward him. Yet his offense arose more from carelessness than deliberate wickedness. He had said she had red hair. Well, she did; but that was no proper way to describe it. When red-haired people belong to a certain social class, their hair is auburn.

Consider this: among these forty-seven captives were five whose names, offenses, and dates of imprisonment were no longer known! One woman and four men—all bent, wrinkled, and mentally extinguished patriarchs. They themselves had forgotten these details long ago; at most, they possessed vague theories about them, nothing definite, and nothing they told twice in the same way. The succession of priests whose duty had been to pray daily with the captives, remind them that God had placed them there for some wise purpose, and teach them that patience, humility, and submission to oppression were what He wished to see in people of an inferior rank, had traditions about these poor human ruins, but nothing more. Those traditions went only a little way, for they concerned merely the length of the imprisonment, not the names of the offenses. Even with the help of tradition, the only fact that could be established was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years; how much longer they had endured this deprivation could not be guessed. The king and queen knew nothing about these poor creatures except that they were heirlooms, assets inherited with the throne from the previous owners. None of their history had been passed on with them, and so their inheriting masters had considered them worthless and taken no interest in them. I said to the queen:

“Then why on earth didn’t you set them free?”

The question baffled her. She did not know why she had not; the thought had never occurred to her. Thus, without realizing it, she was already laying the foundation for the future history of prisoners in the Castle d’If. It seemed clear to me now that, given her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were simply property—nothing more and nothing less. When we inherit property, it does not occur to us to throw it away, even when we place no value on it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open air and the harsh afternoon sunlight—first blindfolding them, out of mercy for eyes so long untroubled by light—they were a sight to behold. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pathetic horrors, every one of them; the most authentic children imaginable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"65fd6b4edef5ce096b39bcd6","rewritten_text":"He always claimed that Peter had written those things for him, but that was a lie: he had gotten every one of them from that young fool we had canoed up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. It gave the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls. It gave the tanyard, which was doing good business, along with some other houses and land worth about seven thousand dollars, and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William. It also said where the six thousand dollars in cash was hidden in the cellar. So the two frauds said they would go get it and make everything proper and honest, and they told me to bring a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag, they poured the money onto the floor. It was a beautiful sight, all those yellow coins. The king’s eyes shone. He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said:

“Oh, this is something, isn’t it? Oh, yes, I reckon it is! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn’t it?”

The duke agreed that it did. They handled the coins, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle onto the floor. Then the king said:

“There’s no use talking; being brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs who have been left behind—that’s the life for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes from trusting Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there isn’t any better way.”

Most people would have been satisfied with the pile and accepted it without question. But no, they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said:

“Damn him, I wonder what he did with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They worried over it for a while and searched everywhere for the missing money. Then the duke said:

“Well, he was a very sick man, and likely he made a mistake—I reckon that’s how it happened. The best thing is to let it go and say nothing about it. We can afford it.”

“Oh, nonsense, yes, we can afford it. I don’t care about that—it’s the counting I’m thinking about. We want to be completely honest and open here, you know. We want to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody—then there won’t be anything suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"331ae1582da1903d12136d1a","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know about me unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that doesn’t matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he told the truth, mostly. There were things he stretched, but mostly he told the truth. That’s nothing. I never knew anybody who didn’t lie once in a while, unless it was Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all mentioned in that book, which is mostly true, with some stretchers, as I said before.

Now this is how the book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars each—all gold. It was a tremendous amount of money when it was piled up. Well, Judge Thatcher took it and put it out at interest, and it brought us a dollar a day apiece all year round—more than a person could figure out what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me as her son and said she would sivilize me; but living in the house all the time was hard, seeing how dreary regular and proper the widow was in everything she did; and when I couldn’t bear it any longer, I took off. I put on my old rags and went back to my sugar-hogshead, and was free and content. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he meant to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I went back to the widow and acted respectable. So I returned.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me plenty of other names too, but she didn’t mean any harm by it. She put me into those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and sweat and feel squeezed up. Well, then the old business started over. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to come right away. When you reached the table, you couldn’t begin eating at once; you had to wait while the widow bowed her head and grumbled a little over the victuals, though there wasn’t really anything wrong with them—that is, nothing except that everything had been cooked separately. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different; the things mix together, the juice sort of trades places, and everything tastes better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was eager to learn all about him; but after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead for a very long time. So then I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t take any interest in dead people."}

{"request_id":"ced9b91b5e48629802114d09","rewritten_text":"“I hope I shall soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, quite willing to believe that this hope was meant as a special compliment to her, smiled very graciously.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I suppose,” he continued, “and know that he is my son, although he does not have my name.”

“Oh, yes, and I shall be very happy to meet him. I am sure Mr. Elton will call on him without delay, and we shall both be delighted to see him at the Vicarage.”

“You are very kind. Frank will be extremely pleased, I am sure. He is expected in town next week, if not sooner. We learned it from a letter today. I came across the letters on my way this morning, and, seeing my son’s handwriting, assumed I might open it—although it was addressed not to me, but to Mrs. Weston. She is his main correspondent, I assure you. I hardly ever receive a letter.”

“And you actually opened a letter addressed to her! Oh, Mr. Weston”—she laughed in an affected way—“I must object to that. What a dangerous example! I beg you not to let your neighbours copy you. Upon my word, if this is what I must expect, we married women will have to defend ourselves! Oh, Mr. Weston, I would never have believed it of you!”

“Yes, we men are a sorry lot. You must look after yourself, Mrs. Elton. This letter tells us—it is a short one, written in haste, only to give us notice—that they are all coming to town at once because of Mrs. Churchill. She has been unwell all winter and thinks Enscombe too cold for her, so they are all moving south without delay.”

“Indeed! From Yorkshire, I believe. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes. They are about one hundred and ninety miles from London, which is a considerable journey.”

“Yes, certainly, very considerable. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance to people with a large fortune, Mr. Weston? You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes travels about. You will hardly believe me, but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back with four horses.”

“The difficulty with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand it, has not been able to leave the sofa for a whole week. In Frank’s last letter, he said she complained of being too weak to reach her conservatory without using both his arm and his uncle’s!”"}

{"request_id":"b95f248667b7528c9942e81c","rewritten_text":"She suddenly felt a strong urge to go to the outer door; she wanted to see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of another reason? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight. She rose from her seat and decided to go. One half of her should not always be wiser than the other, or forever suspecting the other of being worse than it was. She would see if it rained. But in that moment Captain Wentworth entered, with a group of gentlemen and ladies who were clearly his acquaintances and whom he must have joined just below Milsom Street. The sight of her seemed to strike and confuse him more than she had ever seen before; he turned quite red. For the first time since they had renewed their acquaintance, she felt that she was the more composed of the two. She had had a few moments to prepare herself. The first overwhelming, blinding effects of surprise had already passed. Yet she still felt enough: agitation, pain, pleasure, something between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, then turned away. His manner showed embarrassment. She could not have called it cold or friendly, or described it with any certainty except as embarrassed.

After a short while, however, he came toward her and spoke again. They exchanged a few questions about ordinary matters, though neither was probably much wiser for the answers, and Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than before. Because they had spent so much time together, they had learned to speak with apparent calm and indifference; but he could not manage it now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. He was conscious of something. He looked very well, not like someone who had suffered in health or spirits, and he spoke of Uppercross, the Musgroves, and even Louisa. As he mentioned her, he briefly wore his old, teasingly meaningful expression. Yet he was still Captain Wentworth: uncomfortable, uneasy, and unable to pretend otherwise.

It did not surprise Anne, but it saddened her, to see that Elizabeth would not acknowledge him. She saw that he noticed Elizabeth, and that Elizabeth noticed him; each clearly recognized the other. Anne was sure he was ready and expecting to be acknowledged as an acquaintance, and it pained her to watch her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, which Miss Elliot had been waiting for with growing impatience, now arrived. The servant came in to announce it."}

{"request_id":"fd6d2546462ee1b4fc055078","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I will begin my story: it is my final task, and I hope I have enough strength to complete it. I record no crimes; my faults can easily be forgiven, for they came not from evil intentions but from poor judgment. I believe few people would claim that, through different actions and greater wisdom, they could have escaped the misfortunes of which I am the victim. My fate was controlled by necessity, a terrible necessity. It required hands stronger than mine—stronger, I believe, than any human power—to break the thick, unyielding chain that bound me, once filled with nothing but joy and a warm love of goodness, to misery that could end only in death, and now is about to end there. But I am forgetting myself; my story has not yet been told. I will pause for a few moments, wipe my clouded eyes, and try to replace the present dull but heavy unhappiness with the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He had lost his own father when he was young and was raised by a weak mother, who gave him all the indulgence she believed proper for a wealthy nobleman. He was sent to Eton and later to college, and from childhood was allowed the free use of large sums of money. Thus, from his earliest years, he enjoyed the independence that a boy with such advantages always gains at a public school.

Under these influences, his passions found rich soil in which to take root and grow, either as flowers or weeds, according to their nature. Because he had always been allowed to act for himself, his character developed early and strongly, showing a varied surface where a sharp-eyed observer might see the seeds of both virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance led him to spend enormous sums on passing whims, which, because of their apparent force, he dignified with the name of passions. Yet this extravagance often appeared as boundless generosity. While he earnestly concerned himself with the needs of others, his own desires were satisfied completely. He gave his money, but none of his own wishes were sacrificed by his gifts; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was glad to have awakened in any way.

I do not say that, if his desires had been set against those of others, he would have shown excessive selfishness, but he was never put to that test. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wanted to please him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"eabd257fa894d3e14cea3bfe","rewritten_text":"He had, indeed, been entirely unaware of his own influence. He had followed her into the shrubbery without any thought of attempting it. He had come, anxious to see how she endured Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish purpose, no purpose at all beyond trying, if she gave him an opportunity, to comfort or advise her.—What followed had been the work of the moment, the immediate consequence of what he heard upon his feelings. The delightful certainty of her complete indifference to Frank Churchill, of her heart being wholly free from him, had awakened the hope that, in time, he might win her affection for himself;—but it had not been an immediate hope—only, in that instant when eagerness overcame judgment, a wish to be told that she did not reject his effort to attach her.—The higher hopes that gradually unfolded were all the more enchanting.—The affection he had asked permission to create, if he could, was already his!—In less than half an hour, he had gone from a state of profound distress to something so nearly perfect happiness that it could be called by no other name.\n\n_Her_ change had been equal.—That single half-hour had bestowed on each the same precious certainty of being loved, and had removed from each the same measure of ignorance, jealousy, or mistrust.—On his side, there had been a jealousy of long standing, as old as Frank Churchill’s arrival, or even the expectation of it.—He had loved Emma, and been jealous of Frank Churchill, from nearly the same time, one feeling having perhaps revealed the other to him. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that had driven him from the country.—The party at Box Hill had determined him to leave. He would spare himself the sight of such permitted and encouraged attentions again.—He had gone away to learn indifference.—But he had chosen the wrong place. There was too much domestic happiness in his brother’s home; woman appeared in it in too amiable a shape; Isabella was too much like Emma—differing only in those conspicuous deficiencies which always made the other shine more brilliantly before him—for much to have been accomplished, even if his stay had been longer.—Still, he had remained resolutely, day after day—until the morning post brought the account of Jane Fairfax.—Then, with the gladness that must be felt, and which he did not hesitate to feel, since he had never thought Frank Churchill in any way worthy of Emma, there was so much tender concern, so much urgent anxiety for her, that he could remain no longer. He had ridden home through the rain, and had walked up immediately after dinner, to see how this sweetest and best of creatures, faultless despite all her faults, bore the discovery."}

{"request_id":"818984895c8f223bf3029202","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ and therefore assumed that ‘anybody’ meant—well, anybody; that is, everybody.”

“It doth—anybody of noble birth; and better still if he be royal.”

“That, it seemeth to me, may well be so,” said the abbot, who perceived a chance to smooth matters and prevent disaster, “for it were unlikely that so marvelous a gift as this should be granted for revealing the affairs of beings less exalted than those born near the heights of greatness. Our King Arthur—”

“Would you hear of him?” interrupted the enchanter.

“Most gladly, yea, and with gratitude.”

Everyone was instantly filled with awe and interest again, the incorrigible fools. They watched the enchantments with rapt attention, then looked at me with a “There now, what have you to say to that?” expression when the announcement was made:

“The king is weary from the chase, and hath lain in his palace these two hours, sleeping without dreams.”

“God’s blessing upon him!” said the abbot, crossing himself; “may that sleep refresh both body and soul.”

“And so it might, were he asleep,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping; the king is riding.”

There was trouble once more—a clash of authority. No one knew which of us to trust; I still retained some reputation. The magician’s contempt was aroused, and he said:

“Lo, I have seen many wondrous soothsayers, prophets, and magicians in my lifetime, but never one before who could sit idle and perceive the heart of things without a single incantation to aid him.”

“You have dwelt in the woods, and lost much thereby. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood know—but only when the occasion is important.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I reckon I know how to hold my own. That thrust made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and received this answer:

“They are all asleep, having been overcome by weariness, even as the king.”

I said:

“That is merely another falsehood. Half of them are occupied with their amusements; the queen and the rest are not sleeping, but riding. Now perhaps you can exert yourself a little and tell us where the king and queen, and all those riding with them at this moment, are going?”

“They sleep now, as I said; but tomorrow they will ride, for they are journeying toward the sea.”

“And where will they be at vespers the day after tomorrow?”

“Far north of Camelot, with half their journey completed.”

“That is another lie, by a distance of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"5f9ffe1c7f51f322c5108595","rewritten_text":"And Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, and those four knights encountered fiercely, breaking their spears down to their hands. Then Sir Pertolope came from the castle, and Sir Lionel encountered him; there Sir Pertolope, the Green Knight, struck down Sir Lionel, brother to Sir Launcelot. All this was observed by noble heralds, who recorded who bore himself best and their names. Then Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth, but from that blow Sir Bleobaris fell to the ground. When Sir Galihodin saw this, he commanded Sir Gareth to keep him, and Sir Gareth smote him down. Then Sir Galihud took a spear to avenge his brother, and Sir Gareth served him in the same manner, as he did Sir Dinadan and his brother La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage; all these he cast down with one spear. When King Aswisance of Ireland saw Sir Gareth fare so well, he wondered who he could be, for at one time he appeared green, and when he came again he seemed blue. Thus, at every course he rode to and fro, he changed color, so that no king or knight could readily recognize him. Then Sir Agwisance, King of Ireland, encountered Sir Gareth, and Sir Gareth struck him from his horse, saddle and all. After that came King Carados of Scotland, and Sir Gareth brought down both horse and man. In the same fashion he served King Uriens of the land of Gore. Then Sir Bagdemagus entered, and Sir Gareth smote him down, horse and man, to the earth. But Bagdemagus's son Meliganus broke a spear upon Sir Gareth with great strength and knightly skill. Then Sir Galahault, the noble prince, cried aloud, “Knight of the many colors, well hast thou jousted; now prepare thyself, that I may joust with thee.” Sir Gareth heard him, took a great spear, and they encountered together. The prince broke his spear, but Sir Gareth struck him on the left side of his helm, making him reel this way and that; he would have fallen had not his men caught him. “Truly,” said King Arthur, “that knight of the many colors is a good knight.” Therefore the king called Sir Launcelot to him and asked him to encounter that knight. “Sir,” said Launcelot, “I can just as willingly refrain from him at this time, for he has had labor enough today. When a good knight performs so well on a day, it is not the part of a good knight to deprive him of his honor, especially when he sees that a knight has endured such great toil. Perhaps,” said Sir Launcelot, “his cause is here today, and perhaps he is best loved by this lady of all who are here, for I see clearly that he strains and exerts himself to accomplish great deeds. Therefore, as for me, this day he shall have the honor; though it were in my power to take it from him, I would not.”"}

{"request_id":"be965ba5962a59faf3ae1e1e","rewritten_text":"He rose and left the room with my nurse, and a moment later my father entered.

Nothing at that moment could have pleased me more than my father’s arrival. I reached out my hand to him and cried,

“Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father reassured me that they were well and tried, by speaking of matters so dear to my heart, to lift my spirits. But he soon realized that a prison cannot be a cheerful place. “What a place this is that you inhabit, my son!” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and miserable condition of the room. “You travelled in search of happiness, but some fatality seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—”

The name of my unfortunate, murdered friend caused an agitation too great for my weakened state; I began to weep.

“Alas, yes, my father,” I replied. “Some terrible destiny hangs over me, and I must live to fulfil it; otherwise, surely, I would have died upon Henry’s coffin.”

We were not permitted to speak for long, since the precarious state of my health made every precaution necessary to preserve my tranquillity. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted that I must not exhaust my strength through excessive exertion. Yet my father’s presence was like that of my good angel, and I gradually regained my health.

As my illness left me, I became consumed by a dark and hopeless melancholy that nothing could dispel. Clerval’s image was always before me, ghastly and murdered. More than once, the agitation caused by these thoughts made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas, why had they preserved such a miserable and detested life? Surely it was so that I might fulfil my destiny, which was now nearing its end. Soon—oh, very soon—death would silence these throbbing pains and free me from the immense weight of anguish that was bearing me to the grave; and, in carrying out the sentence of justice, I too would sink into rest. At that time death still seemed far away, though the desire for it was always in my thoughts; and I often sat for hours without moving or speaking, longing for some great upheaval that might bury both me and my destroyer beneath its ruins.

The assizes drew near. I had already spent three months in prison, and although I remained weak and constantly in danger of relapse, I was forced to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court was held. Mr. Kirwin took responsibility for every detail of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence."}

{"request_id":"3cab4950902297a6099c1aef","rewritten_text":"He could not help it. And it drove him mad to think that Becky Thatcher had not once noticed that he was even alive. But she had noticed, after all; she knew she was winning their struggle, and she was glad to see him suffer as she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted that he had things to take care of, things that had to be done, and that time was running short. But it was no use—the girl kept talking. Tom thought, “Oh, hang her, am I ever going to get rid of her?” At last he really had to attend to those things, and she innocently said she would be “around” when school ended. He hurried away, hating her for saying it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in the whole town except that Saint Louis show-off who thinks he dresses so well and is some kind of aristocrat! Oh, all right, I beat you the first day you ever came to this town, mister, and I’ll beat you again! Just wait until I catch you alone! I’ll just—”

He acted out a beating of an imaginary boy, punching the air, kicking, and gouging. “Oh, you do, do you? You’re yelling ‘enough,’ are you? Well, let that teach you!” And he finished the imaginary beating to his satisfaction.

Tom ran home at noon. His conscience could not stand any more of Amy’s grateful happiness, and his jealousy could endure no more of the other girl’s suffering. Becky went back to looking at pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes passed and Tom did not come to suffer, her triumph began to fade and she lost interest. She became serious and distracted, then sad. Two or three times she listened hopefully when she heard footsteps, but each time she was disappointed; Tom did not come. At last she became completely miserable and wished she had not taken things so far. Poor Alfred saw that he was losing her, though he did not know why, and kept saying, “Oh, here’s a funny one! Look at this!” Finally she lost patience and said, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care about them!” Then she burst into tears, stood up, and walked away.

Alfred followed close behind and was about to comfort her, but she said:

“Go away and leave me alone, can’t you? I hate you!”

The boy stopped, wondering what he could have done. She had said she would look at pictures with him throughout the lunch break. She walked on, crying. Alfred then went thoughtfully into the empty schoolhouse. He felt humiliated and angry. It was easy for him to understand the truth: the girl had merely used him to take out her spite on Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"92f036b3dbf1bda4c7f660d3","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had come straight from the Speaker’s Levée, wearing their stars and ribbons. All the fashionable women wore their finest dresses, and at the far end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a large, Tartar-looking woman with tiny black eyes and magnificent emeralds. She spoke bad French at the top of her voice and laughed wildly at everything said to her. It was certainly a remarkable mixture of people. Splendid peeresses chatted pleasantly with fierce Radicals, popular preachers rubbed shoulders with famous sceptics, and a whole group of bishops followed a stout opera singer from room to room. Several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, stood on the staircase, and it was said that the supper room had, for a while, been packed with geniuses. In fact, it was one of Lady Windermere’s finest evenings, and the Princess stayed until nearly half past eleven.

As soon as she had left, Lady Windermere returned to the picture gallery, where a famous political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an offended Hungarian virtuoso, and began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. She looked wonderfully beautiful, with her noble ivory throat, her large blue eyes like forget-me-nots, and her thick coils of golden hair. They were truly gold—not the pale straw colour that now wrongly claims that name, but gold like sunlight woven into cloth or hidden in unusual amber. They gave her face something of a saint’s appearance, mixed with no small amount of a sinner’s charm. She was a fascinating psychological study. Early in life, she had discovered the important truth that nothing resembles innocence so closely as an indiscretion. Through a series of reckless adventures, half of them completely harmless, she had gained all the freedoms that came with being an individual. She had changed husbands more than once; indeed, Debrett listed three marriages. But since she had never changed her lover, society had long since stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, had no children, and possessed that intense love of pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she looked eagerly around the room and said in her clear contralto voice, ‘Where is my cheiromantist?’

‘Your what, Gladys?’ exclaimed the Duchess, starting despite herself.

‘My cheiromantist, Duchess. I can’t live without him at present.’

‘Dear Gladys! You are always so original,’ murmured the Duchess, trying to remember what a cheiromantist actually was and hoping it was not the same thing as a chiropodist.

‘He comes to read my hand twice a week, regularly,’ Lady Windermere continued, ‘and he is most interesting about it.’"}

{"request_id":"869dfe5edb3293ddccae92de","rewritten_text":"“And think, ma’am,” said Oliver, as tears rose to his eyes in spite of every effort to restrain them. “Oh! think how young and good she is, and what happiness and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I am sure—certain—quite certain—that, for your sake, who are so good yourself; and for her own; and for the sake of all whom she makes happy; she will not die. Heaven will never allow her to die so young.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, placing her hand upon Oliver’s head. “You reason like a child, poor boy. Yet you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old, and have witnessed enough illness and death to understand the anguish of being parted from those we love. I have seen enough, too, to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them; but this ought to comfort us in our grief, for Heaven is just; and such events teach us, most forcefully, that there is a brighter world than this; and that the journey there is brief. God’s will be done! I love her; and He knows how deeply!”

Oliver was astonished to see that, while Mrs. Maylie spoke these words, she checked her sorrow as if by a single effort; and, straightening herself as she continued, grew calm and resolute. He was even more surprised to discover that this strength endured; and that, throughout all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained prepared and composed: carrying out every duty that had fallen to her, steadily, and, to all outward appearances, even cheerfully. But he was young, and did not understand what powerful minds can accomplish in difficult circumstances. How could he, when those who possess them so rarely understand themselves?

An anxious night followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie’s fears had been only too fully confirmed. Rose was in the first stage of a severe and dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not surrender to fruitless sorrow,” said Mrs. Maylie, placing a finger to her lips as she looked steadily into his face; “this letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne with all possible speed. It must be taken to the market-town: no more than four miles away by the footpath across the fields: and from there sent by a mounted express directly to Chertsey. The people at the inn will undertake this: and I know I can rely on you to see it done.”

Oliver could not answer, but his anxious expression showed that he wished to leave at once."}

{"request_id":"b02eb2b4dac6bf0f21308f43","rewritten_text":"To look at a star in brief glances—to view it obliquely, by turning toward it the outer portions of the _retina_ (which are more sensitive to faint impressions of light than the inner portions)—is to see the star distinctly, and to appreciate its brilliance most fully—a brilliance that fades in exact proportion as we turn our vision _directly_ upon it. More rays actually reach the eye in the latter case, but in the former there is a finer capacity for understanding. Excessive depth confuses and weakens thought; and it is possible to make even Venus herself disappear from the sky through scrutiny that is too prolonged, too concentrated, or too direct.

“As for these murders, let us investigate them ourselves before forming an opinion about them. An inquiry will provide us with amusement,” [I thought this an odd word to use in such a context, but said nothing] “and, besides, Le Bon once did me a service for which I am not ungrateful. We will go and inspect the premises with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and will have no difficulty obtaining the necessary permission.”

The permission was obtained, and we went at once to the Rue Morgue. It is one of those wretched streets lying between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We reached it late in the afternoon, since this district was far from the one where we lived. The house was easy to find; many people were still standing across the street, staring up at its closed shutters with idle curiosity. It was an ordinary Parisian house, with a gateway and, beside it, a glazed watch-box whose window had a sliding panel, marking it as a _loge de concierge._ Before entering, we walked up the street, turned into an alley, and then turned again to pass behind the building—Dupin examining the entire neighborhood, as well as the house, with an attention whose purpose I could not possibly see.

We retraced our steps, returned to the front of the house, rang, and, after showing our credentials, were admitted by the officers in charge. We went upstairs into the room where the body of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been found, and where both victims still lay. As usual, the room had been left in its disordered state. I saw nothing beyond what had been reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin examined everything, including the bodies of the victims. We then entered the other rooms and went into the yard, accompanied throughout by a _gendarme_."}

{"request_id":"993aacfbf155c5f2da37988f","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted that she was somewhat surprised by the match, but she spoke less of her astonishment than of her sincere wish for their happiness; nor could Elizabeth persuade her to think it unlikely. Kitty and Lydia were far from envying Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman; the event affected them in no other way than as news to spread throughout Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant at being able to return to Mrs. Bennet the consolation of having a daughter well married. She called at Longbourn rather more often than usual to say how happy she was, though Mrs. Bennet’s sour expressions and unkind remarks might have been enough to drive happiness away.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a reserve that kept them both silent on the subject, and Elizabeth felt convinced that genuine confidence could never exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn with greater affection toward her sister, whose integrity and delicacy she was certain could never lose her esteem, and for whose happiness she became more anxious each day, as Bingley had now been gone a week and there was still no news of his return.

Jane had sent Caroline an early reply to her letter and was counting the days until she might reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father and written with all the solemn gratitude that a year’s residence with the family might have inspired. Having satisfied his conscience on that point, he went on to inform them, with many expressions of delight, of his happiness at having gained the affection of their amiable neighbour, Miss Lucas. He then explained that it was solely for the pleasure of enjoying her company that he had been so willing to accept their kind invitation to return to Longbourn, where he hoped to come on the Monday in a fortnight. Lady Catherine, he added, approved his marriage so warmly that she wished it to take place as soon as possible; and he trusted this would prove an irresistible argument with his amiable Charlotte for choosing an early date that would make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer a source of pleasure to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was as ready to complain about it as her husband. It was very strange that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge; it was also inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She hated having visitors in the house while her health was so poor, and lovers were the most disagreeable people of all."}

{"request_id":"177f14087d8b7091f4ac3fa1","rewritten_text":"There was something strange in all this that drew me in and enchanted me. He seemed to have awakened from a long, visionary sleep, and felt somewhat like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that charming imitation of an eastern tale: Diana was gone; his friends were altered or dead, and, upon waking, I was all he had left to love on earth.

How precious the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became to me, now that I had so beloved a companion for my rambles. With my father I visited every pleasant place, whether on the islands or beside the waterfalls sheltered by trees; every shaded path and every hollow tangled with underwood and fern. His conversation enlarged my thoughts. I felt newly created, surrounded by all the freshness and vitality of a new being: since his arrival, I seemed transported from a narrow patch of earth into a universe limitless to imagination and understanding. Before, my life had been like a pleasant country stream, never meant to leave its native fields, but destined, when its quiet task was done, to be absorbed without leaving a trace. Now it appeared to me a varied river passing through a fertile and lovely landscape, forever changing and forever beautiful. Alas! I did not know the desert it was soon to reach; the rocks that would rend its waters, or the dreadful scene that would be reflected, more horribly distorted, in its waves. Life was then radiant; I was beginning to learn hope—and what brings a more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should so quickly follow happiness so divine? I drank from an enchanted cup, but gall lay at the bottom of its long-drawn sweetness. My heart was filled with profound affection, yet calm because of its very depth and fullness. I had never imagined that misery could spring from love, and this lesson, which everyone must eventually learn, was taught to me in a way few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and must always mourn, those few brief months of paradisaical bliss; I had broken no command, eaten no apple, and yet was ruthlessly expelled from it. Alas! my companion had, and I was hurled down in his fall. But I stray from my account—let sorrow arrive in its appointed hour; at this point in my story I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship, when my aunt became ill. I spent an entire month nursing her in her chamber, but her illness was fatal, and she died, leaving me for some time inconsolable. Death is terrible to the living; the bonds of habit are so powerful, even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must suffer when they are broken."}

{"request_id":"db3f7c527664ce9b2323219d","rewritten_text":"She would be settled among those who loved her and possessed better judgment than she did; secluded enough to be safe, yet sufficiently occupied to remain cheerful. She would never be guided into temptation, nor left for temptation to discover her. She would be respectable and contented; and Emma acknowledged her to be the most fortunate creature in the world, for having inspired so constant and determined an affection in such a man—or, if not entirely the most fortunate, second only to herself.

Harriet, necessarily drawn away by her commitments to the Martins, was seen less and less at Hartfield; and this was no cause for regret. The closeness between her and Emma must decline; their friendship must become a quieter kind of goodwill; and, happily, what ought to happen, and had to happen, already seemed to be beginning in the gentlest and most natural way.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church, and watched her hand given to Robert Martin with such complete satisfaction that no recollections, even those involving Mr. Elton as he stood before them, could diminish it. Perhaps, indeed, at that moment she scarcely noticed Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might soon be bestowed upon herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last-engaged pair of the three, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Churchills were in town as well, and they were merely waiting for November.

The month between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley had fixed upon, as far as they dared. They had decided that their marriage should take place while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so that the couple might enjoy the planned fortnight away on a seaside tour. John and Isabella, along with every other friend, approved the arrangement. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could Mr. Woodhouse be persuaded to agree? He had never yet spoken of their marriage except as something far in the future.

When the subject was first broached, he was so distressed that they nearly abandoned hope. A second reference to it caused less suffering. He began to believe that it would happen and that he could not prevent it—a very encouraging movement of the mind toward resignation. Yet he was still unhappy. Indeed, he seemed so far from cheerful that his daughter’s courage failed her. She could not endure seeing him suffer or knowing that he imagined himself neglected; and although her reason almost accepted the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys that, once the event had passed, his distress would soon pass as well, she hesitated—she could go no further."}

{"request_id":"405f2470a2b7e2b5e734e841","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at last, “there’s no disputing that, since the new feeding system was introduced, the coffins are somewhat narrower and shallower than they once were; but we must make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Properly seasoned timber is a costly commodity, sir; and all the iron handles are brought by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every business has its disadvantages. A reasonable profit is, naturally, permissible.”

“Certainly, certainly,” replied the undertaker; “and if I fail to profit on one article or another, why, I recover it in the end, you understand—he! he! he!”

“Precisely,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must observe,” continued the undertaker, taking up again the train of remarks which the beadle had broken off: “though I must observe, Mr. Bumble, that I have to struggle against one serious drawback: namely, that all the stout people die off the fastest. Those who have lived more comfortably, and paid rates for years, are the first to decline when they enter the house; and let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches beyond one’s estimate makes a considerable gap in one’s profits: particularly when one has a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry spoke with the proper indignation of a man who had been unfairly treated; and as Mr. Bumble felt that the remark seemed to cast a reflection upon the parish’s honour, the latter considered it prudent to turn the conversation elsewhere. Oliver Twist being foremost in his thoughts, he made him the subject.

“By the bye,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t happen to know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A porochial ’prentis, who is presently a dead weight; a millstone, so to speak, about the porochial throat? Liberal terms, Mr. Sowerberry, liberal terms?” As Mr. Bumble spoke, he lifted his cane to the bill above him and struck three clear taps upon the words “five pounds,” printed there in Roman capitals of enormous size.

“Gadso!” said the undertaker, taking Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat; “that is precisely what I wished to discuss with you. You know—dear me, what an exceedingly handsome button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never observed it before.”

“Yes, I consider it quite attractive,” said the beadle, looking down proudly at the large brass buttons adorning his coat. “The die is identical with the porochial seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and wounded man. The board gave it to me on Newyear’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember putting it on for the first time when I attended the inquest on that impoverished tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"acb2e5bc3b61819d869420f9","rewritten_text":"No bringing him up by hand, then. Not at all!”

Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to accept.

“He gave you a world of trouble, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble sympathetically to my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated; “trouble?” Then she launched into a dreadful list of every illness I had been responsible for, every sleepless night I had caused, every high place from which I had fallen, every low place into which I had tumbled, every injury I had inflicted on myself, and every occasion when she had wished me in my grave, while I had stubbornly refused to go there.

I imagine the Romans must have irritated one another greatly with their noses. Perhaps that was why they became such a restless people. At any rate, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose annoyed me so intensely during the account of my offences that I could have pulled it until he howled. Yet everything I had suffered so far was nothing beside the terrible feelings that seized me when the silence following my sister’s recital was broken—a silence in which everyone had stared at me (as I was painfully aware) with indignation and disgust.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently guiding the company back to the subject from which they had wandered, “Pork—considered as biled—is rich, too; ain’t it?”

“Take a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister.

O Heavens, the moment had come at last! He would discover that it was weak, declare it weak, and I would be ruined! I gripped the table leg beneath the cloth with both hands and awaited my fate.

My sister fetched the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured out his brandy; nobody else took any. The miserable man toyed with his glass—lifted it, examined it against the light, set it down—and lengthened my agony. Meanwhile, Mrs. Joe and Joe were busily clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I could not take my eyes from him. Still clutching the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the wretched creature play with his glass, pick it up, smile, tilt back his head, and swallow the brandy. Immediately afterward, the company was struck with indescribable alarm when he sprang up, spun around several times in a horrifying, spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushed through the door. He then appeared beyond the window, plunging and spitting violently, making the most dreadful faces, and seeming completely out of his mind.

I held on firmly while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him."}

{"request_id":"d8527175b68fcfe938fba036","rewritten_text":"She now felt a strong urge to go to the outer door; she wanted to see whether it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of another motive? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight. She rose from her seat and would go; one half of her should not always be so much wiser than the other, or forever suspecting the other of being worse than it was. She would see whether it rained. But she was turned back at once by the entrance of Captain Wentworth himself, with a party of gentlemen and ladies, evidently acquaintances of his, whom he must have joined a little below Milsom Street. He was more plainly startled and confused by seeing her than she had ever noticed before; he looked quite flushed. For the first time since their renewed acquaintance, she felt that she was showing more feeling than he was. She had the advantage of him, having had the last few moments to prepare herself. All the overwhelming, blinding, bewildering first effects of intense surprise had passed for her. Yet she still had enough to feel! It was agitation, pain, pleasure—a feeling somewhere between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, then turned away. His manner was embarrassed. She could not have called it cold or friendly, nor described it with any certainty except as embarrassed.

After a brief interval, however, he came toward her and spoke again. They exchanged questions about ordinary matters: neither of them was probably much wiser for what they heard, while Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than before. By spending so much time together, they had managed to speak with one another with considerable apparent indifference and calm; but he could not do so now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. There was some kind of awareness between them. He looked very well, not as if his health or spirits had suffered, and he spoke of Uppercross, the Musgroves, and even Louisa, with a brief return of his own teasing significance when he mentioned her; yet he was Captain Wentworth—not comfortable, not at ease, unable to pretend that he was.

It did not surprise Anne, but it grieved her, to see that Elizabeth would not acknowledge him. She saw that he saw Elizabeth, and that Elizabeth saw him; there was complete recognition within each of them. She was convinced that he was ready to be acknowledged as an acquaintance and expected it, and she suffered the pain of watching her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was becoming increasingly impatient, now drew up; the servant entered to announce it."}

{"request_id":"b401a5be8232544c29c5da02","rewritten_text":"It was well past noon when he awoke. His valet had crept into the room several times on tiptoe to see whether he was stirring, wondering what had made his young master sleep so late. At last his bell rang, and Victor entered quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sèvres china. He drew back the olive-satin curtains, with their shimmering blue lining, hanging before the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked drowsily.

“One fifteen, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up and, after sipping some tea, sorted through his letters. One was from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He hesitated briefly, then set it aside. He opened the others without interest. They contained the usual assortment of cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private views, programmes for charity concerts, and similar things showered upon fashionable young men each morning during the season. There was a substantial bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet set, which he still had not dared send to his guardians, extremely old-fashioned people who failed to understand that we live in an age when unnecessary things are our only necessities. There were also several very politely worded notices from Jermyn Street moneylenders, offering to advance any amount at a moment’s notice and at the most reasonable rates of interest.

After about ten minutes he rose and, throwing on an elaborate dressing gown of silk-embroidered cashmere wool, went into the bathroom paved with onyx. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had endured. Once or twice, a vague sense that he had taken part in some strange tragedy returned to him, but it possessed the unreality of a dream.

As soon as he was dressed, he entered the library and sat down to the light French breakfast laid out on a small round table beside the open window. It was an exquisite day. The warm air seemed heavy with spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl filled with sulphur-yellow roses before him. He felt completely happy.

Suddenly his eyes fell on the screen he had placed before the portrait, and he started.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” his valet asked, setting an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"470dbb7d7445a9281f6892d6","rewritten_text":"But do not suppose that I did not consider it an evil in itself.”

“Believe me, they were all entirely comfortable.”

“I might not think better of them for that, perhaps. Such a crowd of women and children have no _right_ to be comfortable aboard ship.”

“My dear Frederick, you are speaking very idly. What would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who often need to be carried from one port to another after our husbands, if everyone shared your feelings?”

“As you see, my feelings did not stop me from taking Mrs Harville and her whole family to Plymouth.”

“But I dislike hearing you speak so much like a fine gentleman, as though women were all fine ladies rather than rational beings. None of us expect smooth water throughout our lives.”

“Ah! my dear,” said the Admiral, “once he has a wife, he will sing another tune. If he marries, and we are fortunate enough to live until another war, we shall see him do as you and I, and many others, have done. We shall find him deeply grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Ay, that we shall.”

“Now I have finished,” cried Captain Wentworth. “Whenever married people begin attacking me with, ‘Oh! you will think quite differently when you are married,’ I can only answer, ‘No, I shall not;’ and then they repeat, ‘Yes, you will,’ and there is no more to say.”

He rose and walked away.

“What a great traveller you must have been, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Fairly so, ma’am, during the fifteen years of my marriage; though many women have travelled farther. I have crossed the Atlantic four times, and gone once to the East Indies and back, only once; besides visiting various places nearer home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never passed the Straits, and was never in the West Indies. Bermuda and Bahama, you know, are not what we call the West Indies.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to say against this; she could not accuse herself of ever having called them anything at all during her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft continued, “that nothing surpasses the accommodations of a man-of-war; I speak, of course, of the higher rates. In a frigate, naturally, one is more confined; yet any reasonable woman may be perfectly happy in one; and I can safely say that the happiest portion of my life was spent aboard ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear."}

{"request_id":"962b46a86750087c1ebc3205","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery horse, the same one that had carried him to victory in Greece; he exhausted himself with punishing exercise, losing the anguish of a troubled mind in physical sensation.

He slowly recovered himself; at last, like someone emerging from the effects of poison, he raised his head above the vapors of fever and passion into the still air of calm reflection. He considered what should be done. He was first struck by the length of time that had passed since madness, rather than any rational impulse, had governed his actions. A month had gone by, and during it he had not seen Evadne. Her power, connected with few of the lasting emotions in his heart, had greatly weakened. He was no longer her slave—no longer her lover: he would never see her again, and, by the completeness of his return, earn Perdita’s confidence.

Yet, as he made this decision, imagination summoned the miserable dwelling of the Greek girl—a dwelling she had refused to exchange for one of greater luxury out of noble and lofty principle. He thought of the splendor of her circumstances and appearance when he had first known her; of her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every feature of Oriental magnificence; of her present poverty, her daily labor, her lonely condition, her faded, famine-stricken cheek. Compassion filled his breast; he would see her once more. He would devise some plan to restore her to society and the enjoyment of her rank; their separation would then follow naturally.

Again he thought of how, during this long month, he had avoided Perdita, fleeing from her as from the stings of his own conscience. But he was awake now; all this would be corrected, and future devotion erase the memory of this single stain upon the serenity of their life. He grew cheerful as he considered it, and calmly and firmly laid out the conduct he would follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita to attend that very evening—the nineteenth of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—a festival held in his honor. May this festival prove a good omen for the happiness of future years. First, he would visit Evadne; he would not remain, but he owed her some explanation, some compensation for his long, unannounced absence; then he would go to Perdita, to the forgotten world, to the duties of society, the splendor of rank, and the enjoyment of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had expected a complete change in Raymond’s manner and conduct. She anticipated open communication and a return to those habits of affectionate companionship that had made up the happiness of her life."}

{"request_id":"08860348d8cfa5a81edc4c4e","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what is the matter now? How is your master?”

“To speak the truth, massa, he isn’t as well as he might be.”

“Not well! I’m truly sorry to hear that. What does he complain of?”

“That’s just it! He never complains of anything—but he’s very sick all the same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so at once? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, he isn’t! He isn’t confined anywhere—that’s exactly where the trouble lies. I’m very worried about poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you’re talking about. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong with him?”

“Well, massa, there’s no use getting angry about it. Massa Will says there’s nothing wrong with him—but then why does he go around looking like this, with his head down and his shoulders raised, and as white as a goose? And then he keeps a cipher all the time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a cipher with figures on the slate—the strangest figures I ever saw. I’m getting frightened, I tell you. I have to keep a very close eye on him wherever he goes. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick cut and ready to give him a devil of a beating when he came back—but I’m such a fool that I couldn’t bring myself to do it after all—he looked so very ill.”

“Eh? What? Ah, yes! On the whole, I think you’d better not be too severe with the poor fellow. Don’t flog him, Jupiter—he can’t very well endure it. But can’t you form any idea what caused this illness, or rather this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, nothing unpleasant has happened since then—I’m afraid it was before then—it was the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Well, massa, I mean the bug—there it is.”

“The what?”

“The bug—I’m certain Massa Will was bitten somewhere around the head by that golden bug.”

“And what reason have you, Jupiter, for such a supposition?”

“Claws enough, massa, and a mouth too. I never saw such a devilish bug—it kicked and bit everything that came near it. Massa Will caught it first, but had to let it go again very quickly, I tell you—that must have been when he got bitten. I didn’t like the look of the bug’s mouth myself, not at all, so I wouldn’t pick it up with my fingers, but I caught it with a piece of paper I found.”"}

{"request_id":"dd5365708f3dd8fe5efb9d55","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that forever produces misery must have been severed, and the malignant fate presiding over it would not allow such a violation of her eternal laws. But why should I lament this? Misery was my element, and nothing miserable could come near me; had Woodville been happy, I should never have known him. And can I, who for so many years was sustained by tears and nourished beneath the dew of grief, hesitate to recount a tale of sorrow and death?

Woodville was compelled to travel into the country and was kept, day after day, in tiresome separation from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her saying that she was somewhat ill, but urging him to hasten to her, since she would draw health from his eyes and his company would be her surest medicine. He was detained three days more, and then hurried to her. His heart, he knew not why, foretold misfortune; he had received no further word from her. He feared she had grown worse, and this fear made him impatient and restless for the instant when he might once again see her standing before him in health and beauty; for a sinister voice seemed continually whispering, “You will never behold her again as she was.”

When he reached her dwelling, everything within was silent. He passed through several rooms, and in one saw a servant weeping bitterly. Faint with terror, he could scarcely ask, “Is she dead?” He could only listen to the terrible reply: “Not yet.” These astonishing words seemed less dreadful than those he had expected; to learn that she still lived, and that hope remained, brought him some relief. He recalled the words of her letter and indulged the wild belief that his kisses, breathing warmth and life, would pour new strength into her, and that she could not die while he was near; his presence, he thought, was the talisman of her life.

He hurried to her sickroom. She lay there, her cheeks burning with fever, while her eyes remained closed and she appeared insensible. He gathered her into his arms, pressed breathless kisses upon her fevered lips, and called to her in a voice of restrained anguish by the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am with you—your life, your love. Return, dearest; you promised me this blessing, that I should restore your health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die beside me. What is death? To see you no more? To be parted from one who is part of myself, without whom I have neither memory nor future?”"}

{"request_id":"fbc73b32b0bf04c580c8a259","rewritten_text":"“I must go, uncertain of what will happen to me; but I shall return here, or follow your party, as soon as I can. A word, a look, will be enough to decide whether I enter your father’s house this evening or never.”

A letter like that was not something she could quickly recover from. Half an hour alone with her thoughts might have calmed her; but the mere ten minutes that passed before she was interrupted, with all the constraints of her situation, could do nothing to restore her composure. Every moment instead brought new agitation. It was overwhelming happiness. And before she had moved beyond the first intensity of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all entered.

The absolute necessity of appearing like herself immediately set off a struggle; but after a while she could do no more. She began to understand nothing they said and had to plead illness and excuse herself. They could then see that she looked very unwell, were shocked and concerned, and would not leave her for anything. This was dreadful. If only they had gone away and left her in the quiet possession of the room, it would have cured her; but having them all standing or waiting around her was unbearable, and in desperation she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” cried Mrs. Musgrove, “go home at once and take care of yourself, so that you may be fit for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no doctor myself. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

But the chair would never do. Worse than everything! To lose the chance of speaking two words to Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk up the town—and she felt almost certain of meeting him—was impossible to bear. She strongly objected to the chair, and Mrs. Musgrove, thinking only of one kind of illness, asked anxiously whether there had been any fall; whether Anne had recently slipped and struck her head; and, once assured that she was certain no such thing had happened, could let her go cheerfully, confident of finding her better that night.

Anxious to leave no possible precaution unattended to, Anne struggled and said—

“I am afraid, ma’am, that this has not been fully understood. Please be so kind as to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your entire party this evening. I am afraid there has been some mistake; and I particularly wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is perfectly understood, I assure you.”"}

{"request_id":"1ecb4bf5c71c6769bd3973ad","rewritten_text":"“Do you often come back?”

“I have never been here since.”

“Nor have I.”

The moon began to rise, and I thought of the calm expression on the white ceiling, which was now gone. The moon began to rise, and I thought of the pressure on my hand when I spoke the last words he had heard on earth.

Estella was the first to break the silence between us.

“I have often hoped and meant to come back, but many things prevented me. Poor, poor old place!”

The first moonlight touched the silver mist, and the same light touched the tears falling from her eyes. Not realizing that I saw them, and trying to control them, she said quietly,—

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left in this state?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground belongs to me. It is the only possession I have not given up. Everything else has been taken from me, little by little, but I kept this. It was the only thing I firmly resisted giving up during all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye before it changes. And you,” she said, with touching concern for a wanderer,—“you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you are doing well, I am sure?”

“I work fairly hard for enough to live on, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” said Estella.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. For a long, difficult time, I kept away the memory of what I had thrown away when I did not understand its value. But since my duty no longer prevented me from admitting that memory, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have always had your place in my heart,” I answered.

Again we were silent until she spoke.

“I never imagined,” said Estella, “that I would say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place. I am very glad to do so.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? To me, parting is painful. The memory of our last parting has always been sad and painful.”

“But you said to me,” Estella replied, very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you will not hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has taught me more powerfully than anything else, and has taught me to understand what your heart once was. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape.”"}

{"request_id":"7fa232ae5509e0c4d633c0f7","rewritten_text":"At the center of this rift I saw a white spot, but at first could not tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus, looked again, and now recognized it as a human skull.

“Upon making this discovery, I was so confident that I considered the enigma solved; for the phrase ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could refer only to the skull’s position on the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ allowed only one interpretation in connection with a search for buried treasure. I understood that the plan was to drop a bullet through the skull’s left eye, and that a bee-line—or, in other words, a straight line—drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’ (the place where the bullet fell), and then extended fifty feet farther, would mark a precise point. Beneath that point, I thought it at least possible, a valuable deposit lay hidden.”

“All this,” I said, “is perfectly clear, and, though ingenious, still simple and explicit. When you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened next?”

“Having carefully taken the tree’s bearings, I turned toward home. The moment I left ‘the devil’s seat,’ however, the circular rift disappeared; and no matter how I turned, I could not see it again. What seems to me the greatest ingenuity in the whole affair is the fact—for repeated experiments have convinced me that it is a fact—that this circular opening can be seen from no other accessible viewpoint than the narrow ledge on the face of the rock.

“On this expedition to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel,’ Jupiter had accompanied me. He had evidently noticed my distracted manner for several weeks and took particular care not to leave me alone. But the next day, rising very early, I managed to slip away from him and went into the hills to search for the tree. After much effort, I found it. When I returned that night, my valet offered to flog me. As for the rest of the adventure, I believe you know it as well as I do.”

“I suppose,” said I, “that you missed the spot on your first attempt at digging because of Jupiter’s stupidity in allowing the bug to fall through the skull’s right eye instead of its left.”

“Exactly. This mistake shifted the ‘shot’—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been directly beneath ‘the shot,’ the error would have mattered little; but ‘the shot’ and the nearest point of the tree served only as two points from which to establish a line of direction. Naturally, the error, however slight at first, grew as we followed the line, and by the time we had gone fifty feet, it led us completely away from the trail.”"}

{"request_id":"7e1dd535b42a079e049808a7","rewritten_text":"He then bowed and left. He saw no one in the street at the time. It is a side street—very lonely.

“_William Bird_, tailor, states that he was one of the group who entered the house. He is an Englishman and has lived in Paris for two years. He was among the first to climb the stairs. He heard the voices arguing. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could make out several words, but cannot now recall them all. He distinctly heard ‘_sacré_’ and ‘_mon Dieu._’ At that moment there was a sound as if several people were struggling—a scraping and scuffling noise. The shrill voice was very loud—louder than the gruff one. He is certain it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be that of a German. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above, being recalled, stated that the door of the chamber where the body of Mademoiselle L. was found had been locked from the inside when the group reached it. Everything was completely silent—there were no groans or noises of any kind. When the door was forced open, no one was seen. The windows of both the back and front rooms were shut and firmly fastened from within. A door between the two rooms was closed but not locked. The door leading from the front room into the passage was locked, with the key inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth floor at the end of the passage, stood open, its door ajar. It was filled with old beds, boxes, and similar items. These were carefully removed and searched. Not an inch of any part of the house was left unexamined. Chimneys were swept from top to bottom. The house had four stories, with attics (_mansardes._) A trapdoor in the roof was nailed shut very securely and did not appear to have been opened for years. Witnesses gave varying estimates of the time between hearing the arguing voices and breaking open the chamber door. Some said as little as three minutes; others as much as five. The door was difficult to open.

“_Alfonzo Garcio_, undertaker, states that he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is a native of Spain. He was one of the group who entered the house but did not go upstairs. He is nervous and feared the effects of agitation. He heard the voices arguing. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could not make out what was said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—of this he is certain.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"f84bf48b00efdb2926281ff4","rewritten_text":"“The stupor and astonishment caused in my mind by this remarkable alteration in the state of affairs was perhaps, in the end, the portion of the adventure most difficult to explain. For the bouleversement itself was not merely natural and unavoidable, but had long been foreseen as something to be expected when I reached that precise stage of my voyage at which the planet’s attraction would be overtaken by that of the satellite—or, more exactly, when the balloon’s gravitation toward the earth became weaker than its gravitation toward the moon. Certainly, I rose from a deep sleep, all my senses bewildered, to witness a most startling phenomenon, one which, though anticipated, had not been expected at that particular instant. The revolution must, naturally, have occurred smoothly and gradually; and it is far from certain that, even had I been awake when it happened, I would have detected it through any inward sign of inversion—that is, through any discomfort or disturbance either in my person or in my apparatus.\n\n“It is scarcely necessary to say that, once I had properly understood my situation and emerged from the terror that had seized every faculty of my soul, my attention was first entirely occupied by the moon’s general physical appearance. It stretched beneath me like a chart—and though I believed it still to be at a considerable distance, the markings of its surface appeared to my sight with a striking and wholly inexplicable sharpness. The complete lack of ocean or sea, and indeed of any lake, river, or water of any kind, struck me at once as the most extraordinary feature of its geological condition. Yet, oddly enough, I saw immense level tracts of a distinctly alluvial character, while much the greater part of the visible hemisphere was covered by countless volcanic mountains, conical in form, and seeming more artificial than naturally formed. The tallest of these rises no more than three and three-quarter miles in perpendicular height; but a map of the volcanic regions of the Campi Phlegraei would give Your Excellencies a more accurate notion of their general surface than any inadequate description I might undertake. Most of them were plainly erupting, and made me dreadfully aware of their violence and strength through the repeated thunder of the misnamed meteoric stones, which now shot upward past the balloon with increasingly alarming frequency.”"}
