{"request_id":"ec5ae9c616e09884a48b4108","rewritten_text":"If, on the other hand, you require one for private use, I can provide an excellent article and guarantee that you will be pleased with the result. May I ask who it is meant for? If it is intended for the police, or for anyone associated with Scotland Yard, I fear I can do nothing for you. English detectives are truly our greatest friends, and I have always discovered that, by counting on their stupidity, we may do precisely as we please. I could not spare one of them.’

‘I assure you,’ said Lord Arthur, ‘that the police have nothing whatever to do with it. Indeed, the clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.’

‘Good heavens! I had no notion that you were so deeply interested in religion, Lord Arthur. Very few young men are nowadays.’

‘I fear you give me too much credit, Herr Winckelkopf,’ said Lord Arthur, blushing. ‘The truth is, I know absolutely nothing about theology.’

‘Then it is entirely a private affair?’

‘Entirely private.’

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged, and went out of the room. A few minutes later he returned carrying a round cake of dynamite, about the size of a penny, together with a charming little French clock topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling upon the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face lit up at the sight. ‘That is exactly what I require,’ he exclaimed. ‘Now tell me how it is set off.’

‘Ah! That is my secret,’ replied Herr Winckelkopf, regarding his invention with a justifiably proud expression. ‘Tell me when you wish it to explode, and I shall set the mechanism for that precise moment.’

‘Well, to-day is Tuesday, and if you could dispatch it immediately—’

‘That cannot be done; I have a great deal of important work in hand for some friends of mine in Moscow. Nevertheless, I may be able to send it to-morrow.’

‘Oh, that will be quite soon enough!’ said Lord Arthur courteously, ‘provided it arrives to-morrow night or on Thursday morning. As for the explosion, let us say Friday at exactly noon. The Dean is invariably at home then.’

‘Friday, at noon,’ repeated Herr Winckelkopf, making a note of it in a large ledger lying on a bureau beside the fireplace.

‘And now,’ said Lord Arthur, getting to his feet, ‘please tell me how much I owe you.’

‘It is such a trifling matter, Lord Arthur, that I do not wish to charge you anything. The dynamite is seven and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and the carriage roughly five shillings. I am delighted to oblige any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.’

‘But your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?’"}

{"request_id":"0ec2c1b7db3a8e96c69acd09","rewritten_text":"But I must warn you in advance that I shall tell Sybil everything. She is coming to lunch with me tomorrow to talk about bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a bad temper, a tendency toward gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I shall certainly tell her all about it.’

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. ‘I am not afraid,’ he replied. ‘Sybil knows me as well as I know her.’

‘Ah! I am a little sorry to hear you say that. The proper foundation for marriage is mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical at all; I have merely gained experience, which is much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is eager to have his palm read. Don’t tell him that he is engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that appeared in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.

‘Dear Lady Windermere,’ cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please let Mr. Podgers stay a little longer. He has just told me I should go on the stage, and I am deeply interested.’

‘If he has told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly take him away. Come here at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.’

‘Well,’ said Lady Jedburgh, making a little _moue_ as she rose from the sofa, ‘if I am not to be allowed to go on the stage, I must at least be allowed to join the audience.’

‘Of course; we are all going to be part of the audience,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘And now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my particular favourites.’

But when Mr. Podgers saw Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned strangely pale and said nothing. A shudder seemed to pass through him, and his thick, bushy eyebrows twitched convulsively, in the odd, irritating manner they assumed whenever he was perplexed. Then large beads of perspiration appeared on his yellow forehead, like poisonous dew, and his fat fingers became cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur could not fail to notice these strange signs of agitation, and for the first time in his life he felt fear himself. His instinct was to rush from the room, but he restrained it. Whatever the truth might be, it was better to know the worst than to remain trapped in this terrible uncertainty.

‘I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We are all waiting,’ cried Lady Windermere in her quick, impatient manner, but the cheiromantist made no answer.

‘I believe Arthur is going on the stage,’ said Lady Jedburgh, ‘and that after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.’"}

{"request_id":"5a8d46ddbbb8eef59d4718b5","rewritten_text":"He couldn’t help it. And it drove him mad to think that Becky Thatcher had not once suspected he was even alive. But she had noticed him after all; she knew she was winning their battle, too, and was pleased to see him suffer as she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted that he had things to attend to, things that had to be done, and that time was running short. But it was useless—the girl kept chirping away. Tom thought, “Oh, damn her, am I ever going to get rid of her?” At last he had to go attend to those things—and she said innocently that she would be “around” when school let out. He hurried away, hating her for it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in the whole town except that Saint Louis smart-aleck who thinks he dresses so well and is some kind of aristocrat! Oh, all right, I beat you the first day you ever saw this town, mister, and I’ll beat you again! Just wait until I catch you alone! I’ll just take and—”

He went through the motions of beating an imaginary boy—punching the air, kicking, and gouging. “Oh, you do, do you? You’re yelling enough, are you? Now then, let that teach you!” And the imaginary beating ended to his satisfaction.

Tom ran home at noon. His conscience could not endure any more of Amy’s grateful happiness, and his jealousy could bear no more of the other misery. Becky went on examining pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes passed and Tom did not come to suffer, her triumph began to fade and she lost interest; seriousness and distraction followed, then sadness. Two or three times she raised her head at the sound of footsteps, but each time it was a false hope; Tom did not come. At last she became completely miserable and wished she had not carried things so far. When poor Alfred, seeing that he was losing her without knowing why, kept exclaiming, “Oh, here’s a funny one! Look at this!” she finally lost patience and said, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care about them!” Then she burst into tears, stood up, and walked away.

Alfred followed close behind and was about to try to comfort her, but she said:

“Go away and leave me alone, can’t you? I hate you!”

The boy stopped, wondering what he could have done—for she had said she would look at pictures throughout the noon break—and she walked on, crying. Then Alfred went thoughtfully into the deserted schoolhouse. He was humiliated and angry. He easily guessed the truth: the girl had simply used him as a means of venting her spite against Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"a43563731729edd47f1f17f0","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologised. He replied, “Not at all,” and continued.

“Miss Havisham was by this time an heiress, and you may imagine that she was watched over as a splendid match. Her half-brother had once more abundant means, but through debts and fresh extravagance he squandered them terribly again. The disagreements between him and her were even greater than those between him and his father, and it is believed that he bore her a deep and deadly resentment, thinking she had helped provoke their father’s anger. Now I come to the cruel part of the story,—pausing only, my dear Handel, to observe that a dinner-napkin cannot be put into a tumbler.”

Why I was attempting to force mine into my tumbler, I am entirely unable to explain. I only know that I found myself, with perseverance deserving a far better purpose, exerting myself most vigorously to squeeze it into that space. Once more I thanked him and apologised, and once more he answered in the most cheerful fashion, “Not at all, I am sure!” and went on.

“There appeared on the scene—at the races, perhaps, or the public balls, or wherever you choose—a certain man who paid his addresses to Miss Havisham. I never saw him (for this occurred five-and-twenty years ago, before you and I were, Handel), but I have heard my father say that he was a flashy man, and just the sort for the purpose. Yet my father insists most emphatically that he was not, without ignorance or prejudice, to be mistaken for a gentleman; for it is one of his principles that no man who was not a true gentleman at heart has ever, since the beginning of the world, been a true gentleman in manner. He says that no polish can conceal the grain of wood; and that the more polish applied, the more plainly the grain will show. Well! This man followed Miss Havisham closely and declared himself devoted to her. I believe she had displayed little susceptibility before then; but all she possessed certainly appeared at that time, and she loved him passionately. There is no question that she worshipped him completely. He exploited her affection so methodically that he obtained large sums of money from her, and persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery (which their father had weakly left to him) at an enormous price, claiming that once he became her husband, he would have to possess and manage the whole concern. Your guardian was not then among Miss Havisham’s advisers, and she was too proud and too deeply in love to accept advice from anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"f69903b9948ae5b313fba5c3","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it, and was preparing to start on the bureau when he was summoned to dress for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a bit of soap. He carried them outside the door and placed the basin on a small bench; then he dipped the soap in the water and set it aside, rolled up his sleeves, poured the water gently onto the ground, and went into the kitchen, where he began diligently rubbing his face with the towel behind the door. But Mary took away the towel and said:

“Now ain’t you ashamed, Tom? You mustn’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was somewhat disconcerted. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a while, summoning his courage; then he drew a deep breath and began. When he presently came into the kitchen, both eyes closed and his hands feeling for the towel, an honorable evidence of soap and water dripped from his face. But after he emerged from the towel he was still not satisfactory, because the clean part ended at his chin and jaws like a mask; below and beyond that boundary lay a dark stretch of untouched soil running down his front and around the back of his neck. Mary took charge of him, and when she had finished, he was a man and a brother, without distinction of color; his soaked hair was neatly brushed, its short curls arranged in a delicate and symmetrical whole. [He privately pressed the curls smooth, with considerable effort, and plastered his hair close against his head; for he considered curls effeminate, and his own made his life bitter.] Then Mary brought out a suit of clothes that had been worn only on Sundays for two years—they were merely known as his “other clothes”—and thus we learn the extent of his wardrobe. After he dressed, the girl “put him to rights”; she buttoned his tidy roundabout to his chin, folded his enormous shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and topped him with his speckled straw hat. He now appeared greatly improved and uncomfortable. He was every bit as uncomfortable as he looked, since the confinement of complete clothing and cleanliness irritated him. He hoped Mary would overlook his shoes, but that hope failed; as was customary, she thoroughly coated them with tallow and brought them out. He lost his temper and declared that he was always being forced to do everything he did not want to do."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d05095ede16ccbc7f34288a3","rewritten_text":"“But, in truth, once an ascent has been made to any particular altitude, the quantity of ponderable air passed through in rising still farther is by no means proportional to the extra height gained (as what has already been said clearly shows), but follows a continually diminishing ratio. It is therefore plain that, however high we ascend, we cannot, strictly speaking, reach a boundary beyond which no atmosphere exists. It must be present, I reasoned, though perhaps in a condition of infinite rarefaction.\n\n“On the other hand, I knew that arguments had been advanced to establish the existence of a genuine and fixed limit to the atmosphere, beyond which there is no air at all. Yet one circumstance, overlooked by those who maintain such a boundary, appeared to me, though not an absolute disproof of their belief, nevertheless deserving the most serious examination. When the intervals between Encke’s comet’s successive returns to perihelion are compared, after the disturbances caused by planetary attractions have been allowed for with the greatest precision, it is found that the periods are gradually shortening; in other words, the major axis of the comet’s ellipse is slowly but steadily decreasing. Now this is exactly what should occur if the comet encountered resistance from an exceedingly rare ethereal medium filling the regions of its orbit. Such a medium, by checking the comet’s speed, must plainly increase its centripetal force by diminishing its centrifugal force. Thus the sun’s attraction would continually gain strength, and the comet would be drawn closer at each revolution. Indeed, there is no other explanation for the change in question. But again:—The actual diameter of this comet’s nebulosity is seen to contract rapidly as it nears the sun, and to expand just as rapidly as it travels away toward its aphelion. Was I not justified, with M. Valz, in supposing that this apparent condensation of volume arose from compression by the same ethereal medium mentioned before, which becomes denser in proportion to its nearness to the sun? The lenticular phenomenon, also known as the zodiacal light, likewise deserved attention. This radiance, so conspicuous in the tropics and not to be confused with any meteoric glow, rises obliquely from the horizon and generally follows the direction of the sun’s equator. It seemed to me plainly to be a rare atmosphere extending outward from the sun, at least beyond Venus’s orbit, and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not imagine this medium restricted to the comet’s elliptical path or to the sun’s immediate vicinity.”"}

{"request_id":"740ab1e3a4da07a75dff89cd","rewritten_text":"Those venerable, feeble people were always visible to the public in the act of bowing, and it was commonly believed that, after bowing a customer out, they continued bowing in the vacant office until they bowed another customer in.

The barrister was perceptive enough to understand that the banker would not have expressed such an opinion on anything less substantial than moral certainty. Though unprepared for the large pill he was obliged to swallow, he managed to get it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, wagging his forensic forefinger at the Temple generally, once it was down, “my way out of this is to prove you all wrong.”

It was a piece of the Old Bailey tactician’s art, and it brought him considerable relief. “You shall not prove me wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver; “I’ll do that for you.”

Accordingly, when Mr. Lorry called that night, as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, amid a heap of books and papers spread about for the purpose, appeared to have nothing less upon his mind than the morning’s subject. He even seemed surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and was altogether absent and preoccupied.

“Well!” said the good-natured emissary, after half an hour of fruitless efforts to bring him back to the matter. “I have been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coldly. “Oh, certainly! What can I have been thinking of!”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in our conversation. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” Mr. Stryver replied in the most friendly manner, “that I am sorry for it on your account, and sorry for it on the poor father’s account. I know this must always be a painful subject with the family; let us say no more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say you don’t,” Stryver answered, nodding in a soothing, conclusive fashion; “never mind, never mind.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, it doesn’t; I assure you it doesn’t. Having imagined sense where there is none, and a praiseworthy ambition where no such ambition exists, I am happily free of my error, and no harm has been done. Young women have made similar follies many times before, and have repented them in poverty and obscurity many times before. From an unselfish standpoint, I am sorry the matter has been abandoned, because it would have been disadvantageous to me in worldly terms; from a selfish standpoint, I am glad it has been abandoned, because it would have been disadvantageous to me in worldly terms—it is scarcely necessary to say that I could have gained nothing by it."}

{"request_id":"0adeb930eb348adb1a7722e6","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?” demanded Oliver.

“Hush!” replied the Dodger. “Do you see that old fellow at the bookstall?”

“The old gentleman across the street?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A fine mark,” said Master Charley Bates.

Oliver looked from one to the other in great surprise, but he had no chance to ask questions. The two boys quietly crossed the road and slipped in behind the old gentleman they had pointed out. Oliver followed a few steps behind them. Unsure whether to go forward or turn back, he stood watching in silent amazement.

The old gentleman looked very respectable, with a powdered head and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar and white trousers, and carried a smart bamboo cane under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood reading it as seriously as if he were sitting in his own study. He may even have imagined himself there, for he was so absorbed that he seemed to notice neither the stall, the street, the boys, nor anything except the book. He read straight through it, turning the page when he reached the bottom and beginning at the top of the next, continuing with the greatest interest and eagerness.

What horror and alarm filled Oliver as he stood a few paces away, his eyes opened as wide as possible, and saw the Dodger thrust his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! He saw him pass it to Charley Bates, and then watched them both run around the corner at full speed!

In an instant, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, watches, jewels, and the Jew came rushing into the boy’s mind.

For a moment he stood there, terror making his blood tingle through every vein until he felt as if he were burning. Then, confused and frightened, he ran off, moving his feet as fast as he could.

It all happened within a minute. Just as Oliver began to run, the old gentleman put his hand into his pocket and discovered that his handkerchief was gone. He turned sharply, saw the boy hurrying away at great speed, and naturally concluded that Oliver was the thief. Shouting “Stop thief!” with all his strength, he ran after him, still holding the book in his hand."}

{"request_id":"0dbb914e9ee180807fc75a55","rewritten_text":"And he always pretended that Peter had written the things for him; but that was a lie: he got every single one of them from that young fool we had canoed up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls; and it left the tanyard, which was doing good business, along with some other houses and land worth about seven thousand, and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and said where the six thousand in cash was hidden in the cellar. So the two frauds said they would go and bring it up, to make everything proper and aboveboard, and told me to come with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag, they poured it out onto the floor. It was a beautiful sight, all those yellow boys. My, how the king’s eyes shone! He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said:

“Oh, this is something, isn’t it? Oh, no doubt about it! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn’t it?”

The duke agreed that it did. They handled the gold pieces, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle onto the floor; and the king said:

“There’s no use talking; being brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs who’ve been left behind is the life for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes of trusting Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there isn’t any better way.”

Most people would have been satisfied with the pile and accepted it on trust; but no, they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said:

“Damn him, I wonder what he did with those four hundred and fifteen dollars?”

They worried over that for a while and searched everywhere for it. Then the duke said:

“Well, he was a very sick man, and likely he made a mistake—I reckon that’s how it was. The best thing is to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can afford it.”

“Oh, nonsense, yes, we can afford it. I don’t care anything about that—it’s the count I’m thinking about. We want to be perfectly honest and open and aboveboard here, you know. We want to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody—then there won’t be anything suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"b71d3b6103d67710c66d8ea0","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray could not escape the influence of this book. Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say that he never tried to escape it. From Paris he ordered no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition and had each bound in a different colour, to match his changing moods and the shifting desires of a nature he sometimes seemed almost unable to control. The hero, that remarkable young Parisian in whom romantic and scientific qualities were strangely combined, became for him a kind of early image of himself. Indeed, the whole book seemed to tell the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one way he was luckier than the novel’s strange hero. He never knew—and had no reason to know—the almost ridiculous fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water that came over the young Parisian so early in life, after the sudden decay of a beauty that had once apparently been extraordinary. He read the later part of the book with an almost cruel pleasure—and perhaps cruelty exists in nearly every joy, as it certainly does in every pleasure. The book gave a truly tragic, though somewhat exaggerated, account of the grief and despair of a man who had lost in himself what he valued most dearly in others and in the world.

The wonderful beauty that had so captivated Basil Hallward, and many others besides him, seemed never to leave Dorian. Even those who had heard the worst things about him—and from time to time strange rumours about his way of life spread through London and became the talk of the clubs—could not believe anything dishonourable about him when they saw him. He always looked like someone who had kept himself untouched by the world. Men who spoke crudely fell silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. There was something pure in his face that made them ashamed. His mere presence seemed to remind them of the innocence they had stained. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have escaped the corruption of an age that was both sordid and sensual.

Often, after returning home from one of those mysterious, lengthy absences that caused such strange speculation among his friends, or those who believed themselves to be his friends, he would creep upstairs to the locked room. He would open the door with the key that now never left him, then stand with a mirror before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him, looking first at the evil, aging face on the canvas and then at the beautiful young face laughing back at him from the polished glass."}

{"request_id":"b04c24c110241614740965c0","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was making a very foolish choice, because there was no doubt that the house was haunted. Lord Canterville himself, a man of the strictest honour, felt obliged to mention this when they met to discuss the sale.

“We have not been willing to live there ourselves,” said Lord Canterville, “since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a fit from which she never truly recovered. Two skeleton hands had been placed on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family have seen the ghost, as has the parish rector, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the unfortunate incident involving the Duchess, none of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville often slept very little because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” replied the Minister, “I will take the furniture and the ghost at their assessed value. I come from a modern country where money can buy everything. With all our lively young men painting the Old World red and carrying off your finest actresses and opera singers, I suppose that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we would soon have it in one of our public museums, or travelling around as a show.”

“I am afraid the ghost does exist,” said Lord Canterville with a smile, “though it may have refused the offers of your ambitious showmen. It has been well known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always appears before a member of our family dies.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, for that matter, Lord Canterville. But there is no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I guess the laws of Nature are not going to be suspended for the British aristocracy.”

“You are certainly very practical in America,” replied Lord Canterville, who did not quite understand Mr. Otis’s last remark. “If you do not mind having a ghost in the house, that is all right. You must only remember that I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was completed, and when the season ended, the Minister and his family went to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who had once been a famous New York beauty as Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, was now a very handsome middle-aged woman, with beautiful eyes and a magnificent profile."}

{"request_id":"3b41a1509702f2a136f4f31c","rewritten_text":"“Yes, it is—and _I_ could have had him if I’d been big enough; I saw him _first_. Who nailed him?”

“It was an old man—a stranger—and he sold his chance in him for forty dollars, becuz he’s got to go up the river and can’t wait. Think of that, now! You bet _I’d_ wait, if it was seven years.”

“That’s me, every time,” says I. “But maybe his chance ain’t worth any more than that, if he’ll sell it so cheap. Maybe there’s something not straight about it.”

“But it _is_, though—straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells everything about him, to a dot—paints him like a picture, and names the plantation he’s frum, below Newr_leans_. No-sirree-_bob_, there ain’t no trouble ’bout _that_ speculation, you bet you. Say, gimme a chaw of tobacker, won’t ye?”

I didn’t have any, so he went away. I went to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t reach any conclusion. I thought until my head ached, but I couldn’t see any way out of the trouble. After all this long journey, and after everything we’d done for those scoundrels, here it had all come to nothing, everything broken up and ruined, because they could have the heart to play Jim such a trick as that, and make him a slave again all his life, among strangers, too, for forty dirty dollars.

Once I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home, where his family was, if he _had_ to be a slave, and that I’d better write Tom Sawyer and tell him to tell Miss Watson where he was. But I soon abandoned that idea for two reasons: she’d be angry and disgusted at his rascality and ungratefulness for leaving her, and would sell him straight down the river again; and if she didn’t, everybody naturally despises an ungrateful nigger, and they’d make Jim feel it constantly, so he’d feel mean and disgraced. And then think of _me!_ It would get around that Huck Finn had helped a nigger gain his freedom; and if I ever saw anybody from that town again, I’d be ready to get down and lick his boots for shame. That’s the way it is: a person does a low-down thing, and then doesn’t want to suffer any consequences from it. He thinks that as long as he can hide it, it isn’t any disgrace. {"request_id":"c2ef8d5cfaadef0abb70bd43","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a very fine-looking old gentleman, and a good-looking younger man with his right arm in a sling. And, my goodness, how the people shouted and laughed and kept it up. But I couldn’t see any joke in it, and I figured it would take some effort for the duke and the king to find one either. I expected them to turn pale. But no, not a trace of paleness did they show. The duke never let on that he suspected anything, but simply went around babbling happily and contentedly, like a jug gurgling out buttermilk; and as for the king, he only gazed sorrowfully at the newcomers, as if the thought that there could be such frauds and scoundrels in the world gave him a stomachache right in his heart. Oh, he did it admirably. Many of the leading people gathered around the king, to show him they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked completely bewildered. Before long he began to speak, and I saw at once that he pronounced his words like an Englishman—not in the king’s manner, though the king’s imitation was fairly good. I can’t reproduce the old gentleman’s words or his accent, but he turned to the crowd and said, more or less like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting; and I’ll admit, honestly and frankly, that I’m not very well prepared to meet it or answer it, because my brother and I have had misfortunes. He has broken his arm, and our baggage was mistakenly put off at a town upriver during the night. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can neither hear nor speak—and can’t even make useful signs now, since he has only one hand to make them with. We are who we claim to be; and in a day or two, when I recover the baggage, I can prove it. But until then I won’t say anything more. I’ll go to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new mute started off; and the king laughed and blurted out:

“Broken his arm—_very_ likely, _isn’t_ it?—and very convenient, too, for a fraud who has to make signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their baggage! That’s _excellent_!—and mighty ingenious—under the _circumstances!_”

So he laughed again, and everybody else did too, except three or four, or perhaps half a dozen. One was the doctor; another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-fashioned carpetbag made of carpet material, who had just come off the steamboat and was speaking to him in a low voice, glancing toward the king now and then and nodding their heads—it was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville; and another was a large, rough, powerful man who had come along and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

content.text: {"request_id":"004b902ea8e8a495c691973a","rewritten_text":"‘Oh, bother my hat! I want Virginia!’ cried the little Duke with a laugh, and they galloped on toward the railway station. There Mr. Otis asked the station-master whether anyone resembling Virginia had been seen on the platform, but learned nothing of her. The station-master, however, telegraphed both ways along the line and assured him that a careful watch would be kept for her. After buying the little Duke a hat from a linen-draper who was just closing his shop, Mr. Otis rode to Bexley, a village about four miles distant, which he had been told was a familiar gypsy haunt because of the large common beside it. There they roused the rural policeman, but obtained no information from him; and, after riding across the entire common, they turned their horses homeward, reaching the Chase at about eleven o’clock, exhausted and nearly heartbroken. At the gate-house they found Washington and the twins waiting with lanterns, for the avenue was very dark. No trace whatever of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been captured on Brockley meadows, but Virginia was not among them. They explained their sudden departure by saying they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and hurried away lest they should be late. In fact, they were greatly distressed to hear of Virginia’s disappearance, being very grateful to Mr. Otis for permitting them to camp in his park, and four of them had remained to assist in the search. The carp-pond had been dragged, and the whole Chase carefully searched, but all without result. It was plain that, for that night at least, Virginia was lost to them. In the deepest gloom Mr. Otis and the boys went up to the house, while the groom followed with the two horses and the pony. In the hall stood a cluster of frightened servants, and in the library poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa, almost beside herself with terror and anxiety, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a mournful meal, for scarcely anyone spoke; even the twins were subdued and awestruck, being deeply attached to their sister. When it was over, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleas, sent them all to bed. Nothing more could be done that night, he said, and in the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard to send detectives down at once."}

{"request_id":"f45c7204b026edc649c09c24","rewritten_text":"“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to figure out where I was. The sun was already up, and I had been sleeping soundly. Pap was standing over me, looking sour and sick as well. He said:

“What are you doing with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t remember anything about what he had been doing, so I said:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was lying in wait for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Well, I tried, but I couldn’t; I couldn’t move you.”

“All right, then. Don’t stand there talking all day. Get out and see whether there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried out along the riverbank. I noticed pieces of branches and other things floating downstream, with bits of bark scattered among them, so I knew the river had begun to rise. I figured I would have a fine time now if I were over in town. The June rise had always been lucky for me, because as soon as it began, cordwood came floating down, along with pieces of log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs together. All you had to do was catch them and sell them to the wood yards and the sawmill.

I went up the bank, keeping one eye out for Pap and the other on whatever the rising water might bring along. Then, all at once, a canoe came drifting by—a beautiful one, too, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I plunged headfirst from the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam toward it. I expected someone would be lying in it, because people often did that to fool others; when a man had pulled a skiff nearly within reach, they would sit up and laugh at him. But it wasn’t so this time. It really was a drift canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it ashore. I thought, the old man will be glad when he sees this—it’s worth ten dollars. But when I reached shore, Pap was still nowhere in sight. As I was pushing it into a little creek like a gully, thickly covered with vines and willows, another idea came to me: I decided to hide it well, and then, instead of taking to the woods when I ran away, I would go downriver about fifty miles and settle in one place for good, so I wouldn’t have such a hard time traveling on foot.

It was fairly close to the shanty, and I thought I heard the old man coming the whole time. But I got it hidden, then stepped out and looked around a clump of willows. There was the old man a little way down the path, taking aim at a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"d28309f5ca38067e9f30bb70","rewritten_text":"These were the events that weighed on Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable member of his family. He could have endured poverty, and while it was the reward of his virtue, he even took pride in it. But the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were sorrows far more bitter and impossible to repair. The Arabian’s arrival now brought new life to his spirit.

“When news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return to her native country. Safie’s generous nature was outraged by this command. She tried to argue with her father, but he angrily left her, repeating his harsh order.

“A few days later, the Turk entered his daughter’s room and hurriedly told her that he had reason to believe his stay in Leghorn had been discovered and that he would soon be handed over to the French government. He had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople, and he would sail within a few hours. He planned to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant, while she followed later with most of his property, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

“When she was alone, Safie considered what she ought to do in this crisis. Living in Turkey was hateful to her; both her religion and her feelings opposed it. From some of her father’s papers that came into her hands, she learned of her lover’s exile and discovered where he was living. She hesitated for some time, but at last made her decision. Taking some jewels that belonged to her and a sum of money, she left Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who understood the common language of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

“She reached a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage safely, but there her attendant became dangerously ill. Safie cared for her with complete devotion, but the poor girl died, leaving the Arabian alone, unable to speak the country’s language and entirely unfamiliar with the ways of the world. Still, she came into good hands. The Italian had mentioned the place they were traveling to, and after her death, the woman whose house they had stayed in made sure that Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.”"}

{"request_id":"260eb79091d4252b4170bebc","rewritten_text":"“Do you heed my words? I have learned the language of despair; I know it by heart, for I am Despair itself—and a strange creature I am: joyous, triumphant Despair. Yet those words are untrue, for the wave may be dark, but it is not bitter. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we awaken, we are free. Come, then, delay no longer, you tardy one! Behold the pleasant potion! Look, I am a spirit of goodness, not a human maiden inviting you, and in persuasive tones—oh, that they might persuade you!—saying, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my eyes fixed upon his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, and his gentle yet earnest expression of deprecation and wonder, even before he spoke, changed the tension of my feelings, stripping away all the sternness of despair and filling me only with the tenderest grief. I saw that his eyes were moist as well when he took both my hands in his; then, sitting beside me, he said:

“This is a sorrowful deed to which you would lead me, dearest friend, and your misery must indeed be profound if it has filled you with such unhappy thoughts. You long for death, yet fear it, and wish me to accompany you. But I have less courage than you, and even with such companionship I dare not die. Hear me, then, and consider whether you ought to win me to your design, even if, through the overbearing eloquence of despair, you could make black death so alluring that fair heaven itself would seem darkness. Listen, I beg you, to one who has himself cherished desperate thoughts and longed impatiently for death, but who has finally trampled that phantom beneath his feet and crushed its sting. Come; since you have played Despair with me, I will play Una with you and lead you unharmed from his dark cavern. Listen, and let yourself be softened by words in which no selfish passion remains.

“We do not know what this wide world signifies, with its strange mingling of good and evil. Yet we have been placed here and commanded to live and hope. I do not know what we are meant to hope for; but some good lies beyond us, and we must seek it—that is our earthly task. If misfortune comes against us, we must struggle with her, cast her aside, and continue onward to discover what it is our nature desires. Whether this expectation of future good prepares us for another existence, I cannot say; or whether it means only that, as laborers in God’s vineyard, we must help smooth the path for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"f4884ea00c389a39c1e10148","rewritten_text":"I am very ignorant, and it troubles me—just a little.”

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative and an orphan like me, whom I love very dearly. She is five years younger than I am, and she lives in a farmer’s house in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has happened to me—for I cannot write—and even if I could, how could I tell her? It is better this way.”

“Yes, yes: better this way.”

“What I was thinking as we came here, and what I am still thinking as I look into your kind, strong face, which gives me so much comfort, is this: If the Republic truly helps the poor, and they become less hungry and suffer less in every way, she may live for a long time. She may even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think”—the calm eyes, filled with so much endurance, fill with tears, and her lips part a little farther and tremble—“that the time will seem long to me while I wait for her in the better land, where I trust that both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot be, my child; there is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much! I am so ignorant. Am I to kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers; they solemnly bless each other. His free hand does not tremble as he lets hers go; nothing worse than a sweet, bright calm remains in the patient face. She goes before him—she is gone; the knitting-women count Twenty-Two.

{"request_id":"57da77877977104fd469b0e9","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had come straight from the Speaker’s Levée in their stars and ribbons, all the fashionable women wore their smartest dresses, and at the far end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a heavy, Tartar-looking woman with tiny black eyes and magnificent emeralds, speaking bad French at the top of her voice and laughing excessively at everything said to her. It was certainly a remarkable mixture of people. Splendid peeresses chatted pleasantly with fierce Radicals, popular preachers rubbed shoulders with eminent sceptics, a whole group of bishops followed a stout prima donna from room to room, several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, stood on the staircase, and it was said that at one point the supper room was packed with geniuses. In fact, it was one of Lady Windermere’s finest evenings, and the Princess stayed until nearly half past eleven.

As soon as she had left, Lady Windermere returned to the picture gallery, where a celebrated political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an outraged Hungarian virtuoso, and began speaking to the Duchess of Paisley. She looked extraordinarily beautiful, with her noble ivory throat, her large blue forget-me-not eyes, and her thick coils of golden hair. Pure gold they were—not that pale straw colour that now usurps the gracious name of gold, but the gold woven into sunbeams or concealed in strange amber; and they gave her face something of the frame of a saint, with no small share of a sinner’s fascination. She was a curious psychological study. Early in life she had discovered the important truth that nothing resembles innocence so closely as an indiscretion; and through a series of reckless escapades, half of them entirely harmless, she had gained all the privileges of a distinctive personality. She had changed her husband more than once; indeed, Debrett credited her with three marriages. But since she had never changed her lover, society had long since stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, childless, and possessed of that excessive passion for pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she looked eagerly around the room and said in her clear contralto voice, ‘Where is my cheiromantist?’

‘Your what, Gladys?’ exclaimed the Duchess, starting involuntarily.

‘My cheiromantist, Duchess; I can’t live without him at present.’

‘Dear Gladys! You are always so original,’ murmured the Duchess, trying to remember exactly what a cheiromantist was and hoping it was not the same thing as a chiropodist.

‘He comes to read my hand twice a week, without fail,’ Lady Windermere continued, ‘and is most interesting about it.’"}

{"request_id":"47e957d2811dc962d34a444e","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at last, “there’s no denying that, since the new feeding system was introduced, the coffins are somewhat narrower and shallower than they used to be; but we must make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Properly seasoned timber is expensive, sir; and all the iron handles come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its disadvantages. A reasonable profit is, of course, permissible.”

“Of course, of course,” replied the undertaker; “and if I fail to profit on one particular item, why, I make it up over time, you see—he! he! he!”

“Exactly,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must say,” continued the undertaker, returning to the line of thought the beadle had interrupted, “though I must say, Mr. Bumble, that I face one very serious disadvantage: all the stout people die the quickest. Those who have been better off, and have paid rates for many years, are the first to collapse when they enter the workhouse; and let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches beyond one’s estimate makes a considerable hole in one’s profits—especially when one has a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry said this with the proper indignation of a mistreated man, and as Mr. Bumble felt that it seemed to cast a reflection on the parish’s honour, the latter thought it best to change the subject. Oliver Twist was foremost in his thoughts, so he made him the topic.

“By the way,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t happen to know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A parish apprentice, who is currently a dead weight; a millstone, as I might say, around the parish’s neck? Generous terms, Mr. Sowerberry, generous terms?” As Mr. Bumble spoke, he raised his cane to the notice above him and gave three distinct taps on the words “five pounds,” printed there in enormous Roman capitals.

“Good heavens!” said the undertaker, taking Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That is exactly what I wanted to speak to you about. You know—dear me, what an elegant button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it is rather handsome,” said the beadle, looking proudly down at the large brass buttons adorning his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and injured man. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember wearing it for the first time when I attended the inquest on that impoverished tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"add6fd25b4ac94a140e175a0","rewritten_text":"“April 7. I rose early and, to my great joy, finally saw what there could be no doubt was the North Pole itself. It lay there beyond question, directly beneath my feet; but, alas, I had risen to such an enormous height that nothing could be made out with precision. Indeed, judging from the sequence of figures recording my altitude at different times between six in the morning on April 2 and twenty minutes before nine that same morning, when the barometer ran down, it might reasonably be concluded that, at four o’clock on the morning of April 7, the balloon had reached a height of at least 7,254 miles above sea level. This elevation may seem immense, but the estimate on which it is based almost certainly fell far short of the truth. In any event, I clearly saw the entire major diameter of the earth; the whole northern hemisphere lay beneath me like an orthographic map, and the equator itself formed the boundary of my horizon. Your Excellencies may readily imagine, however, that the unexplored regions within the Arctic Circle, though directly below me and therefore seen without any apparent foreshortening, were still too small in themselves and too distant from my viewpoint to permit close examination. Nevertheless, what could be seen was strange and compelling. Northward from that enormous rim mentioned earlier—which, with some qualification, may be called the limit of human discovery in these regions—one continuous, or nearly continuous, sheet of ice extended onward. For the first few degrees, its surface was noticeably flattened; farther on, it sank into a level plane; and at last, becoming distinctly concave, it ended at the Pole itself in a sharply defined circular center. Seen from the balloon, this center subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its dark color varied in intensity, but it was always darker than any other point on the visible hemisphere, sometimes deepening into complete, impenetrable blackness. Beyond this, little could be determined. By noon, the circular center had greatly diminished in circumference, and by seven in the evening I had lost sight of it altogether. The balloon passed over the western edge of the ice and drifted rapidly away toward the equator.\n\n“April 8. I noticed a clear reduction in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a significant change in its general color and appearance."}

{"request_id":"355f449a6d7810ac879b2e04","rewritten_text":"After I had sent them in, I could not stay away from the places where they were, but felt that they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near them. In this unreasonable restlessness and distress of mind, I would wander the streets in the evening, passing those offices and houses where I had left the petitions. Even now, the dreary western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their rows of severe, shuttered mansions and their long lines of lamps, seem melancholy to me because of that association.

The daily visits I was allowed to make him were shorter now, and he was watched more closely. Seeing, or imagining, that I was suspected of intending to carry poison to him, I asked to be searched before sitting down at his bedside, and told the officer who was always there that I was willing to do anything that would convince him of the purity of my intentions. No one was harsh with him or with me. There was a duty to perform, and it was performed, but not cruelly. The officer always assured me that he was worse, and some of the other sick prisoners in the room, along with other prisoners who attended them as nurses—criminals, but not incapable of kindness, thank God!—always gave the same report.

As the days passed, I noticed more and more that he would lie peacefully staring at the white ceiling, with no light in his face until some word of mine brightened it for a moment, after which it would fade again. Sometimes he was almost, or entirely, unable to speak; then he would answer me with slight pressures of my hand, and I gradually came to understand him very well.

The days had reached ten when I saw a greater change in him than ever before. His eyes were turned toward the door, and they lit up when I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said as I sat down beside his bed, “I thought you were late. But I knew you couldn’t be.”

“It is exactly the right time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always wait at the gate, don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So I won’t lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand in silence, for I could not forget that I had once intended to desert him.

“And best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable with me since I was under a dark cloud than when the sun was shining.”"}

{"request_id":"980cea26bbb7df2a12377247","rewritten_text":"“But,” I said, handing the slip back to him, “I am as much in the dark as ever. If all the jewels of Golconda were waiting for me to solve this enigma, I am quite certain I could not earn them.”

“And yet,” said Legrand, “the solution is nowhere near as difficult as a first hurried examination of the characters might lead you to believe. These characters, as anyone might readily guess, form a cipher—that is, they convey a meaning. But, knowing what we do of Kidd, I could not imagine him capable of constructing one of the more abstruse cryptographs. I immediately decided that this was a simple kind—one that would nevertheless seem, to the sailor’s crude intellect, completely impossible to solve without the key.”

“And you actually solved it?”

“Easily; I have solved others ten thousand times more obscure. Circumstances, along with a certain inclination of mind, have led me to take an interest in such riddles, and it may well be doubted whether human ingenuity can devise an enigma that human ingenuity cannot, with proper application, unravel. In fact, once I had established a sequence of connected, legible characters, I scarcely gave another thought to the mere difficulty of discovering their meaning.

“In this case—as, indeed, in every case of secret writing—the first question concerns the cipher’s language; for the principles of solution, particularly with the simpler ciphers, depend upon and vary according to the character of the particular language. In general, there is no choice but to test, guided by probability, every language known to the person attempting the solution, until the correct one is found. But with the cipher before us, the signature removed all difficulty. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ can be understood in no language but English. Without that clue, I would have begun with Spanish and French, the languages in which a secret of this kind would most naturally have been written by a pirate of the Spanish Main. As it was, I assumed the cryptograph was English.

“You will notice that there are no spaces between the words. Had there been spaces, the task would have been comparatively easy. In that case, I would have begun by comparing and analyzing the shorter words; and if a one-letter word had appeared, as is most likely—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for example—I would have considered the solution certain. But since there were no divisions, my first step was to determine the most common letters, as well as the rarest.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"bd91cf8f85642fecd47f83c4","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke that morning, he wondered where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and glanced around. Then he understood. It was the cool gray dawn, and a delicious feeling of rest and peace lay in the deep, all-encompassing stillness of the woods. Not a leaf moved; no sound intruded upon great Nature’s meditation. Dewdrops glittered on the leaves and grasses. A white coating of ashes covered the fire, while a thin blue thread of smoke rose straight upward. Joe and Huck were still asleep.\n\nNow, far off in the forest, one bird called; another replied; presently the tapping of a woodpecker could be heard. Little by little the cool, dim gray of morning brightened, and sounds gradually increased as life revealed itself. The wonder of Nature casting off sleep and beginning its work opened before the thoughtful boy. A small green worm crawled across a dewy leaf, repeatedly raising two-thirds of its body into the air and “sniffing around,” then moving on again—for, Tom declared, it was measuring. When the worm drew near him, he sat motionless as a stone, his hopes rising and sinking by turns as the creature continued toward him or appeared ready to go elsewhere; and when, after a painful pause with its curved body raised, it finally settled firmly upon Tom’s leg and began traveling over him, his whole heart rejoiced—for that meant, beyond any doubt, that he would receive a new suit of clothes, a splendid pirate uniform. Next came a procession of ants, appearing from nowhere in particular and attending to their business; one struggled bravely along, carrying a dead spider five times its own size, and hauled it directly up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug climbed the dizzy height of a blade of grass. Tom leaned close and said, “Lady-bug, lady-bug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone,” whereupon she flew off to investigate—which did not surprise the boy, since he had long known that this insect believed readily in fires and had taken advantage of its simplicity more than once. A tumblebug followed, pushing stoutly at its ball, and Tom touched it, watching as it drew its legs against its body and pretended to be dead. By then the birds were fairly celebrating. A catbird, the Northern mockingbird, landed in a tree above Tom’s head and poured out imitations of her neighbors in delighted ecstasy. Then a sharp jay darted down like a flash of blue flame and perched on a twig almost within the boy’s reach, tilting his head and studying the strangers with intense curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large “fox” squirrel came scurrying by, pausing now and then to sit upright, inspect the boys, and chatter at them, for the wild creatures had likely never seen a human being before and hardly knew whether they ought to be frightened."}

content.text: {"request_id":"4a72fd23e8fd6b1dfbfb1779","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was too astonished to think clearly. I knew my design differed greatly in its details, though the general outline was somewhat similar. Soon I took a candle, sat at the far end of the room, and examined the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the other side, exactly as I had drawn it. At first, I was simply amazed by the remarkable similarity of the outlines—the strange coincidence that, without my knowing it, a skull had been on the other side of the parchment, directly beneath my drawing of the _scarabæus_, and that this skull resembled my drawing so closely, not only in shape but also in size. I say that this coincidence completely stunned me for a time. That is the usual effect of such coincidences. The mind tries to find a connection, a chain of cause and effect, and, unable to do so, suffers a kind of temporary paralysis. But when I recovered, another thought gradually came to me, and it startled me even more than the coincidence. I began to remember clearly and certainly that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I sketched the _scarabæus_. I became completely sure of this, because I remembered turning over both sides in search of the cleanest place. If the skull had been there, I could not possibly have failed to see it. This was truly a mystery, one I felt unable to explain. Yet even then, somewhere in the most distant and hidden parts of my mind, there seemed to flicker a faint, glow-worm-like idea of the truth that last night’s adventure would reveal so magnificently. I rose at once, put the parchment safely away, and set aside all further thought until I was alone.\n\n“When you had left, and Jupiter was fast asleep, I began a more careful investigation of the matter. First, I considered how the parchment had come into my possession. The place where we found the _scarabæus_ was on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and only a short distance above the high-water mark. When I picked it up, it gave me a sharp bite, making me drop it. Jupiter, with his usual caution, looked around for a leaf or something similar before grabbing the insect, which had flown toward him."}

{"request_id":"e580b20079c9f22928ec22d9","rewritten_text":"But I wonder how long you would have continued, if you had been left to yourself. I wonder when you would have spoken if I had not asked you! My decision to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had a powerful effect. Too powerful, I fear; for what happens to the moral if our happiness comes from breaking a promise, since I ought not to have mentioned the matter? This will never do.”

“You need not trouble yourself. The moral will be perfectly sound. Lady Catherine’s unjust attempts to separate us were what removed all my doubts. I do not owe my present happiness to your eager wish to express your gratitude. I was not willing to wait for you to begin. My aunt’s information had given me hope, and I was determined to learn everything at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been extremely useful, which ought to please her, since she loves being useful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and feel embarrassed, or had you planned something more serious?”

“My true purpose was to see you and judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me. My stated purpose, or the one I admitted to myself, was to see whether your sister still cared for Bingley and, if she did, to make the confession to him that I have since made.”

“Will you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is going to happen to her?”

“I am more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. But it must be done; and if you will give me a sheet of paper, I will do it at once.”

“And if I did not have a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire the neatness of your handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt as well, who must not be neglected any longer.”

Because she did not wish to admit how much she had exaggerated her closeness with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth had not yet answered Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter. But now she had news to share that she knew would be most welcome, and she was almost ashamed to realize that her uncle and aunt had already lost three days of happiness. She immediately wrote as follows:--

“I should have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, as I ought, for your long, kind, and satisfying account of everything; but, to tell the truth, I was too cross to write. You imagined more than had really happened. But now imagine as much as you like; let your fancy run free and indulge your imagination in every direction the subject allows. Unless you believe me actually married, you cannot be very far wrong."}

{"request_id":"3f36972c7990aae704f3b8ab","rewritten_text":"I now come to my own story. There is little to tell about the early part of my life, so I will be brief. But I must spend some time on my childhood, so it may be understood how, when one hope failed, life became empty; and how, when the only affection I was allowed to cherish was destroyed, my existence seemed to end with it.

I have said that my aunt was very different from my father. I believe that, without having the slightest trace of an evil nature, she had the coldest heart that ever beat in a human breast: it was completely incapable of affection. She took responsibility for me because she believed it was her duty; but she had lived alone for so long, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, that she could not bear to have me disturb her peace. She had never married, and for the last five years had lived entirely alone on an estate she had inherited through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had expressed the wish that she would live with me at his family home, which stood in beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused, however, and as soon as she had settled the affairs left in her care by her brother’s departure, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

The care of me as a baby, and later until I was eight years old, was given to one of my mother’s servants, who had accompanied us into retirement for that purpose. I was kept in a distant part of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed times. This happened twice a day: once around noon, when she came to my nursery, and once after dinner, when I was brought to her. She never showed me affection, and while I remained in the room she seemed constantly afraid that some childish action of mine would annoy her. My good nurse always instructed me very carefully before allowing me to enter the sitting room. The fear inspired by my aunt’s cold looks and few, forced words was so great that I rarely failed to follow my nurse’s lessons or broke the exemplary silence I had been taught to keep during these short visits.

Under my good nurse’s care, I ran freely through our park and the nearby fields. As the child of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the greatest sensitivity of feeling. I cannot express how passionately I loved everything, even the lifeless objects around me."}

content.text: {"request_id":"15e72fd71adaed176d2c36c6","rewritten_text":"Thus I passed two years. Day followed day, and hundreds upon hundreds slipped away; they brought no visible alteration, yet a few of them gradually worked upon my mind as I moved onward toward death. I began to study more, to enter more sympathetically into the thoughts of others as revealed in books; I read history, and lost my individuality among the multitude who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the feeling of immediate suffering diminished, I became more human. Solitude, too, surrendered some of its attractions: I again began to long for sympathy; not that I was ever inclined to seek the crowd, but I wished for a single friend who would love me. You may say, perhaps, that I was slowly becoming fit to return to society. I do not believe it. The sympathy I desired had to be so pure, so free from the influence of outward circumstances, that in the world I could not avoid being disappointed by the coarse materials continually mingled even with its finest feelings. Believe me, I was then less prepared for fellowship with my fellow creatures than before. When I had left them, they had tormented me as pain and sickness might torment: something foreign to the mind, irritating it, which I wished to throw off. But now I would have desired sympathy; I would have wished to join my soul to another’s, and would thereby have prepared myself for abundant draughts of disappointment and suffering; for I was tender as the sensitive plant, all nerve. I did not seek sympathy and assistance in ambition or wisdom, but sweet and mutual affection; smiles to encourage me and gentle words of consolation. I wanted one heart into which I could pour my complaints without restraint, so that, through the heavenly nature of the soil, blessed fruit might grow from such poor seed. Yet how could I find this? The love that forms the soul of friendship is a gentle spirit, seldom discovered except when two amiable beings are united from early youth, or joined by shared suffering and pursuits; it comes to some of the chosen without being sought or recognized; it falls like soft dew upon favored places, which, however barren before, become through its gracious influence fertile with every sweet plant. But when desired, it flees; it mocks the prayers of those who worship it; it will give itself, but cannot be pursued.\n\nI knew all this and did not go in search of sympathy; yet there, upon my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof, where desert lay all around, it came to me like a sunbeam in winter, adorning the snowdrifts even as it helped to melt them.--Alas, the sun shone upon blighted fruit; I did not revive beneath its radiance, for I was too completely ruined to feel its kindly strength."}

{"request_id":"f49fa4fa6c500ca33a29e8ff","rewritten_text":"With my heart pounding and afraid, though I knew not of what, I dismissed the servant, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were the words it held.

“My dear Child

“I have betrayed your trust; I have sought to corrupt your mind, and have made your innocent heart familiar with the looks and language of unlawful and monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes, and must try in some measure to make my punishment answerable to my guilt. You are, I doubt not, prepared for what I am about to declare; we must part and remain separated forever.

“I deprive you of your parent and only friend. You are cast shelterless upon the world: your hopes are destroyed; the peace and safety of your pure mind have been ruined; memory will bring before you dreadful images of guilt, and the anguish of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who bring all this misery upon you; I, who cast you out and without remorse have stamped distrust and agony upon the heart and brow of my own child, who with devilish lightness have tried to take away her loveliness and replace it with the foul deformity of sin; I, in the overflowing torment of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and do, abhor me: but pardon me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me in exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again; never again hear your voice; yet the gentle whispers of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my disordered brain and heart; I am certain I should feel them even in my grave. And I dare strengthen this request by telling how miserably I was betrayed into this snare of fiery anguish, and of all my efforts to free myself: indeed, if your soul were less pure and radiant, I would not try to excuse myself before you; I should fear that, if I led you to regard me with less abhorrence, you might hate vice less: but in speaking to you I feel as though I were appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must strive to obtain it, or despair. I therefore implore you to hear my words, and if, among the good, guilt may in any degree be lessened by sharp agony and remorse that tears the brain as madness perhaps you may believe, though I dare not, that I have some claim to your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our first happy life upon the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from a weary wandering of sixteen years, during which, though I had passed through many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had remained entirely blank."}

{"request_id":"a0fd9c53674c6a10ff19b94d","rewritten_text":"“I must leave, not knowing what my fate may be; but I shall return here, or join your party, as soon as I can. A word, a glance, will suffice to determine whether I enter your father’s house this evening or never.”

A letter of this kind was not easily recovered from. Half an hour alone with her thoughts might have calmed her; but the mere ten minutes that now elapsed before she was disturbed, under all the constraints of her position, could do nothing to restore her composure. Each moment instead increased her agitation. Her happiness was overwhelming. And before she had passed through the first full rush of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta entered together.

The urgent need to appear herself at once brought on a struggle; but after some time she could manage no longer. She began to comprehend nothing they said, and was forced to plead illness and excuse herself. They could plainly see that she looked extremely unwell, and were alarmed and distressed, refusing to leave her for anything. This was terrible. Had they gone away and left her quietly in possession of the room, it would have restored her; but having them all standing or waiting about her was unbearable, and in despair she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” exclaimed Mrs Musgrove, “go home at once, and look after yourself, so that you may be ready for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

But the chair would never do. Worse than anything! To lose the chance of exchanging two words with Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk up the town (and she felt nearly certain of encountering him) was impossible to endure. She earnestly objected to the chair, and Mrs Musgrove, thinking only of one particular kind of illness, had anxiously satisfied herself that there had been no fall; that Anne had not lately slipped and struck her head; that she was entirely certain she had suffered no fall; and could therefore let her depart cheerfully, expecting to find her improved by night.

Eager to neglect no possible precaution, Anne made an effort and said—

“I fear, ma’am, that this has not been fully understood. Pray be kind enough to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your entire party this evening. I am afraid there has been some misunderstanding; and I particularly wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is perfectly understood, I assure you.”"}

{"request_id":"986dbe19de1cddd0e140be66","rewritten_text":"In fact, he was dressed as ‘Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,’ one of his finest impersonations. The Cantervilles had every reason to remember it, since it had truly caused their quarrel with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and, as far as he could tell, everyone was asleep. But as he walked toward the library to see whether any trace of the bloodstain remained, two figures suddenly sprang from a dark corner. They waved their arms wildly over their heads and shouted ‘BOO!’ directly into his ear.

Terrified—which was only natural in the circumstances—he ran toward the staircase, but Washington Otis was waiting there with the large garden syringe. Surrounded by enemies on every side and nearly trapped, he disappeared into the great iron stove, which fortunately was not lit. He then had to make his way home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his room in a dreadful state of dirt, confusion, and despair.

After that, he was never seen on another nighttime expedition. The twins waited for him several times and spread nutshells across the passages every night, greatly annoying their parents and the servants, but nothing came of it. Clearly, his feelings had been so badly hurt that he refused to appear. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his major work on the history of the Democratic Party, which he had been writing for several years. Mrs. Otis arranged a magnificent clam-bake that amazed the entire county. The boys took up lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American games, while Virginia rode her pony along the lanes with the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the final week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. Everyone assumed that the ghost had left. Indeed, Mr. Otis wrote Lord Canterville to say so, and Lord Canterville replied with great pleasure, sending his congratulations to the Minister’s worthy wife.

The Otises were mistaken, however. The ghost was still in the house. Though he was now almost an invalid, he was not ready to give up, especially after hearing that the young Duke of Cheshire was among the guests. The Duke’s great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning, Lord Francis was found lying on the card-room floor in such a helpless, paralyzed condition that, although he lived to a very old age, he was never again able to say anything except ‘Double Sixes.’"}
