{"request_id":"cdbdd2048c43d3b9bbb03466","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was occupied with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note by post, the mere sight of its outside throwing me into a great flutter; for, although I had never seen the handwriting in which it was addressed, I guessed whose hand it was. It had no formal opening, such as Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything, but began in this manner:—

“I am to arrive in London the day after to-morrow by the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you should meet me? At any rate, Miss Havisham has that impression, and I write in obedience to it. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Had there been time, I should likely have ordered several new suits for the occasion; but there was not, and I had to be satisfied with those already in my possession. My appetite disappeared at once, and I knew neither peace nor rest until the day came. Nor did its arrival bring me either; for by then I was worse than ever, and began haunting the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even departed from the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew perfectly well that this was so, I still felt it unsafe to leave the coach-office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a stretch; and in this unreasonable state I had completed the first half-hour of a watch lasting four or five hours, when Wemmick ran into me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said; “how are you? I should scarcely have imagined this was _your_ beat.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both flourishing, thankye,” said Wemmick, “and the Aged especially. He’s in wonderful feather. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I have an idea of firing eighty-two times, if the neighbourhood doesn’t object and that cannon of mine can withstand the pressure. However, that isn’t London conversation. Where do you suppose I’m going?”

“To the office?” I said, since he was moving in that direction.

“Next door to it, as good as,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We have a banker’s-parcel case on hand just now, and I’ve been down the road to take a look at the scene of action; so I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” Wemmick answered, very dryly. “But he is charged with it. You or I might be charged with it just as easily. Either of us might be accused of it, you know.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"4f4af080827325b3c2849054","rewritten_text":"THE following day the ghost was exceedingly weak and exhausted. The dreadful excitement of the past four weeks was beginning to tell on him. His nerves were utterly shattered, and the smallest sound made him start. For five days he remained in his room, and finally resolved to abandon the matter of the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, they plainly did not deserve it. They were evidently persons on a low, material level of existence, wholly unable to appreciate the symbolic significance of sensuous phenomena. The question of phantasmal apparitions and the development of astral bodies was, naturally, another matter, and not really within his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week, and to gibber from the great oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of each month; he could not see how he might honourably evade these obligations. It was certainly true that his life had been most wicked, but, on the other hand, he was extremely conscientious in everything relating to the supernatural. Accordingly, for the next three Saturdays, he paced the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every precaution to avoid being heard or seen. He took off his boots, stepped as softly as possible over the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and carefully used the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit that he adopted this final safeguard only with considerable reluctance. One night, however, while the family were dining, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and carried away the bottle. At first he felt somewhat humiliated, but later had the good sense to recognize the invention’s considerable merits, and it served his purpose to some extent. Even so, he was not allowed to remain unmolested. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor, causing him to stumble in the darkness, and once, while dressed for the role of ‘Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,’ he suffered a serious fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had made from the entrance to the Tapestry Chamber up to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult enraged him so greatly that he resolved on one last attempt to uphold his dignity and social standing, and decided to visit the insolent young Etonians the following night in his famous guise of ‘Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.’\n\nHe had not worn this disguise for over seventy years; indeed, not since he had so terrified pretty Lady Barbara Modish with it that she abruptly ended her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather and eloped to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton, declaring that nothing on earth could persuade her to marry into a family that permitted such a dreadful phantom to pace the terrace at twilight."}

{"request_id":"71ee1e33e1c61d94cf062fd8","rewritten_text":"“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to figure out where I was. The sun was already up, and I had been sleeping soundly. Pap stood over me, looking sour and sick, too. He said:

“What are you doing with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t remember anything about what he had been doing, so I said:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Well, I tried to, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t move you.”

“All right, then. Don’t stand there talking all day. Get out and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried up the riverbank. I noticed pieces of branches and other things floating downstream, along with bits of bark, so I knew the river had started to rise. I figured I would have a great time now if I were over in town. The June rise had always been lucky for me, because as soon as it began, cordwood came floating down, along with pieces of log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs together. All you had to do was catch them and sell them to the wood yards and sawmill.

I walked up the bank, keeping one eye out for Pap and the other for whatever the rising water might bring. Then, all at once, a canoe came floating by—a beautiful one, too, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I jumped headfirst from the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam toward it. I expected someone to be lying in it, because people often did that to fool others; when a man had pulled a skiff almost within reach, they would sit up and laugh at him. But this time there was nobody. It really was a drifting canoe, and I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I thought the old man would be glad when he saw it—it was worth ten dollars. But when I reached shore, Pap was still nowhere in sight. As I was pushing the canoe into a little creek like a gully, covered with vines and willows, I had another idea: I would hide it well, and instead of heading into the woods when I ran away, I would go about fifty miles downriver and settle in one place, so I wouldn’t have such a hard time walking.

The creek was quite close to the shanty, and I thought I heard the old man coming the whole time. But I got the canoe hidden, then stepped out and looked around a clump of willows. There was the old man farther down the path, taking aim at a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"65ceb8c6f6a25501332d25b2","rewritten_text":"With everything settled amicably and to everyone’s satisfaction, the contract was formally confirmed with another teacup of peppermint mixture. This was especially needed because the lady was trembling with excitement. While she drank it, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very good,” said that gentleman, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll call at Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send someone tomorrow morning. Was that what frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything in particular, dear,” the lady replied evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble insisted. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” the lady answered. “One of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” exclaimed Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t some impudence from one of those male paupers—”

“No, no, love!” the lady quickly interrupted.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble continued, “if I thought any one of them had dared to raise his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” the lady replied.

“They had better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, parish or otherwise, presume to do it; and I can tell him he wouldn’t do it a second time!”

Without all the violent gestures, this might not have seemed a very great compliment to the lady’s beauty. But Mr. Bumble accompanied his threat with so many warlike movements that she was deeply touched by this proof of his devotion. She declared, with great admiration, that he was truly a dove.

The dove then turned up his coat collar and put on his cocked hat. After exchanging a long and affectionate embrace with his future partner, he once again faced the cold night wind. He paused only a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward to abuse them a little, so that he could reassure himself that he was capable of filling the workhouse-master’s office with the necessary harshness. Satisfied that he had the right qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building with a light heart and bright dreams of future promotion. These thoughts occupied him until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper. Noah Claypole was never willing to do more physical work than was needed to eat and drink comfortably. So the shop was still open, although it was past the usual closing time. Mr. Bumble tapped the counter several times with his cane, but no one answered. Seeing a light through the glass window of the small parlor at the back, he ventured to look in and see what was happening. When he saw what was happening, he was extremely surprised."}

{"request_id":"e7b616812a520cfbfd1a6839","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue sky of heaven, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my prayer, you shall never see me again while they exist. Go home and begin your labors; I shall watch their progress with indescribable anxiety. And do not fear: when you are ready, I shall appear.”

With that, he suddenly left me, perhaps afraid that my feelings might change. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle’s flight, until he was quickly lost among the undulations of the sea of ice.

His story had taken the entire day, and the sun was near the horizon when he departed. I knew I had to hurry down toward the valley, since darkness would soon surround me; but my heart was heavy, and my steps slow. The effort of winding along the mountain’s narrow paths and placing my feet securely as I advanced confused me, occupied as I was by the emotions the day’s events had stirred. It was deep into the night when I reached the halfway resting place and sat beside the fountain. The stars appeared at intervals as clouds moved across them; dark pines stood before me, and here and there a broken tree lay upon the ground. It was a scene of extraordinary solemnity, awakening strange thoughts within me. I wept bitterly and, clasping my hands in anguish, cried, “Oh, stars and clouds and winds, you are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, crush sensation and memory; let me become nothing. But if you do not, go, go, and leave me in darkness.”

These were wild and miserable thoughts, but I cannot convey how the stars’ eternal twinkling weighed upon me, or how I listened to every blast of wind as though it were a dull, hateful sirocco coming to consume me.

Morning had dawned before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest, but returned at once to Geneva. I could not express my feelings even within my own heart; they pressed upon me with the weight of a mountain, and their excess buried my agony beneath them. Thus I returned home and, entering the house, presented myself to the family. My haggard, wild appearance caused intense alarm, but I answered no questions and scarcely spoke. I felt as though I had been placed under a ban—as though I had no right to claim their sympathy—as though I might never again enjoy their companionship."}

{"request_id":"a81c2b87d56dd0840d8325d1","rewritten_text":"But it is very remarkable that she should always hear Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so distinctly! However, she will not find her grandmama any deafer than she was two years ago; which is saying a great deal at my mother’s time of life—and it really is a full two years, you know, since she was here. We were never so long without seeing her before, and, as I was saying to Mrs. Cole, we shall hardly know how to have enough of her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed!—that must be a very great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You are very kind. Yes, next week. Everybody is so surprised; and everybody says the same obliging things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they can be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell will want the carriage himself on one of those days. So very good of them to send her all the way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, next Friday or Saturday. That is what she writes about. That is why she is writing out of rule, as we call it; for, in the usual course, we should not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, so I imagined. I was afraid there could be little chance of my hearing anything of Miss Fairfax today.”

“So obliging of you! No, we should not have heard, had it not been for this particular circumstance, her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted!—for she is to stay with us at least three months. Three months, she says so positively, as I am going to have the pleasure of reading to you. The case is, you see, that the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her father and mother to come over and see her directly. They had not meant to go until summer, but she is so eager to see them again—for until she married, last October, she had never been away from them even a week, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms, I was going to say, but at any rate different countries, and so she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I declare I do not know which, but we shall see presently in Jane’s letter—written in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, urging them to come over directly, and they would meet them in Dublin and take them back to their country seat, Baly-craig, a beautiful place, I fancy."}

{"request_id":"f739c81f78f3d479adce6585","rewritten_text":"Were our proud hopes destined to vanish thus? Our name had been written “a little lower than the angels;” and yet, behold, we were no more enduring than ephemera. We had styled ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and, lo! we were merely a “quint-essence of dust.” We had lamented that the pyramids survived the embalmed body of their builder. Alas! the humble shepherd’s straw hut we passed upon the road held within its structure the principle of longer endurance than the entire human race. How could this mournful alteration be reconciled with our former aspirations and our seeming powers?

Suddenly, an inward voice, distinct and articulate, appeared to say:—Thus, from eternity, was it ordained: the steeds that carry Time forward had this hour and its fulfilment fastened to them, ever since the void brought forth its burden. Would you read backward the immutable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! eternal, unchanging Necessity! who with tireless fingers art forever weaving the unbreakable chain of events!—I will not complain of thy deeds. If my human understanding cannot admit that all which exists is right; yet, since what exists must exist, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were not born for enjoyment, but for submission and hope.

Will the reader grow weary if I describe in detail our prolonged journey from Paris to Geneva? If I were to set down, day after day, in journal form, the accumulating miseries of our condition, could my hand record, or language supply words for, the variety of our suffering; the jostling and crowding of one dreadful event upon another? Patience, O reader! whoever thou art, wherever thou dwellest, whether of spiritual race, or descended from some surviving pair, thy nature will be human, and thy dwelling the earth; here thou wilt read of the deeds of the vanished race, and wonder whether those who endured what is written were made of frail flesh and delicate organization like thine own. {"request_id":"c0fdbbc44f7a8472c116acbb","rewritten_text":"“This must have been around that period of Mr Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “which has always made me especially curious. It must have been about the same time that he became known to my father and sister. I never knew him myself; I only heard about him. But there was something in his behavior toward my father and sister then, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that I could never fully reconcile with the man we see now. It seemed to show that he was a very different kind of person.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” cried Mrs Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but I heard him speak of them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I may be able to satisfy you about matters you would hardly expect; and as for his marriage, I knew everything about it at the time. I was aware of all the arguments for and against it; I was the friend to whom he confided his hopes and plans. Though I had not known his wife before, since her lower position in society made that impossible, I knew her throughout the rest of her life, or at least until the last two years, and can answer any question you may wish to ask.”

“No,” said Anne, “I have no particular questions about her. I have always understood that they were not a happy couple. But I should like to know why, at that time in his life, he rejected my father’s acquaintance as he did. My father was certainly ready to treat him with kindness and proper attention. Why did Mr Elliot withdraw?”

“Mr Elliot,” replied Mrs Smith, “had one aim at that point in his life: to make his fortune, and by a faster method than the law. He meant to do it through marriage. At least, he was determined not to damage his prospects through an imprudent marriage. I know it was his belief—whether rightly or not, I cannot say—that your father and sister, through their kindness and invitations, were trying to arrange a match between the heir and the young lady. Such a match could never have met his ideas of wealth and independence. That was why he withdrew, I assure you. He told me the whole story. He kept nothing from me. It was curious that, having just left you in Bath, my first and closest acquaintance after my marriage should be your cousin, and that through him I should constantly hear about your father and sister."}

{"request_id":"cb5601eeb8c4be61d26aa513","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams destined to fade like this? Our name had been written “a little lower than the angels”; and yet, behold, we were no better than mayflies. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and now we were a “quintessence of dust.” We had lamented that the pyramids had outlasted the embalmed body of their builder. Alas! The simple shepherd’s straw hut we passed on the road contained within its structure the principle of greater longevity than the entire human race. How could we reconcile this sorrowful change with our former aspirations and apparent powers?

Suddenly an inner voice, clear and articulate, seemed to say: Thus it was decreed from eternity: the steeds that carry Time forward had this hour and its fulfilment chained to them, from the moment the void brought forth its burden. Would you read backward the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! Eternal, changeless Necessity, who with busy fingers are forever weaving the indissoluble chain of events! I will not complain of your acts. If my human mind cannot accept that all that exists is right, yet since what must be, must be, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were not born to enjoy, but to submit and to hope.

Will the reader grow weary if I describe in detail our long journey from Paris to Geneva? If I recorded, day by day, in journal form, the accumulating miseries of our lot, could my hand write—or language provide words—to express the variety of our suffering, the jostling and crowding of one deplorable event upon another? Patience, reader! Whoever you are, wherever you dwell, whether of a spiritual race or descended from some surviving pair, your nature will be human and your home the earth. Here you will read of the deeds of the vanished race, and wonder whether those who endured what is recorded here were made of frail flesh and delicate bodies like your own. Indeed they were—so weep; for surely, solitary being, you will be gentle in disposition. Shed tears of compassion, but meanwhile give your attention to the tale, and learn the deeds and sufferings of your predecessors.

Yet the final events that marked our progress through France were so filled with strange horror and dark misery that I dare not linger over them in my account. If I dissected every incident, each tiny fraction of a second would contain a harrowing tale, whose smallest word would curdle the blood in your young veins. It is right that I should raise this monument of the former race for your instruction, but not that I should drag you through hospital wards or the secret chambers of the charnel house."}

{"request_id":"ab15566f8cb796176ce92ebe","rewritten_text":"_P.S._—Do tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are fashionable.

Lord Arthur looked so serious and unhappy as he read the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

‘My dear Arthur,’ she cried, ‘I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what shall I say about the clock? I think it is an excellent invention, and I should like one myself.’

‘I don’t think much of them,’ said Lord Arthur with a sad smile. After kissing his mother, he left the room.

Upstairs, he threw himself onto a sofa, and his eyes filled with tears. He had done his best to commit the murder, but both times he had failed, through no fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, yet it seemed that Destiny herself had betrayed him. He felt the emptiness of good intentions and the uselessness of trying to be noble. Perhaps it would be better to end the engagement altogether. Sybil would suffer, it was true, but suffering could not truly damage a nature as noble as hers. As for himself, what did it matter? There was always some war in which a man could die, some cause for which he could give his life; and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny bring about his doom. He would do nothing to help her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and Lord Arthur had to dine with them. Their shallow conversation and foolish jokes did not interest him. As soon as coffee was served, he left, making up an engagement to escape. On his way out, the hall porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to come the following evening and see an explosive umbrella that went off as soon as it was opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces. He had decided not to attempt any more experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat beside the river for hours. The moon looked through a mane of golden-brown clouds like a lion’s eye, while countless stars covered the hollow sky like gold dust scattered across a purple dome. From time to time, a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted away with the tide, while the railway signals changed from green to scarlet as trains screamed across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"02d6532c7a4ec89d4bceefb9","rewritten_text":"“I’m gwine, Massa Will—deed I is,” the negro answered promptly—“mos’ to de eend now.”

“_To the end!_” Legrand fairly shrieked. “Do you mean you are at the end of that limb?”

“Soon be at de eend, massa—o-o-o-o-oh! Lor-gol-a-marcy! what’s dis here pon de tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, greatly pleased, “what is it?”

“Why, ’tain’t noffin but a skull—somebody lef’ his head up de tree, and de crows done gobble every bit ob de meat off.”

“A skull, you say! Very well—how is it secured to the limb? What keeps it there?”

“Sure nuff, massa; mus’ look. Why, dis berry curous sarcumstance, pon my word—dare’s a great big nail in de skull, fastenin’ it to de tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do precisely as I tell you—do you hear?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Then pay attention—locate the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! hoo! dat’s good! Why, dare ain’t no eye lef’ at all.”

“Curse your stupidity! Do you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I knows dat—knows all about dat—’tis my lef’ hand what I chops de wood wid.”

“Of course! You are left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. So I suppose you can find the skull’s left eye, or the spot where its left eye was. Have you found it?”

There was a lengthy pause. At last the negro asked,

“Is de lef’ eye ob de skull on de same side as de lef’ hand ob de skull, too?—’cause de skull ain’t got not a bit ob a hand at all—nebber mind! I got de lef’ eye now—here de lef’ eye! What mus’ I do wid it?”

“Let the beetle pass through it, as far as the string reaches—but take care not to release your hold on the string.”

“All dat done, Massa Will; mighty easy ting to put de bug fru de hole—look out for him dare below!”

Throughout this exchange, no part of Jupiter could be seen; but the beetle he had allowed to descend was now visible at the string’s end, shining like a globe of burnished gold in the setting sun’s final rays, some of which still faintly lit the height where we stood. The _scarabæus_ hung entirely free of the branches and, if released, would have dropped at our feet. Legrand at once seized the scythe and used it to clear a circular area three or four yards across directly beneath the insect. When this was done, he ordered Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"cd1b7676e82e59622c1c72ff","rewritten_text":"After a while, twelve o’clock sounded from the tall Westminster tower, and with every stroke of the deep bell the night appeared to quiver. Then the railway lights were extinguished, leaving one lonely lamp shining like a great ruby upon a gigantic mast, while the city’s roar grew more distant.

At two he rose and wandered towards Blackfriars. How unreal it all appeared, how much like some fantastic dream! The houses across the river seemed formed from darkness. One might have thought that silver and shadow had remade the world. The vast dome of St. Paul’s showed through the murky air like a bubble.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he noticed a man bending over the parapet. When he drew closer, the man raised his head, and the gaslight fell directly across his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! The fat, flabby countenance, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the weak, sickly smile, and the sensual mouth could belong to no one else.

Lord Arthur halted. A splendid thought struck him, and he crept quietly up behind. In an instant he had grasped Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There was a rough oath, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over the parapet, but saw nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat spinning in an eddy of moonlit water. Presently that too disappeared, and no sign of Mr. Podgers remained. Once he fancied he saw the bulky, misshapen figure swimming towards the bridge staircase, and a dreadful sense of failure seized him; but it proved only a reflection, and when the moon emerged from behind a cloud, the feeling vanished. At last he believed that destiny’s decree had been fulfilled. He drew a profound sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

‘Have you dropped anything, sir?’ a voice suddenly asked behind him.

He turned and found a policeman holding a bull’s-eye lantern.

‘Nothing of consequence, sergeant,’ he replied with a smile. Hailing a passing hansom, he climbed in and ordered the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For the next several days he swung between hope and fear. At times he almost expected Mr. Podgers to enter the room, while at others he felt that Fate could not treat him so unjustly. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s address in West Moon Street, but could not bring himself to ring. He yearned for certainty and dreaded it.

At last it arrived. He was seated in the club smoking-room, drinking tea and listening somewhat wearily to Surbiton’s description of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered carrying the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"f2e1ae0422d8cb6445776ae9","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery horse, the same that had carried him onward to victory in Greece; he wore himself out with exhausting exercise, drowning the anguish of a troubled mind in bodily sensation.

By degrees he regained command of himself; at length, like one recovering from poison, he raised his head above the vapours of fever and passion into the quiet air of sober reflection. He considered what course was best. He was first impressed by the length of time that had passed since madness, rather than any rational impulse, had governed his conduct. A month had elapsed, and throughout it he had not seen Evadne. Her influence, connected with few of the lasting emotions in his heart, had greatly weakened. He was no longer her slave—no longer her lover: he would never see her again, and, by the completeness of his return, merit Perdita’s confidence.

Yet, as he reached this decision, imagination brought before him the wretched dwelling of the Greek girl—a dwelling she had refused to exchange for greater luxury out of noble and elevated principle. He recalled the splendour of her circumstances and appearance when he had first known her; her life at Constantinople, surrounded by every feature of oriental magnificence; and then her present poverty, her daily labour, her solitary condition, her faded cheek marked by hunger. Compassion filled his heart; he would visit her once more, contrive some means of restoring her to society and the enjoyment of her rank; their separation would then occur naturally.

Once more he reflected on how, during that long month, he had shunned Perdita, fleeing from her as from the pricks of his own conscience. But he was awake now; all this must be corrected, and future devotion wipe away the memory of this single stain upon the tranquillity of their life. The thought made him cheerful, and he calmly and firmly traced the conduct he would pursue. He remembered promising Perdita that he would attend that very evening—the 19th of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—a festival held in his honour. May this festival prove a good omen for the happiness of coming years. First he would call upon Evadne; he would not remain, but owed her some explanation, some recompense for his long, unexplained absence; then he would go to Perdita, to the world he had neglected, to society’s duties, the splendour of rank, and the pleasures of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had expected a complete transformation in Raymond’s manners and behaviour. She looked for open communication and a return to those affectionate habits of intercourse that had once made up the happiness of her life."}

{"request_id":"5378080b4908f24c4d7f3e90","rewritten_text":"Throughout dinner, Mr. Bennet hardly spoke; but once the servants had left, he decided it was time to converse with his guest. He accordingly introduced a topic on which he expected Mr. Collins to excel, remarking that he seemed especially fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort appeared quite extraordinary. Mr. Bennet could not have selected a better subject. Mr. Collins spoke at length in her praise. The topic raised him to an even greater solemnity than usual; and, with an air of the utmost importance, he declared that he had never witnessed such conduct in a person of rank—such affability and condescension as he had experienced from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both sermons he had already had the honour of preaching before her. She had also invited him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the previous Saturday to complete her quadrille party that evening. Many people considered Lady Catherine proud, he knew, but _he_ had never observed anything in her except affability. She had always addressed him as she would any other gentleman; she had not objected in the least to his mixing with the neighbourhood, or to his leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as possible, provided he chose carefully; and she had once visited him at his modest parsonage, where she entirely approved the improvements he had been making, and had even been so kind as to propose some herself—several shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and civil, I am sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very pleasant woman. It is unfortunate that great ladies generally are not more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden surrounding my humble dwelling is separated from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s residence, by no more than a lane.”

“I believe you said she was a widow, sir? Has she any children?”

“She has one daughter only, the heiress of Rosings and of a very considerable estate.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better provided for than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is, indeed, a most charming young lady. Lady Catherine herself declares that, in genuine beauty, Miss de Bourgh is greatly superior to the handsomest of her sex; for there is something in her features that distinguishes the young woman of noble birth.”"}

{"request_id":"d15f82f76c56046c04c22d8f","rewritten_text":"“Is that everything? It is not much, that! Many are under the Republic’s displeasure, and must peer out through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which is he?”

“I am he. Necessarily so, being the last.”

Jarvis Lorry has answered all the questions that came before. Jarvis Lorry has descended and now stands with one hand upon the coach door, replying to a cluster of officials. They stroll at their leisure around the carriage and leisurely climb onto the box, to inspect the scant luggage upon its roof; the country folk loitering nearby press closer to the coach doors and stare greedily inside. A small child, carried by its mother, stretches out its short arm so that it may touch the wife of an aristocrat who has been taken to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.”

“One may leave, citizen?”

“One may leave. Forward, my postilions! A good journey!”

“I salute you, citizens.—And the first danger is past!”

These too are Jarvis Lorry’s words, as he clasps his hands and gazes upward. Terror fills the carriage; there is weeping, and the laboured breathing of the unconscious traveller.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can they not be persuaded to go faster?” asks Lucie, clinging to the old man.

“It would appear that we were fleeing, my darling. I must not press them too hard; it would awaken suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see whether we are followed!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. Thus far, we are not pursued.”

Houses in twos and threes go past, along with lonely farms, crumbling buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and the like, open country, and avenues of bare trees. Beneath us lies the hard, uneven pavement; on either side is soft, deep mud. At times we turn into the bordering mud to escape the stones that clatter beneath and jolt us; at others we become stuck in the ruts and mire. Then the torment of our impatience grows so intense that, in our frantic fear and haste, we are ready to get out and run—hide—do anything rather than remain stopped.

From the open country, back among crumbling buildings, lonely farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like, cottages in twos and threes, avenues of bare trees. Have these men tricked us and brought us back by another road? Is this not the same place appearing twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see whether we are pursued! Hush! The posting-house.

At their leisure, our four horses are removed; at their leisure, the coach waits in the little street, stripped of horses and apparently never likely to move again; at their leisure, the fresh horses gradually appear, one after another; at their leisure, the new postilions come along, sucking and plaiting their whip-lashes; at their leisure, the old postilions count their money, add incorrectly, and reach displeased conclusions."}

{"request_id":"8f01be38e55b83e30f67b49f","rewritten_text":"“Are you speaking of—Mr. Knightley?”

“To be sure I am. I never could have meant anybody else—and so I thought you understood. When we spoke of him, it was perfectly clear.”

“Not quite,” replied Emma, with forced composure, “for everything you said then seemed to me to concern another person. I could almost insist that you had _named_ Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain the service Mr. Frank Churchill had done you, in saving you from the gipsies, was what you mentioned.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how strangely you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly the substance of what I said at the time. I told you I did not wonder at your attachment; that, considering the service he had performed for you, it was entirely natural:—and you agreed, speaking very warmly of your gratitude for that service, and even describing what you had felt when you saw him come forward to rescue you.—The whole impression remains strong in my memory.”

“Oh, dear,” cried Harriet, “now I remember what you mean; but I was thinking of something quite different then. It was not the gipsies—it was not Mr. Frank Churchill I meant. No! (with some emphasis) I was thinking of a far more precious circumstance—of Mr. Knightley’s coming to ask me to dance, when Mr. Elton would not dance with me; and when there was no other partner in the room. That was the kind act; that was the noble benevolence and generosity; that was the service which first made me feel how superior he was to every other person on earth.”

“Good God!” cried Emma, “this has been a most unfortunate—most dreadful mistake!—What can be done?”

“You would not have encouraged me, then, if you had understood me? At least, I cannot be worse off than I would have been if the other had been the person; and now—it _is_ possible—”

She stopped for a few moments. Emma was unable to speak.

“I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she continued, “that you should see a great difference between the two, whether in relation to me or to anybody. You must think one five hundred million times above me compared with the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—that if—strange as it may seem—. Yet you know they were your own words, that _more_ extraordinary things had happened, and matches of _greater disparity_ had taken place than one between Mr. Frank Churchill and me; and therefore it seems possible that even such a thing as this may have happened before—and if I should be fortunate beyond expression, as to—if Mr. Knightley should truly—if _he_ does not object to the disparity, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you will not oppose it, or try to place obstacles in the way.”"}

{"request_id":"0f88b4742b07b4cf3861128c","rewritten_text":"When I saw him in these moods, I often thought about the old philosophy of the Bi-Part Soul, and entertained the idea of a double Dupin—the creative one and the analytical one.

Let no one suppose from this that I am revealing a mystery or writing a romance. What I have described in the Frenchman was simply the result of an excited, or perhaps unhealthy, mind. But an example of the kind of remarks he made at such times will explain it best.

One night we were walking down a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. We both seemed lost in thought, and neither of us had spoken a word for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin said:

“He is a very small man, that is true, and would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_. ”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I replied without thinking. I had been so absorbed in my own thoughts that I did not at first notice how strangely his words matched them. A moment later I realized what had happened, and was deeply astonished.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “I cannot understand this. I admit that I am amazed and can hardly trust my senses. How could you know that I was thinking of ——?” I stopped, wanting to make certain that he really knew whom I had in mind.

“—— Chantilly,” he said. “Why do you stop? You were thinking that his small figure made him unfit for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been thinking. Chantilly had once been a shoemaker on the Rue St. Denis. After becoming obsessed with the theater, he had tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy of that name, and had been widely mocked for it.

“For Heaven’s sake, tell me,” I cried, “how you managed to read my thoughts in this matter—if there is any method behind it.” In truth, I was even more startled than I was willing to admit.

“It was the fruit seller,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the shoemaker was not tall enough to play Xerxes, and so on.”

“The fruit seller! You amaze me. I do not know any fruit seller at all.”

“The man who bumped into you as we entered this street—it may have been fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples had accidentally nearly knocked me down as we passed from the Rue C—— into the street where we stood. But how this could have anything to do with Chantilly, I could not understand at all."}

{"request_id":"16351d5e18891be6049edf64","rewritten_text":"Knights and horses clad in heavy armor could not move very swiftly. They would make the best speed possible, and with the ground now in good shape, free of snow and mud, they could likely manage seven miles at a stretch; they would need to change horses twice; they would reach us around six, or shortly afterward; there would still be ample daylight; they would spot the white cloth I was to bind around my right arm, and I would assume command. We would surround the prison and have the king out almost immediately. All things considered, it would be sufficiently grand and picturesque, though I would have preferred noon, because the scene would then possess a more theatrical quality.

Now, to add more strings to my bow, I decided to seek out some of the people I had once known and make myself recognized. That might get us out of our difficulty without help from the knights. But I had to act carefully, since it was dangerous work. I needed to put on splendid clothing, and it would not do to leap into it all at once. No, I must approach it gradually, purchasing one suit after another in shops far apart, and choosing a slightly finer article each time, until I reached silk and velvet and was prepared for my undertaking. So I set out.

But the plan collapsed like scat! At the very first corner I turned, I ran straight into one of our slaves, prowling about with a watchman. I happened to cough, and he shot me a sudden glance that pierced to my marrow. I supposed he thought he had heard that cough before. I turned at once into a shop and moved down along the counter, pricing goods while keeping watch from the corner of my eye. Those men had halted and were speaking together, peering in through the doorway. I resolved to escape by the rear, if a rear exit existed, and asked the shopwoman whether I might go out there to search for the escaped slave, who was thought to be hiding somewhere behind the shop. I told her I was an officer in disguise, that my partner was at the door with one of the murderers under arrest, and asked whether she would kindly go there and tell him he need not wait, but should immediately proceed to the far end of the back alley and be ready to intercept the man when I drove him out.

She was aflame with eagerness to see one of the already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand without delay."}

{"request_id":"6ef7ed5adf1f8a39f0c864e4","rewritten_text":"He got up and left the room with my nurse, and shortly afterward my father came in.

At that moment, nothing could have pleased me more than my father’s arrival. I reached out my hand to him and exclaimed,

“Are you safe, then—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father reassured me of their safety and tried, by speaking of matters so dear to my heart, to lift my sinking spirits; but he soon perceived that a prison could not be a place of cheerfulness. “What a dwelling this is that you occupy, my son!” he said, gazing sadly at the barred windows and miserable state of the room. “You travelled in search of happiness, yet some fatality appears to follow you. And poor Clerval—”

The mention of my unfortunate, murdered friend caused an agitation too severe for my feeble condition; I burst into tears.

“Alas! Yes, my father,” I answered; “some destiny of the most dreadful nature hangs over me, and I must live to accomplish it, or surely I would have died upon Henry’s coffin.”

We were not permitted to speak for long, since the precarious condition of my health made every measure necessary that might preserve tranquillity. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted that I should not exhaust my strength through excessive exertion. Yet my father’s presence seemed to me like that of my good angel, and I slowly regained my health.

As my illness departed, I became consumed by a dark and gloomy melancholy that nothing could relieve. The image of Clerval, ghastly and murdered, remained forever before me. More than once, the agitation caused by these thoughts made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why had they preserved so wretched and detested a life? Surely it was so that I might accomplish my destiny, which was now nearing its end. Soon—oh, very soon—death would silence these throbbings and free me from the immense burden of anguish that pressed me toward the dust; and, in carrying out the sentence of justice, I too would sink into rest. Death still seemed far away, though the desire for it was constantly in my thoughts; and I often sat for hours without movement or speech, longing for some mighty upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer beneath its ruins.

The assizes drew near. I had already spent three months in prison, and though I remained weak and continually threatened with relapse, I was compelled to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court convened. Mr. Kirwin took upon himself every responsibility of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence."}

{"request_id":"cde0fa85c5d958f0189be4f0","rewritten_text":"‘Well, _monsieur le mauvais sujet_,’ cried the old lady as he entered the room, ‘why haven’t you come to see me all this time?’

‘My dear Lady Clem, I never have a moment to myself,’ said Lord Arthur, smiling.

‘I suppose you mean that you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying _chiffons_ and talking nonsense? I cannot understand why people make such a fuss about marriage. In my day, we never dreamed of flirting in public—or in private, for that matter.’

‘I assure you, I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her dressmakers.’

‘Of course; that is the only reason you come to visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder that you men never learn. _On a fait des folies pour moi_, and now here I am, a poor rheumatic creature with a false front and a bad temper. If it were not for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can find, I do not think I could get through the day. Doctors are useless, except for taking one’s money. They cannot even cure my heartburn.’

‘I have brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,’ said Lord Arthur seriously. ‘It is a wonderful thing, invented by an American.’

‘I do not think I like American inventions, Arthur. I am quite sure I do not. I read some American novels recently, and they were complete nonsense.’

‘Oh, but there is nothing nonsensical about this, Lady Clem! I assure you, it is a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.’ Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and handed it to her.

‘Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a present? That is very sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a _bonbon_. I’ll take it at once.’

‘Good heavens, Lady Clem!’ cried Lord Arthur, catching her hand. ‘You must not do anything of the kind. It is a homoeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it could do you great harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You will be astonished by the result.’

‘I should like to take it now,’ said Lady Clementina, holding the little transparent capsule up to the light, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. ‘I am sure it is delicious. The fact is, although I hate doctors, I love medicines. However, I will keep it until my next attack.’

‘And when will that be?’ Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"f092357cdec885b603974c3d","rewritten_text":"If, however, you want one for home use, I can provide you with an excellent device and guarantee that you will be satisfied with the result. May I ask whom it is intended for? If it is for the police, or for anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I am afraid I can do nothing for you. English detectives are truly our best friends, and I have always found that, by relying on their stupidity, we can do exactly as we please. I could not spare one of them.’

‘I assure you,’ said Lord Arthur, ‘that it has nothing to do with the police. In fact, the clock is intended for the Dean of Chichester.’

‘Good heavens! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do these days.’

‘I am afraid you overestimate me, Herr Winckelkopf,’ said Lord Arthur, blushing. ‘The truth is, I know nothing at all about theology.’

‘Then it is purely a private matter?’

‘Entirely private.’

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room, returning a few minutes later with a round cake of dynamite about the size of a penny and a pretty little French clock, topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face brightened when he saw it. ‘That is exactly what I want,’ he exclaimed. ‘Now tell me how it goes off.’

‘Ah! That is my secret,’ replied Herr Winckelkopf, regarding his invention with justifiable pride. ‘Tell me when you want it to explode, and I will set the mechanism for that exact moment.’

‘Well, today is Tuesday, and if you could send it at once—’

‘That is impossible; I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might send it tomorrow.’

‘Oh, that will be quite soon enough!’ said Lord Arthur politely. ‘If it is delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning, that will do. As for the explosion, say Friday at exactly noon. The Dean is always at home at that hour.’

‘Friday, at noon,’ repeated Herr Winckelkopf, making a note of it in a large ledger lying on a bureau near the fireplace.

‘And now,’ said Lord Arthur, rising, ‘please tell me how much I owe you.’

‘It is such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I do not wish to charge you. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and the carriage about five shillings. I am only too happy to oblige any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.’

‘But your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?’"}

{"request_id":"f072cbb2fa376fc5ff4d8691","rewritten_text":"There was something so striking in the growing intensity of Mr. Wopsle’s eye. He seemed to be turning over so many thoughts and becoming so confused that I could not understand him. I kept thinking about it long after he had risen into the clouds inside a large watch-case, and still I could not understand it. I was thinking about it when I left the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me near the door.

“How are you?” I asked, shaking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It is the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, falling again into his confused expression. “And yet I could swear it was him.”

Alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Whether I would have noticed him at first if you had not been there,” said Mr. Wopsle, continuing in the same confused manner, “I cannot say for certain; but I think I would have.”

Without meaning to, I looked around me, as I had grown used to doing on my way home. His mysterious words sent a chill through me.

“Oh! He cannot be seen now,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I did. I saw him go.”

Because I had reason to be suspicious, I even suspected the poor actor. I feared he was trying to trap me into admitting something. So I watched him as we walked on together, but said nothing.

“I had the foolish idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were completely unaware of him, sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

That earlier chill came over me again, but I was determined not to speak yet. His words could easily mean that someone had sent him to make me connect these hints with Provis. Of course, I was completely certain that Provis had not been there.

“I suppose you wonder at me, Mr. Pip; indeed, I can see that you do. But it is so strange! You will hardly believe what I am about to tell you. I could scarcely believe it myself if you told it to me.”

“Really?” I said.

“Yes, really. Mr. Pip, do you remember a certain Christmas Day long ago, when you were a small child, and I dined at Gargery’s? Some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs repaired.”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember that two convicts were being chased, that we joined the search, that Gargery carried you on his back, and that I led the way while you kept up with me as best you could?”"}

{"request_id":"1e73521e5f123db0e09f94d9","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?” demanded Oliver.

“Hush!” answered the Dodger. “Do you see that old cove at the book-stall?”

“The old gentleman across the way?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A prime plant,” remarked Master Charley Bates.

Oliver glanced from one to the other in profound surprise, but was given no chance to ask questions; for the two boys crept across the road and slipped in close behind the old gentleman to whom they had pointed. Oliver followed a few paces behind them; and, uncertain whether to go forward or turn back, stood watching in silent astonishment.

The old gentleman looked a highly respectable person, with a powdered head and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, white trousers, and carried a smart bamboo cane beneath his arm. He had taken a book from the stall and stood there reading it as intently as though he were seated in his own study, in his elbow-chair. It is quite possible that he imagined himself there; for his abstraction made it clear that he noticed neither the book-stall, nor the street, nor the boys—in short, nothing except the book itself. He read straight through it, turning the leaf upon reaching the bottom of each page, beginning at the top line of the next, and proceeding steadily with the greatest interest and eagerness.

What were Oliver’s horror and alarm, as he stood a few paces away with his eyelids opened as wide as they could go, when he saw the Dodger thrust his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! He watched him pass it to Charley Bates; and then saw them both run around the corner at full speed!

In an instant, the entire mystery of the handkerchiefs, watches, jewels, and the Jew came rushing into the boy’s mind.

For a moment he stood there, the blood tingling through every vein with such terror that he felt as though he were in a blazing fire; then, bewildered and frightened, he turned and ran, making off as quickly as his feet could carry him, without knowing what he was doing.

The whole thing had happened within a minute. At the very moment Oliver started to run, the old gentleman put his hand into his pocket, discovered that his handkerchief was gone, and wheeled sharply around. Seeing the boy hurrying away at such speed, he naturally took him for the thief; and, crying “Stop thief!” at the top of his voice, set off after him, book in hand."}

{"request_id":"a4fd9d6ff2a289086b09ba68","rewritten_text":"At the center of this crack I saw a white spot, but at first I could not tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus and looked again. This time I recognized it as a human skull.

“After making this discovery, I was so confident that I believed the mystery solved. The words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could refer only to the skull’s position on the tree. And ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ could have only one meaning in a search for buried treasure. I understood that a bullet was to be dropped through the skull’s left eye, and that a straight line drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’—the place where the bullet landed—and then extended fifty feet would mark a specific point. Beneath that point, I thought, there might well be a valuable deposit.”

“All this,” I said, “is very clear and, though clever, still simple and exact. What happened after you left the Bishop’s Hotel?”

“Having carefully noted the tree’s position, I turned toward home. But the moment I left ‘the devil’s seat,’ the circular opening disappeared, and no matter how I turned, I could not see it again. To me, the most ingenious part of the whole matter is this fact—for repeated experiments have convinced me it is one: the circular opening can be seen from no other reachable viewpoint than the narrow ledge on the face of the rock.

“Jupiter had accompanied me on this trip to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel.’ He had probably noticed for several weeks how distracted I was, and took special care not to leave me alone. But the next day I rose very early, managed to slip away from him, and went into the hills to look for the tree. After much effort I found it. When I returned that night, my valet offered to flog me. I believe you know the rest of the adventure as well as I do.”

“I suppose,” I said, “that you missed the spot on your first attempt to dig because Jupiter foolishly let the bug fall through the skull’s right eye instead of its left.”

“Exactly. This mistake shifted the ‘shot’—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been directly beneath the ‘shot,’ the error would have mattered little. But ‘the shot’ and the nearest point of the tree were only two points used to establish a direction. Naturally, though the error was small at first, it grew as we followed the line, and after fifty feet it had led us completely away from the treasure.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9f710a144ff51b9587266c2e","rewritten_text":"We both agreed in loving Adrian, though Perdita, still not fully beyond childhood, could not appreciate the extent of his merits as I did, or feel the same sympathy with his pursuits and opinions. I was always with him. There was such sensitivity and sweetness in his nature that it gave our conversations a tender, almost unearthly quality. Yet he could also be as cheerful as a lark singing from its lofty tower, as soaring in thought as an eagle, and as innocent as the gentle-eyed dove. He could dispel Perdita’s seriousness and remove the sting from the tormenting energy of my nature. I looked back on my restless desires and painful struggles with my fellow beings as on a troubled dream, and felt as changed as though I had passed into another form, whose new senses and nervous system had altered the reflection of the visible universe in the mind’s mirror. But I had not changed in that way; I remained the same in strength, in earnest hunger for sympathy, and in my longing for active exertion. My manly virtues had not abandoned me, for the witch Urania spared Samson’s hair while he rested at her feet; yet everything in me had been softened and humanized. Nor did Adrian teach me only the cold facts of history and philosophy. While using them to teach me how to restrain my own reckless and uncultivated spirit, he also opened before me the living page of his own heart and enabled me to feel and understand its wondrous nature.\n\nThe former queen of England had, from her son’s earliest infancy, tried to plant bold and ambitious designs in his mind. She saw that he possessed genius and extraordinary talent, and cultivated these qualities so that she might later use them to advance her own purposes. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even tolerated his untamed love of freedom, hoping that it would, as so often happens, develop into a passion for command. She tried to raise him with resentment toward, and a desire for revenge upon, those who had helped bring about his father’s abdication. In this she failed. The accounts given him, however distorted, of a great and wise nation asserting its right to govern itself awakened his admiration; from an early age he became a republican on principle. Still, his mother did not give up. To his love of power and proud sense of birthright, she added deliberate ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying his character. Through praise, blame, and exhortation, she tried to discover and strike the right chords; and although the music produced by her touch sounded discordant to her, she based her hopes on his talents and remained certain that she would eventually win him over."}

{"request_id":"bec2fa7ac794172260b81ae7","rewritten_text":"It should be said in the young lady’s favor that she did not flatly declare she would not go; she merely expressed an emphatic and earnest wish to be “blessed” if she did—a polite and delicate way of evading the request, showing that she possessed the natural good manners that cannot bear to inflict on another person the pain of a direct and definite refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned from this young lady, dressed gaily, almost extravagantly, in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew soothingly, “what do _you_ say?”

“That it won’t do; so there’s no point trying it on, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes asked, looking up sourly.

“What I said, Bill,” the woman replied calmly.

“Why, you’re exactly the person for it,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody around here knows anything about you.”

“And since I don’t want them to, either,” Nancy replied in the same composed manner, “it’s rather more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes was right. Through a mixture of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman was eventually persuaded to undertake the errand. She was not held back by the same concerns as her agreeable friend; having recently moved to the neighborhood of Field Lane from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she did not fear being recognized by her many acquaintances to the same degree.

Accordingly, with a clean white apron tied over her gown and her curl-papers tucked beneath a straw bonnet—both items supplied from the Jew’s inexhaustible stock—Miss Nancy prepared to set out on her errand.

“Wait a moment, my dear,” said the Jew, producing a small covered basket. “Carry that in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key to carry in the other, Fagin,” said Sikes. “It looks real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, so it does,” said the Jew, hanging a large street-door key from the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There; very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears and wringing the little basket and street-door key in an agony of distress. “What has become of him? Where have they taken him? Oh, have pity, and tell me what has been done with the dear boy, gentlemen; do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"949851dee0fd2ee49fac0999","rewritten_text":"Looking over his letter once more while answering it had so softening an effect that it was especially necessary to strengthen her with a few firm expressions; and she was so deeply troubled by the thought of making him unhappy, considered so much what his mother and sisters would think and say, and was so eager that they should not imagine her ungrateful, that Emma felt, had the young man appeared before her then, he might have been accepted after all.

The letter was nevertheless written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet secure. She was somewhat downcast throughout the evening, but Emma could make allowance for her kindly regrets, sometimes easing them by mentioning her own affection, and sometimes by introducing the thought of Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” she said in a rather mournful voice.

“Nor, if you were, could I ever endure losing you, my Harriet. You are far too necessary at Hartfield to be spared to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I am sure I should never wish to go there; for I am never happy anywhere but at Hartfield.”

After a while she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be greatly surprised if she knew what had occurred. I am sure Miss Nash would—for Miss Nash considers her own sister very respectably married, and she is only a linen-draper.”

“One ought to regret seeing greater pride or refinement in a schoolmistress, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you such a chance of being married. Even this conquest would seem important in her eyes. As for anything better suited to you, I suppose she is entirely ignorant of it. The attentions of a certain person can scarcely yet have entered the gossip of Highbury. So far, I believe you and I are the only ones whose eyes and manners have revealed his meaning.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, and said something about being surprised that people should like her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton was certainly encouraging; yet, after some time, her tender feelings returned towards the rejected Mr. Martin.

“Now that he has received my letter,” she said softly. “I wonder what they are all doing—whether his sisters know—if he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he will not take it too much to heart.”

“Let us think of those absent friends who are more pleasantly occupied,” cried Emma. “At this very moment, perhaps, Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters, saying how much more beautiful the original is, and, after being asked for it five or six times, permitting them to hear your name, your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"64e46a10b3db8cfc9d08b8d7","rewritten_text":"He said nothing about it, however, until their visitor had departed for the night; but the instant he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said,—

“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”

Jane immediately went to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he answered, “and it gives me great pleasure to think that you will be so happily settled. I have no doubt that you will do very well together. Your tempers are not at all unlike. You are both so accommodating that nothing will ever be decided; so trusting that every servant will cheat you; and so liberal that you will always spend beyond your income.”

“I hope not. Carelessness or thoughtlessness with money would be unpardonable in _me_.”

“Spend beyond their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what can you mean? Why, he has four or five thousand a year, and probably more.” Then, turning to her daughter, she continued, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I am certain I shall not sleep a wink tonight. I knew how it would end. I always said it must happen at last. I was sure you could not be so beautiful without attracting someone! I remember, the very first time I saw him, when he came into Hertfordshire last year, I thought it very likely that you would come together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man ever seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were entirely forgotten. Jane was, beyond all comparison, her favourite child. At that moment she cared for nobody else. Her younger daughters soon began appealing to her for pleasures she might one day be able to provide.

Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield; and Kitty earnestly begged for a few balls there each winter.

From this time onward, Bingley was naturally a daily visitor at Longbourn, often arriving before breakfast and always staying until after supper, except when some barbarous neighbour, whom he could not possibly detest enough, had invited him to dinner, an invitation he felt bound to accept.

Elizabeth now had little opportunity to converse with her sister; for whenever he was present, Jane had attention for no one else. Yet Elizabeth found herself quite useful to them both during the periods of separation that occasionally had to occur. When Jane was absent, he always attached himself to Elizabeth for the pleasure of speaking about her; and when Bingley had gone, Jane regularly sought the same consolation.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by telling me that he had been completely unaware of my being in town last spring!"}

{"request_id":"d58636c1eef394b2e57d17d4","rewritten_text":"“What’s the trouble?”

I said:

“Pap, and Mam, and Sis, and—”

Then I broke down. He said:

“Oh, darn it, don’t take on so; we all have our troubles, and this will turn out all right. What’s the matter with them?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman of the boat?”

“Yes,” he said, looking fairly pleased with himself. “I’m the captain and the owner and the mate and the pilot and watchman and head deckhand; and sometimes I’m the freight and passengers. I’m not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be as blameably generous and good to Tom, Dick, and Harry as he is, throwing money around the way he does; but I’ve told him many a time that I wouldn’t trade places with him; for, I say, a sailor’s life is the life for me, and I’m damned if I’d live two miles outside town, where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and as much more besides. I say—”

I broke in and said:

“They’re in terrible trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, Pap and Mam and Sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferryboat and go up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there’s only one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good heavens! What are they doing there, for goodness’ sake?”

“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”

“I bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, they have no chance if they don’t get off mighty quick! How in the world did they ever get into such a mess?”

“Easily enough. Miss Hooker was visiting up there in town—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing—go on.”

“She was visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just at dusk she started across with her Black woman in the horse ferry to spend the night at her friend’s house, Miss What’s-her-name—I’ve forgotten her name—and they lost their steering oar, swung around, and drifted downstream, stern first, about two miles, and struck the wreck broadside. The ferryman, the Black woman, and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker grabbed hold and got aboard the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we came downstream in our trading scow, and it was so dark we didn’t see the wreck until we were right on it; and then we struck it broadside too. But all of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best creature! I almost wish it had been me, I do.”

“My goodness! It’s the most astonishing thing I ever heard.”"}

{"request_id":"0a96e306d854463e8dd4a49d","rewritten_text":"‘Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean, Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?’

‘No, thank you. I never eat anything now; but it is very kind of you all the same, and you are much nicer than the rest of your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ cried Virginia, stamping her foot. ‘You are the one who is rude, horrid, and vulgar. And as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to touch up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, including the vermilion, so I couldn’t paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald green and the chrome yellow, and finally I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white, so I could paint only moonlight scenes, which are always depressing to look at and not at all easy to paint. I never told on you, although I was extremely annoyed, and the whole thing was ridiculous; who ever heard of emerald-green blood?’

‘Well, really,’ said the Ghost, rather meekly, ‘what was I supposed to do? It is very difficult to obtain real blood nowadays, and since your brother started all this with his Paragon Detergent, I certainly saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. As for color, that is always a matter of taste: the Cantervilles have blue blood, for instance—the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don’t care for such things.’

‘You know nothing about it, and the best thing you can do is emigrate and broaden your mind. My father will be only too happy to give you a free passage. And although there is a heavy duty on spirits of every kind, there will be no trouble at Customs, since the officers are all Democrats. Once you reach New York, you are sure to be a great success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars to have a grandfather, and much more than that to have a family Ghost.’

‘ I don’t think I would like America.’

‘I suppose that is because we have no ruins and no curiosities,’ said Virginia sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ replied the Ghost. ‘You have your navy and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I will go and ask Papa to give the twins an extra week’s holiday.’

‘Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I am so lonely and unhappy, and I truly don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, but I cannot.’

‘That is absurd! You only have to go to bed and blow out the candle.’"}

{"request_id":"c456ad424f6337449bcb70a1","rewritten_text":"But how could I, a poor, bewildered village boy, avoid that wonderful inconsistency into which the best and wisest men fall every day?

“It may all be quite true,” I said to Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

In short, when I reached that point, I turned onto my face, seized the hair on either side of my head, and gave it a good wrench. All the while, I knew my heart’s madness was so extreme and misplaced that I was fully aware my face would have deserved it if I had lifted it by my hair and smashed it against the pebbles as punishment for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she tried no further to reason with me. She placed her hand—which was comforting, though roughened by work—on my hands one after another, and gently drew them from my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder to soothe me, while I cried a little with my face against my sleeve, exactly as I had in the brewery yard, and felt vaguely certain that someone, or everyone, was treating me very badly; I couldn’t say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” said Biddy, “and that is that you felt able to confide in me, Pip. And I’m glad of another: you know, of course, that you can rely on me to keep your confidence and always prove worthy of it. If your first teacher—dear me, such a poor one, and so much in need of teaching herself!—were your teacher now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would give you. But it would be a difficult one to learn, and you have gone beyond her, so it is no use now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and said, in a fresh and pleasant tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, rising, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall be, so that means always. Not that I have anything to tell you, because you know everything I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” said Biddy very softly, looking away toward the ships. Then, in the same pleasant tone as before, she repeated, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon faded into the summer evening, and it was very beautiful."}
