{"request_id":"ac6f11ea1b6b8060a9af7699","rewritten_text":"She and the children might stay quite comfortably.”

“Ah! Papa—that is what you have never managed to achieve, and I do not think you ever will. Isabella cannot bear to stay away from her husband.”

This was too true to argue with. Though he disliked it, Mr. Woodhouse could only sigh in submission; and when Emma saw that the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband had lowered his spirits, she quickly turned the conversation to something that would cheer him.

“Harriet must spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I am sure she will enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, are we not, Papa? I wonder which she will think the handsomer, Henry or John?”

“Yes, I wonder which she will. Poor little dears, how happy they will be to come. They are very fond of visiting Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they are, sir. I am sure I do not know anyone who is not.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John looks very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest, and he was named after me, not his father. John, the second, was named after his father. I believe some people are surprised that the eldest was not, but Isabella wanted him called Henry, which I thought was very sweet of her. And he is a very clever boy indeed. They are all remarkably clever, and they have so many charming ways. They come and stand beside my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a piece of string?’ Once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives were made only for grandpapas. I think their father is too rough with them very often.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you are so gentle yourself; but if you compared him with other fathers, you would not think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and strong, and if they misbehave, he may speak sharply to them now and then. But he is an affectionate father—Mr. John Knightley certainly is. The children are all very fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and throws them up to the ceiling in a very frightening way!”

“But they like it, Papa; there is nothing they enjoy more. They find it so delightful that, if their uncle did not make them take turns, whichever one started would never let the other have a turn.”

“Well, I cannot understand it.”

“That is true of all of us, Papa. Half the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other half.”"}

{"request_id":"8734197bc098f45839d8575d","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, began to wonder whether an honest life was not, after all, the best one. Convinced that it certainly was, he turned his back on the scenes of the past and resolved to reform himself in some new sphere of action. For a time he struggled greatly and suffered much; but, possessing a contented nature and a good purpose, he succeeded at last. From being a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he is now the merriest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand that writes these words falters as it nears the end of its task, and would spin out the thread of these adventures a little longer.

I would gladly linger with a few of those among whom I have moved for so long, and share their happiness by trying to portray it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of early womanhood, casting over her secluded path through life a soft, gentle light that fell on all who walked beside her and shone into their hearts. I would paint her as the life and joy of the fireside circle and the lively summer gathering; follow her through the sultry fields at noon, and hear the quiet tones of her sweet voice during the moonlit evening walk. I would watch her in all her goodness and charity abroad, and in the smiling, tireless performance of domestic duties at home. I would paint her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love for each other, spending whole hours together imagining the friends they had lost so sadly. I would summon once more those joyful little faces gathered around her knee, and listen to their merry chatter; recall the sound of that clear laugh, and call up the sympathetic tear shining in the soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks and smiles, and turns of thought and speech—I would gladly recall them all.

How Mr. Brownlow continued, day after day, to fill the mind of his adopted child with knowledge, growing more attached to him as his character unfolded and revealed the flourishing seeds of all he hoped the boy would become—how he discovered in him new traits of his early friend, awakening in his own heart old memories, melancholy yet sweet and comforting—how the two orphans, tested by adversity, remembered its lessons in mercy toward others, mutual love, and fervent gratitude to Him who had protected and preserved them—these are matters that need not be told."}

{"request_id":"6426dc1f0bf20f283dc1b49f","rewritten_text":"It was finally agreed that we would live together during my stay in the city. Since my financial circumstances were somewhat less strained than his, I was allowed to pay for renting and furnishing, in a style suited to the rather fanciful gloom of our shared temperament, a timeworn and grotesque mansion. It had long stood deserted because of superstitions we never investigated, and was slowly collapsing in a secluded, desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If the world had known our routine there, we would have been considered madmen—though perhaps harmless ones. Our isolation was complete. We received no visitors. Indeed, I had carefully concealed the location of our retreat from my former associates, while Dupin had not known, or been known by, anyone in Paris for many years. We lived entirely within ourselves.

My friend had a strange fancy (for what else can I call it?) for loving the night for its own sake; and, as with all his other peculiarities, I quietly adopted it, surrendering myself completely to his wild whims. The dark goddess could not always remain with us, but we could imitate her presence. At dawn we closed every shutter of our old house and lit a pair of strongly scented candles, which gave off only the faintest and most ghastly light. By their glow we occupied our minds with dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the arrival of true Darkness. Then we went out arm in arm, continuing the day’s discussions or wandering far and wide until late, seeking among the crowded city’s shifting lights and shadows that boundless mental stimulation which quiet observation can provide.

On such occasions I could not help noticing and admiring—though his powerful imagination had prepared me for it—a remarkable analytical gift in Dupin. He also seemed to take intense pleasure in using it, if not precisely in displaying it, and openly admitted the satisfaction it gave him. With a low, chuckling laugh, he would boast that most men, as far as he was concerned, wore windows in their chests, and would then support the claim with direct and astonishing demonstrations of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. At such moments his manner was cold and detached; his eyes were blank; and his voice, ordinarily a rich tenor, rose to a treble that would have sounded petulant were it not for the deliberate precision and complete clarity of his speech."}

{"request_id":"b6d5fd06b9a138caf10c0753","rewritten_text":"Saturday at noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke-powders, pawing at the air, and muttering gibberish as energetically as ever. But he looked discouraged, because naturally he had not even started a sweat in that well yet. At last I said:

“How does it look by now, partner?”

“Behold, I am now testing the most powerful enchantment known to the princes of occult magic in the lands of the East. If it fails, nothing can help us. Be silent until I am finished.”

This time he raised so much smoke that it darkened the whole area and must have made things unpleasant for the hermits, since the wind carried it toward them and rolled it over their dens in a thick, billowing fog. He poured out an equal amount of speech and twisted his body, cutting through the air with his hands in the strangest way. After twenty minutes he collapsed, panting and nearly exhausted. Then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns. Behind them came a crowd of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings, all drawn by the enormous smoke and all wildly excited. The abbot anxiously asked about the results. Merlin said:

“If any work a mortal could perform might break the spell binding these waters, the effort I have just made would have done so. It has failed. Therefore I now know that what I feared is true: the most powerful spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name no one may speak and live, has cast his spell upon this well. No mortal breathes, nor ever will, who can discover the secret of that spell, and without that secret no one can break it. The water will never flow again, good Father. I have done all a man could do. Let me go.”

Naturally, this threw the abbot into great confusion. He turned to me, his face showing his distress, and said:

“Ye have heard him. Is it true?”

“Some of it is.”

“Not all, then—not all! Which part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast his spell upon the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we are ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? Ye mean, not certainly?”

“That is what I mean.”

“Then ye also mean that when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he says something that is not necessarily true. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—that is, some small, even trifling, chance—of succeeding.”"}

{"request_id":"de70ade861fd63de1e230bb8","rewritten_text":"“I consider it one of the first refinements of civilized society.”

“Certainly, sir; and it also has the advantage of being popular among the world’s less civilized societies: every savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend dances delightfully,” he continued after a pause, when he saw Bingley join the group; “and I have no doubt that you are skilled in the art yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and I took great pleasure in watching you. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Do you not think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I never pay to any place if I can avoid it.”

“You have a house in town, I suppose?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once considered settling in town myself, for I enjoy the company of refined people; but I was not sure that the air of London would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for an answer, but his companion had no wish to give one. At that moment Elizabeth moved towards them, and Sir William suddenly thought of doing something very gallant. He called to her—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must let me introduce this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot refuse to dance when so much beauty is before you.” Taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy’s, who, though greatly surprised, was willing to accept it. But Elizabeth immediately pulled back and said, somewhat uneasily, to Sir William—

“Indeed, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please do not think I came this way to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with serious courtesy, asked for the honour of her hand, but she refused. Elizabeth was determined, and Sir William’s efforts to persuade her did not change her mind.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you; and although this gentleman generally dislikes the amusement, I am sure he can have no objection to pleasing us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He certainly is. But given the reason, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot be surprised by his willingness; for who would object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave him a playful look and turned away. Her refusal had not offended the gentleman, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him—"}

{"request_id":"5345729f849e611ec839fcd7","rewritten_text":"I want to see you permanently well connected, and for that reason it would be best for you to have as few unusual acquaintances as possible. Therefore, I say that if you are still in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your intimacy with his sisters will not lead you to become acquainted with his wife, who will probably be nothing more than a farmer’s daughter, without education.”

“Certainly. Yes. Not that I think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who had not received some education and been very well brought up. Still, I do not mean to set my opinion against yours—and I am sure I shall not seek his wife’s acquaintance. I shall always feel great regard for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and would be very sorry to give them up, since they are quite as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then certainly I had better not visit her, if I can avoid it.”

Emma watched her throughout these changing remarks and saw no alarming signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted that he had no other hold over her, and that Harriet would offer no serious resistance to any friendly arrangement of her own.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day as they were walking along the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after looking at Emma with great respect, turned to her companion with the most genuine pleasure. Emma was not sorry to have such an opportunity to examine him; and, walking a few yards ahead while they spoke together, she soon made her quick eye sufficiently acquainted with Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was very neat, and he looked like a sensible young man, but he had no other personal advantage. When compared with gentlemen, Emma thought he must lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s affections. Harriet was not indifferent to manners; she had voluntarily remarked upon her father’s gentleness with admiration as well as wonder. Mr. Martin looked as though he had no idea what good manners were.

They stayed together only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting. Harriet then came running to her with a smiling face and a flutter of spirits that Miss Woodhouse hoped to calm very soon.

“Just think of our happening to meet him! How very strange! He said it was pure chance that he had not gone around by Randalls. He did not think we ever walked along this road. He thought we went toward Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"3a83e56de6163d5d4f10690c","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl answered.

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl replied firmly, “one reason the lady knows and will support me in—I know she will, for I have her promise. And for this other reason besides: bad a life as he has led, I have led a bad life too. There are many of us who have followed the same courses together, and I will not turn against them—any of them—who might have turned against me, but did not, bad as they are.”

“Then,” said the gentleman quickly, as though this were the point he had been trying to reach, “place Monks in my hands, and leave me to deal with him.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you that, in that event, if the truth is forced from him, the matter shall end there. There must be circumstances in Oliver’s little history which it would be painful to expose before the public, and once the truth is drawn from him, they shall go free.”

“And if it is not?” the girl suggested.

“Then,” continued the gentleman, “this Fagin shall not be brought to justice without your consent. In such a case, I think I could show you reasons that would persuade you to give it.”

“Have I the lady’s promise for that?” the girl asked.

“You have,” Rose replied. “My true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never discover how you learned what you know?” the girl said, after a brief pause.

“Never,” replied the gentleman. “The information would be used against him in such a way that he could never even guess.”

“I have been a liar, and among liars, since I was a little child,” said the girl after another silence, “but I will trust your word.”

After both had assured her that she could safely do so, she began, in a voice so low that the listener could often scarcely make out even the meaning of her words, to describe by name and location the public-house from which she had been followed that night. From the way she sometimes stopped, it seemed that the gentleman was hastily writing down some of the information she gave him. When she had fully explained the place, the best position for watching it without attracting notice, and the night and hour when Monks most commonly visited it, she appeared to pause for a few moments, trying to bring his features and appearance more clearly to mind.

“He is tall,” said the girl, “and strongly built, though not stout; he has a furtive walk, and as he goes along he is always looking over his shoulder, first to one side and then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"df957051e737382be43504a7","rewritten_text":"Driving a peg carefully into the ground at the exact spot where the beetle had fallen, my friend took a tape measure from his pocket. He fastened one end to that point on the trunk of the tree nearest the peg, unrolled it to the peg, and then continued unrolling it in the direction established by the two points—the tree and the peg—for fifty feet, while Jupiter cleared away the brambles with the scythe. At the place reached, he drove in a second peg and drew around it, as a center, a rough circle about four feet across. He then took a spade himself, handed one to Jupiter and another to me, and urged us to begin digging as quickly as possible.

To tell the truth, I had never particularly enjoyed such work, and at that moment I would gladly have refused; night was approaching, and I was already exhausted from the exercise. But I could see no way out, and I feared that refusing would disturb my poor friend’s composure. If I could have relied on Jupiter’s help, I would not have hesitated to try to force the lunatic home; but I knew the old negro’s character too well to hope that, under any circumstances, he would assist me in a physical struggle with his master. I had no doubt that Legrand had been influenced by one of the countless Southern superstitions about buried treasure, and that his imagination had been strengthened by finding the scarabæus—or perhaps by Jupiter’s stubborn insistence that it was “a bug of real gold.” A mind inclined toward madness could easily be carried away by such suggestions, especially when they agreed with cherished preconceived ideas. I also remembered the poor fellow’s claim that the beetle was “the index of his fortune.” In the end, I was deeply troubled and perplexed, but finally decided to make the best of necessity: I would dig willingly, and so convince the visionary more quickly, through direct evidence, that his beliefs were mistaken.

Once the lanterns had been lit, we all set to work with a zeal better suited to a rational purpose. As their glare fell on our bodies and tools, I could not help thinking what a picturesque group we made, and how strange and suspicious our labor must have seemed to any intruder who happened by our hiding place.

We dug steadily for two hours."}

{"request_id":"42d47189d7964780b8e8221c","rewritten_text":"It is a strange thing, but everyone who vanishes is supposedly seen in San Francisco. It must be a charming city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you suppose has happened to Basil?” Dorian asked, raising his Burgundy to the light and wondering how he could speak of the matter with such composure.

“I haven’t the faintest idea. If Basil elects to conceal himself, that is no concern of mine. If he is dead, I don’t wish to think of him. Death is the one thing that ever frightens me. I detest it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked tiredly.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, drawing the gilt trellis of an open vinaigrette beneath his nostrils, “nowadays one can endure everything except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts in the nineteenth century that cannot be explained away. Let us take our coffee in the music-room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house feels rather lonely without her. Naturally, married life is only a habit, and a bad one. Yet one regrets losing even one’s worst habits. Perhaps those are the habits one regrets most. They form so necessary a part of one’s personality.”

Dorian made no reply, but got up from the table and went into the adjoining room, where he sat at the piano and let his fingers wander over the keys’ black and white ivory. When the coffee arrived, he stopped, glanced across at Lord Henry, and said, “Harry, has it ever occurred to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was extremely popular, and he always carried a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He was not intelligent enough to possess enemies. Certainly, he had extraordinary talent as a painter. But a man may paint like Velasquez and still be utterly dull. Basil was, in truth, rather dull. He interested me only once, when, years ago, he told me that he adored you wildly and that you were the ruling inspiration of his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” Dorian said, sadness audible in his voice. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some of the newspapers do. It does not strike me as likely at all. I know Paris contains dreadful places, but Basil was not the kind of man who would have visited them. He had no curiosity. That was his principal defect.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I had murdered Basil?” the younger man asked."}

{"request_id":"3bec15e8b6eb2b92e2011660","rewritten_text":"The mighty voice—we might call it inorganic, since we could not connect its sound with any mechanism of pipe or key—fell silent, and the girl, turning to help her aged companion, finally noticed us.

He was her father, and since childhood she had guided his sightless steps. They were Germans from Saxony who, having emigrated there only a few years earlier, had formed new bonds with the surrounding villagers. Around the time the pestilence broke out, a young German student had joined them. Their simple history was easy to understand. He, a nobleman, loved the poor musician’s beautiful daughter and followed them in flight from his friends’ persecution; but soon the great leveller came with an unblunted scythe, mowing down the tall flowers of the field along with the grass. The young man was an early victim. She preserved herself for her father’s sake. His blindness allowed her to maintain a deception that had begun by accident—and now, as solitary beings and the only survivors in the land, he remained unaware of the change. He did not know that when he listened to his daughter’s music, the silent mountains, lifeless lake, and unconscious trees were, apart from himself, her only listeners.

On the very day we arrived, she had been struck by the illness’s symptoms. She was paralyzed with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, blind father alone on the empty earth; yet she lacked the courage to reveal the truth, and the sheer force of her desperation drove her to extraordinary effort. At the usual evening hour, she led him to the chapel; and though trembling and weeping for him, she played, without losing the rhythm or missing a note, the hymn written to celebrate the creation of the adorned earth, soon to become her tomb.

We came to her like visitors from heaven itself; her strained courage and barely maintained composure vanished at the sight of relief. With a shriek she rushed toward Adrian, clasped his knees, and, saying only, “O save my father!” opened, amid sobs and hysterical cries, the long-sealed floodgates of her grief.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, and which she had pointed out to us in her final moments. Her father, at last aware of his daughter’s danger but unable to see the changes in her beloved face, stubbornly held her hand until death chilled and stiffened it. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until twelve hours later, when merciful death carried him into unbroken rest. They lie beneath the earth, the tree their monument; the sacred place remains vivid in my memory, framed by the craggy Jura and the distant, immeasurable Alps. The spire of the church they attended still rises among the surrounding trees; and though her hand is cold, I still seem to hear the divine music they loved drifting around them, comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"36c06c5576d0b59391a584cd","rewritten_text":"I was sorry to hear Jim say that; it made him seem so humble. My conscience stirred me more strongly than ever, until at last I said to it, “Leave me alone—it isn’t too late yet. I’ll paddle ashore at first light and tell.” At once I felt easy, happy, and light as a feather. All my troubles were gone. I began watching carefully for a light and half singing to myself. After a while, one appeared. Jim called out:

“We’re safe, Huck, we’re safe! Jump up and click your heels! That’s old Cairo at last, I just know it!”

I said:

“I’ll take the canoe and go see, Jim. It might not be, you know.”

He jumped up, prepared the canoe, put his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. As I pushed off, he said:

“Pretty soon I’ll be shouting for joy, and I’ll say it was all because of Huck. I’m a free man, and I could never have been free if it hadn’t been for Huck. Huck did it. Jim will never forget you, Huck. You’re the best friend Jim’s ever had, and you’re the only friend old Jim has now.”

I paddled away, sweating to tell on him; but when he said this, it seemed to take all the strength out of me. I went more slowly then, and I wasn’t sure whether I was glad I had started or not. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called:

“There you go, faithful Huck—the only white gentleman who ever kept his promise to old Jim.”

I felt sick. But I told myself, I have to do it—I can’t escape it. Just then a skiff came along with two men carrying guns. They stopped, and I stopped too. One of them said:

“What’s that over there?”

“A piece of a raft,” I said.

“Do you belong on it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Are there any men on it?”

“Only one, sir.”

“Well, five escaped slaves ran off tonight up above the bend. Is your man white or black?”

I didn’t answer right away. I tried, but the words wouldn’t come. For a second or two I tried to gather my courage and say it, but I wasn’t brave enough—I didn’t have the courage of a rabbit. I could feel myself weakening, so I stopped trying and said:

“He’s white.”

“I suppose we’ll go see for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I said, “because my father is there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft ashore where the light is.”"}

{"request_id":"e420f7886b43b3c5d9498849","rewritten_text":"“I agree. It’s the best thing. Would you just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, that won’t do for this. That’s good enough for little, worthless common things—especially with girls, because _they_ go back on you anyway and blab if they get angry—but there ought to be writing about a big thing like this. And blood.”

Tom’s whole being applauded the idea. It was deep, dark, and terrible; the hour, the circumstances, and the surroundings suited it perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a small piece of “red keel” from his pocket, turned his work toward the moon, and painfully scrawled these lines, emphasizing every slow downward stroke by clamping his tongue between his teeth and easing the pressure on the upward strokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry was filled with admiration for Tom’s skill at writing and the grandeur of his language. He immediately took a pin from his lapel and was about to prick his flesh, but Tom said:

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin’s brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“It’s poison. That’s what it is. Just swallow some of it once—you’ll see.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was complete. They buried the shingle near the wall with grim ceremonies and incantations, and the fetters binding their tongues were considered locked, with the key thrown away.

A figure now crept stealthily through a gap at the other end of the ruined building, but they did not notice it.

“Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this keep us from _ever_ telling—_always_?”

“Of course it does. It doesn’t matter _what_ happens; we have to keep quiet. We’d drop dead—don’t _you_ know that?”

“Yes, I reckon that’s true.”

They continued whispering for a little while. Presently, a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—less than ten feet away. The boys suddenly clasped each other in terror.

“Which of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, _you_, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t _do_ it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"94b3adb2345fc2949eda936e","rewritten_text":"“Shall I ask them? Or Miss Bates? She is closer.—And I do not know whether Miss Bates may not understand the inclinations of the other people as well as anyone. I think we do need a larger council. Suppose I go and invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you please,” said Mrs. Weston, hesitating a little, “if you think she will be of any use.”

“You will get nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and gratitude, but she will tell you nothing. She will not even listen to your questions. I see no advantage in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so amusing, so extremely amusing! I am very fond of hearing Miss Bates talk. And I need not bring the whole family, you know.”

At this point Mr. Weston joined them, and, hearing what was proposed, gave it his firm approval.

“Yes, do, Frank.—Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle the matter at once. She will enjoy the plan, I am sure; and I do not know a better person for showing us how to overcome difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming a little too particular. She is a constant lesson in how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady—?”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I did not remember at once. Certainly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And away he ran.

Long before he returned, bringing the short, neat, brisk-moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston, like a good-natured woman and a good wife, had examined the passage again and found its problems far less serious than she had first imagined—indeed, very slight; and there the difficulties of deciding ended. Everything else, at least in theory, was perfectly smooth. All the smaller arrangements of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper, seemed to arrange themselves; or were left as mere trifles to be settled at any time between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes.—Everyone invited was certainly to come; Frank had already written to Enscombe to suggest staying a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be refused. And it was to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she most warmly agreed that it must be. As a counsellor she was unnecessary; but as an approver, a much safer role, she was genuinely welcome. Her approval, at once general and detailed, warm and unending, could not fail to please; and for another half-hour they all walked back and forth between the different rooms, some suggesting, some listening, and all happily enjoying the prospect."}

{"request_id":"88882ab0764c6f332abe552e","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was deeply distressed by the marriage being postponed for a second time, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding dress, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. Sybil loved her mother dearly, but she had placed her entire life in Lord Arthur’s hands, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith. Lord Arthur himself took days to recover from his terrible disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely shattered. His excellent common sense soon returned, however, and his practical, sensible mind left him in no doubt about what he should do. Since poison had failed completely, dynamite, or some other kind of explosive, was clearly the next thing to try.

He therefore reviewed the list of his friends and relatives once more and, after careful thought, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of great culture and learning, was passionately fond of clocks and possessed a remarkable collection of timepieces, dating from the fifteenth century to the present day. Lord Arthur thought this hobby of the good Dean’s offered an excellent opportunity to carry out his plan. Finding an explosive device, of course, was an entirely different matter. The London Directory provided no information, and he felt there was little point in going to Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about the dynamite faction’s movements until after an explosion, and not much even then.

Suddenly he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strongly revolutionary views, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a life of Peter the Great and to have come to England to study documents concerning the Tsar’s stay in the country as a ship’s carpenter. It was generally suspected, however, that he was a Nihilist agent, and there was no doubt that the Russian Embassy viewed his presence in London with disapproval. Lord Arthur felt that he was exactly the man he needed, and one morning drove to his lodgings in Bloomsbury to ask for his advice and assistance.

‘So you are taking politics seriously?’ said Count Rouvaloff after Lord Arthur had explained the purpose of his visit. Lord Arthur hated every kind of swagger, however, and felt obliged to admit that he had not the slightest interest in social questions. He wanted the explosive device solely for a private family matter, in which no one but himself was involved."}

{"request_id":"7344610040bd90b3669a9e2c","rewritten_text":"But that is of little importance.”

“I may as well ask,” she replied, “why, when you clearly meant to offend and insult me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, your reason, and even your character. Was that not an excuse for rudeness, if I had been rude? But I have other reasons to resent you. You know I do. If my own feelings had not already decided against you, if they had been indifferent, or even favourable, do you think anything could persuade me to accept the man who has helped ruin, perhaps forever, the happiness of a dearly loved sister?”

As she spoke, Mr. Darcy changed colour; but the emotion quickly passed, and he listened without trying to interrupt her as she continued—

“I have every reason to think badly of you. Nothing can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you played there. You cannot deny that you were the chief, if not the only, cause of separating them; of exposing one to the world’s criticism for being fickle and unstable, and the other to its mockery for disappointed hopes, while bringing them both the deepest misery.”

She paused and saw, with great indignation, that he listened in a way that showed no remorse at all. He even looked at her with a smile of false disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did it?” she repeated.

He then replied with forced calm, “I do not wish to deny that I did everything I could to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. I have treated him more kindly than I have treated myself.”

Elizabeth refused to show that she had noticed this polite remark, but she understood its meaning, and it was unlikely to win her over.

“But this is not the only matter on which my dislike is based,” she continued. “My opinion of you had been settled long before it happened. Your character was revealed in the account Mr. Wickham gave me many months ago. What can you say about that? What imagined act of friendship can you use to defend yourself? Or what false account can you use to deceive others?”

“You take a strong interest in that gentleman’s affairs,” said Darcy, less calmly now, his face growing red.

“Whoever knows what misfortunes he has suffered could help feeling concern for him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated contemptuously. “Yes, his misfortunes have indeed been great.”

“And caused by you!” Elizabeth cried passionately. “You have reduced him to his present state of poverty—comparative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"43467633a5d123fc4868a5fb","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was deeply troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and begged him to reconsider, but the good-natured peer remained firm. At last, he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her. When, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first drawing-room on the occasion of her marriage, her jewels were universally admired. Virginia had received the coronet, the reward of every good little American girl, and married her boyhood sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming, and loved each other so deeply, that everyone rejoiced in the match—except the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had given no fewer than three expensive dinner parties for that purpose, and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis was extremely fond of the young Duke personally, but in principle he objected to titles and, in his own words, ‘was not without apprehension lest, amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity should be forgotten.’ His objections, however, were entirely overruled, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter leaning on his arm, there was no prouder man anywhere in England.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went to Canterville Chase, and the day after they arrived, they walked in the afternoon to the lonely churchyard beside the pine woods. At first there had been much disagreement over the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but in the end it was decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some beautiful roses, which she scattered over the grave. After standing there for some time, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat on a fallen pillar while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up at her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he threw away his cigarette, took her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.’

‘Yes, you do,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never told me what happened to you when you were locked in with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ Virginia said gravely."}

{"request_id":"f2634f6e414128dcaaf65b75","rewritten_text":"It was finally settled that we should share lodgings during my stay in the city; and since my worldly means were somewhat less strained than his, I was allowed to bear the cost of renting and furnishing, in a manner suited to the rather fanciful gloom of our united dispositions, a weathered and grotesque mansion. It had long stood empty because of superstitions we did not trouble to investigate, and was sinking toward ruin in a secluded, desolate quarter of the Faubourg St. Germain.

If the world had known the pattern of our existence there, it would have judged us madmen—though perhaps harmless ones. Our isolation was complete. We received no callers. In fact, I had taken care to conceal the place of our retreat from my former companions; and Dupin had not, for years, either known anyone in Paris or been known there himself. We lived solely within ourselves.

It was one of my friend’s whims (for what other name can I give it?) to love the night for its own sake; and, as with all his other oddities, I quietly adopted this one, surrendering myself wholly to his extravagant fancies. The black goddess could not remain with us at all hours; but we could imitate her presence. At the first light of day we shut every untidy shutter of our old house, and lit two candles whose heavy perfume produced only the most ghastly and feeble illumination. By their aid we occupied our minds with dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the arrival of genuine Darkness. Then we went out arm in arm, continuing the day’s discussions or wandering far and wide until late, seeking among the strange lights and shadows of the crowded city that boundless mental stimulation which quiet observation can provide.

On such occasions I could not fail to notice and admire—though his rich imagination had led me to expect it—a remarkable analytical power in Dupin. He also appeared to take keen pleasure in exercising it, if not precisely in exhibiting it, and openly admitted the satisfaction it gave him. With a soft, chuckling laugh, he would boast that most men, so far as he was concerned, wore windows in their breasts, and would then support the claim with direct and astonishing demonstrations of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. At these moments his manner became cold and abstract; his eyes were blank; and his voice, ordinarily a rich tenor, climbed to a treble that might have seemed petulant had not his delivery been so deliberate and perfectly distinct."}

{"request_id":"9bc684bde41cf210b6b64c2f","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had never happened. She believed he had drunk too much of Mr. Weston’s excellent wine, and was certain he would want to talk nonsense.

To restrain him as much as possible through her own conduct, she immediately prepared to speak with perfect calm and seriousness about the weather and the night. But scarcely had she begun, scarcely had they passed the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, when she found her subject interrupted—her hand seized, her attention demanded, and Mr. Elton actually declaring his love for her: making use of the precious opportunity, expressing feelings that must already have been well known, hoping—fearing—adoring—ready to die if she refused him; yet flattering himself that his ardent attachment, unequalled love, and extraordinary passion could not fail to have some effect, and, in short, firmly determined to be accepted as soon as possible. It was truly so. Without hesitation, without apology, and with scarcely any visible embarrassment, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s lover, was declaring himself _her_ lover. She tried to stop him, but in vain; he continued and said everything. Angry as she was, the thought of the situation made her resolve to control herself when she answered. She felt that half this foolishness must be caused by drink, and therefore hoped it might belong only to the passing moment. Accordingly, with a mixture of seriousness and playfulness, which she hoped would suit his half-and-half condition, she replied,

“I am extremely astonished, Mr. Elton. This to _me_! You have forgotten yourself—you take me for my friend. Any message to Miss Smith I shall be happy to deliver; but no more of this to _me_, if you please.”

“Miss Smith!—A message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean?” And he repeated her words with such confident emphasis and such boastful pretence of amazement that she could not help answering sharply,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behavior! I can explain it in only one way: you are not yourself, or you could not speak either to me or about Harriet in such a manner. Control yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to raise his spirits, not enough to cloud his understanding. He knew perfectly well what he meant; and after warmly protesting that her suspicion was deeply insulting, and briefly mentioning his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—while admitting his surprise that Miss Smith should have been mentioned at all—he returned to the subject of his own passion and pressed urgently for a favorable answer."}

{"request_id":"3953de66eb483f5469f4fcd1","rewritten_text":"You won’t, will you? Oh, you precious flat!”

“It’s naughty, ain’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll get scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. As he spoke, Master Bates seized one end of his neckerchief and held it upright in the air; then he let his head fall onto his shoulder and jerked a strange sound through his teeth, thus showing by a lively pantomime that scragging and hanging meant the same thing.

“That’s what it means,” said Charley. “Look at the way he stares, Jack! I never saw such prime company as that ’ere boy; he’ll be the death of me, I know he will.” Master Charley Bates, after laughing heartily once more, took up his pipe again, tears standing in his eyes.

“You’ve been badly brought up,” said the Dodger, examining his boots with great satisfaction after Oliver had polished them. “Fagin will make something of you, though, or you’ll be the first he ever had who proved unprofitable. You’d better start at once; you’ll come to the trade much sooner than you imagine, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates supported this advice with several moral warnings of his own. When these were exhausted, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into an enthusiastic account of the many pleasures belonging to the life they led, mixed with various hints that Oliver’s best course would be to win Fagin’s favour without delay, by the methods they themselves had used to obtain it.

“And always remember this, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as they heard the Jew unlocking the door above, “if you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the use of talking like that?” interrupted Master Bates; “he doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket-handkerchiefs and watches,” said the Dodger, bringing his speech down to Oliver’s level, “some other fellow will; then the fellows who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too, while nobody will be half a ha’p’orth better except the chaps who get them—and you’ve as good a right to them as they have.”

“Certainly, certainly!” said the Jew, who had entered without Oliver noticing. “It all lies in a nutshell, my dear; in a nutshell—take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together gleefully as he confirmed the Dodger’s reasoning in these words, and chuckled with pleasure at his pupil’s skill.

The conversation went no further then, for the Jew had come home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen before. The Dodger addressed him as Tom Chitling; and, after lingering on the stairs to exchange a few gallantries with the lady, he now appeared."}

{"request_id":"ad7b0a28bd06ea40daf8da6d","rewritten_text":"I hurried along, and we soon reached my college. Then I remembered—with a shudder—that the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there, alive and moving about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might encounter him. I begged him, therefore, to wait a few minutes at the foot of the stairs, while I rushed up toward my room. My hand was already upon the lock before I came to myself. I stopped, seized by a cold trembling. Then I flung the door wide open, as children do when they expect a spectre to be waiting on the other side; but nothing was there. I entered cautiously: the apartment was empty, and my bedroom too had been rid of its hideous guest. I could scarcely believe such good fortune, but once convinced that my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands with delight and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast; yet I could not restrain myself. Joy was not the only feeling possessing me; my flesh tingled with excessive sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for an instant; I leaped over the chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. At first Clerval thought my extraordinary spirits arose from happiness at his arrival, but observing me more closely, he noticed a wildness in my eyes that he could not explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, joyless laughter frightened and amazed him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “what, for God’s sake, is wrong? Do not laugh like that. How ill you are! What causes all this?”

“Do not ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, for I imagined I saw the dreaded spectre glide into the room; “_he_ can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I fancied that the monster had seized me; I struggled violently and fell in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had looked forward to with such joy had been so strangely transformed into bitterness. But I did not witness his sorrow, for I lay senseless and did not regain consciousness for a very long time.

This marked the beginning of a nervous fever that confined me for several months. Throughout that period Henry alone nursed me. I later learned that, aware of my father’s advanced age and inability to undertake so long a journey, and knowing how miserable my illness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this distress by hiding the severity of my condition."}

{"request_id":"0689f30b433d7c176c2d3e09","rewritten_text":"_P.S._—Do tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are fashionable.

Lord Arthur looked so grave and unhappy as he read the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

‘My dear Arthur,’ she cried, ‘I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what am I to say about the clock? I think it is an excellent invention, and I should like to have one myself.’

‘I don’t think much of them,’ said Lord Arthur with a sad smile, and, after kissing his mother, he left the room.

When he reached his room, he threw himself onto a sofa, and his eyes filled with tears. He had done his best to commit the murder, but on both occasions he had failed, through no fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, yet it seemed that Destiny herself had betrayed him. He was overwhelmed by the emptiness of good intentions, by the futility of trying to be noble. Perhaps it would be better to end the marriage altogether. Sybil would suffer, it was true, but suffering could not truly damage a nature as noble as hers. As for himself, what did it matter? There was always some war in which a man could die, some cause to which he could give his life; and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no terror. Let Destiny bring about his doom. He would not lift a finger to help her.

At half past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and Lord Arthur was obliged to dine with them. Their trivial conversation and idle jokes did not interest him, and as soon as coffee was served he left, inventing an engagement to escape. As he was leaving the club, the hall porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to come the following evening and inspect an explosive umbrella that went off as soon as it was opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces. He had decided not to attempt any more experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat for hours beside the river. The moon peered through a mane of tawny clouds like a lion’s eye, while countless stars speckled the hollow sky like gold dust scattered across a purple dome. From time to time a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted away with the tide, and the railway signals changed from green to scarlet as trains rushed shrieking across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"10141f7ea2158177f198f69a","rewritten_text":"He was short in stature, yet remarkably upright, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He opened his lecture with a review of chemistry’s history and the many advances made by learned men, uttering with fervour the names of its most celebrated discoverers. He then briefly surveyed the science’s present condition and explained many of its elementary terms. After conducting several preliminary experiments, he ended with a eulogy of modern chemistry, whose words I shall never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” he said, “promised impossibilities and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted and that the elixir of life is a chimera. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem made only for dabbling in dirt, and whose eyes are fixed upon the microscope or crucible, have truly performed miracles. They penetrate nature’s hidden recesses and reveal how she operates in her secret places. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered how the blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and nearly unlimited powers; they can command the thunder of heaven, imitate the earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows.”

Such were the professor’s words—or rather, let me say, the words of fate—spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as though my soul were wrestling with a tangible enemy; one after another, the keys that composed the mechanism of my being were struck. Chord followed chord, until my mind was filled with a single thought, a single conception, a single purpose. So much has already been accomplished, cried the soul of Frankenstein—far more will I achieve; following the path already marked, I will open a new one, investigate unknown powers, and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner being was in rebellion and confusion; I felt that order would eventually emerge, but lacked the power to bring it forth. Gradually, after dawn, sleep overcame me. I awoke, and the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. Only one resolution remained: to return to my former studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I possessed a natural aptitude. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private, his manner was even gentler and more engaging than in public, for the dignity he displayed during his lecture was replaced in his own home by the greatest affability and kindness."}

{"request_id":"25c3fc37f8d9649678ff42d1","rewritten_text":"This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must know that Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been rented by a wealthy young man from the north of England. He arrived on Monday in a carriage drawn by four horses to see the house, liked it so much that he immediately made an agreement with Mr. Morris, and will move in before Michaelmas. Some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, certainly! A single man with a large fortune—four or five thousand a year. What a wonderful thing for our girls!”

“How so? How could it affect them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “how can you be so tiresome? Surely you know I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that his purpose in moving here?”

“Purpose? Nonsense! How can you say that? But he may very likely fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I see no need for that. You and the girls may go—or you may send them alone, which might be even better; since you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might prefer you.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not claim to be anything special now. When a woman has five grown daughters, she should stop thinking about her own beauty.”

“In such cases, a woman usually has little beauty left to think about.”

“But, my dear, you really must go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes to the neighbourhood.”

“That is more than I can promise, I assure you.”

“But think of your daughters. Just imagine what a fine marriage it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go for that very reason; as you know, they usually do not visit newcomers. Indeed, you must go, because it will be impossible for us to visit him if you do not.”

“You are surely being too careful. I am sure Mr. Bingley will be pleased to see you; and I will send a short note with you, assuring him that I gladly consent to his marrying whichever girl he chooses—though I must say a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“I insist that you do no such thing. Lizzy is no better than the others: and I am sure she is not half as pretty as Jane, nor half as good-natured as Lydia.”"}

{"request_id":"ff507e28aaea28678d058e02","rewritten_text":"While these events were taking place at the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the same room from which the girl had taken Oliver—staring thoughtfully into a dull, smoky fire. He held a pair of bellows on his knees and seemed to have been trying to make the fire burn more brightly. But he had fallen into deep thought. With his arms folded over the bellows and his chin resting on his thumbs, he gazed absently at the rusty bars.

At a table behind him sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist. The Artful was playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. His face, always unusually clever, looked even more interested as he watched the game closely and studied Mr. Chitling’s cards. From time to time, when he had the chance, he gave them serious looks, wisely shaping his own play according to what he observed in his neighbour’s hand. Since it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he needed to drink from a quart pot on the table, already filled with gin and water for everyone.

Master Bates was also paying attention to the game. But, being more excitable than his skilled friend, he reached for the gin and water more often and made many jokes and unrelated comments, all quite improper during a serious game. Indeed, relying on their close friendship, the Artful more than once took the opportunity to lecture his companion solemnly about this bad behavior. Master Bates accepted every warning cheerfully, simply telling his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with another neatly phrased joke of the same kind. Mr. Chitling greatly admired the cleverness of these replies. It was noticeable that he and his partner always lost, and that this seemed to amuse Master Bates rather than anger him. At the end of every deal, Bates laughed loudly and declared that he had never seen such a merry game in all his life.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling sadly, as he took half a crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw such a fellow as you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

{"request_id":"29e66960ccdcc7517350fa3e","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining room, midnight began to boom from the clock tower. When the final stroke sounded, they heard a crash and a sudden, shrill cry. A terrible peal of thunder shook the house, a line of unearthly music drifted through the air, and a panel at the top of the staircase flew open with a loud bang. Virginia stepped onto the landing, looking very pale, with a small casket in her hand. At once they all rushed toward her. Mrs. Otis clasped her fiercely in her arms, the Duke covered her with frantic kisses, and the twins performed a wild war dance around them.

‘Good heavens, child, where have you been?’ Mr. Otis demanded, somewhat angrily, thinking she had played another foolish trick. ‘Cecil and I have ridden all over the country searching for you, and your mother has been frightened half to death. You must never play such practical jokes again.’

‘Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!’ the twins shrieked as they danced around.

‘My darling, thank God we have found you. You must never leave my side again,’ Mrs. Otis murmured, kissing the trembling child and smoothing her tangled golden hair.

‘Papa,’ Virginia said quietly, ‘I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he had done, and before he died he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.’

The entire family stared at her in silent amazement, but Virginia remained grave and composed. Turning around, she led them through the opening in the wood paneling and down a narrow secret passage, while Washington followed with a lighted candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a great oak door studded with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung open on its heavy hinges, revealing a small, low room with a vaulted ceiling and a single tiny barred window. A huge iron ring was set into the wall, and chained to it was a gaunt skeleton stretched full length across the stone floor. It seemed to be reaching with its long, fleshless fingers toward an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just beyond its grasp. The jug had evidently once held water, for its inside was coated with green mold. The trencher held nothing but a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her small hands, and began to pray silently, while the others stared in wonder at the terrible tragedy whose secret had finally been revealed."}

{"request_id":"14835041d53eaf0591efbfb5","rewritten_text":"Emma was not required, by anything she later discovered, to withdraw her poor opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her judgment had been largely correct. As Mrs. Elton appeared to her at this second meeting, so she appeared whenever they met again—self-important, presumptuous, familiar, ignorant, and ill-bred. She possessed a little beauty and a little accomplishment, but so little judgment that she imagined herself arriving with superior knowledge of the world to enliven and improve a country neighbourhood; and she believed Miss Hawkins had occupied such a position in society that only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could exceed it.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton’s opinion differed at all from his wife’s. He seemed not only happy with her, but proud of her. He had the air of congratulating himself on having brought such a woman to Highbury, one whom even Miss Woodhouse could not equal; and most of her new acquaintances, inclined to praise, or unaccustomed to judging, following Miss Bates’s goodwill, or simply assuming that the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she claimed, were perfectly satisfied. Thus Mrs. Elton’s praises passed from one person to another as they naturally would, unchecked by Miss Woodhouse, who readily continued her first contribution and spoke graciously of her as “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings towards Emma changed. Probably offended by the little encouragement her offers of intimacy received, she withdrew in turn and gradually became much colder and more distant; and although the result was agreeable, the ill will that caused it necessarily increased Emma’s dislike. Her manners, and Mr. Elton’s as well, were unpleasant towards Harriet. They were mocking and neglectful. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet; but the feelings that could inspire such conduct lowered them both considerably. There could be no doubt that poor Harriet’s attachment had been offered up to marital openness, and that her own part in the story, presented in the least favourable light for her and the most comforting for him, had very likely been revealed as well. She was, naturally, the object of their shared dislike. When they had nothing else to discuss, it would always be easy to begin attacking Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they dared not show by openly disrespecting her found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong liking to Jane Fairfax, and did so from the beginning. It was not merely that, while she was at war with one young woman, the other might naturally seem more appealing; she had liked Jane from the very first. Nor was she content simply to express a natural and reasonable admiration. Without being asked, invited, or entitled to do so, she insisted on offering her assistance and friendship. Before Emma had lost her confidence, and around their third meeting, she heard all Mrs. Elton’s chivalrous plans on the subject."}

{"request_id":"7e159621399d3fe00481c90b","rewritten_text":"After I had sent them in, I could not stay away from the places where they were, feeling as though they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near. In this unreasonable agitation and distress of mind, I would wander the streets in the evening, passing those offices and houses where I had left the petitions. Even now, the tired western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their lines of severe, closed mansions and their long rows of lamps, seem melancholy to me because of that association.

The daily visits I was allowed to make him had now been shortened, and he was watched more closely. Seeing, or imagining, that I was suspected of intending to carry poison to him, I asked to be searched before sitting beside his bed, and told the officer who was always present that I was ready to do anything that might convince him of the purity of my intentions. No one was unkind to him or to me. There was a duty to perform, and it was performed, but without harshness. The officer always assured me that he was worse, and some of the other sick prisoners in the room, together with prisoners who attended them as nurses—criminals, but, thank God, not without kindness—always gave the same account.

As the days passed, I observed increasingly that he would lie quietly gazing at the white ceiling, his face lacking all brightness until one of my words lit it for a moment, after which the light would fade again. At times he was nearly, or entirely, unable to speak; then he would reply by gently pressing my hand, and I gradually came to understand him very well.

The days had reached ten when I saw a greater change in him than before. His eyes were directed towards the door, and they brightened when I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said, as I sat beside his bed, “I thought you was late. But I knowed you couldn’t be that.”

“It is exactly the time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So as not to lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand without speaking, unable to forget that I had once intended to desert him.

“And the best thing of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable alonger me, since I was under a dark cloud, than when the sun shone.”"}

{"request_id":"48333508de145324a4cc1818","rewritten_text":"If not, and you appeal to my forbearance and to the mercy of those you have deeply injured, sit down without a word in that chair. It has been waiting for you for two whole days.”

Monks muttered some unintelligible words, but still hesitated.

“You will act promptly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and the alternative will be gone forever.”

The man continued to hesitate.

“I have no wish to argue,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and, since I am defending the most precious interests of others, I have no right to do so.”

“Is there—” Monks asked falteringly, “is there—no middle course?”

“None.”

Monks looked anxiously at the old gentleman; but, seeing in his face nothing but severity and determination, he entered the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and return when I ring.”

The men obeyed, leaving the two alone together.

“This is fine treatment, sir,” said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “It is because the hopes and wishes of our young and happy years were bound up with him, and with that fair creature of his blood and family who returned to her God in youth and left me here a solitary, lonely man. It is because he knelt beside me at his only sister’s deathbed when he was still a boy, on the morning that would—but Heaven willed otherwise—have made her my young wife. It is because my scarred heart clung to him from that time onward, through all his trials and errors, until he died. It is because old memories and associations filled my heart, and even seeing you brings back thoughts of him. It is because of all these things that I am moved to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to blush for your unworthiness as the bearer of his name.”

“What does the name have to do with it?” asked the other, after watching, partly in silence and partly with stubborn wonder, his companion’s agitation. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “Nothing to you. But it was hers, and even now, after all these years, it brings back to me, an old man, the warmth and thrill I once felt merely hearing it spoken by a stranger. I am very glad you have changed it—very—very.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks, retaining his assumed name, after a long silence during which he had jerked himself back and forth in sullen defiance while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by one hand."}

content.text: {"request_id":"4f107ad445c2ed16dc7810af","rewritten_text":"This brief explanation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma great pleasure. It became one of the pleasant recollections of the ball, which she strolled about the lawn next morning to savour.—She was exceedingly glad that they had reached so good an understanding concerning the Eltons, and that their opinions of husband and wife agreed so closely; while his praise of Harriet, and his admission in her favour, was especially gratifying. The Eltons’ impertinence, which for several minutes had threatened to spoil the remainder of her evening, had proved the cause of some of its greatest satisfactions; and she anticipated another happy consequence—the cure of Harriet’s infatuation.—From Harriet’s way of describing the matter before they left the ballroom, she entertained strong hopes. It appeared that her eyes had suddenly been opened, and that she could now perceive Mr. Elton was not the superior being she had imagined. The fever had passed, and Emma had little fear that harmful politeness would make the pulse beat quickly again. She relied on the Eltons’ ill feelings to provide all the pointed neglect that might still be needed.—Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not too deeply in love, and Mr. Knightley not disposed to quarrel with her—how happy a summer lay before her! She was not to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her he could not give himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, since he was expected home by midday. She felt no disappointment. Having settled all these matters, examined them from every side, and set them right, she was turning toward the house, her spirits renewed for the claims of the two little boys and their grandfather, when the large iron sweep-gate opened, and two people entered whom she had never expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning upon his arm—Harriet herself!—One moment was enough to assure her that something extraordinary had occurred. Harriet looked pale and terrified, while he was attempting to comfort her.—The iron gates and the front door stood less than twenty yards apart; all three were soon in the hall, and Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted. A young lady who faints must be restored; questions must be answered, and surprises explained. Such occurrences are highly interesting, but their suspense cannot continue long. In a few minutes Emma knew the whole story. Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour-boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also attended the ball, had gone out together and taken the Richmond road, which, though it seemed public enough to be safe, had caused them alarm.—About half a mile beyond Highbury, after a sudden turn and with elms casting deep shade on either side, it became for a considerable distance extremely secluded; and when the young ladies had proceeded some way along it, they suddenly noticed, a short distance ahead, on a wider patch of grass beside the road, a group of gipsies."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e9bc4dae8e41d3e9d2055618","rewritten_text":"“April 19th. This morning, to my great joy, at about nine o’clock, with the moon’s surface frighteningly near and my apprehensions at their height, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs of a change in the atmosphere. By ten, I had reason to believe its density had increased considerably. By eleven, very little effort was needed at the apparatus; and at twelve, with some hesitation, I ventured to unscrew the tourniquet. When I felt no discomfort from doing so, I finally opened the elastic chamber wide and detached it from around the car. As might have been expected, spasms and a violent headache immediately followed an experiment so rash and dangerous. But these and the other difficulties of breathing were not severe enough to endanger my life, so I resolved to endure them as best I could, since I would soon leave them behind as I approached the denser layers near the moon. This approach, however, remained extremely rapid; and it soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably not been mistaken in expecting an atmosphere dense in proportion to the satellite’s mass, I had been wrong to suppose that this density, even at the surface, was sufficient to support the great weight of my balloon’s car. Yet it should have been so, and to the same degree as at Earth, if the actual gravity of bodies on either planet were assumed to correspond to the condensation of its atmosphere. That it was not so, however, was proved well enough by my headlong descent; why it was not so can only be explained by reference to those possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. In any event, I was now close to the planet and descending with terrifying speed. I therefore lost no time in throwing overboard first my ballast, then my water casks, then my condensing apparatus and elastic chamber, and finally every object in the car. But it was useless. I continued to fall with dreadful rapidity and was now no more than half a mile from the surface. As a final measure, after removing my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car itself loose from the balloon; it was of considerable weight. Clinging with both hands to the netting, I had barely time to notice that the entire country, as far as I could see, was thickly dotted with tiny dwellings before I plunged headfirst into the center of a fantastical-looking city, among a vast crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me. They simply stood there like a group of idiots, grinning absurdly and looking sideways at me and my balloon, with their hands planted on their hips.”"}

{"request_id":"75a1cd902d9647c5c56b413e","rewritten_text":"It is a strange thing, but everyone who disappears is said to be seen in San Francisco. It must be a delightful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think happened to Basil?” Dorian asked, holding his Burgundy up to the light and wondering how he could discuss the matter so calmly.

“I haven’t the slightest idea. If Basil chooses to hide, that is none of my concern. If he is dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that truly frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked tiredly.

“Because,” Lord Henry said, passing the gilt lattice of an open vinaigrette beneath his nose, “nowadays one can survive everything except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts of the nineteenth century that cannot be explained away. Let us have coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house feels rather lonely without her. Of course, married life is only a habit, and a bad one. But we regret losing even our worst habits. Perhaps we regret them most. They are such an important part of who we are.”

Dorian said nothing. He rose from the table, went into the next room, sat at the piano, and let his fingers wander over the white and black keys. When the coffee arrived, he stopped and looked across at Lord Henry. “Harry, did you ever think that Basil might have been murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was very popular, and he always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He was not clever enough to have enemies. Of course, he had a remarkable gift for painting. But a man can paint like Velasquez and still be completely dull. Basil was really rather dull. He interested me only once, when he told me years ago that he adored you wildly and that you were the main inspiration for his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” Dorian said, sadness in his voice. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some newspapers do. It doesn’t seem likely to me. I know there are terrible places in Paris, but Basil was not the kind of man who would have gone to them. He had no curiosity. That was his greatest flaw.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I had murdered Basil?” the younger man asked."}
