{"request_id":"138b250dc381b579b3566d7b","rewritten_text":"The insect’s weight was truly remarkable, and, considering everything, I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion of it; but for the life of me, I could not understand Legrand’s agreement with that opinion.

“I sent for you,” he said grandly, after I had finished examining the beetle, “I sent for you so that I might have your counsel and assistance in advancing the designs of Fate and the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I cried, interrupting him, “you are certainly unwell and should take some precautions. You must go to bed, and I will stay with you for a few days, until you recover. You are feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did so and, to tell the truth, found no sign of fever at all.

“But you may be ill without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you this once. First, go to bed. Then—”

“You are mistaken,” he interrupted. “I am as well as I can expect to be under the excitement I am experiencing. If you truly wish me well, you will relieve that excitement.”

“And how is that to be done?”

“Very easily. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and for this expedition we will need the help of someone we can trust. You are the only person we can rely on. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you now see in me will be calmed.”

“I am eager to oblige you in any way,” I replied; “but do you mean that this infernal beetle has anything to do with your expedition into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I can take no part in such an absurd undertaking.”

“I am sorry—very sorry—for we will have to attempt it alone.”

“Attempt it alone! The man must be mad!—but wait! How long do you intend to be gone?”

“Probably all night. We will leave at once and return, in any case, by sunrise.”

“And will you promise me, on your honor, that when this whim of yours is over, and the beetle business—good God!—has been settled to your satisfaction, you will return home and follow my advice without question, as you would that of your physician?”

“Yes, I promise. Now let us go, for we have no time to waste.”

With a heavy heart, I accompanied my friend. We set out at about four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and myself. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, insisting on bearing them all himself—apparently more because he feared trusting either tool within his master’s reach than from any excess of diligence or willingness."}

That was how I tackled brother Dowley. I began speaking in an easy, idle fashion, as though merely passing the time; and the oldest man alive could not have traced my starting point and guessed where I meant to end:

“Boys, there are many strange things about law, custom, usage, and all that sort of matter, when you examine them; yes, and about the course and advance of human opinion and action, too. There are written laws—they perish; but there are unwritten laws—_they_ endure forever. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it declares that they must rise, little by little, throughout the centuries. Observe how it operates. We know what wages are now, in this place and that and yonder; we take an average and call it the wages of to-day. We know what wages were a hundred years ago, and what they were two hundred years ago; that is as far back as we can go, but it is enough to show us the law of progress, the amount and rate of each recurring increase; and thus, without a document to guide us, we can come fairly near deciding what wages were three, four, and five hundred years ago. Good, so far. Do we stop there? No. We cease looking backward, turn about, and apply the law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what people's wages will be at any future date you care to name, for hundreds upon hundreds of years.”

“What, goodman, what!”

“Yes. In seven hundred years wages will have risen to six times their present amount hereabouts, and farm hands will receive 3 cents a day, while mechanics will get 6.”

“I wish I might die now and live then!” interrupted Smug, the wheelwright, a greedy light shining in his eye.

“And that is not all; they will receive their board besides—such as it is: it will not fatten them. Two hundred and fifty years later—mark this now—a mechanic's wages will be—remember, this is law, not guesswork; a mechanic's wages will then be _twenty_ cents a day!”

There was a general gasp of astonishment and awe, while Dickon the mason murmured, with eyes and hands raised:"}

{"request_id":"413dd7da66be4436f2f5bcdd","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates was horrified by Sikes’s crime and began to wonder whether an honest life was, after all, the best one. Deciding that it certainly was, he turned away from his former life and resolved to improve himself in some new line of work. For a while he struggled and suffered greatly; but, with a cheerful nature and a good purpose, he succeeded at last. Once a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he was now the merriest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand that writes these words falters as it nears the end of its task, wishing to spin out the thread of these adventures a little longer.

I would gladly linger with a few of those among whom I have lived for so long, and share their happiness by trying to describe it. I would show Rose Maylie in the full beauty and grace of early womanhood, spreading a soft, gentle light along her quiet path in life, touching everyone who walked it with her and shining into their hearts. I would picture her bringing life and joy to the fireside and the lively summer gathering; follow her through the hot fields at noon; and hear the quiet tones of her sweet voice during an evening walk in the moonlight. I would watch her kindness and charity in public, and her cheerful, tireless care of the household at home. I would show her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love for each other, spending long hours imagining the friends they had lost so sadly. I would bring before me once more the joyful little faces gathered around her knee and listen to their merry chatter; recall the sound of that clear laugh and imagine the sympathetic tear shining in her soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks, smiles, thoughts, and ways of speaking, I would gladly recall, every one.

How Mr. Brownlow continued, day after day, to fill the mind of his adopted child with knowledge, growing more attached to him as his character unfolded and revealed the promising seeds of all he hoped the boy would become; how he discovered in him new qualities of his early friend, awakening old memories in his own heart, sad yet sweet and comforting; how the two orphans, tested by hardship, remembered its lessons in mercy toward others, in mutual love, and in heartfelt thanks to Him who had protected and preserved them—these are matters that need not be told."}

{"request_id":"36ef1dc0b99700176313d464","rewritten_text":"And then I repeated to myself that beautiful passage describing Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise; and I thought how sweet it would be, as I wandered along those lovely banks, to see the car of light descend with my long-lost parent, restored at last to me. While I waited in expectation of that hour, I imagined that I would gather some of the beautiful flowers growing there, weave them into a chaplet, and crown myself in delight: I would sing _sul margine d’un rio_, my father’s favourite song, and my voice, floating through the still air, would tell him, wherever he sat in some bower awaiting our reunion, that his daughter had arrived. Then the mark of misery would have vanished from my brow, and I could lift my eyes without fear to meet his, which always shone with the gentle radiance of innocent love. As I recalled the magical expression of those deep eyes, I wept, though softly, lest my sobs disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely absorbed in this reverie that I continued wandering, paying no attention to my steps, until I actually bent down to pick a flower for my wreath on that barren plain where no flower grew. Then I awoke from my daydream and discovered that I had no idea where I was.

The sun had gone down, and the rosy colour that his setting had cast upon the clouds was almost gone. A wind moved over the plain. I looked about and saw nothing that could tell me my position; I was lost, and tried vainly to recover my path. I went on, while the gathering darkness blurred every mark that might have guided me. At last everything was hidden beneath the profound darkness of the blackest night. I grew tired, and, knowing that my servant was to spend that night in the nearby village, so that my absence would alarm no one, and that in this lonely place I was safe from every intruder, I decided to remain there until morning. In truth, I was too exhausted to go farther: the air was cold, but I paid little heed to bodily discomfort, believing myself well accustomed to the weather after two years of solitude, during which no change of season had interrupted my constant wanderings.

I lay down upon the grass, surrounded by a darkness through which not the faintest ray of light could pass. There was no sound, for the deep night had lulled the insects to sleep, the only creatures inhabiting that desolate place, where no tree or shrub could shelter anything else. A remarkable silence filled the air, soothing my senses while stirring my soul; my thoughts rushed from one image to another and seemed to seize upon eternity."}

content.text: {"request_id":"81d9a8f681ae454010f5b9ee","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was too astonished to think clearly. I knew that my design differed greatly in detail from this one, though the general outline was somewhat similar. After a while I took a candle, sat down at the opposite end of the room, and examined the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the reverse, exactly as I had drawn it. My first thought was simple surprise at the remarkable similarity of the outlines—the strange coincidence that, without my knowing it, a skull should have been on the other side of the parchment, directly beneath my figure of the _scarabæus_, and that this skull should resemble my drawing so closely, not only in outline but also in size. I say that the strangeness of this coincidence completely stunned me for a time. That is the usual effect of such coincidences. The mind struggles to find a connection—a chain of cause and effect—and, unable to do so, undergoes a kind of temporary paralysis. But when I recovered from my stupor, a conviction gradually emerged that startled me far more than the coincidence itself. I began distinctly and certainly to remember that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I sketched the _scarabæus_. I became completely sure of this, because I remembered turning over first one side and then the other, looking for the cleanest place. If the skull had been there, I could not possibly have failed to notice it. Here was a mystery I felt unable to explain; yet even then, faintly, in the most distant and hidden chambers of my mind, there seemed to flicker a glow-worm-like conception of the truth that last night’s adventure would demonstrate so magnificently. I rose at once, put the parchment safely away, and dismissed all further thought of it until I was alone.\n\n“When you had left, and Jupiter was fast asleep, I began a more systematic investigation of the matter. First, I considered how the parchment had come into my possession. The place where we found the _scarabæus_ was on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and only a short distance above the high-water mark. When I picked it up, it gave me a sharp bite, making me drop it. Jupiter, with his usual caution, looked around for a leaf or something similar before taking hold of the insect, which had flown toward him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"4422283fd5a9d7bea6e9d5a7","rewritten_text":"Mrs. Otis has also told me—and I may say that she is no poor judge of Art, having spent several winters in Boston as a girl—that these gems are worth a great deal of money and would bring a high price if sold. Under these circumstances, Lord Canterville, I am sure you will understand why I could not allow them to remain with any member of my family. Such useless ornaments and toys, however suitable or necessary they may be to the dignity of the British aristocracy, would be entirely out of place among people raised on the strict, and, I believe, everlasting principles of republican simplicity. I should perhaps add that Virginia is very eager for you to let her keep the box as a reminder of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. Since it is extremely old and therefore badly damaged, you may decide to grant her request. Personally, I admit that I am rather surprised to find one of my children showing sympathy for medievalism in any form. I can only explain it by remembering that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a trip to Athens.’\n\nLord Canterville listened very seriously to the worthy Minister’s speech, occasionally pulling his grey moustache to hide an involuntary smile. When Mr. Otis had finished, he shook his hand warmly and said, ‘My dear sir, your charming little daughter did my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, a very important service. I and my family are deeply indebted to her for her remarkable courage and spirit. The jewels plainly belong to her, and, by heaven, I believe that if I were heartless enough to take them away, the wicked old fellow would be out of his grave within a fortnight, making my life a misery. As for their being family heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless it is identified as such in a will or other legal document, and no one has known these jewels existed. I assure you that I have no more claim to them than your butler does. When Miss Virginia grows up, I daresay she will be glad to have such pretty things to wear. Besides, Mr. Otis, you forget that you bought the furniture and the ghost at an agreed valuation. Anything belonging to the ghost therefore became yours at once. Whatever activity Sir Simon may have shown in the corridor at night, he was legally dead, and you acquired his property by purchase.’"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cfe20d6687315d45502fc029","rewritten_text":"I rose early and once again managed to escape my creditors’ watchfulness. I hurried to the bookseller’s stall and spent what little cash I had on books about Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. After safely reaching home with them, I used every free moment to read them. Before long, I had learned enough in these subjects, or so I believed, to carry out my plan. During this time, I also did everything I could to win over the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. At last I succeeded—partly by selling enough of my household furniture to pay half their claim, and partly by promising to pay the rest when I completed a small project I said I was planning, and for which I asked their help. Since they were ignorant men, I had little trouble bringing them into my scheme.\n\n“Once these matters were settled, I secretly and cautiously disposed of the property I still owned, with my wife’s help. I also borrowed, in small amounts and under various excuses, a considerable sum of ready money, without giving any thought to how I would repay it. With these funds, I gradually obtained very fine cambric muslin, in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a quantity of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and several other items needed to build and equip a balloon of extraordinary size. I instructed my wife to assemble the balloon as quickly as possible and gave her all the necessary details about how to do it. Meanwhile, I made the twine into a net large enough for the purpose, fitted it with a hoop and the required cords, and bought a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, an ordinary barometer with important modifications, and two astronomical instruments that were not widely known. I then found opportunities to carry, at night, to a secluded place east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks holding about fifty gallons each, along with one larger cask; six tinned-metal tubes, three inches in diameter, properly shaped, and ten feet long; a quantity of a certain metallic or semi-metallic substance, which I will not name; and twelve demijohns of a very common acid. The gas produced from these last materials is one that no one but myself has ever generated—or at least ever used for a similar purpose. I would have no objection to revealing the secret, except that it properly belongs to a citizen of Nantes, France, who shared it with me on the condition that I keep it confidential."}

{"request_id":"b8d1a165e81bb5c407a8a10e","rewritten_text":"‘Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?’

‘No, thank you. I never eat anything now; but it is very kind of you, all the same. You are much nicer than the rest of your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ cried Virginia, stamping her foot. ‘You are the rude, horrid, vulgar one. And as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to touch up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, including the vermilion, so I couldn’t paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald green and the chrome yellow. In the end, I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white, and could paint only moonlight scenes, which are always depressing to look at and very difficult to paint. I never told on you, although I was extremely annoyed. The whole thing was ridiculous; who ever heard of emerald-green blood?’

‘Well, really,’ said the Ghost rather meekly, ‘what was I supposed to do? Real blood is very difficult to get nowadays. And since your brother started it all with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. As for color, that is always a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, for example—the bluest in England. But I know you Americans don’t care about such things.’

‘You know nothing about it. The best thing you can do is emigrate and improve your mind. My father will be delighted to give you a free passage. And although there is a heavy duty on spirits of every kind, there will be no trouble at Customs, since the officers are all Democrats. Once you reach New York, you are sure to be a great success. I know many people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars to have a grandfather, and much more than that to have a family Ghost.’

‘I don’t think I would like America.’

‘I suppose that is because we have no ruins or curiosities,’ said Virginia sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ replied the Ghost. ‘You have your navy and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I will ask Papa to give the twins an extra week’s holiday.’

‘Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I am so lonely and unhappy, and I truly don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, but I cannot.’

‘That is absurd! You only have to go to bed and blow out the candle.’"}

{"request_id":"d90d27f38f23566d03f36134","rewritten_text":"While these events were occurring in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the very room from which the girl had taken Oliver—musing over a dull, smoky fire. A pair of bellows rested on his knee, with which he had seemingly been trying to stir it into livelier flame; but he had sunk into profound thought. His arms folded upon them, his chin supported by his thumbs, he gazed absently at the rusty bars.

At a table behind him sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist; the Artful playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The first-named gentleman’s face, always remarkably intelligent, gained still greater interest from his close attention to the game and his careful study of Mr. Chitling’s hand. Whenever opportunity offered, he cast upon it a number of earnest looks, wisely directing his own play according to what he observed in his neighbour’s cards. As the night was cold, the Dodger wore his hat, as, indeed, he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he found it necessary to seek refreshment from a quart pot on the table, already filled with gin-and-water for the company.

Master Bates likewise watched the play; but, being more excitable than his accomplished friend, he applied himself more often to the gin-and-water and made many jokes and irrelevant observations, all most improper in a scientific rubber. The Artful, relying on their close friendship, took occasion more than once to reason solemnly with his companion about these offences. Master Bates accepted every remonstrance in excellent humour, merely asking his friend to be “blowed,” or to put his head in a sack, or answering with some other neatly fashioned jest of the same description, whose aptness greatly delighted Mr. Chitling. It was curious that the latter gentleman and his partner invariably lost; and that this, instead of angering Master Bates, seemed to amuse him exceedingly, for he laughed uproariously after every deal and declared that he had never witnessed such a jolly game in all his born days.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, with a very lengthened face, as he drew half-a-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never see such a feller as you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

{"request_id":"f914d1a9074bfb63f45dfa38","rewritten_text":"“One more word, Rose. Dearest Rose—just one more!” cried Harry, throwing himself before her. “If I had been less fortunate—if the world had expected me to live some obscure, peaceful life—if I had been poor, sick, or helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or has the prospect of my rising to wealth and honour created this hesitation?”

“Do not force me to answer,” Rose replied. “The question does not arise, and never will. It is unfair, almost cruel, to press me.”

“If your answer is what I hardly dare hope,” Harry said, “it will bring a ray of happiness to my lonely life and light the road ahead. It is no small thing, with a few brief words, to do so much for someone who loves you above all else. Oh, Rose, in the name of my passionate and lasting love; in the name of everything I have suffered for you, and everything you condemn me to endure; answer this one question!”

“Then, if your circumstances had been different,” Rose answered; “if you had been only somewhat, rather than so greatly, above me; if I could have been a help and comfort to you in some humble, peaceful retreat, instead of a burden and disadvantage among ambitious and distinguished people; I would have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be happy—very happy—now. But then, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

As Rose made this confession, memories of old hopes, cherished when she was young, crowded into her mind. But they brought tears, as old hopes often do when they return faded and ruined; and afterward she felt relieved.

“I cannot prevent this weakness, and it makes me more determined,” she said, holding out her hand. “I must leave you now—truly.”

“I ask one promise,” said Harry. “Once, and only once more—within a year, perhaps much sooner—may I speak to you about this for the last time?”

“Not to pressure me into changing my firm decision,” Rose replied with a sad smile. “That would be useless.”

“No,” said Harry. “Only to hear you repeat it, if you will—repeat it finally. I will place at your feet whatever position or fortune I may have gained; and if you still keep your present decision, I will not try, by word or deed, to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose answered. “It is only one more pain, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

She held out her hand again."}

{"request_id":"426cd54832207d6cdaf17526","rewritten_text":"It seemed to be a collection of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, with the look of a rather dull, quiet retreat. Wemmick’s house was a little wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots. Its top had been cut out and painted to look like a battery fitted with guns.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Looks nice, doesn’t it?”

I praised it highly. I believe it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the strangest Gothic windows—most of them false—and a Gothic door almost too small to enter.

“That’s a real flagstaff,” said Wemmick, “and on Sundays I raise a real flag. Now look here. After I cross this bridge, I pull it up—like this—and cut off communication.”

The bridge was a plank crossing a ditch about four feet wide and two feet deep. It was very pleasant to see the pride with which he raised it and secured it, smiling with real enjoyment rather than doing it mechanically.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There it is, you see! And when you hear it go off, I think you’ll agree it’s a Stinger.”

The gun stood in a separate fortress made of latticework. An ingenious little tarpaulin cover, shaped like an umbrella, protected it from the weather.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t spoil the idea of the fortifications—for I believe that if you have an idea, you should carry it out and maintain it—I don’t know whether you agree—”

I said that I certainly did.

“—At the back, there’s a pig, along with chickens and rabbits. Then I put together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers. You’ll judge at supper what kind of salad I can produce. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling again but also speaking seriously as he shook his head, “if you imagine the little place under siege, it could last a devil of a long time for provisions.”

He then led me to a bower about twelve yards away. It was reached by such cleverly twisting paths that it took quite a while to get there. In this retreat, our glasses had already been set out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental lake beside which the bower stood. The lake was circular, with an island in the middle that might have supplied the salad for supper. Wemmick had built a fountain in it; when a small mill was set turning and a cork was removed from a pipe, the fountain played so strongly that it made the back of your hand quite wet."}

{"request_id":"7c97f70b14832c6505c89907","rewritten_text":"Saturday at noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke-powders, pawing the air, and muttering gibberish as vigorously as ever, but he looked rather dispirited, since naturally he had not yet started even a perspiration in that well. At last I said:

“How does the matter promise by now, partner?”

“Behold, I am even now engaged in testing the most powerful enchantment known to the princes of occult arts in the lands of the East; should it fail me, nothing can avail. Peace, until I have finished.”

This time he raised a smoke that darkened the whole region, and must have made things uncomfortable for the hermits, since the wind blew their way and rolled down over their dens in a thick, billowing fog. He poured forth matching volumes of speech, twisted his body, and sawed the air with his hands in the strangest fashion. After twenty minutes he sank down panting and nearly spent. Then came the abbot with several hundred monks and nuns, followed by a multitude of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings, all attracted by the prodigious smoke and all in a high state of excitement. The abbot anxiously asked for the result. Merlin said:

“If any labor of mortal man could break the spell binding these waters, this which I have just attempted would have done so. It has failed; and thereby I now know that what I feared is an established truth: the sign of this failure is that the most potent spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name none may utter and live, has laid his spell upon this well. No mortal breathes, nor ever shall, who can penetrate the secret of that spell, and without that secret none can break it. The water will flow no more forever, good Father. I have done what man could do. Suffer me to depart.”

Of course this threw the abbot into considerable consternation. He turned to me, the signs of it plain upon his face, and said:

“Ye have heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all, then, not all! What part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast his spell upon the well.”

“God’s wounds, then are we ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? Ye mean, not certainly?”

“That is what I mean.”

“Wherefore, ye also mean that when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes, when he says that, he says what is not necessarily true. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—that is, some small, some trifling chance—of succeeding.”"}

{"request_id":"4072ba5559636fb3f5da7b25","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and courtyards eventually opened into a large public space. Pens for animals stood scattered around it, along with other signs of a cattle market. Sikes slowed when they reached the place, for the girl could no longer keep up the rapid pace at which they had been walking. Turning to Oliver, he roughly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes growled as Oliver hesitated and looked around.

They were in a dark corner, well away from the path of passers-by.

Oliver saw clearly enough that resisting would be useless. He held out his hand, and Nancy clasped it tightly.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, seizing Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Listen, boy!” said Sikes, placing his other hand around Oliver’s throat. “If he says even the softest word, hold him! Do you understand?”

The dog growled again. Licking his lips, he watched Oliver as though eager to fasten himself on his throat without delay.

“He’s as willing as a Christian, blind me if he isn’t!” said Sikes, looking at the animal with grim, savage approval. “Now you know what to expect, master, so call out as quickly as you like; the dog will soon stop that. Move on, youngster!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail in response to this unusually affectionate speech and, giving Oliver another warning growl, led the way forward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though for all Oliver knew it might have been Grosvenor Square. The night was dark and foggy. The shop lights could barely penetrate the thickening mist, which wrapped the streets and houses in gloom, making the unfamiliar place seem stranger still to Oliver and deepening his uncertainty and misery.

They had gone only a few paces when a deep church bell struck the hour. At its first stroke, both his guides stopped and turned their heads toward the direction of the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy said when the bell fell silent.

“What’s the point of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes replied.

“I wonder whether they can hear it,” said Nancy.

“Of course they can,” Sikes answered. “It was Bartlemy time when I was locked up, and there wasn’t a penny trumpet at the fair whose squealing I couldn’t hear. After I was shut in for the night, the noise and uproar outside made that thundering old jail so silent that I could almost have beaten my brains out against the iron plates of the door.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"6ef9fc6d313cd5c187309d28","rewritten_text":"We both agreed in loving Adrian, though Perdita, still not fully grown out of childhood, could not value his qualities as I did or share my sympathy with his interests and opinions. I was always with him. His gentle, sensitive nature gave our conversations a tender, almost unearthly quality. Yet he was also as cheerful as a lark singing from its high tower, as lofty in thought as an eagle, and as innocent as a mild-eyed dove. He could lighten Perdita’s seriousness and ease the painful restlessness of my nature. I looked back on my troubled desires and painful struggles with other people as on a disturbed dream. I felt as changed as if I had taken on another body, with new senses and nerves that changed the universe’s reflection in the mind’s mirror. But I had not truly changed. I was still strong, still deeply hungry for sympathy, and still eager for active work. My manly virtues had not left me: the witch Urania had spared Samson’s hair while he rested at her feet. Yet everything in me had become gentler and more human. Adrian taught me more than the cold facts of history and philosophy. Through them, he taught me to control my reckless, uncultivated spirit; and at the same time, he revealed the living page of his own heart, allowing me to feel and understand its wonderful nature.\n\nThe former queen of England had tried, from her son’s earliest childhood, to plant bold and ambitious plans in his mind. She saw that he possessed genius and extraordinary talent, and she developed these qualities so that she could later use them to advance her own aims. She encouraged his hunger for knowledge and his fierce courage. She even accepted his untamed love of freedom, hoping that it would, as it often does, grow into a desire to command. She tried to raise him with resentment toward, and a wish for revenge against, those who had helped bring about his father’s abdication. She failed in this. The reports he received, however distorted, of a great and wise nation claiming the right to govern itself filled him with admiration; from an early age, he became a republican on principle. Still, his mother did not give up. Along with his love of power and proud sense of birth, she encouraged ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying his character. Through praise, blame, and urging, she tried to find and strike the right chords. Though the music produced by her efforts sounded like discord to her, she based her hopes on his talents and remained certain that she would eventually win him over."}

content.text: {"request_id":"989cf8a80aed84934385a178","rewritten_text":"Raymond was exhilarated by the intense sensations of restored health; he felt that, as general of the Athenians, he occupied a position worthy of his ambition. In hoping to conquer Constantinople, he looked toward an event that would stand as a landmark in the wasteland of the ages, an achievement unmatched in human history: a city of immense historical associations, whose beautiful setting was the wonder of the world, and which for many centuries had been the stronghold of the Muslims, would be rescued from slavery and barbarism and restored to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and love of liberty. Perdita relied on his restored society, his love, his hopes, and his fame, as a Sybarite relies on a luxurious couch; every thought was rapture, and every emotion seemed immersed in a congenial, balmy element.\n\nWe reached Kishan on July 7. The weather throughout our journey had been serene. Each day, before dawn, we left our night’s encampment and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and valley, along with the golden splendor announcing the sun’s approach. The accompanying soldiers, with national vivacity, took enthusiastic pleasure in the sight of beautiful nature. The rising of the day-star was greeted by triumphant music, while birdsong, heard in snatches, filled the intervals between the melodies. At noon, we pitched our tents in a shaded valley or a wooded hollow among the mountains, while a stream murmuring over pebbles invited grateful sleep. Our evening march, calmer than the morning, was even more delightful. If the band played, they instinctively chose airs of restrained passion: the farewell of love or lament for absence, followed and concluded by some solemn hymn that harmonized with the tranquil beauty of evening and lifted the soul toward lofty, religious thought. Often every sound was suspended so that we could listen to the nightingale, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travelers. Did we pass through a valley? Gentle shadows surrounded us, and rocks glowed with beautiful colors. If we crossed a mountain, Greece, like a living map, lay spread beneath us, its famous peaks piercing the sky and its rivers tracing silver lines through the fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers surveyed this splendid landscape with ecstasy, so unlike the sober colors and melancholy beauties of our native scenery. When we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer delights; nevertheless, our journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people quickly began moving to honor Lord Raymond."}

Finding no discomfort from this, I at length opened the gum-elastic chamber and detached it from around the car. As might have been anticipated, spasms and severe headache immediately followed an experiment so rash and dangerous. Yet these, along with the other impediments to breathing, were not so serious as to threaten my life; and I resolved to bear them as well as I could, since each moment of my ascent toward the denser strata near the moon would leave them behind. This ascent, however, remained exceedingly rapid; and it soon became distressingly clear that, though I had likely not been mistaken in expecting an atmosphere dense in proportion to the satellite’s mass, I had erred in believing that this density, even at the surface, would sufficiently support the great weight enclosed in my balloon’s car. It ought, nevertheless, to have done so, and to the same extent as at the earth’s surface, the actual gravity of bodies on either planet being presumed to correspond with the atmospheric condensation. That it did not was proved abundantly by my headlong descent; the reason can only be accounted for by referring to those possible geological disturbances I have mentioned before. In any event, I was now near the planet and dropping with dreadful speed. I therefore lost no time in casting out first my ballast, then my water-casks, then my condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every object in the car. All was useless. I continued to fall with frightful velocity and was now less than half a mile above the surface. As a final measure, after removing my coat, hat, and boots, I severed the car itself from the balloon, since it had considerable weight. Clinging with both hands to the netting, I had scarcely time to notice that the entire country, as far as I could see, was thickly dotted with tiny dwellings before I plunged headlong into the center of a strange-looking city, among a huge crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me; instead, they stood like a group of fools, grinning absurdly and casting sidelong looks at me and my balloon, their arms akimbo.”"}

{"request_id":"35edd6fb4172222960cde11d","rewritten_text":"He sprang to his feet and seized her arm roughly. “Show him to me. Which one is he? Point him out. I must see him!” he cried; but just then the Duke of Berwick’s four-in-hand passed between them, and by the time it had cleared the way, the carriage had swept out of the park.

“He’s gone,” Sibyl murmured sadly. “I wish you had seen him.”

“So do I, for as surely as there is a God in heaven, if he ever does you any harm, I shall kill him.”

She stared at him in horror. He repeated the threat. His words struck the air like a dagger. The people nearby began to gape, and a lady standing beside her tittered.

“Come away, Jim; come away,” she whispered. He followed stubbornly as she made her way through the crowd. He was pleased with what he had said.

When they reached the Achilles Statue, she turned back. Pity showed in her eyes, then changed to laughter on her lips. She shook her head at him. “You are foolish, Jim—utterly foolish; only a bad-tempered boy, that is all. How can you say such dreadful things? You don’t know what you are saying. You are merely jealous and unkind. Ah, I wish you would fall in love. Love makes people good, and what you said was wicked.”

“I am sixteen,” he replied, “and I know what I am doing. Mother is no help to you. She doesn’t know how to take care of you. I wish now I wasn’t going to Australia at all. I am half-minded to abandon the whole business. I would, if my articles had not been signed.”

“Oh, don’t be so solemn, Jim. You are like one of the heroes in those foolish melodramas Mother used to enjoy acting in. I am not going to quarrel with you. I have seen him, and oh! seeing him is perfect happiness. We won’t quarrel. I know you would never hurt anyone I love, would you?”

“Not while you love him, I suppose,” came the sullen reply.

“I shall love him forever!” she cried.

“And he?”

“Forever, too!”

“He had better.”

She drew back from him. Then she laughed and laid her hand on his arm. He was only a boy.

At Marble Arch they hailed an omnibus, which set them down near their shabby home in the Euston Road. It was past five, and Sibyl had to lie down for a few hours before acting. Jim insisted that she do so. He said he would rather leave her while their mother was away. She was certain to make a scene, and he hated scenes of every sort."}

{"request_id":"e8d2ea2c629e9d3e43bc65f0","rewritten_text":"Biddy cried; the darkening garden, the lane, and the stars appearing overhead were blurred by my own tears.

“Was nothing ever discovered, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what became of Orlick?”

“Judging by the color of his clothes, I should think he is working in the quarries.”

“Then you have seen him, of course? Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there on the night she died.”

“That was not the last time, either, Biddy?”

“No; I have seen him there since we began walking here. It is useless,” said Biddy, placing her hand on my arm as I tried to run out. “You know I would not deceive you. He was not there for a minute, and then he was gone.”

My anger returned in full force when I learned that this man still followed her, and I felt deep hatred for him. I told her so, and said I would spend any amount of money or take any trouble to drive him from that country. Gradually, she guided me toward calmer subjects and told me how Joe loved me, and how he never complained about anything—she did not say “about me”; she did not need to, for I understood—but always did his duty in his own way, with a strong hand, a quiet tongue, and a gentle heart.

“Indeed, it would be difficult to praise him too highly,” I said. “And Biddy, we must often talk about these things, because I shall certainly be coming here often now. I am not going to leave poor Joe alone.”

Biddy said not a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Leaving aside your calling me Mr. Pip—which seems to me rather improper, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, with a self-righteous air, “I must ask you to explain what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Now, don’t repeat my words,” I replied. “You never used to do that, Biddy.”

“Never used to?” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Never used to!”

Well, I thought I might as well give up that point too. After we had walked silently through the garden once more, I returned to my main argument.

“Biddy,” I said, “I remarked that I would come here often to see Joe, and you answered with a very noticeable silence. Please, Biddy, tell me why.”

“Are you quite sure, then, that you will come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping on the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with clear, honest eyes."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ddef6e51b6749ae354c9213b","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself time to think, and hardly knowing what she felt, Elizabeth finished this letter, immediately seized the other, and opened it with the greatest impatience. It had been written a day after the first letter ended, and read as follows:\n\n“My dearest sister, by now you will have received my hurried letter. I hope this one will be clearer, but although I am not pressed for time, my mind is so confused that I cannot promise to write coherently. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to say, but I have bad news, and it cannot wait. However foolish a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate to learn that it has happened, because there is too much reason to fear that they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, only a few hours after the express. Although Lydia’s brief letter to Mrs. F. led them to believe that she and Wickham were going to Gretna Green, Denny let something slip that showed he believed Wickham never meant to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. This was repeated to Colonel Forster, who immediately became alarmed and set out to follow their route. He traced them easily as far as Clapham, but no farther. On entering that place, they changed into a hackney coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All that is known after that is that they were seen continuing along the London road. I do not know what to think. After making every possible inquiry in that part of London, Colonel Forster came on to Hertfordshire, anxiously asking at every turnpike and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success. No one had seen such people pass through. With the greatest concern, he came to Longbourn and told us his fears in a way that showed how deeply he felt them. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F., but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many things might make it better for them to marry privately in town rather than follow their original plan. And even if he could form such a plan against a young woman of Lydia’s family—which is unlikely—can I believe her so completely without sense or virtue? Impossible! Yet I am troubled to find that Colonel Forster does not trust that they are married. When I expressed my hopes, he shook his head and said he feared Wickham was not a man who could be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"25e5946d3cb9f987a79cf8de","rewritten_text":"MR. Merton was greatly troubled by the marriage being postponed a second time, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding dress, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. Sybil loved her mother dearly, but she had placed her entire life in Lord Arthur’s hands, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith. Lord Arthur himself took several days to recover from his bitter disappointment, and for a while his nerves were thoroughly shattered. His excellent common sense soon returned, however, and his practical, well-balanced mind quickly decided what course to take. Since poison had failed completely, dynamite, or some other explosive, was plainly the next thing to attempt.

He therefore examined the list of his friends and relations once more and, after careful thought, resolved to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of considerable culture and learning, was passionately fond of clocks and possessed a remarkable collection of timepieces, dating from the fifteenth century to the present day. Lord Arthur saw that this interest of the good Dean’s might provide an excellent means of executing his plan. Finding an explosive machine was, naturally, an entirely different problem. The London Directory offered him no help, and he thought there was little point in applying to Scotland Yard, since they never appeared to know anything about the dynamite party’s activities until after an explosion—and not much even then.

Then he suddenly remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strongly revolutionary opinions, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a life of Peter the Great and to have come to England to study documents concerning that Tsar’s stay in the country as a ship’s carpenter; yet it was widely suspected that he was a Nihilist agent, and there was no question that the Russian Embassy viewed his presence in London with displeasure. Lord Arthur thought him exactly the man he needed, and one morning drove to his lodgings in Bloomsbury to seek his advice and help.

‘So you are taking politics seriously?’ said Count Rouvaloff, after Lord Arthur had explained the purpose of his visit. Lord Arthur, who detested every kind of swagger, felt obliged to confess that he had not the least interest in social questions and wanted the explosive machine solely for a family affair, in which nobody but himself was involved."}

{"request_id":"5524add799ce3dcf30552215","rewritten_text":"He never tried a second time. The boys lay there, counting the slow moments until it seemed that time itself must end and eternity begin to fade. Then they were relieved to see that the sun was finally setting.

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, and gave a grim smile at his companion, whose head had fallen onto his knees. He nudged him with his foot and said:

“Here! You’re supposed to be keeping watch, aren’t you? It’s all right, though—nothing’s happened.”

“My! Was I asleep?”

“Oh, only partly. It’s nearly time for us to leave, pard. What shall we do with the little swag we have left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here, like we always do, I suppose. There’s no point taking it away until we head south. Six hundred and fifty dollars in silver is a lot to carry.”

“Well, all right—it won’t hurt to come here one more time.”

“No—but I’d say we should come at night, as we used to. It’s safer.”

“Yes, but listen; it may be a long time before I get the right chance for that job. Accidents could happen, and it isn’t in a very good place. We’ll bury it properly—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said his companion. He crossed the room, knelt down, lifted one of the hearthstones at the back, and pulled out a bag that jingled pleasantly. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to Joe, who was now kneeling in the corner and digging with his bowie knife.

The boys instantly forgot all their fears and misery. With shining eyes, they watched every movement. Luck! The treasure was more wonderful than they could imagine. Six hundred dollars was enough to make half a dozen boys rich! This was treasure hunting at its best—there would be no troublesome uncertainty about where to dig. They nudged each other constantly, and the meaning was clear: “Aren’t you glad now that we’re here!”

Joe’s knife hit something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his companion.

“A half-rotten plank—no, I think it’s a box. Here, give me a hand and we’ll find out what it’s doing here. Never mind, I’ve made a hole.”

He reached inside and pulled out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as excited and delighted as the men.

Joe’s companion said:

“We’ll finish this quickly. There’s an old rusty pick among the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace—I saw it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"85c20b5de1804c9adb18855c","rewritten_text":"Their coming had kindled a sort of fire in the heart of Saint Antoine, spreading swiftly as they advanced, and stirring into flickering flames of faces at nearly every door and window. Yet no one had followed them, and no man spoke when they entered the wine-shop, though every eye within was turned toward them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

Perhaps this served as a signal to loosen the general tongue. It drew back a chorus of “Good day!”

“The weather is bad, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

At this, each man glanced at his neighbour, then all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. Except for one man, who rose and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge aloud, speaking to Madame Defarge, “I have travelled several leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half’s journey from Paris. He is a good child, this road-mender called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender called Jacques. He removed his blue cap to the company and drank. In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse, dark bread; from time to time he ate it, sitting near Madame Defarge’s counter, munching and drinking. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge revived himself with a draught of wine—but took less than he gave the stranger, since wine was no rarity to him—and waited until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He looked at no one present, and no one now looked at him; not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and was working.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked, when the proper time came.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come, then! You shall see the room I told you that you might occupy. It will suit you wonderfully.”

From the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, and from the staircase into a garret—formerly the garret where a white-haired man had sat on a low bench, bent forward and busily making shoes.

No white-haired man was there now; but the three men who had separately left the wine-shop were there. Between them and the distant white-haired man was one small connection: they had once looked in at him through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge carefully shut the door and spoke in a lowered voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness met by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"134ddc3a49ef78785e444dfc","rewritten_text":"Col. Grangerford was a gentleman, you see—one through and through, and so was his family. He was well born, as folks say, and that counts for as much in a man as in a horse, according to the Widow Douglas; and nobody ever disputed that she belonged to the highest aristocracy in our town. Pap said the same thing, too, though he warn’t any more quality than a mudcat. Col. Grangerford was very tall and very thin, with a dark, pale complexion and not a trace of red anywhere. Every morning he shaved his whole narrow face clean, and he had the thinnest lips, the narrowest nostrils, a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and eyes black as could be, set so far back they seemed to be staring at you from caves, you might say. His forehead was high, and his straight black hair fell to his shoulders. His hands were long and slender, and every day he wore a fresh shirt and a complete linen suit, white enough to hurt your eyes; on Sundays he put on a blue tail-coat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane topped with silver. There was no frivolity in him, not the least, and he was never noisy. He was as kind as a man could be—you could sense it, and so you trusted him. Sometimes he smiled, and it was pleasant to see; but when he drew himself up like a liberty-pole and lightning began flashing beneath his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree before finding out what was wrong. He never needed to tell anyone to behave—everybody had good manners in his presence. Everyone liked having him nearby, too; he was nearly always sunshine—I mean, he made things feel like fair weather. When he became a cloudbank, it grew terribly dark for half a minute, and that was sufficient; nothing else would go wrong for a week.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came downstairs in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs and wished them good-day, and nobody sat again until they had taken their seats. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard, where the decanter stood, mixed him a glass of bitters, and handed it over. He held it while they prepared their own, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” They bowed the tiniest bit and replied thank you, and then all three drank. Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and the little bit of whisky or apple brandy at the bottoms of their tumblers, gave it to me and Buck, and we drank to the old people as well."}

{"request_id":"ac0809685183f1b94a7089a1","rewritten_text":"There was something strange in all this that drew me in and enchanted me. He seemed to have awakened from a long, dreamlike sleep, and felt rather like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that lovely imitation of an Eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends had changed or died, and now, upon waking, I was all he had left to love in the world.

How dear the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became to me, now that I had such a beloved companion for my walks. With my father, I visited every beautiful place, whether on the islands or beside waterfalls sheltered by trees; every shaded path and every hollow tangled with undergrowth and fern. His conversation widened my thoughts. I felt renewed, as if I had gained all the freshness and energy of a new life. Since his arrival, I seemed to have been carried from a small corner of earth into a universe without limits to the imagination or understanding. Before, my life had been like a pleasant country stream, never meant to leave its native fields, but destined, when its work was done, to disappear quietly without a trace. Now it seemed like a varied river flowing through a fertile and beautiful landscape, always changing and always lovely. Alas, I did not know what desert it was nearing, what rocks would tear its waters, or what terrible scene would be reflected, even more horribly distorted, in its waves. Life was then brilliant; I was beginning to learn hope—and what brings a more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should so quickly follow such perfect happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, but bitterness lay at the bottom of its long, sweet draught. My heart was filled with deep affection, yet it was calm because of its very depth and fullness. I had no idea that love could bring misery, and this lesson, which everyone must eventually learn, was taught to me in a way few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and must always mourn, those few short months of paradise. I had broken no command and eaten no apple, yet I was cruelly driven from it. Alas, my companion had, and I was thrown down in his fall. But I am straying from my story—let sorrow come in its proper time; at this point I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship, when my aunt became ill. I spent an entire month nursing her in her room, but her illness was fatal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for some time. Death is so terrible to the living; the bonds of habit are so strong, even when affection does not hold them together, that the heart must suffer when they are broken."}

{"request_id":"fe149de85d386354e4384762","rewritten_text":"“Do you understand me? I have learned the language of despair; I know it all by heart, because I am Despair—and a strange being I am: joyous, triumphant Despair. But those words are false, for the wave may be dark, but it is not bitter. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we wake, we are free. Come, then, no more delay, you tardy one! Behold the pleasant potion! Look, I am a spirit of goodness, not a human maiden inviting you, and in winning tones—oh, that they would win you!—saying, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my eyes fixed on his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, and his gentle yet earnest expression of concern and wonder, even before he spoke, changed my overwrought feelings. They took from me all the sternness of despair and filled me only with the softest grief. I saw that his eyes were moist as well when he took both my hands in his. Sitting down beside me, he said:

“This is a sad deed you would lead me to, dearest friend, and your sorrow must indeed be deep to fill you with such unhappy thoughts. You long for death, yet fear it, and wish me to be your companion. But I have less courage than you, and even with such company I dare not die. Listen to me, then reflect on whether you ought to win me to your plan. Even if, with the overbearing eloquence of despair, you could make black death so inviting that fair heaven itself appeared dark. Listen, I beg you, to one who has himself nourished desperate thoughts and longed impatiently for death, but who at last has trampled that phantom underfoot and crushed its sting. Come: since you have played Despair with me, I will play Una’s part with you and bring you unharmed from his dark cavern. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by words in which no selfish passion remains.

“We do not know what this wide world means, with its strange mixture of good and evil. But we have been placed here and told to live and hope. I do not know what we are meant to hope for; yet there is some good beyond us that we must seek, and that is our earthly task. If misfortune comes against us, we must fight it; we must cast it aside and continue onward, discovering what it is our nature to desire. Whether this prospect of future good prepares us for another existence, I do not know; or whether we are merely workmen in God’s vineyard, obliged to lend a hand in smoothing the way for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"628380680b417ccac23b87f8","rewritten_text":"At that moment, his eyes—and mine as well—fell on the scrap of parchment, which I had then taken for paper. It lay half buried in the sand, with one corner sticking out. Near the place where we found it, I noticed the remains of what seemed to be a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have been there for a very long time, because it was barely possible to recognize the timbers as parts of a boat.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon afterward we started home, and on the way we met Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he asked me to let him take it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately put it into his waistcoat pocket, leaving behind the parchment in which it had been wrapped. I had kept that in my hand while he examined the beetle. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind and thought it safest to secure the prize at once—you know how enthusiastic he is about everything connected with Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

“You remember that when I went to the table to draw a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper in its usual place. I looked in the drawer, but there was none there either. I searched my pockets, hoping to find an old letter, and my hand came upon the parchment. I explain exactly how it came into my possession because the circumstances made a strong impression on me.

“No doubt you will think me fanciful—but I had already formed a connection. I had joined two links in a great chain. There was a boat on a seacoast, and not far from it lay a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn upon it. You will naturally ask, ‘What is the connection?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the familiar emblem of the pirate. The death’s-head flag is raised in every engagement.

“I have said that the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is durable—almost impossible to destroy. Things of little importance are rarely written or drawn on parchment, since paper is much better suited to ordinary writing and drawing. This thought suggested that the death’s-head must have some meaning or connection. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. Although one corner had been destroyed by some accident, it was clear that its original shape had been oblong."}

{"request_id":"451cc49561f2ed9e2cee5a3f","rewritten_text":"But he would never have escaped without me. Morgan le Fay hated him with all her heart, and she would never have forgiven him. Yet his offense came more from carelessness than deliberate wickedness. He had said she had red hair. She did, of course, but that was not the proper way to describe it. When red-haired people belong to a certain social class, their hair is called auburn.

Think of it: among these forty-seven prisoners were five whose names, crimes, and dates of imprisonment were no longer known. One woman and four men—all bent, wrinkled, and mentally worn out old men. They themselves had forgotten these facts long ago; at best, they had only uncertain guesses, with nothing definite, and never told the same story twice. The priests who had successively been responsible for praying with the prisoners each day, reminding them that God had placed them there for some wise reason, and teaching them that He approved of patience, humility, and submission to oppression among people of lower rank, had traditions about these poor human wrecks, but nothing more. Even those traditions told little, since they concerned only how long the imprisonment had lasted, not what the crimes were. And even tradition could prove only that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years; no one could guess how much longer they had suffered. The king and queen knew nothing about them except that they were heirlooms, inherited along with the throne from the previous rulers. No history had been passed down with them, so their new owners had considered them worthless and taken no interest in them. I said to the queen:

“Then why on earth didn’t you set them free?”

The question confused her. She did not know why she had not; the thought had never occurred to her. Without realizing it, she was already predicting the future history of prisoners in the Castle d’If. It seemed clear to me then that, because of her upbringing, she regarded these inherited prisoners as property—nothing more and nothing less. After all, when we inherit property, we do not usually throw it away, even if we do not care about it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open air and the bright afternoon sun—first blindfolding them out of kindness, since their eyes had gone so long without light—they were a shocking sight. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pitiful horrors, every one of them; the most genuine children imaginable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"f938bc97535596b0e76ce69d","rewritten_text":"I am not dining at home, so I shall have no need of you.”

“Thank you, sir,” said the man, as he left the room.

“Now, Alan, there is not a moment to lose. How heavy this chest is! I’ll carry it for you. You bring the other things.” He spoke quickly and with authority. Campbell felt himself overborne by him. Together they left the room.

When they reached the upper landing, Dorian took out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he paused, and a troubled expression came into his eyes. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he murmured.

“It means nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. As he did, he saw the face of his portrait leering in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that the previous night, for the first time in his life, he had neglected to conceal the fatal canvas, and was about to hurry forward when he recoiled with a shudder.

What was that disgusting red dew shining, wet and glistening, on one of the hands, as if the canvas had perspired blood? How dreadful it was!—for the moment, it seemed even more dreadful to him than the silent object he knew was stretched across the table, the thing whose grotesque, distorted shadow on the stained carpet showed him that it had not moved, but remained where he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, opened the door a little farther, and, with his eyes half closed and his head turned away, walked swiftly inside, resolved not to look even once at the dead man. Then he bent down, picked up the gold-and-purple hanging, and threw it completely over the picture.

There he stopped, afraid to turn around, his eyes fixed on the intricate pattern before him. He heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other articles he had demanded for his terrible work. He began wondering whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what impression they had formed of each other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, only aware that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a gleaming yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turning in the lock.

It was well after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale, but perfectly composed. “I have done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"faf1da87504b2d72e26d8d1f","rewritten_text":"When I returned, I found the following letter from my father:

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter telling you when to return to us. At first, I was tempted to write only a few lines, simply naming the day I expected you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I cannot do it. What a shock it would be, my son, if you expected a joyful welcome and instead found tears and misery. And how, Victor, can I tell you of our misfortune? Surely absence has not made you indifferent to our happiness and sorrow; but how can I bring pain to my son, who has been away so long? I wish to prepare you for this terrible news, but I know it is impossible. Even now, your eyes must be moving quickly over the page, searching for the words that will reveal the horrible truth.

“William is dead! That sweet child, whose smiles filled my heart with joy and warmth, who was so gentle and yet so cheerful—Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you. I will only tell you what happened.

“Last Thursday, May 7th, my niece, your two brothers, and I went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, and we walked farther than usual. It was already growing dark before we thought of returning. Then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were missing. We sat on a bench and waited for them to come back. Soon Ernest arrived and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said they had been playing, that William had run away to hide, and that he had searched for him without success. He had then waited a long time, but William had not returned.

“This frightened us, and we kept searching until night came. Elizabeth then thought he might have gone back to the house. He was not there. We went out again with torches, for I could not rest while thinking that my dear boy might be lost, exposed to the damp night air and dew. Elizabeth was suffering terribly as well. At about five in the morning, I found my lovely boy. The night before, I had seen him healthy, lively, and full of color; now he lay on the grass, pale and motionless. The mark of the murderer’s fingers was on his neck.

“He was carried home, and the anguish on my face revealed the secret to Elizabeth. She urgently wanted to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she insisted. She entered the room where it lay, quickly examined the victim’s neck, and, clasping her hands, cried, ‘O God!”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"eaffd7db416e1879702051c5","rewritten_text":"He slipped quietly out of the wood paneling, wearing an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled mouth. The moon hid behind a cloud as he passed the great oriel window, where his own arms and those of his murdered wife were shown in blue and gold. He glided onward like an evil shadow, and even the darkness seemed to hate him as he went. Once he thought he heard something call and stopped, but it was only a dog barking from the Red Farm. He continued on, muttering strange sixteenth-century curses and waving the rusty dagger now and then in the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the passage leading to poor Washington’s room. He paused there for a moment, while the wind blew his long gray hair around his head and twisted the dead man’s shroud into grotesque, fantastic shapes. Then the clock struck the quarter-hour, and he knew the time had come. He chuckled and turned the corner. But no sooner had he done so than he fell back with a pitiful cry of terror and hid his pale face in his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a horrible specter, as still as a carved statue and as monstrous as a madman’s dream. Its head was bald and shining; its face was round, fat, and white; and terrible laughter seemed to have twisted its features into a permanent grin. Scarlet rays streamed from its eyes, its mouth was a wide pit of fire, and a dreadful garment, like his own, wrapped its silent, snow-covered body. On its chest hung a sign covered in strange, old-fashioned writing. It seemed to be a scroll of shame, a record of wild sins, or a terrible list of crimes. In its right hand it held a shining steel sword.\n\nSince he had never seen a ghost before, he was naturally terrified. After one quick look at the dreadful phantom, he fled to his room, tripping over his long winding sheet as he hurried down the corridor. At last he dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jackboots, where the butler found it the next morning. Once safely inside his own room, he threw himself onto a small pallet bed and hid his face beneath the blankets. After some time, however, the brave old Canterville spirit returned to him, and he decided to go and speak to the other ghost as soon as daylight came. So, just as dawn began to silver the hills, he went back toward the place where he had first seen the grim phantom. He felt that two ghosts were better than one and that, with his new friend’s help, he might safely face the twins."}

content.text: {"request_id":"f7d56dbf1901178b10d18a30","rewritten_text":"In my time, in my own country, this money was raised through import duties. Citizens imagined that foreign importers paid them, and they found comfort in that belief. In fact, the American people paid them, and the cost was divided so evenly that the annual share of a millionaire and that of a day laborer's newborn child were exactly the same—$6 each. Nothing could be fairer, I suppose. Scotland and Ireland were tributary to Arthur, and the combined population of the British Islands was just under 1,000,000. A mechanic earned an average of 3 cents a day when he paid for his own food and lodging. By that measure, the national government spent $90,000 a year, or about $250 a day. So, by replacing gold with nickels on a king's-evil day, I harmed no one, displeased no one, pleased everyone involved, and saved four-fifths of that day's national expense as well—a saving equal to $800,000 in my America. In making this change, I had relied on wisdom from a very distant source: my boyhood. A true statesman does not reject wisdom because its source is humble. As a boy, I had always saved my pennies and donated buttons to foreign missionaries. Buttons would serve an ignorant savage as well as coins, while coins served me better than buttons; everyone was satisfied, and no one was harmed.\n\nMarinel received the patients as they arrived. He examined each candidate; if the person did not qualify, he was turned away, and if he did, he was sent on to the king. A priest recited the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king rubbed the ulcers while the reading continued. At last, the patient completed the ceremony and received his nickel—the king himself hanging it around his neck—then was sent away. Would you believe that this could cure anyone? It certainly did. Any ritual will cure a patient whose faith in it is strong. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who herded geese there—the girl said so herself. They built the chapel on that spot and hung inside it a picture showing the event, a picture you might think dangerous for a sick person to approach. Yet thousands of the lame and sick came to pray before it every year and left healed and healthy; even the healthy could look at it and survive."}

content.text: {"request_id":"062beb9538b2cf71dffd4247","rewritten_text":"The storm raged violently throughout the night, but nothing noteworthy happened. The following morning, however, when they came down to breakfast, they found the dreadful bloodstain once more upon the floor. ‘I don’t believe the Paragon Detergent can be responsible,’ said Washington, ‘because I have tested it on everything. It must be the ghost.’ He therefore removed the stain again, but on the second morning it had returned. It was there on the third morning too, although Mr. Otis himself had locked the library for the night and taken the key upstairs. The entire family was now deeply interested; Mr. Otis began to wonder whether he had been too absolute in denying the existence of ghosts, Mrs. Otis announced that she meant to join the Psychical Society, and Washington composed a lengthy letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore concerning the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains in Connection with Crime. That night, all uncertainty regarding the objective existence of phantasmata vanished forever.\n\nThe day had been warm and bright, and in the cool evening the whole family went out for a drive. They did not get home until nine, when they ate a light supper. The conversation did not turn toward ghosts, so there were not even those initial conditions of receptive expectation that so often precede the appearance of psychical phenomena. As I have since learned from Mr. Otis, the topics discussed were simply those common to cultivated Americans of the better class: the enormous superiority of Miss Fanny Davenport to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of finding green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the finest English houses; Boston’s importance in the development of the world-soul; the benefits of the baggage-check system in railway travel; and the sweetness of the New York accent compared with the London drawl. The supernatural was not mentioned at all, nor was Sir Simon de Canterville referred to in any manner. At eleven the family retired, and by half-past eleven every light had been extinguished. Some time later, Mr. Otis was awakened by a peculiar sound in the corridor outside his room. It resembled the clinking of metal and appeared to draw nearer with every moment. He rose immediately, struck a match, and checked the time. It was precisely one o’clock. He remained perfectly calm and felt his pulse, which was not in the least feverish. The odd noise continued, and he could now clearly hear footsteps as well. He put on his slippers, took a small oblong phial from his dressing-case, and opened the door."}
