{"request_id":"7822fa1c5193157bcc0e55b4","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I determined to get down the moment we reached the town, and place myself beyond his hearing. I carried out this plan successfully. My small portmanteau lay in the boot beneath my feet; I had only to turn a hinge to release it. I flung it down before me, climbed down after it, and found myself left beside the first lamp, on the first stones of the town pavement. The convicts, meanwhile, continued on with the coach, and I knew where they would be taken away to the river. In imagination, I saw the boat, with its convict crew, waiting for them at the slime-streaked stairs—heard once more the rough “Give way, you!” like an order addressed to dogs—and saw again the wicked Noah’s Ark lying upon the dark water.

I could not have explained what frightened me, since my fear was wholly vague and undefined, but I was possessed by a powerful dread. As I went on toward the hotel, I felt that something far beyond the simple apprehension of an unpleasant or painful recognition caused me to tremble. I am certain it assumed no definite form, and that for a few minutes it was the return of the terror of childhood.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty, and I had not merely ordered my dinner there but had begun eating it before the waiter recognised me. After apologising for his failure of memory, he asked whether he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I replied, “certainly not.”

The waiter—it was he who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound—seemed surprised. At the first opportunity, he placed a dirty, old copy of a local newspaper so squarely before me that I picked it up and read the following paragraph:—

Our readers will learn, not without some interest, concerning the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young artificer in iron from this neighbourhood (what a subject, by the way, for the magic pen of our still not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend was a highly respected person, not wholly unconnected with the corn and seed trade, whose eminently convenient and commodious business premises are situated within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not without regard to our personal feelings that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, since it is gratifying to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

{"request_id":"1b12fc1842e4e98b74e3d56e","rewritten_text":"But no—there was something even more dazzling than that. He would become a pirate! That was it! Now his future stretched clearly before him, blazing with unimaginable glory. How his name would spread through the world and make people tremble! How splendidly he would plow the dancing seas in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grisly flag flying from the bow! And at the height of his fame, how he would suddenly appear in the old village and stride into church, brown and weather-beaten, dressed in his black velvet doublet and trunks, his huge jack-boots, crimson sash, belt bristling with horse-pistols, crime-rusted cutlass at his side, and slouch hat crowned with waving plumes, his black flag unfurled and displaying its skull and crossbones, while he listened in swelling ecstasy to the whispers: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was decided; his career was fixed. He would run away from home and begin it. He would leave the very next morning. So he must start preparing at once. He would gather his resources. Going to a rotten log nearby, he began digging beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he struck wood that gave a hollow sound. He placed his hand there and solemnly pronounced this incantation:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. Lifting it, he revealed a neatly made little treasure-house, its bottom and sides formed of shingles. A marble lay inside. Tom’s astonishment was limitless! He scratched his head in perplexity and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he petulantly tossed the marble away and stood thinking. The fact was, one of his superstitions had failed him—a superstition that he and all his comrades had always considered infallible. If a marble were buried with the proper incantations, left undisturbed for a fortnight, and then the spot opened with the incantation he had just spoken, all the marbles ever lost would have gathered there in the meantime, no matter how far apart they had been. But now the thing had plainly and undeniably failed. Tom’s entire structure of belief was shaken to its foundations. He had often heard of the charm working, but never of its failing. It did not occur to him that he himself had tried it several times before, only to be unable afterward to locate the hiding-places. He puzzled over the matter for a while, and at last concluded that some witch had meddled and broken the charm."}

{"request_id":"9788515101c646f332bfca8d","rewritten_text":"TEN minutes later, his face bleached with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, forcing his way through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered beneath the great striped awning, apparently neither seeing nor hearing anything. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas-lamps around the square flared and wavered in the sharp wind; yet his hands were feverishly hot, and his brow burned like fire. He pressed onward, moving almost like a drunken man. A policeman eyed him curiously as he passed, while a beggar, creeping from an archway to ask for charity, drew back in fright at the sight of misery surpassing his own. Once he paused beneath a lamp and stared at his hands. He fancied he could already see blood upon them, and a faint cry escaped his shaking lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had read there. Murder! The very night seemed aware of it, and the desolate wind seemed to shriek it into his ear. The shadowed corners of the streets were filled with it. It grinned down at him from the housetops.

At first he reached the Park, whose gloomy woodland appeared to hold him spellbound. Weary, he rested against the railings, pressing his brow to the wet metal to cool it, and listening to the trees’ trembling silence. ‘Murder! Murder!’ he repeated continually, as though repeating the word might lessen its horror. The sound of his own voice made him shiver, yet he almost wished Echo would catch it and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. A wild impulse seized him to stop some passer-by and tell him everything.

Then he crossed Oxford Street and entered narrow, disgraceful alleys. Two painted women jeered at him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came curses and the sounds of blows, followed by shrill screams; and crouched on a wet doorstep, he saw the bent forms of poverty and old age. A strange compassion overcame him. Were these children of sin and misery destined to their ends, just as he was destined to his? Were they, like him, only puppets in some monstrous spectacle?

Yet it was not the mystery of suffering but its comedy that impressed him: its utter uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. How disjointed everything appeared! How little harmony there was anywhere! He marvelled at the discord between the shallow optimism of the age and the actual facts of existence. He was still very young.

After some time he found himself before Marylebone Church. The silent road resembled a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there by the dark arabesques of moving shadows."}

And at the height of his fame, how he would suddenly return to the old village and stride into church, brown and weather-beaten, wearing his black velvet jacket and trousers, his huge boots, his crimson sash, his belt bristling with pistols, his cutlass stained with the rust of crime at his side, and his floppy hat crowned with waving feathers. His black flag would be unfurled, displaying its skull and crossbones, and he would hear with swelling delight the whispers: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was decided; his career was settled. He would run away from home and begin it. He would leave the very next morning. So he had to start preparing at once. He would gather all his resources. He went to a nearby rotten log and began digging beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he struck wood that sounded hollow. He placed his hand there and solemnly recited this spell:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. He lifted it and revealed a neat little treasure box, with shingles forming its bottom and sides. Inside lay a marble. Tom was astonished beyond measure! He scratched his head in confusion and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he angrily tossed the marble away and stood thinking. The truth was, one of his superstitions had failed him—a superstition he and all his friends had always considered certain. If you buried a marble with the proper spells, left it alone for two weeks, and then opened the hiding place using the spell he had just spoken, you would find that every marble you had ever lost had gathered there, no matter how far apart they had been. But now the charm had plainly and completely failed. Tom’s entire system of belief was shaken to its foundations. He had often heard of the trick working, but never of it failing. It did not occur to him that he himself had tried it several times before and had simply been unable to find the hiding places afterward. He thought about the matter for a while and finally decided that some witch had interfered and broken the spell."}

{"request_id":"647553ea141957c9bb3b813f","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I says, “I reckon you might tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, _I_ don’t know. But he’s bound to have one. All the nobility has.”

That was his way. If he didn’t feel like explaining something to you, he simply wouldn’t. You could pump him for a week, and it wouldn’t do any good.

He had got the whole coat-of-arms business settled, so now he began finishing the rest of that part of the job, which was to devise a mournful inscription—Jim had to have one, same as they all did. He invented a whole lot, wrote them on a sheet of paper, and read them out, like this:

1. _Here a captive heart busted._

2. _Here a poor prisoner, forsook by the world and friends, fretted out his sorrowful life._

3. _Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity._

4. _Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice shook as he read them, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he couldn’t decide which one Jim ought to scratch onto the wall, they were all so fine; but finally he said he’d have Jim scratch every one of them there. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch so much stuff onto the logs with a nail, and he didn’t know how to form letters, either; but Tom said he’d outline them for him, and then all he’d need to do was follow the lines. Then, after a little while, he says:

“Come to think of it, the logs won’t do; they don’t have log walls in a dungeon: we’ve got to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll bring in a rock.”

Jim said the rock would be worse than the logs; he said it would take him such a terribly long time to carve them into a rock that he’d never get out. But Tom said he’d let me help him. Then he looked over to see how me and Jim were doing with the pens. It was mighty tedious, difficult work, and slow, and gave my hands no chance to heal from the sores, and we didn’t seem to be getting anywhere, hardly; so Tom says:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"9fbb0e30f1829ba468a057dc","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers released Lord Arthur’s right hand and seized his left, bending so low to examine it that the gold rims of his spectacles almost touched the palm. For a moment his face became a white mask of horror, but he quickly regained his composure and, looking up at Lady Windermere, said with a forced smile, “It is the hand of a charming young man.

“Of course it is!” Lady Windermere replied. “But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.”

“All charming young men are,” said Mr. Podgers.

“I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,” Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully. “It is so dangerous.”

“My dear child, they are never too fascinating,” cried Lady Windermere. “But what I want are details. Details are the only things that interest me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?”

“Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—”

“Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!”

“And lose a relative.”

“Not his sister, I hope?” Lady Jedburgh asked in a piteous tone.

“Certainly not his sister,” Mr. Podgers answered, waving his hand dismissively. “Only a distant relative.”

“Well, I am terribly disappointed,” said Lady Windermere. “I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives nowadays. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she had better keep a black silk dress ready; it always comes in useful for church, you know. And now let us go to supper. They are sure to have eaten everything, but perhaps we may find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so agitated about politics at present that I never feel entirely sure of him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep quiet. Duchess, I am sure you are tired?”

“Not at all, dear Gladys,” the Duchess replied, waddling toward the door. “I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the chiropodist—I mean the chiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoiseshell fan be? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, very kind, I’m sure.” The worthy creature finally managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent bottle more than twice.

All this time Lord Arthur Savile had remained standing by the fireplace, still filled with dread and the same sickening sense of approaching evil. He smiled sadly at his sister as she swept past him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking beautiful in her pink brocade and pearls, and he barely heard Lady Windermere call for him to follow her. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the thought that anything might come between them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"1c4e8acb1d8430f9864f1a9b","rewritten_text":"Shall I be carried to the skies, on flowery beds of ease,

While others fight to win the prize, and sail through bloody seas?

He was considered a wonderful reader. At church “sociables” he was always asked to read poetry; and when he finished, the ladies would raise their hands and let them fall helplessly into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn had been sung, the Rev. Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin board and read out “notices” of meetings, societies, and other matters until it seemed the list would last until the crack of doom—a strange custom still maintained in America, even in cities, in this age of abundant newspapers. Often, the less there is to support a traditional custom, the harder it is to abandon it.

And now the minister prayed. It was a good, generous prayer, and it went into detail: he pleaded for the church and the church’s little children; for the village’s other churches; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the State officers; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the officers of the Government; for poor sailors tossed by stormy seas; for the oppressed millions groaning beneath the heel of European monarchies and Oriental despotisms; for those who possessed the light and the good tidings yet had no eyes to see or ears to hear; for the heathen on the far islands of the sea; and he ended by asking that the words he was about to speak might find grace and favor, and be like seed sown in fertile ground, producing in time a grateful harvest of good. Amen.

There was a rustling of dresses, and the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it—if he even did that much. He was restless throughout; he kept count of the prayer’s details unconsciously—for he was not listening, but he knew the territory well and the clergyman’s usual route through it—and whenever a small piece of new material was inserted, his ear caught it and his whole nature resented it; he considered additions unfair and scoundrelly. In the middle of the prayer, a fly landed on the back of the pew before him and tormented his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, clasping its head with its arms, and polishing it so vigorously that it seemed almost to separate from the body, exposing the slender thread of a neck; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them against its body as though they were coat-tails; completing its entire toilet as peacefully as if it knew itself to be perfectly safe."}

{"request_id":"4ff58c6213f7cd47646f0b22","rewritten_text":"Her colour altered, and she said nothing more.

Mrs. Gardiner was standing slightly behind; and when she paused, he asked whether she would do him the honour of presenting him to her friends. This courtesy was wholly unexpected; and she could scarcely restrain a smile at his now seeking the acquaintance of some of those very people against whom his pride had rebelled when he offered himself to her. “What a surprise he will have,” she thought, “when he discovers who they are! He takes them at present for people of fashion.”

The introduction was made at once; and as she explained their relation to her, she cast a sly glance at him, to observe how he endured it, half expecting him to retreat as quickly as possible from such disreputable companions. That he was surprised by the connection was plain: nevertheless, he bore it with fortitude; and instead of withdrawing, turned back with them and began talking to Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help being pleased, nor could she help triumphing. It was comforting that he should learn she had relations of whom she need not be ashamed. She listened with the greatest attention to everything that passed between them, and delighted in every remark, every sentence from her uncle that displayed his intelligence, taste, or good breeding.

Their conversation soon came round to fishing; and she heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the utmost civility, to fish there as often as he pleased while he remained in the neighbourhood, offering also to provide him with fishing tackle and indicating the parts of the stream where sport was generally best. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look full of astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but was exceedingly gratified; the compliment must be intended entirely for her. Yet her wonder was intense, and she kept repeating to herself, “Why is he so changed? What can have caused it? It cannot be for me, it cannot be on my account that his manners have become so gentle. My reproofs at Hunsford could not have produced such an alteration. It is impossible that he should still love me.”

After they had walked for some time in this arrangement, the two ladies ahead and the two gentlemen behind, they returned to their places after going down to the river’s edge to examine more closely a curious water-plant, and there happened to be a slight change. It was brought about by Mrs. Gardiner, who, tired from the morning’s exercise, found Elizabeth’s arm insufficient support and therefore chose her husband’s instead."}

{"request_id":"777fe83de721a80c7c94d967","rewritten_text":"The surrounding oaks were inhabited by a tribe of nightingales—there I am now; Idris, in the cherished prime of youth, stands beside me—remember, I am only twenty-two, and scarcely seventeen summers have passed over the beloved of my heart. The river, swollen with autumn rains, had flooded the lowlands, and Adrian, in his favourite boat, was engaged in the perilous amusement of tearing the highest branch from a submerged oak. Are you weary of life, O Adrian, that you thus trifle with danger?—

He secured his prize and guided his boat through the flood; we watched him anxiously, but the current swept him away from us. He was compelled to land much farther down and take a considerable circuit before he could rejoin us. “He is safe!” said Idris, springing ashore and waving the branch above his head as a sign of triumph; “we will wait for him here.”

We were alone together; the sun had gone down; the nightingales began to sing; and the evening star shone clearly in the flood of light that still lingered unfaded in the west. The blue eyes of my angelic girl rested upon this sweet image of herself. “How the light trembles,” she said, “which is that star’s life. Its wavering radiance seems to declare that its condition, like ours on earth, is uncertain and changeable; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Do not gaze upon the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried; “do not read love in _its_ trembling beams; do not look toward distant worlds; do not speak of the mere fancy of a feeling. I have been silent long—too long, even to the point of sickness, have I yearned to speak to you and surrender my soul, my life, my whole being to you. Do not look at the star, dear love—or look, and let that everlasting spark plead for me; let it stand as my witness and advocate, silent in its shining—love is to me what light is to the star; so long as that light is not extinguished by annihilation, so long will I love you.”

The rapture of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s hardened gaze. Yet I still feel her graceful form pressed against my overflowing heart—still do sight, pulse, and breath falter and fail when I recall that first kiss. Slowly and silently we went to meet Adrian, whose approach we heard.

I begged Adrian to return to me after escorting his sister home. That same evening, as we walked along the moonlit forest paths, I poured out to my friend all my heart, its joy and its hopes. For a moment he appeared troubled. “I might have anticipated this,” he said. “What conflict will now follow!”"}

{"request_id":"9c209f9fec092b190b834637","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is extraordinary! I must meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose and paced around the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is simply an inspiration for my art. You might see nothing in him. I see everything. He is never more present in my work than when I do not paint him. As I have said, he suggests a new style. I find him in the curves of certain lines and in the beauty and subtlety of certain colours. That is all.”

“Then why won’t you display his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I have put into it some expression of this strange artistic worship, which I have naturally never mentioned to him. He knows nothing about it, and he must never know. But the world might guess, and I will not expose my soul to its shallow, prying eyes. My heart will never be placed beneath their microscope. There is too much of me in the painting, Harry—too much of me!”

“Poets are not as careful as you. They know how useful passion can be when it is published. These days, a broken heart can sell many editions.”

“I hate them for that,” Hallward cried. “An artist should create beautiful things, but put none of his own life into them. We live in an age when people treat art as if it were autobiography. We have lost the pure sense of beauty. One day I will show the world what beauty is; and for that reason, the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you are wrong, Basil, but I will not argue. Only the intellectually lost ever argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter thought for a few moments. “He likes me,” he replied after a pause; “I know he does. Of course, I flatter him terribly. I take a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I will regret. Usually he is charming to me, and we sit in the studio talking about a thousand things. Sometimes, however, he is terribly thoughtless and seems to take real pleasure in hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I have given my whole soul to someone who treats it as if it were a flower to wear in his coat—a decoration to satisfy his vanity, an ornament for a summer’s day.”"}

His correspondence with the public enemy had not begun today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that, for longer than that, the prisoner had regularly traveled between France and England on secret business he could not honestly explain. If treasonous schemes could prosper—which, fortunately, they never did—the true wickedness and guilt of this business might have remained hidden. Providence, however, had inspired a man who was fearless and beyond reproach to uncover the prisoner’s plans and, horrified by them, reveal them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would appear before them. His position and conduct were, in every way, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but, discovering his disgrace at once in a fortunate and terrible moment, had decided to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer hold dear on the sacred altar of his country. If Britain, like ancient Greece and Rome, awarded statues to public benefactors, this brilliant citizen would certainly have received one. Since Britain did not award them, he probably would not. Virtue, as the poets had observed in many passages the jury surely knew by heart—though their guilty faces showed that they knew nothing of them—was somehow contagious, especially the shining virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The noble example of this spotless and unquestionable witness for the Crown, whom it was an honour to mention even so unworthily, had spread to the prisoner’s servant. It had inspired him with the holy resolve to search his master’s drawers and pockets and hide his papers. The Attorney-General was ready to hear someone criticize this admirable servant; but, generally speaking, he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters and honoured him more than his own father and mother. He confidently called on the jury to do the same. The evidence of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had discovered, would show that the prisoner had received lists of His Majesty’s forces and their positions and preparations, by sea and land. {"request_id":"e8e2f207354ac6cbac43d204","rewritten_text":"“Well, everyone does it that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it doesn’t make any difference. I’m not everyone, and I can’t stand it. It’s awful being tied down like that. And food comes too easily—I don’t take any interest in meals that way. I have to ask permission to go fishing; I have to ask to go swimming—darned if I don’t have to ask before doing everything. And I had to speak so politely it wasn’t any comfort—I had to go up into the attic and let loose for a while every day, just to get the proper taste back in my mouth, or I would have died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me yell, or yawn, or stretch, or scratch in front of people—” [Then, with a sudden fit of particular irritation and hurt]—“And blast it, she prayed all the time! I never saw such a woman! I had to leave, Tom—I simply had to. And besides, school is about to start, and I would have had to attend it—well, I wouldn’t put up with that, Tom. Listen here, Tom, being rich isn’t what it’s made out to be. It’s nothing but worry and worry, and work and work, and wishing you were dead all the time. Now these clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never going to give them up again. Tom, I never would have gotten into all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money; now you just take my share along with yours, and give me a dime once in a while—not often, because I don’t care about anything unless it’s fairly hard to get—and go ask the widow to excuse me.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It wouldn’t be right; and besides, if you try this a little longer, you’ll come to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed, suffocating houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’m going to stick with them. Damn it all! Just when we had guns and a cave, and everything ready for robbing, this foolishness has to come along and ruin it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Listen here, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from becoming a robber.”

“No! Oh, glory, are you truly serious, Tom?”

“Just as serious as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you join the gang if you aren’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s happiness vanished.

“Can’t let me join, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"41bc47684c90830d7e344683","rewritten_text":"The studio was steeped in the rich fragrance of roses, and whenever the light summer breeze moved among the garden trees, the open door admitted the heavy scent of lilac, or the subtler perfume of the pink-blossomed thorn.

From his corner of the Persian saddle-bag divan, where he lay smoking his customary endless cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could just see the honey-coloured, honey-sweet flowers of a laburnum. Its quivering branches appeared scarcely strong enough to support such a flame-like burden of beauty. From time to time, the fanciful shadows of birds flying past crossed the long curtains of tussore silk drawn before the great window, creating a brief Japanese effect and recalling to him the pale, jade-faced painters of Tokyo, who, through an art necessarily still, attempted to suggest speed and movement. The gloomy humming of bees forcing their way through the tall, uncut grass, or circling monotonously around the dusty golden horns of the wandering woodbine, seemed to deepen the oppressive quiet. London’s muffled roar sounded like the sustained note of a far-off organ.

At the room’s centre, fastened to an upright easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of remarkable beauty. A short distance before it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance several years earlier had caused considerable public excitement and prompted so many strange speculations.

As the painter gazed at the graceful, handsome figure he had so skilfully reproduced in his art, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to remain there. Then he abruptly rose, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against the lids, as if trying to hold within his mind some curious dream from which he feared awakening.

“It is your finest work, Basil—the finest thing you have ever done,” said Lord Henry lazily. “You must surely send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too vast and too vulgar. Whenever I have gone there, there have either been so many people that I could not see the pictures, which was dreadful, or so many pictures that I could not see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is truly the only place.”

“I don’t think I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, throwing back his head in that peculiar manner which had once made his Oxford friends laugh at him."}

{"request_id":"159812f235798d1633c16c48","rewritten_text":"Other chances for forming her observations could hardly fail to arise. Anne had soon been often enough in the company of all four to have formed an opinion, though she was too prudent to admit as much at home, knowing it would have pleased neither husband nor wife; for although she thought Louisa rather the favourite, she could not help believing, so far as memory and experience allowed her to judge, that Captain Wentworth was in love with neither. They were more in love with him; yet even in their case it was not love. It was merely a slight fever of admiration, though it might, and probably must, end in love with one of them. Charles Hayter appeared conscious of being neglected, while Henrietta sometimes seemed divided between the two. Anne longed to make them all understand what they were doing, and to show them some of the dangers to which they were exposing themselves. She imputed guile to none. It was her greatest satisfaction to think that Captain Wentworth was not in the least aware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph—no mean triumph—in his manner. He had probably never heard of, nor considered, any claims Charles Hayter might have had. His only fault was accepting the attentions (for accepting was certainly the word) of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw from the contest. Three days had gone by without his coming once to Uppercross—a very decided alteration. He had even declined one customary invitation to dinner; and when Mr Musgrove found him on that occasion with several large books before him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were convinced that something must be wrong, and spoke solemnly of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had given him an outright dismissal, while her husband lived in continual expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only think that Charles Hayter was acting wisely.

One morning at about this time, while Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at work when the sisters from the Mansion-house appeared at the window.

It was a remarkably fine November day, and the Miss Musgroves crossed the little grounds, stopping only to say that they were going for a _long_ walk, and had therefore assumed that Mary would not care to accompany them. When Mary instantly answered, somewhat jealous at not being considered a good walker, “Oh, yes, I should very much like to join you; I am extremely fond of a long walk,” Anne was convinced, from the looks exchanged by the two girls, that this was exactly what they had not wanted. She again admired the kind of necessity that family habits seemed to create: everything had to be told, and everything had to be done together, however unwelcome or inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"85728c68b008a8578d58d3ec","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that forever brings misery must have been broken, and the malignant fate presiding over it would not allow such a breach of her eternal laws. But why should I complain of this? Misery was my element, and nothing but misery could come near me; if Woodville had been happy, I should never have known him. And can I, who for so many years was fed by tears and nourished beneath the dew of grief, pause to tell a tale of woe and death?

Woodville was required to make a journey into the country and was kept, day after day, in tiresome separation from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her saying that she was slightly ill, but urging him to hurry to her, for she would draw health from his eyes, and his company would be her surest medicine. He was delayed three days longer, and then hastened to her. His heart, though he did not know why, foretold misfortune; he had heard nothing more from her. He feared she might be worse, and this fear made him impatient and restless for the moment when he would see her once again standing before him in health and beauty; for a sinister voice seemed always whispering, “You will never see her as she was again.”

When he reached her home, everything was silent. He passed through several rooms; in one he saw a servant weeping bitterly. Faint with fear, he could scarcely ask, “Is she dead?” and could only listen to the terrible answer: “Not yet.” These astonishing words struck him as less dreadful than those he had expected; to learn that she still lived, and that he might still hope, brought him some relief. He remembered the words of her letter and indulged the wild thought that his kisses, breathing warm love and life, would pour new strength into her, and that she could not die while he was near; his presence was the talisman of her life.

He hurried to her sickroom. She lay there with her cheeks burning from fever, yet her eyes were closed and she seemed insensible. He gathered her into his arms and pressed breathless kisses upon her burning lips. In a voice of restrained anguish, he called her by the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am with you—your life, your love. Return, dearest one. You promised me this gift, that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die beside me. What is death? To see you no more? To be parted from one who is part of myself, without whom I have no memory and no future?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"f20cd3661ea479081d14706b","rewritten_text":"We were united in our love for Adrian, though she, still not wholly beyond childhood, could not value his merits as I did, nor share my sympathy with his pursuits and opinions. I was constantly beside him. There was such tenderness and sweetness in his nature that our conversations took on a gentle, almost unearthly character. Yet he was merry as a lark singing from its airy tower, lofty in thought as an eagle, and innocent as the mild-eyed dove. He could lighten Perdita’s gravity and remove the sting from the tormenting energy of my own nature. I looked back upon my restless longings and painful conflicts with my fellow beings as upon a troubled dream, and seemed as greatly transformed as though I had passed into another form, whose new senses and nervous frame had changed the image of the visible universe in the mind’s mirror. But this was not truly so; I remained the same in strength, in earnest hunger for sympathy, and in my desire for active exertion. My manly virtues had not abandoned me, for the witch Urania spared Sampson’s locks while he rested at her feet; yet everything had become gentler and more humane. Nor did Adrian teach me merely the lifeless truths of history and philosophy. While he used them to help me master my own reckless and uncultivated spirit, he also revealed the living page of his heart, allowing me to feel and comprehend its marvelous character.\n\nThe former queen of England had, from her son’s earliest infancy, tried to plant bold and ambitious schemes within his mind. She perceived that he possessed genius and extraordinary talent, and cultivated these qualities so that she might later employ them in advancing her own purposes. She fostered his thirst for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even endured his untamable love of freedom, hoping that it would, as so often happens, develop into a passion for command. She sought to raise him with resentment toward, and a wish to avenge himself upon, those who had helped bring about his father’s abdication. In this she failed. The reports given him, however distorted, of a great and wise nation claiming the right to govern itself, stirred his admiration; in his early years he became a republican on principle. His mother, nevertheless, did not give up hope. Along with love of authority and proud birth, she cultivated resolute ambition, patience, and self-command. She devoted herself to studying her son’s character. Through praise, blame, and exhortation, she attempted to discover and touch the proper chords; and though the music produced by her efforts sounded discordant to her, she based her hopes on his talents and remained certain that she would eventually win him."}

{"request_id":"80ca192229b7cafdc3d0a09a","rewritten_text":"He made no second attempt. The boys lay there, counting the dragging moments until it seemed that time itself must be finished and eternity turning gray; then they were thankful to see that the sun was finally going down.

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat upright, looked around, and grimly smiled at his companion, whose head had fallen forward onto his knees. He nudged him with his foot and said:

“Here! _You’re_ a watchman, ain’t you! All right, though—nothing’s happened.”

“My! Have I been asleep?”

“Oh, partly, partly. It’s nearly time for us to move, pard. What’ll we do with the little swag we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here as we always have, I reckon. No use carrying it away till we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is something to lug around.”

“Well—all right—it won’t hurt to come here once more.”

“No—but I’d say come at night, like we used to—it’s better.”

“Yes; but look here, it may be a long while before I get the proper chance at that job; accidents could happen; it ain’t in such a good place. We’ll bury it regular—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said his companion. He crossed the room, knelt down, lifted one of the rear hearth-stones, and pulled out a bag that jingled pleasantly. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to Joe, who was now on his knees in the corner, digging with his bowie-knife.

The boys instantly forgot all their fears and misery. With shining, greedy eyes they watched every movement. Luck!—the magnificence of it surpassed anything they could imagine! Six hundred dollars was enough money to make half a dozen boys rich! Here was treasure-hunting under the best possible circumstances—there would be no troublesome uncertainty about where to dig. Every moment they nudged one another—eloquent nudges, easily understood, meaning simply: “Oh, but ain’t you glad _now_ we’re here!”

Joe’s knife hit something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his companion.

“A half-rotten plank—no, I believe it’s a box. Here—lend a hand and we’ll find out what it’s doing here. Never mind, I’ve made a hole.”

He thrust in his hand and pulled it out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men inspected the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as thrilled and delighted as the men themselves.

Joe’s companion said:

“We’ll finish this quickly. There’s an old rusty pick among the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace—I noticed it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"7e27299c7e1201ae4ff807be","rewritten_text":"She studied me sharply for a short while, then said in a low voice,—

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I replied, “that you would not mistake them for the others. They may share the same blood, but, believe me, they are not of the same disposition.”

Still watching me closely, Miss Havisham repeated,—

“What do you want for them?”

“You see, I am not clever enough,” I said, feeling that I coloured slightly, “to conceal from you, even if I wished to, that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would spend the money to render my friend Herbert a lasting service in life, though the circumstances require it to be done without his knowing, I could tell you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowledge?” she asked, resting both hands on her stick so that she could observe me more closely.

“Because,” I said, “I began doing him that service myself, over two years ago, without his knowledge, and I do not wish to be exposed. Why I am unable to complete it, I cannot say. That is part of a secret belonging to someone else, not to me.”

By degrees she took her eyes from me and fixed them on the fire. She watched it for what, in the silence and the glow of the slowly burning-down candles, seemed a long while. Then the falling of some red coals roused her, and she looked back towards me—first absently, then with attention that steadily gathered. Throughout this, Estella continued knitting. When Miss Havisham had settled her gaze upon me, she spoke as though our conversation had not been interrupted,—

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her and striving to steady my trembling voice, “you know that I love you. You know I have loved you for a long time and with all my heart.”

At my words she lifted her eyes to my face, while her fingers continued their work, and regarded me without any change of expression. I noticed Miss Havisham look from me to her, and then from her back to me.

“I ought to have said this earlier, but for my long-standing error. It led me to hope that Miss Havisham intended us for each other. While I believed you were, in a manner, unable to help yourself, I held my tongue. But now I must say it.”

Still keeping her expression unchanged, and with her fingers moving on, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said, replying to that gesture,—“I know. I do not hope ever to call you mine, Estella."}

{"request_id":"bab94eb29d015cf6309f7e19","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Massa Will—truly I am,” the negro replied at once. “I’m almost at the end now.”

“_At the end!_” Legrand shouted. “Do you mean you are at the end of that branch?”

“Almost at de eend, massa—o-o-o-o-oh! Lord have mercy! What is this here on de tree?”

“Well?” cried Legrand, greatly pleased. “What is it?”

“Why, it ain’t nothing but a skull. Somebody left his head up in de tree, and de crows done eat every bit of meat off it.”

“A skull, you say? Very well. How is it attached to the branch? What is holding it there?”

“Sure enough, massa; I must look. Why, this is a very strange thing, I swear—there’s a great big nail in de skull, fastening it to de tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly as I tell you. Do you hear?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Then pay attention. Find the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! Hoo! That’s a good one! Why, there ain’t any left eye at all.”

“Curse your stupidity! Don’t you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that—know all about it. ’Tis my left hand I chop wood with.”

“Of course! You are left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now I suppose you can find the skull’s left eye, or the place where its left eye was. Have you found it?”

There was a long pause. At last the negro asked,

“Is de skull’s left eye on de same side as de skull’s left hand, too? ’Cause de skull ain’t got any hand at all—never mind! I got de left eye now—here it is! What must I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it as far as the string will reach—but be careful not to let go of the string.”

“All done, Massa Will. Mighty easy to put de bug through de hole—watch out for him down there!”

During this exchange, none of Jupiter could be seen. But the beetle he had lowered was now visible at the end of the string, shining like a ball of polished gold in the last rays of the setting sun. Some of that light still faintly reached the hill where we stood. The scarab hung clear of all branches and, if released, would have fallen at our feet. Legrand immediately took the scythe and cut away a circular space three or four yards wide directly beneath the insect. When he had finished, he ordered Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"82d69027142f40bec27194ed","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in any business like that, I says to myself.

When I came downstairs in the morning, the parlor was closed, and the watchers had gone. Nobody was about except the family, the widow Bartley, and our crowd. I studied their faces to see whether anything had happened, but I couldn’t make out.

Toward midday the undertaker arrived with his man, and they placed the coffin in the center of the room on two chairs. Then they arranged all our chairs in rows, borrowing more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining-room were filled. I saw the coffin lid was as it had been before, but I didn’t dare look beneath it with people all around.

Then folks began pouring in, and the beats and girls took places in the front row at the coffin’s head. For half an hour the people passed slowly in single file, looking down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some let fall a tear, and everything was quiet and solemn, except for the girls and beats holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bowed, and sobbing a little. There was no other noise but feet scraping the floor and noses being blown—because people always blow them more at a funeral than anywhere else except church.

When the room was crammed full, the undertaker glided about in his black gloves with his gentle, soothing manner, putting on the final touches, arranging people and things shipshape and comfortable, and making no more noise than a cat. He never said a word; he shifted people, squeezed in latecomers, and opened passages with nods and hand signs. Then he stationed himself against the wall. He was the gentlest, smoothest, stealthiest man I ever saw; and he had no more smile than a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeum—a sick one; and when all was ready, a young woman sat down and worked it. It sounded pretty screechy and colicky, and everybody joined in singing, with Peter the only one who had a good voice, as I figured it. Then Reverend Hobson began speaking, slow and solemn; and right away the most outrageous racket anyone ever heard broke out in the cellar. It was only one dog, but he made an awful din and kept it going; the parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"12726dcb70ce9648f65a85bf","rewritten_text":"There comes a time in every properly raised boy’s life when he desperately wants to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. That desire suddenly seized Tom one day. He went looking for Joe Harper, but couldn’t find him. Then he looked for Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. At last he ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a private spot and quietly explained his plan. Huck was willing. He was always ready to join any adventure that promised fun and cost nothing, since he had far too much free time. “Where’ll we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is treasure buried everywhere?”

“No, of course not. It’s hidden in very particular places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests beneath the end of a branch on an old dead tree, exactly where the shadow falls at midnight; but usually under the floor of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Robbers, naturally—who did you think? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine, I wouldn’t hide it. I’d spend it and have a good time.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do things that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No. They mean to, but they usually forget the signs, or they die. Anyway, it stays there a long time and gets rusty. Then someone finds an old yellow paper explaining how to locate the signs—a paper that takes about a week to decode because it’s mostly symbols and hieroglyphics.”

“Hieroglyphics?”

“Pictures and things, you know, that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Then how are you going to find the signs?”

“I don’t need any signs. They always bury it under a haunted house, on an island, or beneath a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We’ve searched Jackson’s Island a little, and we can try again sometime. Then there’s the old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and there are plenty of dead trees—whole loads of them.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“What a thing to say! No!”

“Then how will you know which one to search?”

“Search them all!”

“Tom, that’ll take the whole summer.”

“Well, so what? Suppose you find a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How would you like that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s excellent. More than excellent for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want any diamonds.”"}

{"request_id":"bf0027e818fc522ded4beadd","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went riding on Brockley Meadows. While climbing through a hedge, she tore her riding habit badly. When she returned home, she decided to use the back staircase so that no one would see her. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door happened to be open, she thought she saw someone inside. Believing it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her work there, she looked in to ask her to mend the torn habit. To her great surprise, however, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees blow through the air and the red leaves whirl wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole manner showed deep sadness. He looked so lonely and so worn-out that little Virginia, who had first meant to run away and lock herself in her room, felt sorry for him and decided to comfort him. Her footsteps were so quiet, and his sadness so deep, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

‘I am very sorry for you,’ she said, ‘but my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow. Then, if you behave yourself, no one will bother you.’

‘It is ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,’ he replied, turning in surprise toward the pretty little girl who had dared to speak to him. ‘Completely ridiculous. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night, if that is what you mean. It is the only reason I exist.’

‘That is no reason to exist at all, and you know you have behaved very wickedly. Mrs. Umney told us on the first day we arrived that you had killed your wife.’

‘Well, I admit it,’ said the Ghost irritably, ‘but it was strictly a family matter and had nothing to do with anyone else.’

‘It is very wrong to kill anyone,’ said Virginia, who sometimes had a gentle, serious Puritan manner inherited from an old New England ancestor.

‘Oh, I hate the cheap harshness of abstract morality! My wife was very plain, never had my ruffs starched properly, and knew nothing about cooking. Why, I once shot a magnificent young buck in Hogley Woods, and do you know how she served it at the table? Still, it does not matter now, because it is all over. And I do not think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.’"}

{"request_id":"92f01b747fbbb70a14d010ff","rewritten_text":"“Then listen! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother, from whom he had long been separated—joined him there, traveling from Paris and taking me with her, supposedly to look after his property, though I cannot say why, since she had little affection for him, and he had none for her. He knew nothing of us, for his senses had failed him, and he slept on until the following day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two, dated on the night his illness began and addressed to you”; he turned to Mr. Brownlow; “with a few short lines enclosed, and a note on the package saying it was not to be sent until after his death. One of the papers was a letter to this girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What did the letter say?” Mr. Brownlow asked.

“The letter? A sheet of paper covered with writing, containing a remorseful confession and prayers to God to help her. He had told the girl some story that a secret matter—to be explained one day—prevented him from marrying her at that time. So she had continued to trust him patiently, until she trusted too far and lost what no one could ever restore to her. She was then only a few months from giving birth. He told her everything he had intended to do, had he lived, to conceal her shame, and begged her, if he died, not to curse his memory or believe that the consequences of their sin would fall upon her or their child; all the guilt, he said, was his. He reminded her of the day he had given her the small locket and the ring engraved with her Christian name, leaving a blank for the name he hoped one day to give her. He begged her still to keep them and wear them next to her heart, as she had before. Then he continued wildly, repeating the same words again and again, as though he had lost his mind. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, as Oliver’s tears fell rapidly.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He spoke of the misery his wife had caused him; of your rebellious nature, vice, malice, and premature evil passions—you, his only son, who had been taught to hate him—and left you and your mother an annuity of eight hundred pounds each. He divided the greater part of his property into two equal shares: one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it were born alive and ever reached adulthood.”"}

“I should have said this earlier, if I had not been mistaken for so long. That mistake made me hope that Miss Havisham intended us for each other. While I believed you could not help yourself, in a sense, I held back from saying it. But I must say it now.”

Keeping her expression unchanged and her fingers still moving, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said, responding to that gesture. “I know. I have no hope that I will ever call you mine, Estella."}

{"request_id":"8594e470ab4431296cf2679c","rewritten_text":"He could not help himself. And it infuriated him to think, as he believed he saw, that Becky Thatcher had not once guessed he was even among the living. Yet she did see him, all the same; and she knew she was winning her battle, too, and was pleased to watch him suffer as she had suffered.

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted that he had matters to attend to; things that had to be done; and that time was passing quickly. But it was useless—the girl kept chirping away. Tom thought, “Oh, hang her, am I never going to get rid of her?” At last he really had to attend to those matters—and she said innocently that she would be “around” when school was dismissed. He hurried off, hating her for saying it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in the whole town except that Saint Louis smarty who thinks he dresses so grand and belongs to the aristocracy! Oh, all right, I licked you the first day you ever set foot in this town, mister, and I’ll lick you again! Just wait till I catch you outside! I’ll just take and—”

Then he acted out the beating of an imaginary boy—pounding the air, kicking, and gouging. “Oh, you do, do you? You yell ’nough, do you? Now then, let that teach you!” And with that the imaginary thrashing ended to his satisfaction.

Tom ran home at noon. His conscience could stand no more of Amy’s thankful happiness, and his jealousy could endure no more of the other misery. Becky went on examining pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes passed and Tom did not appear to suffer, her triumph began to fade and her interest disappeared; seriousness and distraction came next, followed by melancholy. Two or three times she raised her head at the sound of footsteps, but each time it was a false hope; Tom did not come. At last she became thoroughly wretched and wished she had not carried matters so far. When poor Alfred, noticing that he was losing her without knowing why, kept crying, “Oh, here’s a jolly one! Look at this!” she finally lost patience and said, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care about them!” Then she burst into tears, rose, and walked away.

Alfred followed close beside her and was about to try comforting her, but she said:

“Go away and leave me alone, can’t you! I hate you!”

So the boy stopped, wondering what he could possibly have done—for she had said she would look at pictures throughout the noon recess—and she continued on, crying. Then Alfred went thoughtfully into the empty schoolhouse. He was humiliated and angry. It was easy for him to see the truth: the girl had merely used him as a means of venting her spite against Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"011e22e677702190f3bcd459","rewritten_text":"There was something strange in all this that drew me in and enchanted me. He seemed to have awakened from a long, visionary sleep, and felt somewhat like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that beautiful imitation of an Eastern tale: Diana was gone; his friends had changed or died, and now, upon awakening, I was all he had left to love on earth.

How dear the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became to me, now that I had so beloved a companion for my rambles. With my father, I visited every delightful place, whether on the islands or beside the waterfalls sheltered by trees; every shady path and every hollow tangled with undergrowth and fern. His conversation broadened my thoughts. I felt as though I had been recreated, carrying within me all the freshness and vitality of a new being. Since his arrival, I seemed to have been transported from a narrow patch of earth into a universe boundless to the imagination and understanding. Before, my life had been like a pleasant country stream, never meant to leave its native fields, but destined, once its quiet task was done, to be absorbed without leaving a trace. Now it seemed a varied river flowing through a fertile and lovely landscape, forever changing and forever beautiful. Alas! I did not know what desert it was approaching, what rocks would tear its waters, or what hideous scene would be reflected, more horribly distorted, in its waves. Life was then brilliant; I was beginning to learn hope—and what brings more bitter despair to the heart than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should so quickly follow happiness so divine? I drank from an enchanted cup, but gall lay at the bottom of its lingering sweetness. My heart was filled with deep affection, yet it was calm because of its very depth and fullness. I had no idea that misery could arise from love, and this lesson, which everyone must eventually learn, was taught to me in a way few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and must always mourn, those few short months of paradise; I had disobeyed no command, eaten no apple, and yet I was driven ruthlessly from it. Alas! My companion had, and I was cast down in his fall. But I am straying from my account—let sorrow come at its appointed time; at this point in my story, I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship, when my aunt fell ill. I spent an entire month in her room nursing her, but her illness was fatal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for some time. Death is so terrible to the living; the bonds of habit are so strong, even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must be tormented when they are broken."}

{"request_id":"63a9554c69715689f23630a5","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s happened to that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady lowered her spectacles and looked over them around the room; then she raised them and looked beneath them. She almost never looked _through_ them for something as small as a boy; they were her formal pair, the pride of her heart, made for “style,” not usefulness—she could have seen just as well through a pair of stove lids. She looked puzzled for a moment, then said, not angrily, but still loudly enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I swear, if I catch you I’ll—”

She did not finish, because by then she was bending over and jabbing beneath the bed with the broom, and needed breath to punctuate each jab. She brought out nothing but the cat.

“I’ve never seen the equal of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood there, and looked out among the tomato vines and “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at an angle meant to carry and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u, TOM!”

There was a faint sound behind her, and she turned just in time to seize a small boy by the loose back of his jacket and stop his escape.

“There! I should have thought of that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What _is_ that stuff?”

“I don’t know, Aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve told you that if you didn’t leave that jam alone I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch rose into the air—the danger was extreme—

“My! Look behind you, Aunt!”

The old lady spun around and snatched her skirts out of harm’s way. The boy fled at once, scrambled up the tall board fence, and vanished over it.

His Aunt Polly stood astonished for a moment, then began to laugh softly.

“Damn that boy, can’t I ever learn? Hasn’t he played tricks like that on me often enough for me to watch out by now? But old fools are the greatest fools there are. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as they say. But goodness, he never plays the same trick two days in a row, and how is anyone supposed to know what’s coming? He seems to know exactly how long he can torment me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me for a minute or make me laugh, it all fades away and I can’t strike him once.”"}

{"request_id":"04136a991a45108cdcee9f01","rewritten_text":"But do not imagine that I did not consider it an evil in itself.”

“Believe me, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I might not like them any better for that, perhaps. So many women and children have no _right_ to be comfortable aboard ship.”

“My dear Frederick, you are talking complete nonsense. What would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who often need to be carried to one port or another to join our husbands, if everyone shared your feelings?”

“My feelings, as you see, did not stop me from taking Mrs Harville and her entire family to Plymouth.”

“But I hate to hear you speak like such a gentleman, as though women were all delicate ladies instead of rational creatures. None of us expects smooth water throughout our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “once he has a wife, he will sing a different tune. If he marries, and we are fortunate enough to live through another war, we shall see him do as you and I, and many others, have done. We shall see him deeply grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Yes, we shall.”

“Now I am finished,” cried Captain Wentworth. “Whenever married people begin attacking me with, ‘Oh, you will think very differently when you are married,’ I can only answer, ‘No, I shall not.’ Then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that ends the matter.”

He rose and moved away.

“You must have been a great traveller, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Fairly so, ma’am, during the fifteen years of my marriage, though many women have travelled farther. I have crossed the Atlantic four times, and gone once to the East Indies and back; besides visiting various places nearer home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Straits, and was never in the West Indies. We do not count Bermuda or the Bahamas as the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to say in disagreement; she could not accuse herself of ever having called them anything at all during her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft continued, “that nothing can surpass the accommodations aboard a man-of-war; I speak, of course, of the higher rates. In a frigate, naturally, you are more confined, though any reasonable woman may be perfectly happy in one; and I can safely say that the happiest part of my life was spent aboard ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.”"}

{"request_id":"5fd1a87c40bc4ba2ba2a49b3","rewritten_text":"I have said that he was a poet: at three and twenty he published his first poem, and the whole nation greeted it with enthusiasm and delight. His fortunate star seemed always to shine upon him; no reputation had ever been established so swiftly, and his fame was universal. The multitude praised the very poems that astonished the learned man in his study: there was not a single dissenting voice.

It was then, at the summit of his glory, that he became acquainted with Elinor. She was a young heiress of exquisite beauty, living under the guardianship of another: from the first moment they were seen together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not possess Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble, and elevated by youth and by the love she inspired everywhere beyond concern for anything except virtue and excellence. She was lovely; her manners were open and unaffected; her deep blue eyes shone with a radiance that could only arise from sensibility united with wisdom.

They were made for one another, and soon fell in love. Woodville now felt, for the first time, love’s delight; and Elinor was transported to possess the heart of one so beautiful and illustrious among his fellow men. Could anything but unmingled joy proceed from such a union?

Woodville was a Poet—every society sought him, and whenever he appeared all eyes were fixed upon him alone; yet he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian did not object to their mutual affection: Woodville’s merit was too distinguished to invite objection on the ground of his lesser fortune; but her father’s dying will forbade her to marry until she had reached her majority, and her inheritance depended upon her obeying that command. She had only just entered her twentieth year, so she and her lover were compelled to endure the delay. Still, they were constantly together, and their happiness seemed paradisal: they studied side by side, made plans for their future occupations, and, drinking love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, scarcely lamented the postponement of their complete union. Woodville continually advanced in glory; and Elinor grew lovelier and wiser beneath the instruction of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I recount the catastrophe that overtook so much joy? Yet the earth would not be the blighted and sorrowful earth it is if such an angelic pair had been permitted to exist for one another: search the world, and you will find no perfect happiness such as their marriage would have given them; the order of things established among us miserable dwellers on earth would have needed to be overturned before such consummate joy could be allowed."}

{"request_id":"11120a7fe82798a1e4856bb4","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had taken an excellent house in Camden Place, an elevated, dignified setting suited to a man of consequence; and he and Elizabeth were both established there, greatly to their satisfaction.

Anne entered it with a sinking heart, expecting to be imprisoned there for many months, and anxiously asking herself, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Yet the unexpectedly warm welcome she received did her good. Her father and sister were pleased to see her, wanting to show her the house and furnishings, and greeted her kindly. When she sat down to dinner and made a fourth, they treated her presence as an advantage.

Mrs Clay was very agreeable and smiling, but her courtesies and smiles seemed more habitual. Anne had always believed that she would put on the proper appearance when Anne arrived, but the others’ friendliness was unexpected. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and Anne soon heard why. They had no desire to hear about her. After allowing themselves a few compliments about how deeply she must have been missed in their former neighbourhood—compliments Anne could not return—they made only a few weak inquiries before the conversation became entirely their own. Uppercross aroused no interest, and Kellynch very little: everything was Bath.

They had the pleasure of assuring her that Bath had exceeded their expectations in every respect. Their house was unquestionably the finest in Camden Place; their drawing rooms possessed many clear advantages over all the others they had seen or heard about, and the superiority extended equally to the style of the decoration and the taste of the furniture. Their company was eagerly sought. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had declined many introductions, yet people whose names they did not know were constantly leaving cards.

Here were abundant sources of pleasure. Could Anne wonder that her father and sister were happy? She might not wonder, but she had to sigh that her father felt no humiliation in his change of circumstances, saw nothing to regret in the responsibilities and dignity of a resident landowner, and found so much to be proud of in the small distinctions of a town. She had to sigh, smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth flung open the folding doors and walked triumphantly from one drawing room to the other, boasting of their size; at the possibility that the woman who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall could find space between two walls, perhaps thirty feet apart, something to take pride in.

But this was not all they had to make them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

There was no answer. Tom examined his last stroke with an artist’s eye, then gave his brush another gentle sweep and studied the result as before. Ben moved alongside him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stayed with his work. Ben said:

“Hello, old fellow, you have to work, do you?”

Tom turned suddenly and said:

“Why, it’s you, Ben! I wasn’t paying attention.”

“Say—I’m going swimming. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather work, wouldn’t you? Of course you would!”

Tom considered the boy for a moment, then said:

“What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t that work?”

Tom went back to whitewashing and answered casually:

“Well, maybe it is, and maybe it isn’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh, come on, you don’t mean to pretend that you like it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get the chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That made the matter look different. Ben stopped nibbling his apple. Tom moved his brush delicately back and forth, stepped back to judge the effect, added a touch here and there, and criticized the result again. Ben watched every movement, becoming more and more interested and absorbed. At last he said:

“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”

Tom thought it over and was about to agree, but changed his mind:

“No—no—I don’t think it would do, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly is extremely particular about this fence—it’s right here on the street, you know—but if it were the back fence, I wouldn’t mind, and she wouldn’t either. Yes, she’s extremely particular about this fence; it has to be done very carefully. I suppose there isn’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, who can do it the way it has to be done.”

“No—is that so? Oh, come on—let me just try. Only a little—I’d let you if you were me, Tom.”

Yet no one had followed them, and no man spoke when they entered the wine-shop, though every eye there turned toward them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

It may have been a signal that loosened the general tongue. It drew an answering chorus of “Good day!”

“It is bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

At this, every man looked at his neighbour, then all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. Except one man, who rose and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge aloud, addressing Madame Defarge, “I have travelled several leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him—by accident—a day and a half’s journey from Paris. He is a good child, this road-mender called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender called Jacques. He removed his blue cap to the company and drank. In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse dark bread; from time to time he ate it, sitting near Madame Defarge’s counter, munching and drinking. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge refreshed himself with a draught of wine—but took less than he gave the stranger, since wine was no rarity to him—and stood waiting until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He looked at no one present, and now no one looked at him; not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and was working.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked, when the time came.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come, then! You shall see the room I told you that you could occupy. It will suit you perfectly.”

From the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, from the staircase into a garret—formerly the garret where a white-haired man sat on a low bench, bent forward and very busy making shoes.

No white-haired man was there now; but the three men who had left the wine-shop separately were there. And between them and the white-haired man far away was one small link: they had once looked in at him through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge carefully closed the door and spoke in a subdued voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness encountered by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"52aed6f48cf4d0d2964c9e18","rewritten_text":"The elegant gentlemen of the finest breeding wore small hanging ornaments that jingled as they moved lazily. These golden chains rang like tiny, precious bells; together with the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, they stirred the air and drove Saint Antoine and his terrible hunger far away.

Dress was the one unfailing charm used to keep everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Courts of Justice, and all society except the scarecrows, the Fancy Ball reached down to the Common Executioner. To preserve the spell, he was required to work “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was rarely used—Monsieur Paris, as he was called in the episcopal style followed by his fellow Professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans and the rest, presided in this delicate costume. And who among the guests at Monseigneur’s reception in that year of our Lord seventeen hundred and eighty could doubt that a system founded on a frizzled, powdered hangman in gold lace, pumps, and white silk stockings would last until the stars came out?

After Monseigneur had relieved his four bearers of their burdens and drunk his chocolate, he ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holies opened and came out. Then came the submission, the bowing and scraping, the fawning, the servility, and the deepest humiliation! As for bowing in body and spirit, nothing remained for Heaven to receive—which may have been one reason, among others, why Monseigneur’s worshippers never troubled Heaven.

Giving one slave a promise and another a smile, whispering to one fortunate person and waving to another, Monseigneur passed graciously through his rooms to the distant region called the Circumference of Truth. There he turned and came back, and in time had himself shut inside his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, after which he was seen no more.

When the show was over, the flutter in the air became a small storm, and the precious little bells rang down the stairs. Soon only one person remained from the whole crowd. With his hat under his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, he slowly passed among the mirrors toward the exit.

“I devote you,” said this person, stopping at the last door and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he shook the snuff from his fingers as though shaking dust from his feet, and quietly walked downstairs."}
