content.text: {"request_id":"6e943ed0b78a71904f08504c","rewritten_text":"I could recall what conditions had been like during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars a day, reckoned in gold; in the South, he earned fifty, payable in Confederate shinplasters worth a dollar a bushel. In the North, a pair of overalls cost three dollars—a day's pay; in the South, they cost seventy-five—which amounted to two days' wages. Other commodities stood in the same ratio. Thus wages were twice as high in the North as in the South, because one wage possessed twice the purchasing power of the other.\n\nYes, I formed several acquaintances in the hamlet, and one thing that pleased me greatly was discovering our new coins in circulation—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, many nickels, and some silver; all of these among the artisans and ordinary people generally; yes, and even some gold—but that was in the bank, meaning the goldsmith's. I went in while Marco, Marco's son, was bargaining with a shopkeeper over a quarter-pound of salt, and asked to have a twenty-dollar gold piece changed. They did so—after biting the coin, ringing it on the counter, testing it with acid, and asking where I had obtained it, who I was, where I came from, where I was headed, when I expected to arrive, and perhaps two hundred other questions. When they ran out, I continued by supplying information of my own accord: I told them I owned a dog named Watch, that my first wife was a Free Will Baptist, that her grandfather had been a Prohibitionist, that I once knew a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip, who died in hope of a glorious resurrection, and so forth, and so forth, until even that ravenous village inquisitor looked satisfied, and somewhat annoyed as well. Still, he had to respect a man of my financial standing, so he did not talk back to me; I noticed, however, that he vented his feelings on his subordinates, which was entirely natural. Yes, they changed my twenty, though I suspected it put a slight strain on the bank. That was understandable, since it was like entering a poor village store in the nineteenth century and suddenly asking its proprietor to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. He might manage it, perhaps; but he would also wonder how a small farmer came to be carrying so much money in his pocket. That was likely what the goldsmith thought too, for he followed me to the door and stood watching me depart with reverent admiration."}

{"request_id":"867fd69d88b94e50d1801a0f","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know about me unless you had read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he told the truth, mostly. He exaggerated some things, but mostly he told the truth. That’s nothing. I’ve never met anyone who didn’t lie now and then, except Aunt Polly, the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all mentioned in that book, which is mostly true, with some exaggerations, as I said.

This is how the book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars each, all in gold. It was an enormous amount of money when it was piled up. Judge Thatcher took it, invested it, and it earned us a dollar a day each, all year round—more than anyone could know how to spend. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me. But living in her house was hard, because the widow was so strict, proper, and regular in everything she did. When I couldn’t stand it anymore, I ran away. I put on my old rags and went back to my sugar hogshead, and I was free and content. But Tom Sawyer found me and said he was going to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I went back to the widow and acted respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb. She called me plenty of other names, too, but she never meant any harm. She put me back in those new clothes, and all I could do was sweat and feel squeezed up. Then the old routine began again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to come right away. When you reached the table, you couldn’t start eating. You had to wait while the widow bowed her head and grumbled a little over the food, even though there was nothing really wrong with it—except that everything had been cooked separately. In a barrel of leftovers, things are different: they mix together, the juices trade places, and everything tastes better.

After supper she took out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushes. I was eager to learn all about him, but after a while she revealed that Moses had been dead for a very long time. Then I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t have any interest in dead people."}

{"request_id":"bbded702205ba44099261117","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay,” was finally brought to trial.

His judges sat upon the Bench in feathered hats; but the rough red cap and tricoloured cockade were the head-dress otherwise prevailing. Looking at the Jury and the disorderly audience, he might have imagined that the ordinary order of things had been turned upside down, and that the criminals were judging the honest men. The lowest, most cruel, and worst populace of a city, never without its share of the low, cruel, and bad, directed everything there: loudly commenting, applauding, condemning, foreseeing, and hastening the result, without restraint. Most of the men carried weapons of various kinds; among the women, some wore knives, some daggers, some ate and drank as they watched, and many knitted. Among the latter was one who worked with an extra piece of knitting beneath her arm. She sat in the front row, beside a man whom he had not seen since arriving at the Barrier, but whom he immediately recognized as Defarge. He observed that she whispered once or twice in his ear, and seemed to be his wife; but what he chiefly noticed about the pair was that, though they were placed as near him as possible, they never turned their eyes towards him. They appeared to await something with stubborn resolve, and watched the Jury, but nothing else. Beneath the President sat Doctor Manette, in his customary quiet clothing. So far as the prisoner could see, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men there, apart from those connected with the Tribunal, who wore their ordinary clothes and had not put on the coarse dress of the Carmagnole.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was charged by the public prosecutor as an emigrant, whose life was forfeited to the Republic under the decree banishing all emigrants on pain of Death. It mattered nothing that the decree was dated after his return to France. He was there, and the decree was there; he had been captured in France, and his head was demanded.

“Take off his head!” shouted the audience. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to quiet the cries, then asked the prisoner whether it was not true that he had lived for many years in England.

It was unquestionably true.

Then was he not an emigrant? What did he call himself?

Not an emigrant, he hoped, according to the meaning and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President wished to know.

Because he had willingly abandoned a title he disliked, and a position he disliked, and had left his country—he submitted, before the word emigrant had acquired its present meaning in the Tribunal—to live by his own labour in England, rather than upon the labour of France’s overburdened people."}

{"request_id":"68c6450a7894d013d93c3dfe","rewritten_text":"“I now hasten to the most moving part of my story. I shall describe events that filled me with feelings which, changing what I had been, made me what I am.

“Spring advanced quickly; the weather grew fine, and the skies remained cloudless. I was astonished that the place which had once been barren and gloomy should now bloom with the most beautiful flowers and greenery. My senses were delighted and renewed by a thousand pleasant scents and a thousand beautiful sights.

“It was on one of these days, when my cottagers had paused from their work as they often did—the old man playing his guitar while the children listened—that I noticed Felix’s face was sorrowful beyond expression. He sighed repeatedly, and once his father stopped playing; from his manner, I guessed that he was asking his son the reason for his sadness. Felix answered cheerfully, and the old man was beginning his music again when someone knocked at the door.

“It was a woman on horseback, accompanied by a countryman acting as her guide. She wore a dark dress and was covered by a thick black veil. Agatha asked her a question, but the stranger replied only by saying, in a sweet voice, the name Felix. Her voice was musical, though unlike that of either of my friends. At hearing the name, Felix hurried toward her. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, and I beheld a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was shining raven-black and intricately braided; her eyes were dark but gentle, though lively; her features were perfectly proportioned, and her complexion wonderfully fair, with a lovely pink tint in each cheek.

“Felix seemed overwhelmed with delight at the sight of her. Every sign of sorrow disappeared from his face, which instantly expressed such ecstatic joy that I could scarcely have believed it capable of showing so much; his eyes sparkled and his cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment, I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed moved by different feelings; wiping a few tears from her lovely eyes, she extended her hand to Felix, who kissed it passionately and called her, as far as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but smiled. He helped her dismount and, dismissing her guide, led her into the cottage. He and his father exchanged some words, and the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet and tried to kiss his hand, but he raised her and embraced her warmly.

“I soon realized that although the stranger made articulate sounds and seemed to possess a language of her own, neither she nor the cottagers understood the other.”"}

{"request_id":"899b961bd229b16829c2051e","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. If I stay any longer, I’ll be late for lunch. Thank you for giving me the information I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I invited myself and Mr. Gray. He is her newest protégé.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, to stop bothering me with her charity appeals. I’m tired of them. Why, that good woman thinks I have nothing to do except write cheques for her foolish causes.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, but it won’t make any difference. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity. That is their defining quality.”

The old gentleman gave an approving growl and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low arcade into Burlington Street, then headed toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Though it had been told to him bluntly, it had still moved him with the suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness ended by a horrible, treacherous crime. Months of silent suffering, followed by a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy left alone with an old, loveless man. Yes, it was an interesting background. It gave the boy a more complete shape, made him seem more perfect, in a way. Behind every beautiful thing that existed, there was something tragic. Worlds had to struggle and suffer before even the humblest flower could bloom.... And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, sitting across from him at the club with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure, while the red candle shades deepened the rose in his awakening face. Talking to him was like playing an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and movement of the bow.... There was something intensely exciting about influencing someone. No other activity was like it. To project one’s soul into some graceful form and let it remain there for a moment; to hear one’s own ideas returned with all the added music of passion and youth; to pass one’s temperament into another person as if it were a subtle liquid or a strange perfume: there was genuine joy in that—perhaps the most satisfying joy left to us in an age as narrow and vulgar as our own, an age crude in its pleasures and ordinary in its ambitions.... He was a wonderful type, too, this boy whom chance had brought him to in Basil’s studio—or, at least, he could be shaped into a wonderful type."}

{"request_id":"8fbf5ecbf981fe5fd22a6737","rewritten_text":"He said that, while traveling from his home and passing through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke rising from the inn’s chimney. Thinking he might find fellow travelers gathered there, he knocked and was let in. No one was in the house except Lucy and her mother. Her mother had lost the use of her limbs after an attack of rheumatism, and so, one by one, all the remaining people in the country had left, abandoning them alone. Lucy begged the man to stay with her. In a week or two, her mother would be better, and they could then set out; but if they were left helpless and alone, they would surely die. The man replied that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and so, in his view, he could not remain. As a last hope, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to deliver wherever he might meet us. He carried out this task, and Idris received the following letter with deep emotion:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am sure you will remember and pity me, and I dare hope that you will help me; what other hope have I? Forgive the way I write; I am so confused. A month ago, my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already better, and in another month, I am sure, she would be able to travel, as you so kindly said you would arrange for us. But now everyone is gone—everyone. As they left, each person said that perhaps my mother would recover before we were completely deserted. But three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who stayed until the end because of his newborn child. Since his family was large, I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us; but I found the house empty. I have not seen another person since, until this good man arrived. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation; she is so ill that I have kept it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we will die miserably if we remain here. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road; and if, once she recovered, I somehow managed to find the roads and travel so many miles to the sea, you would all be in France, with the great ocean between us—a thing terrible even to sailors.”"}

A quarter of an hour later, amid a remarkable uproar of applause, Sibyl Vane came onto the stage. Yes, she was undeniably beautiful to behold—one of the loveliest beings Lord Henry had ever seen. {"request_id":"642476220aff6036370f7b2e","rewritten_text":"There was a delightful feeling of clearing things up and taking a quiet pause before beginning life anew in our village on Saturday nights, and it encouraged Joe to risk staying out half an hour later on Saturdays than at other times. When the half-hour and the rum and water ran out together, Joe rose to leave and took me by the hand.

“Wait half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I have a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I do, the boy shall have it.”

He found it among a handful of small change, wrapped it in some crumpled paper, and gave it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Mind! Your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him far beyond the limits of good manners and clinging tightly to Joe. He wished Joe good-night, and Mr. Wopsle good-night as well (for he left with us), but gave me only a look with his aiming eye—no, not a look, since he closed it, though wonders can be done with an eye by concealing it.

On the way home, if I had felt like talking, the conversation would have been entirely mine, because Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, while Joe walked all the way home with his mouth wide open, rinsing the rum out with as much air as possible. But I was almost stunned by the reappearance of my old wrongdoing and old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in a particularly bad temper when we entered the kitchen, and Joe was encouraged by that unusual fact to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” said Mrs. Joe triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.”

I took it from the paper, and it turned out to be genuine. “But what’s this?” said Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were nothing less than two thick, overheated one-pound notes that seemed to have enjoyed the closest acquaintance with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran with them to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, fairly certain that the man would not be there.

After a while, Joe returned, saying that the man had gone, but that he, Joe, had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"4603c6eaf350a46b596ce5c5","rewritten_text":"There was something so remarkable in the growing intensity of Mr. Wopsle’s gaze, and he seemed to be turning so many thoughts over in his mind and becoming so confused, that I could not understand it. I sat thinking about it long after he had risen into the clouds inside a large watch-case, and still I could not understand it. I was still thinking of it when I left the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me near the door.

“How are you?” I said, shaking hands with him as we turned down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It is the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, slipping back into his bewildered expression; “and yet I could swear to him.”

Alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Whether I would have noticed him at first if you had not been there,” said Mr. Wopsle, continuing in the same bewildered manner, “I cannot say for certain; yet I think I would have.”

Without meaning to, I looked around me, as I had grown accustomed to do on my way home; for these mysterious words sent a chill through me.

“Oh! He cannot be in sight,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I did. I saw him go.”

Because I had reason to be suspicious, I even suspected the poor actor. I feared he was trying to trap me into making some admission. So I watched him as we walked on together, but said nothing.

“I had the absurd idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were completely unaware of him, sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

The chill I had felt before came over me again, but I was determined not to speak yet, since his words were entirely consistent with his being instructed to make me connect these hints with Provis. Naturally, I was completely certain and secure in knowing that Provis had not been there.

“I expect you wonder at me, Mr. Pip; indeed, I can see that you do. But it is so strange! You will scarcely believe what I am about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself if you told it to me.”

“Really?” I said.

“No, truly. Mr. Pip, you remember, long ago, a certain Christmas Day, when you were a small child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs repaired?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember that two convicts were being pursued, and that we joined the chase, and that Gargery carried you on his back, while I led the way, and you kept up with me as well as you could?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"7fe4e2a62ea215d3f551203e","rewritten_text":"No imagination can picture the sublimity that might have been displayed by a similar phenomenon occurring in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have seemed an appropriate image. Even as it was, my hair stood on end as I gazed far down into the yawning abysses, allowing my imagination, as it were, to descend and wander through the strange vaulted halls, ruddy gulfs, and red, ghastly chasms of that hideous, unfathomable fire. I had indeed made a narrow escape. Had the balloon remained only a little longer within the cloud—that is, had the discomfort of getting wet not prompted me to release the ballast—inevitable ruin would have followed. Such dangers, though rarely considered, are perhaps the greatest that balloons must face. By this time, however, I had reached too great an altitude to feel any further anxiety on that account.\n\n“I was now rising rapidly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of no less than nine and a half miles. I began to have great difficulty breathing. My head, too, was extremely painful; and after noticing moisture on my cheeks for some time, I finally discovered that it was blood, flowing quite rapidly from my eardrums. My eyes also caused me great distress. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to have protruded from their sockets to a considerable degree; and every object in the car, even the balloon itself, appeared distorted. These symptoms exceeded anything I had expected and alarmed me. At that moment, very imprudently and without thinking, I threw three five-pound pieces of ballast from the car. The increased rate of ascent carried me too quickly, without sufficient gradual adjustment, into a highly rarefied layer of the atmosphere, and the result nearly proved fatal to both my expedition and myself. I was suddenly seized by a spasm lasting more than five minutes; and even after it had somewhat subsided, I could draw breath only at long intervals and in gasps—bleeding heavily all the while from my nose and ears, and slightly from my eyes as well. The pigeons appeared extremely distressed and struggled to escape, while the cat mewed piteously and, with her tongue hanging from her mouth, staggered back and forth in the car as though poisoned. Only then did I realize how reckless I had been to release the ballast, and my agitation became extreme. I expected nothing less than death—and death within a few minutes.”"}

{"request_id":"9e0d12c72ac39a7f090ac013","rewritten_text":"Shall I be carried to the skies, on beds of flowers and ease,
While others fight to win the prize, and sail through bloody seas?

He was considered a wonderful reader. At church “sociables,” he was always asked to read poetry. When he finished, the ladies would raise their hands and let them drop helplessly into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say, “Words cannot express it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this mortal earth.”

After the hymn, the Rev. Mr. Sprague became a bulletin board and read aloud “notices” of meetings, societies, and other matters until it seemed the list would last until the end of time—a strange custom still practiced in America, even in cities, in this age of plentiful newspapers. Often, the less reason there is to preserve a traditional custom, the harder it is to abandon it.

Then the minister prayed. It was a good, generous prayer, full of details: he prayed for the church and its little children; for the village’s other churches; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for its officers; for the United States; for the nation’s churches; for Congress; for the President; for government officials; for poor sailors tossed by stormy seas; for oppressed millions groaning under European monarchies and Eastern despotisms; for those who had the light and good news but lacked eyes to see or ears to hear; for the heathen on distant islands; and he ended by asking that the words he was about to speak might find grace and favor, like seeds planted in fertile soil that would eventually produce a thankful harvest of good. Amen.

Dresses rustled, and the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it—if he even did that. He was restless throughout. Without meaning to, he kept count of the prayer’s details, because he was not listening, yet knew the familiar ground and the minister’s usual path across it. Whenever a small new point was inserted, his ear caught it and his whole nature objected. He thought additions were unfair and downright scoundrelly. During the prayer, a fly landed on the back of the pew before him and tormented him by calmly rubbing its hands together, wrapping its arms around its head, and polishing it so hard that it seemed almost to separate from the body, leaving its thin neck exposed; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them against its body as though they were coat-tails; carrying out its entire toilet as peacefully as if it knew it was completely safe."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e4c59dac65995a2f1f168a9e","rewritten_text":"Raymond was exalted by the powerful sensations of restored health; he felt that, as general of the Athenians, he occupied a position worthy of his ambition; and, in hoping to conquer Constantinople, he looked toward an event that would stand as a landmark amid the waste of ages, an achievement without equal in human history. A city of immense historic associations, whose site was the wonder of the world, and which for many centuries had been the stronghold of the Moslems, would be delivered from slavery and barbarism and returned to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and love of liberty. Perdita’s happiness rested upon his restored society, his love, his hopes, and his fame, even as a Sybarite reclines upon a luxurious couch; every thought was rapture, and every emotion seemed steeped in a congenial, balmy element.\n\nWe reached Kishan on the 7th of July. Throughout our journey the weather had remained serene. Each day, before dawn, we departed from our nightly encampment and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and valley before the golden splendour of the approaching sun. The accompanying soldiers, with national vivacity, took enthusiastic pleasure in the spectacle of beautiful nature. The rising star of day was greeted by triumphant music, while birdsong, caught in fragments, filled the pauses between the strains. At noon we set up our tents in some shaded valley or leafy wood among the mountains, while a stream murmuring over pebbles invited grateful sleep. Our evening march, quieter, was even more delightful than the morning’s restless excitement. When the band played, they instinctively selected airs of softened passion: the farewell of love, or a lament for absence, followed and concluded by some solemn hymn that accorded with the peaceful beauty of evening and raised the soul toward lofty, religious thoughts. Often every sound was stilled so that we might hear the nightingale, while fire-flies danced in luminous measure, and the gentle cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travellers. Did we pass through a valley? Tender shadows surrounded us, and rocks glowed with beautiful colours. If we crossed a mountain, Greece, like a living map, lay spread below, her famous peaks piercing the ether and her rivers tracing silver lines through the fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travellers gazed in ecstasy upon this magnificent landscape, so unlike the sober colours and melancholy charms of our native scenery. After leaving Macedonia, the fertile yet low plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties; nevertheless, our journey remained absorbing. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people soon began moving to honour Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"7517d90090325430ad3980cf","rewritten_text":"“These thoughts calmed me, and that afternoon I fell into a deep sleep; but the fever in my blood kept peaceful dreams from me. The terrible scene of the previous day played endlessly before my eyes: the women fleeing, and the enraged Felix dragging me from his father’s feet. I awoke exhausted and, finding that night had already fallen, crept from my hiding place and went in search of food.

“When my hunger was satisfied, I set out along the familiar path leading to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crawled into my hovel and waited silently for the usual hour when the family rose. That hour passed, and the sun climbed high in the sky, but the cottagers did not appear. I trembled violently, fearing some dreadful misfortune. The cottage interior was dark, and I heard no movement; I cannot describe the agony of that suspense.

“Soon two countrymen passed by, then stopped near the cottage and began speaking together, gesturing violently. I could not understand them, however, because they spoke the language of the region, which differed from that of my protectors. Shortly afterward Felix approached with another man. I was surprised, knowing that Felix had not left the cottage that morning, and waited anxiously to learn from their conversation the meaning of these strange events.

“‘Do you realize,’ his companion said, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the produce of your garden? I do not wish to take unfair advantage of you, so I ask you to take a few days to consider your decision.’

“‘It is completely useless,’ Felix replied. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the terrible incident I have told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. I beg you not to argue with me any longer. Take possession of your house and let me flee this place.’

“Felix trembled violently as he spoke. He and his companion entered the cottage, where they remained for a few minutes, and then left. I never saw another member of the De Lacey family.

“I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, sunk in complete and senseless despair. My protectors had gone and severed the only bond that connected me to the world. For the first time, revenge and hatred filled my heart. I made no effort to restrain them; surrendering myself to the current, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death.”"}

{"request_id":"6e8da3d2c8b0e6db34622073","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was completely satisfied with this conversation, so he never troubled himself again, or annoyed his dear sister Elizabeth, by bringing it up. She was glad to see that she had said enough to keep him silent.

The day of his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived, and Mrs. Bennet had to accept a separation which, since her husband had no intention of carrying out her plan for them all to go to Newcastle, would probably last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when shall we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Perhaps not for two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They will have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s farewells were much more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they had left the house, “as I have ever seen. He smiles, flirts, and makes love to us all. I am extremely proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to produce a more valuable son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very gloomy for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that nothing is so bad as parting from one’s friends. One feels so lonely without them.”

“This is the result, you see, madam, of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It should make you more satisfied that your other four are unmarried.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia is not leaving me because she is married, but only because her husband’s regiment happens to be so far away. If it had been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.”

But the gloomy state into which this event had thrown her was soon relieved, and her mind became excited with hope again by a piece of news that began circulating. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been ordered to prepare for her master’s arrival. He was coming in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was extremely agitated. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head, one after another.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” said Mrs. Bennet, after Mrs. Philips had first brought her the news. “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never want to see him again. Still, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield if he wishes.”"}

{"request_id":"6cac0415a658db44a3a286f9","rewritten_text":"“If I can’t live on that, I shan’t ask anyone to give me a lift. Is that satisfactory?”

There was a tremendous roar of applause. Above it, the king’s voice rang out:

“Away with his bonds, and set him free! Let everyone, high and low, rich and poor, honor him, for he has become the king’s right hand. He is clothed with power and authority, and his seat is on the highest step of the throne! Now drive away this creeping night and bring back the light and cheer, so that all the world may bless you.”

But I said:

“That a common man should be shamed before the world is nothing. But it would dishonor the _king_ if anyone who saw his minister naked did not also see him freed from that shame. If I might ask that my clothes be brought back—”

“They are not suitable,” the king interrupted. “Fetch clothing of another kind; dress him like a prince!”

My plan had worked. I wanted to keep matters as they were until the eclipse became total. Otherwise, they would keep trying to make me end the darkness, and of course I could not do that. Sending for the clothes bought some time, but not enough. So I needed another excuse. I said it would be natural for the king to change his mind and regret, at least partly, what he had done in his excitement. Therefore, I would let the darkness deepen for a while; if, after a reasonable time, the king still held to his decision, the darkness would be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else was satisfied with this arrangement, but I had to stand firm.

It grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I struggled with those awkward sixth-century clothes. At last it became completely dark, and the crowd groaned in horror as cold, unnatural night breezes moved through the place and the stars appeared and twinkled overhead. At last the eclipse was total, and I was very glad, though everyone else was miserable—which was only natural. I said:

“The king, by remaining silent, still accepts the terms.” Then I raised my hands and stood that way for a moment. After that I said, with the deepest solemnity: “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass away harmlessly!”

For a moment there was no response in the deep darkness and graveyard silence. But when the sun’s silver rim appeared again a moment or two later, the crowd burst into a huge shout and came rushing down like a flood, smothering me with blessings and gratitude. And Clarence was certainly not the last of them."}

Emma observed her throughout the changing tones of this speech, and detected no alarming signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted that he had no further hold upon her, and that Harriet, on her side, would offer no serious obstacle to any friendly arrangement Emma might make.

They encountered Mr. Martin the very next day while walking along the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after looking at Emma with great respect, turned with the most genuine pleasure toward her companion. Emma was not displeased to have such an opportunity for observation; and, walking a few yards ahead while they spoke together, she soon made her quick eye sufficiently familiar with Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was extremely neat, and he seemed a sensible young man, but his person possessed no other advantage; and when compared with gentlemen, Emma thought he must lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s affections. Harriet was not without a feeling for manners; she had voluntarily remarked upon her father’s gentleness with both admiration and surprise. Mr. Martin looked as though he had no idea what manners were.

They stayed together only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be left waiting; and Harriet then ran up to her with a smiling face and an excited flutter of spirits, which Miss Woodhouse hoped soon to calm.

“Only imagine our happening to meet him!—How very strange! He said it was quite by chance that he had not gone round by Randalls. He did not think we ever walked along this road. He thought we went toward Randalls on most days."}

{"request_id":"d47a2c349244cdffb0fa5074","rewritten_text":"But enough of this. I will begin my tale: it is my final task, and I hope I have enough strength to complete it. I record no crimes; my faults may easily be forgiven, for they arose not from evil motives but from poor judgment. I believe few would claim that, through different conduct and greater wisdom, they could have escaped the misfortunes of which I am the victim. My fate has been ruled by necessity, a terrible necessity. It required hands stronger than mine—stronger, I believe, than any human power—to break the thick, adamantine chain that bound me, once breathing nothing but joy and filled with a warm love and delight in goodness, to misery that can end only, and is now about to end, in death. But I am forgetting myself; my tale remains untold. I will pause for a few moments, wipe my dim eyes, and try to lose the present obscure but heavy feeling of unhappiness in the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank. He had lost his own father early and was educated by a weak mother, with all the indulgence she believed due to a wealthy nobleman. He was sent to Eton and afterward to college, and from childhood was allowed the free use of large sums of money, thereby enjoying from his earliest youth the independence that a boy with such advantages always acquires at a public school.

Under the influence of these circumstances, his passions found deep soil in which they could take root and flourish, as flowers or weeds according to their nature. Having always been permitted to act for himself, his character became strongly marked at an early age and displayed a varied surface on which a keen observer might see the seeds of virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance, which led him to squander immense sums satisfying passing whims—whims whose apparent intensity he dignified with the name of passions—often revealed itself as boundless generosity. Yet while he earnestly concerned himself with the needs of others, his own desires were fulfilled to their fullest extent. He gave his money, but sacrificed none of his wishes to his gifts; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was glad to have awakened in any way.

I do not say that, if his own desires had been set against those of others, he would have shown excessive selfishness; but that test was never made. He was raised in prosperity and surrounded by all its advantages; everyone loved him and wished to please him."}

{"request_id":"4be747a60a674a273512d773","rewritten_text":"WHEN the wedding was held, about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a perfect crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service with the greatest impressiveness, and everyone agreed that they had never seen a more handsome bride and bridegroom. They were not merely handsome, however—they were happy. Lord Arthur never once regretted all he had endured for Sybil, while she, for her part, gave him the finest gifts a woman can offer a man—worship, tenderness, and love. Reality had not destroyed their romance. They always felt young.

Several years later, after two lovely children had been born to them, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, a beautiful old house that the Duke had given his son as a wedding present. One afternoon, while sitting with Lady Arthur beneath a lime-tree in the garden and watching the little boy and girl dart along the rose-walk like wandering sunbeams, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and asked, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, of course I am happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I have no time for happiness, Sybil. I always take a fancy to the last person introduced to me; but generally, once I know people, I grow tired of them.’

‘Don’t your lions keep you satisfied, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh, no! Lions are useful for only one season. Once their manes have been cut, they are the dullest creatures alive. Besides, if you are genuinely kind to them, they behave very badly. Do you remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was a terrible impostor. Naturally, I did not care about that, and I even forgave him when he asked to borrow money, but I could not endure his making love to me. He has made me detest cheiromancy. I practise telepathy now. It is far more entertaining.’

‘You must not say anything against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere; it is the one subject Arthur does not like people to joke about. I assure you, he takes it quite seriously.’

‘You cannot mean that he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him, Lady Windermere—there he is’; and Lord Arthur came up the garden carrying a large bunch of yellow roses, with his two children dancing around him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You cannot mean that you believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Of course I do,’ said the young man with a smile.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe it all the happiness of my life,’ he murmured, sinking into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"91a15184e5b33a4d8ad74374","rewritten_text":"I have said that he was a poet. At twenty-three, he published his first poem, and the whole nation welcomed it with enthusiasm and delight. His good fortune never failed him; no reputation had ever risen so quickly, and his fame was universal. The crowd praised the same poems that amazed the learned scholar in his study: not one voice spoke against them.

It was then, at the height of his glory, that he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of extraordinary beauty, living under her guardian’s care. From the moment they were seen together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not possess Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble. Her youth and the love she inspired lifted her above every concern except virtue and excellence. She was beautiful, with frank, simple manners, and deep blue eyes shining with the light that comes from feeling joined with wisdom.

They were made for each other, and soon fell in love. Woodville felt the joy of love for the first time, while Elinor was delighted to possess the heart of a man so beautiful and honored among his fellow human beings. Could anything but pure happiness come from such a union?

Woodville was a poet, sought by every society, and all eyes turned toward him whenever he appeared. But he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian did not oppose their affection: Woodville’s merit was too great for anyone to object to his lesser fortune. Yet her father’s will forbade her to marry before coming of age, and her inheritance depended on her obeying that command. She had just turned twenty, so she and her lover had to accept the delay. Still, they were always together, and their happiness seemed heavenly. They studied together and planned their future lives. Drinking in love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, they scarcely complained about waiting for their complete union. Woodville’s fame continued to grow, while Elinor became more beautiful and wise under the guidance of her gifted lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I describe the disaster that followed such joy? Yet the earth would not be the sorrowful, blighted place it is if a pair of such angelic beings had been allowed to live entirely for each other. Search the whole world, and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them. The order of things among us miserable inhabitants of earth would have had to change before such complete joy could be permitted."}

“But could you really feel comfortable spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; his father can, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is very careful, and she could send us word every hour about how he was. I really think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terribly worried yesterday, but things are quite different today.”

“Well, if you do not think it too late to let them know you are coming, suppose you went as well as your husband. Leave little Charles in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot think it wrong while I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” cried Mary, her eyes brightening. “Dear me! That is a very good idea, very good indeed. Of course, I may as well go as stay, since I am no use at home—am I? It only makes me anxious. You, who do not have a mother’s feelings, are much better suited to this. You can make little Charles do anything; he always obeys you at once. It will be much better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I shall certainly go. I am sure I ought to, if I can, quite as much as Charles, because they are very eager for me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left alone. It was an excellent idea of yours, Anne. I will go and tell Charles, and get ready at once. You can send for us immediately if anything is wrong; but I dare say there will be nothing to worry you. You may be sure I would not go if I did not feel completely at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was knocking at her husband’s dressing-room door. As Anne followed her upstairs, she arrived in time to hear the whole conversation, which began with Mary saying, in a tone of great excitement—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, because I am no more useful at home than you are. If I shut myself away forever with the child, I could not persuade him to do anything he disliked. Anne will stay; she has offered to remain at home and take care of him. It was Anne’s own idea, so I shall go with you. It will be much better, since I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I should be very glad to have you come; but it seems rather unfair that she should be left at home alone to care for our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"822a60cf999313a4528fc28d","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He appeared deliberately to misunderstand the word she had repeated, and added hastily, “Yes, customers; in banking, we generally call those connected with us our customers. He was a French gentleman; a scientific gentleman; a man of considerable learning—a Doctor.”

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman came from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our connection was in business, but confidential. At that time I was in our French House, and had been there—oh! twenty years.”

“At that time—I may ask, at what time, sir?”

“I mean, miss, twenty years ago. He married—an English lady—and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen and families, were wholly in Tellson’s hands. In much the same manner, I am, or have been, trustee of one sort or another for scores of our customers. These are simply business connections, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing resembling sentiment. Throughout my business life I have moved from one to another, just as I move from one customer to another during my business day; in short, I have no feelings; I am merely a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I am beginning to think”—the strangely furrowed forehead was fixed intently upon him—“that when I was left an orphan, my mother having survived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I am nearly certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small, hesitating hand that trustfully reached toward his, and with some ceremony raised it to his lips. He then led the young lady directly back to her chair and, keeping his left hand on its back while using his right by turns to rub his chin, tug at his wig near the ears, or emphasize his words, stood looking down at her face as she looked up at his.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how accurately I described myself just now, when I said I had no feelings, and that all my relations with my fellow-creatures were merely business relations, when you consider that I have never seen you since. No; you have been Tellson’s ward ever since, and I have been occupied with Tellson’s other business ever since. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my entire life, miss, turning an enormous pecuniary Mangle.”"}

{"request_id":"bc8a9176c4a8e024ed9153dc","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, the blue sky, and the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you shall never see me again while they live. Go home and begin your work; I shall watch its progress with unbearable anxiety. Do not fear: when you are ready, I will appear.”

With that, he suddenly left me, perhaps afraid that I might change my mind. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle flies, until he was soon lost among the waves of ice.

His story had taken the entire day, and the sun was near the horizon when he left. I knew I had to hurry down toward the valley, since darkness would soon surround me; but my heart was heavy, and I walked slowly. The winding mountain paths and the need to place my feet carefully confused me, for I was absorbed by the emotions the day’s events had stirred. It was deep into the night when I reached the halfway resting place and sat beside the fountain. The stars appeared whenever the clouds moved away; dark pines stood before me, and broken trees lay scattered here and there. The scene was deeply solemn and filled me with strange thoughts. I wept bitterly and, clasping my hands in anguish, cried, “Oh, stars, clouds, and winds, you are all about to mock me. If you truly pity me, destroy my senses and memory; let me become nothing. But if you will not, go away, go away, and leave me in darkness.”

These thoughts were wild and miserable, but I cannot express how the stars’ endless flickering weighed on me, or how I listened to every gust of wind as if it were a dull, hateful sirocco coming to consume me.

Morning came before I reached the village of Chamounix. I did not rest, but returned at once to Geneva. I could not even put my feelings into words; they pressed on me with the weight of a mountain, and their force buried my agony beneath them. Thus I returned home and entered the house, where I presented myself to the family. My haggard, wild appearance caused great alarm, but I answered no questions and scarcely spoke. I felt as though I had been placed under a curse—as though I had no right to ask for their sympathy, and could never again enjoy their company."}

{"request_id":"185d3bfabf9e4f40b016c49d","rewritten_text":"Watching him in such moods, I often reflected thoughtfully on the ancient philosophy of the Bi-Part Soul, and entertained the notion of a double Dupin—the creative and the analytical.

Let no one infer from what I have just said that I am revealing any mystery or composing a romance. What I have described in the Frenchman was simply the product of an excited, or perhaps diseased, intellect. Yet an example of the nature of his observations at such times will best explain my meaning.

One night we were walking along a long, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Apparently absorbed in thought, neither of us had uttered a word for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin spoke:

“He is a very small fellow, that is true, and would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

“There can be no doubt of that,” I answered involuntarily, without at first noticing—so deeply was I lost in thought—the remarkable way in which his words corresponded with my own reflections. A moment later I recovered myself, and was profoundly astonished.

“Dupin,” I said solemnly, “this is beyond my understanding. I freely admit that I am amazed and can scarcely trust my senses. How could you know that I was thinking of ——?” I stopped, wishing to determine beyond question whether he truly knew whom I had in mind.

“—— of Chantilly,” he said. “Why do you stop? You were observing to yourself that his small stature made him unfit for tragedy.”

This was exactly the subject of my thoughts. Chantilly had once been a cobbler on the Rue St. Denis who, becoming infatuated with the stage, had attempted the _rôle_ of Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy of that name, and had been notoriously Pasquinaded for his trouble.

“For Heaven’s sake, tell me,” I cried, “the method—if there is a method—by which you have managed to read my mind in this matter.” Indeed, I was even more startled than I would have cared to admit.

“It was the fruiterer,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the mender of soles was not tall enough for Xerxes _et id genus omne_.”

“The fruiterer! You amaze me—I know no fruiterer at all.”

“The man who collided with you as we entered the street—it may have been fifteen minutes ago.”

I now recalled that a fruiterer carrying a large basket of apples had indeed nearly knocked me down accidentally as we passed from the Rue C—— into the thoroughfare where we stood; but how this could relate to Chantilly, I was utterly unable to understand."}

{"request_id":"ecd8bf3338673b52c7f92cfd","rewritten_text":"There was something so extraordinary in the growing brightness of Mr. Wopsle’s eye, and he appeared to be turning over so many matters in his mind while becoming increasingly bewildered, that I could not understand it. I sat pondering it long after he had risen into the clouds inside a large watch-case, and still could not understand it. I was thinking of it still when I left the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me by the door.

“How do you do?” I asked, shaking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Yes, naturally I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It is the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, slipping once more into his absent expression; “and yet I could swear to him.”

Growing alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain what he meant.

“Whether I should have observed him at first if you had not been there,” said Mr. Wopsle, continuing in the same distracted manner, “I cannot say for certain; but I believe I should.”

Without meaning to, I looked around, as I was used to do on my way home; for these mysterious words sent a chill through me.

“Oh! He cannot be visible now,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I did. I saw him go.”

Given the reason I had for suspicion, I even suspected the poor actor himself. I feared he meant to trap me into some confession. So I watched him as we walked on together, but remained silent.

“I had the absurd notion that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw that you were entirely unaware of him, sitting behind you there like a ghost.”

The earlier chill passed over me again, but I determined not to speak yet, since his words were quite compatible with the possibility that he had been prompted to make me connect these allusions with Provis. Naturally, I was completely certain and secure in knowing that Provis had not been there.

“I expect you wonder at me, Mr. Pip; indeed, I can see that you do. But it is so very strange! You will scarcely believe what I am about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself, had you told it to me.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember, long ago, a particular Christmas Day, when you were still a child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs repaired?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you remember there was a pursuit of two convicts, and that we joined it, and that Gargery carried you on his back, while I led the way, and you kept up with me as best you could?”"}

{"request_id":"5e5821b36d4f874bbe8e0b51","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had taken an excellent house in Camden Place, a high and dignified setting suited to a man of importance; he and Elizabeth were both settled there, greatly to their satisfaction.

Anne entered with a heavy heart, expecting to be imprisoned there for many months, and asking herself anxiously, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Yet the unexpectedly warm welcome she received did her good. Her father and sister were pleased to see her, wanting to show her the house and furniture, and they greeted her kindly. When she joined them at dinner, making a party of four, they treated her presence as an advantage.

Mrs Clay was very pleasant and smiling, but her politeness and smiles seemed more routine. Anne had always believed that she would put on the proper appearance when Anne arrived, but the others’ friendliness was unexpected. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and Anne soon learned why. They had no wish to hear about her. After making a few comments about how deeply they had been missed in their former neighbourhood—compliments Anne could not return—they asked only a few weak questions before the conversation became entirely their own. Uppercross interested them not at all, Kellynch only slightly: everything was about Bath.

They were delighted to assure her that Bath had exceeded their expectations in every way. Their house was certainly the finest in Camden Place; its drawing rooms had clear advantages over all the others they had seen or heard about, and the superiority extended to both the decoration and the taste of the furniture. Their company was eagerly sought. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had refused many introductions, yet people they did not know were constantly leaving their cards.

Here was a great supply of happiness. Could Anne wonder that her father and sister were pleased? She might not wonder, but she had to sigh that her father felt no humiliation in the change, saw nothing to regret in giving up the duties and dignity of a country landowner, and found so much to be proud of in the small matters of town life. She had to sigh, smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth opened the folding doors and proudly walked from one drawing room to the other, boasting of their size; she wondered that the former mistress of Kellynch Hall could find space to boast about between two walls perhaps thirty feet apart.

But this was not all they had to make them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

{"request_id":"b43beed2d265bd4d51b0b1d8","rewritten_text":"Had she known that her sister wished to deprive her of such prospects and such realities as these, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood her feelings, having perhaps experienced nearly the same. Lydia’s journey to Brighton was the sole comfort left to her amid the melancholy certainty that her husband never meant to go there himself.

Yet they knew nothing of what had occurred; and their delight continued, with scarcely any interruption, until the very day Lydia departed from home.

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since her return, she had often been in his company, and her agitation had largely subsided; the agitation caused by her former partiality had vanished altogether. She had even learned to perceive, in the very mildness that had first charmed her, an affectation and monotony calculated to disgust and weary. His present conduct toward her gave her another cause for displeasure; for the desire he soon showed to renew the attentions that had distinguished the beginning of their acquaintance could only irritate her after all that had since passed. She ceased to feel any concern for him when she found herself chosen as the object of such empty and frivolous gallantry; and while firmly discouraging it, she could not help feeling the rebuke implied by his assumption that, however long his attentions had been withdrawn, and for whatever reason, her vanity would be pleased and her preference regained whenever he renewed them.

On the final day of the regiment’s stay in Meryton, he dined at Longbourn with several other officers; and Elizabeth was so little inclined to part from him on friendly terms that, when he made some inquiry about how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both stayed three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He appeared surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but, after a moment’s thought and with a returning smile, answered that he had once seen him often. Having remarked that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked how she had liked him. Her reply was warmly favorable. Soon afterward, with an air of indifference, he added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very unlike his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very unlike; but I think Mr. Darcy improves upon acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with an expression she did not miss. “And may I ask—” But checking himself, he continued in a livelier tone, “Is it in his address that he improves?”"}

{"request_id":"9ef66c946a2fa809f9dc008c","rewritten_text":"You must learn some of my philosophy. Think of the past only when remembering it gives you pleasure.”

“I cannot credit you with any philosophy of that kind. _Your_ memories must be entirely free of blame, so the contentment they bring comes not from philosophy, but from something much better: ignorance. But with _me_, it is different. Painful memories intrude, and they cannot, and should not, be pushed away. I have been selfish all my life in practice, though not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was _right_, but not how to control my temper. I was given good principles, yet left to follow them with pride and conceit. Unfortunately, as an only son—and for many years an only _child_—I was spoiled by my parents. Though they were good themselves (my father especially, being entirely benevolent and kind), they allowed, encouraged, almost taught me to be selfish and overbearing; to care for no one beyond my own family; to think poorly of everyone else; and at least to _wish_ to think poorly of their judgment and worth compared with my own. That was what I was, from eight to twenty-eight; and I might still be so but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! How much I owe you! You taught me a lesson that was difficult at first, but immensely beneficial. You humbled me properly. I came to you without the slightest doubt that you would accept me. You showed me how inadequate all my claims were to please a woman worthy of being pleased.”

“Had you then convinced yourself that I would?”

“Indeed I had. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you wished for, and expected, my attentions.”

“My manner must have been at fault, though never intentionally, I assure you. I never meant to deceive you, but my spirits may often have led me astray. How you must have hated me after _that_ evening!”

“Hated you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon found its proper direction.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, indeed. I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise could not have been greater than _mine_ at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special politeness, and I confess I did not expect to receive _more_ than was my due.”

“My purpose _then_,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, through every courtesy within my power, that I was not so mean as to resent the past. I hoped to gain your forgiveness and lessen your poor opinion of me by showing you that I had taken your reproofs to heart.”"}

{"request_id":"806256ba8258864a53447dd5","rewritten_text":"It was well after noon when he woke. His valet had slipped into the room several times on tiptoe to discover whether he was stirring, and had wondered what could make his young master sleep so late. At last the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly with a cup of tea and a heap of letters on a little tray of old Sevres china. He drew aside the olive-satin curtains, their blue lining shimmering, which hung before the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up and, after drinking a little tea, sorted through his letters. One came from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He paused briefly, then set it aside. He opened the rest without interest. They held the customary assortment of cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private views, programmes for charity concerts, and similar things showered upon fashionable young men each morning during the season. There was a substantial bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet-set, which he had not yet dared forward to his guardians, extremely old-fashioned people who failed to understand that we live in an age when useless things are our sole necessities. There were also several most politely phrased notices from Jermyn Street money-lenders, offering to advance any amount at a moment’s notice and on the most reasonable terms.

After roughly ten minutes he rose, threw on an elaborate dressing-gown of silk-embroidered cashmere wool, and went into the bathroom paved with onyx. The cool water revived him after his long sleep. He appeared to have forgotten everything he had endured. Once or twice, a vague impression that he had taken part in some strange tragedy returned to him, but it possessed the unreality of a dream.

When he was dressed, he entered the library and sat down to the light French breakfast arranged for him on a small round table beside the open window. It was a perfect day. The warm air seemed scented with spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl before him, filled with sulphur-yellow roses. He felt entirely happy.

Then his gaze suddenly fell upon the screen he had set before the portrait, and he started.

“Is it too cold for Monsieur?” asked his valet, placing an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"fa1dbd8b783015457caf1dd1","rewritten_text":"After some time, twelve o’clock boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and with every stroke of the resonant bell the night seemed to tremble. Then the railway lights went out, leaving one solitary lamp shining like a great ruby on a giant mast, and the city’s roar grew fainter.

At two o’clock he rose and wandered towards Blackfriars. How unreal everything appeared! How much it resembled a strange dream! The houses across the river seemed built from darkness. One might have thought that silver and shadow had remade the world. The vast dome of St. Paul’s loomed like a bubble through the dim air.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he saw a man leaning over the parapet. When he came closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight fell fully across his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! No one could have mistaken that fat, flabby face, those gold-rimmed spectacles, that sickly, feeble smile, and that sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea flashed through his mind, and he crept quietly up behind him. In an instant he had seized Mr. Podgers by the legs and thrown him into the Thames. There was a coarse oath, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over the parapet, but could see nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat spinning in an eddy of moonlit water. After a while it too sank, and no trace of Mr. Podgers remained. Once he thought he saw the bulky, misshapen figure swimming towards the staircase by the bridge, and a terrible sense of failure seized him, but it proved to be only a reflection. When the moon emerged from behind a cloud, the feeling vanished. At last he seemed to have fulfilled the decree of destiny. He drew a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

‘Have you dropped anything, sir?’ a voice suddenly said behind him.

He turned and saw a policeman carrying a bull’s-eye lantern.

‘Nothing of importance, sergeant,’ he replied with a smile. Hailing a passing hansom, he climbed in and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swung between hope and fear. At times he almost expected Mr. Podgers to enter the room, yet at others he felt that Fate could not be so unjust to him. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s address in West Moon Street, but could not bring himself to ring the bell. He yearned for certainty and dreaded it.

At last it came. He was sitting in the club’s smoking-room, drinking tea and listening rather wearily to Surbiton’s account of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"fe2ab09ea0857dff93d40234","rewritten_text":"I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then I remembered—with a shudder—that the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there, alive and moving about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. I therefore begged him to wait a few minutes at the foot of the stairs while I rushed up to my room. My hand was already on the lock before I came to my senses. I stopped, seized by a cold shiver. Then I flung the door open, as children do when they expect a spectre to be waiting on the other side; but nothing appeared. I stepped inside cautiously: the apartment was empty, and my bedroom had also been freed from its hideous guest. I could scarcely believe such good fortune had come to me, but once I was certain that my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands with joy and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast; but I could not control myself. I was not merely joyful; my flesh tingled with overwhelming sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not remain still for even a moment. I leaped over the chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. At first Clerval thought my unusual excitement came from happiness at his arrival. But when he watched me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes that he could not explain, and my loud, uncontrolled, joyless laughter frightened and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “what, for God’s sake, is wrong? Do not laugh like that. How ill you are! What has caused all this?”

“Do not ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, for I thought I saw the dreaded spectre glide into the room. “_He_ can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined that the monster had seized me; I struggled violently and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had looked forward to with such joy had turned so strangely into bitterness. But I did not witness his grief, for I lay senseless and did not regain consciousness for a very long time.

This marked the beginning of a nervous fever that confined me for several months. Throughout that time, Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that, knowing my father was too old and unfit for such a long journey, and knowing how miserable my illness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this sorrow by concealing the severity of my condition."}

{"request_id":"4a4aa1e3bf78801d7ff73206","rewritten_text":"Mr Elliot looking up with such respect.”

“Absolutely charming!” cried Mrs Clay, though she did not dare turn her eyes towards Anne. “Just like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not call them father and son?”

“Oh! I place no restriction on anyone’s words. If you choose to entertain such notions! But, upon my word, I am hardly aware that his attentions exceed those of other men.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs Clay, raising her hands and eyes, and burying the remainder of her astonishment in a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so frightened on his account. I did invite him, you know. I sent him away smiling. When I discovered that he was truly going to his friends at Thornberry Park for all of tomorrow, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired her friend’s excellent acting, in showing such pleasure as she did both at the expectation and at the actual arrival of the very person whose presence must in reality be obstructing her principal aim. Mrs Clay could hardly fail to hate the sight of Mr Elliot; yet she could put on the most obliging, tranquil expression, and seem entirely content with the reduced opportunity of devoting herself to Sir Walter only half as much as she otherwise would have done.

For Anne herself, it was extremely painful to see Mr Elliot enter the room, and still more painful to have him come near and address her. She had formerly been accustomed to suspect that he was not always perfectly sincere, but now she detected insincerity in everything. His respectful attentions to her father, set against his earlier language, were hateful; and when she remembered his cruel treatment of Mrs Smith, she could scarcely endure the sight of his present smiles and gentleness, or listen to his affected expressions of good feeling.

She intended to avoid any change in her manner that might provoke a remonstrance from him. Escaping all inquiry or public notice was of great importance to her; but she meant to be as decidedly cool towards him as their relationship allowed, and to withdraw, as quietly as possible, the few unnecessary steps of intimacy along which she had gradually been drawn. Accordingly, she was more reserved and cooler than she had been the previous evening.

He wished to revive her curiosity about how and where he might formerly have heard her praised; he greatly desired the satisfaction of being pressed for further information. But the spell was broken: he discovered that the warmth and excitement of a public room were needed to kindle his modest cousin’s vanity; at least, he found that it could not now be accomplished by any of the attempts he might venture amid the more commanding claims of the others."}

{"request_id":"02c59a0d5580e2b595cf4aa2","rewritten_text":"“But do not imagine that I did not consider it an evil in itself.”

“Believe me, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I might not like them better for that. Such a number of women and children have no right to be comfortable on board.”

“My dear Frederick, you are talking nonsense. What would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who often need to be carried to one port or another after our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“My feelings, you see, did not stop me from taking Mrs Harville and all her family to Plymouth.”

“But I hate to hear you speak like such a fine gentleman, as if women were all delicate ladies instead of sensible creatures. None of us expect calm seas all our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has a wife, he will sing a different tune. If he is married, and we are lucky enough to live through another war, we shall see him do as you and I, and many others, have done. We shall see him very grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Yes, we shall.”

“Now I have finished,” cried Captain Wentworth. “Whenever married people begin attacking me with, ‘Oh, you will think very differently when you are married,’ I can only say, ‘No, I shall not.’ Then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that ends the matter.”

He rose and moved away.

“What a great traveller you must have been, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Quite a traveller, ma’am, during the fifteen years of my marriage, though many women have travelled more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times, gone once to the East Indies and back, and visited various places nearer home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Straits, and I was never in the West Indies. Bermuda and the Bahamas are not called the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to say against this; she could not accuse herself of ever having called them anything at all in her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs Croft continued, “that nothing can match the comfort of a man-of-war. I mean, of course, the larger ships. In a frigate, you are more confined; still, any reasonable woman may be perfectly happy in one. I can safely say that the happiest part of my life was spent on board a ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.”"}

{"request_id":"46698065af88293d52687bf0","rewritten_text":"The insect was remarkably heavy, and, considering everything, I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion of it. But I could not understand, no matter how hard I tried, why Legrand agreed with him.

“I sent for you,” he said grandly, after I had finished examining the beetle, “so that I might have your advice and help in carrying out the plans of Fate and the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I cried, interrupting him, “you are clearly unwell and should take some precautions. You must go to bed, and I will stay with you for a few days, until you recover. You are feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did so and, to tell the truth, found no sign of fever at all.

“But you may be ill without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you this once. First, go to bed. Then—”

“You are mistaken,” he interrupted. “I am as well as I can be, considering the excitement I am suffering. If you truly wish to help me, you will relieve that excitement.”

“And how can that be done?”

“Very easily. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and we will need the help of someone we can trust. You are the only person we can rely on. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me will be calmed.”

“I am willing to help you in any way,” I replied, “but do you mean that this cursed beetle has something to do with your expedition into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I cannot take part in such an absurd plan.”

“I am sorry—very sorry—for we will have to attempt it alone.”

“Attempt it alone! The man must be mad! But wait—how long do you expect to be gone?”

“Probably all night. We will leave at once and return, in any case, by sunrise.”

“And will you promise me, on your honor, that when this strange idea is over, and the beetle matter—good God!—has been settled to your satisfaction, you will come home and follow my advice exactly, as you would that of your doctor?”

“Yes, I promise. Now let us go, for we have no time to waste.”

With a heavy heart, I went with my friend. We set out at about four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and me. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, insisting on carrying all of them. It seemed to me that he did so more because he was afraid to leave either tool within his master’s reach than because of any special willingness or helpfulness."}
