{"request_id":"64706d28bea748d213895bb2","rewritten_text":"No later discovery obliged Emma to withdraw her poor opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her judgment had been fairly accurate. As Mrs. Elton seemed to her at this second meeting, so she appeared whenever they encountered one another again—self-important, presumptuous, familiar, uninformed, and ill-mannered. She possessed a little beauty and some accomplishments, but so little judgment that she imagined herself arriving with an advanced knowledge of the world, ready to enliven and improve a country neighbourhood; and she believed Miss Hawkins had occupied a position in society which only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could exceed.

There was no reason to think that Mr. Elton viewed his wife differently. He appeared not only content with her, but proud of her. He seemed to congratulate himself on having brought such a woman to Highbury, one whom even Miss Woodhouse could not surpass; and most of her new acquaintances, being inclined to praise, or unaccustomed to judge, following Miss Bates’s friendly example, or simply assuming that the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she declared herself, were entirely pleased. Thus Mrs. Elton’s praises passed from one person to another as they naturally should, unchecked by Miss Woodhouse, who willingly maintained her first contribution and spoke graciously of her as “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect Mrs. Elton became even less agreeable than she had seemed at first. Her feelings towards Emma changed. Probably offended by the scant encouragement given to her attempts at intimacy, she withdrew in her turn and gradually grew much colder and more distant; and although the result was agreeable, the ill-will that caused it necessarily increased Emma’s dislike. Her behaviour, and Mr. Elton’s as well, was also unpleasant towards Harriet. They were mocking and neglectful. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet; but the feelings capable of producing such conduct lowered them both considerably. It could hardly be doubted that poor Harriet’s attachment had been offered up to conjugal openness, and that her own part in the affair, presented in the least favourable light for her and the most comforting for him, had probably been related too. She was naturally the object of their united dislike. Whenever they had nothing else to discuss, it would always be easy to begin abusing Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they dared not display through open disrespect towards her found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong liking to Jane Fairfax, and did so from the beginning. It was not merely that, during a state of conflict with one young woman, the other might be expected to seem more attractive; from their very first meeting she was interested in Jane. Nor was she content with expressing a natural and reasonable admiration: without being asked, without excuse, and without any particular right, she insisted on offering her assistance and friendship. Before Emma had lost her confidence, and around their third meeting, she heard all of Mrs. Elton’s chivalrous plans on the subject."}

{"request_id":"e83f05a35999e7a4b464951c","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang immediately leaped through the chamber door, ran down the stairs, and then escaped through a window that had unfortunately been left open into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair. The ape still held the razor, sometimes stopping to look back and wave its arms at its pursuer until the man nearly caught up with it. Then it ran on again. The chase continued in this way for a long time. The streets were completely quiet, since it was nearly three in the morning. As it passed through an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive noticed a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s room, on the fourth floor of her house. It rushed to the building, saw the lightning rod, and climbed it with incredible speed. Grasping the shutter, which had been opened fully against the wall, it swung itself onto the headboard of the bed. The entire feat took less than a minute. As the Ourang-Outang entered the room, it kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor was both relieved and confused. He hoped to recapture the animal, since it could hardly escape the trap it had entered except by climbing back down the rod, where he might intercept it. Yet he was also deeply worried about what it might do inside the house. This concern drove him to keep following the fugitive. A lightning rod is easy to climb, especially for a sailor, but when he reached the level of the window, which was far to his left, he could go no farther. The most he could do was lean over and catch a glimpse of the room. At that sight, he nearly lost his grip from horror. Then the terrible screams rose into the night, startling the residents of the Rue Morgue from sleep. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, had apparently been arranging papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been moved to the center of the room. It stood open, with its contents scattered on the floor beside it. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window. Since some time passed between the animal’s entrance and the screams, it probably was not noticed at once. The shutter slamming shut would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked inside, the huge animal had seized Madame L’Espanaye by her hair, which was loose because she had been combing it, and was waving the razor around her face, copying a barber’s movements."}

{"request_id":"2ff92e2b75056e3a57612190","rewritten_text":"He then bowed and left. He saw no one in the street at the time. It is a side street—very lonely.

“_William Bird_, tailor, states that he was one of the group who entered the house. He is an Englishman and has lived in Paris for two years. He was among the first to climb the stairs. He heard the voices arguing. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could make out several words, but cannot now remember them all. He clearly heard ‘_sacré_’ and ‘_mon Dieu._’ At that moment there was a sound like several people struggling—a scraping and scuffling noise. The shrill voice was very loud, louder than the rough one. He is certain it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be a German’s voice. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above, when called again, stated that the door of the room where Mademoiselle L.’s body was found had been locked from the inside when the group reached it. Everything was completely silent—there were no groans or other sounds. When the door was forced open, no one was seen. The windows in both the back and front rooms were shut and firmly fastened from within. A door between the two rooms was closed but not locked. The door from the front room into the passage was locked, with the key inside. A small room at the front of the house, on the fourth floor at the end of the passage, stood open, its door partly ajar. It was filled with old beds, boxes, and other things. These were carefully removed and searched. Not an inch of the house was left unchecked. Chimney sweeps were sent up and down the chimneys. The house had four stories and attics (_mansardes._) A trapdoor in the roof was nailed shut very securely and did not seem to have been opened for years. The witnesses gave different estimates of the time between hearing the arguing voices and breaking open the room door. Some said it was as little as three minutes; others said as much as five. The door was difficult to open.

“_Alfonzo Garcio_, an undertaker, states that he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is a native of Spain. He was one of the group that entered the house but did not go upstairs. He is nervous and feared the effects of excitement. He heard the voices arguing. The rough voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could not make out what was said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—he is certain of this.”"}

{"request_id":"9e0e8caa655896f8922270f3","rewritten_text":"There comes a time in every properly made boy’s life when he feels a fierce desire to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. That desire seized Tom one day. He went out looking for Joe Harper but had no luck. Then he searched for Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. Before long he ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a secluded spot and confided the plan to him. Huck was willing. Huck was always ready to join any enterprise that promised amusement and required no money, since he had an inconvenient excess of the kind of time that is not money. “Where will we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is it buried everywhere?”

“No, of course not. It’s hidden in very specific places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests beneath the end of a branch on an old dead tree, exactly where the shadow falls at midnight; but usually under the floor of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Why, robbers, naturally—who did you think? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine, I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and enjoy myself.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do things that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No, they intend to, but they usually forget the marks, or else they die. Anyway, it lies there for a long time and grows rusty; then someone finds an old yellow paper explaining how to locate the marks—a paper that has to be deciphered for about a week because it’s mostly signs and hieroglyphics.”

“Hieroglyphics?”

“Hieroglyphics—pictures and things, you know, that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Do you have one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Then how are you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t need any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house or on an island, or beneath a dead tree with one branch sticking out. Well, we’ve searched Jackson’s Island a little, and we can try again sometime; and there’s the old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and there are plenty of dead-branch trees—loads of them.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“What are you talking about? No!”

“Then how will you know which one to search?”

“Search them all!”

“Why, Tom, that’ll take the whole summer.”

“Well, so what? Suppose you find a brass pot containing a hundred dollars, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How would that be?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s excellent. More than excellent for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want any diamonds.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"dec79a8cb7821c25c3fa8f4c","rewritten_text":"He crept silently from the wainscoting, wearing a wicked smile upon his cruel, wrinkled lips, while the moon concealed her face behind a cloud as he passed the great oriel window, where his arms and those of his murdered wife were displayed in azure and gold. He glided onward like some evil shadow, and even the darkness appeared to shrink from him. Once he fancied he heard a voice, and halted; but it was merely a dog baying at the Red Farm. So he continued, muttering odd sixteenth-century curses and from time to time flourishing the rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he came to the passage corner leading to luckless Washington’s chamber. There he paused briefly, the wind tossing his long grey locks around his head and twisting the nameless horror of the dead man’s shroud into grotesque, fantastic folds. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he knew the moment had arrived. Chuckling softly, he turned the corner; but scarcely had he done so when, with a pitiful cry of terror, he recoiled and covered his blanched face with his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a dreadful spectre, still as a carved figure and monstrous as a madman’s nightmare! Its head was bald and shining; its face round, fat, and white; and some ghastly laughter seemed to have twisted its features into a permanent grin. Scarlet rays poured from its eyes, its mouth yawned like a broad well of flame, and a hideous garment, resembling his own, wrapped its silent snows around the Titan-like form. A placard hung upon its breast, covered with strange antique lettering—apparently a scroll of disgrace, a record of savage sins, an appalling calendar of crime—and in its right hand it held high a gleaming steel falchion.\n\nHaving never encountered a ghost before, he was naturally terrified. After one hurried second look at the dreadful phantom, he fled toward his room, stumbling over his long winding-sheet as he raced along the corridor, and at last dropping the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jack-boots, where the butler discovered it in the morning. Once safely inside his own chamber, he threw himself upon a little pallet-bed and buried his face beneath the blankets. After some time, however, the courageous old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to seek out the other ghost as soon as daylight came. Thus, just as dawn was silvering the hills, he returned toward the place where he had first seen the grisly phantom, thinking that two ghosts were better than one and that, with his new companion’s help, he might safely confront the twins."}

{"request_id":"f24739623924a28bdf3acd0d","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how strange and mysterious they were! The soul contained something animal, while the body had its flashes of spirituality. The senses might become refined, and the intellect might sink into degradation. Who could tell where the bodily impulse ended and the psychic impulse began? How superficial were the arbitrary distinctions of common psychologists! Yet how hard it was to choose between the claims of the different schools! Was the soul a shadow dwelling in the house of sin? Or was the body truly contained within the soul, as Giordano Bruno had believed? The division of spirit from matter was a mystery, and so too was their union.

He began to ask himself whether psychology could ever become so exact a science that every small spring of life would be exposed to us. As matters stood, we continually misunderstood ourselves and seldom understood anyone else. Experience possessed no ethical value. It was simply the name people gave their errors. Moralists had generally treated it as a form of warning, claimed that it had some ethical power in shaping character, and praised it as something that taught us what to pursue and what to shun. But experience contained no driving force. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly proved was that the future would resemble the past, and that the sin we had once committed with disgust, we would repeat many times, and with delight.

It seemed plain to him that experiment was the sole method by which one could reach a scientific analysis of the passions; and Dorian Gray was plainly a subject ready to hand, promising abundant and valuable results. His sudden, passionate love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon of considerable interest. Curiosity had certainly played a large part in it, along with the longing for fresh experiences, but the passion was not simple; it was exceedingly complex. Whatever purely sensual instinct belonged to boyhood had been altered by the imagination, transformed into something that seemed to the young man himself far removed from the senses, and therefore all the more perilous. It was the passions whose beginnings we misunderstood that ruled us most tyrannically. Our feeblest motives were those whose character we recognized. Often, when we believed we were experimenting upon others, we were in fact experimenting upon ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat pondering these matters, there came a knock at the door. His valet entered and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

“Out in the woods.”

“What will you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell him.”

“All right. He’s a mighty little tick, anyhow.”

“Oh, anybody can chase down a tick that doesn’t belong to them. I’m satisfied with this one. He’s good enough for me.”

“Sho, there are ticks aplenty. I could have a thousand if I wanted them.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know mighty well you can’t. This is a pretty early tick, I reckon. It’s the first I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for him.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom took out a scrap of paper and unrolled it with care. Huckleberry looked at it longingly. The temptation was powerful. At last he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom raised his lip and displayed the gap.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry, “it’s a trade.”

Tom shut the tick inside the percussion-cap box that had recently served as the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom arrived at the small, isolated frame schoolhouse, he marched in briskly, carrying himself like one who had come with all possible honesty and speed. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike haste. The master, enthroned above them in his large splint-bottom armchair, had been dozing to the sleepy murmur of study. The interruption awakened him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that hearing his full name meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to escape into a lie when he noticed two long tails of yellow hair falling down a back he recognized through love’s electric sympathy; beside that figure stood _the only vacant place_ on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He answered at once:

“_I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!_”

The master’s pulse seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The hum of study died away. The pupils wondered whether this reckless boy had lost his senses. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There could be no misunderstanding the words.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astonishing confession I have ever heard. A mere ferule will not suffice for such an offence. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm continued until it was weary and the supply of switches had been greatly reduced. Then came the command:

“Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The titter that passed around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth that effect came more from his reverent awe of his unknown idol and the fearful delight contained in his extraordinary good fortune."}

I feared that the unbroken weight of misfortune had finally disturbed my friend’s reason. Without the slightest hesitation, therefore, I made ready to go with the negro.

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some affection, especially on Lydia’s side, but nothing that caused him any alarm. I feel so sorry for him. His conduct was as attentive and kind as possible. He was coming to us to express his concern before he had any idea that they had not gone to Scotland. When that fear first spread, it hastened his journey.”

“And was Denny convinced that Wickham would not marry? Did he know they planned to run away? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Colonel Forster questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and would not state his true opinion. He did not repeat his belief that they would not marry, and because of that I hope he may have been misunderstood earlier.”

“And until Colonel Forster came in person, none of you doubted, I suppose, that they were truly married?”

“How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt somewhat uneasy—slightly afraid for my sister’s happiness with him as her husband, because I knew his behavior had not always been proper. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only understood how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then admitted, with very natural pride at knowing more than the rest of us, that Lydia’s last letter had prepared her for such a step. It seems she had known for many weeks that they were in love.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I believe not.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit that he did not speak of Wickham as highly as he once had. He believed him imprudent and wasteful; and since this sad affair occurred, people say that he left Meryton deeply in debt. But I hope that is untrue.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secretive, if we had told people what we knew about him, this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But exposing someone’s past faults without knowing what his present feelings were seemed unjustifiable.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"4504338896f9c1ca8b140815","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was disproportionately broad, lending his whole figure a rotundity of highly ridiculous effect. His feet, naturally, were entirely invisible, though a horny substance of doubtful character would sometimes protrude through a tear in the bottom of the car—or, more properly speaking, through the crown of the hat. His hands were immensely large. His hair, exceedingly gray, was gathered behind in a queue. His nose was extraordinarily long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes large, bright, and keen; while his chin and cheeks, though creased by age, were broad, swollen, and double. Yet ears of any description could not be found upon any part of his head. This peculiar little gentleman wore a loose surtout of sky-blue satin, with matching tight breeches secured at the knees by silver buckles. His vest was made of some vivid yellow fabric; a white taffety cap sat jauntily askew upon his head; and, completing his attire, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his throat and descended delicately upon his breast in a fanciful bow of extraordinary size.\n\nHaving descended, as I have already said, to within about a hundred feet of the earth’s surface, the little old gentleman was suddenly overcome by trepidation and seemed unwilling to come any closer to terra firma. He therefore cast out some sand from a canvas bag, which he raised only with considerable effort, and became stationary at once. He then hurriedly and nervously drew from a side pocket of his surtout a large morocco pocketbook. Holding it suspiciously, he regarded it with extreme surprise, plainly astonished by its weight. At last he opened it and took out a huge letter, sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape, which he dropped exactly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent down to retrieve it. But the aeronaut, still deeply agitated and apparently having no further reason to remain in Rotterdam, now began making active preparations to depart. Since he had to release ballast in order to rise again, the six bags he tossed out in succession, without bothering to empty them, all fell most unfortunately upon the burgomaster’s back, rolling him over and over no fewer than twenty-one times before every man in Rotterdam. It cannot be imagined, however, that the great Underduk allowed this insolence from the little old man to go unpunished."}

{"request_id":"9ed3048b22bbfb874306a907","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed ourselves freemen so loudly and earnestly that we drew the interested notice of that liberty-preaching orator and his patriotic company. They clustered around us and took on a very resolute air. The orator said:

“If, indeed, ye are freemen, ye have nought to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain surround ye as shield and shelter! (Applause.) Ye shall soon see. Bring forth your proofs.”

“What proofs?”

“Proof that ye are freemen.”

Ah—I remembered! I came to myself and held my tongue. But the king burst out:

“Thou’rt mad, man. It were more reasonable, and better, that this thief and scoundrel here prove we are _not_ freemen.”

You see, he understood his own laws as people so often understand laws: by their words, not by their consequences. They acquire a _meaning_, and become remarkably vivid, when you have to apply them to yourself.

Everyone shook his head and looked disappointed; some turned away, their interest gone. The orator said—and now his voice had the practical tone of business rather than sentiment:

“An ye know not your country’s laws, it were time ye learned them. Ye are strangers here; that ye will not deny. Ye may be freemen, and we do not deny it; but ye may also be slaves. The law is plain: it doth not demand that the claimant prove ye are slaves; it requireth you to prove ye are not.”

I said:

“Good sir, grant us only time to send to Astolat; or grant us only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man, these are extraordinary requests, and you cannot expect them to be allowed. It would consume much time and cause your master needless inconvenience—”

“_Master_, fool!” the king thundered. “I have no master; I myself am the m—”

“Silence, for God’s sake!”

I managed to get the words out soon enough to stop the king. We were already in trouble enough; it could do us no good to make these people think we were lunatics.

There is no point in dragging out the particulars. The earl housed us and put us up for sale at auction. That same damnable law had existed in our own South in my own day, more than thirteen hundred years afterward, and under it hundreds of freemen unable to prove they were freemen had been sold into lifelong slavery without the fact making any special impression on me; but once the law and auction block entered my own experience, what had previously seemed merely wrong became instantly hellish. Well, that is how we are made.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like swine. In a large town with a brisk market we ought to have fetched a good price; but this place was completely stagnant, and we were sold for a sum that shames me whenever I remember it."}

{"request_id":"e890f3e9efc5ef47a8f80ff1","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was busy with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note in the mail. The sight of its outside threw me into great excitement; although I had never seen the handwriting before, I guessed whose it was. It had no formal opening—not Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or anything else—but began like this:

“I am to come to London the day after tomorrow by the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you should meet me? In any case, Miss Havisham thinks so, and I am writing as she instructed. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If there had been time, I would probably have ordered several new suits for the occasion. But there was not, so I had to be satisfied with the clothes I already owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I had no peace or rest until the day came. Even then I found neither. I was worse than ever, and began haunting the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, before the coach had even left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew perfectly well that it would not arrive for hours, I still felt it unsafe to leave the office out of sight for more than five minutes. In this unreasonable state, I had completed the first half-hour of a four- or five-hour watch when Wemmick ran into me.

“Hello, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I would hardly have expected to find you in this part of town.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and asked about the Castle and the Aged.

“Both doing very well, thank you,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He is in wonderful spirits. He will be eighty-two on his next birthday. I am thinking of firing the cannon eighty-two times, if the neighbors do not object and the cannon can withstand the strain. But that is not London talk. Where do you think I am going?”

“To the office?” I asked, since he was heading that way.

“Almost,” Wemmick replied. “I am going to Newgate. We are handling a banker's-parcel case at present, and I have been down the road to look at the scene of the crime. Now I must have a word with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Good heavens, no,” Wemmick answered very dryly. “But he is accused of it. You or I might be accused of it too. Either of us could be accused, you know.”"}

{"request_id":"8ac5ccfc6ae059efd940e01d","rewritten_text":"Why, we could build a very thrilling superstition around this clue. I suppose you’ll call the bug _scarabæus caput hominis_, or something similar—there are plenty of such names in natural histories. But where are the _antennæ_ you mentioned?”

“The _antennæ!_” said Legrand, who seemed inexplicably heated on the subject. “Surely you can see the _antennæ_. I made them as clear as they are on the actual insect, and I assume that is enough.”

“Well, well,” I said, “perhaps you did—but I still can’t see them.” I handed him the paper without further comment, not wanting to provoke him; but I was greatly surprised by the turn things had taken. His bad temper confused me—and as for the beetle drawing, there were absolutely _no antennæ_ visible, and the whole thing bore a striking resemblance to the usual illustrations of a death’s-head.

He took the paper irritably and was about to crumple it, apparently to throw it into the fire, when a casual glance at the design suddenly fixed his attention. In one instant his face became intensely red; in the next, equally pale. For several minutes he sat scrutinizing the drawing closely. At last he rose, took a candle from the table, and went to sit on a sea chest in the farthest corner of the room. There he examined the paper anxiously again, turning it every way. He said nothing, however, and his behavior astonished me; still, I thought it wiser not to worsen his growing moodiness with any remark. Soon he took a wallet from his coat pocket, placed the paper carefully inside it, and put both into a writing desk, which he locked. He now seemed calmer, but his earlier enthusiasm had completely vanished. He appeared less sullen than distracted. As the evening passed, he became increasingly lost in thought, and none of my attempts at conversation could rouse him. I had planned to spend the night at the hut, as I had often done before, but seeing my host in this state, I thought it best to leave. He did not ask me to stay, but as I departed, he shook my hand with even greater warmth than usual.

About a month later—and during that time I had seen nothing of Legrand—I was visited in Charleston by his servant, Jupiter. I had never seen the good old Black man look so dejected, and I feared that some serious misfortune had overtaken my friend."}

{"request_id":"68cd737c2965994c856ab92b","rewritten_text":"He was short in stature but remarkably upright, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He began his lecture with a review of chemistry’s history and the various advances made by learned men, speaking with fervor the names of its most distinguished discoverers. He then gave a brief account of the science’s present state and explained many of its elementary terms. After conducting a few preliminary experiments, he concluded with a tribute to modern chemistry, whose words I shall never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” he said, “promised impossibilities and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be transmuted and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem made only for dabbling in dirt and whose eyes are fixed upon the microscope or crucible, have truly performed miracles. They penetrate nature’s hidden recesses and reveal how she works in secret. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and almost unlimited powers; they can command the thunder of heaven, imitate the earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows.”

Those were the professor’s words—or rather, let me say, the words of fate, spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as though my soul were wrestling with a tangible enemy. One by one, the keys that formed the mechanism of my being were struck; chord after chord resounded, and soon my mind was filled with a single thought, a single vision, a single purpose. So much has already been accomplished, cried the soul of Frankenstein—far more will I achieve. Following the path already marked, I will open a new one, explore unknown powers, and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner being was in revolt and turmoil; I felt that order would eventually emerge from it, but I had no power to create that order. Gradually, after dawn, sleep came. I awoke, and the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. Only one resolution remained: to return to my former studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I possessed a natural talent. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private, his manner was even gentler and more appealing than in public, for during his lecture there had been a certain dignity in his bearing that, in his own home, was replaced by the greatest warmth and kindness."}

He seemed deliberately to misunderstand the word she had repeated when he added hurriedly, “Yes, customers; in banking, we usually call our clients our customers. He was a French gentleman; a man of science; a man of great learning—a doctor.”

“From Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman was from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our relationship was a business one, but confidential. At that time I was in our French branch, and had been there—oh! twenty years.”

“At that time—I may ask, what time was that, sir?”

“I mean, miss, twenty years ago. He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen and families, were entirely in Tellson’s hands. In the same way, I am, or have been, trustee of one kind or another for dozens of our customers. These are merely business relationships, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing resembling sentiment. Throughout my business life, I have passed from one to another just as I pass from one customer to another during my business day; in short, I have no feelings; I am merely a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I am beginning to think”—the strangely furrowed forehead was fixed intently upon him—“that when I was left an orphan because my mother survived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the hesitant little hand that trustingly reached toward his and, with some ceremony, raised it to his lips. He then led the young lady directly back to her chair and, holding its back with his left hand, using his right by turns to rub his chin, tug at his wig near the ears, or emphasize his words, stood looking down into her face while she looked up at his.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how truthfully I spoke of myself just now, when I said I had no feelings, and that all my relationships with my fellow human beings were merely business relationships, when you consider that I have never seen you since. No; you have been a ward of Tellson’s House ever since, and I have been occupied with Tellson’s other business ever since. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my entire life, miss, turning an enormous financial Mangle.”"}

{"request_id":"f6c713513c89dbaacd430cd6","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind her, except the memory that such things had once existed.

Anne had not set foot in Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and on the few occasions when it might have been possible for her to visit the Hall, she had managed to avoid and escape them. Her first return was to take up her place again in the Lodge’s modern, elegant rooms, and to delight its mistress’s eyes.

Lady Russell’s happiness at seeing her was mingled with some anxiety. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. But fortunately, either Anne had gained in fullness and appearance, or Lady Russell imagined that she had; and while receiving her compliments, Anne enjoyed associating them with her cousin’s silent admiration, and hoped she might be blessed with a second spring of youth and beauty.

As they began to talk, Anne soon perceived a change in her own mind. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, and that she had felt neglected and been obliged to suppress among the Musgroves, had now become matters of only secondary importance. Lately, she had even lost sight of her father, her sister, and Bath. Their affairs had been overwhelmed by those of Uppercross; and when Lady Russell returned to their former hopes and fears, expressing her satisfaction with the house in Camden Place that had been taken, and her regret that Mrs Clay remained with them, Anne would have been embarrassed to have it known how much more she was thinking of Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her acquaintances there; how much more engaging to her were the home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick than her father’s house in Camden Place, or her sister’s intimacy with Mrs Clay. She was truly obliged to make an effort to meet Lady Russell with anything resembling equal concern on subjects that naturally had the first claim upon her.

At first, there was some awkwardness when they spoke of another matter. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had not been there five minutes the previous day before a complete account of it had reached her; yet it must still be discussed. She had to enquire into it, regret the imprudence, lament the consequences, and Captain Wentworth’s name had to be spoken by them both. Anne knew she did not manage this as well as Lady Russell. She could not utter the name while looking directly into Lady Russell’s eyes until she had adopted the expedient of briefly telling her what she thought of the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"cb1c0a2addce1ef698c29a41","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; all the work of maintaining a slow and unsatisfactory correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Breakfast had been over only a short while when Captain and Mrs Harville and Captain Benwick joined them. They had arranged to take their final walk around Lyme together. They needed to leave for Uppercross by one, and until then they meant to stay together outdoors for as long as possible.

Anne found Captain Benwick coming near her as soon as they were properly out in the street. Their conversation the evening before had not made him reluctant to seek her company again. They walked together for some time, speaking as before about Mr Scott and Lord Byron, and still no more able than any other two readers to agree completely about the merits of either, until something caused an almost general change in the group. Then, instead of Captain Benwick, Captain Harville was walking beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” he said, speaking rather quietly, “you have done a good thing by getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he could have company like that more often. I know it is bad for him to be shut away as he is; but what can we do? We cannot leave him.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can easily believe that to be impossible; but perhaps, in time—we know what time does in every kind of grief—and you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may still be considered a young mourner. It was only last summer, I understand.”

“Yes, quite true,” he said with a deep sigh. “Only June.”

“And perhaps he did not know until later.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, having just been made captain of the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, afraid to hear about him. He sent letters, but the Grappler had orders for Portsmouth. The news would have to reach him there, but who was to tell him? Not I. I would almost rather have been hanged from the yard-arm. No one could do it except that good fellow”—he pointed to Captain Wentworth—“The Laconia had arrived at Plymouth the week before, and there was no danger of her being sent to sea again. He took his chance with the rest, applied for leave, but did not wait for the answer. He travelled night and day until he reached Portsmouth, rowed out to the Grappler at once, and never left the poor fellow for a week. That is what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. You can judge, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne considered the question with complete certainty and replied as fully as her own feelings allowed, and as much as he seemed able to bear. He was too deeply moved to continue the subject, and when he spoke again, it was about something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"5070ce87b41daddaa3749cca","rewritten_text":"But my father was beside me to comfort me and drive away painful memories with hopeful thoughts. I felt that there was something sweet in grieving, because he was there to dry my tears.

He also drew my thoughts away from my sorrow by comparing it with his despair after losing my mother. Even then, I shuddered at the picture he painted of his feelings. He had a poet’s imagination, and when he described the storm that had torn through his heart, his words were so vivid that I believed him even as I trembled. I wondered how he could ever return to ordinary life after his wild thoughts had seemed to bring him close to the supernatural. As he spoke, the ideas he expressed were so powerful that the human heart seemed too limited to contain them. His feelings seemed more suited to a spirit living among earthquakes and volcanoes than to a being confined to a mortal body and human form. But those were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was all love and gentleness. When I looked at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips showed me that his heart was filled with the tenderest feelings.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me toward deeper studies than those I had pursued before. My progress delighted him. He stayed with me throughout my studies and helped with, or took part in, every lesson. We met a great deal of society, and each day my father tried to brighten with some new pleasure. His tender love for me, and the love and respect I returned, cast a charm over every moment. The hours passed slowly because we made use of every minute. We lived more in one week than many people do in several months, and the variety and freshness of our pleasures made each one more enjoyable.

We were constantly taking excursions together. Whether we went to see beautiful scenery, admire fine paintings, or simply seek whatever amusement happened to appear, I was always happy when I was near my father. I regretted whenever a third person joined us. Yet if I looked uneasily toward my father, his eyes would meet mine, shining with tenderness, and instantly restore joy to my heart. O, hours of perfect happiness! Though you were brief, memory has made you seem as long as a whole lifetime, when I look back through the fog of grief that rose immediately afterward, as if to hide you from my sight."}

{"request_id":"755d71160649c8e55c53c383","rewritten_text":"“He was delivered to you. You see that I know the circumstances?”

“Such is certainly the fact,” said Defarge. His wife had conveyed to him, by an accidental touch of her elbow as she knitted and hummed, that he would do best to answer, but always briefly.

“It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and from your care she took him, accompanied by a neat brown monsieur—what is his name?—in a little wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—across to England.”

“Such is the fact,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting recollections!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You hear little of them now?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In fact,” madame interposed, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear of them. We received word of their safe arrival, and perhaps one other letter, or perhaps two; but since then they have gradually gone their way in life—we ours—and we have had no correspondence.”

“Precisely so, madame,” replied the spy. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” echoed madame. “She was pretty enough to have married long ago. You English are cold, it seems to me.”

“Oh! You know I am English.”

“I can tell your tongue is,” returned madame; “and what the tongue is, I suppose the man is.”

He did not regard this identification as a compliment; but he made the best of it and dismissed it with a laugh. After drinking his cognac to the last, he continued:

“Yes, Miss Manette is to be married. But not to an Englishman; to one who, like herself, was born French. And speaking of Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!), it is a curious circumstance that she is to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was raised to that height of so many feet; in other words, the present Marquis. But he lives unknown in England, where he is no Marquis; he is Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge continued knitting, but the news plainly affected her husband. However he tried, behind the little counter, to strike a light and light his pipe, he was disturbed, and his hand was unsteady. The spy would not have been a spy had he failed to notice this, or to store it in his mind.

Having made at least this one successful stroke, whatever it might ultimately be worth, and with no customers arriving to assist him in making another, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and departed. Before leaving, he took the opportunity to say, politely, that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b0406b2b6b723813356b157b","rewritten_text":"Having seen our friend duly settled in his new office, we turned our attention towards Windsor. Its proximity to London was enough to remove any sense of painful separation when we left Raymond and Perdita. We took our leave of them in the Protectoral Palace. It was amusing to see my sister enter, as it were, into the spirit of the drama, and strive to occupy her station with suitable dignity. Her inward pride and outward humility were now more than ever at variance. Her timidity was not assumed, but sprang from a fear of being insufficiently valued, that slight consciousness of the world’s neglect which also marked Raymond. Perdita, however, thought more habitually of others than he did; and some of her bashfulness proceeded from a desire to spare those about her any sense of inferiority—a feeling that had never entered her own mind. From the conditions of his birth and education, Idris would have been more suited to the forms of ceremony; but the ease with which such observances came to her through habit made them wearisome, while Perdita plainly took pleasure in her position, despite every disadvantage. She was too occupied by new ideas to suffer much at our departure; she embraced us affectionately and promised soon to visit, but she did not mourn the circumstances that occasioned our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless; he scarcely knew how to employ his newly acquired power. His mind teemed with schemes, though he had settled upon none—but he vowed to himself, his friends, and the world that the era of his Protectorship would be marked by some act of extraordinary glory. Thus we spoke of them and reflected as, with our numbers reduced, we returned to Windsor Castle. We were exceedingly glad to have escaped political turmoil and sought our solitude with renewed eagerness. We were not without occupation; but my ardent nature was now directed solely towards intellectual exertion, and I found severe study an excellent remedy for the fever of spirit which idleness would doubtless have brought upon me. Perdita had allowed us to bring Clara back with us to Windsor; and she, together with my two lovely infants, provided continual interest and amusement.\n\nThe sole circumstance that disturbed our tranquillity was Adrian’s health. It was plainly failing, though no symptom appeared by which we could discover his illness, unless his brightened eyes, lively expression, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption; yet he suffered neither pain nor apprehension. He devoted himself eagerly to books, and rested from his studies in the company he loved best—that of his sister and myself."}

{"request_id":"32106fdab5d8541a381412f3","rewritten_text":"At the centre of this fissure I noticed a white spot, though at first I could not tell what it might be. I altered the telescope’s focus and looked again; now I recognized it as a human skull.

“On making this discovery I was confident enough to believe the riddle solved; for the words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side,’ could signify only the skull’s position on the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ allowed but one meaning in connection with a search for buried treasure. I understood that a bullet was to be dropped from the skull’s left eye, and that a bee-line—or, in other words, a straight line—drawn from the trunk’s nearest point through ‘the shot’ (the place where the bullet landed), and continued fifty feet farther, would mark a precise spot; beneath that spot, I thought it at least possible, lay a valuable deposit.”

“All this,” I said, “is remarkably plain, and, though clever, remains simple and definite. When you departed from the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened next?”

“Why, after carefully taking the tree’s bearings, I turned toward home. Yet the moment I left ‘the devil’s seat,’ the circular fissure disappeared, and no matter how I turned, I could not see it again. What strikes me as the greatest ingenuity in the entire affair is the fact—for repeated trials have convinced me it is one—that this circular opening can be seen from no other accessible viewpoint than the narrow ledge on the rock’s face.

“Jupiter had accompanied me on this journey to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel.’ He had doubtless noticed my absent-minded manner for several weeks, and took particular care not to let me remain alone. But the following day, rising very early, I managed to elude him and went into the hills to look for the tree. After considerable labor I discovered it. When I returned that night, my valet offered to flog me. As for the remainder of the adventure, I believe you know it as well as I do.”

“I presume,” said I, “that you failed to find the spot on your first digging attempt because of Jupiter’s foolishness in allowing the bug to fall through the skull’s right eye rather than the left.”

“Exactly. That error shifted the ‘shot’—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree—by about two and a half inches. Had the treasure lain directly beneath ‘the shot,’ the mistake would have mattered little; but ‘the shot’ and the tree’s nearest point served only as the two points from which a line of direction was established. Naturally, though insignificant at first, the error grew as we followed the line, and after fifty feet had carried us entirely away from the trail.”"}

{"request_id":"b36b071fd93b3dc40065690b","rewritten_text":"“In English, the letter that appears most often is e. After that, the order is: _a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z_. _E_ is so common that it is rare to find a sentence of any length in which it is not the most frequent letter.

“Here, at the very beginning, we have the basis for more than a mere guess. The table is generally useful, though in this particular cipher we will need it only to a limited extent. Since our most common character is 8, we will begin by assuming that it stands for _e_. To test this idea, let us see whether 8 appears often in pairs, since _e_ is frequently doubled in English, as in ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In this case, it appears doubled no fewer than five times, even though the cryptograph is short.

“Let us take 8 as _e_. Now, the most common word in the language is ‘the.’ Let us therefore look for repeated groups of three characters, in the same order, with 8 as the last character. If we find such repeated groups, they will most likely represent ‘the.’ On examination, we find seven of them, each written ;48. We may therefore assume that ; stands for _t_, 4 for _h_, and 8 for _e_—the last conclusion now strongly confirmed. We have made great progress.

“Once we have identified one word, we can determine a very important part of several other words: their beginnings and endings. Consider, for example, the next-to-last occurrence of ;48, near the end of the cipher. We know that the following ; begins a word, and that of the six characters after this ‘the,’ we know five. Writing the letters we have identified and leaving a space for the unknown one, we get:

t eeth.

“We can immediately reject the ‘th’ as part of the word beginning with the first t. By trying every letter of the alphabet in the blank, we see that no word can be formed in which this _th_ belongs. We are therefore left with:

t ee,

“and, by testing the alphabet as before, we arrive at ‘tree’ as the only possible reading.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"f2ea1ec61fd07ba3ba9d4206","rewritten_text":"The next day the ghost was very weak and exhausted. The terrible excitement of the past four weeks was beginning to take its toll. His nerves were completely shattered, and he started at the slightest sound. For five days he stayed in his room, and finally decided to abandon the matter of the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, they clearly did not deserve it. They were evidently people on a low, material level of existence, quite incapable of appreciating the symbolic value of sensuous phenomena. The question of ghostly apparitions and the development of astral bodies was, of course, entirely different, and not really within his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week and gibber from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of every month, and he could not see how he could honorably escape his obligations. It was true that his life had been very wicked, but, on the other hand, he was extremely conscientious in everything connected with the supernatural. Accordingly, for the next three Saturdays, he crossed the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every possible precaution against being heard or seen. He removed his boots, walked as lightly as possible over the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and carefully used Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit that he adopted this final safeguard only with considerable difficulty. However, one night, while the family was at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and carried off the bottle. At first he felt somewhat humiliated, but afterward he was sensible enough to recognize that there was much to recommend the invention, and to some extent it served his purpose. Still, despite everything, he was not left in peace. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor, over which he tripped in the darkness, and once, while dressed for the role of ‘Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,’ he suffered a serious fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had built from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult enraged him so much that he resolved to make one last attempt to assert his dignity and social standing, and decided to visit the insolent young Etonians the following night in his celebrated character of ‘Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.’\n\nHe had not appeared in this disguise for more than seventy years—in fact, not since he had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish so badly with it that she abruptly ended her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton, declaring that nothing in the world could persuade her to marry into a family that allowed such a horrible phantom to walk up and down the terrace at twilight."}

{"request_id":"166e29614c7f35a15cd25bf4","rewritten_text":"I ran to her, gathered her into my arms, showered her with kisses, and pleaded:

“Speak, darling, speak! What is it?”

Her head went limp against my chest, and she gasped, almost inaudibly:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I shouted to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopath and tell him to come!”

Within two minutes I was kneeling beside the child’s crib, while Sandy sent servants hurrying in every direction throughout the palace. I understood the situation almost at once—membranous croup! I bent over her and whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart! Hello-Central.”

She opened her soft eyes languidly and managed to say:

“Papa.”

That comforted me. She was not close to death yet. I sent for sulfur preparations and brought out the croup kettle myself; I do not sit and wait for doctors when Sandy or the child is ill. I knew how to care for both of them and had plenty of experience. This little one had spent much of its short life in my arms, and often I could soothe its troubles and make it laugh through the tears on its eyelashes when even its mother could not.

Sir Launcelot, dressed in his finest armor, came striding down the great hall on his way to the stock board. He was president of the stock board and occupied the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad; for the stock board consisted of the Knights of the Round Table, and they now used the Round Table for business. Seats there were worth—well, you would never believe the price, so there is no point in naming it. Sir Launcelot was a bear. He had cornered one of the new lines and was preparing to squeeze the shorts that day; but what did that matter? He was still the old Launcelot, and when he glanced through the doorway as he passed and learned that his pet was sick, that was enough. Bulls and bears could fight it out without him; he would come in and stand by little Hello-Central with all his strength. And that was exactly what he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute he had put a new wick in the alcohol lamp and was heating the croup kettle. By then Sandy had built a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was ready.

Sir Launcelot raised steam. Together, he and I filled the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a little lactic acid, then filled it with water and pushed the steam spout beneath the canopy. Everything was in order now, and we sat on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"dcbffaaf24183282af1a0609","rewritten_text":"“But it is very strange that she can always hear Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she will not find her grandmother any deafer than she was two years ago; and that is saying a great deal at my mother’s age. It really has been a full two years, you know, since she was here. We have never gone so long without seeing her before, and, as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we shall hardly know how to get enough of her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed! That must be a great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says the same polite things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they will be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell will need the carriage himself on one of those days. It is very kind of them to send her all this way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, next Friday or Saturday. That is what she writes about. It is why she has written earlier than usual, as we call it; normally, we would not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, that is what I thought. I was afraid there was little chance of hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“How kind of you! No, we would not have heard if it were not for this special circumstance, her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted! She is to stay with us for at least three months. Three months—she says so clearly, as I am about to have the pleasure of reading to you. You see, the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to come and see her at once. They had not planned to go until summer, but she is so eager to see them again—for until she married last October, she had never been away from them for even a week. It must seem very strange to be in different kingdoms—or, I should say, different countries. So she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father; I declare, I do not know which, but we shall see in Jane’s letter shortly. She wrote in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, urging them to come immediately. They would meet them in Dublin and take them back to their country estate, Baly-craig, which I imagine is a beautiful place.”"}

{"request_id":"6bcf7492df0a3b0035b71db3","rewritten_text":"I went from shop to shop, buying what was needed to change his appearance. When that was done, I made my way to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but when he saw me enter, he rose at once and stood in front of the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. On the way there, I had thought carefully about what I meant to say.

“Don’t involve yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t involve anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything: I don’t want to know anything; I’m not curious.”

Of course, I understood that he knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to make sure that what I have been told is true. I have no hope that it is false, but at least I can confirm it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head. He did not look at me, but listened toward the floor. “Told suggests that it was said directly. You can’t have spoken directly with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say, informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor who has been unknown to me for so long.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And no one else?” I asked.

“And no one else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you responsible for my mistakes and false conclusions; but I always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” replied Mr. Jaggers, turning his cool eyes on me and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that.”

“And yet it seemed so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart sinking.

“Not the slightest evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat. “Trust nothing because of how it looks; trust everything because of the evidence. There is no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said with a sigh, after standing silent for a while. “I have confirmed what I was told, and that is the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, in all my dealings with you, I have kept to the facts. I have never departed in the least from the facts. You know that perfectly well?”

“Perfectly, sir.”

“When Magwitch first wrote to me—from New South Wales—I told him—from New South Wales—that he must never expect me to depart from the strict facts.”"}

{"request_id":"141e51c4952f3f7993a8ed1e","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and took his left. He bent so low to study it that the gold rims of his spectacles almost touched the palm. For a moment, his face turned into a white mask of horror, but he quickly regained his composure. Looking up at Lady Windermere, he said with a forced smile, ‘It is the hand of a charming young man.’

‘Of course it is!’ replied Lady Windermere. ‘But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.’

‘All charming young men are,’ said Mr. Podgers.

‘I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,’ murmured Lady Jedburgh thoughtfully. ‘It is so dangerous.’

‘My dear child, they are never too fascinating,’ cried Lady Windermere. ‘But I want details. Details are the only things that interest me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will go on a voyage—’

‘Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!’

‘And lose a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I hope?’ said Lady Jedburgh sadly.

‘Certainly not his sister,’ answered Mr. Podgers, waving his hand dismissively. ‘Only a distant relative.’

‘Well, I am terribly disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives nowadays. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she had better keep a black silk dress ready; it is always useful for church, you know. And now let us go to supper. They are sure to have eaten everything, but perhaps we can find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so upset about politics these days that I am never quite sure of him. I do wish General Boulanger would keep quiet. Duchess, I am sure you are tired?’

‘Not at all, dear Gladys,’ answered the Duchess, waddling toward the door. ‘I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the cheiropodist—I mean the cheiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoiseshell fan be? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, very kind, I’m sure.’ The good woman finally managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent bottle more than twice.

All this time, Lord Arthur Savile had remained standing by the fireplace, still filled with dread and the sickening sense that something terrible was coming. He smiled sadly at his sister as she passed him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking beautiful in her pink brocade and pearls. He barely heard Lady Windermere call for him to follow her. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the thought that anything might come between them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"c75544e8da71c0bca8fdc5f5","rewritten_text":"“Well, everybody does it that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it don’t make any difference. I ain’t everybody, and I can’t _stand_ it. It’s terrible being tied down like that. And grub comes too easy—I don’t take no interest in vittles that way. I got to ask before I go fishing; I got to ask before I go swimming—dern’d if I ain’t got to ask to do everything. Why, I had to talk so proper it wasn’t any comfort—I had to go up in the attic and rip out for a spell every day, just to get a taste in my mouth, or I’d have died, Tom. The widder wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me yell, gape, stretch, or scratch in front of folks—” [Then, with a sudden fit of particular irritation and hurt]—“And dad fetch it, she prayed all the time! I never saw such a woman! I _had_ to shove, Tom—I simply had to. And besides, school’s going to start, and I’d have had to go—well, I wouldn’t stand _that_, Tom. Looky-here, Tom, being rich ain’t all it’s cracked up to be. It’s nothing but worry and worry, sweat and sweat, and wishing you was dead every minute. Now these clothes suit me, and this bar’l suits me, and I ain’t ever going to give ’em up again. Tom, I’d never have got into all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money; so you just take my share along with yours, and give me a ten-center now and then—not often, because I don’t give a dern for anything unless it’s tolerable hard to get—and you go beg the widder off for me.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. ’Tain’t fair; and besides, if you’ll stick with it a little longer, you’ll come to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in them cussed smothery houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick with ’em, too. Blame it all! Just when we’d got guns, and a cave, and everything fixed up for robbing, this dern foolishness has to come along and spoil it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Looky-here, Huck, being rich ain’t going to stop me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good-licks; are you in dead earnest, Tom?”

“Just as dead earnest as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang if you ain’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s joy was snuffed out.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"18c1476b24f3d0ce1ed9c99e","rewritten_text":"It is a strange thing, but everyone who disappears is said to be seen in San Francisco. It must be a delightful city, with all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you think happened to Basil?” asked Dorian, holding his Burgundy up to the light and wondering how he could discuss the matter so calmly.

“I haven’t the slightest idea. If Basil chooses to hide himself, that is none of my concern. If he is dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that ever frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked wearily.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, passing the gilt trellis of an open vinaigrette beneath his nostrils, “nowadays one can survive everything except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts in the nineteenth century that cannot be explained away. Let us have our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin exquisitely. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house is rather lonely without her. Of course, married life is merely a habit—a bad habit. But one regrets losing even one’s worst habits. Perhaps one regrets them most of all. They are such an essential part of one’s personality.”

Dorian said nothing, but rose from the table, went into the next room, sat at the piano, and let his fingers wander over the white and black ivory keys. After the coffee was brought in, he stopped and, looking across at Lord Henry, said, “Harry, did it ever occur to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was very popular and always wore a Waterbury watch. Why should he have been murdered? He was not clever enough to have enemies. Of course, he had a remarkable genius for painting. But a man can paint like Velasquez and still be as dull as possible. Basil was really rather dull. He interested me only once, and that was when he told me, years ago, that he had a wild adoration for you and that you were the dominant motive of his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” said Dorian, sadness in his voice. “But don’t people say that he was murdered?”

“Oh, some of the papers do. It does not seem at all likely to me. I know there are dreadful places in Paris, but Basil was not the sort of man who would have gone to them. He had no curiosity. That was his chief defect.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I had murdered Basil?” asked the younger man."}

{"request_id":"997cdaad0c4b67860fc2d9b3","rewritten_text":"With my heart pounding and filled with a fear I could not explain, I dismissed the servant, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were the words it contained.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and have made your innocent heart familiar with the looks and language of unlawful and monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes and try, in some measure, to make my punishment fit my guilt. You are, I doubt not, prepared for what I am about to announce: we must separate and remain divided forever.

“I deprive you of your parent and only friend. You are cast shelterless upon the world; your hopes are destroyed; the peace and security of your pure mind have been ruined. Memory will bring before you terrible images of guilt and the anguish of innocent love betrayed. Yet I am the one who has brought all this misery upon you; I am the one who casts you out and has remorselessly placed the seal of distrust and agony upon the heart and brow of my own child; I, who with devilish recklessness have tried to steal away your loveliness and replace it with the foul deformity of sin. In the overwhelming anguish of my heart, I beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and do, abhor me. But pardon me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me into exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again, never hear your voice; yet the gentle whispers of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my disordered mind and heart. I am certain I would feel it even in my grave. I dare to press this request by telling you how miserably I was drawn into this net of fiery anguish, and of all my struggles to free myself. Indeed, if your soul were less pure and radiant, I would not try to excuse myself to you. I would fear that, if I led you to regard me with less abhorrence, you might hate vice less. But in addressing you, I feel as though I were appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness; I must strive to obtain it, or despair. I therefore implore you to hear my words, and if, among the good, guilt may in any degree be lessened by fierce agony and remorse that tears the mind as madness perhaps does, you may think—though I dare not—that I have some claim to your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of weary wandering, during which, though I had endured many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had remained completely empty."}

{"request_id":"6dc9b6e1b177ea0416758d2a","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I say, “I think you could tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, _I_ don’t know. But he has to have one. All the nobility does.”

That was just his way. If he didn’t feel like explaining something to you, he wouldn’t. You could question him for a week, and it wouldn’t make any difference.

He had finished all that coat-of-arms business, so now he began the rest of that part of the work: planning a mournful inscription. Jim had to have one, he said, just like they all did. He made up several, wrote them on a piece of paper, and read them aloud:

1. _Here a captive heart broke._

2. _Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and friends, worried away his sorrowful life._

3. _Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity._

4. _Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice trembled as he read them, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he couldn’t decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall, because they were all so good. At last he said he would have Jim scratch them all on. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch so much writing onto the logs with a nail, and besides, he didn’t know how to make letters. But Tom said he would draw the letters for him, and then Jim would only have to follow the lines. Then, after a while, he said:

“Come to think of it, the logs won’t do. They don’t have log walls in a dungeon; we have to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll get a rock.”

Jim said the rock would be worse than the logs. He said it would take him such a terribly long time to carve them into a rock that he would never get out. But Tom said he would let me help him. Then he looked over to see how Jim and I were doing with the pens. It was terribly tedious, difficult, and slow work. It gave my hands no chance to heal from the sores, and we hardly seemed to be making any progress. So Tom said:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"f749d158ae65ad4410ed6d90","rewritten_text":"But in that bitter _tirade_ against Chantilly, which appeared in yesterday’s ‘_Musée_,’ the satirist, making some disgraceful allusions to the cobbler’s change of name when he took up the buskin, quoted a Latin line we had often discussed. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I had told you that this referred to Orion, formerly written Urion; and, because of certain sharp points connected with this explanation, I knew you could not have forgotten it. It was therefore clear that you would inevitably connect the two ideas of Orion and Chantilly. That you had made the connection, I saw from the expression of the smile that crossed your lips. You were thinking of the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then, you had been stooping as you walked; but now I saw you straighten to your full height. I was certain that you were reflecting on Chantilly’s small stature. At that moment I interrupted your thoughts by observing that, since he was in fact a very little man—that Chantilly—he would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

Soon afterward, we were reading an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux,” when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“_Extraordinary Murders_.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of terrible screams, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue, known to be occupied solely by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay, caused by an unsuccessful attempt to gain entry in the usual way, the gate was broken open with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors entered with two _gendarmes_. By then the cries had stopped; but as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, two or more harsh voices, angrily arguing, were heard and seemed to come from the upper part of the house. When the second landing was reached, these sounds had also ceased, and everything was completely silent. The group spread out and hurried from room to room. On reaching a large rear chamber on the fourth floor, whose door was found locked with the key inside and was forced open, they saw a scene that filled everyone present with horror and astonishment alike.

“The room was in the greatest disorder—the furniture broken and scattered everywhere. There was only one bedstead; the bed had been taken from it and thrown into the middle of the floor. On a chair lay a razor smeared with blood."}
