{"request_id":"b1a02dc5afbc481dd801df4e","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in any business like that, I said to myself.

When I came downstairs in the morning, the parlor was closed up, and the watchers were gone. Nobody was around except the family, Widow Bartley, and our group. I watched their faces to see whether anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell.

Around midday the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They placed the coffin in the middle of the room on a pair of chairs, then arranged all our chairs in rows and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were full. I saw that the coffin lid was as it had been before, but I didn’t dare look beneath it with people around.

Then people began to stream in. The women and girls took seats in the front row at the head of the coffin, and for half an hour the mourners filed past slowly, one by one, looking down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some shed a tear. Everything was very quiet and solemn, except for the women and girls holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bowed, and sobbing softly. There was no other sound but feet scraping across the floor and noses being blown—because people always blow them more at a funeral than anywhere else except church.

When the place was packed, the undertaker moved about in his black gloves with his gentle, soothing manner, making the final arrangements and getting everyone and everything properly settled, without making more noise than a cat. He never spoke. He shifted people around, squeezed in those who arrived late, and opened passageways, all with nods and hand signals. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the gentlest, smoothest, stealthiest man I had ever seen, and he had no more smile on his face than a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeon—a sickly one. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down and played it. It was shrill and wheezy, and everyone joined in singing, though Peter was the only one who sounded good, in my opinion. Then Reverend Hobson began speaking, slowly and solemnly; and at once the most outrageous racket anyone had ever heard broke out in the cellar. It was only one dog, but he made an enormous noise and kept it up without stopping. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"533aba441cbbc794bdf2ff13","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I rushed to the king and said into his ear:

“Out the door at once, sire! The woman is dying of the disease that ravaged Camelot two years ago.”

He did not move.

“Indeed, I shall remain—and help as well.”

I whispered again:

“King, you must not. You must leave.”

“You mean well, and you speak wisely enough. But it would be shameful for a king to show fear, and shameful for a knight in armor to withhold his hand where there are those in need of help. Be at peace; I will not go. You are the one who must leave. The Church’s ban is not upon me, but it forbids you to be here, and it will deal harshly with you if word reaches it of your trespass.”

It was a desperate position for him, and might cost him his life, but there was no use arguing. If he believed his knightly honor was at stake, that ended the matter; he would stay, and nothing could stop him. I knew that, and so I dropped the subject. The woman spoke:

“Good sir, out of your kindness, will you climb the ladder there and bring me news of what you find? Do not be afraid to tell me, for there are times when even a mother’s heart is beyond breaking—because it is already broken.”

“Stay,” said the king, “and give the woman something to eat. I will go.” And he set down the knapsack.

I turned to begin, but the king had already started. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in the dim light, who had not noticed us until then or spoken.

“Is he your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“Thank God for that one mercy, yes—for three hours now. Where can I fully repay my gratitude? My heart is bursting with it for the sleep he sleeps now.”

I said:

“We will be careful. We will not wake him.”

“Ah, no, you will not, for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a triumph it is to know it! No one can harm him, and no one can insult him again. He is in heaven now and happy; or, if not there, he remains in hell and is content, for in that place he will find neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together; we were man and wife for twenty-five years, and never separated until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer together. This morning he was out of his mind, and in his fancy we were boy and girl again, wandering through the happy fields. So, in that innocent, joyful conversation, he wandered farther and farther, still chatting lightly, and entered those other fields we know nothing of, where he was shut away from mortal sight."}

{"request_id":"43d3980f30a7f4b429b46c7b","rewritten_text":"“‘We have been to your residence,’ said the first, ‘and, unfortunately, did not find you there. We were told that you were probably walking in this direction, so we followed in the hope of catching up with you. Will you please enter the carriage?’

“The manner of both men was imperious, and as these words were spoken, they moved to place me between themselves and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘forgive me; but I generally ask who is doing me the honour of requesting my assistance, and what kind of case I am being summoned to attend.’

“The second speaker replied. ‘Doctor, your clients are people of standing. As for the nature of the case, our confidence in your skill assures us that you will determine it more accurately than we could describe it. Enough. Will you please enter the carriage?’

“I could do nothing but comply, and entered in silence. They followed me inside—the last man leaping in after raising the steps. The carriage turned around and continued at its previous speed.

“I repeat this conversation exactly as it occurred. I have no doubt that it is the same word for word. I describe everything precisely as it happened, forcing my mind not to stray from the task. Where I make the broken marks that follow, I stop for the time being and place my paper in its hiding place.

*****

“The carriage left the streets behind, passed through the North Barrier, and emerged onto the country road. About two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier—it was not until later, when I traveled the route, that I estimated the distance—it turned off the main avenue and soon stopped at an isolated house. All three of us got out and walked along a damp, soft path through a garden where an unattended fountain had overflowed, toward the house door. The door did not open at once when the bell was rung, and one of my two escorts struck the man who answered it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“There was nothing in this act that especially caught my attention, since I had seen ordinary people struck more often than dogs. But the other man, also angered, struck him in the same way with his arm. The brothers’ expressions and manner were then so exactly alike that I realized for the first time that they were twins.

“From the moment we got out at the outer gate—which we found locked, and which one brother opened to let us in before locking it again—I had heard cries coming from an upper room."}

{"request_id":"83dc60695c1dc31cd82027f2","rewritten_text":"He made her understand that Frank admired her greatly—thought her very beautiful and charming; and since there was so much to be said in his favor, she felt she must not judge him too harshly. As Mrs. Weston observed, “all young people would have their little whims.”

Among his new acquaintances in Surrey, one person was not so forgiving. In general, people throughout Donwell and Highbury judged him fairly; they made generous allowances for the small excesses of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well. But one person could not be softened in his criticism by bows or smiles: Mr. Knightley. The news was told to him at Hartfield. He was silent for the moment, but Emma soon heard him say to himself, while looking over a newspaper, “Hum! just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She was half inclined to resent this, but after watching him for a moment, she saw that he had said it only to ease his own feelings, not to provoke her; so she let it pass.

Although Mr. and Mrs. Weston had brought bad news in one respect, their visit that morning was especially well timed in another. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma want their advice; and, even more fortunately, she wanted exactly the advice they gave.

This was what happened: The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years and were very good people—friendly, generous, and unassuming. On the other hand, they came from a low social background, were in trade, and were only moderately genteel. When they first moved to the country, they lived quietly within their income, kept little company, and spent little on it. But during the last year or two, their means had greatly increased: the business in town had become more profitable, and fortune had generally favored them. As their wealth grew, so did their ambitions—their need for a larger house and their desire for more company. They enlarged their house, increased their staff, and raised all their expenses; by now, in wealth and style of living, they were second only to the family at Hartfield. Their love of society and their new dining-room made everyone expect them to give dinner parties, and a few gatherings, mostly for single men, had already taken place. Emma could hardly imagine that they would dare invite the regular and most important families—not Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. Nothing would persuade her to attend if they did, and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal seem less significant than she wished."}

{"request_id":"2edb551af85efedfdbd97081","rewritten_text":"On that subject, therefore, I shall remain entirely silent; and you may be sure that no ungenerous reproach will ever pass my lips once we are married.”

It was absolutely necessary to interrupt him now.

“You are too hasty, sir,” she cried. “You forget that I have given no answer. Let me do so without further delay. Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me. I am very sensible of the honour of your proposal, but it is impossible for me to do anything other than decline it.”

“I am not now learning,” replied Mr. Collins, with a formal wave of his hand, “that it is customary for young ladies to reject the advances of the man they secretly intend to accept when he first seeks their favour; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second or even a third time. I am therefore not at all discouraged by what you have just said, and shall hope to lead you to the altar before long.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “your hope is a rather extraordinary one after my declaration. I assure you that I am not one of those young ladies—if such young ladies exist—who are so daring as to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am perfectly serious in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who could make you so. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am persuaded she would find me entirely unqualified for the position.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins, very gravely, “but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you in the least. And you may be certain that, when I have the honour of seeing her again, I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty, economy, and other amiable qualities.”

“Indeed, Mr. Collins, all praise of me will be unnecessary. You must allow me to judge for myself, and do me the courtesy of believing what I say. I wish you to be very happy and very rich, and by refusing your hand, I do everything in my power to prevent your being otherwise. In making me this offer, you must have satisfied the delicacy of your feelings toward my family, and may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it falls to you without any self-reproach. This matter may therefore be regarded as finally settled.” Rising as she spoke, she would have left the room, had not Mr. Collins addressed her again:

“When I have the honour of speaking to you next on this subject, I shall hope to receive a more favourable answer than the one you have now given me; though I am far from accusing you of cruelty at present, because I know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man upon his first application, and perhaps you have even now said as much to encourage my suit as would be consistent with the true delicacy of the female character.”"}

{"request_id":"8a2ac913035fca4391acbf50","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that always brings misery must have been broken, and the evil fate ruling it would not allow such a breach of her eternal laws. But why should I complain? Misery was my element, and nothing but misery could come near me; if Woodville had been happy, I would never have known him. And can I, who for so many years was fed by tears and nourished by the dew of grief, hesitate to tell a story of sorrow and death?

Woodville had to travel into the country and was kept away, day after day, from his lovely bride. He received a letter saying that she was slightly ill, but urging him to hurry to her, because she would find health in his eyes and his company would be her surest medicine. He was delayed for three more days, and then hurried to her. His heart, though he did not know why, warned him of misfortune. He had heard nothing more from her; he feared she had grown worse. This fear made him impatient and restless to see her once again standing before him in health and beauty, while a sinister voice seemed always to whisper, “You will never see her as she was again.”

When he reached her home, everything was silent. He passed through several rooms and saw a servant weeping bitterly in one of them. Faint with fear, he could barely ask, “Is she dead?” He could only listen to the terrible answer: “Not yet.” These shocking words seemed less frightening than the answer he had expected. Learning that she still lived, and that he might still hope, brought him some relief. He remembered her letter and gave himself to the wild belief that his kisses, warm with love and life, would restore her strength; that with him beside her, she could not die; that his presence was the charm protecting her life.

He hurried to her sickroom. She lay there with fever burning in her cheeks, her eyes closed and apparently without sense. He gathered her into his arms and covered her burning lips with desperate kisses. In a voice of quiet anguish, he called her by the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am with you—your life, your love. Return, dearest one. You promised me this gift, that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die while I am near. What is death? To see you no more? To lose one who is part of myself, without whom I have no memory and no future?”"}

{"request_id":"83d02d69efaeaa5ea55af203","rewritten_text":"Great God! Had I for a single moment imagined the hellish purpose of my fiendish enemy, I would sooner have exiled myself forever from my native land and roamed the earth as a friendless outcast than agreed to this wretched marriage. But, as though endowed with magical powers, the monster had concealed his true intentions from me; and while I believed I had prepared only for my own death, I hastened that of a victim far dearer to me.

As the appointed time of our marriage approached, whether through cowardice or some prophetic instinct, my heart seemed to sink within me. Yet I hid my feelings beneath an appearance of cheerfulness that brought smiles and happiness to my father’s face, though it scarcely deceived Elizabeth’s ever-watchful and discerning eye. She anticipated our union with calm satisfaction, mingled with a slight fear, impressed upon her by former misfortunes: that the happiness now seeming so certain and real might soon vanish like an airy dream, leaving behind only profound and lasting regret.

Preparations for the event were completed, congratulatory visitors arrived, and everything wore a cheerful aspect. As best I could, I confined to my own heart the anxiety consuming me, and entered with apparent sincerity into my father’s arrangements, though they might serve only as ornaments for my tragedy. Through my father’s efforts, the Austrian government had restored part of Elizabeth’s inheritance to her. She possessed a small estate on the shores of Como. It was decided that, immediately after our marriage, we would travel to Villa Lavenza and spend the first days of our happiness beside the beautiful lake on which it stood.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to protect myself should the fiend openly attack me. I constantly carried pistols and a dagger, and remained continually alert against deception; by these measures I obtained a greater measure of peace. Indeed, as the time drew near, the threat seemed increasingly like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing my tranquillity, while the happiness I expected from marriage appeared more certain as the appointed day of its solemnisation approached and I heard it repeatedly spoken of as an event no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth appeared happy, and my composed manner did much to soothe her. But on the day destined to fulfil both my wishes and my fate, she was melancholy, and a foreboding of evil possessed her; perhaps, too, she was thinking of the terrible secret I had promised to disclose to her the next day."}

{"request_id":"4148f4a118e2748cd002f9db","rewritten_text":"“I now examined the death’s-head carefully. Its outer edges—the parts of the drawing closest to the edge of the vellum—were much clearer than the rest. It was obvious that the heat had acted unevenly or not strongly enough. I immediately lit a fire and held every part of the parchment over the glowing heat. At first, the only result was that the faint lines of the skull grew darker. But when I continued the experiment, a figure appeared at the corner of the slip, diagonally opposite the death’s-head. At first I thought it was a goat. Looking more closely, however, I saw that it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! Ha!” I said. “Of course, I have no right to laugh at you—a million and a half dollars is too serious a matter for jokes—but you are not going to add a third link to your chain. You will not find any special connection between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, as you know, have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming world.”

“But I have just said that the figure was not a goat.”

“Well, a kid, then—much the same thing.”

“Much the same, but not entirely,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately took the animal’s figure as a kind of punning, hieroglyphic signature. I call it a signature because its position on the vellum suggested that idea. The death’s-head at the diagonally opposite corner likewise looked like a stamp or seal. But I was deeply troubled by the absence of everything else—the body of the instrument I had imagined, and the text that would give meaning to its context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I felt irresistibly that some great good fortune was about to come to me. I can hardly say why. Perhaps it was more a wish than a real belief. But do you know that Jupiter’s foolish words about the bug being made of solid gold had a remarkable effect on my imagination? Then there was the whole series of accidents and coincidences, which was truly extraordinary. Do you see how accidental it was that these events happened on the only day of the year when it was, or might be, cool enough for a fire? Without the fire—or without the dog appearing at exactly the moment he did—I would never have noticed the death’s-head, and therefore would never have possessed the treasure?”"}

{"request_id":"96f1b5fd7204732456f09c46","rewritten_text":"Nothing Emma later discovered made her take back her poor opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her first judgment had been quite accurate. Mrs. Elton was exactly as she had seemed at their second meeting whenever they met again: self-important, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and badly mannered. She had a little beauty and some accomplishments, but so little good sense that she believed she had come with superior knowledge of the world to brighten and improve a country neighborhood. She imagined that Miss Hawkins had occupied such a position in society that only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could exceed it.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton viewed his wife any differently. He seemed not only happy with her but proud of her. He appeared to congratulate himself on bringing such a woman to Highbury, one whom even Miss Woodhouse could not equal. Most of her new acquaintances, eager to praise her or unused to judging others, followed Miss Bates’s friendly example or simply assumed that the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she claimed. They were therefore quite satisfied. Mrs. Elton’s praises passed from one person to another, as they naturally would, without being stopped by Miss Woodhouse, who willingly continued her first contribution and spoke graciously of Mrs. Elton as “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one way, Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had seemed at first. Her feelings toward Emma changed. Probably offended by the little encouragement Emma gave her attempts at friendship, she withdrew in return and gradually became much colder and more distant. Although this change was pleasant for Emma, the ill will behind it naturally increased her dislike. Mrs. Elton’s behavior toward Harriet was unpleasant too, as was Mr. Elton’s. They were mocking and careless. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet of her attachment, but the feelings that could inspire such behavior lowered them both greatly. It was clear that poor Harriet’s attachment had been revealed in the openness of married life, and that her part in the story had probably been told in the least favorable way for her and the most comforting for him. Harriet was, of course, the object of their shared dislike. Whenever they had nothing else to discuss, it would always be easy to start criticizing Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they dared not show through open disrespect toward Emma found a wider outlet in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton took a strong liking to Jane Fairfax, and did so from the very beginning. It was not merely because, while she was at war with one young woman, another might seem especially appealing; she had liked Jane from their first meeting. Nor was she content simply to express a natural and reasonable admiration. Without being asked, invited, or given any special right, she insisted on offering Jane her help and friendship. Before Emma had lost her confidence, and around their third meeting, she heard all about Mrs. Elton’s heroic plans on Jane’s behalf."}

{"request_id":"eb0f780a5141b7424006dad0","rewritten_text":"“And think of this, ma’am,” said Oliver, as tears filled his eyes despite his efforts to hold them back. “Oh! Think how young and good she is, and how much pleasure and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I am sure—certain—quite certain—that, for your sake, since you are so good yourself; for her own sake; and for the sake of everyone she makes happy, she will not die. Heaven would never let her die so young.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, placing her hand on Oliver’s head. “You think like a child, poor boy. But you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, though I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old and have seen enough illness and death to know the pain of losing those we love. I have also seen enough to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them. But this should comfort us in our sorrow, for Heaven is just. Such things teach us clearly that there is a brighter world than this one, and that the journey to it may be short. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how deeply!”

Oliver was surprised to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke, she stopped her grieving as if by a single effort. Straightening herself, she became calm and firm. He was even more astonished to find that this strength lasted, and that throughout all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie was always ready and composed. She carried out every duty that had fallen to her steadily and, to all appearances, even cheerfully. But Oliver was young and did not know what strong minds can endure in difficult times. How could he, when those who possess such strength so rarely understand it themselves?

An anxious night followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie’s fears had proved only too accurate. Rose was in the first stage of a severe and dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not give in to useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, placing a finger to her lips as she looked steadily into his face. “This letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne as quickly as possible. It must be taken to the market town, which is no more than four miles away by the footpath across the fields, and then sent by a rider straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will arrange this, and I know I can trust you to make sure it is done.”

Oliver could not answer, but his anxious expression showed that he was ready to leave at once."}

{"request_id":"6060ff5b5bcdf8f8d641d98f","rewritten_text":"You must learn some of my philosophy. Think of the past only when remembering it gives you pleasure.”

“I cannot credit you with that kind of philosophy. Your memories must be entirely free of blame, so the peace they bring comes not from philosophy but, much better, from ignorance. But that is not true for me. Painful memories return, and they cannot, and should not, be pushed away. I have been selfish all my life in practice, though not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was right, but not how to control my temper. I was given good principles, but left to follow them with pride and conceit. Sadly, as an only son—and for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents. Though they were good people, my father especially being kind and generous, they allowed, encouraged, and almost taught me to be selfish and overbearing; to care about no one outside my family; to think poorly of everyone else; and at least to wish to believe that their judgment and worth were less than my own. That was how I was from eight to twenty-eight, and I might still be that way if not for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! How much I owe you! You taught me a lesson that was difficult at first, but greatly benefited me. You humbled me as I needed to be humbled. I came to you certain that you would welcome me. You showed me how inadequate all my claims were to please a woman worthy of being pleased.”

“Had you really convinced yourself that I would?”

“Indeed I had. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you wanted and expected me to propose.”

“My manner must have been at fault, though I assure you it was not intentional. I never meant to deceive you, but my feelings may often have led me astray. How you must have hated me after that evening!”

“Hated you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon found its proper direction.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, indeed. I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise could not have been greater than mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special politeness, and I admit I did not expect to receive more than I was owed.”

“My purpose then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, through every courtesy I could offer, that I was not so petty as to resent the past. I hoped to gain your forgiveness and reduce your poor opinion of me by showing you that I had taken your criticisms to heart.”"}

{"request_id":"3169746532903f71f411e65b","rewritten_text":"And if he asked me why I wanted it, and why I believed I had any right to it, I would tell him—though he cared little for such humble dreams—that I had loved Estella deeply and for a long time, and that although I had lost her and must live a life of bereavement, anything connected with her was still nearer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing that Mr. Jaggers remained completely still and silent, apparently unmoved by my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you are a man with a gentle heart. I have seen your pleasant home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways in which you renew yourself after your business life. I beg you to say a word for me to Mr. Jaggers, and to point out to him that, considering everything, he ought to be more open with me!”

I have never seen two men look at each other more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this appeal. At first, I feared that Wemmick would be dismissed from his employment at once; but that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers soften into something like a smile, and Wemmick grow more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father, and you, with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the most cunning impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” Wemmick replied, growing bolder still. “I think you’re another.”

Again they exchanged the same strange looks, each apparently still uncertain whether the other was making fun of him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it be so. Now, looking at you, sir, I shouldn’t be surprised if you were planning and arranging to have a pleasant home of your own one of these days, when you’ve grown tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t speak of ‘poor dreams’; you know more about such matters than I do, having much fresher experience of them. But now, about this other matter. I’ll put a case to you. Mind! I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say that I fully understood he had expressly stated that he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “suppose this case. Suppose a woman, in circumstances such as you have described, kept her child concealed and was forced to tell the fact to her legal adviser, because he had represented to her that, considering the scope of his defense, he needed to know the truth about that child."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5e7fa874feaa4eada007e40a","rewritten_text":"“They must matter to you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You don’t want people speaking of you as vile and degraded. Of course, you have your position, your wealth, and all the rest. But position and wealth are not everything. Mind you, I don’t believe these rumours at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin writes itself on a man’s face. It cannot be hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices. There are no such things. If a miserable man has a vice, it appears in the lines of his mouth, the droop of his eyelids, even in the shape of his hands. Someone—I won’t name him, but you know whom I mean—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never seen him before and knew nothing about him then, though I have heard plenty since. He offered me an enormous price. I refused him. There was something about the shape of his fingers that I disliked. I now know that my instinct about him was completely right. His life is terrible. But you, Dorian, with your pure, bright, innocent face and your wonderfully peaceful youth—I cannot believe anything against you. And yet I see you so rarely, you never come to the studio now, and when I am away from you and hear all the horrible things people whisper about you, I don’t know what to say. Why is it, Dorian, that a man like the Duke of Berwick leaves a club room when you enter? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse either to visit your house or invite you to theirs? You used to be friends with Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up while we were discussing the miniatures you lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that you might have the most artistic tastes, but you were a man no pure-minded girl should be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was your friend and asked what he meant. He told me. He said it openly, in front of everyone. It was horrible! Why is your friendship so destructive to young men? There was that poor boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were his closest friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with his reputation ruined.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"7a1825d0a6c85022d15ec6e0","rewritten_text":"“The shock and surprise caused in my mind by this extraordinary change in my situation were perhaps, after all, the part of the adventure hardest to explain. For the change itself was not only natural and unavoidable, but had long been expected whenever I reached that exact point in my journey where the moon’s attraction replaced the planet’s—or, more precisely, where the balloon was pulled toward the earth less strongly than toward the moon. Certainly, I woke from a deep sleep with all my senses confused and found myself facing a very startling sight, one that I had expected but not at that particular moment. The change in direction must, of course, have happened smoothly and gradually. It is not at all certain that, even if I had been awake when it occurred, I would have noticed any physical sign of the reversal—any discomfort or disturbance in my body or in my equipment.\n\n“It is hardly necessary to say that, once I fully understood my situation and recovered from the terror that had overwhelmed every faculty of my mind, my attention first turned entirely to the moon’s general physical appearance. It lay below me like a map. Although I believed it was still at a considerable distance, the markings on its surface appeared with astonishing and completely inexplicable clarity. At first glance, the complete absence of oceans or seas—and indeed of any lake, river, or body of water—seemed the most remarkable feature of its geology. Yet, strangely, I saw vast, level regions that were clearly alluvial, while most of the visible hemisphere was covered with countless volcanic mountains. They were cone-shaped and looked more like artificial than natural formations. The tallest rose no more than three and three-quarter miles straight upward; but a map of the volcanic regions of the Campi Phlegraei would give Your Excellencies a better idea of their general appearance than any inadequate description I could offer. Most of them were plainly erupting, and their repeated thunder showed me, with terrifying force, their violence and power. The wrongly named meteoric stones now shot upward past the balloon with ever more frightening frequency.”"}

{"request_id":"4e56aea14a36683fcc5a035d","rewritten_text":"She would be placed among people who loved her and had better judgment than she did; secluded enough to be safe, yet occupied enough to remain cheerful. She would never be led into temptation, nor left for temptation to discover her. She would be respectable and happy; and Emma admitted that she was the luckiest creature in the world, having inspired such a steady and enduring affection in such a man—or, if not quite the luckiest, second only to herself.

Harriet, necessarily drawn away by her commitments to the Martins, was seen less and less at Hartfield, which was no cause for regret. The intimacy between her and Emma had to diminish; their friendship had to become a calmer kind of goodwill. Fortunately, what ought to happen, and what must happen, already seemed to be beginning, in the most gradual and natural way.

Before the end of September, Emma accompanied Harriet to church and watched her give her hand to Robert Martin with such complete satisfaction that no memories, even those connected with Mr. Elton as he stood before them, could diminish it. Perhaps, indeed, at that moment she scarcely saw Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might soon be bestowed on herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Churchills were also in town, and they were only waiting for November.

The month between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley had fixed upon, as far as they dared. They had decided that their marriage should take place while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so that the couple could spend the planned fortnight away on a seaside tour. John and Isabella, along with every other friend, approved the arrangement. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could Mr. Woodhouse be persuaded to consent? He had never yet referred to their marriage except as something far in the future.

When the subject was first raised with him, he was so miserable that they nearly lost hope. A second mention caused less distress. He began to think that it would happen and that he could not prevent it—a very encouraging movement of the mind toward resignation. Still, he was not happy. Indeed, he seemed so far from it that his daughter’s courage failed. She could not bear to see him suffer or to know that he imagined himself neglected; and although her reason almost accepted the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys that, once the event was over, his distress would soon end as well, she hesitated—she could not go on."}

{"request_id":"71b5b6216bf896bded940d0b","rewritten_text":"But he had oppressed no one, imprisoned no one; so far from harshly demanding payment of his dues, he had voluntarily surrendered them, cast himself upon a world offering him no favour, secured his own private position there, and earned his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had administered the impoverished, encumbered estate under written instructions: to spare the people, to provide whatever little could be provided—fuel in winter, insofar as the heavy creditors allowed it, and produce in summer, insofar as it could be rescued from that same grasp—and doubtless he had set out these facts in his plea and evidence, for his own protection, so that they must now come to light.

This strengthened the desperate determination Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the mariner of the old tale, the winds and currents had carried him within the Loadstone Rock’s influence; it was drawing him toward itself, and he must go. Every thought that rose before him swept him onward, faster and faster, with increasing certainty, toward that terrible attraction. His hidden uneasiness had been that evil purposes were being carried out in his unhappy country by evil instruments, while he, who could not help knowing himself better than they, was absent instead of attempting to check the bloodshed and uphold the claims of mercy and humanity. With this uneasiness partly smothered and partly reproaching him, he had been led to compare himself pointedly with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so powerful; and immediately after that comparison, so damaging to himself, came Monseigneur’s sneers, which had wounded him deeply, followed by Stryver’s, coarser and more galling than all, for reasons long remembered. Then came Gabelle’s letter: an innocent prisoner’s appeal, in peril of death, to his justice, honour, and good name.

His decision was made. He must go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he must sail onward until he struck it. He knew of no rock and scarcely perceived any danger. The purpose behind his actions, though he had left them unfinished, showed them to him in a light that France would gratefully recognize when he appeared to uphold it. Then there rose before him that splendid vision of doing good, so often the hopeful mirage of generous minds; and in the illusion he even pictured himself possessing some influence with which to guide the raging Revolution that was running so terribly wild."}

{"request_id":"bb1e7773523953171764b8e7","rewritten_text":"“Then listen! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill at Rome, my mother, his wife, joined him there. They had long been separated; she travelled from Paris and took me with her—to attend to his property, for all I know, since she had little affection for him, and he none for her. He knew nothing of us, his senses having failed him, and slept on until the following day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two, dated on the night his illness began and addressed to you”; he turned to Mr. Brownlow; “with a few brief lines enclosed, and a notice on the packet that it was not to be delivered until after his death. One of the papers was a letter to this girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What did the letter say?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter?—It was a sheet covered with writing, crossed and recrossed, containing a remorseful confession and prayers that God might aid her. He had told the girl some story that a hidden mystery—to be revealed one day—kept him from marrying her at that time; and she had continued to trust him patiently, until she trusted too much and lost what no one could ever restore. She was then only a few months from her confinement. He explained all he had intended to do, had he lived, to conceal her shame, and begged that, if he died, she would neither curse his memory nor believe that the results of their sin would fall upon her or their young child; all the guilt, he said, was his. He recalled the day he had given her the little locket and the ring bearing her Christian name, with a blank space left for the name he hoped someday to give her—begged her still to keep them and wear them next to her heart, as she had done before—and then continued wildly, repeating the same words again and again, as though he had lost his reason. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, while Oliver’s tears streamed down.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He spoke of the misery his wife had caused him; of your rebellious nature, vice, spite, and early evil passions, you being his only son and raised to hate him; and left you and your mother an annuity of eight hundred pounds each. The greater part of his property he divided equally—one share for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it were born alive and ever reached adulthood.”"}

{"request_id":"39d505a808b2db5fbb0930fc","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s happened to that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady lowered her spectacles and looked over them around the room; then she raised them and looked beneath them. She almost never looked _through_ them for something as small as a boy. They were her formal pair, the pride of her heart, made for “style,” not usefulness—she could have seen just as well through two stove lids. She looked puzzled for a moment, then said, not angrily, but loudly enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I swear, if I catch you I’ll—”

She did not finish, because she was now bending down and poking under the bed with the broom, needing breath to mark each jab. She found nothing except the cat.

“I never saw the equal of that boy!”

She went to the open door and stood there, looking among the tomato vines and “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at an angle meant to carry and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind her. She turned just in time to grab a small boy by the loose back of his jacket and stop him from escaping.

“There! I should have thought of that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What _is_ that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve told you that if you didn’t leave that jam alone, I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch rose into the air—the danger was serious—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady spun around and pulled her skirts out of danger. At once the boy ran, scrambled over the tall board fence, and vanished on the other side.

His Aunt Polly stood stunned for a moment, then began to laugh softly.

“Damn that boy, can’t I ever learn? Hasn’t he played tricks like that on me often enough for me to watch out by now? But old fools are the biggest fools there are. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, as they say. But goodness, he never plays the same trick two days in a row, so how is anyone supposed to know what he’ll do? He seems to know exactly how long he can torment me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me for a minute or make me laugh, my anger disappears and I can’t hit him even once.”"}

{"request_id":"b5449c233f87b8051f4aeab5","rewritten_text":"I don’t want to get mixed up in any business like that, I told myself.

When I came downstairs in the morning, the parlor was closed, and the watchers were gone. No one was there except the family, Widow Bartley, and our group. I studied their faces to see whether anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell.

Around midday, the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They placed the coffin in the middle of the room on two chairs, then arranged all our chairs in rows and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were full. I saw that the coffin lid was as it had been before, but I didn’t dare look beneath it with so many people around.

Then people began to arrive. The women and girls took seats in the front row at the head of the coffin, and for half an hour the visitors filed past slowly, one at a time, looking down at the dead man’s face for a minute. Some shed a tear. Everything was quiet and solemn, except for the women and girls holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, keeping their heads bowed, and sobbing softly. The only other sounds were feet scraping across the floor and people blowing their noses—because people always blow their noses more at a funeral than anywhere else except church.

When the room was packed, the undertaker moved about in his black gloves with gentle, soothing manners, making final adjustments and arranging people and things neatly and comfortably without making more noise than a cat. He never spoke. He shifted people around, squeezed in late arrivals, and opened paths through the crowd with nods and hand signals. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the gentlest, smoothest, quietest man I had ever seen, and he had no more smile on his face than a ham does.

They had borrowed a melodeon—a sick-sounding one. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down and played it. It sounded shrill and wheezy, but everyone joined in singing, and Peter was the only one who sounded good, as far as I could tell. Then Reverend Hobson began speaking slowly and solemnly. At once, the most outrageous noise anyone had ever heard broke out in the cellar. It was only one dog, but he made an enormous racket and kept it up. The preacher had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"d9b8d26e62f900f92e3f8fdb","rewritten_text":"At least, that was what he thought. But who could know? ... No. There had been nothing more. He had spared her out of vanity. He had pretended to be good out of hypocrisy. Out of curiosity, he had tried denying himself. He understood that now.

But would this murder haunt him all his life? Would he always be weighed down by his past? Was he truly going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him. The picture itself—that was the evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it for so long? Once, he had enjoyed watching it change and grow old. Recently, he had felt no pleasure in it. It had kept him awake at night. Whenever he was away, he had been terrified that other eyes might see it. It had cast sadness over his passions. Even the memory of it had spoiled many moments of happiness. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

He looked around and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it many times until not a stain remained. It was bright and gleaming. Just as it had killed the painter, it would kill the painter’s work and everything that work represented. It would kill the past, and once the past was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous life of the soul, and without its terrible warnings, he would be at peace. He grabbed the knife and drove it into the picture.

A cry rang out, followed by a crash. The cry was so horribly full of pain that the frightened servants woke and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing through the square below stopped and looked up at the large house. They continued on until they met a policeman, then brought him back. The policeman rang the bell several times, but no one answered. Except for a light in one of the upper windows, the house was completely dark. After a while, he left and stood beneath a nearby portico, watching.

“Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” the policeman replied.

As they walked away, the two men looked at each other and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed servants spoke to one another in low whispers. Old Mrs. Leaf was crying and wringing her hands. Francis was as pale as death.

After about fifteen minutes, he took the coachman and one of the footmen and crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"c5a6fbca1867536461636565","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know who I am unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he told the truth, mostly. There were things he exaggerated, but mostly he told the truth. That’s nothing. I’ve never known anybody who didn’t lie now and then, except Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all mentioned in that book, which is mostly true, with some exaggerations, as I said before.

Now, this is how the book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers had hidden in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars apiece—all in gold. It was an enormous amount of money when it was piled up. Well, Judge Thatcher took it and invested it, and it earned us a dollar a day apiece all year round—more than anyone could know what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me; but living in the house all the time was hard, considering how strictly regular and proper the widow was in everything she did. So when I couldn’t stand it any longer, I ran away. I put on my old rags and went back to my sugar hogshead, and I was free and content. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was going to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I went back to the widow and behaved respectably. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, along with a lot of other names, but she never meant any harm by it. She put me into those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and feel cramped. Then the old routine began again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to come immediately. When you reached the table, you couldn’t start eating at once; you had to wait for the widow to lower her head and grumble a little over the food, though there was really nothing wrong with it—except that everything had been cooked separately. In a barrel of odds and ends, it’s different: things get mixed together, the juices trade places, and everything tastes better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushes, and I was eager to learn all about him. But after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead for a very long time. So then I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t have any interest in dead people."}

{"request_id":"ab62bfb67a6f1635ba7ef4fd","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, will you? Oh, you precious little fool!”

“It’s naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll end up being hanged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. As he spoke, Master Bates seized one end of his neckerchief and held it upright in the air. Then he dropped his head onto his shoulder and jerked a strange sound through his teeth, vividly acting out that being scragged and being hanged meant the same thing.

“That’s what it means,” said Charley. “Look how he stares, Jack! I’ve never seen such splendid company as that boy; he’ll be the death of me, I know he will.” Master Charley Bates, having laughed heartily once more, took up his pipe again, tears in his eyes.

“You’ve been badly brought up,” said the Dodger, examining his boots with great satisfaction after Oliver had polished them. “Fagin will make something of you, though, or you’ll be the first boy he’s ever had who proved unprofitable. You’d better start at once; you’ll come into the trade long before you expect it, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates supported this advice with several moral warnings of his own. When these were exhausted, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into an enthusiastic account of the many pleasures belonging to the life they led, mixed with various hints that the best thing Oliver could do was to win Fagin’s favor without delay, by the methods they themselves had used to earn it.

“And always remember this, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as they heard the Jew unlocking the door above, “if you don’t take handkerchiefs and watches—”

“What’s the use of talking like that?” interrupted Master Bates. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket handkerchiefs and watches,” said the Dodger, lowering his language to Oliver’s level, “someone else will. Then the people who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too, while nobody will be even half a farthing better off except the fellows who get them—and you’ve just as much right to them as they do.”

“Of course, of course!” said the Jew, who had entered without Oliver noticing. “It all comes down to that, my dear; take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the principles of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together gleefully as he confirmed the Dodger’s reasoning in these words, and chuckled with delight at his pupil’s skill.

The conversation went no further at that time, because the Jew had returned home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen before. The Dodger addressed him as Tom Chitling; after lingering on the stairs to exchange a few flirtatious remarks with the lady, he now appeared."}

{"request_id":"2627246356b994f19b4d273c","rewritten_text":"He made her understand that Frank admired her greatly—thought her very beautiful and charming; and with so much to recommend him overall, she felt she could not judge him harshly. As Mrs. Weston observed, “all young people would have their little whims.”

There was one person among his new acquaintances in Surrey who was not so lenient. In general, he was judged throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury with great fairness; generous allowances were made for the minor excesses of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well. But there was one spirit among them that bows or smiles could not soften in its power of criticism—Mr. Knightley. The news was told to him at Hartfield; for the moment, he was silent. But Emma heard him almost immediately afterward say to himself, over the newspaper in his hand, “Hum! Just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She was half inclined to resent it; but a moment’s observation convinced her that he had said it only to ease his own feelings, not to provoke her, and so she let it pass.

Although Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit that morning had made them, in one respect, bearers of unwelcome news, in another it was particularly timely. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma want their advice; and, even more fortunately, she wanted exactly the advice they gave.

This was what happened: The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years and were very good sort of people—friendly, generous, and unassuming; but, on the other hand, they were of humble origin, in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they had first come to the country, they had lived according to their income, quietly, keeping little company, and spending little on it. But the last year or two had brought them a considerable increase in means—their house in town had produced greater profits, and fortune in general had smiled upon them. As their wealth grew, so did their ambitions: they wanted a larger house and more company. They enlarged their house, increased their number of servants, and raised their expenses in every way; and by this time they were, in fortune and style of living, second only to the family at Hartfield. Their love of society and their new dining room prepared everyone for their giving dinner parties, and a few gatherings, chiefly among the single men, had already taken place. Emma could hardly imagine that they would presume to invite the established and best families—not Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. Nothing would tempt her to go if they did, and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal seem less meaningful than she wished."}

{"request_id":"5046e7a8d62815e3cc3d7647","rewritten_text":"“What’s the trouble?”

I said:

“Pap, and Mam, and Sis, and—”

Then I broke down. He said:

“Oh, dang it, don’t take on so; we all have our troubles, and this one will turn out all right. What’s the matter with them?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman of the boat?”

“Yes,” he said, looking quite pleased with himself. “I’m the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and head deckhand; and sometimes I’m the freight and passengers too. I’m not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be as generous and good to Tom, Dick, and Harry as he is, throwing money around the way he does; but I’ve told him many a time that I wouldn’t trade places with him. A sailor’s life is the life for me, I say, and I’m darned if I’d live two miles out of town, where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and as much more besides. I say—”

I interrupted him and said:

“They’re in terrible trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, Pap and Mam and Sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferryboat and go up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there’s only one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good land! What are they doing there, for goodness’ sake?”

“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”

“I bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, they have no chance if they don’t get off mighty quick! How in the world did they ever get into such a mess?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting up at the town—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing—go on.”

“She was visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and just as evening began, she started across in the horse ferry with her Black woman to spend the night at her friend’s house, Miss What-you-may-call-her—I’ve forgotten her name. They lost their steering oar, swung around, and floated downstream, stern first, for about two miles. Then they struck the wreck, and the ferryman, the Black woman, and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker grabbed hold and got aboard the wreck. About an hour after dark, we came downstream in our trading scow. It was so dark that we didn’t see the wreck until we were right on it, and then we struck it too. But all of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best creature! I almost wish it had been me, I really do.”

“My goodness! It’s the strangest thing I ever heard.”"}

However, she will not find her grandmother any deafer than she was two years ago; which is saying a great deal at my mother’s age—and it really has been a full two years, you know, since she was here. We have never gone so long without seeing her before, and as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we shall hardly know how to get enough of her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed!—that must be a very great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised; and everyone says the same obliging things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they can be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell will need the carriage himself on one of those days. It is so very good of them to send her all this way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, next Friday or Saturday. That is what she writes about. That is why she is writing earlier than usual, as we call it; for ordinarily we should not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, so I imagined. I was afraid there could be little chance of my hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“So obliging of you! No, we should not have heard if it had not been for this particular circumstance, her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted!—for she is to stay with us at least three months. Three months, she says so positively, as I am about to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is this, you see: the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her father and mother to come over and see her at once. They had not intended to go until summer, but she is so eager to see them again—for until she married last October, she had never been away from them for even a week, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms, I was going to say, but in any case different countries—and so she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I declare I do not know which, but we shall see presently in Jane’s letter—writing in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, urging them to come over immediately. They would meet them in Dublin and take them back to their country estate, Baly-craig, a beautiful place, I imagine."}

{"request_id":"3e63acc848c16f82160f35d9","rewritten_text":"I want to see you permanently well connected, and for that reason it would be best for you to have as few unsuitable acquaintances as possible. So, if you are still in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with the sisters will not lead you to become acquainted with his wife, who will probably be some uneducated farmer’s daughter.”

“To be sure. Yes. Not that I think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who had not received some education and been very well brought up. Still, I do not mean to oppose my opinion to yours—and I am sure I shall not seek his wife’s acquaintance. I shall always feel great affection for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and would be very sorry to give them up, since they are quite as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then certainly I had better not visit her, if I can avoid it.”

Emma watched her as she spoke, noting every change in her manner, and saw no troubling signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted that he had no other hold over her and that Harriet would offer no serious resistance to any friendly plan of her own.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day while walking along the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after looking at Emma with great respect, he turned to her companion with obvious pleasure. Emma was glad to have the chance to examine him. She walked a few yards ahead while they talked, and soon her sharp eyes had formed a clear opinion of Mr. Robert Martin. He was very neat and looked like a sensible young man, but he had no other advantage in appearance. When compared with gentlemen, Emma thought he would lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s feelings. Harriet was not indifferent to good manners; she had noticed her father’s gentleness herself, admiring it as much as she wondered at it. Mr. Martin looked as if he had no idea what good manners were.

They stayed together only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting. Harriet then ran back to her with a smiling face and such excitement that Miss Woodhouse hoped to calm her very soon.

“Just think of our happening to meet him! How very strange! He said it was pure chance that he had not gone around by Randalls. He did not think we ever walked along this road. He thought we went toward Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"7016d748e5c86406ebb502d8","rewritten_text":"“No raising him by hand, then. Not at all!”

Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to accept.

“He caused you endless trouble, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble sympathetically to my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” Then she launched into a dreadful catalogue of every illness I had suffered, every sleepless night I had caused, every high place I had fallen from, every low place I had fallen into, every injury I had inflicted on myself, and every time she had wished me in my grave, while I had stubbornly refused to go there.

I think the Romans must have irritated one another greatly with their noses. Perhaps that was why they became such a restless people. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose annoyed me so much during the account of my misdeeds that I would have liked to pull it until he howled. But everything I had endured so far was nothing compared with the terrible feelings that seized me when the silence following my sister’s recital was broken. During that silence, everyone had looked at me—with indignation and disgust, as I painfully knew.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently guiding the company back to the subject from which they had wandered, “pork—considered as boiled—is rich too, isn’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister.

Heaven help me, the moment had finally come! He would discover that it was weak, say that it was weak, and I would be ruined! I gripped the table leg beneath the cloth with both hands and waited for my fate.

My sister went for the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured out his brandy; no one else took any. The miserable man toyed with his glass—lifting it, holding it up to the light, then setting it down—and prolonged my suffering. All the while, Mrs. Joe and Joe were busily clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I could not take my eyes off him. Still clinging to the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the wretched man playfully touch his glass, pick it up, smile, tilt back his head, and drink the brandy. Immediately afterward, the company was overcome with indescribable alarm when he sprang to his feet, spun around several times in a terrifying, spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and rushed out the door. Through the window he could then be seen plunging violently and spitting, making the most hideous faces, and apparently out of his mind.

I held on tightly while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him."}

{"request_id":"67fba371508931164dc0acbc","rewritten_text":"“So, now, tell me all about it.”

“Well, you see, it happened this way. The old mistress—that’s Miss Watson—keeps picking on me and treats me pretty harshly, but she always said she wouldn’t sell me down to New Orleans. Still, I’d noticed a slave trader hanging around the place quite a bit lately, and I began to feel uneasy. One night I crept to the door pretty late. It wasn’t fully closed, and I heard the old mistress telling the widow she was going to sell me down to New Orleans. She said she didn’t want to, but she could get eight hundred dollars for me, and it was such a large sum she couldn’t resist. The widow tried to make her promise she wouldn’t do it, but I didn’t wait to hear the rest. I got out of there mighty fast, I can tell you.

“I ran down the hill, expecting to steal a skiff somewhere along the shore above town, but people were still moving about, so I hid in the old, falling-down cooper’s shop on the bank and waited for everyone to leave. Well, I stayed there all night. There was somebody around the whole time. Around six in the morning, skiffs began passing by, and by eight or nine, every skiff that went along was talking about how your father had come to town and said you’d been killed. Those later skiffs were full of ladies and gentlemen going over to see the place. Sometimes they stopped at the shore and rested before crossing, so from their talk I learned everything about the killing. I was terribly sorry you’d been killed, Huck, but I’m not anymore.

“I lay there under the shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn’t afraid, because I knew the old mistress and the widow were going to leave for the camp meeting right after breakfast and be gone all day. They knew I went off with the cattle around daylight, so they wouldn’t expect to see me around the place and wouldn’t miss me until evening, after dark. The other servants wouldn’t miss me either, because they’d slip away and take a holiday as soon as the old people were out of the way.

“Well, when it got dark, I set out along the river road and went about two miles or more, to where there weren’t any houses. I’d made up my mind what I was going to do. You see, if I kept trying to escape on foot, the dogs would track me. If I stole a skiff to cross over, they’d notice that skiff was missing, and they’d know about where I’d landed on the other side and where to pick up my trail.”"}

{"request_id":"8c982422c3916788fbff7458","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to keep in her old position at Lady Canterville’s strong request. She gave each of them a low curtsey as they got out and said in a quaint, old-fashioned way, ‘I welcome you to Canterville Chase.’ They followed her through the fine Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room lined with black oak panels, with a large stained-glass window at the far end. Tea had been prepared for them there. After removing their wraps, they sat down and looked around while Mrs. Umney served them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor beside the fireplace. Not knowing what it meant, she said to Mrs. Umney, ‘I’m afraid something has been spilled there.’

‘Yes, madam,’ replied the old housekeeper softly. ‘Blood was spilled on that spot.’

‘How horrible,’ cried Mrs. Otis. ‘I don’t like bloodstains in a sitting room at all. It must be removed immediately.’

The old woman smiled and answered in the same quiet, mysterious voice, ‘It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered there by her own husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived for nine more years, then disappeared suddenly under very mysterious circumstances. His body was never found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. Tourists and others have greatly admired the bloodstain, and it cannot be removed.’

‘That is nonsense,’ cried Washington Otis. ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it in no time.’ Before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he dropped to his knees and quickly scrubbed the floor with a small stick of what looked like black cosmetics. Within moments, no trace of the bloodstain remained.

‘I knew Pinkerton would do it,’ he said triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family. But no sooner had he spoken than a terrible flash of lightning lit the dark room, a frightening crash of thunder made them all jump to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

‘What an awful climate!’ said the American Minister calmly as he lit a long cheroot. ‘I suppose the old country is so overcrowded that there isn’t enough decent weather for everyone. I have always believed that emigration is England’s only solution.’

‘My dear Hiram,’ cried Mrs. Otis, ‘what can we do with a woman who faints?’

‘Charge it to her as breakage,’ answered the Minister. ‘She won’t faint again after that.’ And within a few moments Mrs. Umney had certainly recovered."}

{"request_id":"6928736f5938be2d5eebf0ff","rewritten_text":"“You have not been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy the evening parties here.”

“Oh, no. Their usual character has nothing to offer me. I do not play cards.”

“I know you did not formerly. You used not to like cards; but time brings many changes.”

“I am not yet so greatly changed,” cried Anne, then stopped, afraid of some misunderstanding she could scarcely define. After waiting a few moments, he said, as though the words had been forced from him by immediate feeling, “It is a period, indeed! Eight and a half years is a period.”

Whether he would have gone further was left for Anne to consider in a calmer hour; for, while she was still hearing the words he had spoken, Henrietta startled her into other thoughts, eager to use the present leisure to get out, and calling on her companions to lose no time, lest someone else should arrive.

They had to move. Anne said she was quite ready and tried to appear so; but she felt that, if Henrietta had known the regret and reluctance in her heart as she left that chair and prepared to leave the room, she would have found, in all her own feelings for her cousin, and in the very certainty of Captain Wentworth’s affection, enough to pity her.

Their preparations, however, were abruptly interrupted. Alarming sounds were heard; other visitors approached, and the door opened for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose entrance seemed to chill everyone. Anne felt an immediate oppression, and wherever she looked, she saw signs of the same feeling. The room’s comfort, ease, and gaiety were over, subdued into cold composure, deliberate silence, or dull conversation, to suit the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How humiliating to feel that it was so!

Her jealous eye was satisfied in one respect. Captain Wentworth was acknowledged again by both of them, Elizabeth more graciously than before. She even spoke to him once and looked at him more than once. Elizabeth was, in fact, considering an important plan. Its outcome soon explained it. After wasting a few minutes on the proper empty remarks, she began to give the invitation meant to include all the Musgroves’ remaining obligations. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends: no formal party.” She said it with great grace, and the cards she had brought with her, marked “Miss Elliot at home,” were placed on the table with a courteous, inclusive smile for everyone, and one smile and one card more distinctly intended for Captain Wentworth. The truth was that Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to understand the value of a man with such an air and appearance as his."}

{"request_id":"603eea467e9ca0af6bcdf6ad","rewritten_text":"There comes a point in every properly made boy’s life when he burns to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. That longing seized Tom one day. He went out looking for Joe Harper, but could not find him. Then he tried Ben Rogers, who had gone fishing. Before long he came across Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a secluded spot and confided the plan to him. Huck was agreeable. Huck was always ready to join any venture that promised amusement and cost nothing, since he possessed an inconvenient excess of the kind of time that is not money. “Where’ll we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is it buried everywhere?”

“No, it ain’t. It’s hidden in very particular places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests beneath the end of a branch on an old dead tree, exactly where the shadow falls at midnight; but usually under the floor of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Why, robbers, naturally—who did you suppose? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it belonged to me, I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and enjoy myself.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t act that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No, they mean to, but usually forget the signs, or else they die. Anyway, it lies there a long while and grows rusty; then somebody discovers an old yellow paper explaining how to find the marks—a paper that has to be worked out for about a week because it’s mostly signs and hy’roglyphics.”

“Hyro-what?”

“Hy’roglyphics—pictures and such, you know, that don’t appear to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well, then, how are you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t need any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house or on an island, or beneath a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We’ve searched Jackson’s Island a little, and we can try again sometime; and there’s the old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and plenty of dead-limb trees—whole loads of them.”

“Is it under every one?”

“What a question! No!”

“Then how’ll you know which one to try?”

“Try them all!”

“Why, Tom, that’ll take the whole summer.”

“Well, so what? Suppose you find a brass pot containing a hundred dollars, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest packed with diamonds. How would that be?”

Huck’s eyes shone.

“That’s bully. Bully enough for me. Just give me the hundred dollars, and I don’t want any diamonds.”"}
