{"request_id":"ddcc8f88f0f642f0e6b40f71","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often, you’d see one poke his nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she had to keep things nearby to throw at them when she was alone, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot and said she was usually a good shot with it, but she had strained her arm a day or two before and didn’t know whether she could aim straight now. Still, she watched for a chance and soon threw it at a rat. She missed badly and cried, “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to get away before the old man returned, but of course I didn’t show it. I took the lead, and when the first rat poked out his nose, I threw it. If he had stayed where he was, he would have been a very sick rat. She said that was excellent and guessed I would hit the next one. She went to get the lump of lead and brought it back, along with a hank of yarn she wanted me to help her with. I held up both hands, and she placed the yarn over them while continuing to talk about her affairs and her husband’s. But she stopped to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, where it’s handy.”

She dropped the lump into my lap at that moment, and I clamped my legs around it while she went on talking. But only for about a minute. Then she removed the yarn, looked me straight in the face pleasantly, and said:

“Come now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or what is it?”

I think I shook like a leaf, and I hardly knew what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you, either. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it; and, more than that, I’ll help you. My old man will too, if you want him to. You see, you’re only a runaway apprentice. It isn’t anything. There’s no harm in it. You were treated badly, and you decided to run away. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"976a1803d8571863d9ce45c3","rewritten_text":"A FEW days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went riding across Brockley meadows. In forcing her way through a hedge, she tore her habit so badly that, when she got home, she resolved to use the back staircase so that no one would see her. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door stood open, she thought she caught sight of someone within. Supposing it to be her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her work there, she looked in to ask her to repair the habit. To her great astonishment, however, it was the Canterville Ghost himself! He sat beside the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees whirl through the air and the red leaves dance wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his entire posture expressed profound dejection. Indeed, he looked so wretched and so thoroughly out of repair that little Virginia, whose first impulse had been to flee and lock herself in her room, was overcome with pity and resolved to comfort him. Her step was so quiet, and his melancholy so deep, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

‘I am very sorry for you,’ she said, ‘but my brothers are returning to Eton to-morrow, and then, if you behave yourself, nobody will trouble you.’

‘It is ridiculous to ask me to behave myself,’ he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to address him, ‘perfectly ridiculous. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and wander about at night, if that is what you mean. It is the sole purpose of my existence.’

‘That is no purpose for existing at all, and you know you have behaved very wickedly. Mrs. Umney told us, on the first day we came here, that you had murdered your wife.’

‘Well, I freely confess it,’ said the Ghost peevishly, ‘but it was strictly a family affair, and involved nobody else.’

‘It is very wrong to murder anyone,’ said Virginia, who sometimes possessed a gentle Puritan solemnity inherited from an old New England ancestor.

‘Oh, I detest the cheap harshness of abstract morality! My wife was extremely plain, never had my ruffs starched properly, and understood nothing about cooking. Why, there was a buck I had shot in Hogley Woods, a splendid pricket, and do you know how she had it served at table? Still, it does not matter now, since it is finished, and I do not think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I had killed her.’"}

{"request_id":"d6ca51789cac0a0d4e1ee036","rewritten_text":"It was at Warwick Castle that I met the curious stranger I am about to describe. Three things drew me to him: his open simplicity, his amazing knowledge of ancient armor, and how relaxing his company was—for he did all the talking. Like other modest people, we had fallen in at the back of the group being led through the castle, and he immediately began saying things that interested me. As he spoke in a soft, pleasant, flowing way, he seemed to drift quietly out of the present world and time into some distant age and forgotten land. Gradually, he cast such a spell over me that I felt I was moving among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mold of a gray antiquity, speaking with one of its surviving relics. He spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other famous knights of the Round Table exactly as I would speak of my closest friends, enemies, or neighbors. And as he continued, he began to look terribly, impossibly old—faded, dry, musty, and ancient. At last he turned to me and said, as casually as someone discussing the weather:

“You know about the transmigration of souls; do you know about the transposition of ages—and bodies?”

I said I had never heard of it. He seemed no more interested than if we had been discussing the weather, and did not even notice whether I answered. There was a brief silence, broken at once by the droning voice of the paid guide:

“Ancient hauberk, dating from the sixth century, the time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous. Observe the round hole through the chain mail in the left breast. Its cause is unknown; it is thought to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not with a modern smile, but with one that must have disappeared from common use many centuries ago—and murmured, apparently to himself:

“Know this well: I saw it done.” Then, after a pause, he added, “I did it myself.”

Before I had recovered from the shock of this statement, he was gone.

That evening I sat beside the fire at the Warwick Arms, lost in a dream of the old days, while rain struck the windows and wind roared around the eaves and corners. From time to time I opened old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, feasted on its rich tales of wonders and adventures, breathed in the perfume of its outdated names, and dreamed again."}

{"request_id":"f981c47f902745bc9f130959","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and every kind of low vagabond were mixed together in one mass. Drovers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and struggled, sheep bleated, and pigs grunted and squealed. Hawkers cried out, while shouts, curses, and quarrels rose from every side. Bells rang, and every public-house poured out a roar of voices. People crowded, pushed, drove, beat, whooped, and yelled. The ugly, clashing noise echoed through every corner of the market, while unwashed, unshaven, ragged, and dirty figures ran constantly back and forth, bursting in and out of the crowd. Altogether, it was a deafening and confusing scene that overwhelmed the senses.

Mr. Sikes, pulling Oliver behind him, forced his way through the thickest part of the crowd and paid little attention to the many sights and sounds that amazed the boy. He nodded two or three times to friends who passed, and refused several invitations to have a morning drink. He kept moving until they had escaped the noise and made their way through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, looking up at the clock of St. Andrew’s Church. “Nearly seven! You must walk faster. Come on—don’t start lagging behind already, Lazy-legs!”

As he spoke, Mr. Sikes jerked his little companion by the wrist. Oliver quickened his pace to a trot, somewhere between walking and running, and did his best to keep up with the housebreaker’s long, quick strides.

They continued at that speed until they had passed Hyde Park Corner and were heading toward Kensington. Then Sikes slowed down until an empty cart, some distance behind them, caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” written on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could, whether he would carry them as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes, he’s my boy,” replied Sikes, staring hard at Oliver and absently putting his hand into the pocket where he kept the pistol.

“Your father walks a little too fast for you, doesn’t he, my lad?” the driver asked, noticing that Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” Sikes cut in. “He’s used to it. Here, take my hand, Ned. Get in!”

Speaking to Oliver in this way, he helped him into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told him to lie there and rest.

As they passed one milestone after another, Oliver wondered more and more where his companion intended to take him. They passed Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, yet continued steadily on as if their journey had only just begun."}

{"request_id":"594e5331fdc8be644c7196ca","rewritten_text":"The following day was fixed for the production (so that our honour might not grow cold through delay), and on that day Drummle appeared with a small, polite acknowledgment in Estella’s handwriting, stating that she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. This left me no alternative but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, generally speaking, to deny as untenable the notion that I was to be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove contradicted everybody indiscriminately, and at last the advancement of good feeling was pronounced to have proceeded at a remarkable speed.

I describe this casually, but it was anything but casual to me. I cannot properly convey the pain I felt at the thought of Estella showing favour to such a contemptible, awkward, sullen fool, so far beneath the common level. Even now, I believe it must have arisen from some pure flame of generosity and selflessness in my love for her, that I could not bear the idea of her stooping to that hound. Certainly I should have been wretched whatever person she had favoured; but a more deserving object would have produced distress of another sort and intensity.

It was not difficult for me to discover, and I soon did discover, that Drummle had begun following her closely, and that she permitted him to do so. Before long he was constantly after her, and he and I encountered each other every day. He persisted in a dull, stubborn fashion, while Estella kept him in pursuit; sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes nearly flattering him, sometimes plainly scorning him, sometimes seeming to know him perfectly, and sometimes hardly recalling who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had named him, was accustomed to waiting in ambush, and possessed the patience of his kind. Besides this, he had a thick-headed faith in his wealth and his family’s importance, which occasionally served him well—almost supplying the place of focus and resolute intention. Thus the Spider, watching Estella with dogged persistence, outlasted many more brilliant insects, and would often uncoil himself and drop down at precisely the right moment.

At a certain Assembly Ball in Richmond (there were Assembly Balls in most places in those days), where Estella had surpassed all the other beauties, this clumsy Drummle lingered so persistently around her, and with such tolerance from her, that I determined to speak with her about him. I seized the next opportunity, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home and sat apart among some flowers, prepared to leave."}

{"request_id":"ed6721e8209a6f0227f554f6","rewritten_text":"After some time, twelve o’clock boomed from the tall tower at Westminster. With every stroke of the deep bell, the night seemed to shake. Then the railway lights went out, leaving one lonely lamp shining like a large ruby on a giant mast, and the city’s roar grew quieter.

At two o’clock he rose and walked toward Blackfriars. Everything looked unreal, like a strange dream. The houses across the river seemed made of darkness. It was as though silver and shadow had remade the world. The great dome of St. Paul’s appeared through the dim air like a bubble.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle, he saw a man leaning over the parapet. When he came closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight fell fully across his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! No one could mistake that fat, flabby face, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the weak, sickly smile, or the sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea came to him, and he quietly crept up behind. In an instant he seized Mr. Podgers by the legs and threw him into the Thames. There was a rough oath, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur looked anxiously over the parapet, but could see nothing of the cheiromantist except a tall hat spinning in a whirl of moonlit water. After a while it sank too, and no sign of Mr. Podgers remained. Once he thought he saw the large, misshapen figure swimming toward the bridge staircase, and a terrible sense of failure seized him. But it was only a reflection, and when the moon came out from behind a cloud, the feeling disappeared. At last he seemed to have carried out the decree of destiny. He breathed a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

‘Have you dropped anything, sir?’ a voice suddenly asked behind him.

He turned and saw a policeman holding a bull’s-eye lantern.

‘Nothing important, sergeant,’ he replied with a smile. Hailing a passing hansom, he climbed in and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he moved between hope and fear. At times he almost expected Mr. Podgers to walk into the room, yet at others he felt that Fate could not treat him so unfairly. Twice he went to the cheiromantist’s address in West Moon Street, but he could not make himself ring the bell. He wanted certainty, but was afraid of it.

At last it came. He was sitting in the club’s smoking-room, drinking tea and listening rather wearily to Surbiton’s account of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"20d96d5a925a59de93417536","rewritten_text":"“If, however, you want one for home use, I can provide an excellent device and guarantee that you will be satisfied with the result. May I ask who it is for? If it is for the police, or anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I am afraid I can do nothing for you. English detectives are really our best friends. I have always found that, by relying on their stupidity, we can do exactly as we please. I could not spare one of them.”

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “that it has nothing to do with the police. In fact, the clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Dear me! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do these days.”

“I am afraid you overestimate me, Herr Winckelkopf,” said Lord Arthur, blushing. “The truth is, I know nothing about theology.”

“Then it is purely a private matter?”

“Purely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room. A few minutes later he returned with a round piece of dynamite about the size of a penny and a pretty little French clock, topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face brightened when he saw it. “That is exactly what I want,” he cried. “Now tell me how it goes off.”

“Ah! That is my secret,” replied Herr Winckelkopf, looking at his invention with justifiable pride. “Tell me when you want it to explode, and I will set the mechanism for that exact moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday. If you could send it at once—”

“That is impossible. I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might send it tomorrow.”

“Oh, that will be quite soon enough,” said Lord Arthur politely, “if it is delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning. As for the explosion, let us say Friday at exactly noon. The Dean is always at home then.”

“Friday, at noon,” repeated Herr Winckelkopf. He wrote it down in a large ledger lying on a desk near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising, “please tell me how much I owe you.”

“It is such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I do not wish to charge you. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and the carriage about five shillings. I am only too happy to oblige a friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"63a9859283c5189c3f3a3052","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, still unsure where to go. “At Tellson’s bank at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise to show myself in the meantime? I think so. These people should know that a man like me is here; it is a sensible precaution, and may be necessary preparation. But care, care, care! Let me think it through!”

He stopped himself from following the direction his steps had begun to take, turned once or twice through the darkening street, and considered what might follow from the idea. His first impression was confirmed. “It is best,” he said at last, having made up his mind, “that these people should know that a man like me is here.” Then he turned towards Saint Antoine.

Defarge had described himself that day as the keeper of a wine-shop in the Saint Antoine suburb. Anyone who knew the city well could find his house without asking questions. After locating it, Carton left the narrower streets and ate dinner at a place serving refreshments, then fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in many years, he had no strong drink. Since the previous night, he had taken nothing but a little weak, light wine; and the night before, he had slowly poured the brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man who had finished with it.

It was seven o’clock when he awoke refreshed and went out into the streets again. On his way to Saint Antoine, he stopped at a shop window with a mirror and slightly fixed his loose cravat, coat collar, and untidy hair. Then he went straight to Defarge’s and entered.

There was no customer in the shop except Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and croaking voice. Carton had seen this man on the Jury. He stood drinking at the small counter and talking with the Defarges, husband and wife. The Vengeance joined in, as though she were a regular member of the establishment.

Carton entered, sat down, and asked, in very poor French, for a small measure of wine. Madame Defarge gave him a careless glance, then a sharper one, and then another sharper one. At last she came over and asked what he had ordered.

He repeated what he had already said.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, raising her dark eyebrows with interest.

He looked at her as though even one French word took him time to understand, then answered in the same strong foreign accent as before."}

{"request_id":"b5a01f906bcb8ba95ee7daa6","rewritten_text":"Now that he had no work to occupy him, he placed the knuckles of his right hand in the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left hand in the hollow of his right, and then passed a hand over his bearded chin, repeating these movements in regular alternation without a moment’s pause. Calling him back from the wandering state into which he always fell after speaking was like rousing a very weak person from a faint, or trying, in the hope of some revelation, to hold back the spirit of a dying man.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“Certainly I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a weary sound that was neither a sigh nor a groan, he bent over his work again, until the silence was broken once more.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, looking steadily at him.

His haggard eyes turned toward Defarge, as though he wished to pass the question on to him; but when no help came from that direction, they dropped to the ground and then returned to the questioner.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away again, for several minutes, continuing those measured movements of his hands all the while. At last his eyes slowly returned to the face from which they had wandered. When they settled on it, he started and continued like a sleeper suddenly awakened, returning to a subject from the previous night.

“I asked permission to teach myself, and after a long time, with great difficulty, I received it, and I have made shoes ever since.”

As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry said, still looking steadily into his face:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the ground, and he sat staring fixedly at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry placed his hand on Defarge’s arm—“do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time rising in your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

As the captive of so many years sat staring in turn at Mr. Lorry and Defarge, some long-erased traces of an intensely active intelligence in the center of his forehead gradually pushed through the black mist that had fallen over him. They were clouded again, grew fainter, and disappeared; but they had been there."}

{"request_id":"2cf13d7581c039076b44ee20","rewritten_text":"But that same peaceful Saturday afternoon brought no merriment to the little town. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were plunged into mourning, amid deep sorrow and many tears. An uncommon stillness lay over the village, though it was quiet enough at the best of times. The villagers went about their affairs absently and spoke little, but sighed frequently. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children. They had no spirit for their games and gradually abandoned them.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering sadly around the empty schoolhouse yard, feeling very low. Yet she discovered nothing there to console her. She spoke to herself:

“Oh, if only I had a brass andiron-knob again! But now I haven’t anything to remember him by.” And she swallowed a small sob.

After a while she stopped and said inwardly:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could live it over, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for anything in the world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought overcame her, and she wandered off, tears running down her cheeks. Then a fairly large group of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came along and stood gazing over the picket fence, speaking solemnly of how Tom had done this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe had said some little thing (now plainly full of dreadful prophecy!)—and each one indicated the precise place where the missing boys had stood, then added something like, “and I was standing just so—just as I am now, and if you were him—I was this close—and he smiled, just like this—and then something seemed to pass all over me, sort of—awful, you know—and I never guessed what it meant, of course, but I understand now!”

Then they argued over who had seen the dead boys last while they were alive. Many claimed the gloomy honor and produced evidence, more or less altered by the witness. When it was finally settled who really had seen the departed last and spoken the final words to them, those fortunate ones assumed a kind of sacred importance, while everyone else stared at and envied them. One poor fellow, having no other distinction to present, said with plainly visible pride in the memory:

“Well, Tom Sawyer licked me once.”

But that attempt at glory failed. Most of the boys could say the same, which made the distinction far too common. The group drifted away, still remembering the lost heroes in hushed, reverent voices."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e9b6e5b94dfc04ea2a12aba7","rewritten_text":"The next day the ghost was very weak and tired. The terrible excitement of the past four weeks was beginning to affect him. His nerves were completely shattered, and he jumped at the slightest noise. He stayed in his room for five days, and finally decided to give up trying to remove the bloodstain from the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, they clearly did not deserve it. They were obviously people living on a low, material level and were quite unable to appreciate the symbolic meaning of physical phenomena. The question of ghostly appearances and the development of astral bodies was, of course, entirely different and really beyond his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week and to groan from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of every month, and he could not see how he could honorably avoid these duties. It was true that his life had been very wicked, but, on the other hand, he was extremely conscientious about everything connected with the supernatural. For the next three Saturdays, therefore, he walked through the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every possible precaution not to be heard or seen. He removed his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and carefully used Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit that it was difficult for him to accept this last form of protection. However, one night, while the family was at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and took the bottle. At first he felt slightly humiliated, but later he sensibly recognized that the invention had much to recommend it, and it served his purpose to some extent. Even so, he was not left in peace. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor, and he tripped over them in the dark. On one occasion, while dressed as ‘Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,’ he suffered a serious fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had built from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult made him so angry that he decided to make one last attempt to defend his dignity and social position. He resolved to visit the insolent young Etonians the following night in his famous role of ‘Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.’\n\nHe had not worn this disguise for more than seventy years—in fact, not since he had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish so badly with it that she suddenly ended her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. She declared that nothing in the world could persuade her to marry into a family that allowed such a horrible ghost to walk up and down the terrace at twilight."}

But the good-natured peer stood firm and finally persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her. When, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire appeared at the Queen’s first drawing-room after her marriage, everyone admired her jewels. Virginia had received the coronet, the reward given to all good little American girls, and had married her childhood sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming, and loved each other so deeply, that everyone was pleased by the marriage—except the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to win the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had held three costly dinner parties for that purpose. Strangely enough, Mr. Otis was also displeased. He was very fond of the young Duke personally, but in principle he disliked titles and, as he put it, ‘feared that, among the weakening influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity might be forgotten.’ His objections were completely overruled, however, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter on his arm, there was no prouder man anywhere in England.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went to Canterville Chase. The day after they arrived, they walked in the afternoon to the lonely churchyard beside the pine woods. At first, there had been much disagreement about the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone. In the end, it was decided to carve only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some beautiful roses, which she scattered over the grave. After standing there for a while, they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up at her lovely eyes. Suddenly, he threw away his cigarette, took her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.’

‘Yes, you have,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never told me what happened when you were locked in with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ Virginia said seriously."}

{"request_id":"04e3d4a1ca0f15bed9a2ba09","rewritten_text":"With my heart pounding and fear I could not explain, I dismissed the servant, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were the words it contained.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and have made your innocent heart familiar with the looks and language of forbidden and monstrous passion. I must atone for these crimes and try, in some measure, to make my punishment fit my guilt. You are, I doubt not, prepared for what I am about to tell you: we must separate and be parted forever.

“I am taking away your parent and only friend. You are cast helpless and without shelter upon the world. Your hopes are destroyed, and the peace and safety of your pure mind have been ruined. Memory will bring you terrible images of guilt and the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I am the one who has brought all this misery upon you; I am the one who casts you out and has cruelly placed distrust and anguish upon the heart and face of my own child. With devilish carelessness, I have tried to take away her loveliness and replace it with the ugly deformity of sin. Therefore, in the overwhelming anguish of my heart, I beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must, and do, hate me. But forgive me, Mathilda, and do not think of me in my exile with unending anger. I must never see you again or hear your voice. Yet the gentle whispers of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning in my troubled mind and heart; I am sure I would feel them even in my grave. I dare support this request by telling you how miserably I was drawn into this net of fiery anguish and describing all my efforts to escape it. If your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to defend myself to you. I would fear that, if I made you hate me less, you might hate vice less as well. But when I speak to you, I feel as though I were appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness. I must try to win it, or I must despair. I therefore beg you to hear my words. If, among the good, guilt may be lessened at all by severe suffering and remorse that tears the mind as madness might, perhaps you may believe—though I dare not—that I have some claim to your compassion.

“I beg you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of weary wandering. During that time, though I had endured many dangers and misfortunes, my affections had remained completely empty."}

{"request_id":"40acc37a8dc6c8c241922664","rewritten_text":"I have said that he was a poet: at twenty-three he published his first poem, and the entire nation greeted it with enthusiasm and delight. His good fortune never deserted him; no reputation had ever been made so quickly, and his fame was universal. The multitude praised the same poems that astonished the scholar in his study: there was not a single dissenting voice.

It was then, at the height of his glory, that he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of exquisite beauty, living under the care of her guardian; from the moment they were seen together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor did not possess Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble, and elevated by her youth and by the love she inspired everywhere beyond any knowledge except that of virtue and excellence. She was lovely; her manner was frank and simple; her deep blue eyes shone with a radiance that could come only from sensibility joined with wisdom.

They were made for each other, and soon fell in love. Woodville felt the joy of love for the first time, while Elinor was enraptured to possess the heart of one so beautiful and celebrated among his fellow men. Could anything but unalloyed happiness come from such a union?

Woodville was a poet—every society sought him, and all eyes turned toward him alone when he appeared; but he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian did not object to their mutual affection: Woodville’s merit was too distinguished to invite criticism on account of his lesser fortune. But her father’s dying will forbade her to marry before she came of age, and her inheritance depended on her obeying this command. She had just entered her twentieth year, and she and her lover were forced to submit to the delay. Yet they were always together, and their happiness seemed almost paradisal: they studied together and made plans for their future lives; absorbing love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, they scarcely complained about postponing their complete union. Woodville’s fame continued to rise, and Elinor became more lovely and wise beneath the instruction of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one; everything was ready for their union. How can I describe the catastrophe that followed such happiness? Yet the earth would not be the blighted, sorrowful place it is if a pair of such angelic beings had been allowed to live for each other. Search the whole world, and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have brought them; the order of things established among us miserable inhabitants of earth would have had to change before such complete joy could be permitted."}

{"request_id":"33cc79a3502c65deb34899dc","rewritten_text":"It was at that moment that his eyes, and mine as well, fell on the scrap of parchment, which I had then taken for paper. It lay half buried in the sand, with one corner protruding. Near the place where we found it, I noticed the remains of what seemed to have been a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have lain there for a very long time, since its resemblance to boat timbers could scarcely be discerned.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Shortly afterward we set off for home, and on the way encountered Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he asked me to let him take it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately put it into his waistcoat pocket, leaving behind the parchment in which it had been wrapped, which I had kept in my hand while he examined it. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind and thought it best to secure the prize at once—you know how enthusiastic he is about everything connected with Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

“You remember that when I went to the table to make a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper where it was normally kept. I looked in the drawer, but found none there. I searched my pockets, hoping to find an old letter, when my hand came upon the parchment. I describe exactly how it came into my possession because the circumstances affected me with unusual force.

“No doubt you will think me fanciful—but I had already formed a kind of connection. I had joined two links of a great chain. There was a boat on a sea-coast, and not far from the boat lay a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn upon it. You will naturally ask, ‘Where is the connection?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the familiar emblem of the pirate. The death’s-head flag is raised in every engagement.

“I have said that the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is durable—almost imperishable. Matters of little importance are seldom committed to parchment, since for ordinary drawing or writing it is far less suitable than paper. This thought suggested that the death’s-head must have some meaning—some relevance. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. Although one corner had been destroyed by some accident, it was clear that its original form had been oblong."}

{"request_id":"6d1b985d48de3614a116ce47","rewritten_text":"He then bowed and went away. He saw no one in the street at that moment. It is a side street—very solitary.

“_William Bird_, tailor, states that he was among the party who entered the house. He is an Englishman, and has lived in Paris for two years. He was one of the first to go up the stairs. He heard the voices arguing. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could distinguish several words, but cannot now recall them all. He heard ‘_sacré_’ and ‘_mon Dieu_’ distinctly. At that instant there was a noise as though several people were struggling—a scraping and scuffling sound. The shrill voice was extremely loud—louder than the gruff voice. He is certain it was not the voice of an Englishman. It seemed to be that of a German. It might have been a woman’s voice. He does not understand German.

“Four of the witnesses named above, being recalled, testified that the chamber door where the body of Mademoiselle L. was discovered had been locked from within when the party reached it. Everything was entirely quiet—there were no groans or sounds of any sort. When the door was forced, no one was visible. The windows of both the front and back rooms were shut and securely fastened from the inside. A door connecting the two rooms was closed, though not locked. The door from the front room into the passage was locked, its key being on the inside. A small room at the head of the passage, in the front of the house on the fourth story, stood open, its door ajar. It was filled with old beds, boxes, and similar articles. These were removed and searched with care. Not an inch of any part of the house was left unexamined. Chimneys were swept from top to bottom. The house had four stories, with garrets (_mansardes._) A trapdoor in the roof was nailed down very firmly and did not seem to have been opened for years. The witnesses gave differing estimates of the interval between hearing the voices quarrelling and forcing open the chamber door. Some said it was no more than three minutes; others said as much as five. The door was difficult to open.

“_Alfonzo Garcio_, undertaker, states that he lives in the Rue Morgue. He is a native of Spain. He was among the party that entered the house, but did not go upstairs. Being nervous, he feared the effects of excitement. He heard the voices arguing. The gruff voice was that of a Frenchman. He could not make out what was said. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—of this he is certain.”"}

{"request_id":"b43d52b16ac77e4eda96f7b1","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently placing his hand on the Doctor’s arm again, after a brief silence on both sides, “what would you attribute this attack to?”

“I believe,” replied Doctor Manette, “that there had been a powerful and extraordinary revival of the chain of thought and memory that first caused the illness. Some intense associations of an extremely distressing nature were vividly brought back, I think. It is likely that a fear had long been hidden in his mind: that those associations might return—under certain circumstances, perhaps, or on a particular occasion. He tried unsuccessfully to prepare himself; perhaps the effort to prepare made him less able to endure it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, with understandable hesitation.

The Doctor looked miserably around the room, shook his head, and answered in a low voice, “Not at all.”

“And as for the future?” Mr. Lorry prompted.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining his firmness, “I should have great hope. Since Heaven, in its mercy, restored him so quickly, I should have great hope. He yielded beneath the pressure of something complicated, long feared, dimly anticipated, and resisted for a long time; and, recovering after the cloud had broken and passed, I should hope that the worst was over.”

“Well, well! That is good news. I am thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am thankful!” repeated the Doctor, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other matters,” said Mr. Lorry, “about which I am anxious to be informed. May I continue?”

“You cannot do your friend a greater service.” The Doctor offered him his hand.

“Then, the first. He is studious by nature and unusually energetic; he devotes himself with great enthusiasm to gaining professional knowledge, conducting experiments, and many other pursuits. Now, does he do too much?”

“I think not. It may be the nature of his mind to require constant occupation in an unusual degree. That may be partly natural to him and partly the result of suffering. The less he occupied himself with healthy matters, the more danger there would be of his mind turning in an unhealthy direction. He may have observed this in himself and discovered it.”

“You are certain that he is not under too much strain?”

“I believe I am quite certain.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt whether that would be easy. There has been violent pressure in one direction, and it requires a counterweight.”

“Forgive me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose for a moment that he was overworked; would it reveal itself through some recurrence of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"14653526da35811b90050242","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said when we reached its base, “come here! Was the skull nailed to the branch with its face turned outward, or toward the branch?”

“De face was out, massa, so de crows could get at de eyes good, widout any trouble.”

“Well, then, was it through this eye or that one that you dropped the beetle?” Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes.

“’Twas dis eye, massa—the lef eye—jis as you tell me,” and he pointed to his right eye.

“That will do—we must try it again.”

My friend’s madness now seemed, or perhaps only appeared, to show some method. He moved the peg marking where the beetle had fallen to a spot about three inches west of its former position. Then he measured from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, as before, and extended the line straight for fifty feet. This marked a spot several yards away from where we had been digging.

We drew a circle around the new spot, somewhat larger than the first, and began digging again. I was terribly tired, but, without quite understanding what had changed in my thoughts, I no longer strongly disliked the work. I had become strangely interested—even excited. Perhaps, despite Legrand’s wild behavior, there was something thoughtful and deliberate about him that affected me. I dug eagerly and sometimes caught myself looking almost expectantly for the imagined treasure whose vision had driven my unfortunate companion mad. When these strange thoughts had taken their strongest hold on me, and after we had worked for perhaps an hour and a half, the dog’s violent howling interrupted us again. At first his restlessness had clearly been caused by playfulness or whim, but now his cries became harsh and serious. When Jupiter tried once more to muzzle him, the dog resisted fiercely, leaped into the hole, and frantically clawed at the soil. Within seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones—two complete skeletons—mixed with several metal buttons and what seemed to be the dust of decayed woolen cloth. One or two strokes of a spade turned up the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug farther, three or four loose gold and silver coins appeared."}

{"request_id":"bdcd1b02147a49ed77a3cee1","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; all the work of maintaining a slow and unsatisfactory correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Breakfast had been over only a short while when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick joined them. They had arranged to take their final walk around Lyme together. They ought to leave for Uppercross by one, and until then they meant to stay together and outdoors for as long as possible.

Anne found Captain Benwick drawing near her as soon as they were properly out in the street. Their conversation the previous evening had not discouraged him from seeking her company again; and they walked together for some time, speaking as before of Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, still as unable as before—and as unable as any two readers—to agree exactly about the merits of either, until something caused an almost general rearrangement among the party, and Captain Harville was beside her instead of Captain Benwick.

“Miss Elliot,” he said, speaking rather quietly, “you have done a good deed by making that poor fellow talk so much. I wish he could have such company more often. I know it is bad for him to be shut up as he is; but what can we do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can easily believe that to be impossible; but perhaps, in time—we know what time does in every case of grief, and you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may still be called a young mourner—only last summer, as I understand.”

“Yes, quite true,” he said with a deep sigh, “only June.”

“And perhaps he did not know until rather later.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, having just been appointed to the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, dreading to hear of him; he sent in letters, but the Grappler was under orders for Portsmouth. The news would have to follow him there, but who was to tell him? Not I. I would sooner have been hanged from the yard-arm. No one could do it but that good fellow”—he pointed to Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had arrived at Plymouth the week before, with no danger of being sent to sea again. He took his chance with the rest; applied for leave of absence, but without waiting for the reply, travelled night and day until he reached Portsmouth, rowed out to the Grappler at once, and never left the poor fellow for a week. That is what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. You may judge, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne considered the question with complete certainty, and said as much in reply as her own feelings could express, or as his seemed able to endure, for he was too deeply moved to continue the subject. When he spoke again, it was about something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"271fec49e3e45d191682c4a0","rewritten_text":"“If I can’t live on that, I won’t ask anyone to give me a lift. Is that satisfactory?”

There was an enormous roar of applause, and from its midst the king’s voice rose:

“Remove his bonds and set him free! Let all, high and low, rich and poor, pay him homage, for he has become the king’s right hand, clothed with power and authority, and his seat is on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this creeping night and bring back the light and cheer, so that all the world may bless you.”

But I said:

“That an ordinary man should be shamed before the world is nothing; but it would dishonor the _king_ if anyone who saw his minister naked did not also see him freed from his shame. If I might ask that my clothes be brought back—”

“They are not suitable,” the king interrupted. “Fetch garments of another kind; dress him like a prince!”

My plan worked. I wanted to keep matters as they were until the eclipse became total; otherwise they would try again to make me dismiss the darkness, and of course I could not do that. Sending for the clothes bought some time, but not enough. So I needed another excuse. I said it would be only natural for the king to change his mind and regret, at least somewhat, what he had done in the excitement; therefore I would let the darkness deepen for a while, and if, after a reasonable time, the king still held to his decision, the darkness would be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else was satisfied with this arrangement, but I had to stand firm.

It grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I struggled with those awkward sixth-century clothes. At last it became completely dark, and the multitude groaned in horror as the cold, uncanny night breezes moved through the place and the stars appeared and twinkled overhead. At last the eclipse was total, and I was very glad, though everyone else was miserable—which was only natural. I said:

“The king, by remaining silent, still stands by the terms.” Then I raised my hands and held them there for a moment. Then I said, with the most terrible solemnity: “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass away harmlessly!”

For a moment there was no response in that profound darkness and graveyard silence. But when the sun’s silver rim emerged a moment or two later, the assembly erupted in a tremendous shout and came pouring down like a flood to smother me with blessings and gratitude; and Clarence was certainly not the last of the wave."}

{"request_id":"99f1b70dc70dac644a53861e","rewritten_text":"‘Well, _monsieur le mauvais sujet_,’ exclaimed the old lady when he came into the room, ‘why have you neglected me for so long?’

‘My dear Lady Clem, I never get a moment to myself,’ Lord Arthur replied with a smile.

‘I suppose you mean that you spend the whole day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying _chiffons_ and talking rubbish? I cannot see why people make so much fuss over being married. In my time we never thought of billing and cooing in public—or in private, for that matter.’

‘I assure you, Lady Clem, I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours. As far as I can tell, she is wholly occupied with her milliners.’

‘Naturally; that is the sole reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder men never take warning. _On a fait des folies pour moi_, and now here I am, a wretched rheumatic creature with a false front and an unpleasant temper. Why, were it not for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me every dreadful French novel she can discover, I doubt I could survive the day. Doctors are utterly useless, except for extracting fees. They cannot even cure my heartburn.’

‘Then I have brought you a remedy for it, Lady Clem,’ said Lord Arthur solemnly. ‘It is a remarkable thing, invented by an American.’

‘I do not think I approve of American inventions, Arthur. I am certain I do not. I read several American novels recently, and they were complete nonsense.’

‘Oh, but there is not the slightest nonsense about this, Lady Clem! I assure you it is an infallible cure. You must promise to try it’; and Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and gave it to her.

‘Well, the box is delightful, Arthur. Is it truly a gift? How very kind of you. And is this the marvelous medicine? It looks like a _bonbon_. I shall take it immediately.’

‘Good heavens, Lady Clem!’ cried Lord Arthur, seizing her hand. ‘You must not do anything of the sort. It is a homoeopathic medicine, and taking it when you have no heartburn might do you tremendous harm. Wait until an attack comes, and take it then. You will be amazed by the result.’

‘I should like to take it now,’ said Lady Clementina, raising the small transparent capsule toward the light, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. ‘I am sure it must be delicious. The truth is, although I detest doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I shall save it for my next attack.’

‘And when will that be?’ Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"37f2a65eb65d62feda5177a0","rewritten_text":"It was the beginning of February, and Anne, who had been in Bath for a month, was becoming very eager for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to hear far more than Mary had told her. It had been three weeks since she had received any news at all. She knew only that Henrietta had returned home, and that Louisa, though thought to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. One evening, while thinking deeply about them all, she received a letter from Mary, thicker than usual, and, to make the pleasure and surprise greater, it came with the compliments of Admiral and Mrs Croft.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was interesting news. They were people toward whom her heart naturally turned.

“What is this?” cried Sir Walter. “The Crofts have arrived in Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! Such letters are useful passports. They secure an introduction. Still, I should have visited Admiral Croft in any case. I know what is owed to my tenant.”

Anne could listen no longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion escaped notice. Her letter held all her attention. It had been started several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

I will not apologize for my silence, because I know how little people think about letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to care about Uppercross, which, as you know, offers very little to write about. We had a very dull Christmas; Mr and Mrs Musgrove did not give a single dinner party during the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anyone. The holidays are finally over; I believe no children ever had such long ones. I am sure I never did. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear that they have not gone home. Mrs Harville must be an unusual mother to keep them away so long. I cannot understand it. They are not at all well-behaved children, in my opinion; but Mrs Musgrove seems to like them just as much, if not more, than her grandchildren. What terrible weather we have had! You may not notice it in Bath, with your fine pavements, but in the country it matters greatly. No one has visited me since the second week of January, except Charles Hayter, who had been calling much more often than I wanted. Between ourselves, I think it is a great pity Henrietta did not stay in Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little farther from him.”"}

{"request_id":"5412f78d974f4cc2e05cc8bf","rewritten_text":"“I agree. It’s the best way. Would you just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, that won’t do for this. That’s good enough for small, ordinary things—especially with girls, because they go back on you anyway and tell if they get angry—but something this important ought to be written down. And sealed with blood.”

Tom’s whole being applauded the idea. It was deep, dark, and terrible; the hour, the circumstances, and the surroundings suited it perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a small piece of red chalk from his pocket, turned it toward the moon, and painfully wrote these lines. He pressed down hard on every slow downward stroke, holding his tongue between his teeth, and eased the pressure on the upward strokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry admired Tom’s skill at writing and the grandeur of his words. He immediately took a pin from his lapel and was about to prick his skin, but Tom stopped him.

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin is brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“It’s poison. That’s what it is. Just swallow some once—you’ll see.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was complete. They buried the shingle near the wall with gloomy ceremonies and incantations. The chains binding their tongues were considered locked, and the key thrown away.

A figure now crept quietly through a gap at the other end of the ruined building, but they did not notice it.

“Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this mean we can _never_ tell—_ever_?”

“Of course it does. No matter _what_ happens, we have to keep quiet. We’d drop dead—you _know_ that, don’t you?”

“Yes, I suppose that’s true.”

They continued whispering for a while. Then a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—less than ten feet away. The boys suddenly grabbed each other, terrified.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, _you_, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t _do_ it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"63768fc8e409fb3f4484cd68","rewritten_text":"It seemed to consist of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, giving the impression of a somewhat dreary seclusion. Wemmick’s house was a tiny wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, with its upper part shaped and painted like a battery fitted with guns.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Looks well; doesn’t it?”

I praised it highly. I believe it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the strangest Gothic windows (most of them sham, by a long way), and a Gothic door almost too narrow to enter.

“That’s a genuine flagstaff, you see,” said Wemmick, “and on Sundays I hoist a real flag. Now look here. Once I’ve crossed this bridge, I raise it up—so—and cut off communication.”

The bridge was merely a plank, spanning a chasm about four feet across and two feet deep. Still, it was delightful to observe the pride with which he lifted it and secured it, smiling with genuine enjoyment rather than doing it mechanically.

“At nine every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun goes off. There he is, you see! And when you hear him fire, I think you’ll call him a Stinger.”

The cannon in question stood in a separate fortress made of lattice-work. An ingenious little tarpaulin arrangement, rather like an umbrella, sheltered it from the weather.

“Then, at the rear,” said Wemmick, “out of sight, so it doesn’t interfere with the fortification idea—for it’s a rule of mine that if you have an idea, you should carry it through and maintain it—I don’t know whether you agree—”

I said that I certainly did.

“—At the rear, there’s a pig, along with fowls and rabbits; then I put together my own little frame, you see, and grow cucumbers. At supper you’ll see what kind of salad I can produce. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling once more, though quite seriously as he shook his head, “if you imagine the little place under siege, it could last a devil of a long time for provisions.”

He then led me to a bower about a dozen yards away, though it was reached by such cleverly winding paths that it took a considerable time to arrive. In this retreat our glasses had already been laid out. Our punch was cooling in an ornamental lake beside which the bower stood. The water, with an island in its centre that might have supplied the supper salad, was circular, and he had built a fountain in it. When a small mill was set in motion and a cork removed from a pipe, the fountain played with such force that it thoroughly wetted the back of your hand."}

{"request_id":"8cd61b2930a17d6e4b3b4302","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, fell to considering whether an honest life was not, after all, the best. Having decided that it certainly was, he turned away from the scenes of his past, resolved to reform himself in some new sphere of action. For a while he struggled greatly and suffered much; but, possessing a contented nature and a worthy purpose, he succeeded at last; and, from having been a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s lad, he is now the merriest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand that writes these words falters as it draws near the end of its task, and would spin out, for a little longer, the thread of these adventures.

I would gladly linger still with a few of those among whom I have moved so long, and share their happiness by trying to portray it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of early womanhood, casting upon her secluded path through life a soft, gentle light, which fell on all who walked it beside her and shone into their hearts. I would depict her the life and joy of the fireside circle and the lively summer company; I would follow her across the sultry fields at noon, and hear the quiet tones of her sweet voice during the moonlit evening walk; I would watch her in all her goodness and charity abroad, and in the smiling, tireless performance of domestic duties at home; I would paint her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love for each other, spending whole hours together imagining the friends they had so sadly lost; I would call before me once more those joyous little faces gathered around her knee, and listen to their merry chatter; I would recall the sound of that clear laugh, and summon up the sympathetic tear that sparkled in the soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks and smiles, and turns of thought and speech—I would gladly recall them all.

How Mr. Brownlow continued, day after day, to fill the mind of his adopted child with stores of knowledge, growing more attached to him as his character unfolded and revealed the flourishing seeds of all he hoped the boy would become—how he discovered in him fresh traits of his early friend, awakening in his own heart old memories, melancholy yet sweet and comforting—how the two orphans, tested by adversity, remembered its lessons in mercy toward others, mutual love, and fervent gratitude to Him who had guarded and preserved them—these are matters that need not be related."}

{"request_id":"78c63ce90dd29340bd0f474c","rewritten_text":"I now come to my own story. There is little to tell about the early part of my life, and I will be brief; but I must be permitted to dwell somewhat on my childhood, so that it may be understood how, when one hope failed, all life would become a blank; and how, when the only affection I was allowed to cherish was destroyed, my existence was extinguished with it.

I have said that my aunt was very unlike my father. I believe that, without the slightest trace of an evil nature, she possessed the coldest heart that ever beat in a human breast: it was entirely incapable of affection. She took me under her protection because she believed it her duty; but she had lived alone for so long, undisturbed by the noise and chatter of children, that she could not bear to have her quiet disturbed. She had never married; and for the last five years had lived in complete solitude on an estate inherited through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had expressed the wish that she would live with me at his family home, situated in beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this proposal, but as soon as she had settled the affairs that her brother’s departure had placed in her care, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

The care of me as a baby, and afterward until I had reached my eighth year, fell to a servant of my mother’s who had accompanied us into retirement for that purpose. I was kept in a distant part of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed times. This happened twice each day: once around noon, when she came to my nursery, and once after dinner, when I was brought to her. She never caressed me, and throughout the time I remained in the room she seemed afraid that some childish impulse might annoy her. My good nurse always instructed me with the greatest care before allowing me to enter the parlor—and the fear inspired by my aunt’s cold looks and few, restrained words was so great that I rarely failed in my lessons or broke the exemplary stillness I had been taught to maintain during these brief visits.

Under my good nurse’s care, I ran freely through our park and the neighboring fields. As the child of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the greatest sensitivity of feeling. I cannot express how passionately I loved everything, even the inanimate objects that surrounded me."}

{"request_id":"8ebee0ab5a4a7745ba33ed69","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. If I stay any longer, I shall be late for lunch. Thank you for giving me the information I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I have invited myself and Mr. Gray. He is her newest _protégé_.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to trouble me again with her charitable appeals. I am tired of them. Why, the good woman imagines I have nothing to do except write cheques for her foolish causes.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, though it will make no difference. Philanthropic people lose every sense of humanity. That is what sets them apart.”

The old gentleman gave an approving growl and rang for his servant. Lord Henry went through the low arcade into Burlington Street, then turned towards Berkeley Square.

So that was the account of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Though it had been told him crudely, it had nevertheless moved him with the promise of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A handful of wild, happy weeks ended by a hideous and treacherous crime. Months of silent suffering, followed by a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy abandoned to loneliness and the rule of an old, loveless man. Yes, it made an interesting background. It gave the boy a pose, made him more complete, so to speak. Behind every exquisite thing in existence, there was something tragic. Worlds had to labour, that even the humblest flower might bloom.... And how delightful he had been at dinner the previous night, sitting opposite him at the club with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure, the red candle-shades deepening into rose the awakening wonder in his face. Speaking with him was like playing an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and tremor of the bow.... There was something profoundly fascinating in exercising influence. No other occupation resembled it. To cast one’s soul into some gracious form and allow it to remain there briefly; to hear one’s own intellectual opinions returned with all the added music of youth and passion; to pass one’s temperament into another as if it were a delicate fluid or unfamiliar perfume: there was genuine pleasure in that—perhaps the most satisfying pleasure left to us in an age as narrow and vulgar as our own, an age grossly sensual in its pleasures and grossly ordinary in its ambitions.... This boy was a wonderful type, too, whom by such a curious chance he had encountered in Basil’s studio—or, at least, could be shaped into a wonderful type."}

{"request_id":"84c38864278a47b566a7ebb6","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, will you? Oh, you precious little fool!”

“It’s naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll get scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. He caught hold of one end of his neckerchief and held it up in the air. Then he dropped his head to one side and made a strange sound through his teeth, showing by this lively pantomime that scragging meant hanging.

“That’s what it means,” said Charley. “Look at how he stares, Jack! I never saw such fine company as that boy. He’ll be the death of me, I know he will.” Master Charley Bates laughed heartily again, then took up his pipe, tears in his eyes.

“You’ve been badly brought up,” said the Dodger, looking with great satisfaction at his boots after Oliver had polished them. “Fagin will make something of you, though, or you’ll be the first boy he ever had who turned out useless. You’d better start at once, because you’ll join the trade long before you expect it; and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates supported this advice with several moral warnings of his own. When he had finished, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins gave Oliver an enthusiastic account of the many pleasures of their life. They also offered him several hints that the best thing he could do was to win Fagin’s favor without delay, using the same methods they had used themselves.

“And always remember this, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as they heard the Jew unlocking the door above, “if you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the use of talking like that?” interrupted Master Bates. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket handkerchiefs and watches,” said the Dodger, simplifying his words for Oliver, “someone else will. Then the people who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off too, while nobody will be even half a farthing better off except the fellows who get them—and you have just as much right to them as they do.”

“Of course, of course!” said the Jew, who had entered without Oliver noticing. “It’s all very simple, my dear; as simple as can be. Take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! Ha! Ha! He knows the lessons of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands together happily as he agreed with the Dodger’s reasoning, and he chuckled with delight at his pupil’s skill.

The conversation went no further at that time, because the Jew had returned home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen before. The Dodger greeted him as Tom Chitling. He had paused on the stairs to exchange a few flirtatious words with the lady, and now came in."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5a46f6325bec91ea0232d7b3","rewritten_text":"Deprived of ordinary resources, the analyst casts himself into the spirit of his adversary, identifies himself with him, and not infrequently perceives at once the only means—sometimes absurdly simple ones—by which he may lure him into error or hasten him into miscalculation.\n\nWhist has long been remarked for its influence upon what is called the calculating faculty; and men of the highest intellectual order have been known to find in it an apparently inexplicable pleasure, while rejecting chess as frivolous. There is certainly no similar pursuit that so severely exercises the power of analysis. The finest chess-player in Christendom _may_ be little more than the finest player of chess; but skill at whist implies an ability to succeed in all those more serious enterprises in which one mind contends with another. By skill, I mean that perfection of the game which embraces an understanding of _all_ the sources from which legitimate advantage can be obtained. These are not merely numerous but varied, and often lie in regions of thought wholly inaccessible to ordinary comprehension. To watch closely is to remember accurately; and in this respect the concentrated chess-player will perform well at whist, while Hoyle’s rules (being founded upon the game’s simple mechanism) are generally easy enough to understand. Thus a retentive memory, together with adherence to “the book,” is commonly considered the whole of good play. Yet the analyst’s ability appears in matters beyond the boundaries of mere rule. He silently makes countless observations and deductions. His companions may do the same; but the difference in the amount of information acquired lies less in the soundness of the inference than in the quality of the observation. The essential knowledge is knowing _what_ to observe. Our player limits himself in no way; and because the game is his object, he does not dismiss deductions drawn from matters outside it. He studies his partner’s face, comparing it closely with the countenance of each opponent. He examines how the cards are arranged in every hand; often counting trump by trump and honor by honor, through the looks their holders cast upon one another. He marks every change of expression as the play advances, collecting a store of thought from differences showing certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered, he decides whether the person who took it can win another in that suit. He detects a card played as a feint by the manner in which it is cast upon the table. A careless or unintended word; the accidental dropping or turning of a card, together with the concern or indifference shown about hiding it; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are placed; confusion, hesitation, eagerness, or alarm—all furnish his seemingly intuitive perception with signs of the actual state of affairs."}

{"request_id":"c8c0a1ee160b345e1ddf34a3","rewritten_text":"But I must give you warning that I shall tell Sybil everything. She is lunching with me to-morrow to discuss bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a violent temper, a tendency toward gout, or a wife residing in Bayswater, I shall certainly inform her of it all.’

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. ‘I am not afraid,’ he replied. ‘Sybil knows me as thoroughly as I know her.’

‘Ah! I am rather sorry to hear you say that. The soundest foundation for marriage is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical at all; I have simply acquired experience, which amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is longing to have his hand read. Do not tell him that he is engaged to one of the loveliest girls in London, for that was printed in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.

‘My dear Lady Windermere,’ exclaimed the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please let Mr. Podgers remain a little longer. He has just said that I ought to go on the stage, and I am deeply interested.’

‘If he has told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly carry him off. Come here at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.’

‘Well,’ said Lady Jedburgh, making a small _moue_ as she rose from the sofa, ‘if I am not permitted to go on the stage, I must at least be permitted to join the audience.’

‘Naturally; we are all going to be in the audience,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘And now, Mr. Podgers, be certain to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my particular favourites.’

But when Mr. Podgers looked at Lord Arthur’s hand, he became strangely pale and remained silent. A shiver appeared to run through him, while his large bushy eyebrows jerked convulsively, in the peculiar, irritating fashion they assumed when he was perplexed. Then several great drops of sweat appeared upon his yellow brow, like poisonous dew, and his fat fingers became cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur could not help observing these unusual signs of agitation, and for the first time in his life he felt afraid. His first impulse was to flee the room, but he mastered it. Whatever the truth might be, it was better to know the worst than to remain trapped in this dreadful uncertainty.

‘I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We are all waiting,’ cried Lady Windermere in her brisk, impatient fashion, but the cheiromantist gave no answer.

‘I believe Arthur is going on the stage,’ said Lady Jedburgh, ‘and that, after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.’"}

{"request_id":"b29d8071b87cafc4be2eb477","rewritten_text":"But no—there was something even more spectacular than this. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future lay clear before him, glowing with unimaginable splendor. How his name would spread across the world and make people shudder! How gloriously he would plow through the dancing seas in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grisly flag flying at the bow! And at the height of his fame, how he would suddenly appear in the old village and stride into church, brown and weather-beaten, dressed in his black velvet doublet and breeches, his great jackboots, his crimson sash, his belt bristling with horse pistols, his crime-rusted cutlass at his side, his slouch hat crowned with waving plumes, his black flag unfurled, the skull and crossbones displayed upon it—and hear, with swelling ecstasy, the whispers: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was settled; his career was decided. He would run away from home and begin it. He would leave the very next morning. So he had to start preparing at once. He would gather his resources. He went to a rotten log nearby and began digging beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he struck wood that sounded hollow. He placed his hand there and pronounced this incantation solemnly:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. He lifted it and revealed a neatly made little treasure house, its bottom and sides formed of shingles. A marble lay inside. Tom’s astonishment was boundless! He scratched his head in confusion and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he tossed the marble away irritably and stood thinking. The truth was, one of his superstitions had failed him—a superstition that he and all his comrades had always considered infallible. If you buried a marble with the proper incantations, left it undisturbed for two weeks, and then opened the place using the incantation he had just spoken, you would find that every marble you had ever lost had gathered there in the meantime, no matter how far apart they had been. But now the thing had actually, unquestionably failed. Tom’s entire structure of faith was shaken to its foundations. He had often heard of it working, but never of it failing before. It did not occur to him that he himself had tried it several times and afterward could never locate the hiding places. He puzzled over the matter for some time, then finally decided that a witch had interfered and broken the charm."}
