{"request_id":"92b840d493e66ac8b64080a0","rewritten_text":"All this, and much more besides, I would gladly set forth in detail. But, to be concise, I must receive my reward. I long to return to my family and my home; and as the price of any further communication from me—in view of the light I am able to cast upon many highly important branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must request, through the influence of your honorable body, a pardon for the crime I committed in causing the creditors’ deaths upon my departure from Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of the present paper. Its bearer, a resident of the moon, whom I have persuaded and suitably instructed to serve as my messenger to the earth, will await your Excellencies’ pleasure and return to me with the pardon, should it be possible by any means to obtain it.

“I have the honor to be, etc., your Excellencies’ most humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

When Professor Rub-a-dub had finished reading this most extraordinary document, it is said that, in the height of his astonishment, he let his pipe fall to the ground. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and put them in his pocket; then, so completely forgetting both himself and his dignity, he spun around three times on his heel in the very essence of amazement and admiration. There could be no doubt—the pardon must be secured. So Professor Rub-a-dub swore with a hearty oath, and so at last concluded the illustrious Von Underduk, who took his fellow scientist’s arm and, without uttering a word, began making his way home to consider what measures should be taken. On reaching the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor ventured to observe that, since the messenger had seen fit to vanish—doubtless terrified to death by the savage-looking burghers of Rotterdam—the pardon would be of little value, for no one but a man from the moon would undertake a journey across so immense a distance. The burgomaster agreed that this was true, and the matter consequently ended there. Rumors and conjectures, however, did not end with it. Once the letter was published, it produced a host of gossip and opinions. Some of the excessively wise even made themselves absurd by denouncing the entire affair as nothing more than a hoax. {"request_id":"5290df2043738a60f9b22f86","rewritten_text":"Then they went past deserted brickfields. The fog was thinner there, and he could make out the odd bottle-shaped kilns, their orange flames spreading like fans. A dog barked as they passed, while somewhere far off in the darkness a roaming sea-gull cried. The horse stumbled into a rut, swerved, and then broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and clattered once more along streets paved with rough stones. Most windows were unlit, though now and again fantastic shadows appeared against a blind glowing with lamplight. He watched them with curiosity. They moved like monstrous puppets and gestured like living creatures. He loathed them. A heavy anger filled his heart. As they rounded a corner, a woman shouted something from an open doorway, and two men pursued the hansom for nearly a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

It is said that passion causes a person to think in circles. Certainly, with dreadful repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips formed and re-formed those subtle words concerning soul and sense, until he discovered in them, so to speak, the complete expression of his mood, and gave intellectual sanction to passions that would otherwise still have ruled his temper. From one cell of his brain to another crept the same thought; and the fierce desire to live, the most terrible of all human appetites, gathered strength in every trembling nerve and fibre. Ugliness, once hateful to him because it made things real, had now become precious for that very reason. Ugliness was the sole reality. The coarse quarrel, the revolting den, the raw violence of a life thrown into disorder, even the utter degradation of thief and outcast, seemed more vivid in their intense actuality than all the gracious forms of art and the dreamlike shadows of song. These were what he required for forgetfulness. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver pulled up sharply at the head of a dark lane. Above the low roofs and uneven chimney-stacks rose the black masts of ships. Coils of white mist clung to the yards like spectral sails.

“Somewhere around here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked about him. “This will do,” he replied; then, getting out quickly and paying the driver the extra fare he had promised, he walked swiftly toward the quay. Here and there, a lantern shone at the stern of some enormous merchant vessel. Its light trembled and broke apart in the puddles. A red glow came from a steamer bound outward and taking on coal. The slimy pavement resembled a wet mackintosh."}

{"request_id":"ef50cee9203a91417e5c17ed","rewritten_text":"“Mr Elliot looking up with so much respect.”

“Quite delightful!” cried Mrs Clay, though she did not dare look towards Anne. “Exactly like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not say father and son?”

“Oh! I place no restriction on anyone’s words. If you choose to think so! But, truly, I am hardly aware that his attentions are greater than those of other men.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs Clay, raising her hands and eyes, then hiding the rest of her astonishment in a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so worried about him. I did invite him, you know. I sent him away smiling. When I discovered that he really meant to spend all of tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired her friend’s acting. Mrs Clay was able to show such pleasure at the expected and actual arrival of the very man whose presence must be interfering with her main purpose. Mrs Clay could not possibly enjoy seeing Mr Elliot; yet she wore a calm, obliging expression and seemed entirely satisfied with being able to devote only half as much attention to Sir Walter as she otherwise would have done.

For Anne herself, seeing Mr Elliot enter the room was extremely distressing, and having him come near and speak to her was painful. She had already felt that he could not always be sincere, but now she saw insincerity in everything. His respectful attention to her father, compared with what he had said before, was hateful; and when she remembered his cruel treatment of Mrs Smith, she could scarcely endure his present smiles and gentleness, or listen to his false expressions of good feeling.

She intended to avoid changing her manner so much that he might challenge her about it. It was very important to escape any questions or public scene; but she meant to be as clearly cool towards him as their family relationship allowed, and to quietly withdraw from the unnecessary intimacy into which she had gradually been drawn. Accordingly, she was more guarded and cooler than she had been the previous evening.

He wanted to revive her curiosity about how and where he had once heard her praised, and very much wished to enjoy being questioned further. But the spell was broken. He realized that the excitement and liveliness of a public room were needed to stir his modest cousin’s vanity; at least, he saw that he could not achieve it now through any of the attempts he could make while the others’ stronger claims occupied her attention."}

content.text: {"request_id":"439558861a33628227d7b36e","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the dead man’s luxury was a marvel.\n\nHe next gave his attention to embroideries and tapestries, which served as frescoes in the cold chambers of northern Europe. As he pursued the subject—and he possessed an extraordinary ability to become wholly absorbed, for the time being, in whatever occupied him—he was nearly saddened by the thought of the destruction time wrought upon beautiful and wondrous things. He, at least, had escaped such decay. Summer came after summer, and the yellow jonquils flowered and faded again and again, while nights of horror repeated the tale of their disgrace, yet he remained unchanged. No winter damaged his face or dimmed his flowerlike freshness. How unlike this was the fate of material things! What had become of them? Where was the vast crocus-coloured robe, embroidered by brown girls for Athena’s delight, upon which the gods battled the giants? Where was the enormous velarium Nero had spread over the Colosseum at Rome—that purple Titan’s sail depicting the starry heavens, with Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white steeds with gilded reins? He wished to see the strange table-napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, displaying every delicacy and dish that might be desired at a feast; the funeral cloth of King Chilperic, bearing its three hundred golden bees; the extravagant robes that provoked the Bishop of Pontus and were decorated with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—all, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat once worn by Charles of Orleans, whose sleeves carried the verses of a song beginning “_Madame, je suis tout joyeux_,” with its musical accompaniment worked in gold thread, every note—square-shaped in those days—made from four pearls. He read of the chamber prepared at the palace in Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in broidery, and blazoned with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly ornamented with the arms of the queen, the whole worked in gold.” Catherine de Medicis had a mourning-bed made of black velvet, sprinkled with crescents and suns. Its damask curtains bore leafy wreaths and garlands against a ground of gold and silver, their edges trimmed with pearl embroidery, and it stood in a room hung with rows of the queen’s devices, cut in black velvet on cloth of silver. Louis XIV. had fifteen-foot-high caryatides embroidered in gold in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"875da5cf29d2c43429ce447f","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in astonishment for several moments, then, perceiving that he was perfectly serious, wrote an address on a sheet of paper, put his initials to it, and passed it across the table.

‘Scotland Yard would pay handsomely to learn this address, my dear fellow.’

‘They won’t get it,’ cried Lord Arthur, laughing. After warmly shaking the young Russian’s hand, he hurried downstairs, looked at the paper, and ordered the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

Once there, he dismissed the man and wandered along Greek Street until he reached a place known as Bayle’s Court. Passing beneath the archway, he entered a strange _cul-de-sac_, seemingly occupied by a French Laundry, for a complete web of clothes-lines ran from house to house, with white linen fluttering in the morning breeze. He went to the very end and knocked at a small green house. After a delay, during which every window in the court turned into a blurred cluster of watching faces, the door was opened by a somewhat rough foreigner, who asked in very poor English what he wanted. Lord Arthur gave him the paper Count Rouvaloff had supplied. On seeing it, the man bowed and ushered Lord Arthur into a shabby front parlour on the ground floor. A few moments later Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in, a wine-stained napkin tied around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

‘Count Rouvaloff has given me a letter of introduction to you,’ said Lord Arthur, bowing, ‘and I should like a brief interview concerning a business matter. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I wish you to provide me with an explosive clock.’

‘Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,’ said the genial little German with a laugh. ‘You need not look so startled; it is my business to know everyone, and I recall seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I trust her ladyship is in excellent health. Will you sit with me while I finish breakfast? There is some splendid _pâté_, and my friends are good enough to claim that my Rhine wine is superior to anything served at the German Embassy.’ Before Lord Arthur had recovered from his surprise at being recognised, he was seated in the back room, drinking the most exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale-yellow hock glass bearing the Imperial monogram, and conversing as amicably as possible with the celebrated conspirator.

‘Explosive clocks,’ said Herr Winckelkopf, ‘are not especially suitable for export abroad, because even when they manage to pass through Customs, the trains run so irregularly that they generally explode before reaching their intended destination.’"}

{"request_id":"77b2f5a200bf0b8b86c3dc4e","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire, never picked up any book for his own amusement except the Baronetage. There he found occupation for an idle hour and comfort in a troubled one; there his faculties were stirred to admiration and respect as he contemplated the small surviving number of the earliest patents; there any unpleasant feelings caused by domestic affairs naturally changed into pity and contempt as he turned through the nearly endless creations of the last century; and there, if every other page failed him, he could read his own history with an interest that never diminished. This was the page at which his favourite volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by whom (who died in 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a stillborn son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

That was exactly how the paragraph had originally come from the printer; but Sir Walter had improved it by adding, for his own and his family’s information, these words after the date of Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and by inserting with perfect accuracy the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

Then came the history and rise of the ancient and respectable family, in the usual language: how it had first settled in Cheshire; how it was mentioned by Dugdale; how its members had served as high sheriff, represented a borough in three successive parliaments, shown loyalty, and received the dignity of a baronet in the first year of Charles II, along with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. Altogether, it filled two handsome duodecimo pages and ended with the arms and motto: “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed once more by Sir Walter’s handwriting:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity of appearance and of position. He had been remarkably handsome in his youth and, at fifty-four, was still a very fine man. Few women could care more about their appearance than he did, nor could the valet of any newly made lord be more pleased with the place he occupied in society. He considered the blessing of beauty inferior only to the blessing of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, who possessed both gifts, was the constant object of his deepest respect and devotion.

His good looks and rank had one legitimate claim on his attachment, since to them he must have owed a wife of far superior character to anything his own deserved."}

{"request_id":"5df56e97abb647b3d83c1fe7","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had secured a very fine house in Camden Place, an elevated and dignified position, suited to a man of consequence; and he and Elizabeth were both established there, greatly to their satisfaction.

Anne entered it with a sinking heart, expecting to be confined there for many months, and saying anxiously to herself, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Yet the welcome she received was unexpectedly cordial, and did her good. Her father and sister were pleased to see her, partly so that they might show her the house and its furnishings, and they greeted her kindly. When she made a fourth at dinner, her presence was remarked upon as an advantage.

Mrs Clay was very agreeable, and smiled a great deal, though her politeness and smiles seemed more habitual. Anne had always supposed that she would make the proper pretence upon her arrival, but the others’ attentions were unforeseen. They were plainly in excellent spirits, and she soon heard the reasons. They had no desire to hear from her. After allowing for some compliments about being greatly missed in their former neighbourhood, which Anne could not offer, they made only a few weak enquiries before the conversation became entirely their own. Uppercross inspired no interest, and Kellynch very little: everything was Bath.

They were delighted to assure her that Bath had surpassed their expectations in every particular. Their house was certainly the finest in Camden Place; their drawing-rooms possessed many clear advantages over all the others they had seen or heard about, and the superiority extended equally to the manner of decoration and the taste of the furniture. Their acquaintance was eagerly sought. Everyone wished to visit them. They had declined many introductions, yet people whose names they did not know were constantly leaving cards.

Here were abundant sources of pleasure. Could Anne be surprised that her father and sister were happy? She might not be surprised, but she had to sigh that her father felt no humiliation in the change, saw nothing to regret in the responsibilities and dignity of a resident landowner, and found so much to boast of in the small distinctions of a town; and she had to sigh, smile, and wonder as Elizabeth flung open the folding doors and walked proudly from one drawing-room into the other, boasting of their size; at the thought that the woman who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall could find room for pride between two walls perhaps thirty feet apart.

But this was not all they had to make them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

{"request_id":"cbad5c555e17256c65f2a9ad","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse was handsome, clever, and rich. With a comfortable home and a cheerful nature, she seemed to possess many of life’s greatest blessings, and had lived almost twenty-one years with very little to trouble or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters born to a deeply loving, indulgent father. After her sister married, Emma had become the mistress of his house at a very young age. Her mother had died so long before that Emma could remember little more than a vague sense of her affection. Her place had been filled by an excellent governess who had come close to being a mother in her love for Emma.

Miss Taylor had been part of Mr. Woodhouse’s household for sixteen years, acting less as a governess than as a friend. She loved both daughters, but Emma especially. Between them, the relationship was more like that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor officially stopped being governess, her gentle nature had kept her from imposing much control. Now that any authority she had once held was long gone, they lived together as two very close friends. Emma did whatever she pleased, respecting Miss Taylor’s judgment but usually following her own.

The true problems in Emma’s situation were that she had too much power to get her own way and thought rather too highly of herself. These weaknesses threatened to spoil her many pleasures. But she was not yet aware of the danger, and did not consider them misfortunes at all.

Then sorrow came—a mild sorrow, but not in the form of any unpleasant realization. Miss Taylor married. Losing Miss Taylor was what first brought Emma real grief. On the wedding day of her beloved friend, Emma first sat sadly thinking about a future without her. After the wedding, when the newly married couple had left, Emma and her father were alone at dinner, with no third person to brighten the long evening. As usual, her father fell asleep after dinner, leaving her only to sit and think about what she had lost.

The marriage promised every kind of happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston had an excellent character, a comfortable fortune, an appropriate age, and pleasant manners. Emma could take some satisfaction in remembering how generously and selflessly she had encouraged and helped bring about the match. Still, it had been a miserable morning for her. She would feel Miss Taylor’s absence every hour of every day. She remembered her past kindness—the love and care of sixteen years: how Miss Taylor had taught and played with her from the age of five, devoted all her energy to keeping her happy and entertained when she was well, and cared for her through the many illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"77e275e906603da5971a53c6","rewritten_text":"“This must have been around that particular period of Mr Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “which has always aroused my special curiosity. It must have been about the same time that he became acquainted with my father and sister. I never knew him personally; I only heard about him; but there was something in his behaviour then, towards my father and sister, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, which I could never quite reconcile with his present character. It seemed to indicate a very different kind of man.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” cried Mrs Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but I heard him talk of them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he declined to go. I may be able to satisfy you on matters you would scarcely expect; and as for his marriage, I knew everything about it at the time. I was acquainted with all the arguments on both sides; I was the friend to whom he confided his hopes and intentions; and although I had not known his wife before—her lower position in society, indeed, made that impossible—I knew her throughout the rest of her life, or at least until the last two years, and can answer anything you may wish to ask.”

“Nay,” said Anne, “I have no particular inquiry to make concerning her. I have always understood that they were not a happy couple. But I should like to know why, at that stage of his life, he slighted my father’s acquaintance as he did. My father was certainly inclined to show him every kind and proper attention. Why did Mr Elliot withdraw?”

“Mr Elliot,” replied Mrs Smith, “had one aim at that time: to make his fortune, and by a somewhat faster means than the law. He resolved to achieve it through marriage. At least, he was determined not to damage it by marrying imprudently; and I know it was his opinion—whether rightly or not, I cannot of course judge—that your father and sister, in their civilities and invitations, intended a match between the heir and the young lady, and that such a marriage could never satisfy his notions of wealth and independence. That was why he withdrew, I assure you. He told me the entire story. He kept nothing from me. It was curious that, having just left you in Bath, my first and chief acquaintance after marrying should be your cousin; and that, through him, I should continually hear about your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"3723ed09f216183f99987f34","rewritten_text":"This brief explanation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma considerable pleasure. It was one of the pleasant memories of the ball, which she walked around the lawn the next morning to enjoy. She was extremely glad that they had reached such a good understanding about the Eltons, and that their opinions of both husband and wife were so similar; and his praise of Harriet, his concession in her favour, was especially gratifying. The Eltons’ impertinence, which for a few minutes had threatened to ruin the rest of her evening, had become the cause of some of its greatest satisfactions; and she looked forward to another happy result—the cure of Harriet’s infatuation. From Harriet’s way of speaking about the incident before they left the ballroom, she had strong hopes. It seemed as if Harriet’s eyes had suddenly been opened, enabling her to see that Mr. Elton was not the superior creature she had believed him to be. The fever was over, and Emma could have little fear that harmful politeness would quicken the pulse again. She relied on the Eltons’ ill feeling to provide all the pointed neglect that might still be necessary. Harriet rational, Frank Churchill not too deeply in love, and Mr. Knightley unwilling to quarrel with her—how happy a summer must lie before her!

She was not to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her that he could not allow himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, since he was expected home by midday. She did not regret it.

Having arranged all these matters, examined them from every angle, and set them right, she was just turning toward the house, her spirits renewed for the demands of the two little boys as well as their grandfather, when the great iron sweep-gate opened, and two people entered whom she had never expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—Harriet herself! One moment was enough to convince her that something extraordinary had occurred. Harriet looked pale and frightened, while he was trying to comfort her. The iron gates and the front door were not twenty yards apart; all three were soon in the hall, and Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted.

A young lady who faints must be revived; questions must be answered, and surprises explained. Such events are deeply interesting, but their suspense cannot last long. Within a few minutes Emma knew the whole story.

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also attended the ball, had gone out walking together and taken the Richmond road, which, though it appeared public enough to be safe, had soon alarmed them. About half a mile beyond Highbury, after a sudden turn, and heavily shaded by elms on both sides, it became secluded for a considerable distance; and when the young ladies had gone some way along it, they suddenly saw, a short distance ahead, on a wider patch of grass beside the road, a group of gypsies."}

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote to his brother again. The main purpose of his letter was to tell them that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

“It was very much my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree that leaving that regiment is highly advisable, both for his sake and my niece’s. Mr. Wickham intends to join the Regulars; and among his former friends there are still some able and willing to help him in the army. He has been promised an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, now stationed in the north. It is an advantage that it should be so far from this part of the kingdom. He gives fair promises; and I hope that, among different people, where each will have a reputation to protect, they will both behave more prudently. I have written to Colonel Forster, informing him of our present arrangements and asking him to satisfy Mr. Wickham’s various creditors in and near Brighton by promising speedy payment, for which I have made myself responsible. Will you also take the trouble to give similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton? I shall enclose a list, based on the information he has given. {"request_id":"42ca43f139890e9fdd2c8a23","rewritten_text":"“Well, everybody lives that way, Huck.”

“Tom, it makes no difference. I ain’t everybody, and I can’t stand it. It’s awful being tied down like that. And food comes too easily—I don’t care about eating when it’s that way. I have to ask before I can go fishing; I have to ask before I can go swimming—darned if I don’t have to ask before doing everything. And I had to talk so politely that it wasn’t any fun. Every day I had to go up into the attic and let loose for a while, just to get the proper taste back in my mouth, or I’d have died, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me yell, gape, stretch, or scratch in front of people—” [Then, with a sudden burst of special anger and hurt]—“And blast it, she prayed all the time! I never saw such a woman! I had to shove off, Tom—I simply had to. Besides, school is about to start, and I would have had to go. Well, I wouldn’t stand that, Tom. Look here, Tom, being rich isn’t what people say it is. It’s nothing but worry and worry, sweat and sweat, and wishing you were dead all the time. These clothes suit me now, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never going to leave them again. Tom, I never would have gotten into all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money. So you take my share along with yours, give me a dime once in a while—not often, because I don’t care about anything unless it’s pretty hard to get—and go ask the widow to let me go.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It wouldn’t be fair. Besides, if you try living this way a little longer, you’ll come to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—the way I’d like sitting on a hot stove if I sat there long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed, stuffy houses. I like the woods, the river, and hogsheads, and I’m going to stick with them. Blast it all! Just when we had guns, a cave, and everything ready for robbing, this foolish business has to come up and ruin it all!”

Tom saw his chance—

“Look here, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from becoming a robber.”

“No! Oh, good luck; are you really serious, Tom?”

“Just as serious as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you join the gang if you aren’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s happiness disappeared.

“Can’t let me join, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"f8de2c575c5b28a76331d11e","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?” demanded Oliver.

“Hush!” replied the Dodger. “Do you see that old fellow at the bookstall?”

“The old gentleman across the street?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A first-rate mark,” observed Master Charley Bates.

Oliver looked from one to the other in the greatest surprise, but he was given no chance to ask questions; the two boys had already crossed the road stealthily and slipped in behind the old gentleman toward whom his attention had been directed. Oliver followed a few paces behind them and, uncertain whether to go forward or turn back, stood watching in silent amazement.

The old gentleman looked thoroughly respectable, with a powdered head and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar and white trousers, and carried a smart bamboo cane beneath his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood there reading as intently as though he were seated in his own study, in his favorite chair. It was quite possible that he imagined himself there; for his absorption made it clear that he noticed neither the bookstall, nor the street, nor the boys, nor anything at all except the book itself. He read straight through it, turning the page when he reached the bottom, beginning at the top line of the next, and continuing steadily with the greatest interest and eagerness.

What were Oliver’s horror and alarm, as he stood a few paces away with his eyes opened as wide as they could go, when he saw the Dodger thrust his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief? He watched him pass it to Charley Bates, and then saw them both run around the corner at full speed!

In an instant, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, watches, jewels, and the Jew rushed into the boy’s mind.

For a moment he stood there, his blood tingling through every vein with terror until he felt as though he were standing in a fire. Then, confused and frightened, he ran; without knowing what he was doing, he fled as fast as his feet could carry him.

It all happened within a minute. At the very moment Oliver began to run, the old gentleman put his hand into his pocket, discovered that his handkerchief was gone, and turned sharply around. Seeing the boy racing away at such speed, he naturally concluded that Oliver was the thief. Shouting “Stop, thief!” with all his strength, he ran after him, still holding the book."}

{"request_id":"63be236c4d2d6776058e5a38","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but wait a little. Go on, Joseph. Well done! Go on!”

“What would the company present say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That abject hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded once more and said, with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Follow her up, Joseph!”

“Then, to finish the matter,” said Joe, handing the bag delightedly to my sister, “it’s five-and-twenty pounds.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pounds, Mum,” echoed that basest of swindlers, Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand; “and it’s no more than your merits (as I said when my opinion was requested), and I wish you joy of the money!”

Had the villain stopped there, his case would have been bad enough, but he deepened his guilt by proceeding to take me into custody, with a patronage that made all his former criminality seem insignificant.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always carry through whatever they begin. This boy must be bound, immediately. That’s _my_ way. Bound immediately.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister, clutching the money, “we’re deeply indebted to you.”

“Never mind me, Mum,” returned that diabolical cornchandler. “A pleasure is a pleasure everywhere. But this boy, you know; we must have him bound. I said I would see to it—to tell you the truth.”

The Justices were sitting in the nearby Town Hall, and we went over at once to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the presence of the Magistrates. I say we went over, but Pumblechook pushed me along exactly as though I had just picked a pocket or set fire to a hayrick; indeed, the general belief in Court was that I had been caught red-handed. As Pumblechook shoved me ahead of him through the crowd, I heard some people say, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s a young ’un, too, but looks bad, don’t he?” One person with a mild and benevolent face even gave me a tract decorated with a woodcut of a malicious young man equipped with a complete sausage-shop of fetters, and entitled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall seemed a strange place to me, with pews higher than those in a church—and people leaning over them to watch—and mighty Justices, one with a powdered head, reclining in chairs with folded arms, or taking snuff, or sleeping, or writing, or reading the newspapers—and several shining black portraits on the walls, which my unartistic eye saw as a mixture of hardbake and sticking-plaster."}

{"request_id":"68f04781ca23263404bbadfd","rewritten_text":"But my father was at my side to comfort me and banish painful memories with brighter hopes: I thought it sweet to grieve, since he might dry my tears.

Again, he turned my thoughts from sorrow by comparing it with his own despair when he lost my mother. Even then I shuddered at the picture he painted of his passions: he possessed a poet’s imagination, and when he described the whirlwind that had torn through his feelings, he gave his words such a vivid stamp of life that I believed him even as I trembled. I wondered how he could ever have returned to the duties of life after his wild thoughts had seemed to bring him into kinship with the unearthly; as he spoke, the ideas he conveyed were so tremendous that it seemed the human heart was far too limited to contain them. His feelings appeared more suited to a spirit dwelling amid earthquakes and volcanoes than to one enclosed in a mortal body and human form. But these were only memories; he had changed since then. Now he was all affection and gentleness; and whenever I looked up at him in wonder as he spoke, the smile upon his lips assured me that his heart was filled with the mildest passions.

Two months after my aunt’s death, we moved to London, where my father guided me toward deeper studies than those that had previously occupied me. My progress delighted him; he remained with me throughout my studies and helped with, or took part in, every lesson. We saw much of society, and no day passed without my father trying to adorn it with some fresh pleasure. The tender attachment he felt for me, and the love and reverence with which I returned it, cast a charm over every moment. The hours passed slowly, for every minute was put to use; we lived more in a week than many people do in several months, and the variety and novelty of our pleasures gave each one its relish.

We were constantly making excursions together. Whether to visit lovely scenery, admire fine paintings, or sometimes merely to seek whatever amusement chance might offer, I was always happy when near my father. I regretted whenever a third person joined us; yet if I glanced uneasily toward my father, his eyes would rest upon me, shining with tenderness, and instantly restore joy to my heart. O, hours of profound delight! Brief as you were, memory makes you last as long as an entire life when viewed through the veil of grief that rose immediately afterward, as though to hide you from my sight."}

{"request_id":"3178bb8943b9aebd06d3aa2f","rewritten_text":"“Nothing but a tick.”

“Where did you get him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What will you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell him.”

“All right. It’s a mighty small tick, anyway.”

“Oh, anyone can catch a tick that doesn’t belong to them. I’m satisfied with it. It’s good enough for me.”

“Sure, there are ticks everywhere. I could have a thousand if I wanted to.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know perfectly well you can’t. This is an early tick, I reckon. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for him.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom took out a scrap of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it wistfully. The temptation was very strong. At last he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the gap.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry, “it’s a trade.”

Tom shut the tick inside the percussion-cap box that had recently served as the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom reached the small, isolated frame schoolhouse, he walked in briskly, with the manner of someone who had come as quickly and honestly as possible. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike speed. The master, enthroned in his large splint-bottom armchair, had been dozing, lulled by the sleepy hum of study. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that when his full name was spoken, trouble was coming.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to take refuge in a lie when he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized through love’s electric sympathy; beside that figure was the only vacant place on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He said at once:

“_I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!_”

The master’s pulse seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The hum of study died away. The pupils wondered whether this reckless boy had lost his mind. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no mistaking the words.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astonishing confession I have ever heard. A mere whipping will not answer for this offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm continued until it was tired and the supply of switches had been noticeably reduced. Then came the order:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The titter that rippled around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth that effect came more from his reverent awe of his unknown idol and the fearful delight contained in his extraordinary good fortune.”"}

{"request_id":"7128bb25a3b6a8ebb85af254","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father, of course, may spare you, if your mother can. Daughters are never so important to a father. And if you stay another _month_ in full, I shall be able to take one of you as far as London, since I am going there in early June for a week; and as Dawson has no objection to the barouche-box, there will be ample room for one of you—and, indeed, if the weather happens to be cool, I should not object to taking you both, since neither of you is large.”

“You are very kind, madam; but I believe we must follow our original plan.”

Lady Catherine appeared resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot endure the thought of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is highly improper. You must find some way to send someone. I have the greatest dislike in the world to that sort of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended, according to their position in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two male servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne could not have appeared properly in any other manner. I am extremely attentive to such matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad I thought to mention it; for it would truly be discreditable to _you_ to let them go alone.”

“My uncle is sending a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a male servant, does he? I am very glad you have someone who considers such matters. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you mention my name at the Bell, they will attend to you.”

Lady Catherine had many other questions about their journey; and since she did not answer them all herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention—which she considered fortunate; for, with her mind so occupied, she might otherwise have forgotten where she was. Reflection had to be saved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she surrendered to it as her greatest relief; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, during which she could indulge in all the pleasure of painful memories.

She was well on her way to knowing Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She studied every sentence; and her feelings toward its writer were sometimes entirely different. When she recalled the manner in which he had addressed her, she was still filled with indignation; but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and reproached him, her anger turned upon herself, and his disappointed feelings became an object of compassion."}

{"request_id":"19abad86b6a7a3078431eac7","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” said the spy in the most contemptuous manner, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness to ask this other gentleman, so much your junior, whether he can possibly reconcile it with his position to play that Ace he mentioned. I admit that I am a spy, and that it is considered a disreputable position—though someone must fill it; but this gentleman is no spy, so why should he lower himself by becoming one?”

“I play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, answering for himself and checking his watch, “without the slightest hesitation, in a very few minutes.”

“I should have hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the discussion, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I could show no greater respect for your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I have made up my mind completely.”

The spy’s polished manner, strangely at odds with his deliberately rough clothing, and probably with his usual behavior, was so checked by Carton’s unreadable expression—Carton was a mystery even to men wiser and more honest than Barsad—that it faltered and failed him. While he hesitated, Carton resumed his former pose of studying the cards and said:

“And now that I think of it, I have a strong feeling that I hold another good card not yet mentioned. That friend and fellow Sheep who said he had been pasturing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” the spy replied quickly.

“French, eh?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, seeming not to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well, he may be.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy, “though it isn’t important.”

“Though it isn’t important,” Carton repeated mechanically—“though it isn’t important—No, it isn’t important. No. And yet I know the face.”

“I don’t think so. I’m sure you don’t. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“Can’t be,” Sydney Carton muttered, looking back over the matter and idly swirling his glass, which fortunately was a small one. “Can’t be. He spoke good French. Yet I thought he seemed like a foreigner?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, striking his open hand against the table as the truth suddenly became clear to him. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now you’re being hasty, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that tilted his aquiline nose even farther to one side. “There you truly give me an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"a1aa94277872d86870b80a53","rewritten_text":"“What conclusion, then, follows? What impression has this made upon your imagination?”

I felt my flesh creep as Dupin asked me this. “A madman,” I said, “has committed the deed—some raving lunatic escaped from a nearby _Maison de Santé._”

“In some respects,” he replied, “your idea is not without merit. But the voices of madmen, even during their wildest fits, never resemble that peculiar voice heard upon the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and their language, however incoherent in meaning, always retains the coherence of syllables. Besides, a madman’s hair is not like what I now hold in my hand. I pulled this small tuft from Madame L’Espanaye’s tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I cried, completely shaken; “this hair is extraordinary—this is not _human_ hair.”

“I have not claimed that it is,” he said; “but before we settle that question, I want you to examine the little sketch I have drawn on this paper. It is a _fac-simile_ of what one part of the testimony described as ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of fingernails,’ upon the throat of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and another part (by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne) called a ‘series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’

“You will see,” my friend continued, spreading the paper on the table before us, “that this drawing suggests a firm, unyielding grip. There is no sign of _slipping_. Each finger has held—perhaps until the victim died—the terrible grasp by which it first sank into the flesh. Now try to place all your fingers simultaneously into the corresponding impressions as you see them.”

I tried, but failed.

“Perhaps we are not testing this fairly,” he said. “The paper lies on a flat surface, while the human throat is cylindrical. Here is a piece of wood whose circumference is approximately that of the throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.”

I did so, but the difficulty was even clearer than before. “This,” I said, “is the mark of no human hand.”

“Now read,” Dupin replied, “this passage from Cuvier.”

It was a detailed anatomical and general description of the large fulvous Ourang-Outang of the East Indian Islands. The gigantic size, immense strength and agility, savage ferocity, and imitative tendencies of these mammals are well known to everyone. At once, I understood the full horror of the murder.

“The description of the digits,” I said when I finished reading, “corresponds exactly with this drawing.”"}

{"request_id":"306432aad8dd203b6d9c7c55","rewritten_text":"The exquisite gentlemen of the highest breeding wore small dangling ornaments that tinkled as they moved languidly; these golden fetters sounded like tiny precious bells. Together with the rustling of silk, brocade, and fine linen, their noise stirred a flutter in the air that wafted Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger far away.

Dress was the one unfailing talisman and charm for keeping everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals of Justice, and all society (save the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball descended to the Common Executioner, who, in obedience to the charm, was obliged to officiate “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe being uncommon—Monsieur Paris, as it was the episcopal fashion among his fellow Professors of the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, to call him, presided in this elegant attire. And who among the company at Monseigneur’s reception in that year of our Lord seventeen hundred and eighty could doubt that a system founded upon a frizzled, powdered, gold-laced, pumped, white-silk-stockinged hangman would last until the stars went out?

When Monseigneur had relieved his four bearers of their burdens and drunk his chocolate, he ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holiests opened and came forth. Then there was submission, cringing and fawning, servility, and abject humiliation! As for bowing in body and spirit, nothing remained in that regard for Heaven—which may have been one reason, among others, that Monseigneur’s worshippers never troubled it.

Giving one fortunate slave a word of promise and another a smile, whispering to one and waving his hand to the next, Monseigneur passed affably through his rooms toward the distant region of the Circumference of Truth. There, he turned and came back, and in due time had himself shut within his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, after which he was seen no more.

The spectacle ended, the flutter in the air grew into quite a small storm, and the precious little bells rang down the stairs. Soon only one person remained of the whole crowd. With his hat beneath his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, he slowly made his way among the mirrors toward the exit.

“I devote you,” said this person, pausing at the last door and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he shook the snuff from his fingers as though shaking dust from his feet, and quietly walked downstairs."}

{"request_id":"4ad6610170cf972f4e060059","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often, you’d see one poke its nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she had to keep things nearby to throw at them when she was alone, or they wouldn’t leave her in peace. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot and said she was generally a good shot with it, but she had strained her arm a day or two before and didn’t know whether she could throw accurately now. Still, she watched for an opportunity and immediately hurled it at a rat; but she missed badly and cried, “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to get away before the old man returned, but naturally I didn’t show it. I took the lead, and when the first rat poked out its nose, I threw; if it had stayed where it was, it would have been a very sick rat. She said that was excellent and reckoned I would hit the next one. She went to retrieve the lump of lead and brought it back, along with a hank of yarn she wanted me to help her with. I held up both hands, and she placed the hank over them, continuing to talk about her affairs and her husband’s. But she broke off to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, where it’s handy.”

So she dropped the lump into my lap at that very moment. I clamped my legs together over it, and she continued talking. But only for about a minute. Then she removed the hank, looked me directly in the face with a pleasant expression, and said:

“Come now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—or what is it?”

I suppose I shook like a leaf, and I hardly knew what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you, either. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it; and, more than that, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice, that’s all. It isn’t anything. There’s no harm in it. You were treated badly, and you decided to run away. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"6dd3c6ef20e35c64dca60269","rewritten_text":"Then I repeated to myself the beautiful passage describing Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise. I thought how sweet it would be, as I wandered along those lovely banks, to see the chariot of light descend with my long-lost parent, restored to me at last. While I waited for that moment, I imagined gathering the flowers that grew there into a wreath and crowning myself with joy. I would sing _sul margine d’un rio_, my father’s favorite song, and my voice, drifting through the still air, would tell him, wherever he sat waiting for our reunion, that his daughter had come. Then the mark of misery would have vanished from my brow, and I could raise my eyes without fear to meet his, which always shone with the gentle light of innocent love. When I thought of the magical expression in those deep eyes, I wept, but softly, afraid that my sobs might disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely lost in this dream that I walked on without noticing where I was going. At last I bent down to pick a flower for my wreath on that barren plain, where no flower grew. Then I awoke from my daydream and realized that I did not know where I was.

The sun had set, and the rosy color it had given the clouds was almost gone. Wind swept across the plain. I looked around but saw nothing that showed me where I was. I had lost my way and tried in vain to find the path. I continued wandering, while the growing darkness erased every mark that might have guided me. At last everything was hidden in the deepest night. I grew tired, and since my servant was to spend the night in the nearby village, my absence would alarm no one. I was safe in that lonely place from every intruder, so I decided to remain there until morning. In truth, I was too tired to walk farther. The air was cold, but I did not care about my physical discomfort. During my two years of solitude, I had become used to every kind of weather, since no change of season had stopped my constant wandering.

I lay on the grass, surrounded by darkness that not even the faintest ray of light could enter. There was no sound, for the deep night had put the insects to sleep—the only creatures living in that lonely place, where no tree or bush could shelter anything else. A wonderful silence filled the air. It calmed my senses while stirring my soul; my mind rushed from one image to another and seemed to grasp eternity."}

{"request_id":"5b6917414b7c736fd2c7203a","rewritten_text":"But that is of little consequence.”

“I may as well ask,” she replied, “why, with such an obvious intention of offending and insulting me, you thought fit to tell me that you liked me against your will, your reason, and even your character? Was that not some excuse for rudeness, if I _was_ rude? But I have other causes for resentment. You know that I have. If my own feelings had not already decided against you, if they had been indifferent, or even favourable, do you imagine that anything could persuade me to accept the man who has been the instrument of destroying, perhaps forever, the happiness of a dearly loved sister?”

As she spoke these words, Mr. Darcy changed colour; but the emotion soon passed, and he listened without trying to interrupt her as she went on,--

“I have every reason to think badly of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous conduct you displayed _there_. You cannot deny that you were the chief, if not the sole, means of separating them, of exposing one to the world’s censure for fickleness and instability, the other to its ridicule for disappointed hopes, and of involving them both in the deepest misery.”

She stopped, and observed with considerable indignation that he listened in a manner showing himself entirely untouched by remorse. He even regarded her with a smile of affected disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did so?” she repeated.

He then answered with assumed calmness, “I have no intention of denying that I did all within my power to part my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. I have treated _him_ more kindly than I have treated myself.”

Elizabeth scorned the appearance of noticing this courteous remark, though its meaning was not lost on her, nor was it likely to win her over.

“But this is not the only matter,” she continued, “on which my dislike rests. My opinion of you had been formed long before it occurred. Your character was revealed in the account I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. What have you to say on that subject? By what fancied act of friendship can you defend yourself here? or beneath what false representation can you deceive others?”

“You take a lively interest in that gentleman’s affairs,” said Darcy, in a less composed tone and with a deeper flush.

“Who, knowing what his misfortunes have been, could help taking an interest in him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated contemptuously,--“yes, his misfortunes have indeed been considerable.”

“And caused by you,” cried Elizabeth energetically; “You have brought him to his present condition of poverty--comparative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"d86c09c18e0a722fdedb65b7","rewritten_text":"“What conclusion, then, has followed? What impression have I produced upon your imagination?”

A shudder passed over me as Dupin put the question. “A madman,” I answered, “has committed the deed—some raving lunatic escaped from a neighboring _Maison de Santé._”

“In certain respects,” he replied, “your notion is not without relevance. Yet the voices of madmen, even during their wildest paroxysms, are never found to correspond with that singular voice heard upon the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and their speech, however incoherent in its words, always possesses the coherence of syllabification. Moreover, a madman’s hair is not like that which I now hold. I drew this small tuft from the tightly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you can infer from it.”

“Dupin!” I cried, thoroughly unnerved; “this hair is extraordinary—this is not _human_ hair.”

“I have not claimed that it is,” said he; “but before settling that question, I want you to examine the little sketch I have made on this paper. It is a _fac-simile_ of what one part of the testimony calls ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails,’ upon Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what another portion (given by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne) describes as a ‘series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’

“You will observe,” my friend continued, laying the paper upon the table between us, “that the drawing suggests a firm, unchanging grip. There is no sign of _slipping_. Each finger has remained—perhaps until the victim’s death—in the dreadful grasp by which it first sank into the flesh. Now try placing all your fingers simultaneously into the corresponding impressions as they appear here.”

I tried, but could not do so.

“Perhaps we are not testing the matter fairly,” he said. “The paper lies upon a flat surface, whereas the human throat is cylindrical. Here is a piece of wood whose circumference is approximately that of the throat. Wrap the drawing around it, and make the attempt once more.”

I did as he instructed; but the difficulty was still more apparent. “This,” I said, “is the mark of no human hand.”

“Now read,” Dupin answered, “this passage from Cuvier.”

It was a detailed anatomical and general description of the great fulvous Ourang-Outang of the East Indian Islands. The enormous size, extraordinary strength and agility, savage ferocity, and imitative tendencies of these mammals are sufficiently familiar to everyone. At once I grasped the full horror of the murder.

“The description of the digits,” I said when I had finished reading, “corresponds exactly with this drawing.”"}

{"request_id":"53d9dcdac9eaeef4fb0f3894","rewritten_text":"His understanding and disposition, though different from her own, would have fulfilled all her hopes. Their union must have benefited them both: her ease and animation might have softened his mind and improved his manners; while from his judgment, knowledge, and experience of the world, she would have gained advantages of greater consequence.

But no such fortunate marriage could now show the admiring multitude what true conjugal happiness was. A union of an entirely different character, and one that made the other impossible, was soon to take place in their family.

How Wickham and Lydia were to be maintained in tolerable independence, she could not conceive. Yet how little lasting happiness could belong to a couple brought together only because their passions had proved stronger than their virtue, she could readily imagine.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote once more to his brother. In answer to Mr. Bennet’s acknowledgments, he replied briefly, assuring him of his eagerness to advance the welfare of any member of his family; and ended by begging that the matter might never be mentioned to him again. The chief purpose of his letter was to tell them that Mr. Wickham had determined to leave the militia.

“It was my earnest wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I believe you will agree with me in thinking a removal from that corps highly advisable, both for his sake and my niece’s. Mr. Wickham means to enter the Regulars; and among his former friends are still some who can and will assist him in the army. He has been promised an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, now stationed in the north. It is an advantage that it should be so far from this part of the kingdom. He makes a fair promise; and I hope that, among new people, where each will have a character to maintain, they will both act with greater prudence. I have written to Colonel Forster, informing him of our present arrangements, and asking him to satisfy Mr. Wickham’s several creditors in and around Brighton with assurances of speedy payment, for which I have made myself responsible. Will you also take the trouble of carrying similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, whose names I shall enclose according to his account? He has declared all his debts; at least, I hope he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be settled within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and Mrs. Gardiner tells me that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south."}

content.text: {"request_id":"33376603c19d0ed2db0c25a1","rewritten_text":"Poor Jack was later shot in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, while Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended, so in every respect it had been a great success. It was, however, an exceedingly difficult ‘make-up,’ if I may use that theatrical phrase in connection with one of the greatest mysteries of the supernatural—or, in more scientific language, the higher-natural—world, and his preparations occupied a full three hours. At length all was ready, and he was delighted with his appearance. The large leather riding-boots belonging to the costume were slightly too big for him, and he had managed to find only one of the two horse-pistols, but on the whole he was satisfied. At a quarter past one he slipped out of the wainscoting and crept along the corridor. When he reached the twins’ room, known as the Blue Bed Chamber because of the colour of its hangings, he saw that the door stood slightly open. Desiring to make an impressive entrance, he flung it wide, whereupon a heavy jug of water dropped directly upon him, soaking him to the skin and missing his left shoulder by only a couple of inches. At the same instant he heard muffled shrieks of laughter coming from the four-post bed. The shock to his nerves was so severe that he ran back to his room as fast as possible, and the following day he was confined there with a bad cold. The sole consolation he found in the entire affair was that he had not brought his head along, since, had he done so, the results might have been extremely serious.\n\nHe now abandoned all hope of ever frightening the impolite American family, and generally contented himself with creeping through the passages in list slippers, a thick red muffler wrapped around his throat against draughts, and a little arquebuse in case the twins attacked him. The final blow came on the 19th of September. He had gone down to the great entrance-hall, convinced that there, at least, he would be left in peace, and was entertaining himself by making sarcastic comments on the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which had replaced the Canterville family portraits. He was dressed simply but neatly in a long shroud flecked with churchyard mould, had bound up his jaw with a strip of yellow linen, and carried a small lantern and a sexton’s spade."}

{"request_id":"1e602c80e8d0fef7377b704e","rewritten_text":"The nephew looked at him as he passed toward the door, but the uncle did not return his look.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Light Monsieur my nephew to his room there—and burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you like,” he added to himself, before ringing his little bell again and calling his valet to his own bedroom.

After the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis walked back and forth in his loose chamber robe, gently preparing for sleep on that hot, still night. His softly slippered feet made no sound on the floor. Moving around the room, he looked like a polished tiger—like an enchanted marquis from a story, one of the hopelessly wicked kind, whose regular change into tiger form was either ending or beginning.

He crossed his luxurious bedroom from end to end, thinking again of the scenes from the day’s journey that had returned to his mind: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the setting sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on the cliff, the little village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road mender in his blue cap pointing out the chain beneath the carriage. The fountain brought to mind the fountain in Paris, the small bundle lying on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, crying, “Dead!”

“I am calm now,” said Monsieur the Marquis, “and can go to bed.”

Leaving only one light burning on the broad hearth, he let the thin gauze curtains fall around him. As he settled down to sleep, he heard the night break its silence with a long sigh.

For three long hours, the stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the black night. During those same hours, the horses in the stables rattled their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound that hardly resembled the one poets traditionally give to owls. But creatures of that kind stubbornly refuse to say what people have written for them.

For three long hours, the stone faces of the chateau—lions and human faces—stared blindly into the night. Complete darkness covered the landscape, and its silence joined the dust settling quietly on every road. The burial ground had become so dark that its small mounds of poor grass could no longer be told apart; for all anyone could see, the figure on the Cross might have climbed down. In the village, both tax collectors and taxpayers slept deeply. Perhaps they dreamed of feasts, as starving people often do, and of comfort and rest, as driven slaves and yoked oxen may dream. Its thin inhabitants slept soundly, fed and free in their dreams."}

{"request_id":"ae6de7961f5e24b107fd601a","rewritten_text":"But he had oppressed no one and imprisoned no one. Far from harshly demanding payment of what he was owed, he had willingly given it up, faced a world that offered him no favor, made a place for himself there, and earned his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the poor, debt-ridden estate according to written instructions: to spare the people, giving them what little could be given—fuel in winter, if the powerful creditors allowed it, and whatever produce could be saved from their grip in summer. No doubt he had included these facts in his defense and evidence, for his own protection, so that they could not fail to appear now.

This strengthened the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor in the old story, the winds and currents had carried him into the reach of the Loadstone Rock. It was pulling him toward itself, and he had to go. Everything that came to his mind pushed him onward, faster and more steadily, toward that terrible attraction. His hidden uneasiness had been that evil men were carrying out evil purposes in his unhappy country, while he, knowing himself better than they were, was not there trying to stop the bloodshed and defend mercy and humanity. With this uneasiness partly suppressed and partly accusing him, he had been led to compare himself with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong. That comparison, which made him look bad, was immediately followed by Monseigneur’s sneers, which had wounded him deeply, and then by Stryver’s, which were especially crude and painful because of old reasons. After these came Gabelle’s letter: an innocent prisoner’s appeal to his justice, honor, and good name, with death threatening him.

His decision was made. He had to go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he had to sail on until he struck it. He knew of no rock and saw hardly any danger. The purpose behind what he had done, even though he had left it unfinished, made his actions appear in a light that France would gratefully recognize when he arrived to defend them. Then the glorious vision of doing good—the hopeful illusion that so often rises before many good minds—appeared before him. He even imagined that he might have some influence in guiding the raging Revolution, which was running so terribly out of control."}

{"request_id":"8aa9f8910cc73427f04a5ce5","rewritten_text":"Indeed, he was attired as ‘Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,’ one of his finest impersonations, and one the Cantervilles had every cause to recall, since it was the true beginning of their quarrel with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and, so far as he could tell, nobody was awake. Yet as he wandered towards the library to discover whether any traces of the blood-stain remained, two figures suddenly sprang upon him from a shadowy corner, flung their arms wildly over their heads, and shrieked ‘BOO!’ directly into his ear.

Overcome by a panic that was, in the circumstances, quite natural, he dashed towards the staircase, only to find Washington Otis stationed there with the large garden-syringe. Thus surrounded by foes on every side and nearly driven to bay, he disappeared into the great iron stove, which luckily was unlit, and was forced to travel home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his own room in a dreadful condition of dirt, confusion, and despair.

After that, he was never seen on another nocturnal expedition. The twins ambushed him several times and scattered nutshells across the passages each night, greatly irritating their parents and the servants, but all without result. It was perfectly clear that his feelings had been so hurt that he refused to show himself. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his major work on the history of the Democratic Party, upon which he had laboured for several years; Mrs. Otis arranged a magnificent clam-bake that astonished the entire county; the boys devoted themselves to lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games; and Virginia rode her pony along the lanes, accompanied by the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the final week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. Everyone supposed that the ghost had departed, and indeed Mr. Otis wrote Lord Canterville to say so. In reply, Lord Canterville conveyed his great delight at the news and sent his warmest congratulations to the Minister’s worthy wife.

The Otises, however, were mistaken, for the ghost remained in the house. Though by now almost an invalid, he was far from willing to let the matter end, especially after learning that the young Duke of Cheshire was among the visitors. The Duke’s grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost, and had been discovered the following morning lying on the card-room floor in so helpless a paralytic condition that, although he lived to a very advanced age, he was never again able to say anything except ‘Double Sixes.’"}

{"request_id":"0856e1ff5eb1312743ec870f","rewritten_text":"These reflections soothed me, and during the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep; yet the fever in my blood prevented any tranquil dreams. The dreadful scene of the previous day continually unfolded before my eyes: the women fleeing, and the furious Felix dragging me from his father’s feet. I awoke worn out, and, discovering that night had come, slipped from my hiding-place to seek food.

“When my hunger had been satisfied, I turned toward the familiar path leading to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I crawled into my hovel and waited silently for the usual hour when the family rose. That hour came and went, the sun climbed high overhead, but the cottagers did not emerge. I shook violently, fearing some terrible calamity. The cottage interior was dark, and I heard no sound; I cannot express the torment of that uncertainty.

“Soon two peasants passed by, but stopped near the cottage and began speaking together with vehement gestures. I could not understand them, since they spoke the language of the region, unlike that of my protectors. Shortly afterward Felix came near with another man. I was astonished, knowing he had not left the cottage that morning, and waited anxiously to learn from their conversation the cause of these strange events.

“‘Do you realize,’ his companion said, ‘that you must pay three months’ rent and surrender the produce of your garden? I do not wish to profit unfairly, and therefore ask you to take several days before deciding.’

“‘It is completely pointless,’ Felix answered; ‘we can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in the greatest danger because of the terrible event I have described. My wife and sister will never recover from their fright. I beg you not to argue with me further. Reclaim your dwelling and allow me to flee this place.’

“Felix shook violently as he spoke. He and his companion went inside the cottage, where they stayed for a few minutes, and then left. I never again saw any member of the De Lacey family.

“I remained in my hovel for the rest of the day, sunk in complete and senseless despair. My protectors had gone, severing the sole bond that connected me with the world. For the first time, revenge and hatred filled my heart. I made no effort to restrain them; surrendering to their current, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death."}

content.text: {"request_id":"521f60934e6f87368dc41a38","rewritten_text":"“April 7th. I rose early and, to my great joy, finally saw what I could only assume was the North Pole itself. It was there beyond doubt, directly beneath my feet. But, alas, I had risen to such an enormous height that nothing could be seen clearly. Judging from the sequence of figures showing my altitude at different times between six A.M. on April 2nd and twenty minutes before nine A.M. that same day, when the barometer stopped working, it was reasonable to conclude that by four o’clock on the morning of April 7th the balloon had reached a height of at least 7,254 miles above sea level. This height may seem enormous, but the estimate used to calculate it was probably far below the truth. In any case, I could certainly see the earth’s entire major diameter. The whole northern hemisphere lay below me like a map drawn in projection, and the equator itself formed the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies can easily imagine that the unexplored regions within the Arctic Circle, though directly beneath me and therefore seen without foreshortening, were still too small in themselves and too far from my viewpoint to be examined with much accuracy. Even so, what I could see was strange and exciting. North of that great rim mentioned earlier, which may—with some qualification—be called the limit of human discovery in these regions, one continuous, or nearly continuous, sheet of ice stretched onward. During the first few degrees of its course, its surface became noticeably flatter; farther on, it sank into a level plane; and at last, growing somewhat concave, it ended at the Pole in a sharply defined circular center. Seen from the balloon, this center appeared to measure about sixty-five seconds of arc. Its dark color varied in intensity, but it was always darker than any other point on the visible hemisphere, sometimes deepening into complete, impenetrable blackness. Beyond this, little could be determined. By noon, the circular center had greatly decreased in size, and by seven P.M. I had lost sight of it altogether. The balloon had passed over the western edge of the ice and was moving rapidly away toward the equator.\n\n“April 8th. I noticed that the earth’s apparent diameter had decreased, and that its general color and appearance had also changed considerably."}
