{"request_id":"a087100be6c7976ceb3cd2ed","rewritten_text":"Could not determine whether the voice belonged to a man or a woman. Could not understand what was spoken, but thought the language was Spanish. This witness described the condition of the room and the bodies as we described it yesterday.

“_Henri Duval_, a neighbor and silversmith by occupation, states that he was among the group who first entered the house. In general, he confirms Musèt’s testimony. Immediately after forcing their way in, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which gathered very quickly despite the late hour. This witness believed the shrill voice to be that of an Italian. He was certain it was not French. He could not tell whether it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He did not know Italian. Though unable to distinguish the words, he was persuaded by the intonation that the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter, and had often spoken with both. He was certain the shrill voice belonged to neither of the deceased.

“——_Odenheimer, restaurateur._ This witness offered his evidence voluntarily. As he did not speak French, his examination was conducted through an interpreter. He was born in Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the shrieks began. They continued for several minutes—perhaps ten. They were prolonged and loud—terrible and distressing. He was among those who entered the building. In every respect except one, he confirmed the preceding testimony. He was certain the shrill voice was a man’s—that of a Frenchman. He could not make out the words. They were loud, rapid, and uneven, apparently uttered in fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh—not truly shrill, but harsh. He could not describe it as a shrill voice. The gruff voice repeatedly said ‘_sacré_,’ ‘_diable_,’ and once ‘_mon Dieu._’

“_Jules Mignaud_, banker, of Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye possessed some property. In the spring of the year—eight years earlier—she opened an account with his banking house. She made frequent deposits of small amounts. She drew nothing until the third day before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs. The money was paid in gold, and a clerk carried it to her home.

“_Adolphe Le Bon_, clerk at Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence with the 4000 francs, packed in two bags. When the door was opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from him, while the old lady took the other.”"}

{"request_id":"88f41c16285a996e5d45a375","rewritten_text":"Saturday at noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke powders, pawing the air, and muttering gibberish as vigorously as ever, but he looked rather discouraged, since naturally he had not yet raised even a sweat in that well. At last I said:

“How does the matter look by now, partner?”

“Behold, I am even now engaged in testing the most powerful enchantment known to the princes of occult arts in the lands of the East; should it fail me, nothing can help. Silence, until I am finished.”

This time he raised a smoke that darkened the whole region and must have made things unpleasant for the hermits, since the wind was blowing toward them and rolled over their dens in a thick, billowing fog. He poured out an equal volume of words, twisted his body, and sawed the air with his hands in the most extraordinary fashion. After twenty minutes he collapsed, panting and nearly exhausted. Then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, followed by a multitude of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings, all drawn by the enormous smoke and all in a state of great excitement. The abbot anxiously asked for the result. Merlin said:

“If any labor a mortal could perform might break the spell binding these waters, the one I have just attempted would have done so. It has failed; therefore I now know that what I feared is an established truth: the sign of this failure is that the most powerful spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name no one may speak and live, has cast his spell upon this well. No mortal breathes, nor ever will, who can discover the secret of that spell, and without that secret no one can break it. The water will never flow again, good Father. I have done what a man could do. Let me go.”

Naturally, this threw the abbot into considerable consternation. He turned to me, the signs of it plain on his face, and said:

“You have heard him. Is it true?”

“Some of it is.”

“Not all, then—not all! Which part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast his spell upon the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we are ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean, not certainly?”

“That is what I mean.”

“Then you also mean that when he says no one can break the spell—”

“Yes. When he says that, he says something that is not necessarily true. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—that is, some small, some trifling chance—of succeeding.”"}

{"request_id":"a4cc214164437d167ea023a8","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced angrily up and down the room. I stood ready to hear and answer his reproaches. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is completely absurd,” he cried. “If you were schoolboys, you could not behave more unreasonably.”

“You do not understand,” said Raymond. “This is only part of a larger system—a plan of tyranny to which I will never submit. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in its empire? Must my privacy be invaded, my actions criticized, and my friends insulted? But I will end all of it at once. Let this be your witness.” He took the star, the symbol of his office, from his breast and threw it onto the table. “I renounce my office. I give up my power—let whoever can take it!”

“Let him take it,” Adrian exclaimed, “if he can declare himself, or be declared by the world, your superior. There is no man in England with enough arrogance to do so. Know your own worth, Raymond, and your anger will fade; your confidence will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country or ourselves, we also prayed for the Protector’s life and welfare, since they were inseparably tied to ours. You devoted your hours to our benefit, and your ambition was to earn our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, gave us useful institutions, and made the land richly fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your judgment seat, while the poor and oppressed rose like flowers waking at dawn beneath the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we are all shocked and grieving when this seems to have changed? But come, this gloomy fit has already passed. Resume your duties; your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will be silenced, and our love, respect, and loyalty will again be shown to you. Control yourself, Raymond, and the world will obey you.”

“All this would be very sensible if it were spoken to someone else,” Raymond replied bitterly. “Take your own advice, and you, the first peer in the land, may become its sovereign. You, the good, wise, and just man, may rule every heart. But I have realized—too soon for my happiness, too late for England’s good—that I accepted a task beyond my ability. I cannot control myself. My passions rule me; even my smallest impulse is my tyrant. Do you think I gave up the Protectorate—and I have given it up—in a moment of anger? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that bauble again, never again burden myself with the care and misery whose visible sign it is."}

{"request_id":"5078c586eff0b453a1e8db8e","rewritten_text":"Then they passed lonely brickfields. The fog was thinner here, and he could see the strange, bottle-shaped kilns, their orange flames spreading like fans. A dog barked as they went by, and somewhere far off in the darkness a wandering seagull cried. The horse stumbled in a rut, swerved, and then broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled once more over streets paved with rough stones. Most of the windows were dark, but now and then strange shadows appeared against a blind lit from behind. He watched them with curiosity. They moved like huge puppets and gestured like living creatures. He hated them. A dull anger filled his heart. As they turned a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open doorway, and two men chased the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver struck at them with his whip.

It is said that passion makes a person think in circles. Certainly, with terrible repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips formed and re-formed those subtle words about soul and sense, until he found in them a complete expression of his mood. By approving them intellectually, he justified passions that would still have controlled him without that excuse. From one part of his mind to another crept the same thought; and the wild desire to live, the most terrible of all human appetites, stirred every trembling nerve and fibre into action. Ugliness, which had once disgusted him because it made things real, now became precious to him for that very reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The rough fight, the filthy den, the crude violence of a life without order, even the degradation of thieves and outcasts, seemed more vivid in their powerful reality than all the beautiful forms of art and the dreamy shadows of song. They were what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver stopped with a jerk at the top of a dark lane. Above the low roofs and uneven chimney stacks rose the black masts of ships. Coils of white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere around here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked around. “This will do,” he replied. He got out quickly, paid the driver the extra fare he had promised, and walked swiftly toward the quay. Here and there, a lantern shone at the stern of a huge merchant ship. Its light trembled and broke apart in the puddles. A red glow came from a steamer heading out to sea as it took on coal. The slimy pavement looked like a wet raincoat."}

{"request_id":"73fcfb95ebd905cafa4f8ffd","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. You told me to wake you.”

“Oh! I remember. Very well, very well.”

After making several dull attempts to fall asleep again, which the man skillfully prevented by stirring the fire for five minutes, he got up, put on his hat, and went out. He turned into the Temple and, after reviving himself by walking twice along King’s Bench Walk and Paper Buildings, entered Stryver’s chambers.

Stryver’s clerk, who never took part in these meetings, had gone home, so Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing gown, with his throat bare for comfort. Around his eyes was the wild, strained, worn look seen in heavy drinkers of his kind, from the portrait of Jeffries onward, and visible in different forms in the portraits of every age of drinking.

“You’re a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time; perhaps a quarter of an hour later.”

They entered a gloomy room lined with books and covered with papers, where a bright fire burned. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the scattered papers stood a shining table covered with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

“You’ve had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I was dining with the day’s client—or watching him dine; it’s the same thing!”

“That was an excellent point, Sydney, the one you used to establish the identification. How did you think of it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was a rather handsome fellow, and that I might have been much the same kind of man if I’d had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his prematurely large belly shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

The jackal sullenly loosened his clothes, went into the next room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and two towels. He soaked the towels, partly wrung them out, folded them around his head in a horrible fashion, sat at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much reducing to do tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, as he searched through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“There they are, Sydney. Begin!”

The lion then settled on his back on a sofa beside the drinking table, while the jackal sat at his own paper-covered desk across from him, with bottles and glasses within easy reach."}

{"request_id":"27b5a7744f7edd37fa90084c","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I hurried to the king and spoke into his ear:

“Out the door at once, sire! The woman is dying of the disease that ravaged Camelot two years ago.”

He did not move.

“Indeed, I shall remain—and help as well.”

I whispered once more:

“King, you must not. You must leave.”

“Your purpose is good, and your words are not unwise. Yet it would shame a king to show fear, and shame a belted knight to hold back his hand where there are those in need of aid. Peace, I will not go. You are the one who must leave. The Church’s ban is not laid upon me, but it forbids you to remain here, and she will treat you harshly should word reach her of your trespass.”

It was a perilous position for him, and could cost him his life, but arguing was useless. If he believed his knightly honor was involved, that settled the matter; he would stay, and nothing could stop him. I knew this, and therefore let the subject drop. The woman spoke:

“Good sir, out of your kindness, will you climb that ladder and bring me word of what you discover? Do not fear to tell me, for there are times when even a mother’s heart is beyond breaking—having already broken.”

“Stay,” said the king, “and give the woman food. I will go.” And he set down the knapsack.

I turned to begin, but the king had already gone ahead. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in the dim light, who had not noticed us until then or spoken.

“Is that your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he sleeping?”

“God be thanked for that one mercy, yes—for three hours now. Where may I repay my gratitude in full? My heart is overflowing with thanks for the sleep he sleeps now.”

I said:

“We shall be careful. We will not wake him.”

“Ah, no, that you will not, for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a triumph it is to know it! No one can hurt him, and no one can insult him again. He is in heaven now and happy; or, if not there, he remains in hell and is content, for there he will find neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together; we were husband and wife for these five-and-twenty years, never parted until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer side by side. This morning he was out of his mind, imagining that we were boy and girl again, wandering through the joyful fields; and so, in that innocent, happy talk, he wandered farther and farther, still lightly chatting, and entered those other fields of which we know nothing, shut away from mortal sight."}

{"request_id":"cb2772b1bf1316b63d999ee7","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Master Will—I truly am,” the Black man replied promptly. “I’m almost at the end now.”

“_At the end!_” Legrand cried, nearly screaming. “Do you mean you’re at the end of that limb?”

“Almost at de end, massa—o-o-o-o-oh! Lord have mercy! What is this here on the tree?”

“Well?” Legrand cried, greatly pleased. “What is it?”

“Why, it’s nothing but a skull—somebody left his head up in the tree, and the crows have eaten every bit of flesh off it.”

“A skull, you say? Very well—how is it fastened to the limb? What holds it there?”

“Sure enough, massa; I must look. Why, this is a very curious thing, upon my word—there’s a great big nail in the skull, fastening it to the tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly as I tell you—do you hear?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Pay attention, then—find the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! Hoo! That’s a good one! Why, there isn’t any left eye at all.”

“Curse your stupidity! Do you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that—I know all about it. It’s my left hand that I chop wood with.”

“Of course! You’re left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now, I suppose you can find the skull’s left eye, or the place where its left eye was. Have you found it?”

There was a long pause. At last the Black man asked,

“Is de skull’s lef eye on de same side as de skull’s lef hand, too?—’cause de skull ain’t got no hand at all—never mind! I got de lef eye now—here’s de lef eye! What must I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it, as far as the string will reach—but be careful not to release your hold on the string.”

“All done, Master Will; mighty easy thing to put de bug through de hole—look out for him down below!”

During this exchange, no part of Jupiter could be seen; but the beetle he had allowed to descend was now visible at the end of the string, shining like a globe of polished gold in the last rays of the setting sun, some of which still faintly lit the height where we stood. The scarab hung completely clear of the branches and, if released, would have fallen at our feet. Legrand immediately took the scythe and cut a circular space three or four yards across directly beneath the insect. When he had finished, he ordered Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"84920ce54c425697275c7876","rewritten_text":"“I regard it as one of the earliest refinements of civilized society.”

“Certainly, sir; and it has the further advantage of being fashionable even among the world’s less polished societies: every savage can dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. “Your friend dances delightfully,” he continued after a pause, when he saw Bingley join the group; “and I have no doubt that you are an expert in the art yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and found no small pleasure in watching you. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Do you not think it would be a fitting compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I never pay any place if I can avoid it.”

“You have a house in town, I presume?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once considered settling in town myself, for I am fond of distinguished society; but I was not entirely sure that the air of London would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for an answer, but his companion had no inclination to give one. At that moment Elizabeth moved towards them, and Sir William was seized by the idea of doing something especially gallant. He called to her—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to introduce this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot refuse to dance when so much beauty is before you.” Taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy’s, who, though greatly surprised, was not unwilling to accept it. But Elizabeth immediately drew back and said, somewhat flustered, to Sir William—

“Indeed, sir, I have not the slightest intention of dancing. I beg you not to imagine that I came this way in order to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with grave courtesy, requested the honour of her hand, but without success. Elizabeth was resolute, and Sir William’s efforts to persuade her did nothing to change her mind.

“You dance so excellently, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of seeing you; and although this gentleman generally dislikes the amusement, I am sure he can have no objection to obliging us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He certainly is; but given the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot be surprised by his compliance. Who could object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave him a mischievous look and turned away. Her refusal had not diminished her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him—"}

{"request_id":"637e478a568843a3f43dcd42","rewritten_text":"But how could I, a poor, confused village boy, escape the strange contradiction that even the best and wisest people fall into every day?

“It may all be true,” I said to Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

In short, when I reached that point, I turned onto my face, grabbed the hair on both sides of my head, and pulled hard. All the while, I knew my heart’s madness was so extreme and misplaced that I felt my face deserved punishment for belonging to such a fool. I almost thought I should lift it by my hair and bang it against the pebbles.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she tried no longer to reason with me. Her hand was comforting, though rough from work. She placed it over my hands one after another and gently drew them from my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder to soothe me. With my face against my sleeve, I cried a little—just as I had in the brewery yard—and vaguely felt that someone, or perhaps everyone, had treated me very badly. I could not say which.

“I am glad of one thing,” said Biddy. “You have felt able to trust me, Pip. And I am glad of another: you know, of course, that you can rely on me to keep your confidence and always deserve it. If your first teacher—dear me, such a poor teacher, and one who needed teaching herself!—were teaching you now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would give you. But it would be a difficult one to learn, and you have already gone beyond her, so it is no use now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and said, in a fresh, pleasant tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, rising, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Until you become a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall, so that means always. Not that I have anything to tell you, because you know everything I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” said Biddy softly, looking away toward the ships. Then, in the same pleasant tone as before, she repeated, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon slowly faded into evening, and it was very beautiful."}

{"request_id":"91abe3efef607bdcd7547395","rewritten_text":"When we got back to the raft, he counted his earnings and found he had collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also brought along a three-gallon jug of whisky that he found under a wagon while starting home through the woods. The king said that, all together, it beat any day he had ever spent as a missionary. He said there was no use comparing heathens with pirates when it came to working a camp meeting.

The duke had thought he was doing pretty well until the king showed up, but afterward he was not so sure. He had printed two small jobs for farmers at the printing office—horse bills—and collected four dollars. He had also sold ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper, agreeing to print them for four dollars if they paid in advance, which they did. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he took three subscriptions at fifty cents each, provided they paid in advance. They had planned to pay in cordwood and onions as usual, but he said he had just bought the paper, had lowered the price as far as he could, and would now run it for cash. He also set up a short poem he had written himself—three verses, sweet and sad. It was called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart,” and he left it ready to print without charging anything. Altogether, he took in nine dollars and fifty cents and said he had earned a fair day’s pay.

Then he showed us another small job he had printed without charging us. It showed a runaway Black man carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” beneath it. The notice was all about Jim and described him exactly. It said he had run away from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, the previous winter, and had probably gone north. Whoever caught him and returned him would receive the reward and expenses.

“Now,” said the duke, “after tonight we can travel during the day if we want. Whenever we see anyone coming, we can tie Jim hand and foot with a rope, lay him in the wigwam, show them this handbill, and say we captured him up the river. We were too poor to travel by steamboat, so our friends gave us this little raft on credit, and we’re going down to collect the reward.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"5476b05476f1d786d66ddd79","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later, the bell rang for tea. Since Virginia did not come downstairs, Mrs. Otis sent a footman up to call her. After a while he returned and said he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. She usually went into the garden each evening to pick flowers for the dinner table, so Mrs. Otis was not worried at first. But when six o’clock came and Virginia still had not appeared, she became very anxious. She sent the boys to search outside while she and Mr. Otis looked through every room in the house. At half-past six, the boys returned and said they had found no sign of their sister. Everyone was now extremely upset and unsure what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that a few days earlier he had allowed a group of gypsies to camp in the park. He immediately set out for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they had been staying, accompanied by his eldest son and two farm servants. The little Duke of Cheshire, frantic with worry, begged to come too, but Mr. Otis refused because he feared there might be a fight. When they reached the camp, however, he found that the gypsies had gone. Their departure had clearly been sudden: the fire was still burning, and several plates lay on the grass. He sent Washington and the two men to search the area, then hurried home and telegraphed every police inspector in the county, telling them to look for a little girl who had been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then had his horse brought around and, after making his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode off along the Ascot Road with a groom. He had gone barely two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Turning, he saw the little Duke riding up on his pony, his face flushed and his head bare. ‘I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy gasped, ‘but I can’t eat any dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry with me. If you had let us become engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!’\n\nThe Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young troublemaker, and he was deeply touched by the boy’s devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted him kindly on the shoulders and said, ‘Well, Cecil, if you refuse to go back, I suppose you must come with me. But I’ll have to get you a hat at Ascot.’"}

{"request_id":"7c81b05cf11111f11b63115d","rewritten_text":"“And I call upon you, spirits of the dead, and upon you, wandering servants of vengeance, to help and guide me in my work. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink deeply of agony; let him feel the despair that now torments me.”

I had begun my invocation solemnly, with a sense of awe that almost convinced me the spirits of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion. But as I finished, the furies took hold of me, and rage choked my voice.

The stillness of the night was broken by a loud, demonic laugh. It rang in my ears for a long time; the mountains echoed it, and I felt as though all hell surrounded me with mockery and laughter. Surely, in that moment, I would have gone mad and ended my miserable life, if my vow had not been heard and I had not been kept alive for vengeance. The laughter faded, and a familiar, hated voice, apparently close beside my ear, spoke in a clear whisper: “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have decided to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed toward the place from which the sound had come, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly, the moon’s broad disk rose and shone directly upon his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with more than human speed.

I pursued him, and for many months this has been my task. Following a faint clue, I traced the winding Rhone, but without success. Then the blue Mediterranean came into view, and by a strange chance I saw the fiend enter it at night and hide aboard a ship bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same vessel, but somehow he escaped me.

Through the wild regions of Tartary and Russia, though he continued to evade me, I always followed his trail. Sometimes peasants, frightened by this horrible apparition, told me where he had gone. Sometimes he himself, fearing that if I lost every trace of him I would despair and die, left a sign to guide me. Snow fell upon my head, and I saw the mark of his enormous foot across the white plain. How can you, just beginning life, knowing nothing yet of care or agony, understand what I have suffered and still suffer? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my pains. Some devil had cursed me, and I carried an eternal hell within me. Yet a good spirit still followed and guided my steps, and whenever I complained most, it would suddenly free me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger overcame me and nature collapsed from exhaustion, a meal had been prepared for me in the wilderness, restoring my strength and courage."}

{"request_id":"bbf8dc2fb0a14c6d42a4b44e","rewritten_text":"But there was no laughter in the little town that peaceful Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were going into mourning, with deep grief and many tears. An unusual silence filled the village, though it was quiet enough at the best of times. The villagers went about their business distractedly and spoke little, but they sighed often. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children. They had no interest in their games and gradually abandoned them.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering sadly around the empty schoolhouse yard. But there was nothing there to comfort her. She said to herself:

“Oh, if only I had a brass andiron knob again! But now I have nothing to remember him by.” And she held back a small sob.

After a moment she stopped and thought:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for anything in the world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought overwhelmed her, and she wandered away with tears running down her cheeks. Then a group of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came by and stood looking over the picket fence. In solemn voices they talked about how Tom had done this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe had said some small thing that now seemed full of terrible meaning. Each speaker pointed to the exact place where the lost boys had stood, then added something like, “And I was standing just so—just as I am now, and if you were him—I was this close—and he smiled, just like this—and then something seemed to go all over me, something awful, you know—and I never guessed what it meant, of course, but I can see now!”

Then they argued over who had seen the dead boys last while they were alive. Many claimed that sad honor and offered evidence, though the witnesses had altered it to some degree. When they finally decided who really had seen the boys last and spoken the final words to them, those lucky ones assumed a kind of sacred importance. Everyone else stared at them and envied them. One poor boy, with no other glory to claim, said with obvious pride:

“Well, Tom Sawyer licked me once.”

But that attempt at fame failed. Most of the boys could say the same, which made the distinction seem too common. The group slowly drifted away, still remembering the lost heroes in hushed, respectful voices."}

{"request_id":"afb67465f546b7d4ee7b201e","rewritten_text":"“I must go, not knowing what will happen to me; but I will return here, or join your party, as soon as I can. One word or look will decide whether I enter your father’s house this evening or never again.”

A letter like this could not be recovered from quickly. Half an hour alone with her thoughts might have calmed her; but the ten minutes that passed before she was interrupted, with all the limits imposed by her situation, could do nothing to restore her peace. Each moment only brought new agitation. Her happiness was overwhelming. And before she had moved beyond the first rush of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all entered.

The need to appear like herself immediately caused a struggle; but after a while she could do no more. She began to understand nothing they said and had to claim that she felt unwell and excuse herself. They could then see that she looked very ill, and were shocked and worried. They would not leave her for anything. This was terrible. If they had only gone away and left her quietly in that room, it would have cured her; but having them all standing or waiting around her was unbearable, and in desperation she said she would go home.

“By all means, my dear,” cried Mrs. Musgrove. “Go home at once and take care of yourself, so that you may be well enough for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring for a chair. She must not walk.”

But the chair would never do. It was worse than anything! To lose the chance of speaking two words to Captain Wentworth during a quiet, solitary walk up the town—and she felt almost certain of meeting him—was impossible to bear. She strongly objected to the chair. Mrs. Musgrove, who thought only of one kind of illness, asked anxiously whether Anne had fallen; whether she had recently slipped and struck her head; and, after becoming fully convinced that there had been no fall, was able to let her leave cheerfully, expecting to find her better that night.

Anxious to leave no possible precaution unmentioned, Anne struggled to say—

“I am afraid, ma’am, that this has not been fully understood. Please be so kind as to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your entire party this evening. I am afraid there has been some mistake; and I especially wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is perfectly understood, I assure you.”"}

{"request_id":"8764fb82d94d6f80282b9884","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had taken him aboard, and ever afterward, I kept a wary lookout for any sign that we were suspected. I had seen none. We certainly had not been, and at that moment just as certainly were not, accompanied or followed by any boat. Had one been waiting on us, I would have run ashore and forced her either to proceed or to make her purpose plain. But we continued on without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and seemed, as I have said, a natural part of the scene. It was striking—though perhaps the miserable life he had led explained it—that he was the least troubled of us all. He was not unconcerned, for he told me he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign land; nor, as I understood him, was he willing simply to submit or resign himself. But he had no intention of going halfway to meet danger. When danger came to him, he faced it; until then, he would not trouble himself about it.

“If you knowed, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here alonger my dear boy and smoke, arter being day after day betwixt four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I believe I know the pleasures of freedom,” I replied.

“Ah,” said he, shaking his head solemnly. “But you don’t know it equal to me. You must have been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it equal to me—but I ain’t a-going to be low.”

It seemed inconsistent to me that, for any ruling idea, he should have risked his freedom, and even his life. But I considered that perhaps freedom without danger was so unlike the whole habit of his existence that it could not mean to him what it would mean to another man. I was not far wrong, for after smoking a little he said:—

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, t’other side the world, I was always looking toward this side; and it come flat to be there, though I was growing rich. Everybody knowed Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody’s head would be troubled about him. They ain’t so easy concerning me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, leastways, if they knowed where I was.”

“If everything goes well,” I said, “you will be entirely free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he answered, drawing a deep breath, “I hope so.”

“And believe so?”"}

{"request_id":"e1c6c10d8c636d64e73bb4ea","rewritten_text":"But in that bitter tirade against Chantilly, which appeared in yesterday’s Musée, the satirist made some disgraceful references to the cobbler’s change of name when he took up acting, and quoted a Latin line we had often discussed. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I had told you that this referred to Orion, once written Urion; and because of certain sharp points in that explanation, I knew you could not have forgotten it. So it was clear that you would connect the ideas of Orion and Chantilly. I saw that you had done so from the kind of smile that crossed your lips. You were thinking of the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then, you had been walking bent over; but now I saw you straighten to your full height. I was sure that you were thinking of Chantilly’s small figure. At that moment I interrupted your thoughts by observing that, since he was in fact a very little man—that Chantilly—he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Soon afterward, we were reading an evening edition of the Gazette des Tribunaux when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of terrible screams, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue. The house was known to be occupied only by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After an unsuccessful attempt to enter in the usual way, the gate was broken open with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors went inside with two gendarmes. By then the screams had stopped; but as the group hurried up the first flight of stairs, two or more harsh voices arguing angrily were heard, apparently coming from the upper part of the house. When they reached the second landing, those sounds had also stopped, and everything was completely quiet. The group spread out and rushed from room to room. When they reached a large back room on the fourth floor, they found the door locked, with the key inside, and forced it open. What they saw filled everyone present with both horror and astonishment.

“The room was in complete disorder, with furniture broken and scattered everywhere. There was only one bedstead; the bed had been taken off it and thrown into the middle of the floor. A razor covered with blood lay on a chair."}

{"request_id":"70bf53e1978e0ed425ed6006","rewritten_text":"I ran to her, gathered her into my arms, covered her with kisses, and pleaded:

“Speak, darling, speak! What is it?”

Her head went limp against my chest, and she gasped so softly I could hardly hear her:

“HELLO-CENTRAL!”

“Quick!” I shouted to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopath and tell him to come!”

Within two minutes I was kneeling beside the child’s crib, while Sandy sent servants rushing in every direction throughout the palace. I understood the situation almost at once—membranous croup! I bent over her and whispered:

“Wake up, sweetheart! Hello-Central.”

She opened her gentle eyes slowly and managed to say:

“Papa.”

That comforted me. She was not close to death yet. I sent for sulfur preparations and brought out the croup kettle myself; I do not sit and wait for doctors when Sandy or the child is ill. I knew how to care for both of them and had plenty of experience. This little one had spent much of its short life in my arms, and often I could ease its troubles and make it laugh through the tears on its eyelashes when even its mother could not.

Sir Launcelot, wearing his finest armor, came striding down the great hall on his way to the stock board. He was its president and occupied the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad. The stock board consisted of the Knights of the Round Table, who now used the Round Table for business. Seats there were worth—well, you would never believe the price, so there is no point in naming it. Sir Launcelot was a bear, and he had cornered one of the new lines. He was preparing to squeeze the shorts that day; but what did that matter? He was still the old Launcelot, and when he glanced through the doorway, learned that his pet was sick, and saw her condition, nothing else mattered. Bulls and bears could fight among themselves; he would come in and stand by little Hello-Central with all his strength. And that was exactly what he did. He tossed his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute had put a new wick in the alcohol lamp and was heating the croup kettle. By then Sandy had built a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was ready.

Sir Launcelot brought the kettle to a boil. Together, he and I filled it with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a little lactic acid, then poured in water and placed the steam spout beneath the canopy. Everything was in order now, and we sat on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch."}

content.text: {"request_id":"070e09c3a18747a0f0e1df26","rewritten_text":"“April 19th. This morning, to my great joy, at about nine o’clock, with the moon’s surface frighteningly near and my fears at their highest, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs of a change in the atmosphere. By ten, I had reason to believe its density had increased greatly. By eleven, the apparatus required very little effort; and at noon, after some hesitation, I dared to unscrew the tourniquet. When I felt no discomfort from doing so, I opened the rubber chamber completely and removed it from around the car. As might be expected, spasms and severe headaches immediately followed an experiment so sudden and dangerous. But these troubles, along with the other difficulties of breathing, were not severe enough to threaten my life. I therefore resolved to endure them as best I could, since I was rapidly leaving them behind as I approached the denser layers near the moon. My descent, however, remained extremely rapid; and it soon became alarmingly clear that, although I had probably been right to expect an atmosphere whose density matched the satellite’s mass, I had been wrong to suppose that even at the surface it would be dense enough to support the great weight of my balloon’s car. Yet it should have done so, to the same degree as at Earth, if the actual gravity of bodies on either planet corresponded to the condensation of its atmosphere. My steep fall proved that this was not so; the reason can only be explained by those possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. In any case, I was now close to the planet and descending with terrifying speed. I immediately threw overboard my ballast, then my water kegs, then the condenser and rubber chamber, and finally every object in the car. But none of this helped. I continued to fall horribly fast and was now less than half a mile from the surface. As a final measure, after removing my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car itself loose from the balloon. It was quite heavy, and, clinging with both hands to the netting, I had barely time to notice that the entire country, as far as I could see, was thickly dotted with tiny houses before I plunged headfirst into the center of a strange-looking city and into the middle of a huge crowd of ugly little people. Not one spoke a word or made the slightest effort to help me. They simply stood there like a group of idiots, grinning foolishly and looking sideways at me and my balloon, with their arms akimbo.”"}

{"request_id":"e129b704e2f6b48a6c2eae0b","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is extraordinary! I must see Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from his seat and paced up and down the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is simply a motive in art to me. You might see nothing in him. I see everything in him. He is never more present in my work than when no image of him appears. As I have said, he suggests a new manner. I find him in the curves of certain lines, in the beauty and subtlety of certain colours. That is all.”

“Then why won’t you exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I have put into it some expression of all this strange artistic idolatry, which, of course, I have never wanted to mention to him. He knows nothing about it. He must never know anything about it. But the world might guess, and I will not expose my soul to their shallow, prying eyes. My heart will never be placed beneath their microscope. There is too much of myself in the thing, Harry—too much of myself!”

“Poets are not as scrupulous as you. They know how useful passion can be for publication. These days, a broken heart will go through many editions.”

“I hate them for it,” Hallward cried. “An artist should create beautiful things, but put none of his own life into them. We live in an age when men treat art as though it were meant to be autobiography. We have lost the abstract sense of beauty. One day I will show the world what it is; and for that reason the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you are wrong, Basil, but I will not argue with you. Only the intellectually lost ever argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter thought for a few moments. “He likes me,” he replied after a pause; “I know he likes me. Of course, I flatter him terribly. I take a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I will regret having said. Usually, he is charming to me, and we sit in the studio talking about a thousand things. Sometimes, however, he is horribly thoughtless and seems to take genuine delight in hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I have given my entire soul to someone who treats it as though it were a flower to place in his coat, a piece of decoration to flatter his vanity, an ornament for a summer’s day.”"}

{"request_id":"e8962ea13be7121610666eff","rewritten_text":"Those venerable, feeble men were always seen by the public bowing, and people commonly believed that, after bowing a customer out, they continued bowing in the empty office until they bowed another customer in.

The barrister was perceptive enough to understand that the banker would not have expressed such an opinion on anything less substantial than moral certainty. Though unprepared for the large pill he had to swallow, he managed to get it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking his forensic forefinger at the Temple in general once it was down, “my way out of this is to prove you all wrong.”

It was a piece of Old Bailey tactician’s skill, and it brought him considerable relief. “You shall not prove me wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver; “I’ll do that for you.”

Accordingly, when Mr. Lorry called that night, as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, surrounded by books and papers spread out for the purpose, appeared to have nothing less on his mind than the morning’s subject. He even seemed surprised to see Mr. Lorry and was altogether absent and preoccupied.

“Well!” said the good-natured emissary, after half an hour of fruitless attempts to bring him back to the matter. “I have been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coldly. “Oh, of course! What am I thinking of!”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in the conversation we had. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” replied Mr. Stryver in the friendliest manner, “that I am sorry for it on your account, and sorry for it on the poor father’s account. I know this must always be a painful subject for the family; let us say no more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say you don’t,” Stryver replied, nodding in a soothing, conclusive way; “never mind, never mind.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, it doesn’t; I assure you it doesn’t. Having imagined sense where there is none, and a worthy ambition where there is no worthy ambition, I am glad to have escaped my mistake, and no harm has been done. Young women have made similar follies many times before, and have repented them in poverty and obscurity many times before. From an unselfish point of view, I am sorry the matter has been abandoned, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms; from a selfish point of view, I am glad it has been abandoned, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms—it is scarcely necessary to say that I could have gained nothing from it."}

I had spent most of that time at school and could spell, read, and write a little. I could also recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five, and I don’t believe I could ever get beyond that, even if I lived forever. I don’t care much for mathematics anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I learned to tolerate it. Whenever I got especially tired, I played hooky, and the beating I received the next day actually did me good and cheered me up. So the longer I attended, the easier it became. I was also getting used to the widow’s ways, and they didn’t bother me quite so much. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed weighed on me most of the time, but before the cold weather came, I sometimes slipped away and slept in the woods, which gave me a break. I still preferred the old ways, but I was beginning to like the new ones a little, too. The widow said I was improving slowly but surely and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast, I accidentally knocked over the saltcellar. I reached for some salt as quickly as I could, meaning to throw it over my left shoulder and prevent bad luck, but Miss Watson got there first and stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; you’re always making such a mess!” The widow tried to say something kind for me, but I knew that wouldn’t keep the bad luck away. After breakfast I went outside feeling nervous and uneasy, wondering where the bad luck would strike me and what form it would take. There are ways to prevent some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of them. So I didn’t try to do anything; I just walked along sadly, keeping watch.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the tall board fence. An inch of fresh snow covered the ground, and I saw someone’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry, stood near the stile for a while, and then continued around the garden fence. It was strange that they hadn’t come in after lingering there so long. I couldn’t understand it. Somehow, it seemed very curious. I was about to follow the tracks around, but first I bent down to examine them."}

{"request_id":"b87b609e1cbc0ef4f9047b51","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by them to Adrian, chosen as arbiter; and they had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and desolate country, all the while indulging a fierce hatred of one another; and now they argued their respective causes with unabated party spirit.

By examining the deputies separately, and after much inquiry, we discovered the real condition of affairs at Paris. Since parliament had appointed him Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had yielded to Adrian. He was our captain, to conduct us from our native land to unknown regions, our lawgiver, and our protector. When our plan of emigration was first arranged, no lasting separation of our members had been intended, and command of the entire body, rising by successive degrees of authority, culminated in the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen events altered our plans and caused most of our number to remain divided from the supreme chief for nearly two months. They had crossed over in two separate groups; and upon reaching Paris, disagreement sprang up between them.

They had discovered Paris to be deserted. When the plague first appeared, returning travellers and merchants, together with letters, regularly informed us of the destruction wrought by disease upon the continent. But as mortality increased, this intercourse diminished and finally stopped. Even in England, communication between one part of the island and another grew slow and infrequent. No vessel crossed the current separating Calais from Dover; or, if some sorrowful voyager, eager to learn whether his relatives lived or died, departed from the French coast to rejoin us, the hungry sea often swallowed his small craft, or within a day or two the disorder seized him, and he died before he could relate the story of France’s desolation. We were therefore largely ignorant of the continent’s condition, and still entertained some faint hope of finding many companions scattered across its broad extent. Yet the same causes that had so terribly reduced the English population had possessed even greater opportunity for destruction in the neighboring country. France was empty; along the whole road from Calais to Paris, not a single human being appeared. In Paris a few remained, perhaps a hundred, who, resigned to their approaching fate, wandered through the capital’s streets and gathered to speak of former times, with that liveliness and even cheerfulness which rarely abandons the people of this nation.

The English entered Paris without opposition. Its tall buildings and narrow streets were without life. A few pallid figures could be seen at their customary meeting place in the Tuileries; they wondered why the islanders had come to their doomed city—for in the extremity of misery, sufferers always believe their own portion of calamity the most severe, just as, when enduring intense pain, we would exchange the particular torment under which we writhe for any other inflicted upon another part of the body."}

{"request_id":"e05069793e52b59f4e2abdbe","rewritten_text":"Yet despite all this, the boy grew more and more gloomy, pale, and miserable. She added hot baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges. The boy stayed as dismal as a hearse. She began supporting the water treatment with a thin oatmeal diet and blister plasters. She measured his capacity as if he were a jug and filled him every day with patent medicines.

By this time Tom had become used to being persecuted. This stage filled the old lady’s heart with alarm. His indifference had to be broken at any cost. Then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a large supply at once. She tasted it and felt deeply grateful. It was pure fire in liquid form. She abandoned the water treatment and everything else, placing all her faith in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched anxiously for the result. Her troubles immediately vanished and her spirit was at peace again, because his “indifference” had been destroyed. The boy could not have shown a livelier, stronger interest if she had built a fire beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to wake up; this kind of life might be romantic enough in his ruined condition, but it was becoming too lacking in feeling and too full of distracting variety. He considered several ways to escape and finally decided to pretend that he liked Pain-killer. He asked for it so often that he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have enjoyed it without any doubts; but because it was Tom, she secretly watched the bottle. She saw that the medicine really was disappearing, but it never occurred to her that the boy was repairing a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One day Tom was pouring medicine into the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat came by, purring, staring greedily at the teaspoon, and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it clear that he did want it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now that you’ve asked for it, I’ll give it to you, because there’s nothing mean about me. But if you find you don’t like it, you must blame no one but yourself.”

Peter agreed. So Tom forced open his mouth and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped several feet into the air, gave a war whoop, and raced around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and causing complete chaos."}

{"request_id":"ef19a0f446bbcc69ca1c1e3a","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man; a very pleasant, kindly-looking old man when I woke him. I told him my brother and me had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and had camped on part of a raft we found. About midnight, I said, he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over there and mend it, without saying anything or letting anybody know, because we meant to come home this evening and surprise the family.

“Who are your folks?” he asks.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. Then, after a moment:

“How did you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“Remarkable dream,” he says.

Then he lit his lantern, fetched his saddle-bags, and we set off. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like her appearance—said she was large enough for one, but didn’t seem safe enough for two. I says:

“Oh, you needn’t be scared, sir; she carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and _the guns;_ that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

Still, he put his foot on the gunwale and rocked her, then shook his head and said he reckoned he’d look for a larger one. But all the others were locked and chained; so he took my canoe and told me to wait until he returned, or search farther around, or perhaps go home and get things ready for the surprise if I wanted to. But I said I didn’t; so I explained exactly how to find the raft, and he started off.

I got an idea soon afterward. I says to myself, suppose he can’t mend that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do—hang around there until he gives the whole thing away? No, sir; I know what _I’ll_ do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back, if he says he has to go again, I’ll get down there too, even if I have to swim; then we’ll tie him up, keep him, and push off down the river. When Tom is finished with him, we’ll pay him whatever it’s worth, or all we have, and then let him get ashore.

So I crawled into a lumber pile to sleep; and the next time I woke, the sun was high above my head! I rushed out and went to the doctor’s house, but they told me he had left sometime during the night and hadn’t returned yet."}

{"request_id":"0a91c433d8efea75266bbfa9","rewritten_text":"Great God! If for a single moment I had imagined the hellish purpose of my fiendish enemy, I would sooner have exiled myself forever from my native land and wandered friendless across the earth than agreed to this wretched marriage. But, as though endowed with magical powers, the monster had blinded me to his true intentions; and while I believed I had prepared only my own death, I hastened that of a far more beloved victim.

As the date set for our marriage approached, whether through cowardice or some prophetic instinct, I felt my heart sink within me. Yet I concealed my feelings beneath an appearance of cheerfulness that brought smiles and happiness to my father’s face, though it scarcely deceived Elizabeth’s ever-watchful, discerning eyes. She anticipated our union with calm contentment, mixed with a little fear born of the misfortunes of the past: the fear that what now seemed certain, tangible happiness might soon dissolve into an airy dream, leaving behind only profound and lasting regret.

Preparations were made, congratulatory visits were received, and everything wore a cheerful aspect. As best I could, I locked within my own heart the anxiety that consumed me and entered with apparent sincerity into my father’s plans, though they might serve only as decorations for my tragedy. Through my father’s efforts, the Austrian government had restored part of Elizabeth’s inheritance to her. She possessed a small estate on the shores of Lake Como. It was agreed that immediately after our marriage we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend the first days of our happiness beside the beautiful lake on which it stood.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to protect myself should the fiend attack me openly. I constantly carried pistols and a dagger, remained alert against every deception, and by these means gained some measure of peace. Indeed, as the date drew near, the threat began to seem more like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing my calm; while the happiness I expected from marriage appeared increasingly certain as the appointed day of its solemnization approached and I heard it continually discussed as an event no accident could possibly prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy, and my calm manner did much to soothe her. But on the day meant to fulfill my hopes and my destiny, she was melancholy, overcome by a foreboding of evil; perhaps she was also thinking of the terrible secret I had promised to reveal to her the next day."}

{"request_id":"20316fcf2c84ebe5d5e7d84f","rewritten_text":"On that subject, therefore, I shall remain completely silent; and you may be sure that, once we are married, no ungenerous reproach will ever pass my lips.”

It was now absolutely necessary to interrupt him.

“You are too hasty, sir,” she cried. “You forget that I have given no answer. Let me give it without any further delay. Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me. I am very aware of the honour of your proposal, but I cannot do anything except refuse it.”

“I am not now learning,” replied Mr. Collins, with a formal wave of his hand, “that young ladies commonly reject the advances of the man they secretly intend to accept when he first asks for their favour; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second or even a third time. I am therefore not at all discouraged by what you have just said, and hope to lead you to the altar before long.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “that is a very strange hope after what I have declared. I assure you that I am not one of those young ladies—if such young ladies exist—who are bold enough to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked a second time. I am completely serious in refusing you. You could not make me happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who could make you happy. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am sure she would find me entirely unfit for the position.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins very seriously, “but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you at all. And you may be sure that, when I have the honour of seeing her again, I shall speak in the highest terms of your modesty, thrift, and other pleasing qualities.”

“Indeed, Mr. Collins, all praise of me will be unnecessary. You must allow me to judge for myself, and do me the courtesy of believing what I say. I wish you to be very happy and very rich, and by refusing your hand, I am doing everything I can to prevent you from being otherwise. In making me this offer, you must have satisfied your sense of duty toward my family, and you may take possession of the Longbourn estate when it comes to you without any guilt. This matter may therefore be considered finally settled.” As she spoke, she rose and would have left the room, had not Mr. Collins addressed her again:

“When I have the honour of speaking to you next about this matter, I hope to receive a more favourable answer than the one you have now given me. Still, I am far from accusing you of cruelty at present, because I know it is the established custom of your sex to reject a man the first time he proposes; and perhaps you have already said as much as would encourage my suit while remaining consistent with the true delicacy of a woman’s character.”"}

{"request_id":"3aab911a4ae02526aae28b38","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse, handsome, intelligent, and wealthy, with a comfortable home and cheerful nature, appeared to possess many of life’s greatest blessings; and had spent almost twenty-one years in the world with scarcely anything to trouble or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters belonging to a most loving and indulgent father; and, after her sister’s marriage, had become mistress of his household at a very early age. Her mother had been dead too long for Emma to retain more than a vague memory of her tenderness; and her place had been filled by an excellent governess, who had come scarcely short of a mother in affection.

Miss Taylor had been part of Mr. Woodhouse’s family for sixteen years, serving less as a governess than as a friend, deeply fond of both daughters, but especially of Emma. Between _them_, the closeness was rather that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor had formally given up her position as governess, the gentleness of her disposition had scarcely permitted her to enforce restraint; and with the appearance of authority now long gone, they had lived together as two mutually devoted friends, Emma doing exactly as she pleased; she valued Miss Taylor’s judgment highly, but was guided chiefly by her own.

The true drawbacks of Emma’s situation were, in fact, the ability to have nearly everything her own way, and a tendency to think somewhat too highly of herself; these were the faults that threatened to diminish her many pleasures. Yet the danger was currently so unnoticed that she did not regard them as misfortunes in the least.

Sorrow arrived—a mild sorrow—but not in the form of any unpleasant self-awareness.—Miss Taylor married. It was the loss of Miss Taylor that first brought Emma grief. On the wedding-day of this beloved friend, Emma first sat in sustained melancholy. Once the wedding was over and the newly married couple had departed, she and her father were left to dine together, with no expectation of a third person to brighten a long evening. Her father settled himself to sleep after dinner, as he usually did, leaving her only to sit and reflect on what she had lost.

The marriage promised complete happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of irreproachable character, comfortable means, appropriate age, and agreeable manners; and Emma found some comfort in remembering the selfless, generous friendship with which she had always desired and encouraged the match. Still, it had been a dark morning’s business for her. Miss Taylor’s absence would be felt every hour of every day. She remembered her former kindness—the kindness and affection of sixteen years—how Miss Taylor had taught her and played with her from the age of five—how she had devoted all her abilities to keeping Emma attached and entertained when she was well—and how she had nursed her through the many illnesses of childhood."}

{"request_id":"98ac4c7e7f30f63f9d26c1ea","rewritten_text":"After dinner, the whole gang went out onto the sandbar to hunt for turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and whenever they found a soft spot, they dropped to their knees and dug with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. The eggs were perfectly round and white, a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a splendid fried-egg feast, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast, they went whooping and prancing onto the bar, chasing one another in circles and shedding their clothes as they ran until they were naked. Then they carried on their frolic far up the bar’s shallow water, struggling against the strong current, which repeatedly knocked their legs out from under them and made the fun even greater. From time to time they gathered together and splashed water into one another’s faces with their palms, gradually drawing closer, their faces turned away to escape the choking spray. At last they seized and wrestled with one another until the strongest ducked his neighbor, and then all of them went under in a tangle of pale legs and arms. They surfaced blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for breath all at once.

When they were thoroughly worn out, they ran ashore and sprawled on the dry, hot sand, lying there and covering themselves with it. Before long they would rush back into the water and repeat the whole performance. Finally, they realized that their bare skin served quite well as flesh-colored “tights.” They drew a circle in the sand and put on a circus—with three clowns, since none of them would surrender that most honored position to another.

Next they brought out their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until the game lost its appeal. Then Joe and Huck went swimming again, but Tom refused, because when he kicked off his trousers, he had also kicked the string of rattlesnake rattles from his ankle. He wondered how he had avoided cramps for so long without the protection of that mysterious charm. He would not go back into the water until he found it, and by then the other boys were tired and ready to rest. Gradually they drifted apart, sank into the “dumps,” and gazed wistfully across the broad river toward the village, which lay dozing in the sunlight. Tom caught himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe. He scratched it out and was angry at himself for being so weak. But he wrote it again anyway; he could not help himself. He erased it once more, then escaped the temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"d4265c5eb5ba2f9167d737ad","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the orangutan immediately sprang through the chamber door, down the stairs, and then through a window—unfortunately left open—into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair. The ape, still holding the razor, would sometimes stop to look back and gesture at its pursuer until he had nearly caught up with it. Then it would flee again. The chase continued in this way for a long time. The streets were utterly quiet, since it was nearly three in the morning. While passing through an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive noticed a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s room, on the fourth floor of her house. It rushed toward the building, saw the lightning rod, and climbed it with astonishing agility. Grasping the shutter, which had been thrown fully back against the wall, it swung itself onto the bed’s headboard. The entire feat took less than a minute. As the orangutan entered the room, it kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor was both relieved and bewildered. He hoped strongly that he could now recapture the animal, since it could hardly escape the trap it had entered except by the rod, where he might intercept it on its way down. Yet he was also deeply anxious about what it might do inside the house. This concern drove him to continue after the fugitive. A lightning rod is not difficult to climb, especially for a sailor; but when he reached the height of the window, which was far to his left, his progress stopped. The most he could do was lean over far enough to glimpse the room’s interior. At that sight, he nearly lost his grip from sheer horror. It was then that the terrible shrieks rose into the night, startling the residents of the Rue Morgue from sleep. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, had apparently been arranging papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been rolled into the center of the room. It stood open, with its contents scattered on the floor beside it. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window; and, judging by the time between the animal’s entrance and the screams, they probably did not notice it at once. The shutter slamming closed would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked inside, the huge animal seized Madame L’Espanaye by the hair, which hung loose because she had been combing it, and waved the razor around her face, imitating a barber’s movements."}

{"request_id":"ec2a18c50bf2d810537fe53a","rewritten_text":"“I hope I shall soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, quite willing to believe that such a hope was meant as a special compliment to her, smiled most graciously.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I suppose,” he continued—“and know him to be my son, although he does not bear my name.”

“Oh! yes, and I shall be very happy to make his acquaintance. I am sure Mr. Elton will lose no time in calling on him; and we shall both be delighted to see him at the Vicarage.”

“You are very obliging.—Frank will be extremely pleased, I am sure.—He is to be in town next week, if not sooner. We received notice of it in a letter today. I came across the letters on my way this morning, and, seeing my son’s handwriting, assumed I might open it—although it was not addressed to me—it was for Mrs. Weston. She is his chief correspondent, I assure you. I hardly ever receive a letter.”

“And so you actually opened one addressed to her! Oh! Mr. Weston—” (laughing affectedly) “I must protest against that.—What a dangerous precedent!—I beg you not to let your neighbours follow your example.—Upon my word, if this is what I am to expect, we married women must begin to defend ourselves!—Oh! Mr. Weston, I could never have believed it of you!”

“Yes, we men are wretched creatures. You must look after yourself, Mrs. Elton.—This letter tells us—it is a short letter—written in haste, merely to give us notice—it tells us that they are all coming to town immediately, because of Mrs. Churchill—she has been unwell throughout the winter, and considers Enscombe too cold for her—so they are all to move south without delay.”

“Indeed!—from Yorkshire, I think. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, they are about one hundred and ninety miles from London, a considerable journey.”

“Yes, upon my word, very considerable. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of great fortune?—You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes travels about. You will scarcely believe me—but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back with four horses.”

“The difficulty with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand, has not been able to leave the sofa for a whole week. In Frank’s last letter, he said she complained of being too weak to reach her conservatory without both his arm and his uncle’s!”"}

{"request_id":"0daa5a128f04b88d1b354d61","rewritten_text":"The studio was full of the rich scent of roses, and whenever the light summer breeze moved through the garden trees, the heavy fragrance of lilac or the gentler perfume of the pink-flowering hawthorn drifted in through the open door.

From the corner of the Persian saddlebag divan where he lay smoking, as usual, countless cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could just see the gleam of the laburnum’s honey-sweet, honey-coloured blossoms. Its trembling branches seemed barely able to support such flame-like beauty. From time to time, the strange shadows of flying birds passed over the long tussore-silk curtains drawn across the enormous window, creating a brief Japanese effect and reminding him of the pale, jade-faced painters of Tokyo who, through an art necessarily still, tried to suggest speed and movement. The brooding hum of bees forcing their way through the tall, uncut grass, or circling monotonously around the dusty golden horns of the wandering honeysuckle, seemed to make the silence more oppressive. The muted roar of London sounded like the sustained note of a distant organ.

At the centre of the room, fixed to an upright easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of remarkable beauty. A short distance before it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance several years earlier had caused great public excitement and inspired so many strange theories.

As the painter studied the graceful, handsome figure he had so skilfully reproduced in his art, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to remain there. But he suddenly rose, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against the lids, as if trying to hold inside his mind some curious dream from which he feared he might wake.

“It is your finest work, Basil—the best thing you have ever done,” Lord Henry said lazily. “You must certainly send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too large and too vulgar. Whenever I have gone there, there have either been so many people that I could not see the pictures, which was dreadful, or so many pictures that I could not see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I’ll send it anywhere,” he replied, throwing his head back in that peculiar manner that had once made his friends laugh at him at Oxford."}
