{"request_id":"1f498a5fd0ed5ae59144439e","rewritten_text":"“I must take the liberty of observing, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he put down the newspaper, “that the present moment is greatly in our favour. This peace will be sending all our wealthy naval officers ashore. They will all be seeking a home. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, for choosing tenants—very responsible tenants. Many a noble fortune has been made during the war. If a rich admiral should come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” replied Sir Walter; “that is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would indeed be a prize to him; perhaps the greatest prize of all, though he may have taken ever so many before; hey, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he was expected to do, at this wit, and then continued—

“I presume to remark, Sir Walter, that, in business matters, gentlemen of the navy are very agreeable to deal with. I have gained some knowledge of their methods; and I freely confess that they hold very liberal opinions, and are as likely to prove desirable tenants as any class of people one could encounter. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would venture to suggest is, that if, through any rumours spreading of your intention—which must be considered possible, since we know how difficult it is to keep the actions and plans of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of another; consequence has its price—I, John Shepherd, might conceal any family affairs I pleased, for no one would think it worthwhile to watch me; but Sir Walter Elliot has eyes upon him which may be very hard to escape; and so far I will venture, that it will not greatly surprise me if, despite all our caution, some report of the truth should circulate; in which case, as I was about to say, since applications will certainly follow, I should consider those from our wealthy naval commanders especially deserving attention; and beg leave to add that, at any time, two hours will bring me over, to spare you the trouble of answering.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. But shortly afterwards, getting up and walking about the room, he observed sarcastically—

“There are few among the gentlemen of the navy, I imagine, who would not be astonished to find themselves in a house of this character.”

“They would look about them, no doubt, and bless their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, for Mrs Clay was present: her father had driven her over, since nothing benefited Mrs Clay’s health so much as a drive to Kellynch; “but I entirely agree with my father in thinking that a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"fa24f2cd943d7832886be85a","rewritten_text":"His account was this: while travelling from his home and passing through Datchet, he was astonished to see smoke rising from the inn chimney. Thinking he might find fellow travellers gathered there, he knocked and was admitted. No one was in the house except Lucy and her mother; the latter had lost the use of her limbs through an attack of rheumatism, and thus, one after another, all the remaining inhabitants of the country had departed, leaving the two of them alone. Lucy begged the man to remain with her; within a week or two her mother would improve, and they could then set out, but if left so helpless and abandoned, they must perish. The man replied that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and therefore, as he saw it, he could not stay. As a final expedient, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to be delivered wherever he might meet us. This duty at least he performed, and Idris received, deeply moved, the following letter:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am certain you will remember and pity me, and I dare hope that you will help me; what other hope remains to me? Forgive the way I write, for I am so confused. A month ago my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already somewhat better, and in another month, I am sure, she would be able to travel, in the manner you were so kind as to say you would arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone—as they left, each one said that perhaps my mother would recover before we were entirely deserted. But three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who, because of his new-born child, stayed until the last; and since there were many of them, I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us. But I found the house empty. I have seen no one since, until this good man arrived. —What will become of us? My mother does not know our condition; she is so ill that I have concealed it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? Surely we must perish miserably if we remain as we are. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die upon the road; and if, once she recovered, I could somehow discover the roads and travel so many miles to the sea, you would all be in France, with the vast ocean between us, which is dreadful even to sailors."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3bb2aaf3370086fa3ad47c86","rewritten_text":"So the ringmaster made a short speech, saying he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance, and that if the man promised not to cause more trouble, he would let him ride, provided he thought he could stay on the horse. Everybody laughed and said all right, and the man climbed aboard. The instant he was up, the horse began to rip and tear, jumping and cavorting, while two circus men clung to his bridle and tried to restrain him, and the drunk man hung onto his neck, his heels flying up with every leap. The whole crowd stood shouting and laughing until tears ran down their faces. At last, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse broke free and went off like the very nation, racing around the ring with the sot sprawled over him and gripping his neck, one leg dangling nearly to the ground on one side, then the other on the other side, while the people went clean crazy. It wasn’t funny to me, though; I trembled to see the man in such danger. But soon he struggled upright astride the horse and seized the bridle, reeling this way and that. Then, the next minute, he sprang up, let go of the bridle, and stood! The horse was still going like a house afire. He stood there, sailing around as easily and comfortably as if he had never been drunk in his life—and then began stripping off his clothes and flinging them away. He shed them so rapidly they seemed to clog the air, and altogether he threw off seventeen suits. Then there he was, slim and handsome, dressed in the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you ever saw. He laid into the horse with his whip and made him fairly hum, then finally skipped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing-room, while everybody howled with delight and astonishment.\n\nThen the ringmaster saw how completely he had been fooled, and he was the sickest ringmaster you ever saw, I reckon. Why, it was one of his own men! He had invented the whole joke himself and never told a soul. Well, I felt sheepish enough at being taken in, but I wouldn’t have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. I don’t know; there may be better circuses than that one, but I’ve never come across them yet. Anyway, it was good enough for me; and wherever I find it, it can have all my custom every time."}

{"request_id":"cab5b7e94e01d10c01497e9f","rewritten_text":"He mounted the fiery horse that had carried him to victory in Greece. He wore himself out with exhausting exercise, dulling the pain of his troubled mind through physical sensation.

Slowly, he recovered his senses. At last, like someone emerging from the effects of poison, he raised his head above the vapours of fever and passion into the calm air of reflection. He considered what should be done. He was first struck by how much time had passed since madness, rather than reason, had guided his actions. A month had gone by, and in all that time he had not seen Evadne. Her hold over him, tied to only a few of the lasting feelings in his heart, had greatly weakened. He was no longer her slave, nor her lover. He would never see her again, and by fully returning to Perdita, he would earn her trust.

Yet, as he made this decision, his imagination brought before him the miserable home of the Greek girl—a home she had refused to exchange for greater luxury because of her noble principles. He remembered the splendour of her appearance and circumstances when he had first known her. He remembered her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every sign of Eastern magnificence; and he thought of her present poverty, her daily labour, her lonely condition, and her faded, hunger-stricken face. Compassion filled his heart. He would see her once more. He would find some way to restore her to society and to the enjoyment of her rank. After that, their separation would happen naturally.

Then he thought again of how, throughout this long month, he had avoided Perdita, fleeing from her as though from the stings of his own conscience. But he was awake now. All this would be corrected, and future devotion would erase the memory of this single stain on the peace of their life. The thought made him cheerful, and he calmly and firmly planned the conduct he would follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita to attend that very evening—19 October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—a festival held in his honour. May the festival prove a good sign of the happiness of the years ahead. First, he would visit Evadne briefly. He would not remain, but he owed her an explanation and some compensation for his long, unexplained absence. Then he would go to Perdita, to the world he had forgotten, to the duties of society, the splendour of rank, and the enjoyment of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had expected a complete change in Raymond’s manner and conduct. She looked forward to open communication and a return to the affectionate habits that had once made her life so happy."}

{"request_id":"8fa60f2bcc146121c5b48510","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction, and though I had fully expected it, the event gave me the most unmistakable pleasure. After reaching, on its previous course, approximately the twentieth parallel of southern latitude, it suddenly veered eastward at a sharp angle, and continued in that direction throughout the day, keeping almost, if not entirely, within the exact plane of the lunar ellipse. One notable result of this alteration in course was a very distinct swaying of the car—a motion that continued, to a greater or lesser extent, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again greatly frightened by a recurrence of the loud, crackling noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I reflected long on the matter, but could reach no satisfactory explanation. The earth’s apparent diameter had diminished considerably, now subtending from the balloon an angle of scarcely more than twenty-five degrees. The moon was wholly invisible, being nearly at my zenith. I remained in the plane of the ellipse, but advanced only slightly eastward.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter decreased with extraordinary rapidity. To-day I became firmly convinced that the balloon was actually ascending the line of apsides toward the point of perigee—in other words, following the direct path that would carry it straight to the moon at the portion of its orbit nearest the earth. The moon itself was immediately overhead and therefore concealed from my sight. Much prolonged labor was required to condense the atmosphere.

“April 15th. The continents and seas upon the earth could no longer be distinguished, even in outline, with anything like clarity. About noon I became conscious, for the third time, of that dreadful sound which had previously so amazed me. This time, however, it lasted several moments and grew louder as it continued. At last, while I stood stupefied and terrified, expecting some unknown and horrible destruction, the car shook with tremendous violence, and a vast flaming mass of material, whose nature I could not discern, rushed past the balloon with the roar and thunder of a thousand voices. When my fear and astonishment had somewhat abated, I found little difficulty in believing it to be some enormous volcanic fragment cast out from the world toward which I was rapidly drawing, and probably belonging to that peculiar class of substances sometimes found upon the earth and called meteoric stones for lack of a better name.

“April 16th. To-day, looking upward as best I could through each side window in turn, I saw, to my great delight, a very small part of the moon’s disk extending, as it were, on every side beyond the balloon’s enormous circumference."}

{"request_id":"862ba42cc33b3b63f88e5856","rewritten_text":"Smallpox!

I rushed to the king and whispered in his ear:

“Leave at once, sire! The woman is dying of the disease that ravaged Camelot two years ago.”

He did not move.

“Indeed, I shall stay—and help as well.”

I whispered again:

“King, you must not. You must go.”

“You mean well, and your words are not foolish. But it would be shameful for a king to show fear, and shameful for a knight in armor to hold back his hand when people need help. Be quiet; I will not go. You are the one who must leave. The Church’s ban is not upon me, but it forbids you to be here, and it will punish you severely if it hears of your trespass.”

It was a desperate situation for him and might cost him his life, but there was no use arguing. If he believed his knightly honor was at stake, that ended the matter; he would stay, and nothing could stop him. I knew that, so I dropped the subject. The woman spoke:

“Good sir, would you kindly climb that ladder and tell me what you find? Do not be afraid to report it, for there are times when even a mother’s heart is beyond breaking—because it is already broken.”

“Stay,” said the king, “and give the woman something to eat. I will go.” He set down the knapsack.

I turned to leave, but the king had already begun. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in the dim light, who had not noticed us or spoken.

“Is he your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“Thank God for that one kindness, yes—for three hours. Where can I fully repay my gratitude? My heart is overflowing with it because he sleeps now.”

I said:

“We will be careful. We will not wake him.”

“Oh no, you will not, for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes. What a victory it is to know that! No one can hurt him or insult him again. He is in heaven now and happy; or, if he is not there, he remains in hell and is content, for there he will find neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together, and man and wife for twenty-five years, never separated until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer together. This morning he was out of his mind, imagining that we were boy and girl again, wandering through happy fields. So, in that innocent, joyful conversation, he wandered farther and farther, still talking lightly, and entered those other fields we know nothing about, shut away from mortal sight."}

{"request_id":"7d38c01153256ead69bc4ce1","rewritten_text":"The day went by much as the preceding one had. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley had passed part of the morning with the invalid, who continued, though slowly, to recover; and, in the evening, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was not brought out. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley, seated beside him, watched his letter taking shape and repeatedly diverted his attention with messages for her sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was watching their game.

Elizabeth took up her needlework and found sufficient amusement in observing what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s continual praises, whether of his handwriting, the regularity of his lines, or the length of his letter, together with the complete indifference with which he received them, made a curious dialogue, and perfectly agreed with Elizabeth’s opinion of both.

“How pleased Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!”

He made no reply.

“You write remarkably quickly.”

“You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write over the course of a year! Business letters as well! How detestable I should find them!”

“It is fortunate, then, that they fall to me rather than to you.”

“Pray tell your sister that I am eager to see her.”

“I have already told her so once, at your request.”

“I fear you do not like your pen. Let me mend it for you. I am remarkably good at mending pens.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He remained silent.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and pray inform her that I am quite enchanted by her lovely little design for a table, which I consider infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to postpone your raptures until I write again? At present I have not space to do them justice.”

“Oh, it is of no importance. I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charmingly long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long; but whether they are always charming, I am not the proper judge.”

“It is my rule that anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write badly.”

“That will not serve as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” cried her brother, “for he does not write with ease. He thinks too carefully over words of four syllables. Do you not, Darcy?”

“My manner of writing is quite different from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless manner imaginable."}

Will you kindly enter the carriage?’

“The manner of both men was imperious, and as these words were spoken they moved to position me between themselves and the carriage door. They were armed; I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ said I, ‘forgive me; but I generally ask who has the honour of requesting my assistance, and what is the nature of the case for which I am summoned.’

“The answer came from the one who had spoken second. ‘Doctor, your clients are persons of condition. As for the nature of the case, our confidence in your ability assures us that you will discover it more readily than we could explain it. Enough. Will you kindly enter the carriage?’

“I could do nothing except comply, and entered in silence. They followed me in—the last springing aboard after raising the steps. The carriage turned and continued at its previous speed.

“I repeat this conversation precisely as it occurred. I have no doubt it is the same word for word. I relate everything exactly as it happened, forcing my mind not to stray from the task. At the broken marks that follow, I stop for the moment and place my paper in its hiding-place.

*****

“The carriage left the streets behind, passed through the North Barrier, and came out upon the country road. Two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier—it was not until afterwards, when I travelled the distance, that I estimated it—it turned from the main avenue and soon stopped before a solitary house. All three of us alighted and walked along a damp, yielding footpath through a garden where an unattended fountain had overflowed, to the house door. The door was not opened at once when the bell was rung, and one of my two conductors struck the man who opened it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“There was nothing in this act to draw my special notice, since I had seen common people struck more often than dogs. But the other man, angered as well, struck him in the same fashion with his arm; the brothers’ expressions and bearing were then so precisely alike that I first understood they were twins.

“From the moment we alighted at the outer gate—which we found locked, and which one brother opened to let us in before locking it again—I had heard cries coming from an upper chamber."}

{"request_id":"5b299e5ef8f38b9114a622a2","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The omission had been punished upon the sinner; for when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no letter of condolence arrived at Kellynch, and there was therefore too much reason to fear that the Dalrymples regarded the connection as ended. How this troublesome matter might be repaired, and they be received again as cousins, was the question; and, in a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot considered it insignificant. “Family connections were always worth preserving, and good society always worth pursuing; Lady Dalrymple had taken a house in Laura Place for three months, and would be living handsomely. She had been at Bath the previous year, and Lady Russell had heard her described as a charming woman. It was greatly to be wished that the connection might be restored, if it could be done without any sacrifice of propriety on the Elliots’ part.”

Sir Walter, however, would employ his own methods, and eventually wrote his right honourable cousin a very elegant letter, full of explanation, regret, and entreaty. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot admired it; but it achieved its purpose, producing three lines of scrawl from the Dowager Viscountess: “She was highly honoured, and would be happy in their acquaintance.” The labour of the affair was finished, and its pleasures began. They paid visits in Laura Place, obtained the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, to be displayed wherever they would be most conspicuous; and “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—were mentioned to everyone.

Anne felt ashamed. Even had Lady Dalrymple and her daughter been particularly agreeable, she would have been embarrassed by the excitement they caused; but they were nothing. They possessed no superiority of manner, accomplishment, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the reputation of “a charming woman” because she smiled and gave every person a civil reply. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and awkward that she could never have been admitted into Camden Place except for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected more; yet “it was an acquaintance worth having.” And when Anne ventured to express her opinion of them to Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but still insisted that, as a family connection, as good society, and as people capable of gathering good society about them, they had their importance. Anne smiled and said,

“My notion of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of intelligent, well-informed people, who have much to say; that is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"349a96f0c7c1b3c634f5569a","rewritten_text":"“I agree. It’s the best plan. Will you hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh, no, that won’t do for this. That’s good enough for little, common rubbish—especially with gals, ’cause _they_ go back on you anyhow, and blab when they get mad—but there ought to be writing about a big thing like this. And blood.”

Tom’s entire being applauded the notion. It was profound, gloomy, and terrible; the hour, the circumstances, and the surroundings suited it perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, drew a small piece of “red keel” from his pocket, turned his work toward the moon, and painfully scratched out these words, stressing every slow down-stroke by gripping his tongue between his teeth and easing the pressure on the up-strokes.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry was full of wonder at Tom’s skill with writing and the grandeur of his language. He immediately pulled a pin from his lapel and was about to prick himself, but Tom stopped him:

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin’s brass. It may have verdigrease on it.”

“What’s verdigrease?”

“It’s poison. That’s what it is. You just swallow some once—you’ll find out.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked the ball of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he taught Huckleberry to form an H and an F, and the oath was finished. They buried the shingle near the wall with gloomy ceremonies and incantations, and the fetters binding their tongues were thought to be locked, with the key thrown away.

A figure now crept silently through a gap at the far end of the ruined building, but they failed to notice it.

“Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this stop us from _ever_ telling—_always_?”

“Of course it does. No matter _what_ happens, we’ve got to keep mum. We’d drop dead—don’t _you_ know that?”

“Yes, I reckon that’s true.”

They went on whispering for a while. Presently, a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—less than ten feet away. The boys suddenly seized each other, terrified.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, _you_, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t _do_ it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"24f9a36dd448cfaf43400021","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, the force of gravity would steadily diminish in proportion to the squares of the distances, and so, with a velocity increasing enormously, I would eventually reach those remote regions where the earth’s attraction was overtaken by the moon’s. For that reason, I did not think it necessary to burden myself with provisions for more than forty days.

“There remained, however, another difficulty that caused me some concern. It has been observed that, during balloon ascents to any considerable height, people suffer not only pain in breathing but also great discomfort in the head and body, often accompanied by nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms, all becoming more troublesome as the altitude increases. This was a somewhat disturbing thought. Was it not likely that these symptoms would continue to worsen, perhaps until death itself brought them to an end? In the end, I decided that they would not. Their cause was to be found in the gradual removal of the usual atmospheric pressure from the body’s surface, and the resulting swelling of the superficial blood vessels—not in any actual breakdown of the animal system, as occurs in difficulty breathing, when the atmosphere is too thin to renew the blood properly in one of the heart’s ventricles. Except for the failure of that renewal, I could see no reason why life could not continue even in a vacuum; for the expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is purely muscular action, and the cause rather than the effect of respiration. In short, I believed that, as the body grew accustomed to the absence of atmospheric pressure, the painful sensations would gradually lessen—and to endure them while they lasted, I trusted confidently in the iron strength of my constitution.

“Thus, Your Excellencies, I have described some, though by no means all, of the considerations that led me to conceive the plan of a journey to the moon. I shall now present the result of an attempt so audacious in conception and, in any case, so entirely without precedent in human history.

“After reaching the altitude mentioned earlier—that is, three miles and three-quarters—I threw a quantity of feathers from the car and found that I was still rising rapidly enough; there was therefore no need to release any ballast. I was pleased by this, since I wished to keep with me as much weight as I could carry, for reasons that will be explained later."}

{"request_id":"70434b3694f3fea1ddfc4263","rewritten_text":"They know what a clever lad he is; he’ll be a lifer. They’ll make the Artful nothing less than a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “Why talk to me like that? Why don’t you speak so I can understand you?”

Fagin was about to translate these mysterious expressions into plain language. Once explained, Mr. Bolter would have learned that they meant “transportation for life,” but the conversation was interrupted by the arrival of Master Bates, his hands in his breeches-pockets and his face twisted into a half-comical look of misery.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” said Charley, after he and his new companion had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to identify him; and the Artful’s booked for a passage out,” replied Master Bates. “I must have a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband, so I can visit him in them before he sets off on his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad for a common, cheap snuffbox! I never thought he’d have done it for less than a gold watch, chain, and seals. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables and go out like a gentleman, instead of as a common thief, without any honour or glory!”

After expressing these feelings for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates sat down on the nearest chair, looking bitter and discouraged.

“What do you mean, saying he has neither honour nor glory?” exclaimed Fagin, casting an angry look at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best among you all? Is there one of you who could match him or come close to him at any job? Eh?”

“Not one,” replied Master Bates, his voice made hoarse by regret; “not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin replied angrily. “What are you crying for?”

“Because it won’t be in the record, will it?” said Charley, driven into openly defying his old friend by his grief. “Because it can’t appear in the indictment; because nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he appear in the Newgate Calendar? Perhaps he won’t be there at all. Oh, my eye, my eye, what a blow it is!”

“Ha! Ha!” cried Fagin, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter in a fit of laughter that shook him as if he had the palsy. “See how proud they are of their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"907d1d53216fe13eede345a3","rewritten_text":"“One word more, Rose. Dearest Rose—just one more!” cried Harry, throwing himself before her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world would call it—if some obscure and peaceful life had been my destiny—if I had been poor, sick, helpless—would you have turned from me then? Or has my likely rise to wealth and honour given birth to this scruple?”

“Do not force me to answer,” Rose replied. “The question does not arise, and never will. It is unfair, almost unkind, to press me.”

“If your answer is what I scarcely dare hope,” Harry returned, “it will cast a gleam of happiness upon my lonely path and light the way before me. It is no small thing to do so much, with a few brief words, for one who loves you above everything else. Oh, Rose: in the name of my passionate and lasting devotion; in the name of all I have suffered for you, and all you condemn me to endure; answer me this one question!”

“Then, if your lot had been different,” Rose answered; “if you had been even a little, though not so far, above me; if I could have been a help and comfort to you in some humble life of peace and retirement, rather than a blemish and burden among ambitious and distinguished people; I would have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be happy—very happy—now; but then, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

As Rose made this confession, crowded memories of old hopes, cherished long ago when she was a girl, filled her mind; but they brought tears with them, as old hopes do when they return withered, and the tears brought her relief.

“I cannot help this weakness, and it strengthens my resolve,” she said, extending her hand. “I must leave you now, truly.”

“I ask one promise,” said Harry. “Once, and only once more—say within a year, though it may be much sooner—I may speak to you again on this subject, for the last time.”

“Not to urge me to change my rightful decision,” Rose replied, with a melancholy smile; “it will be useless.”

“No,” said Harry; “to hear you repeat it, if you will—repeat it finally! I will lay at your feet whatever position or fortune I may possess; and if you still hold to your present resolution, I will not try, by word or deed, to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose replied; “it is only one more pang, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

She extended her hand again."}

{"request_id":"0cb35ebc25aee5a97ccee0be","rewritten_text":"On the morning chosen for Admiral and Mrs Croft to view Kellynch Hall, Anne found it most natural to take her almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s and stay away until everything was finished; afterward, she found it equally natural to regret missing the chance to see them.

The meeting between the two parties was highly satisfactory and settled the whole matter at once. Both ladies were already well inclined toward an agreement and therefore saw only good manners in each other. As for the gentlemen, the Admiral showed such warm good humor and open, trusting generosity that he could not help influencing Sir Walter. Sir Walter had also been flattered into his finest and most polished behavior by Mr Shepherd’s assurance that the Admiral knew him by reputation as a model of good breeding.

The house, grounds, and furniture were approved; the Crofts were approved; the terms, timing, everything, and everyone were satisfactory. Mr Shepherd’s clerks began their work without a single preliminary disagreement to alter in all that “This indenture sheweth.”

Sir Walter declared without hesitation that the Admiral was the best-looking sailor he had ever met. He even said that, if his own servant had been allowed to arrange the Admiral’s hair, he would not have been ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. As the Admiral and his wife drove back through the park, he remarked with equal warmth, “I thought we should soon reach an agreement, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—compliments that would have been considered fairly equal.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas. Since Sir Walter planned to move to Bath during the previous month, there was no time to lose in making all the necessary arrangements.

Lady Russell was convinced that Anne would not be allowed any useful or important part in choosing the house they were about to secure. She was therefore very unwilling to have Anne sent away so soon and wanted her to remain until Lady Russell could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. But Lady Russell had commitments of her own that would keep her away from Kellynch for several weeks, so she could not offer the full invitation she wished. Anne dreaded the possible September heat in Bath’s bright white glare and grieved to give up the autumn months in the country, with all their gentle and painful influence; yet, considering everything, she did not think she wished to stay."}

{"request_id":"72c4245e675068d01d4593b7","rewritten_text":"“Men marry because they are tired; women because they are curious: both end up disappointed.”

“I don’t think I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your aphorisms. I’m putting it into practice, as I do everything you say.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“An actress,” said Dorian Gray, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That’s a rather commonplace beginning.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard of her.”

“No one has. They will someday, though. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are a decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they say it charmingly. Women represent the triumph of matter over mind, just as men represent the triumph of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you say that?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s quite true. I’m analyzing women at present, so I ought to know. The subject isn’t as obscure as I thought. I find that, ultimately, there are only two kinds of women: the plain and the painted. Plain women are very useful. If you want to gain a reputation for respectability, you only have to take them down to supper. The others are very charming. They make one mistake, however. They paint themselves to look young. Our grandmothers painted themselves in order to speak brilliantly. Rouge and wit used to go together. That’s all over now. As long as a woman can look ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s perfectly satisfied. As for conversation, there are only five women in London worth talking to, and two of them can’t be admitted into decent society. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah, Harry, your views terrify me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you mustn’t be unsympathetic. After all, it never would have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. For days after meeting you, something seemed to throb in my veins. As I lounged in the park or strolled down Piccadilly, I would look at everyone who passed and wonder, with a mad curiosity, what kind of lives they led. Some fascinated me. Others filled me with terror. There was an exquisite poison in the air. I had a passion for sensations....”"}

{"request_id":"8924c33fa5d07fea688b0276","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, still unsure where to go. “At Tellson’s bank at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise, in the meantime, to show myself? I think so. It is best that these people should know there is such a man as I here; it is a sound precaution, and may be necessary preparation. But care, care, care! Let me think it through!”

He checked his steps, which had begun to carry him toward a destination, turned once or twice through the already darkening street, and followed the thought in his mind to its possible consequences. His first impression was confirmed. “It is best,” he said at last, firmly resolved, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” And he turned toward Saint Antoine.

Defarge had described himself that day as the keeper of a wine-shop in the Saint Antoine suburb. Anyone who knew the city well could find his house without asking questions. After locating it, Carton came out of the narrower streets again, dined at a place serving refreshments, and fell sound asleep afterward. For the first time in many years, he had no strong drink. Since the previous night he had taken nothing but a little light, thin wine, and the night before he had slowly poured the brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth like a man who had finished with it.

It was as late as seven o’clock when he awoke refreshed and went out into the streets again. As he walked toward Saint Antoine, he stopped at a shop window containing a mirror and slightly rearranged his loose cravat, his coat collar, and his wild hair. Then he went straight to Defarge’s and entered.

There happened to be no customer in the shop except Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and croaking voice. This man, whom Carton had seen on the Jury, stood drinking at the small counter and talking with the Defarges, husband and wife. The Vengeance joined in the conversation like a regular member of the establishment.

When Carton entered, took a seat, and asked, in very indifferent French, for a small measure of wine, Madame Defarge gave him a careless glance, then a sharper one, then a sharper still, and finally approached him herself to ask what he had ordered.

He repeated what he had already said.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, raising her dark eyebrows inquisitively.

After looking at her as though even the sound of a single French word took him time to understand, he answered in the same strong foreign accent as before."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7cf892cd572d43d455a9cf84","rewritten_text":"The mental qualities called analytical are, by themselves, difficult to analyze. We recognize them only by their effects. Among other things, we know that, when possessed to an unusual degree, they give their owner intense pleasure. Just as a strong man takes pride in his physical power and enjoys exercises that use his muscles, so the analyst delights in the mental activity that untangles problems. He enjoys even the simplest tasks that bring his talent into play. He likes riddles, puzzles, and hieroglyphics, and in solving each he shows a sharpness of insight that seems almost supernatural to ordinary minds. His conclusions, reached through the very essence of method, seem in fact to have all the appearance of intuition.\n\nThe ability to solve problems may be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by its highest branch, which has been unfairly called analysis merely because it works backward. Yet calculation is not, by itself, analysis. A chess player, for example, calculates without analyzing. It follows that the effect of chess on the mind is widely misunderstood. I am not writing a treatise, but merely introducing a somewhat unusual narrative with observations made almost at random; I will therefore say that the higher and more useful powers of the reflective mind are exercised more clearly by the quiet game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and unusual ways and have changing values, people mistake complexity for depth, as they often do. Attention is intensely engaged. If it weakens for even a moment, an oversight occurs and leads to harm or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but complicated, such oversights become more likely; and in nine games out of ten, the more focused player defeats the more naturally clever one. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are distinctive and vary little, mistakes caused by carelessness are less likely. Since simple attention is left relatively unused, any advantage either player gains comes from superior insight. To make this less abstract, imagine a game of draughts reduced to four kings, where, naturally, no oversight need be expected. It is clear that, if the players are otherwise equal, victory can be decided only by some unusual move resulting from a powerful effort of intellect."}

{"request_id":"0eb2560ff9e66594c4d72ffe","rewritten_text":"“Do you often come back?”

“I have never been here since.”

“Nor have I.”

The moon began to rise, and I thought of the calm expression on the white ceiling, which had vanished. The moon began to rise, and I thought of the pressure on my hand when I spoke the last words he heard on earth.

Estella was the next to break the silence between us.

“I have often hoped and meant to come back, but many circumstances prevented me. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the moon’s first rays, and those same rays touched the tears falling from her eyes. Unaware that I saw them, and trying to master them, she said quietly,

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left in this condition?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground belongs to me. It is the only possession I have not given up. Everything else has gone from me, little by little, but I have kept this. It was the only matter over which I made a determined stand throughout all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built on?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say goodbye to it before it changes. And you,” she said, with touching interest in the wanderer, “you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you do well, I am sure?”

“I work fairly hard to earn enough to live, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” said Estella.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long, difficult time when I kept far from me the memory of what I had thrown away while completely unaware of its value. But since my duty no longer conflicted with admitting that memory, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have always held your place in my heart,” I replied.

Again we were silent, until she spoke.

“I never imagined,” said Estella, “that I would say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place. I am very glad to do so.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? To me, parting is painful. The memory of our last parting has always been sorrowful and painful to me.”

“But you said to me,” Estella answered, very earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you will not hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has taught me more powerfully than anything else, and has taught me to understand what your heart once was. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"82b24a6d3ea40efc992177fd","rewritten_text":"Having seen our friend properly settled in his new office, we turned our attention toward Windsor. Its nearness to London was enough to remove any sense of painful separation when we left Raymond and Perdita. We said goodbye to them in the Protectoral Palace. It was charming to see my sister enter, as it were, into the spirit of the drama and try to fill her position with appropriate dignity. Her inward pride and modesty were now more than ever at war. Her shyness was not affected, but arose from a fear of not being properly valued, that slight sense of the world’s neglect which also marked Raymond. Yet Perdita thought more constantly of others than he did; and part of her bashfulness came from a desire to spare those around her any feeling of inferiority—a feeling that never entered her own mind. Given his birth and education, Idris would have been better suited to the forms of ceremony; but the ease with which habit enabled him to perform such actions made them tedious, whereas Perdita, despite every disadvantage, plainly enjoyed her situation. She was too full of new ideas to feel much sorrow at our departure. She took an affectionate leave of us and promised to visit soon, but she did not regret the circumstances that had brought about our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless; he did not know what to do with his newly acquired power. His head was crowded with plans, though he had settled on none; but he promised himself, his friends, and the world that the era of his Protectorship would be marked by some act of extraordinary glory. Thus we spoke of them and reflected as, with our numbers reduced, we returned to Windsor Castle. We were intensely relieved to have escaped political turmoil and sought our solitude with renewed eagerness. We had no lack of occupation; but my restless energy was now directed solely toward intellectual effort, and I found hard study an excellent remedy for the fever of spirit that, in idleness, would surely have overtaken me. Perdita had allowed us to bring Clara back with us to Windsor, and she, together with my two lovely infants, was a constant source of interest and amusement.\n\nThe only thing that disturbed our peace was Adrian’s health. It was clearly failing, though he showed no symptom that could reveal his illness—unless his brighter eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption. Yet he suffered neither pain nor apprehension. He devoted himself eagerly to books and rested from his studies in the company he loved best: his sister and me."}

{"request_id":"abb3ddb98a370c594384dda9","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water with which to finish the feast. After a while Becky suggested that they move on again. Tom was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“Becky, can you bear it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face went pale, but she thought she could.

“Well, then, Becky, we must stay here, where there’s water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!”

Becky burst into tears and sobs. Tom did what he could to comfort her, but with little effect. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and search for us!”

“Yes, they will! Certainly they will!”

“Maybe they’re searching for us now, Tom.”

“Why, I suppose they may be. I hope they are.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I suppose.”

“Tom, it might be dark then—would they notice that we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But in any case, your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

The frightened look on Becky’s face brought Tom to his senses, and he realized he had made a mistake. Becky was not supposed to have gone home that night! The children fell silent and thoughtful. A moment later, a fresh outburst of grief from Becky showed Tom that the thought in his mind had struck hers as well—that Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher discovered that Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children fixed their eyes on their piece of candle and watched it melt slowly and mercilessly away; saw the half-inch wick stand alone at last; saw the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, linger at its top for a moment, and then—the horror of complete darkness descended!

How long afterward it was that Becky slowly became aware she was crying in Tom’s arms, neither of them could tell. All they knew was that, after what seemed an immense stretch of time, both awoke from a dead stupor of sleep and returned to their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday now—perhaps Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but her sorrow was too overwhelming; all her hope was gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and surely the search was continuing. He would shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried it, but in the darkness the distant echoes sounded so terrible that he did not try again.

The hours dragged away, and hunger came to torment the captives once more. A portion of Tom’s half of the cake remained; they divided it and ate. But they seemed hungrier than before."}

{"request_id":"5732f9e48abed5099d140bc0","rewritten_text":"“Next, we constructed a wire fence.”

“A wire fence?”

“Yes. You yourself suggested it two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—the occasion when the Church first tested her strength against us, and soon decided it wiser to wait for a more hopeful season. Well, how have you laid out the fence?”

“I run twelve enormously strong wires—bare, not insulated—from a large dynamo in the cave—a dynamo with no brushes but one positive and one negative—”

“Yes, exactly.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a circle of level ground one hundred yards across; they form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—that is, twelve circles inside one another—and their ends return to the cave.”

“Good; continue.”

“The fences are attached to stout oak posts spaced only three feet apart, and the posts are buried five feet deep.”

“That is solid enough.”

“Yes. Outside the cave, the wires have no ground connection. They leave from the dynamo’s positive brush; there is a ground connection through the negative brush; the opposite ends return to the cave, each grounded separately.”

“No, no, that will never do!”

“Why not?”

“It costs too much—it wastes power. You need no ground connection except the one through the negative brush. Bring the other end of every wire back into the cave and secure each one separately, but _without_ grounding it. Now consider the saving. A cavalry charge rushes at the fence; you use no power and spend no money, because there is only one ground connection until the horses strike the wire. The instant they touch it, they make a connection with the negative brush _through the ground_ and fall dead. Don’t you understand? You expend no energy until it is required; the lightning is waiting, ready, like a charge in a gun, but costs nothing until you discharge it. Yes, the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I can’t imagine how I missed that. It is not merely cheaper, but more effective than the other arrangement, since broken or tangled wires would do no damage.”

“No, particularly if we keep a telltale in the cave and cut off the broken wire. Well, proceed. The gatlings?”

“Yes—that has been arranged. In the middle of the innermost circle, on a broad platform six feet high, I have placed a battery of thirteen Gatling guns and stocked it with ample ammunition.”

“That is right. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights come, there will be music. The edge of the precipice above the cave—”

“I have put a wire fence there, along with a Gatling.”"}

{"request_id":"bf620139a49643232c2b5919","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I decided to get out as soon as we reached the town and place myself beyond his hearing. I carried out this plan successfully. My small portmanteau was in the boot beneath my feet; I only had to turn a hinge to remove it. I threw it down in front of me, climbed down after it, and was left beside the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement. As for the convicts, they continued on with the coach, and I knew where they would be taken off to the river. In my imagination, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-covered steps—heard again the rough “Give way, you!” like an order given to dogs—and saw once more the wicked Noah’s Ark lying on the black water.

I could not have explained what I feared, because my fear was entirely vague and undefined, but I was seized by a powerful terror. As I walked on toward the hotel, I felt that a dread far greater than the simple fear of an unpleasant or painful recognition made me tremble. I am certain it had taken no definite form, and that for a few minutes it was the return of my childhood terror.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had not only ordered my dinner there but had sat down to eat it before the waiter recognised me. After apologising for his faulty memory, he asked whether he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said, “certainly not.”

The waiter—it was he who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound—seemed surprised. At the first opportunity, he placed a dirty, old copy of a local newspaper so directly in my path that I picked it up and read this paragraph:—

Our readers will learn, with no small interest, concerning the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young ironworker from this neighbourhood (what a subject, incidentally, for the magic pen of our still not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!), that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend was a highly respected man not wholly unconnected with the corn and seed trade, whose remarkably convenient and spacious business premises are located within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not without personal feeling that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is gratifying to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

{"request_id":"e6e131a810513afff7f894b7","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray was unable to escape this book’s influence. Or perhaps it would be truer to say that he never wished to escape it. From Paris he obtained no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition, having each bound in a different colour to match his shifting moods and the changing fancies of a nature over which he sometimes seemed almost wholly to have lost command. The hero, that extraordinary young Parisian in whom romantic and scientific temperaments were so oddly mingled, became for him a sort of prophetic image of himself. Indeed, the entire book appeared to tell the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic hero. He never knew—nor, in truth, had any reason to know—that rather grotesque fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water which overtook the young Parisian so early, caused by the sudden decay of a beauty that had once apparently been so remarkable. With an almost cruel delight—and perhaps cruelty has a place in nearly every joy, as surely as it does in every pleasure—he would read the book’s final portion, with its genuinely tragic, though somewhat exaggerated, account of the grief and despair of a man who had himself lost what he had valued most dearly in others and in the world.

For the remarkable beauty that had so captivated Basil Hallward, and many others besides, seemed never to desert him. Even those who had heard the worst things about him—and from time to time strange rumours of his way of life spread through London and became the talk of the clubs—could not believe anything dishonourable of him when they saw him. He always appeared like one who had kept himself unstained by the world. Men who spoke coarsely fell silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. There was something in the purity of his face that reproached them. His mere presence seemed to bring back the memory of the innocence they had corrupted. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have escaped the taint of an age both sordid and sensual.

Often, after returning from one of those mysterious, lengthy absences that prompted such strange speculation among those who were his friends, or believed themselves to be, he would steal upstairs to the locked room, unlock the door with the key that now never left him, and stand with a mirror before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him, looking first at the wicked, aging face on the canvas, and then at the beautiful young face smiling back from the polished glass."}

{"request_id":"df7d5089ace82265350a849f","rewritten_text":"These were the events that tormented Felix and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable member of his family. He could have endured poverty, and while this suffering was the reward of his virtue, he took pride in it; but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were misfortunes more bitter and beyond repair. The Arabian’s arrival now breathed new life into his soul.

“When news reached Leghorn that Felix had been stripped of his wealth and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return to her native country. Safie’s generous nature rebelled against this command; she tried to argue with her father, but he angrily left her, repeating his tyrannical order.

“A few days later, the Turk entered his daughter’s room and hurriedly told her that he had reason to believe his residence in Leghorn had been discovered and that he would soon be handed over to the French government. He had therefore hired a vessel to take him to Constantinople, and he was to sail within a few hours. He intended to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant, who would follow at her convenience with most of his property, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

“When she was alone, Safie considered what course it would be proper for her to take in this emergency. Living in Turkey was abhorrent to her; both her religion and her feelings opposed it. From some of her father’s papers that came into her possession, she learned of her lover’s exile and discovered the name of the place where he was then living. She hesitated for some time, but at last made her decision. Taking some jewels that belonged to her and a sum of money, she left Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who understood the common language of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

“She reached a town safely, about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, when her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie nursed her with the greatest devotion, but the poor girl died, leaving the Arabian alone, unfamiliar with the country’s language and completely ignorant of the ways of the world. Yet she fell into good hands. The Italian had mentioned the place they were traveling to, and after her death, the woman of the house where they had stayed made sure that Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"42a086850f75274379e1dae4","rewritten_text":"“Oh, damn my hat! I want Virginia!” cried the little Duke, laughing, and they galloped on to the railway station. There Mr. Otis asked the stationmaster whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but he learned nothing. The stationmaster, however, telegraphed along the line in both directions and assured him that a close watch would be kept for her. After buying a hat for the little Duke from a linen draper who was just closing his shop, Mr. Otis rode on to Bexley, a village about four miles away, which he had been told was a well-known gypsy haunt because of the large common beside it. There they roused the local policeman, but he could give them no information. After riding all over the common, they turned their horses toward home and reached the Chase at about eleven o’clock, exhausted and nearly heartbroken. Washington and the twins were waiting for them at the gatehouse with lanterns, since the avenue was very dark. Not the slightest trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley Meadows, but Virginia was not with them. They explained their sudden departure by saying that they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and had hurried away for fear of being late. In fact, they had been deeply distressed to hear of Virginia’s disappearance, since they were very grateful to Mr. Otis for allowing them to camp in his park, and four of them had remained behind to help with the search. The carp pond had been dragged, and the entire Chase had been thoroughly searched, but without result. It was clear that, for that night at least, Virginia was lost to them. In the deepest depression, Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, while the groom followed with the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a group of frightened servants. In the library, poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa, almost out of her mind with terror and anxiety, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau de cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted that she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a melancholy meal, for hardly anyone spoke. Even the twins were subdued and awestruck, as they were very fond of their sister. When they had finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleas, ordered them all to bed. Nothing more could be done that night, he said, and in the morning he would telegraph Scotland Yard to send detectives at once."}

{"request_id":"6dcda22cfb6fc454ce0236df","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months slipped by, and winter was well along by then. I had been attending school nearly all the time and could spell, read, and write a little, and could recite the multiplication table as far as six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t believe I could ever have gone beyond that, even if I lived forever. I never had much faith in mathematics, anyhow.

At first I hated school, but after a while I got so I could endure it. Whenever I grew especially tired, I played hookey, and the whipping I received the next day did me good and lifted my spirits. Thus, the longer I attended, the easier it became. I was also getting somewhat accustomed to the widow’s ways, and they didn’t grate on me quite so much. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed weighed on me pretty heavily most of the time, but before the cold weather came I would sometimes slip away and sleep in the woods, which gave me a rest. I still preferred the old ways, though I was beginning to like the new ones a little, too. The widow said I was improving slowly but surely and doing very satisfactorily. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I happened to knock over the salt-cellar. I reached for some salt as quickly as I could, intending to toss it over my left shoulder and ward off the bad luck, but Miss Watson got there first and stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; what a mess you are always making!” The widow spoke up kindly for me, but I knew well enough that wouldn’t prevent the bad luck. After breakfast I went out feeling anxious and unsteady, wondering where it would strike me and what form it would take. There are ways to avoid certain kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of those kinds; so I didn’t try to do anything, but merely trudged along downhearted and watchful.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the high board fence. An inch of fresh snow covered the ground, and I noticed someone’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry, lingered around the stile for a while, and then continued along the garden fence. It was strange that they hadn’t come in after waiting there so long. I couldn’t understand it. Somehow, it was very curious. I meant to follow the tracks around, but first I bent down to examine them."}

{"request_id":"78bd89f4557d9f24bf67955d","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was making a very foolish decision, since there was no doubt the place was haunted. Indeed, Lord Canterville himself, a man of scrupulous honour, had felt obliged to mention the fact to Mr. Otis when they discussed the terms.

“We have not wished to live there ourselves,” said Lord Canterville, “since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a fit from which she never truly recovered. Two skeleton hands had been placed on her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. And I feel bound to tell you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several living members of my family, as well as by the parish rector, the Reverend Augustus Dampier, who is a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the unfortunate incident involving the Duchess, none of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville often slept very little at night because of the mysterious noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” replied the Minister, “I will take the furniture and the ghost at an assessed value. I come from a modern country, where we have everything money can buy; and with all our lively young men painting the Old World red and carrying off your finest actresses and prima donnas, I suppose that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we would have it at home very soon, either in one of our public museums or traveling the roads as a show.”

“I fear the ghost does exist,” said Lord Canterville with a smile, “though it may have resisted the offers of your enterprising impresarios. It has been well known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always appears before the death of a member of our family.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, for that matter, Lord Canterville. But there is no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I suppose the laws of Nature are not going to be suspended for the sake of the British aristocracy.”

“You are certainly very natural in America,” answered Lord Canterville, who did not entirely understand Mr. Otis’s last remark. “If you do not mind having a ghost in the house, then everything is settled. Only remember that I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was completed, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who, as Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, had been a celebrated New York belle, was now a very handsome middle-aged woman, with fine eyes and a superb profile."}

{"request_id":"4acff0ffc802e66b81b577a8","rewritten_text":"His manner was stubborn in the extreme, and “dat deuced bug” were the only words that passed his lips during the journey. As for me, I carried a pair of dark lanterns, while Legrand occupied himself with the _scarabæus_, which he had fastened to the end of a piece of whip-cord and swung back and forth with the manner of a conjuror as he walked. When I noticed this final, unmistakable proof of my friend’s mental derangement, I could hardly keep from weeping. Still, I thought it wiser to indulge his fancy for the moment, or until I could take some stronger action with a reasonable prospect of success. Meanwhile, I tried, without result, to learn from him the purpose of the expedition. After persuading me to come along, he appeared unwilling to discuss any subject of lesser importance, and answered all my questions only with “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s upper end in a skiff, then climbed the high ground along the mainland shore and traveled northwest through country so wild and desolate that no sign of a human footprint appeared anywhere. Legrand went ahead confidently, stopping only briefly from time to time to consult what seemed to be landmarks he had arranged on an earlier occasion.

We continued in this fashion for nearly two hours, and the sun was just going down when we entered a district far more dreary than any we had yet encountered. It was a kind of plateau near the top of an almost impassable hill, thickly forested from its base to its summit and scattered with enormous rocks that seemed to rest loosely on the earth. In many places, they were kept from plunging into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines running in different directions lent the landscape an even sterner solemnity.

The natural platform we had climbed was densely covered with brambles, and we soon found that it would have been impossible to push through them without the scythe. At his master’s command, Jupiter began cutting a passage for us toward the foot of an immensely tall tulip-tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, yet surpassed them all—and every other tree I had ever seen—in the beauty of its leaves and shape, the broad reach of its branches, and the majestic character of its whole appearance."}

{"request_id":"702aed4a85d5cfd40c306539","rewritten_text":"The surrounding oaks were home to a tribe of nightingales—and there I am now; Idris, in the cherished prime of youth, is beside me. Remember, I am only twenty-two, and scarcely seventeen summers have passed over the beloved of my heart. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian, in his favorite boat, was engaged in the dangerous sport of tearing the highest branch from a submerged oak. Are you weary of life, Adrian, that you play with danger in this way?—

He secured his prize and steered his boat through the flood. We watched him anxiously, but the current carried him away from us; he had to land much farther downstream and make a considerable detour before he could rejoin us. “He is safe!” said Idris, as he sprang ashore and waved the branch above his head in triumph. “We will wait for him here.”

We were alone together. The sun had set; the nightingales began to sing; and the evening star shone clearly in the still-bright flood of light lingering in the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes rested on this sweet emblem of herself. “How the light trembles,” she said, “as though that star’s life were in it. Its wavering radiance seems to say that its condition, like ours on earth, is uncertain and changeable; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Do not gaze at the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Do not read love in its trembling rays; do not look toward distant worlds; do not speak of the mere imagination of a feeling. I have been silent for so long—so long, and with such painful longing, have I wished to speak to you and surrender my soul, my life, my whole being to you. Do not look at the star, dear love—or do, and let that eternal spark plead for me; let it be my witness and advocate, silent as it shines. Love is to me what light is to the star; so long as that light is not extinguished by annihilation, so long will I love you.”

The rapture of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s hardened eyes. I can still feel her graceful form pressed against my overflowing heart; still, at the memory of that first kiss, sight, pulse, and breath grow faint and fail. Slowly and silently, we went to meet Adrian, whom we heard approaching.

I begged Adrian to return to me after escorting his sister home. That same evening, as we walked along the moonlit forest paths, I poured out my entire heart—its joy and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he looked troubled. “I might have foreseen this,” he said. “What conflict will now follow!”"}

{"request_id":"30d0f4c073a7f8625aca9f44","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean to say—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook; “but wait a moment. Go on, Joseph. Good for you! Go on!”

“What would everyone here say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Handsome would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That miserable hypocrite, Pumblechook, nodded again and said, with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Good again! Press her, Joseph!”

“Then, to finish the matter,” said Joe, happily handing the bag to my sister, “it’s twenty-five pounds.”

“It’s twenty-five pounds, Mum,” echoed that lowest of swindlers, Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand; “and it’s no more than your merits deserve (as I said when my opinion was requested), and I wish you joy of the money!”

If the villain had stopped there, his case would have been bad enough, but he made his guilt still darker by taking me into custody, with a patronizing authority that made all his earlier crimes seem insignificant.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, taking me by the arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always carry through whatever they begin. This boy must be bound immediately. That’s _my_ way. Bound immediately.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister, clutching the money, “we’re deeply indebted to you.”

“Don’t mention me, Mum,” replied that devilish corn merchant. “A pleasure is a pleasure everywhere. But this boy, you understand; we must have him bound. I said I’d take care of it—to tell you the truth.”

The Justices were sitting in the nearby Town Hall, and we went there at once to have me bound apprentice to Joe in the presence of the magistrates. I say we went there, but Pumblechook pushed me along as if I had just picked someone’s pocket or set fire to a haystack; indeed, everyone in court seemed to think I had been caught red-handed. As Pumblechook shoved me through the crowd ahead of him, I heard some people say, “What has he done?” and others, “He’s only a youngster, too, but he looks bad, doesn’t he?” One person with a mild, kindly face even gave me a tract decorated with a woodcut of a wicked young man covered in a complete sausage-shop of chains, and titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall seemed a strange place to me, with pews higher than those in a church—and people leaning over them to watch—and imposing Justices, one with a powdered head, reclining in chairs with folded arms, taking snuff, falling asleep, writing, or reading newspapers. On the walls hung several glossy black portraits, which my untrained eye saw as a mixture of hardbake and sticking-plaster."}

{"request_id":"ca2d83ec0e5157029219dcf6","rewritten_text":"In fact, he was dressed as ‘Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,’ one of his most remarkable impersonations, and one the Cantervilles had every reason to remember, since it was the true origin of their quarrel with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and, as far as he could tell, no one was awake. As he strolled towards the library, however, to see whether any traces of the bloodstain remained, two figures suddenly sprang out at him from a dark corner, waving their arms wildly above their heads and shrieking ‘BOO!’ into his ear.

Overcome by a panic that, in the circumstances, was only natural, he rushed towards the staircase, but found Washington Otis waiting there with the large garden syringe. Hemmed in by his enemies on every side and driven almost to bay, he disappeared into the great iron stove, which fortunately was unlit, and had to make his way home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his room in a dreadful state of dirt, disarray, and despair.

After that, he was never seen on another nocturnal expedition. The twins lay in wait for him several times and scattered nutshells across the passages every night, greatly annoying their parents and the servants, but it was useless. It was clear that his feelings had been so deeply hurt that he would not appear. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his major work on the history of the Democratic Party, on which he had been engaged for several years; Mrs. Otis organised a magnificent clam bake that astonished the entire county; the boys took up lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games; and Virginia rode through the lanes on her pony, accompanied by the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the final week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. It was generally believed that the ghost had gone away. Indeed, Mr. Otis wrote Lord Canterville to say so, and Lord Canterville replied with great pleasure, sending his warmest congratulations to the Minister’s worthy wife.

The Otises, however, were mistaken, for the ghost was still in the house. Though now almost an invalid, he was far from willing to let matters rest, especially after hearing that the guests included the young Duke of Cheshire. The Duke’s great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. The next morning, Lord Francis was found lying on the card-room floor in such a helpless paralytic condition that, although he lived to a great age, he was never again able to say anything except ‘Double Sixes.’"}
