{"request_id":"b46cbb9ce0166f1079646186","rewritten_text":"Directly before him, in the pale moonlight, stood a frightening old man. His eyes glowed like red coals; long gray hair hung over his shoulders in tangled coils; his old-fashioned clothes were dirty and torn, and heavy manacles and rusty chains hung from his wrists and ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains. For that purpose, I have brought you a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. It is said to work perfectly after one application, and the wrapper carries several testimonials from some of our most respected native clergymen. I shall leave it here beside the bedroom candles, and will gladly provide more if you need it.” With that, the United States Minister placed the bottle on a marble table, shut his door, and went to bed.

For a moment, the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still in offended outrage. Then he hurled the bottle onto the polished floor and fled down the corridor, groaning hollowly and giving off a terrible green light. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open, two small figures in white appeared, and a large pillow shot past his head! Clearly, there was no time to waste. He quickly used the Fourth Dimension of Space as a means of escape, vanished through the wood paneling, and left the house completely silent.

When he reached a small secret room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to understand his situation. Never, during his brilliant and uninterrupted career of three hundred years, had he been so deeply insulted. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a fit while she stood before the mirror in her lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids, who had fallen into hysterics when he merely grinned at them through the curtains of a spare bedroom; of the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out as he returned late one night from the library, leaving him under Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a complete victim of nervous illness; and of old Madame de Tremouillac, who had woken early one morning to see a skeleton sitting in an armchair by the fire and reading her diary. She had been confined to bed for six weeks with brain fever, and after recovering had returned to the Church and ended her association with that notorious skeptic, Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"f92bf7350ce93262a40a89f8","rewritten_text":"I have not the nerves for such a thing.”

“But could you really feel at ease spending the entire evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; you see, his papa can, so why should not I? Jemima is so attentive, and she could send us word every hour about him. I truly think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I am no more frightened about little Charles now than he is. Yesterday I was terribly alarmed, but today the situation is quite different.”

“Well, if you do not think it too late to give notice for yourself, suppose you went as well as your husband. Leave little Charles in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot object while I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” cried Mary, her eyes lighting up. “Dear me! That is an excellent idea, truly. Of course, I may as well go as stay, since I am of no use at home—is that not so? It only worries me. You, who have no mother’s feelings, are much the more suitable person. You can make little Charles do anything; he always obeys you at once. It will be far better than leaving him with Jemima alone. Oh, I shall certainly go; I am sure I ought to, if I can, every bit as much as Charles, because they are extremely eager for me to become acquainted with Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left by yourself. It was an excellent thought of yours, Anne. I will go tell Charles and get ready immediately. You can send for us at a moment’s notice, you know, if anything is wrong; but I dare say there will be nothing to frighten you. You may be certain I would not go unless I felt completely easy about my dear child.”

The next moment she was knocking at her husband’s dressing-room door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she arrived in time to hear the entire conversation, which began with Mary saying, in a voice of great triumph—

“I intend to go with you, Charles, since I am no more useful at home than you are. If I shut myself away forever with the child, I should not be able to persuade him to do anything he disliked. Anne will stay; Anne has offered to remain at home and care for him. It was Anne’s own suggestion, and so I shall go with you, which will be much better, for I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I should be very pleased to have you come; but it seems rather unfair that she should be left at home alone to nurse our sick child.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"38e230edf8acd3febfc77af0","rewritten_text":"For a while I was too astonished to think clearly. I knew that my design differed greatly in its details from this one—though the general outline bore a certain resemblance. Presently I took up a candle, seated myself at the opposite end of the room, and examined the parchment more carefully. On turning it over, I found my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had drawn it. My first thought was simply amazement at the extraordinary likeness of outline—the strange coincidence that, unknown to me, a skull should have been on the other side of the parchment, directly beneath my figure of the _scarabæus_, and that this skull should resemble my drawing so closely, not only in shape but in size. I repeat, the oddness of this coincidence completely bewildered me for some time. Such is commonly the effect of coincidences of this kind. The mind attempts to form a connection—a chain of cause and effect—and, failing to do so, undergoes a sort of temporary paralysis. But after I had recovered from my stupor, another conviction gradually arose, one that startled me far more than the coincidence itself. I began clearly and firmly to remember that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I sketched the _scarabæus_. I became entirely certain of this, because I recalled turning over one side and then the other, looking for the cleanest place. If the skull had been there, naturally I could not have failed to see it. Here was a mystery I felt unable to explain; yet even then, faintly, in the most distant and hidden chambers of my mind, there seemed to flicker a glow-worm-like notion of the truth that last night’s adventure had demonstrated so magnificently. I rose immediately, secured the parchment, and put all further thought aside until I could be alone.\n\n“When you had departed, and Jupiter was sound asleep, I began a more systematic examination of the matter. First I considered how the parchment had come into my possession. The place where we found the _scarabæus_ lay on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island, and only a short distance above high-water mark. When I picked it up, it gave me a sharp bite, making me drop it. Jupiter, with his usual caution, before taking hold of the insect, which had flown toward him, searched around for a leaf or something similar with which to seize it."}

{"request_id":"f122fe4bcc02276faa42201b","rewritten_text":"But there was no laughter in the little town that peaceful Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were being plunged into mourning, with profound grief and many tears. An unusual silence settled over the village, though it was quiet enough under ordinary circumstances. The villagers went about their affairs distractedly and spoke little; but they sighed often. The Saturday holiday seemed a burden to the children. They had no enthusiasm for their games and gradually abandoned them.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering sadly around the deserted schoolhouse yard, feeling deeply melancholy. But she found nothing there to comfort her. She spoke to herself:

“Oh, if only I had a brass andiron knob again! But now I have nothing to remember him by.” And she stifled a small sob.

After a while she stopped and said to herself:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over again, I wouldn’t say that—I wouldn’t say it for anything in the world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought overwhelmed her, and she wandered away with tears running down her cheeks. Then a fairly large group of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came by and stood looking over the picket fence, speaking reverently about how Tom had done this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe had said one small thing or another (filled with terrible prophecy, as they could easily recognize now). Each speaker pointed out the exact place where the lost boys had stood, then added something like, “And I was standing just so—just as I am now, and if you were him—I was this close—and he smiled, just like this—and then something seemed to pass all over me, like—awful, you know—and I never guessed what it meant, of course, but I can see now!”

Then they argued over who had seen the dead boys last while they were alive. Many claimed that mournful distinction and offered evidence, more or less altered by the witness. When it was finally decided who really had seen the departed boys last and exchanged the final words with them, the fortunate ones assumed a kind of sacred importance and were stared at and envied by everyone else. One poor fellow, who had no other glory to offer, said with obvious pride in the memory:

“Well, Tom Sawyer licked me once.”

But that attempt at glory failed. Most of the boys could say the same, which made the distinction far too common. The group drifted away, still recalling the lost heroes in hushed, awed voices."}

{"request_id":"f0a021c6277b9077c91cd38e","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced at him, but in vain, as he proceeded toward the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I expect the pleasure of seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Light Monsieur my nephew to his chamber there!--And burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you please,” he added to himself, before ringing his little bell once more and calling his valet to his own bedroom.

After the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis paced back and forth in his loose chamber-robe, gently preparing himself for sleep on that hot, still night. Rustling around the room, his softly slippered feet making no sound upon the floor, he moved like a cultivated tiger: he looked like some enchanted marquis of the irredeemably wicked kind in a tale, whose recurring transformation into tiger-shape was either ending or beginning.

He crossed his luxurious bedroom from end to end, again reviewing the fragments of the day’s journey that rose unbidden in his thoughts: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sinking sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the little village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender in his blue cap pointing beneath the carriage to the chain. That fountain brought to mind the Paris fountain, the small bundle on the step, the women stooping over it, and the tall man with raised arms crying, “Dead!”

“I am cool now,” said Monsieur the Marquis, “and can go to bed.”

Accordingly, leaving only one light burning upon the broad hearth, he allowed his thin gauze curtains to fall around him, and heard the night break its silence with a long sigh as he settled himself to sleep.

The stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the black night for three long hours; for three long hours, the horses in the stables rattled at their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound bearing very little likeness to the sound men-poets conventionally assign to owls. Yet it is the stubborn habit of such creatures almost never to say what has been written down for them.

For three long hours, the stone faces of the chateau, lion and human, stared blindly into the night. Dead darkness covered the whole landscape, and dead darkness added its hush to the dust settling quietly along every road. The burial-place had reached such a state that its small mounds of poor grass could no longer be distinguished from one another; the figure upon the Cross might have descended, for anything visible of it. In the village, taxers and taxed slept soundly. Dreaming, perhaps, of feasts, as the starving commonly do, and of comfort and rest, as the driven slave and yoked ox may, its gaunt inhabitants slept deeply, and were fed and freed."}

{"request_id":"a4e57901b1e6239d861e913c","rewritten_text":"“Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, uptown?” said Joe.

“Is there any Miss Havisham downtown?” my sister replied.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he’s going. He’d better play there, too,” said my sister, shaking her head at me to encourage me to be extremely light and playful, “or I’ll work him.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham uptown—everyone for miles around had heard of Miss Havisham uptown—as an immensely rich and grim woman who lived in a large, gloomy house barricaded against robbers and led a secluded life.

“Well, to be sure!” said Joe, astonished. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Noodle!” cried my sister. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Which some person,” Joe politely hinted again, “mentioned when he said she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? Isn’t it just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook might be one of her tenants, and that he might sometimes—we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, since that would demand too much of you—but sometimes—go there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, always considerate and thoughtful toward us—though you may not think so, Joseph,” she added in a tone of deepest reproach, as if he were the most heartless of nephews, “then mention this boy, standing prancing here”—which I solemnly declare I was not doing—“to whom I have forever been a willing slave?”

“Good again!” cried Uncle Pumblechook. “Well put! Nicely pointed! Very good! Now, Joseph, you know the case.”

“No, Joseph,” said my sister, still reproachful, while Joe apologetically rubbed the back of his hand repeatedly across his nose, “you do not yet—though you may not think so—know the case. You may believe that you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that, for all we know, this boy’s fortune may be made by his going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, keep him there tonight, and take him himself to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And mercy me!” cried my sister, suddenly throwing off her bonnet in desperation, “here I stand talking to mere mooncalves, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the mare is catching cold at the door, and the boy is covered with soot and dirt from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"8282d5f1a8c89e907e1158f8","rewritten_text":"For this reason, I decided to get out as soon as we reached the town and place myself beyond his hearing. I carried out this plan successfully. My small portmanteau was in the boot beneath my feet; I only had to turn a hinge to remove it. I threw it down before me, climbed down after it, and was left beside the first lamp, on the first stones of the town pavement. As for the convicts, they continued on with the coach, and I knew where they would be taken away to the river. In my imagination, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-covered steps—heard again the rough “Give way, you!” like an order given to dogs—and saw again the wicked Noah’s Ark lying on the black water.

I could not have explained what I feared, because my fear was completely vague and undefined, but I was filled with terror. As I walked toward the hotel, I felt that a dread far greater than the simple fear of an unpleasant or painful meeting made me tremble. I am sure it had no clear shape, and that for a few minutes it was the return of my childhood terror.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had ordered my dinner there and sat down to eat it before the waiter recognized me. After apologizing for failing to remember me, he asked whether he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said, “certainly not.”

The waiter—it was he who had brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound—seemed surprised. At the first opportunity, he placed a dirty, old copy of a local newspaper directly in my path. I picked it up and read this paragraph:—

Our readers will learn, with some interest, concerning the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young ironworker from this neighbourhood (what a subject, by the way, for the magic pen of our still not universally acknowledged townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!), that the youth’s first patron, companion, and friend was a highly respected man connected in some way with the corn and seed trade. His extremely convenient and spacious business premises are located within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not without personal feeling that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is pleasing to know that our town produced the founder of the young man’s fortune."}

{"request_id":"a49d7acf9c38c9807363b688","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so completely satisfied with this conversation that he never again troubled himself, or annoyed his dear sister Elizabeth, by bringing up the subject; and she was glad to find that she had said enough to keep him silent.

The day of his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived, and Mrs. Bennet was forced to endure a separation which, since her husband had no intention of joining her plan for them all to go to Newcastle, was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when shall we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Perhaps not for two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time for writing. My sisters may write to me. They will have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s farewells were much more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they had left the house, “as I have ever seen. He simpers, smirks, and makes love to us all. I am immensely proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas himself to produce a more valuable son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very low for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that there is nothing so dreadful as parting from one’s friends. One feels so forlorn without them.”

“This is the consequence, you see, madam, of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It must make you more content that your other four are unmarried.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia does not leave me because she is married, but only because her husband’s regiment happens to be so far away. If it had been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.”

But the dispirited state into which this event had thrown her was soon relieved, and her mind opened again to the excitement of hope through a piece of news that had begun circulating. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for her master’s arrival. He was coming in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was extremely agitated. By turns, she looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” said Mrs. Bennet, for Mrs. Philips had first brought her the news. “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never want to see him again. But still, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield if he wishes.”"}

{"request_id":"f019120692a0609bc7397658","rewritten_text":"But how could I, a poor, bewildered country boy, escape that remarkable inconsistency into which the finest and wisest men fall every day?

“It may all be perfectly true,” I said to Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

In short, when I reached that point, I rolled over onto my face, seized the hair on either side of my head, and gave it a good wrench. All the while I knew that the madness of my heart was so utterly mad and misplaced that I was fully aware my face would have deserved it if I had hauled it up by my hair and dashed it against the pebbles as punishment for belonging to such a fool.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she attempted no further reasoning with me. She laid her hand—which was a comforting hand, though roughened by work—on my hands in turn, and gently drew them from my hair. Then she patted my shoulder softly and soothingly, while I cried a little with my face against my sleeve, just as I had done in the brewery yard, and felt dimly certain that somebody, or perhaps everybody, had treated me very badly; I could not say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” said Biddy, “and that is that you’ve felt able to trust me, Pip. And I’m glad of another: you know, of course, that you can rely on me to keep your confidence and always be worthy of it. If your first teacher—dear! such a poor teacher, and herself so much in need of teaching—were teaching you now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would give you. But it would be a difficult one to learn, and you have gone beyond her, so it is useless now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and said, in a newly cheerful tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, rising, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall be, so that means always. Not that I have anything to tell you, since you know everything I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” said Biddy very softly, looking away toward the ships. Then, returning to her earlier pleasant tone, she repeated, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy that we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon gradually softened into summer evening, and it was very beautiful."}

{"request_id":"bc981841d297ace8982ef22a","rewritten_text":"A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from a citizen who was away and set off at once. When they were several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now you can see that this bluff looks the same all the way down from Cave Hollow—no houses, no woodpiles, bushes all alike. But do you see that white spot up there where there’s been a landslide? Well, that’s one of my marks. We’ll go ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing, you could touch the hole I escaped from with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched all around but found nothing. Tom proudly walked into a thick clump of sumac bushes and said:

“There you are! Look at it, Huck; it’s the snugest hole in this country. Just keep quiet about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I’d need a place like this, and finding one was the trouble. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret—except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in, because of course there has to be a Gang, or there wouldn’t be any style to it. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“Well, it certainly does, Tom. And who will we rob?”

“Oh, almost anybody. Ambush people—that’s mostly how it’s done.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not always. Keep them in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get all they can from their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if it still hasn’t been raised, then you kill them. That’s the usual way. Only you don’t kill the women. You lock them up, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and terribly frightened. You take their watches and things, but you always remove your hat and speak politely. Nobody is as polite as robbers—you’ll see that in any book. Then the women fall in love with you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two, they stop crying, and after that you couldn’t make them leave. If you drove them out, they’d turn around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, that’s really great, Tom. I believe it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home and circuses and everything.”

By then everything was ready, and the boys entered the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, then secured their joined kite strings and moved on."}

{"request_id":"3572fdbd0d42ab088ea05bb1","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent by them to Adrian, who had been chosen as arbiter. They had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and desolate countryside, all the while indulging a fierce hatred of one another; and now they argued their respective causes with unabated partisan spirit.

By questioning the deputies separately and conducting a lengthy investigation, we learned the true state of affairs in Paris. Since Parliament had appointed him Ryland’s deputy, all the surviving English had submitted to Adrian. He was our captain, to lead us from our native soil into unknown lands; our lawgiver and our protector. When our plan of emigration was first arranged, no lasting separation of our members had been intended, and command of the entire body, rising through successive degrees of authority, culminated in the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen circumstances altered our plans and caused most of our number to remain separated from the supreme chief for nearly two months. They had crossed over in two separate groups, and upon reaching Paris, disagreement arose between them.

They had found Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, returning travellers and merchants, together with letters, regularly informed us of the disease’s ravages across the continent. But as mortality increased, this communication diminished and finally ceased. Even in England, communication from one part of the island to another became slow and infrequent. No vessel crossed the waters between Calais and Dover; or, if some melancholy voyager, wishing to learn whether his relatives lived or had died, departed from the French shore to rejoin us, the greedy ocean often swallowed his small craft. Otherwise, after a day or two, he was infected by the disease and died before he could recount the desolation of France. We were therefore largely ignorant of conditions on the continent, and still held some vague hope of finding many companions scattered across its broad expanse. But the same causes that had so terribly reduced the English nation had found even greater opportunity for destruction in the neighboring country. France was empty. Along the entire road from Calais to Paris, not one human being was seen. In Paris, a few remained—perhaps a hundred—who, resigned to their approaching fate, wandered through the capital’s streets and gathered to speak of former times, with the liveliness and even gaiety that rarely abandons the people of that nation.

The English took possession of Paris without opposition. Its tall buildings and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at their customary meeting place in the Tuileries. They wondered why the islanders had come to their doomed city—for in the depths of misery, sufferers always believe their share of the calamity the most bitter, just as, when enduring intense pain, we would exchange the particular torment wracking us for any other that might afflict another part of the body."}

{"request_id":"e4831bbef4cda0d8a6cb6876","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost completed their course. It was now the end of May; the woods were dressed in their freshest green, and the sweet scent of newly mown grass filled the fields. I thought that the mild air and Nature’s lovely aspect might help awaken gentle sensations in him, and inspire feelings of peace and affection, preparing him for the confidence I resolved to gain from him.

I therefore selected the evening of one of these days for my attempt. I asked him to walk with me, and conducted him to a nearby beech wood, whose light shade protected us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After walking for some time in silence, I sat down with him upon a mossy hillock. It is strange, but even now I seem to see the place: many of the slender, smooth trunks were entwined with ivy, whose shining leaves of deepest green stood out against the white bark and the pale leaves of the young beech shoots growing from their parent trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss and partly covered by the dead leaves of the previous autumn, which the winds had gathered here and there into little mounds. A few stumps, thick with moss, stood around us. The leaves stirred softly in the breeze, and through their green canopy the bright blue sky could be seen. As evening advanced, the distant trunks were reddened by the sun, and the wind fell completely still, while a few birds flew past us toward their evening rest.

It was here, then, that we sat together; and when you hear all that passed—all that terrible suffering which tore our souls even in this peaceful place, which might, but for strange passions, have been a paradise to us—you will not wonder that I remember it as I looked upon it, hoping its calm would bring calm to me and inspire me not only with courage, but with persuasive words. I saw all these things and observed them absently in my mind while trying to arrange my thoughts in proper order for the attempt. My heart beat rapidly as I gathered strength to speak to him, for I was resolved not to be repulsed, yet trembled to imagine what effect my words might produce. At last, with much hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness toward me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—you showed me when you first returned will, I hope, excuse me in your eyes for daring to speak to you, though with the tender love of a daughter, yet also with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"491bd0a047951774eb043967","rewritten_text":"The exquisitely dressed gentlemen of the finest breeding wore small dangling ornaments that chimed as they moved languidly; these golden fetters rang like tiny precious bells. Together with the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, their sound stirred a flutter in the air that wafted Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger far away.

Dress was the one unfailing talisman and charm for keeping everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that was never meant to end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals of Justice, and all society (except the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball descended to the Common Executioner, who, in keeping with the charm, was required to officiate “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was rarely used—Monsieur Paris, as it was the episcopal fashion among his fellow Professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, presided in this elegant dress. And who among the company at Monseigneur’s reception in that year seventeen hundred and eighty of our Lord could possibly doubt that a system founded on a frizzled, powdered, gold-laced, pump-wearing, white-silk-stockinged hangman would last until the stars went out?

After Monseigneur had relieved his four bearers of their burdens and taken his chocolate, he ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holies thrown open and emerged. Then came such submission, such cringing and fawning, such servility and abject humiliation! As for bowing down in body and spirit, nothing remained for Heaven—which may have been one reason, among others, why Monseigneur’s worshippers never troubled it.

Offering a word of promise here and a smile there, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a wave of his hand to another, Monseigneur graciously passed through his rooms to the distant region of the Circumference of Truth. There, Monseigneur turned and came back again, and in due time had himself shut inside his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, after which he was seen no more.

When the spectacle was over, the flutter in the air became a small storm, and the precious little bells rang down the stairs. Soon only one person remained from the entire crowd. With his hat beneath his arm and his snuff-box in his hand, he slowly made his way among the mirrors toward the exit.

“I devote you,” said this person, stopping at the last door and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he shook the snuff from his fingers as though shaking dust from his feet, and quietly walked downstairs."}

{"request_id":"3c49b70088a879d548d76ff7","rewritten_text":"I know she would!”

Widow Douglas’s splendid hospitality was a tempting lure, and it, along with Tom’s persuasion, soon won the day. They decided not to tell anyone about the night’s plans. Then it occurred to Tom that Huck might come that very night and give the signal. The thought took much of the excitement out of his anticipation. Still, he could not bear to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’s. And why should he, he reasoned? The signal had not come the night before, so why was it any more likely to come tonight? The certain pleasure of the evening outweighed the uncertain treasure; and, like a boy, he decided to follow the stronger impulse and not let himself think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd swarmed ashore, and soon the distant forest and craggy heights echoed with shouts and laughter. Every possible way of becoming hot and tired was tried, and eventually the rovers straggled back to camp with hearty appetites. Then the destruction of the good food began. After the feast came a refreshing period of rest and conversation beneath the spreading oaks. Presently someone shouted:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were gathered, and at once there was a general scramble up the hill. The cave’s entrance was partway up the hillside, shaped like the letter A. Its massive oak door stood open. Inside was a small chamber, cold as an icehouse, its walls made by Nature of solid limestone damp with a cold sweat. It was romantic and mysterious to stand there in the deep gloom and look out at the green valley shining in the sun. But the scene soon lost its power, and the roughhousing began again. As soon as a candle was lit, everyone rushed at its owner; a struggle and brave defense followed, but the candle was soon knocked down or blown out, bringing delighted laughter and another chase. Yet everything ends. Before long, the procession filed down the steep slope of the main passage, its flickering line of lights dimly revealing the towering rock walls almost to where they met sixty feet overhead. This main passage was no more than eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other tall, narrower crevices branched off on either side—for McDougal’s cave was a vast labyrinth of crooked passages that crossed one another, emerged again, and led nowhere."}

{"request_id":"9c749ae38370eab9c0b25f13","rewritten_text":"“No bringing him up by hand, then. Not at all!”

Joe offered me more gravy, but I was afraid to accept it.

“He was a great deal of trouble to you, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble sympathetically to my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” Then she began a terrible list of all the illnesses I had caused her, all the sleepless nights I had given her, all the high places I had fallen from, all the low places I had fallen into, all the injuries I had done myself, and all the times she had wished me dead, while I had stubbornly refused to die.

I think the Romans must have annoyed one another greatly with their noses. Perhaps that was why they became such a restless people. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose annoyed me so much during the account of my misdeeds that I wanted to pull it until he howled. But everything I had suffered so far was nothing compared with the terrible feelings that seized me when the silence following my sister’s speech was finally broken. During that silence, everyone had looked at me—with, as I painfully knew, anger and disgust.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently bringing everyone back to the subject they had left, “pork, when boiled, is rich too, isn’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister.

Oh heavens, it had finally come! He would discover that it was weak. He would say it was weak, and I would be ruined! I gripped the table leg beneath the cloth with both hands and waited for my fate.

My sister went for the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured out his brandy. No one else took any. The miserable man played with his glass—lifting it, holding it up to the light, and setting it down again—making my misery last longer. Meanwhile, Mrs. Joe and Joe busily cleared the table for the pie and pudding.

I could not take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with my hands and feet, I watched the wretched man toy with his glass, pick it up, smile, throw back his head, and drink the brandy. Immediately afterward, everyone was overcome with horror when he sprang to his feet, spun around several times in a frightening, jerking dance like a whooping cough fit, and rushed out the door. Through the window, we could then see him plunging about violently and spitting, making the most horrible faces, and seeming completely out of his mind.

I held on tightly while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran to him."}

{"request_id":"b9da1740ca3398bee57d653a","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from these beloved friends—a secret he had cherished from his earliest years; and though he loved his fellow collegiates, he would not entrust it to the delicacy or sympathy of any one among them. He was in love. He feared that the force of his passion might become an object of their mockery; and he could not endure their profaning it by deeming trivial and fleeting what he felt to be the very life of his life.

There was a gentleman of modest fortune living near his family mansion who had three beautiful daughters. The eldest was by far the most lovely, but her beauty merely enhanced her other virtues—her understanding was clear and vigorous, and her temper angelically mild. She and my father had been playmates from infancy. Diana, even as a child, had been a favourite of his mother; that preference increased as the beautiful and lively girl grew older, and so, during his school and college vacations, they were constantly together. Novels, and all the other means by which young people in civilized society are brought to know of passions before they truly experience them, had deeply influenced one so unusually open to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his favourite companion in play, yet he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older than he, her upbringing had left her more childish, at least in understanding and expressing emotion; she received his ardent declarations innocently, and returned them without knowing their meaning. She had read no novels and kept company only with her younger sisters—what could she understand of the distinction between love and friendship? And when the growth of her understanding revealed the true character of their intercourse, her affections were already fixed upon her friend, and her only fear was that other attractions or inconstancy might lead him to break his childhood vows.

But each day they grew more passionate and tender. It was a love that had matured with his own growth, woven itself into every faculty and feeling, and destined to end only with life. No one knew of their attachment but their two hearts; yet although in every other matter, and even in this, he feared his companions’ judgment for loving one beneath him in fortune, nothing could for an instant disturb his resolve to unite himself with her as soon as he could summon enough courage to face the obstacles he was determined to overcome.

Diana was entirely deserving of his deepest affection."}

{"request_id":"95fe789fc0d9a3f1e9bd0066","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, his face bleached with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile rushed out of Bentinck House, forcing his way through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, seeming neither to see nor hear anything. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind; but his hands burned with fever, and his forehead felt like fire. He walked on and on, almost with the unsteady gait of a drunk. A policeman watched him curiously as he passed, and a beggar who shuffled out from an archway to ask for alms grew frightened when he saw misery greater than his own. Once Arthur stopped beneath a lamp and looked at his hands. He thought he could already see blood upon them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had seen there. Murder! The very night seemed to know it, and the desolate wind seemed to howl it into his ear. The dark corners of the streets were filled with it. It grinned at him from the rooftops.

First he reached the Park, whose gloomy woodland seemed to hold him spellbound. Weary, he leaned against the railings, cooling his brow against the wet metal and listening to the trees’ trembling silence. “Murder! Murder!” he kept repeating, as though saying the word again and again might lessen its horror. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he almost hoped Echo would hear him and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a mad urge to stop some passer-by and tell him everything.

Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, shameful alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came oaths and blows, followed by shrill screams, and huddled on a damp doorstep he saw the crooked forms of poverty and old age. A strange pity came over him. Were these children of sin and misery destined for their end, as he was for his? Were they, like him, merely puppets in a monstrous show?

And yet it was not the mystery but the comedy of suffering that struck him: its utter uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. How incoherent everything seemed! How completely without harmony! He was astonished by the discord between the shallow optimism of the age and the actual facts of existence. He was still very young.

After some time he found himself before Marylebone Church. The silent roadway looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there by the dark arabesques of shifting shadows."}

{"request_id":"02dd82d50fdce65b0f51619c","rewritten_text":"Winters at the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are rarely severe, and in autumn it is an unusual event for a fire to be considered necessary. Yet around the middle of October, 18—, there came a day of extraordinary cold. Just before sunset, I made my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, which I had not visited for several weeks. At that time I lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and travel there and back was far less convenient than it is today. When I reached the hut, I knocked as usual. Receiving no answer, I found the key where I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and entered. A bright fire was burning on the hearth. It was a novelty, and a welcome one. I removed my overcoat, settled into an armchair beside the crackling logs, and patiently awaited the arrival of my hosts.

Soon after dark they came in and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, hurried about preparing marsh-hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—what else can I call them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unknown bivalve, belonging to a new genus; and, beyond that, with Jupiter’s help, he had tracked down and captured a _scarabæus_ he believed to be entirely new. He wanted my opinion of it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands over the fire and wishing the entire tribe of _scarabæi_ to the devil.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” Legrand said. “But it has been so long since I saw you; how could I have expected you to visit me on this particular night? On my way home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, foolishly, lent him the beetle. So you cannot see it until morning. Stay here tonight, and I will send Jup down for it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in creation!”

“What? Sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No—the beetle. It is a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and another, somewhat longer, at the other. The antennae are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep tellin’ you,” Jupiter interrupted. “De bug is a goole bug, solid, every bit of him, inside and all, ’cept his wing—never feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"f4e09200cc77a19afccb50f0","rewritten_text":"According to the latest reports from Rotterdam, that city appears to be in a state of intense philosophical excitement. Indeed, events have occurred there so wholly unexpected—so entirely new—so completely opposed to accepted ideas—that I have no doubt all Europe is already in an uproar, all physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at war with each other.

It seems that on the—— day of—— (I am not certain of the date), a vast crowd had gathered, for reasons not specifically stated, in the great square of the Exchange in the prosperous city of Rotterdam. The day was warm—unusually warm for the season—and scarcely a breath of air was moving. The crowd was in no bad mood at being occasionally sprinkled by brief, friendly showers falling from large white clouds that crossed the blue sky in shifting patterns. Nevertheless, around noon, a slight but remarkable disturbance became visible among them: the clatter of ten thousand voices began; and, a moment later, ten thousand faces turned toward the heavens, ten thousand pipes dropped at once from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a cry, comparable to nothing but the roar of Niagara, rang out long, loudly, and furiously across the whole area around Rotterdam.

The cause of this uproar soon became clear. From behind the enormous bulk of one of the sharply outlined clouds already mentioned, a strange, irregular, yet apparently solid object slowly emerged into an open patch of blue. Its shape was so peculiar, and its parts so whimsically assembled, that the sturdy burghers standing below could neither understand it nor admire it enough. What could it be? In the name of every woman and devil in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? No one knew; no one could guess. No one—not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—had the slightest clue for solving the mystery. So, since nothing more sensible could be done, every man carefully put his pipe back into the corner of his mouth, raised his right eye toward the phenomenon, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally puffed again.

Meanwhile, the object that had inspired so much curiosity and produced so much smoke descended lower and lower toward the good city. Within a few minutes it came close enough to be seen clearly. It appeared to be—yes, it was certainly a kind of balloon; but surely no balloon like it had ever been seen in Rotterdam before."}

{"request_id":"68cbd3ff147825495c5b7a41","rewritten_text":"Biddy cried; the darkening garden, the lane, and the stars appearing overhead were blurred in my own sight.

“Nothing was ever discovered, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what became of Orlick?”

“Judging by the color of his clothes, I should think he is working in the quarries.”

“Then of course you have seen him? Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there on the night she died.”

“That was not the last time either, Biddy?”

“No; I have seen him there since we began walking here. It is useless,” said Biddy, placing her hand on my arm as I was about to run out, “you know I would not deceive you; he was not there a minute, and he is gone.”

My indignation was renewed by the discovery that this fellow still pursued her, and I felt an enduring hatred for him. I told her so, and said I would spend any amount of money or take any trouble to drive him from that country. Gradually she led me into calmer conversation, and told me how Joe loved me, and how Joe never complained of anything—she did not say, of me; she had no need; I understood what she meant—but always did his duty in his station, with a strong hand, a quiet tongue, and a gentle heart.

“Indeed, it would be difficult to say too much in his praise,” I said; “and Biddy, we must often speak of these things, because of course I shall be coming down here often now. I am not going to leave poor Joe alone.”

Biddy said not a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Leaving aside your calling me Mr. Pip—which seems to me in poor taste, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, in a self-righteously assertive tone, “I must ask you to tell me what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Now, don’t repeat my words,” I retorted. “You never used to do that, Biddy.”

“Never used to!” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Never used to!”

Well, I rather thought I would abandon that point too. After another silent circuit of the garden, I returned to my main argument.

“Biddy,” I said, “I remarked that I would be coming down here often to see Joe, and you answered with a deliberate silence. Please, Biddy, tell me why.”

“Are you quite certain, then, that you will come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping in the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with a clear, honest gaze."}

Emma amused herself by declaring that it was indeed very extraordinary, and that she had not a word to say in his defence.

“I cannot conceive,” said Mrs. Elton, (feeling the affront as a wife ought,) “I cannot conceive how he could behave so to you, of all people in the world! The very last person one would expect to be forgotten!—My dear Mr. E., he must certainly have left a message for you.—Even Knightley could not be so exceedingly eccentric;—his servants must have forgotten it. Depend upon it, that was what happened: and it is very likely with the Donwell servants, who, as I have often noticed, are all extremely awkward and negligent.—I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry standing at our sideboard for any consideration. {"request_id":"679ff5f904bf7a0c8662e098","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier went riding across Brockley Meadows. She tore her riding habit badly while forcing her way through a hedge, and when she returned home, decided to go upstairs by the back staircase so no one would see her. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door happened to be open, she thought she saw someone inside. Assuming it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her work there, she looked in to ask her to mend the habit. To her immense surprise, however, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees blow through the air and the red leaves dance wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole posture expressed profound depression. Indeed, he looked so forlorn and so thoroughly worn out that little Virginia, whose first impulse had been to run away and lock herself in her room, felt sorry for him and resolved to comfort him. Her step was so light, and his melancholy so deep, that he did not notice her until she spoke.

‘I’m so sorry for you,’ she said, ‘but my brothers are returning to Eton tomorrow, and then, if you behave yourself, no one will bother you.’

‘It is absurd to ask me to behave myself,’ he replied, turning in astonishment toward the pretty little girl who had dared to address him. ‘Completely absurd. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night, if that is what you mean. It is my only reason for existing.’

‘That is no reason to exist at all, and you know you have behaved very wickedly. Mrs. Umney told us, on the first day we arrived here, that you had killed your wife.’

‘Well, I freely admit it,’ said the Ghost petulantly, ‘but it was strictly a family matter and concerned no one else.’

‘It is very wrong to kill anyone,’ said Virginia, who sometimes possessed a gentle Puritan seriousness inherited from an old New England ancestor.

‘Oh, I detest the cheap severity of abstract morality! My wife was extremely plain, never had my ruffs properly starched, and knew nothing about cooking. Why, there was a buck I had shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket—and do you know how she had it served at table? Still, it does not matter now, because it is all over. And I do not think it was very kind of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.’"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b1fea25d5ac8b5e47afb2f1d","rewritten_text":"The Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner before them, though young in years, was old in the treasonable practices that demanded the forfeiture of his life. This correspondence with the public enemy was not a matter of today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that, for longer than that, the prisoner had regularly travelled between France and England on secret business for which he could give no honest account. If treasonous schemes were capable of prospering—which, happily, they never were—the true wickedness and guilt of his dealings might have remained hidden. Providence, however, had moved a person beyond fear and reproach to investigate the nature of the prisoner’s plans and, horrified by what he discovered, reveal them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would be brought before them. His position and bearing were, in every respect, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend; but, discovering his infamy at once in a fortunate and disastrous hour, he had resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer cherish in his heart upon the sacred altar of his country. If Britain, like ancient Greece and Rome, awarded statues to public benefactors, this brilliant citizen would certainly have received one. Since Britain did not award them, he probably would not. Virtue, as the poets had observed in many passages the jury surely knew word for word—though their faces showed the guilty awareness that they knew none of them—was, in some sense, contagious; especially the radiant virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The noble example of this spotless and unimpeachable witness for the Crown, whom it was an honour even to mention unworthily, had spread to the prisoner’s servant. It had inspired him with the holy resolve to search his master’s drawers and pockets and conceal his papers. He, the Attorney-General, expected some attempt might be made to disparage this admirable servant; but, generally speaking, he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters, and honoured him more than his own father and mother. He confidently called upon the jury to do the same. The testimony of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had discovered and which would be produced, would prove that the prisoner had been supplied with lists of His Majesty’s forces and details of their deployment and preparation, by sea and land, leaving no doubt that he had habitually transmitted such information to a hostile power."}

{"request_id":"10e814f3143508de45f76803","rewritten_text":"His face was deeply sunburned and more than half covered by whiskers and a mustache. He carried a huge oak club but seemed otherwise unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and wished us “good evening” in a French accent. Though somewhat Neufchatel-like, it still clearly suggested that he came from Paris.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I suppose you have come about the orangutan. I almost envy you for owning him; he is an unusually fine animal and surely very valuable. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew a long breath, like a man freed from an unbearable burden, and answered confidently:

“I have no way of knowing—but he cannot be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no. We had no suitable place to keep him here. He is at a livery stable on the Rue Dubourg, very close by. You can collect him in the morning. Of course, you are ready to prove that he belongs to you?”

“Certainly, sir.”

“I shall be sorry to give him up,” said Dupin.

“I don’t mean for you to go to all this trouble without payment, sir,” said the man. “I could not expect that. I am quite willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” replied my friend, “that is only fair. Let me think! What should I ask? Oh, I know. My reward will be this: you must give me all the information you can about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words very softly and calmly. With the same calmness, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from inside his coat and placed it on the table without the slightest agitation.

The sailor’s face reddened as though he were fighting for breath. He sprang to his feet and seized his club, but a moment later sank back into his chair, shaking violently, his face as pale as death. He said nothing. I felt deep pity for him.

“My friend,” said Dupin gently, “you are frightening yourself for no reason—you truly are. We mean you no harm at all. I give you my word, as a gentleman and a Frenchman, that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the crimes in the Rue Morgue. Still, you cannot deny that you are involved in them to some extent.”"}

{"request_id":"7bc6e5668f1d9c70bb985a74","rewritten_text":"In my younger days, discontent never entered my thoughts, and whenever _ennui_ did overcome me, the sight of nature’s beauty, or the contemplation of what was excellent and sublime in human works, could always engage my heart and restore elasticity to my spirits. But I am a blasted tree; the bolt has pierced my soul; and I then felt that I must live on to display what I shall soon become—a wretched spectacle of ruined humanity, pitied by others and unbearable to myself.

We remained a considerable time at Oxford, wandering through its environs and trying to recognize every place connected with the most stirring period of English history. Our small excursions of discovery were often lengthened by the succession of objects that appeared before us. We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, my soul rose above its degrading and miserable fears to contemplate the divine principles of liberty and self-sacrifice that these sights commemorated and recalled. For an instant I dared cast off my chains and look about me with a free and elevated spirit; but the iron had sunk into my flesh, and once more I fell, trembling and without hope, into my wretched self.

We quitted Oxford reluctantly and travelled to Matlock, our next resting-place. The country around this village bore a stronger resemblance to the scenery of Switzerland; yet everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the distant crown of white Alps that always accompanies the pine-clad mountains of my native land. We saw the wondrous cave and the small cabinets of natural history, where the curiosities were arranged in the same fashion as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name caused me to tremble when Henry uttered it, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which had thus become linked with that dreadful scene.

From Derby, still travelling northward, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could now almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow remaining on the northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing of the rocky streams were all familiar and beloved sights. Here, too, we formed several acquaintances, who nearly succeeded in deceiving me into happiness. Clerval’s pleasure was proportionately greater than mine; among men of talent his mind expanded, and he discovered in his own nature capacities and resources greater than he could have imagined possessing while he had associated with his inferiors."}

{"request_id":"637303cfb39e230e3eb7cc3f","rewritten_text":"Her position was, indeed, one of extraordinary trial and difficulty. Though she felt the keenest, most ardent desire to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s history, she could not violate the confidence entrusted to her by the wretched woman with whom she had just spoken, who had confided in her as a young and innocent girl. The woman’s words and manner had moved Rose Maylie deeply; and, joined to her love for her young charge, and scarcely less sincere or fervent, was her earnest hope of bringing the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They intended to stay in London for only three days before leaving for several weeks in a distant coastal region. It was now midnight on the first day. What plan could she settle upon and carry out within forty-eight hours? Or how could she delay their departure without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was staying with them and would remain for the next two days; but Rose knew the worthy gentleman’s impetuous nature too well, and could too plainly foresee the anger with which, in the first burst of his indignation, he would view the means by which Oliver had been recaptured, to entrust him with the secret while no experienced person was available to support her plea on the girl’s behalf. For the same reasons, she had to exercise the utmost caution and discretion in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first instinct would certainly be to consult the good doctor about it. Seeking legal advice, even had she known where to turn, was hardly conceivable for the same cause. Once she thought of asking Harry for help; but this brought back the memory of their last parting, and it seemed unworthy to summon him when—tears came to her eyes as she followed the thought—he might by now have learned to forget her and be happier at a distance.

Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, leaning first toward one course and then another, only to shrink from each as new objections arose, Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. After further reflection the next day, she reached the desperate decision to consult Harry.

“If returning here would cause him pain,” she thought, “how much pain it will cause me! Yet perhaps he will not return; he may write, or come himself while carefully avoiding me—he did so when he left. I scarcely expected it then; but it was better for us both.” At this point Rose let the pen fall and turned aside, as if even the paper that was to carry her message must not witness her tears."}

{"request_id":"b18de13747cafc7e79d5cbec","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologized. He said, “Not at all,” and continued.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you may imagine that she was pursued as a highly desirable match. Her half-brother once again had ample means, but between debts and renewed madness, he squandered them most terribly. The differences between him and her were even greater than those between him and his father, and it was suspected that he held a deep and deadly grudge against her for having influenced their father’s anger. Now I come to the cruel part of the story—pausing only, my dear Handel, to observe that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to force mine into my tumbler, I cannot say at all. I only know that I found myself, with perseverance worthy of a far better cause, making the most determined efforts to compress it within those limits. Again I thanked him and apologized, and again he said in the most cheerful manner, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“There appeared on the scene—at the races, perhaps, or the public balls, or anywhere else you please—a certain man who courted Miss Havisham. I never saw him, for this happened twenty-five years ago, before you and I were born, Handel, but I have heard my father say that he was a flashy man, and exactly the sort for the purpose. Yet my father insists most strongly that he was not, without ignorance or prejudice, to be mistaken for a gentleman; for it is his principle that no man who was not a true gentleman at heart has ever, since the world began, been a true gentleman in manner. He says that no varnish can conceal the grain of the wood, and that the more varnish you apply, the more clearly the grain will show. Well! This man pursued Miss Havisham relentlessly and claimed to be devoted to her. I believe she had shown little susceptibility before that time; but all she possessed certainly emerged then, and she loved him passionately. There is no doubt that she idolized him completely. He exploited her affection so methodically that he obtained large sums of money from her, and persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery—which their father had weakly left him—at an enormous price, claiming that once he became her husband, he would have to own and manage the whole concern. Your guardian was not yet involved in Miss Havisham’s affairs, and she was too proud and too deeply in love to accept advice from anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"1fa77b69b5359ba074c2444c","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, purchased Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was acting most foolishly, since there was no question that the house was haunted. Indeed, Lord Canterville himself, a gentleman of the strictest honour, had considered it his duty to inform Mr. Otis of the fact while they were negotiating the terms.

‘We have not chosen to live there ourselves,’ said Lord Canterville, ‘ever since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was so terrified that she suffered a fit from which she never truly recovered. Two skeleton hands had been laid upon her shoulders while she was dressing for dinner. And I feel obliged to tell you, Mr. Otis, that the ghost has been seen by several living members of my family, as well as by the parish rector, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, who is a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the Duchess’s unfortunate accident, none of our younger servants would remain with us, and Lady Canterville frequently slept very little at night because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.’

‘My Lord,’ replied the Minister, ‘I will take the furniture and the ghost at their assessed value. I come from a modern country, where money can purchase everything; and with all our lively young men painting the Old World red, while carrying away your finest actresses and prima-donnas, I suppose that if there were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we should soon have it at home, either in one of our public museums or travelling about as a spectacle.’

‘I am afraid the ghost does exist,’ said Lord Canterville with a smile, ‘although it may have declined the offers of your enterprising showmen. It has been known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always appears before the death of a member of our family.’

‘Well, so does the family doctor, for that matter, Lord Canterville. But there is no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I reckon the laws of Nature are not about to be suspended for the sake of the British aristocracy.’

‘You are certainly very natural in America,’ answered Lord Canterville, who had not entirely understood Mr. Otis’s last remark, ‘and if you have no objection to a ghost in the house, then all is well. You must only remember that I warned you.’

A few weeks later the purchase was completed, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, who as Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street had been a celebrated New York belle, was now a very handsome middle-aged woman, with beautiful eyes and a magnificent profile."}

content.text: {"request_id":"da40b12b2fb9d83761c54fea","rewritten_text":"In truth, he had not suspected his own influence at all. He had followed her into the shrubbery without any thought of trying to use it. Anxious to see how she would bear the news of Frank Churchill’s engagement, he had come with no selfish purpose, indeed with no plan beyond trying, if she gave him the chance, to comfort or advise her.—Everything else had been the work of the moment, the immediate result of what he heard and felt. The wonderful certainty that she was completely indifferent to Frank Churchill, that her heart was entirely free of him, had awakened the hope that, in time, he might win her affection himself;—but it was not a present hope. In that brief moment, when eagerness overcame judgment, he had only dared to hope she would say that she did not forbid him to try to win her.—The greater hopes that gradually appeared were all the more delightful.—The affection he had asked permission to create, if he could, was already his!—In less than half an hour, he had gone from deep distress to something so close to perfect happiness that it could be called nothing else.\n\n_Her_ change was just as great.—That half-hour had given them both the same precious certainty that they were loved, and had removed from each the same measure of ignorance, jealousy, and doubt.—On his side, the jealousy had lasted a long time, beginning with Frank Churchill’s arrival, or even with the expectation of it.—He had been in love with Emma and jealous of Frank Churchill from nearly the same time; one feeling had probably revealed the other to him. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that had driven him away from the country.—The party at Box Hill had decided him to leave. He would spare himself the sight of such openly allowed and encouraged attentions again.—He had gone away to learn indifference.—But he had chosen the wrong place. There was too much family happiness in his brother’s home; women appeared too kindly there; and Isabella was too much like Emma—differing only in those obvious weaknesses that made Emma’s brilliance stand out before him—for much progress to be possible, even if he had stayed longer.—Still, he had remained, firmly, day after day, until the morning’s post brought the story of Jane Fairfax.—Then, with a happiness he had every right, and did not hesitate, to feel, since he had never thought Frank Churchill worthy of Emma, he became so deeply concerned and anxious for her that he could stay no longer. He had ridden home through the rain and, immediately after dinner, walked up to see how this sweetest and best of all creatures, faultless despite all her faults, had borne the discovery."}

{"request_id":"855d6ffef308cf9e3e4df76b","rewritten_text":"“Listen, then! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother—joined him there. They had been separated for a long time. She traveled from Paris and took me with her, supposedly to look after his property, though I cannot say why, since she had little affection for him, and he had little for her. He knew nothing of us, for his senses had failed him, and he slept on until the next day, when he died. Among the papers in his desk were two, dated on the night his illness began and addressed to you”—he turned to Mr. Brownlow—“enclosed in a few short lines, with a note on the package saying it was not to be sent until after his death. One paper was a letter to this girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What did the letter say?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter? It was a sheet of paper covered with writing, containing a sorrowful confession and prayers asking God to help her. He had told the girl that some secret matter—which he would explain one day—prevented him from marrying her at that time. She had trusted him patiently until she trusted him too far, and lost what no one could ever give back to her. She was then only a few months from giving birth. He told her what he had planned to do, if he lived, to conceal her shame. If he died, he begged her not to curse his memory or believe that the results of their sin would fall upon her or their child, since all the guilt was his. He reminded her of the day he had given her the little locket and the ring engraved with her Christian name, leaving a blank for the name he hoped one day to give her. He begged her to keep them and wear them against her heart, as she had done before. Then he continued wildly, repeating the same words again and again, as though he had lost his mind. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, as Oliver’s tears fell rapidly.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He spoke of the misery his wife had caused him, and of the rebellious nature, wickedness, spite, and early evil passions of you, his only son, whom she had raised to hate him. He left you and your mother an annuity of eight hundred pounds each. He divided the greater part of his property into two equal shares: one for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, if it was born alive and ever reached adulthood.”"}

{"request_id":"eeb65af109bb267e69fcccff","rewritten_text":"“Men marry because they are weary; women, because they are curious: both end by being disappointed.”

“I don’t think I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your aphorisms. I’m putting it into practice, as I do everything you say.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“An actress,” said Dorian Gray, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That is a rather commonplace _début_.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard of her.”

“No one has. They will someday, though. She is a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are a decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they say it charmingly. Women represent matter’s triumph over mind, just as men represent mind’s triumph over morals.”

“Harry, how can you say that?”

“My dear Dorian, it is perfectly true. I am studying women at present, so I ought to know. The subject is not as abstruse as I once thought. Ultimately, I find, there are only two kinds of women, the plain and the coloured. Plain women are extremely useful. If you wish to acquire a reputation for respectability, you need only take them down to supper. The others are very charming. They make one mistake, however. They paint themselves in an attempt to look young. Our grandmothers painted in an attempt to speak brilliantly. _Rouge_ and _esprit_ once went together. That is finished now. So long as a woman can appear ten years younger than her own daughter, she is entirely content. As for conversation, only five women in London are worth talking to, and two of them cannot be admitted to decent society. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah, Harry, your opinions frighten me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you mustn’t be unsympathetic. After all, it would never have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. {"request_id":"ea10be0a72ad7f670ad551b3","rewritten_text":"“Mr Elliot looking up with such respect.”

“Absolutely delightful!” cried Mrs Clay, though she did not dare turn her eyes toward Anne. “Exactly like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not say father and son?”

“Oh! I place no restriction on anyone’s words. If you choose to entertain such ideas! But, upon my word, I am scarcely aware that his attentions go beyond those of other men.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs Clay, raising her hands and eyes, then burying the rest of her astonishment in a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so alarmed about him. I did invite him, you know. I sent him away smiling. When I discovered that he was truly going to spend all of tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired her friend’s excellent acting, in being able to show such pleasure as she did at the expectation and actual arrival of the very person whose presence must truly interfere with her principal aim. Mrs Clay could hardly fail to hate the sight of Mr Elliot; yet she could assume the most obliging, calm expression, and appear entirely satisfied with the reduced opportunity of devoting herself only half as much to Sir Walter as she otherwise would have done.

For Anne herself, it was deeply distressing to see Mr Elliot enter the room, and quite painful to have him come near and speak to her. She had previously felt that he could not always be entirely sincere, but now she saw insincerity in everything. His respectful attention to her father, set against his former words, was hateful; and when she remembered his cruel treatment of Mrs Smith, she could scarcely endure the sight of his present smiles and gentleness, or the sound of his artificial expressions of good feeling.

She intended to avoid any change in her manner that might provoke a remonstrance from him. It was very important to escape all questioning or public display; but she meant to be as decidedly cool toward him as their relationship allowed, and to retrace, as quietly as possible, the few unnecessary steps of intimacy along which she had gradually been led. Accordingly, she was more guarded and cooler than she had been the previous evening.

He wished to revive her curiosity about how and where he might formerly have heard her praised; he greatly desired the satisfaction of being pressed for more information. But the spell was broken: he discovered that the warmth and excitement of a public room were necessary to kindle his modest cousin’s vanity; at least, he found that it could not now be done by any of the attempts he could risk amid the others’ more commanding claims."}
