{"request_id":"160d084cdd6fabbf3dedec3b","rewritten_text":"His face, deeply sunburned, was more than half concealed by whiskers and a mustache. He carried a huge oaken cudgel but appeared otherwise unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and wished us “good evening” in a French accent which, though somewhat Neufchâtel-like, still clearly suggested a Parisian origin.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I suppose you have come about the orangutan. Upon my word, I almost envy you for possessing him—a remarkably fine and no doubt very valuable animal. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew a long breath, like a man relieved of some unbearable burden, and then replied confidently:

“I have no way of knowing—but he cannot be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no; we had no facilities for keeping him here. He is at a livery stable on the Rue Dubourg, just nearby. You can collect him in the morning. Of course, you are prepared to identify the property?”

“Certainly, sir.”

“I shall be sorry to part with him,” said Dupin.

“I don’t mean for you to go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” said the man. “I couldn’t expect that. I am quite willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” replied my friend, “that is entirely fair, certainly. Let me think—what should I ask? Oh, I know. My reward will be this: you must give me all the information you can about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words very softly and calmly. With equal calm, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. He then drew a pistol from inside his coat and placed it on the table without the slightest agitation.

The sailor’s face flushed as though he were fighting for breath. He sprang to his feet and seized his cudgel, but the next moment sank back into his chair, trembling violently, his face like death itself. He said nothing. I pitied him with all my heart.

“My friend,” said Dupin gently, “you are needlessly alarming yourself—you truly are. We mean you no harm at all. I give you my word of honor, as a gentleman and a Frenchman, that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. Still, it will not do to deny that you are involved in them to some extent.”"}

{"request_id":"43b9738c9e475f8a9662c56c","rewritten_text":"“One word more, Rose. Dearest Rose—one more!” cried Harry, throwing himself before her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world would call it—if some obscure and peaceful life had been allotted me—if I had been poor, sick, helpless—would you have rejected me then? Or has my likely rise to wealth and honour given birth to this scruple?”

“Do not force me to answer,” replied Rose. “The question does not arise, and never will. It is unfair, almost unkind, to press it.”

“If your answer is what I scarcely dare hope,” returned Harry, “it will cast a gleam of happiness across my lonely path, and illuminate the road before me. It is no small thing to do so much, by speaking a few brief words, for one who loves you above everything. Oh, Rose: in the name of my passionate and lasting devotion; in the name of all I have suffered for you, and all you condemn me to endure; answer me this one question!”

“Then, if your lot had been differently appointed,” rejoined Rose; “if you had been even somewhat, though not so greatly, above me; if I could have been a help and comfort to you in some humble life of peace and retirement, rather than a stain and hindrance amid ambitious and distinguished society; I should have been spared this ordeal. I have every reason to be happy—very happy—now; but then, Harry, I confess I should have been happier.”

Crowded memories of old hopes, cherished long ago when she was a girl, filled Rose’s mind as she made this confession; but they brought tears with them, as old hopes do when they return withered, and the tears brought her relief.

“I cannot overcome this weakness, and it strengthens my resolve,” said Rose, holding out her hand. “I must leave you now, truly.”

“I ask one promise,” said Harry. “Once, and only once more—within a year, perhaps, though it may be much sooner—I may speak to you again on this matter, for the final time.”

“Not to urge me to change my rightful decision,” replied Rose, with a melancholy smile; “that would be useless.”

“No,” said Harry; “only to hear you repeat it, if you will—repeat it finally! I will place at your feet whatever rank or fortune I may possess; and if you still maintain your present resolution, I will not seek, by word or deed, to alter it.”

“Then let it be so,” rejoined Rose; “it is only one pain more, and by then I may be better able to endure it.”

She held out her hand once again."}

{"request_id":"2d5d174b9570b4f0edc19766","rewritten_text":"He was short but remarkably upright, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He began his lecture by reviewing the history of chemistry and the improvements made by different learned men, speaking with passion as he pronounced the names of the most distinguished discoverers. He then gave a brief account of the science as it stood and explained many of its basic terms. After performing a few preliminary experiments, he ended with a praise of modern chemistry, whose words I shall never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” he said, “promised impossibilities and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be changed into one another and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem made only for dabbling in dirt and whose eyes are fixed on the microscope or crucible, have truly performed miracles. They enter nature’s hidden places and reveal how she works there. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and almost unlimited powers; they can command the thunder, imitate an earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows.”

Those were the professor’s words—or rather, the words of fate, spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as though my soul were struggling with a real enemy. One by one, the keys that formed the mechanism of my being were pressed; chord after chord sounded, and soon my mind held one thought, one idea, one purpose. So much has been done, cried the soul of Frankenstein—far more will I achieve. Following the path already marked, I will open a new one, explore unknown powers, and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner being was in rebellion and turmoil; I felt that order would come from it, but I had no power to create that order. Gradually, after dawn, sleep came. I awoke, and the thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. Only one decision remained: to return to my former studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private, his manner was even gentler and more appealing than in public. During his lecture, there had been a certain dignity in his bearing; in his own home, this was replaced by the greatest friendliness and kindness."}

{"request_id":"b24506a2daafbe8d6b6806eb","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost completed their cycle. It was now the end of May; the woods were covered in their freshest green, and the sweet scent of newly mown grass filled the fields. I thought the gentle air and beautiful face of Nature might help awaken mild feelings in him, giving him a peaceful and loving mood before I tried to gain the confidence I had resolved to seek.

I therefore chose the evening of one of these days for my attempt. I invited him to walk with me and led him to a nearby beech wood, whose light shade protected us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After walking silently for some time, I sat with him on a mossy hillock. It is strange, but even now I seem to see the place. Many of the slender, smooth trunks were wrapped in ivy, whose shining, darkest-green leaves stood out against the white bark and the pale leaves of the young beech shoots growing from their parent trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss and partly covered by the dead leaves of the previous autumn, which the wind had gathered here and there into little mounds. A few moss-covered stumps stood nearby. The leaves moved gently in the breeze, and through their green canopy we could see the bright blue sky. As evening approached, the distant trunks turned red in the sunlight, and the wind died completely, while a few birds flew past us toward their evening rest.

Here we sat together. When you hear all that happened—all that terrible suffering that tore our souls even in this peaceful place, which might have been a paradise to us without those strange passions—you will not wonder that I remember it as I looked upon it. Its calm helped calm me and gave me not only courage but persuasive words. I saw all these things and noted them absently while trying to arrange my thoughts in the right order for my attempt. My heart beat quickly as I prepared to speak, for I was determined not to be rejected, yet I trembled to imagine what effect my words might have on him. At last, after much hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—you showed me when you first returned will, I hope, excuse me for daring to speak to you, though with the tender affection of a daughter, yet also with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"805c390427ccb6ddedbc9883","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father, certainly, may spare you, if your mother is able. Daughters are never of such importance to a father. And if you remain another _month_ in full, I shall be able to take one of you as far as London, since I am going there at the beginning of June, for a week; and as Dawson has no objection to the barouche-box, there will be ample room for one of you—and, indeed, should the weather prove cool, I should not mind taking you both, as neither of you is large.”

“You are all kindness, madam; but I believe we must adhere to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine appeared resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot endure the thought of two young women travelling post alone. It is highly improper. You must find some way to send someone. I have the greatest dislike in the world to that kind of thing. Young women ought always to be properly protected and attended, in keeping with their station in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two men-servants accompany her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne, could not properly have appeared otherwise. I am extremely particular about such matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad it occurred to me to say so; for it would truly be discreditable to _you_ to allow them to go alone.”

“My uncle is to send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, does he? I am very pleased that you have someone who attends to such matters. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, naturally. If you give my name at the Bell, you will be properly attended.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions concerning their journey; and since she did not answer every one herself, attention was required—which Elizabeth considered fortunate; for, with her mind so engaged, she might otherwise have forgotten where she was. Reflection had to be saved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she surrendered to it as the greatest relief; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, during which she could indulge in all the pleasure of disagreeable recollections.

She was well on her way to knowing Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She examined every sentence; and her feelings toward its writer were sometimes entirely different. When she recalled the manner of his address, she remained filled with indignation: but when she reflected on how unjustly she had condemned and reproached him, her anger turned upon herself; and his disappointed feelings became objects of compassion."}

It was, however, an extremely difficult “make-up,” if I may use that theatrical term for one of the greatest mysteries of the supernatural—or, in more scientific language, the higher-natural—world, and it took him a full three hours to prepare. At last everything was ready, and he was very pleased with his appearance. The large leather riding boots that went with the costume were slightly too big for him, and he could find only one of the two horse pistols, but overall he was satisfied. At a quarter past one, he slipped out of the wainscoting and crept down the corridor. When he reached the twins’ room, which was called the Blue Bed Chamber because of the color of its curtains, he found the door slightly open. Wanting to make a dramatic entrance, he threw it wide open. A heavy jug of water immediately fell on him, soaking him completely and missing his left shoulder by only a few inches. At the same moment, he heard muffled laughter coming from the four-poster bed. The shock was so great that he ran back to his room as fast as he could, and the next day he was confined to bed with a severe cold. The only thing that comforted him was that he had not brought his head with him, because if he had, the results might have been very serious.\n\nHe now abandoned all hope of ever frightening this rude American family. Usually, he contented himself with creeping through the passages in soft slippers, wearing a thick red scarf around his throat to protect against drafts, and carrying a small arquebus in case the twins attacked him. The final blow came on September 19. He had gone downstairs to the great entrance hall, certain that there, at least, he would be left alone. He was amusing himself by making sarcastic comments about the large Sarony photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which had replaced the Canterville family portraits. He was dressed simply but neatly in a long shroud spotted with churchyard mold, had tied his jaw with a strip of yellow linen, and carried a small lantern and a sexton’s spade."}

{"request_id":"8eed299b871e26596b7fff6c","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; all the labor of maintaining a slow and unsatisfactory correspondence with Elizabeth fell to Anne.

Breakfast had scarcely been over when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick joined them; they had arranged to take their final walk around Lyme together. They should leave for Uppercross by one, and until then they meant to remain together and outside for as long as possible.

Anne discovered Captain Benwick drawing near her as soon as they were properly in the street. Their conversation of the previous evening had not made him reluctant to seek her company again; and for some time they walked together, speaking as before about Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, still no more able than before—or than any other two readers—to agree precisely about the merits of either, until something caused an almost general rearrangement of the party, and Captain Harville took Captain Benwick’s place beside her.

“Miss Elliot,” he said, in a rather quiet voice, “you have done a good thing by getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he could have such companionship more often. I know it is bad for him to be confined as he is; but what can we do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can readily believe that impossible; but perhaps, with time—we know what time accomplishes in every kind of sorrow, and you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend may still be considered a young mourner—only last summer, as I understand.”

“Ay, quite true,” (with a heavy sigh) “only June.”

“And perhaps he did not know until rather later.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he returned from the Cape, having just been made captain of the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, fearing to hear of him; he sent in letters, but the Grappler had orders for Portsmouth. The news would have to reach him there, but who was to deliver it? not I. I would almost as soon have been hanged from the yard-arm. No one could do it except that good fellow” (pointing to Captain Wentworth). “The Laconia had entered Plymouth the week before, and there was no likelihood of her being sent to sea again. He took his chance with the rest; applied for leave of absence, but without waiting for the answer travelled night and day until he reached Portsmouth, rowed out to the Grappler at once, and did not leave the poor fellow for a week. That is what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. You may judge, Miss Elliot, whether he is dear to us!”

Anne considered the question with complete certainty, and answered as fully as her own feelings allowed, or as much as his seemed able to endure, for he was too deeply moved to continue the subject; and when he spoke again, it was about something entirely different."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6bd488ef44da8180dd593eea","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the dead man's luxury was wonderful.\n\nThen he turned to embroidery and to the tapestries that served as frescoes in the cold rooms of northern Europe. As he studied the subject—and he had an extraordinary ability to become completely absorbed in whatever he was doing—he was almost saddened by the thought of how time destroyed beautiful and marvelous things. He, at least, had escaped that fate. Summer came after summer, and the yellow jonquils bloomed and died many times, while nights of horror repeated the story of their shame, but he remained unchanged. No winter damaged his face or dulled his flowerlike beauty. How different it was with material things! Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe, made by brown girls for Athena's pleasure, on which the gods fought the giants? Where was the enormous canopy Nero stretched across Rome's Colosseum, that purple Titan's sail showing the starry sky and Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white horses with golden reins? He longed to see the strange tablecloths made for the Priest of the Sun, displaying every delicacy and dish needed for a feast; King Chilperic's burial cloth, with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastic robes that angered the Bishop of Pontus, decorated with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—all, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat once worn by Charles of Orleans, whose sleeves carried the verses of a song beginning “_Madame, je suis tout joyeux_.” The music was embroidered in gold thread, and each note, square-shaped in those days, was made with four pearls. He read about the room prepared at the palace in Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in embroidery, and bearing the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly marked with the queen’s arms, the whole worked in gold.” Catherine de Medicis had a mourning bed made of black velvet covered with crescents and suns. Its damask curtains showed leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold-and-silver background, with pearl embroidery along the edges. It stood in a room hung with rows of the queen’s emblems, cut from black velvet and set against silver cloth. Louis XIV had gold-embroidered caryatids fifteen feet high in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"6eaf438e1c346d0d0ba63347","rewritten_text":"I then went from shop to shop, buying whatever was needed to alter his appearance. When that was done, I made my way, for my own purposes, to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but when he saw me enter, he rose at once and stood before the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. On the way there, I had thought carefully about what I meant to say.

“Don’t commit yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t commit anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything: I don’t want to know anything; I’m not curious.”

Of course, I understood that he knew the man had arrived.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to satisfy myself that what I have been told is true. I have no hope that it is untrue, but at least I can verify it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head to one side. He did not look at me, but listened intently toward the floor. “Told would suggest verbal communication. You can’t have verbal communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I’ll say, informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the benefactor who has been unknown to me for so long.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And no one else?” I asked.

“And no one else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you responsible for my mistakes and false conclusions; but I always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied, turning his cool eyes on me and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it seemed so much like it, sir,” I pleaded, my heart sinking.

“Not a particle of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat. “Trust nothing by appearances; trust everything to evidence. There is no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I said with a sigh, after standing silent for a while. “I have verified my information, and that is the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout my communications with you, I have kept to the exact line of fact. There has never been the slightest departure from that line. You are fully aware of this?”

“Quite, sir.”

“I told Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must never expect me to depart from the exact line of fact.”"}

{"request_id":"37014b6adf18852d95aa2651","rewritten_text":"“I am not eating at home, so I shall not need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” said the man as he left the room.

“Now, Alan, there is no time to lose. How heavy this chest is! I’ll carry it for you. You bring the other things.” He spoke quickly and with authority. Campbell felt himself being controlled by him. They left the room together.

When they reached the top landing, Dorian took out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he stopped, and a troubled expression came over his face. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he whispered.

“It means nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. At once he saw the face of his portrait leering in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that the night before, for the first time in his life, he had forgotten to cover the fatal canvas. He was about to rush forward, but drew back with a shudder.

What was that disgusting red moisture shining wetly on one of the hands, as if the canvas had sweated blood? How horrible it was! For a moment, it seemed even more horrible than the silent thing he knew was stretched across the table—the thing whose grotesque, misshapen shadow on the stained carpet showed that it had not moved, but was still there, just as he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, opened the door a little farther, and, with his eyes half closed and his head turned away, walked quickly inside, determined not to look even once at the dead man. Then he bent down, picked up the gold-and-purple hanging, and threw it over the picture.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around, and fixed his eyes on the complicated pattern before him. He heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other things he had requested for his terrible work. He began to wonder whether he and Basil Hallward had ever met, and, if they had, what they had thought of each other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, only noticing that the dead man had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a shining yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turning in the lock.

It was well after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale, but completely calm. “I have done what you asked me to do,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"48f1ebad83ca83c4941ee608","rewritten_text":"“In English, the letter that occurs most often is e. After that, the order is: _a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z_. _E_ is so dominant that it is rare to find a sentence of any length in which it is not the prevailing character.

“Here, then, at the very outset, we have the basis for something more than a mere guess. The table’s general usefulness is obvious—but in this particular cipher, we shall need its assistance only to a limited extent. Since our most frequent character is 8, we will begin by assuming that it represents the _e_ of the ordinary alphabet. To test this assumption, let us see whether 8 appears often in pairs—for _e_ is frequently doubled in English, in words such as ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In this case, we find it doubled no fewer than five times, although the cryptograph is short.

“Let us therefore take 8 as _e_. Now, of all _words_ in the language, ‘the’ is the most common; let us see whether there are repetitions of any three characters, in the same order, with the last of them being 8. If we find such repeated sequences, they will most likely represent the word ‘the.’ On examination, we find no fewer than seven such sequences, the characters being ;48. We may therefore assume that ; represents _t_, 4 represents _h_, and 8 represents _e_—the last now being firmly confirmed. Thus, a major step has been made.

“But once we have established a single word, we can establish a highly important point: several beginnings and endings of other words. Let us consider, for example, the next-to-last occurrence of the combination ;48, not far from the cipher’s end. We know that the ; immediately following it begins a word, and that of the six characters after this ‘the,’ we know five. Let us write those characters using the letters we know they represent, leaving a space for the unknown—

t eeth.

“Here we can immediately reject the ‘th’ as forming no part of the word beginning with the first t; for, by trying every letter of the alphabet in the blank, we see that no word can be formed in which this _th_ belongs. We are therefore reduced to

t ee,

and, by going through the alphabet as before if necessary, we arrive at the word ‘tree’ as the only possible reading.”"}

{"request_id":"d0bd407ee8366750cd21f916","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction, and although I had fully expected it, it gave me the greatest pleasure. After reaching about the twentieth parallel of southern latitude on its previous course, it suddenly turned eastward at a sharp angle. It continued in that direction throughout the day, staying almost exactly in the plane of the moon’s orbit. One notable result of this change was a very noticeable swaying of the car, which continued, to some degree, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again greatly frightened by the return of the loud, crackling noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought about it for a long time but could reach no satisfactory conclusion. The earth’s apparent diameter had decreased greatly; from the balloon it now measured only a little more than twenty-five degrees. The moon could not be seen at all, since it was nearly directly overhead. I remained in the plane of the moon’s orbit but made little progress eastward.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter decreased with extreme speed. Today I became convinced that the balloon was actually traveling along the line of apsides toward the point of perigee—in other words, following the direct course that would take it to the moon at the part of its orbit nearest the earth. The moon itself was directly overhead and therefore hidden from my sight. A great deal of prolonged effort was needed to condense the atmosphere.

“April 15th. The outlines of continents and seas could no longer be seen on the earth with anything like clarity. Around noon, I heard for the third time the terrifying sound that had astonished me before. This time it lasted several moments and grew louder as it continued. At last, while I stood stunned and terrified, expecting some terrible destruction but not knowing what, the car shook violently. Then a huge, flaming mass of material, whose nature I could not identify, roared and thundered past the balloon. When my fear and astonishment had somewhat faded, I had little trouble believing it was a massive volcanic fragment thrown from the world I was rapidly approaching. In all likelihood, it belonged to the strange class of objects sometimes found on earth and called meteoric stones for lack of a better name.

“April 16th. Today, looking upward as best I could through each side window in turn, I saw, to my great delight, a very small part of the moon’s disk extending beyond the balloon’s enormous circumference on every side."}

{"request_id":"7bfc9ed3480ceeb712e3ee56","rewritten_text":"Her colour changed, and she said no more.

Mrs. Gardiner was standing a little behind them. When she paused, he asked whether she would do him the honour of introducing him to her friends. This polite request caught her completely unprepared, and she could barely hide a smile. He was now seeking the acquaintance of people whose company his pride had rejected when he had offered himself to her. “How surprised he will be,” she thought, “when he discovers who they are! He thinks they are people of fashion.”

The introduction was made at once. As she explained how they were related to her, she gave him a sly glance to see how he took it, expecting him to leave as quickly as possible rather than remain with such disgraceful companions. He was clearly surprised by the connection, but he bore it bravely. Instead of going away, he turned back with them and began talking to Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help being pleased and triumphant. It was comforting that he should learn she had relatives of whom she had no reason to be ashamed. She listened closely to everything they said and took pride in every remark and sentence from her uncle that showed his intelligence, taste, or good manners.

The conversation soon turned to fishing. Elizabeth heard Mr. Darcy invite her uncle, with the greatest politeness, to fish there whenever he wished while he remained in the area. He also offered to provide fishing equipment and pointed out the parts of the stream where the best sport was usually found. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look of astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but she was deeply pleased; the compliment must have been meant entirely for her. Yet she remained extremely puzzled and kept asking herself, “Why is he so changed? What could have caused it? It cannot be for me, it cannot be because of me, that his manner has become so gentle. My criticisms at Hunsford could not have produced such a change. It is impossible that he should still love me.”

After they had walked this way for some time, with the two ladies ahead and the two gentlemen behind, they changed places slightly after going down to the riverbank to examine a curious water plant more closely. The change began with Mrs. Gardiner. Tired from the morning’s exercise, she found Elizabeth’s arm unable to support her well enough and therefore chose her husband’s instead."}

content.text: {"request_id":"17dbeb761ec9a58b6ca17b9e","rewritten_text":"Weeks passed, and I became increasingly absorbed in you. Then something new occurred. I had painted you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis wearing a huntsman’s cloak and carrying a polished boar-spear. With heavy lotus blossoms crowning you, you had sat at the prow of Adrian’s barge, looking over the green, muddy Nile. You had bent above the quiet pool of a Greek woodland and seen, in the water’s soundless silver, the wonder of your own face. And all of it had been what art ought to be—unconscious, ideal, and distant. One day, a fatal day, I sometimes think, I decided to paint a magnificent portrait of you as you truly were, not dressed in the fashion of vanished ages, but in your own clothes and your own time. Whether it was the realism of the method, or simply the extraordinary force of your personality, shown to me so directly, without mist or veil, I cannot say. But I know that, as I worked, every flake and film of colour seemed to disclose my secret. I became frightened that others might discover my idolatry. I felt, Dorian, that I had revealed too much, that I had placed too much of myself in it. Then I resolved never to let the picture be exhibited. You were somewhat irritated; but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, whom I spoke to about it, laughed at me. I did not care. When the portrait was complete, and I sat alone with it, I knew I had been right.... Well, after a few days the thing left my studio, and once I had escaped the unbearable fascination of its presence, I thought I had been foolish to imagine I had seen anything in it beyond the fact that you were exceptionally handsome and that I could paint. Even now I cannot help thinking it mistaken to suppose that the passion felt during creation is ever truly displayed in the work produced. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and colour speak to us of form and colour—that is all. It often seems to me that art hides the artist far more completely than it reveals him. And so, when I received this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the chief work in my exhibition. It never entered my mind that you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The picture must not be shown. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for telling you this."}

{"request_id":"cad10be38ea2342e80247e1d","rewritten_text":"The studio was full of the rich scent of roses. When the light summer wind moved through the garden trees, the heavy smell of lilac, or the gentler perfume of the pink-flowering thorn, drifted in through the open door.

From the corner of the Persian saddlebag divan where he lay smoking his usual endless cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could just see the honey-colored, honey-sweet flowers of a laburnum. Its trembling branches seemed barely able to carry such flame-like beauty. Now and then, the strange shadows of flying birds passed over the long tussore-silk curtains hanging before the huge window. They created a brief Japanese effect and made him think of the pale, jade-faced painters of Tokyo, who use an art that cannot move to suggest speed and motion. The dull buzzing of bees pushing through the tall, uncut grass, or circling stubbornly around the dusty golden horns of the wandering woodbine, seemed to make the silence heavier. The distant rumble of London sounded like the low note of a faraway organ.

In the middle of the room, fixed to a tall easel, stood a full-length portrait of a remarkably handsome young man. A short distance in front of it sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance several years earlier had caused great public excitement and led to many strange guesses.

As the painter studied the graceful, beautiful figure he had so skillfully captured in his art, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to remain there. But he suddenly rose, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers against his lids, as if trying to hold inside his mind some strange dream from which he feared he might wake.

“It is your finest work, Basil—the best thing you have ever done,” said Lord Henry lazily. “You must certainly send it next year to the Grosvenor. The Academy is too large and too vulgar. Whenever I have gone there, either there have been so many people that I could not see the pictures, which was terrible, or so many pictures that I could not see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, throwing his head back in that odd manner that had once made his friends laugh at him at Oxford."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d5bc36547b7bcc7ef32bec69","rewritten_text":"So the ringmaster made a short speech. He said he hoped there would be no trouble, and that if the man promised not to cause any more, he would let him ride, if he thought he could stay on the horse. Everyone laughed and agreed, and the man climbed on. The moment he was mounted, the horse began to buck, rear, and leap wildly. Two circus men clung to its bridle, trying to hold it, while the drunk man hung onto its neck, his heels flying up with every jump. The whole crowd stood shouting and laughing until tears ran down their faces. At last, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse broke free and raced around the ring like mad. The drunk man lay across it, clinging to its neck, with one leg nearly dragging on one side, then the other leg on the other side, while the crowd went wild. It wasn’t funny to me; I trembled to see how much danger he was in. But soon he struggled upright, astride the horse, and seized the bridle, swaying from side to side. The next moment he sprang up, dropped the bridle, and stood! The horse was still racing like a house on fire. He stood there, sailing around as easily and comfortably as if he had never been drunk in his life. Then he began pulling off his clothes and throwing them away. He shed them so quickly that they seemed to clog the air, and altogether he removed seventeen suits. Then there he was, slim and handsome, dressed in the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you ever saw. He attacked the horse with his whip and made it hum, then finally leaped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing room. Everyone was howling with delight and amazement.\n\nThen the ringmaster realized how completely he had been fooled, and he was the sickest-looking ringmaster you ever saw, I reckon. Why, the man was one of his own performers! He had planned the whole joke himself and had told nobody. I felt foolish enough to have been taken in, but I wouldn’t have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. I don’t know; there may be better circuses than that one, but I have never found them. Anyway, it was more than good enough for me, and wherever I come across it, it can have all my business every time."}

As our wedding day drew near, whether from cowardice or some prophetic feeling, I felt my heart sink. Yet I hid my feelings behind a show of cheerfulness that brought smiles and happiness to my father’s face, though it scarcely deceived Elizabeth’s ever-watchful, perceptive eyes. She looked forward to our marriage with calm contentment, mixed with a little fear born of past misfortunes: the happiness that now seemed certain and real might soon vanish like a dream, leaving behind only deep and lasting regret.

Preparations were made, congratulatory visitors arrived, and everything appeared cheerful. I kept the anxiety eating at my heart as hidden as I could and joined my father’s plans with apparent sincerity, though they might serve only as decorations for my tragedy. Through my father’s efforts, the Austrian government had returned part of Elizabeth’s inheritance to her. She owned a small estate on the shores of Lake Como. We agreed that immediately after our marriage we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend our first happy days beside the beautiful lake.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to protect myself if the fiend attacked me openly. I constantly carried pistols and a dagger, and remained alert against any trick. These measures gave me some peace. Indeed, as the day approached, the threat seemed more like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing me, while the happiness I expected from marriage seemed increasingly certain. The wedding was spoken of so often as an event that no accident could prevent that I began to believe it so.

{"request_id":"9ed9dbf0e1cf1efbbdb7b791","rewritten_text":"But I wonder how long you would have continued, if you had been left to yourself. I wonder when you would have spoken if I had not asked you! My decision to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had a powerful effect. Too powerful, I fear; for what becomes of the moral if our happiness comes from a broken promise, since I ought not to have mentioned the subject? This will never do.”

“You need not trouble yourself. The moral will be entirely sound. Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable efforts to separate us were what removed all my doubts. I do not owe my present happiness to your eager wish to express your gratitude. I was not in the mood to wait for you to begin. My aunt’s information had given me hope, and I was determined to learn everything at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been immensely useful, which ought to please her, since she loves being useful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and feel embarrassed? Or had you intended something more serious?”

“My true purpose was to see you and judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope to make you love me. My declared purpose—or the one I admitted to myself—was to see whether your sister still cared for Bingley and, if she did, to make the confession to him that I have since made.”

“Will you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is going to happen to her?”

“I am more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. But it must be done; and if you will give me a sheet of paper, I shall do it immediately.”

“And if I did not have a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire the steadiness of your handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt as well, who must not be neglected any longer.”

Because she was unwilling to admit how greatly she had exaggerated her intimacy with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter. But now she had something to tell her that she knew would be most welcome, and she was almost ashamed to realize that her uncle and aunt had already lost three days of happiness. She immediately wrote as follows:—

“I should have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, as I ought, for your long, kind, and satisfying account of everything; but, to tell the truth, I was too cross to write. You imagined more than truly existed. But now imagine as much as you please; let your fancy run free and indulge your imagination in every direction the subject allows, and unless you believe me actually married, you cannot be very far wrong."}

{"request_id":"a1c08ee1c025d80ba42d179b","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind her, except the memory that such things had existed.

Anne had not entered Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and on the few occasions when it might have been possible for her to go to the Hall, she had managed to avoid and escape it. Her first return was to take up her place in the Lodge’s modern, elegant rooms and delight its mistress.

Some anxiety mingled with Lady Russell’s joy at seeing her. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. But fortunately, either Anne had improved in fullness and appearance, or Lady Russell imagined that she had; and as Anne accepted her compliments, she enjoyed connecting them with her cousin’s silent admiration and hoped she might be blessed with a second spring of youth and beauty.

When they began to talk, Anne soon became aware of a change in her mind. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, and that she had felt neglected and been forced to suppress among the Musgroves, had now become matters of secondary importance. She had lately even lost sight of her father, her sister, and Bath. Their concerns had been overwhelmed by those of Uppercross; and when Lady Russell returned to their former hopes and fears, expressing her satisfaction with the house in Camden Place that had been taken and her regret that Mrs Clay should still remain with them, Anne would have been ashamed to admit how much more she was thinking of Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her acquaintances there; how much more interesting to her were the home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick than her father’s house in Camden Place or her sister’s intimacy with Mrs Clay. She was actually obliged to make an effort to meet Lady Russell with anything resembling equal concern on subjects that naturally had the first claim upon her.

At first, there was some awkwardness when they spoke of another subject. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had been at the house scarcely five minutes the previous day when a complete account of it had burst upon her; but it still had to be discussed. She had to make enquiries, regret the imprudence, lament the outcome, and Captain Wentworth’s name had to be mentioned by both of them. Anne knew she did not manage it as well as Lady Russell. She could not say the name and look directly into Lady Russell’s eyes until she had adopted the expedient of briefly telling her what she thought of the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"eb896d4d82c26b4fdf736c0b","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s feelings had overcome her self-interest, and for the young man’s sake she had given up the chance to scheme any longer for Sir Walter. She has abilities as well as feelings, however, and it is still uncertain whether his cleverness or hers will win in the end; whether, after stopping her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may not finally be persuaded and charmed into making her the wife of Sir William.

There was no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and humiliated by losing their companion and discovering that she had deceived them. They could, of course, turn to their distinguished cousins for comfort; but they would long feel that flattering and following others, without being flattered and followed themselves, offered only half the pleasure.

Anne, having learned early that Lady Russell intended to love Captain Wentworth as she ought, had only one shadow over the happiness she expected: she knew she had no relations to offer him whom a sensible man could value. She felt her own inferiority very deeply in this respect. The difference in their fortunes meant nothing to her and caused not a moment’s regret. But she had no family who could properly welcome and appreciate him—nothing respectable, harmonious, or warm to offer in return for the worth and immediate kindness she had found in his brothers and sisters. This caused her as much pain as she could feel in circumstances otherwise filled with happiness. She had only two friends in the world to add to his circle: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. He was, however, very willing to become attached to them. Despite all her former mistakes, he could now value Lady Russell sincerely. He was not required to admit that she had been right to separate them at first, but he was ready to say almost everything else in her favour. As for Mrs Smith, she had many claims that quickly and permanently recommended her to him.

Anne’s recent kindness to her would have been enough on its own, and their marriage, instead of taking away one friend, gave her two. She was the first to visit them after they had settled into married life. Captain Wentworth also fully repaid everything she had done, or ever intended to do, for his wife. He helped her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies by writing letters, taking action on her behalf, and guiding her through every minor difficulty with the energy of a fearless man and a determined friend."}

{"request_id":"bb507f611ea4c557167789bd","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost completed their cycle. It was now the end of May; the woods were dressed in their freshest green, and the sweet scent of newly mown grass filled the fields. I thought the gentle air and Nature’s lovely face might help awaken mild sensations in him, and inspire peaceful, loving feelings before I sought the confidence I was determined to gain from him.

I therefore chose the evening of one of those days for my attempt. I invited him to walk with me and led him to a nearby beech wood, whose light shade protected us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After walking in silence for some time, I sat with him on a mossy hillock. It is strange, but even now I seem to see the place: many of the slender, smooth trunks were wrapped in ivy, whose shining, deepest-green leaves contrasted with the white bark and the pale leaves of the young beech shoots growing from their parent trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss and partly covered by the dead leaves of the previous autumn, which the winds had gathered here and there into little mounds. A few moss-covered stumps stood nearby. The leaves stirred gently in the breeze, and through their green canopy one could see the bright blue sky. As evening approached, the distant trunks were reddened by the sun, and the wind died completely, while a few birds flew past us toward their evening rest.

It was here that we sat together. When you hear all that happened—all that terrible suffering that tore our souls even in this peaceful place, which might have been a paradise for us but for those strange passions—you will not wonder that I remember it as I looked upon it, hoping its calm would give me calm and inspire me not only with courage but with persuasive words. I saw all these things and absently recorded them in my mind while trying to arrange my thoughts in the proper order for my attempt. My heart beat rapidly as I gathered the strength to speak to him. I was determined not to be rejected, yet I trembled to imagine what effect my words might have on him. At last, after much hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness toward me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—you showed me when you first returned will, I hope, excuse me in your eyes for daring to speak to you, though with the tender affection of a daughter, yet also with the freedom of a friend and an equal.”"}

{"request_id":"c72c32c6039da19bd5774a0b","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends—a secret he had cherished from his earliest years. Although he loved his fellow students, he would not entrust it to the delicacy or sympathy of any one of them. He was in love. He feared that the intensity of his passion might become an object of their ridicule, and he could not bear for them to profane it by treating as trivial and temporary what he felt to be the very life of his life.

A gentleman of modest means lived near his family home and had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty was merely an addition to her other qualities: her understanding was clear and strong, and her nature angelically gentle. She and my father had been playmates from infancy. Diana had been a favorite of his mother even as a child, and that partiality grew as the beautiful, lively girl matured. Thus, during his school and college vacations, they were constantly together. Novels, and all the other ways by which young people in civilized society are introduced to the existence of passion before they truly feel it, had deeply affected him, for he was unusually susceptible to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his favorite playmate, but he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older than he, her upbringing had left her more childish, at least in her understanding and expression of feeling. She received his ardent declarations innocently and returned them without knowing what they meant. She had read no novels and associated only with her younger sisters; what could she know of the difference between love and friendship? And when the growth of her understanding revealed the true nature of their relationship, her affections were already devoted to her friend. All she feared was that other attractions or fickleness might lead him to break the vows of his childhood.

But each day they became more ardent and tender. It was a passion that had grown with him; it had become woven into every faculty and feeling, and could end only with his life. No one knew of their love except their two hearts. Yet although he feared his companions’ judgment in all things, and even in this—because he truly loved someone beneath him in fortune—nothing could for a moment shake his resolve to unite himself with her as soon as he could gather enough courage to face the difficulties he was determined to overcome.

Diana was entirely worthy of his deepest affection."}

“Our little friend Harriet Smith, too, is just the same sort of pretty young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very glad to hear it—but Jane Fairfax alone is known to be so remarkably accomplished and superior!—and precisely Emma’s age.”

This subject was discussed with great satisfaction, and others of equal importance followed, all passing with the same good agreement; but the evening did not end without a slight return of uneasiness. The gruel arrived and furnished abundant conversation—much praise and many observations—an unquestioning declaration of its wholesomeness for every constitution, and rather sharp Philippics against the many houses where it was never made tolerably;—but, unfortunately, among the failures which the daughter was obliged to mention, the latest, and therefore most conspicuous, was her own cook at South End, a young woman engaged temporarily, who had never been able to understand what she meant by a basin of nice, smooth gruel, thin, though not too thin. However often she had desired and ordered it, she had never obtained anything tolerable. Here was a perilous opening.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern.—The ejaculation in Emma’s ear conveyed, “Ah! there is no end to the sad consequences of your going to South End. It is not a subject to be discussed.” For a little while she hoped he would not pursue it, and that silent reflection might be enough to restore him to his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After several minutes, however, he began,

“I shall always be very sorry that you went to the sea this autumn, instead of coming here.”

“But why should you be sorry, sir?—I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you were obliged to go to the sea, it would have been better not to choose South End. South End is an unhealthy place. Perry was surprised to hear that you had settled on South End.”

“I know many people have that notion, but it is really quite a mistake, sir.—We all remained perfectly well there, and never suffered the least inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield says it is wholly mistaken to suppose the place unhealthy; and I am sure he can be relied on, for he thoroughly understands the nature of the air, and his own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere.—Perry spent a week at Cromer once, and considers it the finest of all the sea-bathing places."}

“Tell me what it is.”

Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of my fate—for I cannot write—and if I could, how could I tell her? It is better as it is.”

“Yes, yes: better as it is.”

“What I have been thinking as we came along, and what I am still thinking now, as I look into your kind, strong face, which gives me so much support, is this: If the Republic truly helps the poor, and they become less hungry and suffer less in every way, she may live a long time; she may even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“It cannot be, my child; there is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much! I am so ignorant. Am I to kiss you now? Has the moment come?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers; they solemnly bless each other. His free hand does not tremble as he releases hers; nothing worse than a sweet, bright constancy appears in his patient face. She goes before him next—is gone; the knitting-women count Twenty-Two.

{"request_id":"c4a2c57b4039644a0f5cc030","rewritten_text":"If I cannot live on that, I shall not ask anyone to give me a lift. Is that satisfactory?”

A tremendous roar of applause followed, and from its midst the king’s voice rang out:

“Remove his bonds and set him free! Let high and low, rich and poor, pay him homage, for he has become the king’s right hand, is clothed in power and authority, and sits upon the throne’s highest step! Now sweep away this creeping night and restore the light and cheer, that all the world may bless thee.”

But I said:

“That a common man should be shamed before the world is nothing; but it would dishonor the _king_ if anyone who saw his minister naked did not also see him freed from his shame. If I might ask that my clothes be brought back—”

“They are not suitable,” the king interrupted. “Fetch garments of another kind; dress him as a prince!”

My plan had succeeded. I wished to leave matters as they stood until the eclipse became total, since otherwise they would try again to make me banish the darkness, and naturally I could not do that. Sending for the clothes bought some time, but not enough. I therefore needed another excuse. I said it would be only natural for the king to change his mind and regret, in some measure, what he had done in his excitement; so I would allow the darkness to deepen for a while, and if, after a reasonable interval, the king still held to his decision, the darkness would be dismissed. Neither the king nor anyone else approved of this arrangement, but I had to insist upon it.

It grew steadily darker and blacker while I wrestled with those inconvenient sixth-century clothes. At last it became completely dark, and the crowd groaned in terror as the cold, uncanny night winds moved through the place and the stars appeared, glittering overhead. Finally the eclipse was total, and I was delighted, though everyone else was miserable; which was only natural. I said:

“The king, by remaining silent, still stands by the terms.” Then I raised my hands and held them so for a moment; then, with the most terrible solemnity, I said: “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass away harmlessly!”

For a moment there was no answer, amid that profound darkness and cemetery-like silence. But when the sun’s silver rim emerged a moment or two later, the assembly erupted in a mighty shout and came rushing down like a flood, smothering me with blessings and gratitude; and Clarence was certainly not the last of the deluge."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c6f77d595f1c2f119b66c481","rewritten_text":"“But, in fact, once we have risen to any given altitude, the amount of air overcome by rising still farther is by no means proportional to the additional height climbed (as can plainly be seen from what was stated earlier), but follows a continually diminishing ratio. It is therefore clear that, however high we may ascend, we cannot, strictly speaking, reach a boundary beyond which no atmosphere exists. It must continue, I argued, though perhaps in a state of infinite rarefaction.\n\n“On the other hand, I knew that arguments had been advanced to prove the existence of a real and definite limit to the atmosphere, beyond which there is absolutely no air. Yet one circumstance, overlooked by those who maintained such a limit, seemed to me—though not a positive refutation of their belief—nevertheless worthy of the most serious investigation. When the intervals between Encke’s comet’s successive arrivals at perihelion are compared, after allowing with the greatest accuracy for all disturbances caused by the planets, the periods appear gradually to diminish; that is, the major axis of the comet’s ellipse is slowly but steadily growing shorter. Now this is exactly what should occur if the comet encountered resistance from an extremely rare ethereal medium filling the regions of its orbit. Such a medium, by slowing the comet’s velocity, must increase its centripetal force by weakening its centrifugal force. In other words, the sun’s attraction would continually gain strength, and the comet would be drawn closer at every revolution. Indeed, there is no other way to explain the variation in question. But again: the actual diameter of this comet’s nebulosity is observed to contract rapidly as it approaches the sun, and to expand just as rapidly as it travels away toward its aphelion. Was I not justified, with M. Valz, in supposing that this apparent condensation of volume arose from compression by the same ethereal medium I have already mentioned, which becomes denser in proportion to its nearness to the sun? The lenticular phenomenon also called the zodiacal light deserved attention. This radiance, so conspicuous in the tropics and impossible to mistake for any meteoric glow, extends obliquely upward from the horizon and generally follows the direction of the sun’s equator. It seemed to me clearly to be a rare atmosphere extending outward from the sun, at least beyond Venus’s orbit, and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not suppose this medium confined to the comet’s elliptical path or to the sun’s immediate neighborhood.”"}

{"request_id":"3a1091782ed6c70f9dee5c46","rewritten_text":"Her situation was truly one of extraordinary trial and difficulty. Though she felt the strongest, most urgent desire to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s history, she could not betray the confidence placed in her by the wretched woman with whom she had just spoken, who had trusted her as a young and innocent girl. The woman’s words and manner had touched Rose Maylie’s heart; and, joined to her love for her young charge, and scarcely less sincere or fervent, was her earnest wish to bring the outcast back to repentance and hope.

They intended to remain in London for only three days before leaving for several weeks in a distant part of the coast. It was now midnight on the first day. What action could she decide upon that might be carried out within forty-eight hours? Or how could she delay the journey without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them and would remain for the next two days; but Rose knew the excellent gentleman’s impulsive nature too well, and could too clearly foresee the anger with which, in the first burst of his indignation, he would view the person responsible for Oliver’s recapture, to entrust him with the secret while no experienced person was present to support her arguments on the girl’s behalf. These considerations made the greatest caution and discretion necessary in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first instinct would certainly be to consult the worthy doctor about the matter. Seeking legal advice, even had she known how to do so, was hardly possible for the same reason. For a moment she thought of asking Harry for help; but this brought back the memory of their last parting, and it seemed unworthy of her to summon him when—tears rising to her eyes as she followed the thought—he might by now have learned to forget her and be happier away.

Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, leaning first toward one course and then another, and shrinking from each as new considerations arose, Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. After further reflection the next day, she reached the desperate decision to consult Harry.

“If it pains him to return here,” she thought, “how much more it will pain me! But perhaps he will not come; he may write, or he may come in person and carefully avoid seeing me—he did so when he left. I scarcely expected it; but it was better for both of us.” At this point Rose let the pen fall and turned away, as though the very paper that would carry her message must not witness her tears."}

{"request_id":"4f05e10462f3aa34c68ae686","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed ourselves freemen so loudly and earnestly that we drew the interested attention of the liberty-preaching orator and his patriotic crowd. They gathered around us and took up a very determined stance. The orator said:

“If you are truly freemen, you have nothing to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain surround you as shield and shelter!” (Applause.) “You shall soon see. Produce your proof.”

“What proof?”

“Proof that you are freemen.”

Ah—I remembered! I came to my senses and said nothing. But the king burst out:

“You’re insane, man. It would be more reasonable for this thief and scoundrel here to prove that we are _not_ freemen.”

You see, he knew his own laws as other people so often know laws: by their words, not their effects. They take on a _meaning_ and become very vivid when you have to apply them to yourself.

Everyone shook his head and looked disappointed; some turned away, no longer interested. The orator said—and this time in the tones of business, not sentiment:

“If you do not know your country’s laws, it is time you learned them. You are strangers to us; you will not deny that. You may be freemen—we do not deny it—but you may also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove that you are slaves; it requires you to prove that you are not.”

I said:

“Dear sir, give us only time to send to Astolat; or give us only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you cannot expect them to be granted. It would take much time and cause your master unreasonable inconvenience—”

“_Master_, idiot!” the king stormed. “I have no master; I myself am the m—”

“Silence, for God’s sake!”

I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in enough trouble; it could not help us to give these people the idea that we were lunatics.

There is no point in dragging out the details. The earl housed us and sold us at auction. That same infernal law had existed in our own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later, and under it hundreds of freemen who could not prove they were freemen had been sold into lifelong slavery without making any particular impression on me. But the moment the law and auction block entered my personal experience, something that had merely seemed improper became suddenly hellish. Well, that is how we are made.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like swine. In a large town with an active market, we should have brought a good price; but this place was utterly stagnant, and we were sold for a figure that shames me whenever I think of it."}

{"request_id":"36ed5eb85c518785f20df116","rewritten_text":"On that subject, therefore, I shall remain entirely silent; and you may be assured that, once we are married, no ungenerous reproach shall ever escape me.”

It was now absolutely necessary to stop him.

“You are too hasty, sir,” she exclaimed. “You forget that I have given no answer. Let me do so without further delay. Accept my thanks for the compliment you offer me. I am very sensible of the honour of your proposals, but it is impossible for me to do anything but refuse them.”

“I am not now to be informed,” replied Mr. Collins, with a formal gesture of the hand, “that it is customary for young ladies to reject the addresses of the man they secretly intend to accept when he first seeks their favour; and that the refusal is sometimes repeated a second, or even a third, time. I am therefore not at all discouraged by what you have just said, and shall hope to conduct you to the altar before long.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “your hope is a most extraordinary one after my declaration. I assure you that I am not one of those young ladies (if any such exist) who are bold enough to risk their happiness on the possibility of being asked a second time. I am entirely serious in my refusal. You could not make _me_ happy, and I am convinced that I am the last woman in the world who could make _you_ so. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am persuaded she would consider me wholly unfit for the position.”

“Were it certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins, very gravely—“but I cannot suppose that her Ladyship would disapprove of you in the least. And you may be sure that, when I have the honour of seeing her again, I shall speak in the strongest terms of your modesty, economy, and other agreeable qualities.”

“Indeed, Mr. Collins, all commendation of me will be needless. You must allow me to judge for myself, and do me the compliment of believing what I say. I wish you every happiness and great wealth, and by refusing your hand, do everything in my power to keep you from being otherwise. In making me this offer, you must have satisfied the delicacy of your feelings toward my family, and may take possession of the Longbourn estate whenever it falls to you without any self-reproach. This matter may therefore be regarded as finally settled.” As she spoke, she rose and would have left the room, had not Mr. Collins addressed her in this manner—

“When I have the honour of speaking to you again on this subject, I shall hope to receive a more favourable answer than the one you have now given me; though I am far from accusing you of cruelty at present, since I know it to be the established custom of your sex to reject a man upon his first application, and perhaps you have even now said as much as would encourage my suit while remaining consistent with the true delicacy of the female character.”"}

{"request_id":"a42ea76b92be2efb6103538c","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was deeply upset by the marriage being postponed for a second time, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding dress, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. But although Sybil loved her mother dearly, she had placed her whole life in Lord Arthur’s hands, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith. Lord Arthur himself took days to recover from his terrible disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely shattered. Soon, however, his excellent common sense returned, and his practical mind quickly decided what he must do. Since poison had failed completely, dynamite, or some other explosive, was clearly the next thing to try.

He therefore reviewed the list of his friends and relatives once more and, after careful thought, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a highly educated man who loved clocks and possessed a remarkable collection of timepieces, dating from the fifteenth century to the present. Lord Arthur felt that this hobby gave him an excellent chance to carry out his plan. Finding an explosive device, of course, was another matter entirely. The London Directory offered no help, and he thought there was little point in asking Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about the dynamite faction’s activities until after an explosion—and not much even then.

Then he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strongly revolutionary views, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a life of Peter the Great and to have come to England to study documents about the Tsar’s time there as a ship carpenter. But people generally suspected that he was a Nihilist agent, and it was certain that the Russian Embassy did not welcome his presence in London. Lord Arthur thought he was exactly the man he needed, and one morning drove to his lodgings in Bloomsbury to ask for his advice and help.

‘So you are taking politics seriously?’ Count Rouvaloff said after Lord Arthur explained why he had come. But Lord Arthur disliked boasting of any kind, and felt obliged to admit that he had no interest at all in social questions. He wanted the explosive device only for a private family matter, in which no one but himself was involved."}

{"request_id":"019eaa7e587a4a3a64a8685d","rewritten_text":"Then I repeated to myself that beautiful passage describing Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise, and thought how sweet it would be, as I wandered along those lovely banks, to see the chariot of light descend with my long-lost parent, restored at last to me. As I waited in expectation of that moment, I imagined that, from the beautiful flowers growing there, I would weave a wreath and crown myself for joy. I would sing _sul margine d’un rio_, my father’s favourite song, and my voice, drifting through the still air, would tell him, wherever he sat awaiting our reunion, that his daughter had come. Then the mark of misery would have vanished from my brow, and I would lift my eyes without fear to meet his, which always shone with the gentle radiance of innocent love. When I thought of the magical expression in those deep eyes, I wept, but softly, lest my sobs disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely absorbed in this reverie that I continued walking without noticing where my feet carried me. I actually bent down to pick a flower for my wreath on that barren plain, where no flower grew, before awakening from my daydream and discovering that I had no idea where I was.

The sun had set, and the rosy colour it had cast upon the clouds during its descent had almost faded. A wind swept across the plain. I looked around and saw nothing that could tell me where I was; I had lost my way and tried in vain to find the path. I wandered on, while the gathering darkness blurred every trace that might have guided me. At last everything was hidden beneath the profound darkness of night. I grew tired, and, knowing that my servant was to sleep that night in the neighbouring village, so that my absence would alarm no one, and that in this wild place I was safe from every intruder, I resolved to spend the night where I was. Indeed, I was too weary to walk farther. The air was cold, but I paid no attention to the discomfort, thinking myself well accustomed to the weather after two years of solitude, during which no change of season had interrupted my continual wanderings.

I lay on the grass, surrounded by darkness that no faint ray of light penetrated. There was no sound, for the deep night had lulled the insects to sleep—the only creatures living in that lonely place, where no tree or shrub could shelter anything else. A wondrous silence filled the air, calming my senses while stirring my soul. My mind rushed from one image to another and seemed to grasp eternity."}

{"request_id":"f71cde4f8f54e10e62b0ed3c","rewritten_text":"“Do you often return?”

“I have never been here since.”

“Nor have I.”

The moon started to rise, and I thought of the calm expression on the white ceiling, which had vanished. The moon started to rise, and I remembered the pressure of my hand when I had spoken the final words he had heard on earth.

Estella was the first to break the silence that had fallen between us.

“I have often wished and meant to come back, but many circumstances have kept me away. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the moon’s first rays, and those same rays touched the tears falling from her eyes. Unaware that I saw them, and quietly striving to master them, she said,—

“Were you wondering, as you came along, how it happened to be left in this state?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground is mine. It is the one possession I have not surrendered. Everything else has slipped away from me, little by little, but I have held on to this. It was the subject of the only firm resistance I made throughout all those miserable years.”

“Is it going to be built upon?”

“At last, it is. I came here to say farewell before it is changed. And you,” she said, with a voice of touching concern for a wanderer,—“you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And prosper, I am sure?”

“I work fairly hard for enough to live on, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought about you,” said Estella.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long and difficult time when I kept away from me the memory of what I had cast aside while wholly unaware of its value. But since my duty no longer prevented me from admitting that memory, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have always kept your place in mine,” I replied.

Again we were silent, until she spoke.

“I scarcely imagined,” said Estella, “that in saying farewell to this place I would also say farewell to you. I am very glad to do so.”

“Glad to part once more, Estella? To me, parting is painful. To me, the memory of our last separation has always been sorrowful and painful.”

“But you said to me,” Estella answered, with great earnestness, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that to me then, you will not be unwilling to say it now,—now, when suffering has been a stronger teacher than anything else, and has taught me to understand what your heart once was. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better form.”"}
