{"request_id":"5e5e1fc6f2f24f3495d5a9e5","rewritten_text":"Good heavens, she was a masterful talker. It would not have been proper for me to suggest that it was very late, that I was tired, and that I was desperately sleepy. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to endure it; there was no other choice. So she went on and on, her voice tinkling through the otherwise profound, ghostly silence of the sleeping castle, until at last there came, as though from far beneath us, a distant sound like a muffled shriek—with such agony in it that my flesh crawled. The queen stopped, and pleasure lit her eyes; she tilted her graceful head as a bird does when listening. Again the sound forced its way upward through the stillness.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a truly stubborn soul, and has endured long. It has been many hours now.”

“Endured what?”

“The rack. Come—you shall see a cheerful sight. If he does not yield his secret now, you shall see him torn apart.”

What a smooth, silky hellion she was; and how calm and serene she remained, while the cords running down my legs ached in sympathy with that man’s suffering. Escorted by armored guards carrying blazing torches, we marched along echoing corridors and down stone stairways, damp and dripping, smelling of mold and centuries of imprisoned darkness—a cold, uncanny journey, and a long one, made neither shorter nor more pleasant by the sorceress’s conversation, which concerned the prisoner and his crime. He had been accused by an anonymous informer of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony is not really sufficient, Your Highness. It would be fairer to confront the accused with his accuser.”

“I had not considered that, since it is of little importance. But even if I wished to, I could not, because the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, and immediately departed again, so the forester does not know him.”

“Then this Unknown is the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Indeed, no man saw the killing, but this Unknown saw the bold wretch near the place where the stag lay, and came with loyal zeal to betray him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag as well? Is it not possible that he killed it himself? His loyal zeal—in a mask—seems just a little suspicious. But what does Your Highness hope to gain by racking the prisoner? Where is the benefit?”

“He will not confess otherwise, and then his soul would be lost. By law, his life is forfeited for his crime—and I will certainly see that he pays for it!—but it would endanger my own soul to let him die without confession or absolution.”"}

{"request_id":"7bc27e1bcd4aa499720c856a","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it and was preparing to start on the bureau when he was called away to dress for Sunday school.

Mary gave him a tin basin of water and a piece of soap. He went outside the door, set the basin on a small bench, dipped the soap in the water, and put it down. He rolled up his sleeves, gently poured the water onto the ground, then went into the kitchen and began diligently wiping his face on the towel behind the door. But Mary took away the towel and said:

“Now aren’t you ashamed, Tom? You mustn’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was somewhat unsettled. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it for a while, gathering his courage. He drew a deep breath and began. When he soon entered the kitchen, both eyes shut and feeling around for the towel, an honorable evidence of soap and water dripped from his face. But when he emerged from the towel, he still was not satisfactory, because the clean area ended at his chin and jaws like a mask. Below and beyond that line stretched a dark expanse of untouched soil, running down his front and around the back of his neck. Mary took charge of him, and when she finished, he was a man and a brother, with no distinction of color. His soaked hair was neatly brushed, its short curls arranged into a delicate, symmetrical whole. [He privately flattened the curls, with effort and difficulty, and plastered his hair close to his head, because he considered curls effeminate, and his own made his life bitter.] Then Mary brought out a suit of clothes that had been worn only on Sundays for two years—they were simply called his “other clothes”—which tells us the size of his wardrobe. After he dressed, the girl “put him to rights”: she buttoned his tidy roundabout to his chin, folded his enormous shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and crowned him with his speckled straw hat. He now looked greatly improved and uncomfortable. He was every bit as uncomfortable as he looked, because the confinement of complete clothing and cleanliness irritated him. He hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that hope failed; as was customary, she thoroughly coated them with tallow and brought them out. He lost his temper and said he was always being forced to do everything he did not want to do."}

{"request_id":"5cfe1156780b3ce708a02a9d","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what is wrong now? How is your master?”

“To tell de troof, massa, him not berry well as he mought be.”

“Not well! I am truly sorry to hear that. What does he complain of?”

“Dar! Dat’s it! Him neber complain of notin’—but him berry sick all de same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so at once? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, dat he aint! He aint confined nowhar—that’s just whar de shoe pinch. My mind is berry heavy ’bout poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I should like to understand what you mean. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what is wrong with him?”

“Why, massa, ’taint worth getting mad about—Massa Will say there aint nothin’ wrong wid him—but den what make him go about looking dis way, wid he head down and he shoulders up, and as white as a goose? And den he keep a cipher all de time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a cipher wid de figures on de slate—de strangest figures I ever did see. Ise getting scared, I tell you. Hab for to keep a mighty close eye ’pon him always. T’other day he gave me de slip before sunrise and was gone de whole blessed day. I had a big stick cut and ready to give him a very good beating when he came back—but Ise such a fool dat I hadn’t de heart after all—he looked so berry poorly.”

“Eh? What? Ah, yes! On the whole, I think you had better not be too hard on the poor fellow. Don’t flog him, Jupiter—he can’t stand it very well. But can you form no idea what caused this illness, or rather this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, dey aint bin nothin’ unpleasant since den—’twas before den, I fear—’twas de very day you was dare.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, massa, I mean de bug—dare now.”

“The what?”

“De bug—I’m berry certain Massa Will was bitten somewhere ’bout de head by dat gold-bug.”

“And what reason have you, Jupiter, for such a belief?”

“Claws enough, massa, and a mouth too. I never did see such a devilish bug—he kicked and bit everything that came near him. Massa Will caught him first, but had to let him go again mighty quick, I tell you—that must have been when he got bitten. I didn’t like de look of de bug’s mouth myself, nohow, so I wouldn’t take hold of him wid my fingers, but I caught him with a piece of paper dat I found.”"}

{"request_id":"46bf51a01c7e04e78b51f4a8","rewritten_text":"To look at a star in brief, sideways glances—to turn the outer parts of the retina toward it, which are more sensitive to faint light than the inner parts—is to see the star clearly and appreciate its brightness best. That brightness fades as soon as we look directly at it. More rays reach the eye in the second case, but the first gives us a finer ability to understand what we see. Too much depth can confuse and weaken thought; even Venus can disappear from the sky if we examine it too steadily, intensely, or directly.

“As for these murders, let us investigate them ourselves before forming an opinion. An inquiry will amuse us,” [I thought this an odd word to use, but said nothing] “and, besides, Le Bon once did me a service for which I am grateful. We will see the place with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and can easily obtain the necessary permission.”

The permission was obtained, and we went at once to the Rue Morgue. It is one of those miserable streets between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. We reached it late in the afternoon, since this area was far from where we lived. The house was easy to find; many people were still staring at its closed shutters with pointless curiosity from across the street. It was an ordinary Parisian house, with a gateway and, beside it, a glass watch-box with a sliding window panel, marking the concierge’s lodge. Before entering, we walked up the street, turned into an alley, and then turned again to pass behind the building. All the while, Dupin examined the entire neighborhood and the house with such careful attention that I could see no purpose in it.

We retraced our steps, returned to the front of the house, rang, and showed our credentials. The officers in charge admitted us. We went upstairs to the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found, and where both bodies still lay. As usual, the room had been left in disorder. I saw nothing beyond what had been reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin examined everything, including the victims’ bodies. We then went through the other rooms and into the yard, with a gendarme accompanying us the entire time."}

content.text: {"request_id":"bc1a51519827897d42e0d5d6","rewritten_text":"Deprived of ordinary resources, the analyst enters the mind of his opponent, identifies with him, and often sees at once the only ways—sometimes absurdly simple ones—in which he can lure him into error or rush him into miscalculation.\n\nWhist has long been recognized for its effect on what is called the calculating faculty; and men of the highest intellect have been known to take an apparently inexplicable delight in it while dismissing chess as frivolous. Certainly, nothing of a similar kind places so great a demand upon the power of analysis. The finest chess player in Christendom may be little more than the finest player of chess; but skill at whist implies an ability to succeed in all those more important undertakings in which one mind contends with another. By skill, I mean perfection in the game that includes an understanding of every source from which legitimate advantage may be gained. These sources are not only numerous but varied, and often lie in regions of thought entirely inaccessible to ordinary understanding. To observe attentively is to remember clearly; and in this respect the focused chess player will do very well at whist, while Hoyle’s rules—which are themselves based on the game’s simple mechanics—are generally easy enough to understand. Thus a retentive memory and playing “by the book” are commonly considered the whole of good play. But the analyst’s skill appears in matters beyond the limits of mere rules. He silently makes countless observations and deductions. His companions may do the same; the difference in the amount of information gained lies less in the soundness of the deduction than in the quality of the observation. The essential knowledge is knowing what to observe. Our player limits himself in no way; and because the game is his object, he does not dismiss deductions drawn from things outside it. He studies his partner’s face, comparing it carefully with the faces of each opponent. He considers how the cards are arranged in every hand, often counting trump by trump and honor by honor through the glances their holders cast at one another. He notices every change of expression as play proceeds, drawing a wealth of information from differences in the signs of certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered, he judges whether the player who takes it can win another in that suit. He recognizes a feint by the manner in which the card is laid upon the table. A casual or careless word; the accidental dropping or turning of a card, together with the anxiety or indifference shown about hiding it; the counting of tricks and the order in which they are arranged; embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or fear—all provide his seemingly intuitive perception with clues to the true state of affairs."}

{"request_id":"af46cb5710d38848517c9533","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers released Lord Arthur’s right hand and grasped his left, stooping so far over it that the gold rims of his spectacles appeared almost to brush the palm. For an instant his face turned into a white mask of terror, but he quickly regained his _sang-froid_, and, looking up at Lady Windermere, said with an artificial smile, ‘It is the hand of a charming young man.

‘Of course it is!’ replied Lady Windermere, ‘but will he make a charming husband? That is what I wish to discover.’

‘All charming young men do,’ said Mr. Podgers.

‘I don’t believe a husband ought to be too fascinating,’ murmured Lady Jedburgh thoughtfully; ‘it is so dangerous.’

‘My dear child, they are never too fascinating,’ cried Lady Windermere. ‘But I want particulars. Particulars are the only things that matter. What is to happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, during the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—’

‘Oh yes, his honeymoon, naturally!’

‘And lose a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I hope?’ said Lady Jedburgh, her voice full of distress.

‘Certainly not his sister,’ answered Mr. Podgers, waving his hand deprecatingly; ‘merely a distant relative.’

‘Well, I am terribly disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I shall have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. Nobody cares about distant relatives nowadays. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she had better keep a black silk dress ready; it always serves for church, you know. And now let us go to supper. They are certain to have eaten everything, but perhaps we shall find some hot soup. François once made excellent soup, but he is so disturbed by politics at present that I never feel entirely sure of him. I do wish General Boulanger would be quiet. Duchess, surely you are tired?’

‘Not in the least, dear Gladys,’ answered the Duchess, waddling toward the door. ‘I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the cheiropodist—I mean the cheiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, where can my tortoise-shell fan be? Oh, thank you so much, Sir Thomas. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, very kind, I’m sure’; and the worthy creature at last succeeded in reaching the lower floor without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.

Throughout it all Lord Arthur Savile had stood beside the fireplace, oppressed by the same dread and the same sickening sense of approaching evil. He smiled sadly at his sister as she passed him on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking beautiful in pink brocade and pearls, and scarcely heard Lady Windermere call for him to follow. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the thought that anything might separate them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"4c78ac55f8a1b5c5e32e515f","rewritten_text":"“What conclusion, then, have you reached? What impression has this made on your imagination?”

A chill ran over me as Dupin asked the question. “A madman,” I said, “committed the deed—some raving lunatic who escaped from a nearby _Maison de Santé._”

“In some ways,” he replied, “your idea is not unreasonable. But the voices of madmen, even during their wildest fits, never sound like that strange voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and however confused their words may be, their syllables still follow the patterns of a language. Besides, a madman’s hair would not be like what I now hold in my hand. I pulled this small tuft from Madame L’Espanaye’s tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I cried, completely shaken. “This hair is extremely strange—this is not _human_ hair.”

“I have not claimed that it is,” he said. “But before we settle that question, look at the small drawing I have made on this paper. It is a _fac-simile_ of what one part of the testimony described as ‘dark bruises, and deep indentations of finger nails’ on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what another account, by Messrs. Dumas and Etienne, called a ‘series of livid spots, evidently the impression of fingers.’

“You will see,” my friend continued, spreading the paper on the table before us, “that the drawing suggests a firm, unchanging grip. There is no sign of _slipping._ Each finger kept its position—perhaps until the victim died—and left the terrible marks where it first pressed into the flesh. Now try placing all your fingers at once into the corresponding impressions.”

I tried, but could not do it.

“Perhaps we are not testing this fairly,” he said. “The paper lies on a flat surface, while a human throat is cylindrical. Here is a piece of wood whose circumference is about the same as the throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.”

I did so, but the difficulty was even clearer. “This,” I said, “is the mark of no human hand.”

“Now read this passage from Cuvier,” Dupin replied.

It was a detailed anatomical and general description of the large, tawny Ourang-Outang of the East Indian Islands. Everyone knows enough of these animals’ enormous size, tremendous strength and agility, savage nature, and tendency to imitate. At once, I understood the full horror of the murders.

“As I finish reading,” I said, “the description of the fingers exactly matches this drawing.”"}

{"request_id":"e2eb89b06c366a19ffce1713","rewritten_text":"“I now examined the death’s-head closely. Its outer edges—the edges of the drawing nearest the vellum’s border—were much clearer than the rest. It was evident that the caloric had acted imperfectly or unevenly. I at once lit a fire and exposed every part of the parchment to a glowing heat. At first, the sole result was that the skull’s faint lines grew stronger; but, after I continued the experiment, there appeared at the corner of the slip, diagonally opposite the place where the death’s-head had been drawn, the figure of what I initially took to be a goat. A more careful inspection, however, convinced me that it was meant for a kid.”

“Ha! ha!” said I, “certainly I have no right to laugh at you—a million and a half in money is far too serious a matter for jesting—but you are not going to form a third link in your chain—you will not discover any particular connection between your pirates and a goat—pirates, you know, have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming interest.”

“But I have just said that the figure was not a goat.”

“Well, then, a kid—much the same thing.”

“Much the same, but not entirely,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately regarded the animal’s figure as a sort of punning or hieroglyphic signature. I call it a signature because its position on the vellum suggested that interpretation. The death’s-head at the diagonally opposite corner likewise seemed to have the character of a stamp or seal. Yet I was greatly perplexed by the absence of everything else—of the body belonging to my imagined instrument, and of the text required by my context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something of that sort. In truth, I felt irresistibly possessed by a foreboding of some immense good fortune about to arrive. I can hardly explain why. Perhaps it was, after all, more a wish than a genuine belief; but do you know that Jupiter’s foolish remark about the bug being made of solid gold had a remarkable influence on my imagination? And then there was the succession of accidents and coincidences—they were extraordinarily striking. Do you see how accidental it was that these events should have taken place on the one day in the entire year when it has been, or might be, cool enough for a fire, and that without the fire, or without the dog’s intervention at the exact moment of his appearance, I should never have noticed the death’s-head, and thus never become the possessor of the treasure?”"}

{"request_id":"eecaed0b09da8ed40c69b604","rewritten_text":"To observe a star by glimpses—to see it obliquely, by turning toward it the outer parts of the _retina_ (more responsive to faint impressions of light than the inner portions), is to see the star clearly—is to gain the fullest sense of its brilliance—a brilliance that fades exactly as we direct our sight _fully_ upon it. More rays actually reach the eye in the latter instance, but in the former there is a finer power of apprehension. Excessive depth confuses and weakens thought; and it is possible to cause even Venus herself to disappear from the heavens through an examination too prolonged, too fixed, or too direct.

“As to these murders, let us conduct some investigations of our own before forming an opinion about them. An inquiry will provide us with amusement,” [I thought this a strange word to use in such a connection, but said nothing] “and, moreover, Le Bon once did me a service for which I am not ungrateful. We shall go and inspect the premises ourselves. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and will have no trouble securing the required permission.”

The permission was secured, and we immediately set out for the Rue Morgue. It is one of those wretched streets lying between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late afternoon when we arrived, since this district was far from the one in which we lived. The house was easy to locate; many people were still staring at its shuttered windows with idle curiosity from across the street. It was an ordinary Parisian dwelling, with a gateway and, beside it, a glazed watch-box whose window had a sliding panel, marking it as a _loge de concierge._ Before entering, we walked up the street, turned into an alley, and then turned again to pass behind the building—Dupin all the while inspecting the entire neighborhood, as well as the house, with an attentiveness whose purpose I could not imagine.

We retraced our route, returned to the front of the house, rang, and, after presenting our credentials, were admitted by the officers in charge. We went upstairs into the room where the body of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been discovered, and where both victims still lay. As usual, the room’s disorder had been left untouched. I saw nothing beyond what had already appeared in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin examined everything, including the bodies of the victims. We then entered the remaining rooms and went out into the yard, accompanied throughout by a _gendarme_."}

{"request_id":"54eae051492593e3bedf98cd","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” said I, “what is the trouble now?—how is your master?”

“Why, to speak de troof, massa, him not so berry well as mought be.”

“Not well! I am truly sorry to hear that. What does he complain of?”

“Dar! dat’s it!—him neber ’plain of notin’—but him berry sick for all dat.”

“_Very_ sick, Jupiter!—why did you not say so at once? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, dat he aint!—he aint ’fin’d nowhar—dat’s just whar de shoe pinch—my mind is got to be berry hebby ’bout poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I should like to understand what you mean. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what ails him?”

“Why, massa, ’taint worf while for to git mad about de matter—Massa Will say noffin at all aint de matter wid him—but den what make him go about looking dis here way, wid he head down and he soldiers up, and as white as a gose? And den he keep a syphon all de time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a syphon wid de figgurs on de slate—de queerest figgurs I ebber did see. Ise gittin’ skeered, I tell you. Hab for to keep mighty tight eye ’pon him ’noovers. Todder day he gib me slip ’fore de sun up and was gone de whole ob de blessed day. I had a big stick ready cut for to gib him deuced good beating when he did come—but Ise sich a fool dat I hadn’t de heart arter all—he look so berry poorly.”

“Eh?—what?—ah yes!—upon the whole I think you had better not be too severe with the poor fellow—don’t flog him, Jupiter—he can’t very well stand it—but can you form no idea what has occasioned this illness, or rather this change of conduct? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, dey aint bin noffin onpleasant _since_ den—‘twas _’fore_ den I’m feared—‘twas de berry day you was dare.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, massa, I mean de bug—dare now.”

“The what?”

“De bug,—I’m berry sartain dat Massa Will bin bit somewhere ’bout de head by dat goole-bug.”

“And what reason have you, Jupiter, for such a supposition?”

“Claws enuff, massa, and mouff too. I nebber did see sick a deuced bug—he kick and he bite ebery ting what cum near him. Massa Will cotch him fuss, but had for to let him go ’gin mighty quick, I tell you—den was de time he must ha’ got de bite. I did n’t like de look oh de bug mouff, myself, no how, so I would n’t take hold ob him wid my finger, but I cotch him wid a piece ob paper dat I found.”"}

{"request_id":"be955deb3ef44062359277be","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” replied Duff.

“And, translating the word ‘yokel’ for the ladies, I take it you mean that this attempt was not made by a countryman?” said Mr. Losberne, smiling.

“That’s right, sir,” replied Blathers. “This is all about the robbery, is it?”

“All of it,” replied the doctor.

“Now, what is this about the boy the servants have been talking about?” asked Blathers.

“Nothing at all,” replied the doctor. “One frightened servant decided that the boy had something to do with this attempt to break into the house; but it’s nonsense—complete absurdity.”

“Easy enough to settle, if that’s true,” remarked Duff.

“What he says is quite right,” observed Blathers, nodding firmly and idly playing with the handcuffs as though they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What story does he tell about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t fall out of the clouds, did he, sir?”

“Of course not,” replied the doctor, glancing nervously at the two ladies. “I know his entire history, but we can discuss that later. You would like to see the place where the thieves tried to get in first, I suppose?”

“Certainly,” replied Mr. Blathers. “We had better inspect the house first and question the servants afterward. That is the usual way of doing things.”

Lights were brought, and Messrs. Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and everyone else, went into the little room at the end of the passage and looked out of the window. Then they went around across the lawn and looked in through it. After that, they had a candle brought out to examine the shutter, a lantern to follow the footprints, and a pitchfork to search the bushes. When this was finished, to the breathless interest of everyone watching, they came back inside. Mr. Giles and Brittles were then made to act out their parts in the previous night’s events. They performed it about six times, contradicting each other in only one important detail the first time, and in at least a dozen by the last. Once this was done, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a long private discussion. Compared with its secrecy and seriousness, a meeting of great doctors debating the hardest problem in medicine would have seemed like child’s play.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced uneasily in the next room, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with worried faces.

“Upon my word,” he said, stopping after many quick turns, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"13f0cd530e6e5cbd1bdd37b6","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so entirely content with this conversation that he never again troubled himself, or annoyed his dear sister Elizabeth, by bringing up the subject; and she was glad to discover that she had said enough to keep him silent.

The day of his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived; and Mrs. Bennet was obliged to endure a separation which, since her husband had no intention of joining her plan for them all to go to Newcastle, was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she exclaimed, “when shall we see you again?”

“Oh, Lord! I cannot say. Perhaps not for two or three years.”

“Write to me very frequently, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women have little time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They will have nothing else to occupy them.”

Mr. Wickham’s farewells were far more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, appeared handsome, and uttered many agreeable things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they had left the house, “as ever I saw. He simpers, smirks, and makes love to us all. I am excessively proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas to produce a more valuable son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very melancholy for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that there is nothing so dreadful as parting from one’s friends. One feels so desolate without them.”

“This is the result, you see, madam, of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It should make you more content that your other four remain single.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia does not leave me because she is married, but merely because her husband’s regiment happens to be so distant. Had it been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.”

Yet the dispirited state into which this event had cast her was soon eased, and her mind once more opened to the excitement of hope through a piece of news then beginning to circulate. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to prepare for her master’s arrival, as he was coming down in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was all agitation. By turns, she looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head.

“Well, well, and so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for Mrs. Philips had first brought her the news). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never wish to see him again. But still, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield, if he chooses.”"}

{"request_id":"913f7f4b2799140f623842bb","rewritten_text":"This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must know that Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a young man of considerable fortune from the north of England; that he arrived on Monday in a chaise and four to inspect the place, and was so pleased with it that he immediately agreed with Mr. Morris; that he is to move in before Michaelmas, and that some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, certainly! A single man of great fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a splendid thing for our girls!”

“How so? How can it concern them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “how can you be so tiresome? Surely you know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that his purpose in settling here?”

“Purpose? Nonsense, how can you say such a thing! But it is very possible that he may fall in love with one of them, and so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I see no reason for that. You and the girls may go—or you may send them alone, which might be even better; for since you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley may prefer you to the whole party.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not claim to be anything remarkable now. When a woman has five grown daughters, she ought to stop dwelling on her own beauty.”

“In such circumstances, a woman does not often have much beauty to dwell upon.”

“But, my dear, you really must go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into the neighbourhood.”

“That is more than I can promise, I assure you.”

“But think of your daughters. Just imagine what a fine establishment it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are resolved to go, solely for that reason; for ordinarily, you know, they visit no newcomers. Indeed, you must go, because it will be impossible for us to visit him if you do not.”

“You are surely too scrupulous. I dare say Mr. Bingley will be delighted to see you; and I will send a few lines with you to assure him of my hearty consent to his marrying whichever of the girls he chooses—though I must say a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“I insist that you do no such thing. Lizzy is not in the least better than the others: and I am sure she is not half as handsome as Jane, nor half as good-humoured as Lydia.”"}

{"request_id":"0f1d5e315267a18e888c0d5d","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was greatly troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the good-natured peer remained resolute. At last, he persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her. Thus, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first drawing-room in the spring of 1890, on the occasion of her marriage, everyone admired her jewels. Virginia had received the coronet, the reward of every well-behaved American girl, and married her boy-lover as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming, and so deeply in love, that everyone rejoiced in the match—except the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had given no fewer than three costly dinner-parties to that end, and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis was very fond of the young Duke personally, but in principle he disliked titles and, as he put it, ‘was not without apprehension lest, amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity should be forgotten.’ His objections were entirely overruled, however, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter on his arm, there was no prouder man anywhere in England.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went to Canterville Chase, and the afternoon after their arrival they walked to the lonely churchyard beside the pine-woods. At first there had been much dispute over the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but in the end it was decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some beautiful roses, which she scattered over the grave, and after standing there for a while they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat on a fallen pillar, while her husband reclined at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up at her lovely eyes. Suddenly he tossed away his cigarette, took her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife should keep no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.’

‘Yes, you have,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never told me what happened when you were shut up with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ Virginia said gravely."}

{"request_id":"328643b59fa05264427312ab","rewritten_text":"Other chances to make her observations could not fail to arise. Anne had soon been in the company of all four together often enough to form an opinion, though she was too wise to admit as much at home, where she knew it would satisfy neither husband nor wife. For while she considered Louisa to be rather the favourite, she could not help thinking, as far as she dared judge from memory and experience, that Captain Wentworth was in love with neither of them. They were more in love with him; yet even in their case it was not love. It was a slight fever of admiration, but it might, and probably must, end in love with one of them. Charles Hayter seemed conscious of being slighted, while Henrietta sometimes appeared divided between the two. Anne longed for the power to explain to them all what they were doing, and to point out some of the dangers to which they were exposing themselves. She attributed guile to none of them. It was deeply satisfying to believe that Captain Wentworth was not in the least aware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph—no pitiful triumph—in his manner. He had probably never heard, and never considered, any claims Charles Hayter might have had. He was only wrong in accepting the attentions—for accepting was the proper word—of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to leave the field. Three days had passed without his coming once to Uppercross: a most decisive change. He had even refused a regular invitation to dinner; and when Mr Musgrove found him on that occasion with some large books before him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were certain that all could not be right, and spoke gravely of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had given him a definite dismissal, while her husband lived in constant expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only think that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning around this time, while Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at work when the sisters from the Mansion-house appeared at the window.

It was a very fine November day, and the Miss Musgroves crossed the small grounds and stopped for no purpose except to say that they were going to take a _long_ walk, and therefore assumed that Mary would not wish to go with them. When Mary immediately replied, somewhat jealous at not being considered a good walker, “Oh, yes, I should very much like to join you; I am very fond of a long walk,” Anne felt certain, from the looks of the two girls, that this was precisely what they did not want. She again admired the kind of necessity that family habits seemed to create: everything had to be communicated, and everything had to be done together, however unwanted or inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"2a272adab01fc675c14e7056","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to reassure you quite a lot. But what made you react that way? What did you think we had found?”

Huck was trapped—the man was watching him closely. He would have given anything for a believable answer, but nothing came to him. The questioning eyes seemed to bore deeper and deeper. A foolish reply occurred to him, and there was no time to consider it, so he blurted it out weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too upset to smile, but the old man laughed loudly and happily, shaking all over from head to foot. At last he said that a laugh like that was worth money because it reduced a man’s doctor bills enormously. Then he added:

“Poor fellow, you’re pale and worn out—you’re not well at all. No wonder you’re nervous and confused. But you’ll recover. Rest and sleep should set you right, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed with himself for acting like such a fool and showing such suspicious excitement. He had abandoned the idea that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard the conversation at the widow’s stile. He had only decided that it probably was not the treasure; he had not known for certain. So the suggestion that a bundle had been captured was too much for him to handle calmly. Still, he was glad the incident had happened, because now he knew beyond any doubt that this bundle was not the bundle. His mind was peaceful and completely at ease. In fact, everything now seemed to be going exactly as it should. The treasure had to remain in No. 2, the men would be caught and jailed that day, and he and Tom could take the gold that night without trouble or fear of interruption.

Just as breakfast ended, someone knocked at the door. Huck rushed to find a hiding place, since he did not want even the slightest connection with what had happened during the night. The Welshman admitted several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and noticed groups of townspeople climbing the hill to look at the stile. So the news had spread. The Welshman had to tell the visitors the story of the night. The widow openly expressed her gratitude for being saved.

“Please don’t mention it, ma’am. There is someone to whom you may owe more than you owe me and my boys, but he won’t let me reveal his name. We would not have been there without him.”"}

{"request_id":"5ab2843fdd1f12923d48c99f","rewritten_text":"And I call upon you, spirits of the dead, and upon you, wandering ministers of vengeance, to aid me and guide me in my work. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink deeply of agony; let him feel the despair that now torments me.”

I had begun my invocation solemnly, with an awe that almost convinced me the shades of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion. But as I finished, the furies took hold of me, and rage choked my voice.

Through the stillness of night, I was answered by a loud, fiendish laugh. It rang long and heavily in my ears; the mountains echoed it, and I felt as though all hell surrounded me with mockery and laughter. Surely, in that moment, frenzy would have seized me and I would have ended my miserable existence, had not my vow been heard and my life been reserved for vengeance. The laughter faded, and then a familiar, hated voice, apparently close beside my ear, addressed me in an audible whisper: “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have resolved to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed toward the place from which the sound had come, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly, the moon’s broad disk rose and shone directly upon his ghastly, distorted form as he fled with more than human speed.

I pursued him, and for many months this has been my task. Following a faint clue, I traced the winding course of the Rhône, but in vain. The blue Mediterranean came into view, and by a strange chance I saw the fiend enter it by night and conceal himself aboard a vessel bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same ship, but somehow he escaped me.

Across the wilds of Tartary and Russia, though he continued to elude me, I have always followed his trail. Sometimes peasants, terrified by the dreadful apparition, told me where he had gone; sometimes he himself, fearing that if I lost every trace of him I would despair and die, left some sign to guide me. Snow fell upon my head, and I saw the imprint of his enormous foot across the white plain. You, who are only beginning life, to whom care is unfamiliar and agony unknown, how can you understand what I have suffered and still suffer? Cold, hunger, and fatigue were the least of the pains I was destined to endure. I was cursed by some devil and carried my eternal hell with me; yet a benevolent spirit continued to follow and direct my steps, and whenever I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly free me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger overcame nature and exhaustion brought me down, a meal had been prepared for me in the desert, restoring and strengthening me."}

{"request_id":"871eac3c316656ef91737ad7","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed ourselves freemen so loudly and earnestly that the liberty-preaching orator and his patriotic crowd took an interested notice of us. They gathered around and adopted a very determined attitude. The orator said:

“If you truly are freemen, you have nothing to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain surround you as shield and shelter! (Applause.) You shall soon see. Bring out your proof.”

“What proof?”

“Proof that you are freemen.”

Ah—I remembered! I came to my senses and said nothing. But the king angrily burst out:

“You’re insane, man. It would be more reasonable for this thief and scoundrel here to prove that we are not freemen.”

You see, he understood his own laws the way people so often understand laws: by their words, not by their effects. They take on a meaning, and become very vivid, when you have to apply them to yourself.

Everyone shook his head and looked disappointed; some turned away, no longer interested. The orator spoke again, this time in the practical tone of business rather than feeling:

“If you do not know your country’s laws, it is time you learned them. You are strangers here; you will not deny that. You may be freemen—we do not deny it—but you may also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove that you are slaves; it requires you to prove that you are not.”

I said:

“Dear sir, give us only time to send to Astolat; or give us only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Peace, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you cannot expect them to be granted. It would take a great deal of time and unfairly inconvenience your master—”

“Master, idiot!” the king shouted. “I have no master. I myself am the m—”

“Silence, for God’s sake!”

I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in enough trouble; it could not help us to make these people think we were lunatics.

There is no point in giving all the details. The earl housed us and then put us up for auction. That same terrible law had existed in our own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later. Under it, hundreds of freemen who could not prove they were freemen had been sold into lifelong slavery, without making any particular impression on me. But the moment the law and auction block became part of my own experience, something that had merely seemed wrong before suddenly became hellish. Well, that is how we are made.

Yes, we were sold at auction, like pigs. In a large town with a busy market, we would have brought a good price. But this place was completely stagnant, and we were sold for an amount that still makes me ashamed whenever I think of it."}

{"request_id":"69835daa1ba8a77147d3dcfe","rewritten_text":"I don’t have the nerve for that sort of thing.”

“But could you really be comfortable spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; you see, his papa can, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour about how he was. I really think Charles might as well have told his father that we would all come. I am no more alarmed about little Charles now than he is. I was dreadfully alarmed yesterday, but the situation is very different today.”

“Well, if you don’t think it too late to give notice for yourself, suppose you went as well as your husband. Leave little Charles in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot think it wrong while I remain with him.”

“Are you serious?” cried Mary, her eyes brightening. “Dear me! That is a very good idea, very good indeed. Of course, I may as well go as not, since I am no use at home—isn’t that so? And staying here only harasses me. You, who have no mother’s feelings, are much the more suitable person. You can make little Charles do anything; he always obeys you at once. It will be much better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I shall certainly go; I am sure I ought to, if I can, quite as much as Charles, because they are extremely eager for me to become acquainted with Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left alone. It was an excellent idea of yours, Anne, truly. I will go and tell Charles, and get ready at once. You can send for us, you know, at a moment’s notice, if anything is wrong; but I dare say there will be nothing to alarm you. You may be sure I would not go if I did not feel completely at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was knocking at her husband’s dressing-room door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she arrived in time to hear the entire conversation, which began with Mary saying, in a tone of great triumph—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, because I am no more useful at home than you are. If I shut myself away forever with the child, I should not be able to persuade him to do anything he disliked. Anne will stay; Anne has offered to remain at home and take care of him. It was Anne’s own suggestion, and so I shall go with you, which will be much better, since I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I should be very glad to have you go; but it seems rather hard that she should be left at home alone to nurse our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"e06c2f233d778303313dd9ea","rewritten_text":"There was a delightful feeling of clearing things up and taking a quiet pause before beginning life anew in our village on Saturday nights, which encouraged Joe to risk staying out half an hour later on Saturdays than at other times. When the half-hour and the rum and water had run out together, Joe rose to leave and took me by the hand.

“Wait half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I believe I have a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I have, the boy shall have it.”

He picked it from a handful of small change, wrapped it in some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Mind! Your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him much longer than good manners allowed, and clinging tightly to Joe. He wished Joe good-night, and Mr. Wopsle good-night (who left with us), while he gave me only a look from his aiming eye—no, not a look, since he closed it, though wonders can be performed with an eye by concealing it.

On the way home, had I felt inclined to talk, the conversation would have been entirely mine, for Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked all the way home with his mouth wide open, rinsing the rum away with as much air as possible. But I was somehow stunned by the return of my old wrongdoing and old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in a particularly bad temper when we appeared in the kitchen, and Joe, encouraged by this uncommon circumstance, told her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” said Mrs. Joe triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.”

I took it from the paper, and it turned out to be genuine. “But what’s this?” said Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were nothing less than two thick, overheated one-pound notes that seemed to have enjoyed the closest acquaintance with every cattle-market in the county. Joe seized his hat again and hurried with them to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, fairly certain that the man would not be there.

Soon Joe returned, saying the man had gone, but that he, Joe, had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"00110d422957ac1bda2a0656","rewritten_text":"But in that bitter _tirade_ against Chantilly, which appeared in yesterday’s ‘_Musée_,’ the satirist, making some shameful allusions to the cobbler’s change of name when he assumed the buskin, quoted a Latin line about which we had often spoken. I mean the line

Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I had told you that this referred to Orion, once written Urion; and, from certain pungent associations attached to the explanation, I knew you could not have forgotten it. It was evident, then, that you would inevitably unite the two notions of Orion and Chantilly. That you had united them I perceived from the nature of the smile which crossed your lips. You were thinking of the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then, you had been stooping as you walked; but now I saw you straighten yourself to your full height. I was consequently certain that your thoughts had turned to Chantilly’s diminutive stature. At that moment I broke into your reflections by observing that, since he was really a very small fellow—that Chantilly—he would be better suited to the _Théâtre des Variétés_.”

Soon afterward, we were examining an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux,” when the following paragraphs caught our notice.

“_Extraordinary Murders_.—This morning, at about three o’clock, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by a series of dreadful shrieks, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue, known to be occupied solely by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay, caused by an unsuccessful effort to gain entrance in the ordinary way, the gateway was forced with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors entered, accompanied by two _gendarmes_. By then the cries had stopped; but as the group hurried up the first staircase, two or more harsh voices, angrily disputing, were heard and seemed to come from the upper portion of the house. When the second landing was reached, these sounds too had ceased, and all was completely silent. The party dispersed and rushed from room to room. On reaching a large rear chamber on the fourth floor, (the door having been found locked, with the key within, and therefore forced open,) a scene met their eyes that filled everyone present with horror as well as astonishment.

“The room was in the greatest confusion—the furniture broken and scattered everywhere. There was but one bedstead; the bed had been taken from it and cast into the center of the floor. Upon a chair lay a razor, stained with blood."}

{"request_id":"5861a48ee0c3f60b87bc5c9b","rewritten_text":"“I must point out, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, as he put down the newspaper, “that the present situation is very much in our favour. This peace will be putting all our wealthy naval officers ashore. They will all be looking for a home. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, to have a choice of tenants—very responsible tenants. Many a great fortune was made during the war. If a rich admiral should come our way, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” replied Sir Walter; “that is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would indeed be a prize to him; perhaps the greatest prize of all, however many he may have taken before; eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he was expected to, and then continued—

“I venture to observe, Sir Walter, that, in business, gentlemen of the navy are good people to deal with. I have had some experience of their methods; and I freely admit that they hold very liberal views, and are as likely to make desirable tenants as any class of people one could meet. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would suggest is this: if, as a result of rumours spreading about your intentions—which must be considered possible, since we know how difficult it is to keep the actions and plans of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of another; prominence has its price—I, John Shepherd, might conceal any family matters I wished, because no one would think it worth observing me; but Sir Walter Elliot has eyes upon him that may be very difficult to evade. Therefore, I venture to say that it will not greatly surprise me if, despite all our caution, some rumour of the truth should spread. In that event, as I was about to observe, applications will certainly follow, and I should consider those from wealthy naval commanders especially worth attending to; and I beg leave to add that I can come over at any time within two hours, to spare you the trouble of replying.”

Sir Walter merely nodded. But soon afterward, rising and walking about the room, he remarked sarcastically—

“There are few among the gentlemen of the navy, I imagine, who would not be surprised to find themselves in a house of this kind.”

“They would look around them, no doubt, and bless their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, who was present; her father had driven her over, since nothing benefited Mrs Clay’s health so much as a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely agree with my father that a sailor might be a very desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"1fa2d7df9096e6d3ef6fd242","rewritten_text":"It should be said in the young lady’s favor that she did not expressly declare she would not, but only voiced an emphatic and earnest wish to be “blessed” if she did; a courteous and delicate way of evading the request, showing that she possessed the natural good manners which cannot endure causing a fellow-creature the pain of a blunt and direct refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned from this young lady, who was gaily, almost splendidly dressed in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, to the other female.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew soothingly, “what do _you_ say?”

“That it won’t do; so there’s no use trying it on, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” asked Mr. Sikes, looking up surlily.

“What I say, Bill,” the lady answered calmly.

“Why, you’re exactly the person for it,” argued Mr. Sikes; “nobody round here knows anything about you.”

“And since I don’t want ’em to, either,” Nancy replied in the same composed tone, “it’s rather more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes was right. Through a mixture of threats, promises, and bribes, the lady was at last persuaded to undertake the commission. She was not restrained by the same concerns as her agreeable companion; for, having lately moved into the neighborhood of Field Lane from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she had no equal fear of being recognized by her many acquaintances.

Accordingly, with a clean white apron fastened over her gown and her curl-papers tucked beneath a straw bonnet—both garments supplied from the Jew’s inexhaustible stores—Miss Nancy prepared to set out upon her errand.

“Wait a moment, my dear,” said the Jew, producing a small covered basket. “Carry that in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door-key for the other one, Fagin,” said Sikes; “it makes the thing look real and genivine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, so it does,” said the Jew, hanging a large street-door key upon the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There; very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” said the Jew, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” cried Nancy, bursting into tears and wringing the little basket and street-door key in an agony of distress. “What has become of him? Where have they taken him? Oh, have pity, and tell me what has been done with the dear boy, gentlemen; do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"1651b5ed2fd927a38116ab7c","rewritten_text":"“You have not been in Bath long enough,” said he, “to take pleasure in the evening parties here.”

“Oh! no. Their usual nature has no attraction for me. I do not play cards.”

“I know you did not formerly. You once disliked cards; but time brings many alterations.”

“I am not changed so much yet,” cried Anne, and then stopped, afraid she scarcely knew how he might misunderstand her. After a few moments’ silence, he said, as though speaking from an immediate impulse, “It is a period, indeed! Eight years and a half is a period.”

Whether he would have said more, Anne was left to consider in some calmer hour; for, while the words were still sounding in her ears, Henrietta drew her attention to other matters, anxious to take advantage of the present leisure to go out, and urging her companions to make haste, lest another visitor should arrive.

They were forced to move. Anne spoke of being quite ready, and endeavoured to appear so; but she felt that, if Henrietta had understood the regret and reluctance in her heart as she left that chair and prepared to leave the room, she would have discovered, in all her own feelings for her cousin, and in the very certainty of his affection, enough to pity her.

Their preparations, however, were suddenly interrupted. Alarming sounds were heard; other visitors drew near, and the door opened to admit Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose arrival appeared to cast a general chill. Anne felt an immediate oppression, and wherever she looked she saw signs of the same feeling. The room’s comfort, ease, and liveliness had vanished, subdued into cold restraint, deliberate silence, or dull conversation, to suit the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How mortifying it was to know that this should be so!

Her jealous eye was gratified in one respect. Captain Wentworth was once more acknowledged by both, Elizabeth being more gracious to him than before. She even spoke to him once, and looked at him more than once. Elizabeth was, in truth, considering an important measure. Its result soon made the matter clear. After spending a few minutes in uttering the proper commonplaces, she began the invitation intended to include all the Musgroves’ remaining obligations. “To-morrow evening, to meet a few friends: no formal party.” She delivered it with great grace, and placed upon the table the cards she had brought with her, marked “Miss Elliot at home,” accompanied by a courteous, inclusive smile for everyone, and one smile and one card more distinctly intended for Captain Wentworth. The fact was, Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to appreciate the value of a man possessing such an air and appearance as his."}

{"request_id":"590dd219c889d00b60691ecc","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret lowering herself enough to visit the Coles. The visit gave her many pleasant memories the next day; and whatever she might be thought to have sacrificed in dignified seclusion would be more than repaid by the glory of popularity. She must have delighted the Coles—worthy people who deserved to be made happy!—and left behind her a name that would not soon fade.

Perfect happiness, even in memory, is uncommon; and there were two matters about which she was not entirely at ease. She wondered whether, as one woman to another, she had not violated her duty by revealing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings to Frank Churchill. It was hardly right; but the idea had been so powerful that it had escaped her, and his acceptance of everything she told him was such a compliment to her insight that she could not be completely sure she ought to have kept silent.

The other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and in that case she had no doubt. She sincerely and unmistakably regretted the inferiority of her own playing and singing. She deeply mourned the idleness of her childhood—and sat down to practise energetically for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival interrupted her; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she might soon have been consoled.

“Oh! If only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than a lamp is like sunlight.”

“Oh, dear—I think you play the better of the two. I think you play quite as well as she does. I am sure I would much rather hear you. Everyone said last night how well you played.”

“Anyone who knew anything about it must have noticed the difference. The truth is, Harriet, that my playing is merely good enough to be praised, while Jane Fairfax’s is far beyond that.”

“Well, I shall always think you play quite as well as she does, or that, if there is any difference, no one could ever detect it. Mr. Cole said how much taste you had; and Mr. Frank Churchill spoke at length about your taste, saying that he valued taste much more than execution.”

“Ah! But Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw that she had execution, but I did not know she had any taste. No one mentioned it. And I hate Italian singing—there is no understanding a word of it. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it is no more than she is required to do, since she will have to teach.”"}

{"request_id":"89d024e0c4fd07d79160d4f8","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams meant to fade like this? Our name was written “a little lower than the angels”; yet we were no better than mayflies. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and now we were a “quintessence of dust.” We had complained that the pyramids had outlasted the embalmed body of their builder. Alas, even the simple shepherd’s straw hut we passed on the road held within its structure the promise of a longer life than the entire human race. How could we reconcile this sad change with our former hopes and our apparent powers?

Suddenly, an inner voice, clear and distinct, seemed to say: Thus it was decreed from eternity. The horses that carry Time forward had this hour and its fulfillment chained to them from the moment the void gave birth to its burden. Would you read backward the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Almighty! Eternal, unchanging Necessity, who with busy fingers are always weaving the unbreakable chain of events—I will not complain of your actions. If my human mind cannot accept that all things are right, then, since whatever happens must happen, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly, we were not born to enjoy, but to submit and to hope.

Will the reader grow tired if I describe in detail our long journey from Paris to Geneva? If I recorded, day by day, the countless miseries of our condition in journal form, could my hand write, or language provide words to express, the variety of our suffering—the crowding of one terrible event upon another? Have patience, reader, whoever you are and wherever you live. Whether you are a spiritual being or descended from some surviving pair, your nature will be human and your home will be the earth. Here you will read of the deeds of the vanished race, and wonder whether those who endured what is recorded here were made of fragile flesh and delicate bodies like your own. Indeed they were—so weep; for surely, solitary being, you will be gentle in spirit. Shed tears of compassion, but meanwhile attend to this tale and learn the deeds and sufferings of your predecessors.

Yet the final events that marked our passage through France were so filled with strange horror and dark misery that I dare not linger over them. If I examined every incident, each tiny fraction of a second would contain a dreadful story, whose smallest word would chill the blood in your young veins. It is right that I should raise this monument of the former race for your instruction, but not that I should lead you through hospital wards or the hidden rooms of a charnel house."}

content.text: {"request_id":"49a50d80a92e12b65487eaf7","rewritten_text":"I am also informed by Mrs. Otis, who, I may say, is no minor authority on art—having had the privilege of spending several winters in Boston as a girl—that these gems are worth a great deal of money and would command a high price if sold. Under these circumstances, Lord Canterville, I am sure you will understand how impossible it would be for me to let them remain in the possession of any member of my family; indeed, all such empty ornaments and toys, however appropriate or necessary to the dignity of the British aristocracy, would be entirely out of place among people raised according to the strict, and, I believe, immortal principles of republican simplicity. I should perhaps add that Virginia is very eager for you to let her keep the box as a memento of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. Since it is extremely old and therefore rather badly damaged, you may perhaps decide to grant her request. For my part, I admit that I am quite surprised to find a child of mine showing sympathy with medievalism in any form, and can explain it only by the fact that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a trip to Athens.’\n\nLord Canterville listened with great seriousness to the worthy Minister’s speech, occasionally tugging at his grey moustache to conceal an involuntary smile. When Mr. Otis had finished, he shook his hand warmly and said, ‘My dear sir, your charming little daughter rendered my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, a very important service, and my family and I are deeply indebted to her for her extraordinary courage and spirit. The jewels plainly belong to her, and, by heaven, I believe that if I were heartless enough to take them away, the wicked old fellow would be out of his grave within a fortnight, making my life a misery. As for their being heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless it is identified as such in a will or other legal document, and the existence of these jewels was entirely unknown. I assure you that I have no more claim to them than your butler does, and when Miss Virginia grows up, I daresay she will be glad to have pretty things to wear. Besides, you forget, Mr. Otis, that you bought the furniture and the ghost at an assessed value, and anything belonging to the ghost passed immediately into your possession. Whatever activity Sir Simon may have displayed in the corridor at night, legally speaking he was dead, and you acquired his property by purchase.’"}

{"request_id":"9722edbb94ba49be3b836017","rewritten_text":"I would gladly explain all this, and much more besides. But, to be brief, I must have my reward. I long to return to my family and my home; and as the price of any further information from me—in view of the light I can shed on many important areas of physical and metaphysical science—I must ask, through the influence of your honorable body, for a pardon for the crime I committed in causing the creditors’ deaths when I left Rotterdam. This, then, is the purpose of this paper. Its bearer, a resident of the moon whom I have persuaded and properly trained to serve as my messenger to Earth, will await your Excellencies’ decision and return to me with the pardon, if it can be obtained by any means.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

After reading this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe on the ground in utter surprise. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and put them in his pocket; then, forgetting both himself and his dignity, he turned around three times on his heel in complete astonishment and admiration. There was no doubt about it—the pardon had to be obtained. So Professor Rub-a-dub swore emphatically, and the illustrious Von Underduk finally agreed, as he took his fellow scientist’s arm and, without a word, began making his way home to discuss what should be done. When they reached the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor suggested that since the messenger had chosen to disappear—probably terrified by the savage appearance of Rotterdam’s burghers—the pardon would be useless, because no one but a man from the moon would attempt such a distant journey. The burgomaster agreed, and the matter ended there. The rumors and speculation did not. Once published, the letter produced all kinds of gossip and opinions. Some of the supposedly wise even made fools of themselves by dismissing the whole affair as nothing more than a hoax. But “hoax,” among such people, is, I believe, simply a general word for anything beyond their understanding. For my part, I cannot imagine what evidence led them to make such an accusation. Let us see what they say:"}

{"request_id":"e873084bccea92c004d64355","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.

His face immediately took on an expression of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To find someone who fled from me.”

“And did the man you pursued travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we have seen him, for the day before we picked you up, we saw some dogs pulling a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked many questions about the route the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Soon afterward, when he was alone with me, he said, “I have surely aroused your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you are too considerate to ask questions.”

“Certainly; it would be very rude and inhuman of me to trouble you with my curiosity.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and dangerous situation; you have kindly brought me back to life.”

Soon afterward he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied that I could not say with certainty, since the ice had not broken until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety before then; but I had no way of knowing.

From that time, a new energy seemed to animate the stranger’s failing body. He was extremely eager to go on deck and watch for the sledge that had appeared before; but I persuaded him to remain in the cabin, because he was far too weak to endure the cold air. I promised that someone would watch for him and tell him at once if anything new came into view.

This is my journal of everything connected with this strange event up to the present day. The stranger’s health has gradually improved, but he is very quiet and seems uneasy whenever anyone except me enters his cabin. Still, his manner is so gentle and pleasant that all the sailors are interested in him, although they have spoken with him very little. As for me, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant, profound sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in better days, for even now, despite his ruin, he is so attractive and kind.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the open ocean; yet I have found a man whom, before misery had broken his spirit, I would have been glad to have as the brother of my heart."}

{"request_id":"b357eba22c59d8452a088c69","rewritten_text":"We would wake after a while and look around to see what had caused it, and perhaps spot a steamboat coughing upstream, so far off toward the opposite bank that you couldn’t tell anything about her except whether she was a stern-wheeler or a side-wheeler. Then for about an hour there would be nothing to hear or see—only complete loneliness. Next you might see a raft drifting by, far away, and perhaps a fellow on it chopping, because they are almost always doing that on a raft; you would see the axe flash and fall—you heard nothing; you saw the axe rise again, and by the time it was above the man’s head, then you heard the _k’chunk!_—it had taken all that time to cross the water. So we spent the day idling around, listening to the silence. Once there was a heavy fog, and the rafts and other things passing by were beating tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run them down. A scow or raft passed so close that we could hear them talking, cursing, and laughing—hear them clearly; but we couldn’t see any sign of them. It made you feel uneasy; it was like spirits carrying on in the air. Jim said he believed they were spirits, but I said:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Damn this damn fog.’”

As soon as night fell we pushed off; when we had reached about the middle, we left her alone and let her drift wherever the current carried her. Then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes allowed it. The new clothes Buck’s family had made for me were too fine to be comfortable, and besides, I never cared much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we had the whole river to ourselves for a very long time. There were the banks and islands over there, across the water; perhaps a spark—which was a candle in a cabin window; and sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two—on a raft or scow, you know. Maybe you could hear a fiddle or a song drifting over from one of those boats. It is wonderful to live on a raft. We had the sky above us, scattered with stars, and we would lie on our backs and look up at them, discussing whether they had been made or had simply happened. Jim believed they had been made, but I thought they had happened; I figured it would have taken too long to _make_ so many."}

{"request_id":"6140da2ae335232d55df477f","rewritten_text":"“He was brought to you. You see that I know the circumstances?”

“That is certainly true,” said Defarge. His wife had signaled with an accidental touch of her elbow as she knitted and hummed that he should answer, but always briefly.

“It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and it was from your care that she took him, accompanied by a neat brown gentleman—what was his name?—wearing a little wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—to England.”

“That is true,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You do not hear much about them now?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In fact,” Madame Defarge interrupted, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear about them. We received word that they had arrived safely, and perhaps one other letter, or perhaps two. Since then, they have gone their way in life—we have gone ours—and we have had no correspondence.”

“Exactly so, madame,” replied the spy. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” Madame Defarge echoed. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English seem cold to me.”

“Oh! You know I am English.”

“I can hear it in your speech,” Madame Defarge replied; “and I suppose a man is like his tongue.”

He did not take this as a compliment, but he made light of it with a laugh. After finishing his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman; to someone who, like her, was born French. And speaking of Gaspard—poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!—it is a curious thing that she is going to marry the nephew of the Marquis for whom Gaspard was raised to that great height of so many feet; in other words, the present Marquis. But he lives unknown in England. He is not a Marquis there; he is Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge continued knitting, but the news clearly affected her husband. Whatever he did behind the little counter, whether striking a match or lighting his pipe, he was troubled, and his hand was unsteady. The spy would not have been a spy if he had failed to notice this and remember it.

Having made at least this one useful discovery, whatever it might be worth, and with no customers arriving to give him another opportunity, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and left. Before departing, he took care to say politely that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}
