{"request_id":"e53c236427c4c6ea418ad587","rewritten_text":"It was the beginning of February, and Anne, who had been in Bath for a month, was becoming very eager for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to hear far more than Mary had told her. It had been three weeks since she had heard anything at all. She knew only that Henrietta was home again, and that Louisa, though thought to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. She was thinking of them all very intently one evening when a letter from Mary, thicker than usual, was delivered to her; and, to increase the pleasure and surprise, it came with the compliments of Admiral and Mrs Croft.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was something to interest her. They were people toward whom her heart naturally turned.

“What is this?” cried Sir Walter. “The Crofts have arrived in Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! Such letters are useful passports. They secure an introduction. I should have called on Admiral Croft in any case. I know what is owed to my tenant.”

Anne could listen no longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion escaped notice. Her letter absorbed her attention. It had been begun several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

I make no apology for my silence, because I know how little people think about letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to care about Uppercross, which, as you know very well, offers little to write about. We have had a very dull Christmas; Mr and Mrs Musgrove have not held a single dinner party throughout the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anyone. The holidays, however, are finally over: I believe no children ever had such long ones. I am sure I never did. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear that they have never gone home. Mrs Harville must be an unusual mother to part with them for so long. I cannot understand it. They are not at all well-behaved children, in my opinion; but Mrs Musgrove seems to like them quite as much, if not more, than her grandchildren. What dreadful weather we have had! It may not be noticed in Bath, with your fine pavements; but in the country it is a serious matter. No one has called on me since the second week of January, except Charles Hayter, who had been calling much more often than was welcome. Between ourselves, I think it a great pity Henrietta did not remain in Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little farther from him.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"0c236bf68317cac74f07dade","rewritten_text":"Dawn had come when I set the Manuscript aside. The rain had nearly stopped; the world was gray and mournful, and the spent storm sighed and sobbed itself to sleep. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his door, which stood slightly open. I could hear his voice, so I knocked. There was no answer, though the voice continued. I peered inside. The man lay on his back in bed, speaking brokenly but with spirit, punctuating his words with his arms, which he flung about restlessly, as the sick do in delirium. I slipped in quietly and bent over him. His mutterings and exclamations continued. I spoke—only a word, to draw his attention. At once, his glassy eyes and ashen face lit with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome:\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you have come at last—how I have longed for you! Sit beside me—do not leave me—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand? Give it to me, dear; let me hold it—there—now all is well, all is peace, and I am happy again—we are happy again, are we not, Sandy? You are so dim, so indistinct; you are only a mist, a cloud, but you are here, and that is blessing enough. And I have your hand; do not take it away—it is only for a little while. I shall not need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello, Central!... She does not answer. Asleep, perhaps? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say good-bye.... Sandy! Yes, you are there. I lost myself for a moment and thought you had gone.... Have I been ill long? It must be so; it seems months to me. And such dreams! Such strange and terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality—delirium, of course, but so real! Why, I thought the king was dead; I thought you were in Gaul and could not get home; I thought there was a revolution. In the fantastic frenzy of those dreams, I thought Clarence and I and a handful of my cadets fought and destroyed the entire chivalry of England! But even that was not the strangest. I seemed to be a creature from a distant, unborn age, centuries in the future, and even that was as real as the rest! Yes, I seemed to have flown back from that age into our own, then forward to it again, and been set down, a stranger and abandoned, in that strange England, with an abyss of thirteen centuries yawning between you and me—between me and my home and my friends—between me and everything dear to me, everything that could make life worth living!”"}

Emma amused herself by agreeing that it was indeed very strange, and that she had not a word to say in his defense.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, feeling the insult as a wife ought to, “I cannot imagine how he could treat you this way, of all people! You are the very last person anyone would expect him to forget! My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message for you; I am sure he must have. Even Knightley could not be so eccentric—and his servants must have forgotten it. Depend on it, that was what happened. It would be very likely with the Donwell servants, who, as I have often noticed, are extremely awkward and careless. I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry standing beside our sideboard for any price. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her indeed. She promised Wright a receipt and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” Mr. Elton continued, “as I approached the house, and he told me I would not find his master at home, but I did not believe him. William seemed rather annoyed. {"request_id":"fe195c1d2d33dec625a94a89","rewritten_text":"Good heavens, she was a masterful talker. It would not have been proper for me to say that it was very late, that I was tired, and that I could hardly keep my eyes open. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to endure it; there was no other choice. So she went on and on, her voice tinkling through the otherwise deep, ghostly silence of the sleeping castle. At last there came, as if from far beneath us, a distant sound like a muffled shriek—with such agony in it that my flesh crawled. The queen stopped, and her eyes shone with pleasure. She tilted her graceful head like a bird listening for a sound. Again the cry forced its way up through the silence.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a stubborn soul, and has endured long. It has been many hours now.”

“Endured what?”

“The rack. Come—you shall see a cheerful sight. If he does not reveal his secret now, you shall see him torn apart.”

What a smooth, heartless devil she was, remaining so calm and serene while the cords in my legs ached in sympathy with that man's suffering. Armored guards carrying blazing torches led us through echoing corridors and down damp, dripping stone stairs that smelled of mold and centuries of trapped darkness. It was a long, cold, frightening journey, made neither shorter nor more pleasant by the sorceress's talk about the prisoner and his crime. An anonymous informer had accused him of killing a stag in the royal hunting grounds. I said:

“Anonymous testimony is not really fair, Your Highness. It would be better to confront the accused with his accuser.”

“I had not considered that, since it seemed of little importance. But even if I wished to, I could not, because the accuser came masked at night, told the forester, and immediately departed again. Thus the forester does not know him.”

“Then was this Unknown the only person who saw the stag being killed?”

“Indeed, no man saw the killing. But this Unknown saw the bold fellow near the place where the stag lay, and, out of loyal zeal, reported him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag as well? Is it not possible that he killed it himself? His loyal zeal—while masked—seems somewhat suspicious. But why do you intend to torture the prisoner? What good will it do?”

“He will not confess otherwise, and then his soul would be lost. By law, his crime has cost him his life—and I will certainly see that he pays it!—but I would endanger my own soul if I allowed him to die without confessing and receiving absolution.”"}

{"request_id":"c1953fdfeadb3295db0532d4","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ and assumed that ‘anybody’ included—well, anybody; that is, everybody.”

“It does—anybody of noble birth; and preferably royal.”

“That, it seems to me, may well be,” said the abbot, who saw a chance to smooth matters and avert disaster, “for surely so marvelous a gift would not be granted to reveal the affairs of beings lesser than those born near the heights of greatness. Our King Arthur—”

“Would you know about him?” the enchanter interrupted.

“Most gladly, and with gratitude.”

Everyone was immediately filled with awe and interest again, the incorrigible idiots. They watched the incantations intently, then looked at me with a “There, now, what can you say to that?” expression when the announcement came:

“The king is weary from the hunt and has lain in his palace these two hours, sleeping dreamlessly.”

“God’s blessing upon him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep refresh both body and soul.”

“And so it might, if he were asleep,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping; the king is riding.”

There was trouble again—a conflict of authority. No one knew which of us to believe; I still had some reputation left. The magician’s scorn was aroused, and he said:

“Behold, I have seen many wonderful soothsayers, prophets, and magicians in my lifetime, but never one who could sit idle and see into the heart of things without a single incantation to help him.”

“You have lived in the woods and lost much by it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood knows—but only on important occasions.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I reckon I know how to hold my own. That jab made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and received this answer:

“They are all asleep, overcome by fatigue, just as the king is.”

I said:

“That is merely another lie. Half of them are occupied with their amusements; the queen and the other half are not sleeping—they are riding. Now perhaps you can exert yourself a little and tell us where the king and queen, and all those riding with them, are going at this moment.”

“They sleep now, as I said; but tomorrow they will ride, for they are setting out on a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be the day after tomorrow at vespers?”

“Far north of Camelot, with half their journey completed.”

“That is another lie—by a distance of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"c78ae69a4919492cf9d56ef4","rewritten_text":"Her complexion changed, and she said no more.

Mrs. Gardiner was standing a little behind, and when she paused, he asked whether she would do him the honour of introducing him to her friends. This display of civility caught her completely unprepared; she could scarcely suppress a smile at his now seeking the acquaintance of some of the very people against whom his pride had rebelled when he proposed to her. “How surprised he will be,” she thought, “when he discovers who they are! He takes them for people of fashion.”

The introduction was made at once; and as she explained their relationship to her, she stole a sly glance at him to see how he endured it, half expecting him to retreat as quickly as possible from such disgraceful companions. That he was surprised by the connection was obvious; nevertheless, he bore it with fortitude. Far from leaving, he turned back with them and began speaking with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help being pleased—could not help feeling triumphant. It was comforting that he should know she had relations of whom there was no reason to be ashamed. She listened with the greatest attention to everything that passed between them and took pride in every expression, every sentence from her uncle that revealed his intelligence, taste, or good manners.

The conversation soon turned to fishing, and she heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the utmost civility, to fish there as often as he wished while he remained in the neighbourhood. He offered at the same time to provide him with fishing tackle and pointed out the parts of the stream where the best sport was usually found. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look that expressed her astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but was deeply gratified; the compliment must be intended entirely for her. Yet her amazement was extreme, and she kept repeating to herself, “Why is he so changed? What could have caused it? It cannot be for me; it cannot be on my account that his manner has softened so much. My reproofs at Hunsford could not have produced such a change. It is impossible that he should still love me.”

After they had walked this way for some time, with the two ladies ahead and the two gentlemen behind, a small change occurred when they resumed their places after going down to the riverbank to examine more closely a curious water plant. It began with Mrs. Gardiner, who, tired from the morning’s exercise, found Elizabeth’s arm insufficient support and therefore chose her husband’s instead."}

{"request_id":"35f06d4021a5dc0a5262a329","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to ease your mind considerably. But what caused that change in you? What did _you_ think we had found?”

Huck was in a tight spot—the questioning eye was fixed on him—and he would have given anything for some material from which to shape a believable answer. Nothing came to him. The eye seemed to bore deeper and deeper. A foolish reply suggested itself, and there was no time to consider it, so he blurted it out at random, weakly:

“Sunday-school books, perhaps.”

Poor Huck was too troubled to laugh, but the old man roared with delight, shaking every part of himself from head to foot. At last he declared that a laugh like that was money in a man’s pocket, since it reduced the doctor’s bill enormously. Then he continued:

“Poor fellow, you’re pale and worn—you’re not well at all. No wonder you’re somewhat flighty and unsteady. But you’ll recover. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed to realize what a fool he had made of himself and how suspiciously excited he had appeared. He had abandoned the notion that the parcel brought from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard the conversation at the widow’s stile. Yet he had only concluded that it was not the treasure; he had not known for certain that it wasn’t. Thus the mention of a captured bundle had overwhelmed his self-control. Still, on the whole, he was glad the incident had occurred, because he now knew beyond any doubt that this bundle was not _the_ bundle, and his mind was consequently peaceful and thoroughly at ease. Indeed, everything now seemed to be moving in exactly the right direction. The treasure must still be in No. 2, the men would be caught and imprisoned that day, and he and Tom could take the gold that night without difficulty or fear of interruption.

Breakfast had scarcely ended when someone knocked at the door. Huck sprang toward a hiding-place, unwilling to be connected in even the slightest way with the recent affair. The Welshman admitted several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and observed groups of townspeople making their way up the hill to gaze at the stile. The news had evidently spread. The Welshman was obliged to recount the night’s events to his visitors. The widow openly expressed her gratitude for being saved.

“Please don’t mention it, madam. There is someone to whom you may owe more than you do to me and my boys, perhaps, but he won’t permit me to reveal his name. We would not have been there without him.”"}

{"request_id":"1078770e2d7a81e5b6b8d01a","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis, at Lady Canterville’s earnest request, had agreed to retain in her former position. She gave each of them a low curtsey as they got out and said in a quaint, old-fashioned manner, “I welcome you to Canterville Chase.” Following her, they went through the fine Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room panelled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at the far end. Tea had been prepared for them there, and, after removing their wraps, they sat down and began looking around while Mrs. Umney waited on them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor beside the fireplace and, unaware of what it really meant, said to Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” replied the old housekeeper in a low voice, “blood has been spilled on that spot.”

“How dreadful,” cried Mrs. Otis. “I don’t like bloodstains in a sitting room at all. It must be removed immediately.”

The old woman smiled and answered in the same low, mysterious voice, “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered on that very spot by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon survived her by nine years, then disappeared suddenly under very mysterious circumstances. His body has never been found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. Tourists and others have greatly admired the bloodstain, and it cannot be removed.”

“That is nonsense,” cried Washington Otis. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it up in no time.” Before the terrified housekeeper could stop him, he had dropped to his knees and was vigorously scrubbing the floor with a small stick of what appeared to be black cosmetic. Within moments, no trace of the bloodstain remained.

“I knew Pinkerton would do it,” he exclaimed triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family. But no sooner had he spoken than a terrible flash of lightning illuminated the gloomy room, a frightening peal of thunder made them all leap to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What an outrageous climate!” said the American Minister calmly as he lit a long cheroot. “I suppose the old country is so overpopulated that there isn’t enough decent weather for everyone. I have always believed that emigration is the only solution for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” cried Mrs. Otis, “what are we to do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge it to her as breakage,” answered the Minister. “She won’t faint again after that.” And within a few moments Mrs. Umney certainly recovered."}

{"request_id":"7b1d853f6c6fbbf5bcf9b129","rewritten_text":"The oaks around us were home to a tribe of nightingales—there I am now; Idris, in the precious prime of youth, is beside me. Remember, I am only twenty-two, and barely seventeen summers have passed over the beloved of my heart. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian, in his favorite boat, was engaged in the dangerous sport of plucking the highest branch from a submerged oak. Are you tired of life, Adrian, that you play so carelessly with danger?—

He secured his prize and guided his boat through the flood. We watched him anxiously, but the current carried him away from us. He had to land much farther downstream and take a long route before he could rejoin us. “He is safe!” said Idris, leaping ashore and waving the branch above his head as a sign of victory. “We will wait for him here.”

We were alone together. The sun had set, the nightingales began to sing, and the evening star shone clearly in the light that still lingered unfaded in the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes rested on this sweet image of herself. “How the light trembles,” she said, “as though that trembling were the star’s life. Its shifting brightness seems to say that its condition, like ours on earth, is uncertain and changeable; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Do not gaze at the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Do not read love in its trembling rays; do not look toward distant worlds or speak of the mere idea of a feeling. I have been silent for a long time—so long that the desire to speak has made me ill—and I have wished to place my soul, my life, my whole being in your hands. Do not look at the star, dear love—or do, and let that eternal spark speak for me. Let it be my witness and advocate, silent as it shines. Love is to me what light is to the star; as long as that light is not extinguished by annihilation, I will love you.”

The joy of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s hardened eyes. I can still feel her graceful body pressed against my overflowing heart; even now, sight, pulse, and breath weaken and fail when I remember that first kiss. Slowly and silently, we went to meet Adrian, whom we heard approaching.

I begged Adrian to return to me after taking his sister home. That same evening, as we walked along the moonlit forest paths, I poured out my whole heart—its joy and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he looked troubled. “I might have expected this,” he said. “What conflict will now follow!”"}

{"request_id":"9539e6516572dc38e56453b9","rewritten_text":"I know she would!”

The Widow Douglas’s splendid hospitality was a tempting lure, and it, together with Tom’s urging, soon carried the decision. They resolved to tell no one about the night’s plans. Presently Tom thought that perhaps Huck might come that very night and give the signal. The idea took much of the eagerness from his expectations. Yet he could not endure giving up the entertainment at Widow Douglas’s. And why should he, he argued—the signal had not come the night before, so why was it any more likely tonight? The certain pleasure of the evening outweighed the doubtful treasure; and, like a boy, he decided to follow the stronger impulse and not think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat halted at the entrance to a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the distant forest and jagged heights rang on every side with shouts and laughter. Every possible way of becoming hot and tired was tried, and presently the rovers straggled back to camp, armed with hearty appetites; then the destruction of the good things commenced. After the meal came a pleasant period of resting and talking beneath the spreading oaks. Presently someone called out:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were obtained, and at once there was a general scramble up the hill. The cave’s mouth opened partway up the hillside, shaped like the letter A. Its huge oaken door stood open. Inside was a little chamber, cold as an icehouse, its walls formed by Nature from solid limestone damp with a chilly sweat. It was romantic and mysterious to stand there in the deep darkness and gaze out over the green valley gleaming in the sunlight. But the solemnity of the scene soon faded, and the rough play began again. As soon as a candle was lit, everyone rushed at its owner; a struggle and brave defense followed, but the candle was quickly knocked down or blown out, bringing a delighted uproar of laughter and another chase. Yet everything ends. By-and-by the procession filed down the steep slope of the main passage, its flickering line of lights faintly showing the towering rock walls nearly to where they met sixty feet above. This main passage was only eight or ten feet across. Every few steps, other high, narrower cracks branched away on either side—for McDougal’s cave was merely a huge maze of twisting aisles that joined one another, emerged again, and led nowhere."}

She would wait—and, sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was settled: Jane was to go. Quite a surprise to me! I had not the slightest notion! Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and immediately told her that, after considering the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s situation, she had resolved to accept it. I knew nothing of it until the whole matter was settled.”

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us; Mrs. Elton insisted that we should come. It was arranged on the hill, while we were walking about with Mr. Knightley. ‘You _must_ _all_ spend your evening with us,’ she said—‘I absolutely must have you _all_ come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he refused from the beginning; and although I thought he would come, since Mrs. Elton declared she would not excuse him, he did not—but my mother, Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very agreeable evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, must always seem agreeable, though everyone appeared rather tired after the morning’s party. Even pleasure, you know, can be exhausting—and I cannot say that any of them seemed to have enjoyed it very much. Still, _I_ shall always consider it a pleasant party, and feel deeply obliged to the kind friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you did not know it, had been deciding the whole day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time comes, it must be unwelcome to her and all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every possible advantage—I mean, in regard to the family’s character and manners.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, it contains everything in the world that could make her happy. Except the Sucklings and Bragges, there is no other nursery establishment in all Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance so liberal and elegant. Mrs. Smallridge is a most delightful woman!—A style of living almost equal to Maple Grove—and as for the children, except the little Sucklings and little Bragges, there are nowhere such elegant, sweet children. Jane will be treated with such consideration and kindness!—It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary!—I really cannot presume to tell you what her salary is, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"faa594650690df9463663877","rewritten_text":"“Well,” I said, “I needed the watermelon.” But he said I didn’t need it to escape from prison; that was the difference. He said if I’d wanted it to hide a knife in and smuggle it to Jim so he could kill the seneschal, it would have been all right. So I let it go, though I couldn’t see any advantage in pretending to be a prisoner if I had to sit down and chew over a lot of fine distinctions like that every time I saw a chance to grab a watermelon.

Well, as I was saying, that morning we waited until everyone had settled down to work and no one was in sight around the yard. Then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood a little way off to keep watch. After a while he came out, and we went and sat on the woodpile to talk. He said:

“Everything’s all right now except the tools; and that’s easy to fix.”

“Tools?” I said.

“Yes.”

“Tools for what?”

“Why, to dig with. We aren’t going to _gnaw_ him out, are we?”

“Aren’t those old crippled picks and things in there good enough to dig a Black man out with?” I said.

He turned on me, looking so pitying he could have made anyone cry, and said:

“Huck Finn, have you _ever_ heard of a prisoner having picks and shovels, with all the modern conveniences in his wardrobe to dig himself out with? Now I want to ask you—if you have any sense at all—what kind of chance would _that_ give him to be a hero? Why, they might as well lend him the key and be done with it. Picks and shovels—why, they wouldn’t provide them even to a king.”

“Well, then,” I said, “if we don’t want the picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of case knives.”

“To dig the foundations out from under that cabin?”

“Yes.”

“Damn it, Tom, that’s foolish.”

“It doesn’t matter how foolish it is; it’s the _right_ way—and it’s the usual way. And there isn’t any _other_ way that I’ve ever heard of, and I’ve read all the books that give information about these things. They always dig out with a case knife—and not through dirt, mind you; usually it’s through solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever and ever. Why, look at one of those prisoners in the bottom dungeon of the Château d’If, in the harbor of Marseilles, who dug himself out that way; how long do you suppose _he_ worked at it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don’t know. A month and a half.”"}

{"request_id":"4d607690ec6e417781ab923f","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind her, except the memory that such things had once existed.

Anne had not returned to Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and whenever it had been possible for her to go to the Hall, she had found a way to avoid it. Her first return was to take her place again in the Lodge’s modern, elegant rooms and delight its mistress.

Lady Russell’s joy at seeing her was mixed with some anxiety. She knew who had been spending time at Uppercross. Fortunately, either Anne had grown healthier and better-looking, or Lady Russell imagined that she had; and as Anne accepted her compliments, she amused herself by connecting them with her cousin’s silent admiration and hoping that she might enjoy a second spring of youth and beauty.

As they talked, Anne soon noticed a change in her own mind. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, and that she had felt neglected and been forced to suppress among the Musgroves, had now become matters of only secondary importance. She had lately lost sight even of her father, her sister, and Bath. The concerns of Uppercross had pushed everything else aside. When Lady Russell returned to their former hopes and fears, expressed her satisfaction that a house in Camden Place had been taken, and regretted that Mrs Clay was still living with them, Anne would have been ashamed to admit how much more she was thinking about Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her acquaintances there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick interested her far more than her father’s house in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness to Mrs Clay. She actually had to make an effort to show Lady Russell anything like equal concern about subjects that naturally deserved her first attention.

At first, there was some awkwardness when they spoke of another matter. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had been at the Lodge less than five minutes the previous day when the full story had reached her; but it still had to be discussed. She had to ask questions, regret the imprudence, mourn the result, and both of them had to mention Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne knew she did not manage this as well as Lady Russell. She could not say his name while looking directly at Lady Russell until she had found a way to explain briefly what she thought of his attachment to Louisa."}

{"request_id":"ef48347e3a6817f70b2a620d","rewritten_text":"“This must have been around that very period of Mr Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “which has always aroused my particular curiosity. It must have been about the same time that he became known to my father and sister. I never knew him myself; I only heard about him; but there was something in his conduct then, toward my father and sister, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, which I could never quite reconcile with his present character. It seemed to reveal a very different kind of man.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” cried Mrs Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but I heard him speak of them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I may be able to satisfy you on points you would hardly expect; and as for his marriage, I knew everything about it at the time. I was aware of all the arguments for and against it; I was the friend to whom he confided his hopes and plans; and although I had not known his wife before—her inferior position in society, in fact, made that impossible—I knew her throughout the rest of her life, or at least until the last two years, and can answer any question you may wish to ask.”

“No,” said Anne, “I have no particular inquiry to make about her. I have always understood that they were not a happy couple. But I should like to know why, at that stage of his life, he slighted my father’s acquaintance as he did. My father was certainly inclined to treat him with great kindness and proper attention. Why did Mr Elliot withdraw?”

“Mr Elliot,” replied Mrs Smith, “at that period of his life, had one aim: to make his fortune, and by a somewhat faster method than the law. He was determined to do it through marriage. At least, he was determined not to damage it through an imprudent marriage; and I know it was his belief—whether rightly or not, I cannot of course decide—that your father and sister, in their courtesies and invitations, were planning a match between the heir and the young lady, and it was impossible that such a match could satisfy his ideas of wealth and independence. That was why he withdrew, I assure you. He told me the whole story. He kept nothing from me. It was curious that, having just left you behind in Bath, my first and closest acquaintance after marrying should be your cousin; and that, through him, I should continually hear about your father and sister.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"48fb6272cb552e3acf54d33c","rewritten_text":"I would pretend to die; my satisfied heirs would take possession of my wealth, and I would gain my freedom. But I would have to plan carefully. I could not be left without means; I had to secure some money. Alas, what shameful measures I was forced to take! Yet a whole life of deceit was otherwise my fate. Whenever remorse at planning a fraud made me draw back, I was driven back to it and confirmed in my purpose by the visit of some aunt or cousin. They would tell me that death came to everyone. Then they would say that my father had surely lost his mind since my mother’s death; that he was mad, and that I was lucky, because in one of his fits he might have killed me instead of destroying his own troubled mind. All this, of course, was said delicately—not in plain words, lest my feelings be hurt, but in dark hints, whispered softly and quietly, with lowered eyes and sympathetic smiles or whimpers. I listened with a calm face while every nerve in me trembled; I, who dared not say yes or no to any of this blasphemy. Oh, what a delightful life, entirely free of deceit! I had the look of a dove and the heart of a fox. In truth, I felt only the shame of lying, not any sacred sense of innocent purpose that might redeem it. I, who had once clothed myself in the bright dress of sincerity, must now borrow one of many colors. It might fit awkwardly at first, but practice would teach me to arrange its folds elegantly and to lie with grace. Yes, I might stain my soul with falsehood until I had completely hidden its natural color. Oh, beloved father! Accept the pure heart of your unhappy daughter; let me join you as untainted as I was, or you will not recognize what I have become. Just as grief might change Constance, deceit would change me, until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy both now and when we meet again, I must flee from this life, which is a mockery to someone like me. Only in solitude can I be myself; in solitude I shall be yours.\n\nAlas, even now I look back with disgust at the tricks and schemes by which, after many painful struggles, I managed to escape. I could give a long account of the methods I used, first to secure a small income for the rest of my life and then to make certain that everyone believed I was dead. I could, but I will not."}

{"request_id":"05047ff19c53311f2a85f76b","rewritten_text":"“You’ve fostered an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am, quite unbecoming to a person of his station: as the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, who are practical philosophers, will tell you. What business have paupers with soul or spirit? It’s sufficient that we allow ’em living bodies. If you’d kept the boy on gruel, ma’am, this would never have occurred.”

“Dear, dear!” ejaculated Mrs. Sowerberry, devoutly lifting her eyes toward the kitchen ceiling: “this is the result of being liberal!”

Mrs. Sowerberry’s liberality toward Oliver had consisted in lavishly giving him all the dirty scraps and odds and ends nobody else would eat; so there was considerable meekness and self-sacrifice in her willingly enduring Mr. Bumble’s severe accusation, of which, to do her justice, she was entirely innocent in thought, word, and deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, when the lady lowered her eyes to earth once more; “the only course now, as I understand it, is to leave him in the cellar for a day or two, until he’s somewhat starved down; then bring him out, and keep him on gruel throughout the apprenticeship. He comes from a bad family. Excitable dispositions, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both nurse and doctor said that his mother forced her way here, through difficulties and pain that would have killed any respectable woman, weeks beforehand.”

At this stage of Mr. Bumble’s speech, Oliver, hearing enough to understand that his mother was being mentioned, began kicking again, with such force that every other sound was drowned. Sowerberry returned at that moment. Oliver’s offence having been described to him, with whatever exaggerations the ladies considered most likely to inflame his anger, he unlocked the cellar door in an instant and hauled his rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver’s clothes had been ripped during the beating he had suffered; his face was bruised and scratched, and his hair lay scattered across his forehead. The angry flush had not faded, however; and when dragged from his prison, he glared boldly at Noah and appeared entirely undaunted.

“Now, you’re a fine young fellow, aren’t you?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and boxing his ear.

“He called my mother names,” Oliver answered.

“Well, and what if he did, you little ungrateful wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved what he said, and worse.”

“She didn’t,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“It’s a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry broke into a torrent of tears.

That torrent of tears left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Had he paused for even a moment before punishing Oliver with the utmost severity, it must be obvious to every experienced reader that, according to all established precedents in matrimonial disputes, he would have been a brute, an unnatural husband, an insulting creature, a poor counterfeit of a man, and several other agreeable characters too numerous to list within this chapter’s limits."}

{"request_id":"493a6916368ae7f4bc374903","rewritten_text":"Of course, he was very amusing and all that, but I was terribly disappointed; and when I asked him about the coat of mail, he merely laughed and said it was far too cold to wear in England. Ah, here is Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you must remove your glove. No, not the left hand—the other.’

‘Dear Gladys, I really don’t think this is quite proper,’ said the Duchess, weakly unbuttoning a rather dirty kid glove.

‘Nothing interesting ever is,’ said Lady Windermere: ‘_on a fait le monde ainsi_. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favorite cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley, and if you say that she has a larger mount of the moon than I do, I shall never believe in you again.’

‘I am sure, Gladys, there is nothing of the sort in my hand,’ said the Duchess solemnly.

‘Your Grace is quite right,’ said Mr. Podgers, examining the small, plump hand with its short square fingers. ‘The mount of the moon is not developed. The life line, however, is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three distinct lines on the _rascette_! You will live to a very advanced age, Duchess, and be extremely happy. Ambition—very moderate; line of intellect not exaggerated; line of heart—’

‘Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Nothing would give me greater pleasure,’ said Mr. Podgers, bowing, ‘if the Duchess had ever been so, but I am sorry to say that I see great constancy of affection, combined with a strong sense of duty.’

‘Please continue, Mr. Podgers,’ said the Duchess, looking thoroughly pleased.

‘Economy is not the least of Your Grace’s virtues,’ Mr. Podgers continued, and Lady Windermere burst into laughter.

‘Economy is a very good thing,’ remarked the Duchess complacently. ‘When I married Paisley, he had eleven castles and not a single house fit to live in.’

‘And now he has twelve houses and not a single castle!’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Well, my dear,’ said the Duchess, ‘I like—’

‘Comfort,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘and modern conveniences, with hot water supplied to every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only thing our civilisation can give us.

‘You have described the Duchess’s character admirably, Mr. Podgers, and now you must read Lady Flora’s.’ At a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and prominent shoulder blades stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa and held out a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

‘Ah, a pianist! I see,’ said Mr. Podgers. ‘An excellent pianist, but perhaps scarcely a musician.’"}

{"request_id":"6a42f47ba113c16fd9d15dec","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret her condescension in visiting the Coles. The call supplied her with many agreeable memories on the following day; and whatever she might be thought to have sacrificed in dignified retirement would be fully compensated by the splendour of popularity. She must have given the Coles—worthy people, who deserved to be made happy!—great pleasure, and left behind her a name not soon to fade.

Perfect happiness, even in recollection, is uncommon; and there were two matters about which she was not entirely at ease. She questioned whether, in revealing her suspicions of Jane Fairfax’s feelings to Frank Churchill, she had not violated the duty of woman toward woman. It was scarcely proper; yet the thought had been so powerful that it escaped her, and his readiness to accept everything she said was such a compliment to her discernment that she could not quite decide whether silence would have been better.

The other regret concerned Jane Fairfax as well; and in that case she had no uncertainty. She sincerely and completely lamented the inferiority of her own playing and singing. She deeply mourned the idleness of her childhood—and sat down to practise energetically for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival then interrupted her; and had Harriet’s praise been enough to satisfy her, she might soon have recovered her comfort.

“Oh! if only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Do not put us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh! dear—I think you play the better of the two. I think you play quite as well as she does. I am certain I would much rather listen to you. Everyone last night said how well you played.”

“Anyone who understood the matter must have perceived the difference. The truth is, Harriet, that my playing is merely good enough to be praised, while Jane Fairfax’s is far beyond it.”

“Well, I shall always think you play quite as well as she does, or that, if there is a difference, no one could ever discover it. Mr. Cole said how much taste you possessed; and Mr. Frank Churchill spoke at length of your taste, saying he valued taste much more than execution.”

“Ah! but Jane Fairfax possesses both, Harriet.”

“Are you certain? I saw that she had execution, but I did not know she had taste. No one mentioned it. And I detest Italian singing.—One cannot understand a word. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it is only what she is required to do, since she will have to teach.”"}

{"request_id":"4acf743273c4a628ec523f","rewritten_text":"‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he really is some kind of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I hope he is a foreigner, at least. That would make it rather less unpleasant.’

‘I must certainly present him to you.’

‘Present him!’ exclaimed the Duchess. ‘You don’t mean that he is here?’ She began searching for a little tortoiseshell fan and a very ragged lace shawl, ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here; I should never think of giving a party without him. He says that I have a perfectly psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even slightly shorter, I would have become a confirmed pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I understand!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘Misfortunes as well,’ replied Lady Windermere, ‘and in enormous quantities. Next year, for example, I am in serious danger on both land and sea, so I intend to live in a balloon and have my dinner hauled up to me in a basket every evening. It is all written on my little finger—or perhaps in the palm of my hand; I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence is capable of resisting temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their hands read once a month, simply to learn what they should avoid doing. Naturally, one does it anyway, but being warned is so agreeable. Now, if someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Allow me to go, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man who stood nearby, listening to the conversation with an amused smile.

‘Thank you very much, Lord Arthur; but I am afraid you would not know him.’

‘If he is as remarkable as you claim, Lady Windermere, I could hardly fail to find him. Describe him to me, and I will bring him here at once.’

‘Well, he does not resemble a chiromantist in the least. I mean, he is neither mysterious, nor esoteric, nor romantic in appearance. He is a short, stout man with an amusing bald head and enormous gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country solicitor. I am truly sorry, but it is not my fault. People are so irritating. All my pianists look precisely like poets, and all my poets look precisely like pianists. I remember last season inviting a most terrible conspirator to dinner, a man who had blown up countless people, always wore a coat of mail, and carried a dagger up his sleeve; and do you know, when he arrived, he looked exactly like a pleasant old clergyman and spent the whole evening telling jokes?’"}

{"request_id":"7b098393136809ee2593fbb7","rewritten_text":"“Are you speaking of—Mr. Knightley?”

“To be sure I am. I never imagined you could mean anyone else—and I thought you understood me. When we talked about him, it seemed perfectly clear.”

“Not quite,” Emma replied, forcing herself to remain calm. “Everything you said then seemed to me to concern someone else. I could almost swear that you had named Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain you spoke of the service Mr. Frank Churchill had done you by protecting you from the gypsies.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how can you forget?”

“My dear Harriet, I remember exactly what I said. I told you that I did not wonder at your attachment; that, considering the service he had done you, it was perfectly natural. You agreed, speaking very warmly of your gratitude and even describing what you had felt when he came forward to rescue you. I remember it clearly.”

“Oh, dear,” cried Harriet, “now I understand what you mean; but I was thinking of something quite different then. It was not the gypsies—it was not Mr. Frank Churchill I meant. No!” she added with some pride. “I was thinking of something far more precious—Mr. Knightley’s coming to ask me to dance when Mr. Elton would not dance with me, and there was no other partner in the room. That was the kind action; that was the noble kindness and generosity; that was the service that first made me feel how much better he was than every other person on earth.”

“Good God!” cried Emma. “This has been a most unfortunate—most terrible mistake! What can be done?”

“You would not have encouraged me if you had understood me? Still, I cannot be worse off than I would have been if I had meant the other man; and now—it is possible—”

She stopped for a few moments. Emma could not speak.

“I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she continued, “that you see a great difference between the two, whether you consider me or anyone else. You must think one five hundred million times above me compared with the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—that if—strange as it may seem—. You know you said yourself that more wonderful things had happened, and that matches of greater inequality had taken place than one between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it seems that even such a thing as this may have happened before. And if I should be fortunate beyond words—if Mr. Knightley should truly—if he does not mind the difference, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, that you will not oppose it or try to create difficulties.”"}

{"request_id":"ca4b03de6a168043658cbaf7","rewritten_text":"To look at him, one might have thought Nemesis had taken Pallas’s shield and revealed the Gorgon’s head to him. He appeared petrified, his face marble-like in its melancholy. He had enjoyed the refined and luxurious existence of a young man born to wealth and position, a life made exquisite by its freedom from vulgar anxieties and its graceful, youthful carelessness; but now, for the first time, he understood the dreadful mystery of Destiny, the terrible significance of Doom.

How insane and monstrous it all appeared! Could it be that upon his hand, in letters he himself could not decipher but another man could read, there lay some dreadful secret of sin, some blood-red mark of guilt? Was escape impossible? Were we merely chessmen, shifted by an invisible force, vessels shaped by the potter’s whim for honour or disgrace? His reason rebelled, yet he felt that tragedy was descending upon him, and that he had suddenly been required to carry an unbearable burden. Actors were fortunate indeed. They could decide whether to enter tragedy or comedy, whether to suffer or rejoice, laugh or weep. Real life was otherwise. Most men and women were compelled to play parts for which they were wholly unsuited. Our Guildensterns perform Hamlet for us, while our Hamlets must jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the casting is wretched.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers came into the room. On seeing Lord Arthur, he started, and his coarse, heavy face turned a kind of greenish yellow. Their eyes met, and for a moment neither spoke.

‘The Duchess has left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and has sent me to return it to her,’ Mr. Podgers said at last. ‘Ah, there it is on the sofa! Good evening.’

‘Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me a direct answer to a question I am about to ask you.’

‘Some other time, Lord Arthur, but the Duchess is waiting. I fear I must leave.’

‘You will not leave. The Duchess can wait.’

‘Ladies ought not to be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,’ said Mr. Podgers, with his sickly smile. ‘The fair sex is inclined to impatience.’

Lord Arthur’s finely carved lips twisted with irritated disdain. At that moment the unfortunate Duchess seemed scarcely important to him. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and extended his hand.

‘Tell me what you saw there,’ he said. ‘Tell me the truth. I must know. I am not a child.’"}

{"request_id":"5245bb6399d6d74b8d6e79eb","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man—a very pleasant, kind-looking old man when I woke him. I told him that my brother and I had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and had camped on part of a raft we found. Around midnight, I said, he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over there, fix it, and say nothing about it or let anyone know, because we wanted to come home that evening and surprise the family.

“Who is your family?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down there.”

“Oh,” he said. After a moment, he asked:

“How did you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”

“Strange dream,” he said.

Then he lit his lantern, got his saddlebags, and we set out. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the look of it. He said it was large enough for one, but didn’t seem very safe for two. I said:

“Oh, you needn’t be afraid, sir. It carried the three of us easily enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and _the guns_; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he said.

But he put his foot on the gunwale, rocked the canoe, shook his head, and said he supposed he’d look around for a larger one. They were all locked and chained, though, so he took my canoe and told me to wait until he returned. I could search farther, or perhaps go home and get everyone ready for the surprise, if I wanted to. But I said I didn’t, so I explained exactly how to find the raft, and he started off.

I had an idea soon afterward. I said to myself, suppose he can’t fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do—stay there until he gives everything away? No, sir; I knew what I would do. I’d wait, and when he came back, if he said he had to go anywhere else, I’d get down there too, even if I had to swim. Then we’d tie him up, keep him, and head downriver; and when Tom was finished with him, we’d pay him whatever it was worth—or all we had—and then let him get ashore.

So I crawled into a lumber pile to sleep. The next time I woke, the sun was high overhead! I rushed out and went to the doctor’s house, but they told me he had left sometime during the night and had not returned yet."}

content.text: {"request_id":"92050f2b66ac2d3022447f13","rewritten_text":"How long I remained in this condition, it is impossible to say. It must, however, have been a considerable time, for when I partly recovered my awareness, I found dawn breaking, the balloon at a tremendous height above a wilderness of ocean, and no sign of land anywhere within the immense horizon. Yet my sensations on recovering were by no means as agonizing as might have been expected. Indeed, there was something almost like the beginning of madness in the calm inspection I began to make of my situation. I raised each of my hands to my eyes in turn and wondered what event could have caused the swelling of the veins and the terrible blackness of my fingernails. I then carefully examined my head, shaking it repeatedly and feeling it with close attention, until I managed to convince myself that it was not, as I had half suspected, larger than my balloon. Next, with an air of understanding, I felt in both my trouser pockets and, finding a set of tablets and a toothpick case missing, tried to account for their disappearance. Unable to do so, I felt deeply frustrated. It now occurred to me that I was suffering severe discomfort in the joint of my left ankle, and a faint awareness of my situation began to emerge in my mind. But, strangely enough, I was neither astonished nor horrified. If I felt any emotion at all, it was a sort of amused satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to show in freeing myself from this predicament; and I never for a moment regarded my eventual safety as doubtful. For several minutes I remained absorbed in the deepest thought. I distinctly remember repeatedly pressing my lips together, placing my forefinger beside my nose, and making other gestures and grimaces familiar to men who, comfortably settled in their armchairs, ponder matters of difficulty or importance. Having, as I believed, gathered my thoughts sufficiently, I now, with great caution and deliberation, put my hands behind my back and unfastened the large iron buckle belonging to the waistband of my trousers. The buckle had three prongs, which, being somewhat rusty, turned only with great difficulty on their axes. After some effort, however, I brought them to right angles with the body of the buckle, and was pleased to find that they stayed firmly in that position. Holding the instrument I had made between my teeth, I then began to untie my cravat. I had to pause several times before I could complete this maneuver, but at last I succeeded."}

{"request_id":"9690d3b203283c19207bed1f","rewritten_text":"“And consider, ma’am,” said Oliver, as tears forced their way into his eyes despite his efforts to hold them back. “Oh! Consider how young and good she is, and how much pleasure and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I am sure—certain, completely certain—that, for your sake, since you are so good yourself; for her own sake; and for the sake of all she makes happy, she will not die. Heaven will never let her die so young.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, placing her hand on Oliver’s head. “You think like a child, poor boy. But you remind me of my duty, nevertheless. I had forgotten it for a moment, Oliver, though I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old and have witnessed enough illness and death to know the agony of being separated from those we love. I have seen enough, too, to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them; but this should comfort us in our sorrow, for Heaven is just. Such things teach us, with terrible clarity, that there is a brighter world than this, and that the journey to it is swift. God’s will be done! I love her; and He knows how deeply!”

Oliver was surprised to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke these words, she checked her grief as if by a single effort; and, straightening herself as she spoke, became calm and resolute. He was even more astonished to find that this strength endured, and that throughout all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie was always ready and composed, carrying out every duty that had fallen to her steadily and, to all outward appearances, even cheerfully. But he was young and did not know what strong minds can endure under trying circumstances. How could he, when those who possess them so rarely understand their own strength?

An anxious night followed. When morning came, Mrs. Maylie’s fears had been only too fully confirmed. Rose was in the first stage of a severe and dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not surrender to useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, placing a finger to her lips as she looked steadily into his face. “This letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne as quickly as possible. It must be taken to the market town, which is no more than four miles away by the footpath across the fields, and from there sent by a mounted messenger directly to Chertsey. The people at the inn will arrange this, and I know I can trust you to see it done.”

Oliver could not reply, but his anxious expression showed that he wanted to leave at once."}

{"request_id":"acc6d016f015a2621f828c3c","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke warmly in praise of his sister’s skill.

“I am very pleased to hear so favorable an account of her,” said Lady Catherine; “and pray tell her from me that she cannot hope to excel unless she practises a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he answered, “that she has no need of such advice. She practises very regularly.”

“So much the better. One cannot practise too much; and when I next write to her, I shall insist that she neglect it on no account. I often tell young ladies that no musical excellence can be gained without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play truly well unless she practises more; and though Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is quite welcome, as I have often said, to come to Rosings every day and play the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She would be in no one’s way there, you know, in that part of the house.”

Mr. Darcy appeared somewhat embarrassed by his aunt’s lack of manners and made no reply.

When coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth that she had promised to play for him, and she immediately sat down at the instrument. He brought a chair close beside her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then resumed her conversation with her other nephew, until he moved away from her and, proceeding with his customary deliberation toward the pianoforte, placed himself where he had a full view of the fair performer’s face. Elizabeth noticed his purpose, and at the first suitable pause turned to him with a mischievous smile.

“You intend to frighten me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in such solemn state to hear me. But I shall not be alarmed, though your sister does play so well. I have a stubbornness that cannot endure being frightened at another person’s pleasure. My courage always increases with every effort to intimidate me.”

“I shall not say that you are mistaken,” he replied, “because you could not truly suppose that I meant to alarm you; and I have known you long enough to understand that you take great pleasure in sometimes declaring opinions which are not really your own.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this portrait of herself, and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very amusing idea of me, and teach you never to believe a word I say. I am especially unfortunate to meet someone so capable of revealing my true character, in a part of the world where I had hoped to present myself with some credit.”"}

{"request_id":"c7be3d527054655d6d13d502","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis, at Lady Canterville’s earnest request, had agreed to retain in her old position. She gave each of them a low curtsey as they stepped down, and said in a quaint, old-fashioned way, ‘I welcome you to Canterville Chase.’ They followed her through the handsome Tudor hall into the library, a long, low chamber panelled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at the far end. Tea had been prepared for them there, and, after removing their wraps, they sat down and began looking about while Mrs. Umney attended to them.

All at once Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red mark on the floor beside the fireplace and, quite unaware of its true meaning, said to Mrs. Umney, ‘I fear something has been spilled there.’

‘Yes, madam,’ answered the old housekeeper softly, ‘blood was spilled in that place.’

‘How dreadful,’ exclaimed Mrs. Otis; ‘I really dislike bloodstains in a sitting-room. It must be cleaned away immediately.’

The old woman smiled and replied in the same quiet, mysterious tone, ‘It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered on that very spot by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine years beyond her, then vanished suddenly in circumstances of the greatest mystery. His body has never been found, but his guilty ghost still haunts the Chase. Tourists and others have greatly admired the stain, and it cannot be removed.’

‘That is complete nonsense,’ cried Washington Otis; ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will take it off in no time.’ Before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he had dropped to his knees and was vigorously scrubbing the floor with a little stick of what appeared to be black cosmetic. Within moments, not a trace of the bloodstain remained.

‘I knew Pinkerton would manage it,’ he declared proudly, glancing around at his admiring family. But scarcely had he spoken when a dreadful flash of lightning illuminated the gloomy room, a terrifying crash of thunder sent them all springing to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

‘What an outrageous climate!’ said the American Minister calmly, lighting a long cheroot. ‘I suppose the old country is so crowded that there isn’t enough respectable weather to go around. I have always believed emigration is England’s only solution.’

‘My dear Hiram,’ cried Mrs. Otis, ‘what are we to do with a woman who faints?’

‘Put it down as breakage,’ replied the Minister; ‘she won’t faint again after that.’ And within a few moments Mrs. Umney had indeed recovered."}

{"request_id":"64ec38bd8120d525083f637f","rewritten_text":"At least, that was what he thought. But who could say? ... No. There had been nothing else. He had spared her out of vanity. He had put on the mask of goodness through hypocrisy. For curiosity, he had attempted self-denial. He understood that now.

But this murder—would it pursue him all his life? Was he forever to be weighed down by his past? Was he truly going to confess? Never. There was only one piece of evidence remaining against him. The picture itself—that was evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it for so long? Once, he had taken pleasure in watching it change and grow old. Lately, he had found no pleasure in it. It had kept him awake at night. When he was away, terror had filled him at the thought of other eyes seeing it. It had cast melancholy over his passions. The mere recollection of it had spoiled many joyful moments. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

He glanced around and saw the knife with which he had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it repeatedly, until not a trace remained upon it. It was bright and gleaming. Just as it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and everything that work signified. It would destroy the past, and once the past was dead, he would be free. It would end this monstrous life of the soul, and without its hideous warnings, he would be at peace. He grasped the knife and drove it into the picture.

A cry rang out, followed by a crash. The cry was so terrible in its agony that the frightened servants awoke and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing through the square below stopped and looked up at the great house. They continued on until they encountered a policeman, whom they brought back with them. The man rang the bell several times, but no one answered. Apart from a light in one of the upper windows, the house was completely dark. After a while, he went away and stood beneath a neighboring portico, watching.

“Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” the policeman replied.

As they walked away, they looked at one another and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed domestics spoke to one another in hushed whispers. Old Mrs. Leaf wept and wrung her hands. Francis was pale as death.

After roughly a quarter of an hour, he took the coachman and one of the footmen and crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"32748ce178f9bc2925fdf084","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had never happened. She supposed he had drunk too freely of Mr. Weston’s excellent wine, and was certain he would be inclined to talk absurdly.

To restrain him as far as her own conduct could, she at once prepared to speak with perfect calm and solemnity about the weather and the night. Yet scarcely had she started, scarcely had they passed the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, when she found her topic interrupted—her hand taken, her attention claimed, and Mr. Elton actually making passionate love to her: seizing the valuable opportunity, declaring feelings that must already be known, hoping—fearing—adoring—prepared to die if she rejected him; while flattering himself that his fervent attachment, incomparable love, and unprecedented passion could not fail to produce some effect, and, in short, being firmly determined to be accepted seriously as soon as possible. It was truly so. Without hesitation—without apology—and with little visible embarrassment, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s lover, was declaring himself _her_ lover. She attempted to stop him, but without success; he continued, saying everything. Angry though she was, the thought of the situation made her resolve to control herself when she answered. She felt that half this foolishness must be caused by drink, and could therefore hope it might belong only to the present hour. Accordingly, combining seriousness with playfulness, as she hoped would best suit his divided condition, she replied,

“I am exceedingly astonished, Mr. Elton. This to _me_! You have forgotten yourself—you mistake me for my friend—any message for Miss Smith I shall gladly deliver; but no more of this to _me_, if you please.”

“Miss Smith!—a message for Miss Smith!—What could she possibly mean?”—And he repeated her words with such confident emphasis, such boastful display of astonishment, that she could not help answering sharply,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behaviour! I can explain it in only one way: you are not yourself, or you could not speak either to me, or about Harriet, in such a fashion. Control yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to raise his spirits, not enough to cloud his understanding. He knew perfectly well what he meant; and after warmly protesting that her suspicion was deeply insulting, and briefly mentioning his regard for Miss Smith as her friend—while admitting his surprise that Miss Smith had been brought up at all—he returned to the subject of his own passion and pressed very earnestly for a favourable answer."}

{"request_id":"f0617b38ce740fdc756cbd70","rewritten_text":"Dear me, she was a wonderful talker. It would not have been fitting for me to hint that it was very late, that I was tired, and that sleep weighed heavily upon me. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the opportunity. Now I had to endure it; there was no alternative. So she tinkled on and on through the otherwise deep, ghostly silence of the sleeping castle, until presently there arose, seemingly from far beneath us, a distant sound like a muffled shriek—with such agony in it that my flesh crept. The queen paused, and pleasure shone in her eyes; she inclined her graceful head as a bird does when listening. Again the sound forced its way upward through the stillness.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and endureth long. It is many hours now.”

“Endureth what?”

“The rack. Come—ye shall see a merry sight. If he yield not his secret now, ye shall see him torn apart.”

What a smooth-tongued fiend she was; and how calm and tranquil, while the cords running down my legs ached in sympathy with that man's suffering. Led by armored guards carrying blazing torches, we marched through echoing passages and down damp, dripping stone stairs that smelled of mold and centuries of captive darkness—a cold, eerie journey, and a lengthy one, made neither shorter nor more pleasant by the sorceress's account of the prisoner and his offense. An anonymous informer had accused him of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony is not quite the proper thing, your Highness. It would be fairer to confront the accused with his accuser.”

“I had not considered it, since it seemed a matter of little importance. But if I wished to do so, I could not, because the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, and immediately departed again, so that the forester knoweth him not.”

“Then was this Unknown the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Marry, _no_ man _saw_ the killing, but this Unknown saw this bold wretch near the place where the stag lay, and came with most loyal zeal and betrayed him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag as well? Is it not possible that he killed it himself? His loyal zeal—in a mask—seems somewhat suspicious. But what does your Highness hope to gain by racking the prisoner? Where is the benefit?”

“He will not confess otherwise; and then his soul would be lost. By law his life is forfeited for the crime—and surely will I see that he pay it!—but it would endanger my own soul to let him die without confession and absolution."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e2ccd8e25c6d7b4558df61ad","rewritten_text":"Dawn had arrived when I put the Manuscript away. The rain was nearly over; the world looked gray and mournful, while the spent storm sighed and sobbed itself into rest. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his door, which stood slightly open. I could hear his voice, and knocked. No answer came, though the voice continued. I peered inside. The man lay on his back in bed, speaking in broken phrases but with animation, emphasizing them with his arms, which he flung about restlessly, as the sick do in delirium. I entered quietly and leaned over him. His mutterings and exclamations continued. I spoke—only a word, to attract his notice. At once his glassy eyes and ashen face brightened with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome:\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you have come at last—how I have yearned for you! Sit beside me—do not go—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand?—give it to me, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is well, everything is peaceful, and I am happy again—we are happy again, are we not, Sandy? You are so indistinct, so shadowy, merely a mist, a cloud, but you are here, and that is blessedness enough; and I have your hand; do not withdraw it—it will be only for a little while, and I shall not need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello—Central!... she does not answer. Perhaps she is asleep? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say good-bye.... Sandy! Yes, you are there. I lost myself for a moment and thought you had gone.... Have I been ill long? It must be so; it seems months to me. And such dreams! such strange and terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality—delirium, of course, but so real! Why, I thought the king was dead, that you were in Gaul and unable to return, that there had been a revolution; in the wild frenzy of those dreams, I thought Clarence and I and a small band of my cadets fought and destroyed all the chivalry of England! Yet even that was not the strangest. I seemed to be a being from some distant unborn age, centuries ahead, and even that felt as real as everything else! Yes, I seemed to have flown backward from that age into our own, then forward to it once more, and to have been left, a stranger and forsaken, in that strange England, with an abyss thirteen centuries wide gaping between you and me! between me and my home and my friends! between me and everything dear to me, everything that could make life worth living!"}

{"request_id":"e55bee03d4940b18cf3e0a9a","rewritten_text":"My father’s family name was Pirrip, and my Christian name was Philip. But my baby tongue could not say either name properly, so I called myself Pip, and everyone else came to call me Pip.

I know Pirrip was my father’s family name because it was written on his tombstone, and because my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, told me so. She was married to the blacksmith. I never saw my father or mother, and never saw a picture of either of them, since they lived before photographs existed. So my first ideas about their appearance came foolishly from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on my father’s stone made me imagine him as a short, broad, dark man with curly black hair. From the wording and style of the inscription, “_Also Georgiana Wife of the Above_,” I decided, as a child, that my mother had freckles and poor health. Beside their grave stood five small stone markers, each about a foot and a half long, arranged in a neat row. They honored my five little brothers, who had given up trying to survive in this world very early. Because of them, I firmly believed that they had all been born lying on their backs with their hands in their trouser pockets, and had never removed them during their lives.

We lived in the marsh country, beside the river and, following its winding course, twenty miles from the sea. My first clear and powerful understanding of the world came on a cold, raw afternoon near evening. Then I learned for certain that this bleak place, covered with nettles, was the churchyard; that Philip Pirrip, formerly of this parish, and Georgiana, his wife, were dead and buried; that Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, their infant children, were also dead and buried; and that the dark, flat wilderness beyond the churchyard, crossed by ditches, raised banks, and gates, with cattle scattered across it, was the marshes. I learned that the low, dull line in the distance was the river; that the wild, distant place from which the wind came rushing was the sea; and that the small, shivering child who was growing frightened and beginning to cry was Pip.

“Be quiet!” shouted a terrible voice, as a man rose among the graves beside the church porch. “Stay still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”

He was a frightening man dressed all in rough gray clothes, with a large iron shackle on his leg."}

{"request_id":"0351c22e2274484b938c6f54","rewritten_text":"Knights and horses in heavy armor could not travel very fast. They would make the best time they could, and now that the ground was in good condition, without snow or mud, they would probably manage seven miles an hour; they would have to change horses a couple of times; they would arrive around six, or shortly afterward; it would still be light enough; they would see the white cloth I was to tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround that prison and have the king out in no time. It would be showy and picturesque enough, all things considered, though I would have preferred noon, because the whole affair would have been more theatrical then.

Now, to add another string to my bow, I thought I would look up some of the people I had formerly recognized and make myself known. That might get us out of our trouble without the knights. But I had to proceed cautiously, for it was risky. I needed to get into sumptuous clothing, and it would not do to rush into it. No, I had to work up to it gradually, buying one suit after another in shops far apart, choosing a slightly finer article each time, until I finally reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I began.

But the scheme collapsed completely! At the first corner I turned, I came straight upon one of our slaves, prowling around with a watchman. I coughed at that moment, and he gave me a sudden look that pierced to my marrow. I judged that he thought he had heard that cough before. I immediately turned into a shop and moved along the counter, pricing things and watching from the corner of my eye. Those men had stopped, talking together and looking in through the door. I decided to escape by the back way, if there was one, and asked the shopwoman whether I could step outside and search for the escaped slave, who was believed to be hiding somewhere back there. I told her I was an officer in disguise, that my partner was at the door with one of the murderers in custody, and asked whether she would kindly go out and tell him he need not wait, but should hurry to the far end of the back alley and be ready to head the slave off when I drove him out.

She was bursting with eagerness to see one of the already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand at once."}
