{"request_id":"af336f07c9b8b95f279315b5","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water with which to end the feast. After a while Becky proposed that they go on again. Tom remained quiet for a moment, then said:

“Becky, can you stand it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face grew pale, but she believed she could.

“Well, then, Becky, we have to stay here, where there’s water to drink. That small piece is our last candle!”

Becky burst into tears and lamentations. Tom tried to comfort her, but with little success. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and search for us!”

“Yes, they will! Of course they will!”

“Perhaps they’re looking for us now, Tom.”

“Why, I suppose they may be. I hope they are.”

“When will they miss us, Tom?”

“When they return to the boat, I suppose.”

“Tom, it may be dark by then—would they notice that we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But your mother would miss you as soon as they reached home.”

The frightened expression on Becky’s face brought Tom back to his senses, and he realized he had blundered. Becky was not supposed to have gone home that night! The children fell silent and thoughtful. Soon another outburst of grief from Becky showed Tom that the thought in his own mind had entered hers as well—that Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher learned that Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children fixed their eyes on their little piece of candle and watched it slowly and mercilessly melt away; saw the last half-inch of wick stand by itself; saw the weak flame rise and sink, climb the slender pillar of smoke, pause at its top for a moment, and then—the terror of complete darkness descended!

How much later it was when Becky slowly became aware that she was weeping in Tom’s arms, neither of them could say. They knew only that, after what seemed an immense span of time, both awoke from a deathlike stupor of sleep and returned once more to their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday now—perhaps Monday. He tried to make Becky talk, but her sorrow weighed too heavily; all her hope had vanished. Tom said they must have been missed long before, and surely the search was continuing. He would shout, and perhaps someone would come. He tried, but in the darkness the far-off echoes sounded so dreadful that he did not try again.

The hours slipped away, and hunger came to torment the captives once more. A piece of Tom’s half of the cake remained; they divided it and ate. Yet they seemed hungrier than before."}

{"request_id":"05de974b2f3fa6b072b9ac73","rewritten_text":"The following day was set for the production (lest our honour grow cold through delay), and on that day Drummle appeared with a polite little statement in Estella’s handwriting, saying that she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. This left me no choice but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, on the whole, to reject as untenable the idea that I was to be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove engaged in indiscriminate contradiction, and at last the promotion of good feeling was pronounced to have advanced at an astonishing rate.

I speak of this lightly, but it was no light matter to me. I cannot adequately express the pain it caused me to think that Estella should show any favour to a contemptible, clumsy, sulky fool, so far below the average. Even now, I believe it was due to some pure fire of generosity and selflessness in my love for her that I could not bear the thought of her stooping to that hound. No doubt I should have been miserable whoever she had favoured; but a worthier object would have caused me a different sort and degree of distress.

It was easy for me to discover, and I soon did discover, that Drummle had begun following her closely, and that she permitted him to do so. Before long, he was always pursuing her, and he and I crossed paths every day. He persisted in a dull, stubborn way, and Estella kept him at it: sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes almost flattering him, sometimes openly despising him, sometimes seeming to know him perfectly, and sometimes scarcely remembering who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had called him, was accustomed to lying in wait, however, and possessed the patience of his kind. Besides, he had a blockheaded confidence in his money and his family’s greatness, which sometimes served him well—almost taking the place of concentration and determined purpose. Thus the Spider, doggedly watching Estella, outwaited many brighter insects, and would often uncoil himself and drop at exactly the right moment.

At a certain Assembly Ball in Richmond (there used to be Assembly Balls in most places then), where Estella had outshone every other beauty, this blundering Drummle lingered around her so persistently, and with such tolerance on her part, that I resolved to speak to her about him. I took the next opportunity, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home and was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave."}

{"request_id":"3642342bb4b9ce779cec0ed6","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, the force of gravity would steadily decrease according to the square of the distance. As my speed increased enormously, I would eventually reach those distant regions where the moon’s attraction replaced the earth’s. For that reason, I did not think it necessary to carry more provisions than would last forty days.

“There was, however, another difficulty that caused me some concern. It has been observed that during balloon ascents to great heights, people suffer not only pain when breathing but also severe discomfort in the head and body, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms. These troubles become worse as the altitude increases. This was a disturbing thought. Was it not likely that the symptoms would continue to grow, perhaps until death ended them? In the end, I decided that this was not so. They seemed to result from the gradual removal of the usual atmospheric pressure from the body’s surface, which caused the small blood vessels near the skin to expand. They did not arise from any actual breakdown of the body, as breathing difficulties do when the air is too thin to renew the blood properly in one of the heart’s chambers. If the blood could still be renewed, I saw no reason why life could not continue even in a vacuum. The expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is purely muscular action, and is the cause rather than the result of respiration. In short, I believed that as the body grew used to the lack of atmospheric pressure, the painful sensations would gradually lessen. Until then, I trusted in the iron strength of my constitution to endure them.

“Thus, Your Excellencies, I have described some, though certainly not all, of the thoughts that led me to plan a journey to the moon. I shall now tell you what happened when I attempted a voyage so daring in its design and, in any case, entirely without precedent in human history.

“After reaching the altitude I mentioned earlier—three miles and three-quarters—I threw a quantity of feathers out of the car and found that I was still rising fast enough. There was therefore no need to release any ballast. I was pleased, because I wanted to keep as much weight with me as possible, for reasons that will be explained later."}

content.text: {"request_id":"4d8bd01c8f0b6729d840a105","rewritten_text":"In my time, in my own country, this money was raised through imposts, and the citizen fancied that the foreign importer paid it, finding comfort in that belief; but in truth it was paid by the American people, distributed among them so evenly and exactly that the yearly cost to the hundred-millionaire and to the day-laborer’s nursing infant was exactly alike—each paid $6. I reckon nothing could be fairer. Now, Scotland and Ireland were tributary to Arthur, and the combined population of the British Islands was somewhat under 1,000,000. A mechanic’s average wage was 3 cents a day, when he supported himself. By that measure, the national government’s expenses came to $90,000 annually, or roughly $250 per day. So, by replacing gold with nickels on a king’s-evil day, I harmed nobody, displeased nobody, pleased everyone concerned, and besides saved four-fifths of that day’s national expense—a saving equal to $800,000 in my America. In making the exchange I had borrowed wisdom from a very distant source—my boyhood—for a true statesman scorns no wisdom, however humble its origin: as a boy I had always saved my pennies and given buttons to the foreign missionary cause. Buttons would serve the ignorant savage as well as coin, while coin served me better than buttons; everyone was satisfied and no one was injured.\n\nMarinel received the patients as they arrived. He inspected each candidate; if the person failed to qualify, he was turned away; if he passed, he was sent on to the king. A priest recited the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king rubbed the ulcers while the reading went on; at last the patient completed the process, received his nickel—the king himself hanging it about his neck—and was dismissed. Would you suppose that this could cure? It certainly could. Any ceremony will cure when the patient’s faith in it is strong. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who herded geese there—the girl herself said so—and they built the chapel on that very spot and hung within it a picture depicting the event, a picture you might think unsafe for a sick person to approach. Yet thousands of the lame and ill came each year to pray before it and departed healed and sound; even the healthy could gaze upon it and live."}

{"request_id":"42c12b82c33a19f705a462f6","rewritten_text":"“I now hasten to the most affecting portion of my story. I shall describe events that filled me with emotions which, from what I had once been, have made me what I now am.

“Spring progressed swiftly; the weather grew pleasant and the skies remained without a cloud. I was astonished that the place which had formerly seemed barren and gloomy should now flourish with the loveliest flowers and greenery. My senses were delighted and renewed by countless pleasant fragrances and innumerable scenes of beauty.

“It was during one of these days, when my cottagers took their regular rest from work—the old man playing his guitar while the children listened—that I noticed Felix’s face was melancholy beyond expression. He sighed often, and once his father stopped playing; from his manner, I guessed that he asked the reason for his son’s sadness. Felix answered in a cheerful tone, and the old man was beginning his music again when someone knocked at the door.

“It was a lady on horseback, attended by a countryman serving as her guide. She wore a dark dress and was concealed beneath a heavy black veil. Agatha asked her something, but the stranger answered only by speaking Felix’s name in a sweet voice. Her voice was musical, though unlike that of either of my companions. At hearing the name, Felix hurried toward the lady. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, and I beheld a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was glossy raven-black and intricately braided; her eyes were dark, yet gentle and lively; her features were perfectly proportioned, and her remarkably fair complexion was touched with a lovely flush in each cheek.

“Felix appeared transported with joy at seeing her. Every sign of sorrow disappeared, and his face immediately showed an ecstatic happiness I could scarcely have imagined it capable of expressing. His eyes glittered and his cheeks reddened with pleasure; at that instant, I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed moved by other emotions; brushing several tears from her lovely eyes, she extended her hand to Felix, who kissed it passionately and called her, as far as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but smiled. He helped her dismount and, sending away her guide, led her into the cottage. He exchanged some words with his father, while the young stranger knelt before the old man and tried to kiss his hand; but he lifted her up and embraced her warmly.

“I soon discovered that, although the stranger made articulate sounds and seemed to possess a language of her own, neither she nor the cottagers understood the other.”"}

{"request_id":"919de07b5e2792991004dee7","rewritten_text":"“Now, in English, the letter appearing most often is e. After that, the order is: _a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z_. _E_ is so overwhelmingly common that a sentence of almost any length is seldom found without its being the dominant character.

“Here, then, at the outset, we have the basis of something more substantial than a mere conjecture. The table’s general usefulness is evident—but with this particular cipher, we shall need its assistance only to a limited extent. Since our most frequent character is 8, we shall begin by supposing it to be the _e_ of the ordinary alphabet. To test this idea, let us see whether 8 occurs in pairs—for _e_ is very often doubled in English—in words such as ‘meet,’ ‘.fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In this case, we find it doubled no fewer than five times, though the cryptograph is short.

“Let us, then, take 8 for _e_. Now, among all _words_ in the language, ‘the’ occurs most frequently; let us consequently determine whether any three characters are repeated in the same order, with the last being 8. If we find such repeated groups, they will very likely stand for ‘the.’ On examination, we discover no fewer than seven such combinations, the characters being ;48. We may therefore suppose that ; is _t_, 4 is _h_, and 8 is _e_—the last conclusion now being strongly confirmed. Thus we have made considerable progress.

“But once a single word has been established, we can determine a highly important matter: several beginnings and endings of other words. Consider, for instance, the next-to-last occurrence of ;48, situated near the cipher’s end. We know that the following ; begins a word, and of the six characters after this ‘the,’ we know five. Let us write them down using the letters whose meanings we have established, leaving a blank for the unknown one—

t eeth.

“Here we can immediately reject the ‘th’ as belonging to the word beginning with the first t; for, by trying every alphabetic letter in the vacant place, we see that no word can be made in which this _th_ forms part. We are therefore reduced to

t ee,

and, by running through the alphabet if needed, as before, we reach the word ‘tree’ as the only possible reading.”"}

{"request_id":"9c02a74a44a997ff6c8359e5","rewritten_text":"I now turn to my own history. There is little to tell of the earlier part of my life, and I shall pass over it quickly; yet I must linger somewhat upon my childhood, so that it may be understood how, when one hope failed, all existence would have become a blank; and how, when the sole affection I was allowed to cherish was destroyed, my life was extinguished along with it.

I have already said that my aunt differed greatly from my father. I believe that, without the least trace of an evil heart, she possessed the coldest that ever occupied a human breast: it was wholly incapable of affection. She took charge of me because she believed it her duty; but having lived too long alone, undisturbed by the noise and prattle of children, she could not permit me to interrupt her tranquillity. She had never married; and for the preceding five years had lived in complete solitude upon an estate inherited through her mother, on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters my father had expressed the wish that she would live with me at his family residence, situated in a beautiful district near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this proposal; but once she had settled the affairs which her brother’s departure had placed in her hands, she left England and carried me with her to her Scottish estate.

The care of me as an infant, and afterward until I had reached my eighth year, fell to a servant of my mother’s who had accompanied us into retirement for that purpose. I was lodged in a distant part of the house and saw my aunt only at appointed times. This happened twice each day: once, around noon, she came to my nursery; and once, after dinner, I was brought to her. She never embraced me, and during the whole time I remained in the room seemed afraid that some childish prank might trouble her. My excellent nurse always instructed me with the utmost care before allowing me to enter the parlour—and the dread inspired by my aunt’s cold looks and few, constrained words was so strong that I rarely failed in her lessons or departed from the exemplary quiet I had been taught to maintain during these brief visits.

Under my good nurse’s care I roamed freely through our park and the neighbouring fields. As the child of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the greatest tenderness of feeling. I cannot express the passion with which I loved everything, even the lifeless objects that surrounded me."}

{"request_id":"6459c79c4192a2253bb45015","rewritten_text":"The party was divided between two adjoining benches. Anne sat on the front one, and Mr Elliot had managed, with help from his friend Colonel Wallis, to secure a seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and the main focus of Colonel Wallis’s attention, was perfectly satisfied.

Anne was in an ideal mood for the evening’s entertainment. It gave her just enough to occupy her: she had feeling for the tender music, energy for the lively, attention for the scientific, and patience for the dull. She had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first act. Near its end, during the interval after an Italian song, she explained the song’s words to Mr Elliot. A concert programme lay between them.

“This,” she said, “is almost the meaning—or rather, the general idea of the words. One must not really speak of the meaning of an Italian love song. Still, this is as close as I can come, since I do not claim to understand the language. I am a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I can see that. I can see you know nothing about it. You know only enough of the language to translate, at sight, these inverted, rearranged, shortened Italian lines into clear, understandable, elegant English. You need say no more about your ignorance. Here is complete proof.”

“I will not argue with such generous politeness; but I should be sorry to be tested by a true expert.”

“I have not had the pleasure of visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot. I consider her a woman too modest for the world to know even half her accomplishments, and too accomplished for such modesty to be natural in any other woman.”

“For shame! For shame! That is far too much flattery. I have forgotten what comes next,” she said, turning to the programme.

“Perhaps,” Mr Elliot said quietly, “I have known your character longer than you realize.”

“Indeed? How could that be? You can have known it only since I came to Bath, unless you heard me spoken of earlier by my own family.”

“I knew of you by reputation long before you came to Bath. I had heard you described by people who knew you well. I have known your character for many years. Your appearance, your nature, your accomplishments, your manner—they were all familiar to me.”

Mr Elliot had achieved the interest he hoped to awaken. No one can resist the attraction of such a mystery."}

{"request_id":"3d38837f751276944bb338b3","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man—a very pleasant, kind-looking old man when I woke him. I told him that my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday afternoon, had camped on part of a raft we found, and that around midnight my brother must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go there, fix it, and keep quiet about it, because we planned to come home that evening and surprise the family.

“Who is your family?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he said. After a moment, he asked, “How did you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”

“Strange dream,” he said.

Then he lit his lantern, got his saddlebags, and we started. But when he saw the canoe, he did not like the look of it. He said it was big enough for one person, but did not seem safe for two. I said:

“Oh, you needn’t be afraid, sir. It carried the three of us easily enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he said.

But he put his foot on the gunwale, rocked the canoe, shook his head, and said he thought he would look for a bigger one. They were all locked and chained, though, so he took my canoe and told me to wait until he returned. He said I could search farther, or perhaps go home and get everyone ready for the surprise, if I wanted to. But I said I did not. I told him exactly how to find the raft, and then he left.

I had an idea soon afterward. I said to myself, suppose he cannot fix that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, as the saying goes? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What will we do—stay there until he gives everything away? No, sir; I knew what I would do. I would wait, and when he came back, if he said he had to go anywhere else, I would get down there too, even if I had to swim. We would tie him up, keep him there, and push off down the river. When Tom was finished with him, we would pay him whatever it was worth—or all the money we had—and then let him go ashore.

So I crawled into a lumber pile to sleep. The next time I woke, the sun was high overhead. I rushed out and went to the doctor’s house, but they told me he had left sometime during the night and had not returned yet."}

{"request_id":"021945a4091dd36f619d3853","rewritten_text":"After dinner, the whole gang went out onto the sandbar to hunt turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and whenever they found a soft spot, they knelt down and dug with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. The eggs were perfectly round and white, a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a grand feast of fried eggs, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast, they went whooping and prancing onto the bar. They chased one another in circles, taking off their clothes as they ran, until they were naked. Then they continued their game far up the shallow water, fighting against the strong current. Every so often it knocked their legs out from under them, which made the fun even greater. Sometimes they gathered together and splashed water into one another’s faces with their hands. They slowly moved closer, turning their faces away to avoid the choking sprays, until they grabbed and wrestled. The strongest boy ducked his neighbor, and then they all went under in a tangle of pale arms and legs. They came up blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for breath all at once.

When they were thoroughly tired, they ran out onto the dry, hot sand, sprawled there, and covered themselves with it. Soon they rushed back into the water and repeated the whole performance. At last they realized that their bare skin looked much like flesh-colored “tights.” They drew a circle in the sand and put on a circus, with three clowns, since none of them would give up that proudest role to another.

Next they took out their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until they grew tired of that too. Then Joe and Huck went swimming again, but Tom refused. While kicking off his trousers, he had knocked the string of rattlesnake rattles from his ankle, and he wondered how he had avoided cramps so long without the protection of that mysterious charm. He would not swim again until he found it. By then, the other boys were tired and ready to rest. They slowly drifted apart, sank into the “dumps,” and gazed wistfully across the broad river toward the village, which lay sleeping in the sun. Tom caught himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe. He rubbed it out and felt angry at his own weakness. But he wrote it again anyway; he could not stop himself. He erased it once more, then escaped the temptation by gathering the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"261381bec62e7a475609a196","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by heaven’s blue sky, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you shall never see me again while they exist. Return to your home and begin your labours; I shall watch their progress with indescribable anxiety. And do not fear: when you are ready, I shall appear.”

With these words, he abruptly left me, perhaps afraid that my feelings might change. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle flies, until he was soon lost among the waves of the sea of ice.

His story had taken the entire day, and the sun stood near the horizon when he departed. I knew I must hurry down toward the valley, since darkness would soon surround me; yet my heart was burdened and my steps were slow. The work of winding along the mountain’s narrow paths and planting my feet securely as I went confused me, occupied as I was by the emotions the day’s events had awakened. It was deep into the night when I reached the halfway resting-place and sat beside the fountain. The stars appeared at intervals as clouds moved across them; the dark pines stood before me, and here and there a shattered tree lay upon the ground. It was a scene of extraordinary solemnity, stirring unfamiliar thoughts within me. I wept bitterly and, clasping my hands in anguish, cried, “Oh! stars and clouds and winds, you are all about to mock me; if you truly pity me, crush sensation and memory; let me become nothing. But if you will not, depart, depart, and leave me in darkness.”

These were frantic and wretched thoughts, but I cannot tell you how the stars’ everlasting glitter oppressed me, or how I heard every gust of wind as though it were a dull, hateful sirocco coming to consume me.

Morning broke before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest, but went straight back to Geneva. I could not even give my feelings expression within my own heart—they pressed upon me with the weight of a mountain, and their excess buried my agony beneath them. Thus I returned home and, entering the house, presented myself to the family. My haggard, wild appearance filled them with alarm, but I answered no questions and scarcely spoke. I felt as though I had been placed under a ban—as though I had no right to seek their sympathy—as though I could never again enjoy their companionship."}

{"request_id":"e294252bf12464d492116528","rewritten_text":"‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he really is some kind of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I hope he is at least a foreigner. That would make it a little less bad.’

‘I must introduce him to you.’

‘Introduce him!’ cried the Duchess. ‘You don’t mean to say he is here?’ She began searching for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very worn lace shawl, so she could leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here. I would never give a party without him. He says I have a purely psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even slightly shorter, I would have become a complete pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I see!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘And misfortunes too,’ Lady Windermere replied, ‘and plenty of them. Next year, for example, I am in great danger both on land and at sea, so I am going to live in a balloon and have my dinner lifted up to me in a basket every evening. It is all written on my little finger—or on the palm of my hand; I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their hands read once a month, so they know what not to do. Of course, one does it anyway, but it is so pleasant to be warned. Now, if someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Let me go, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man who stood nearby, listening with an amused smile.

‘Thank you so much, Lord Arthur; but I am afraid you would not recognise him.’

‘If he is as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, I could hardly miss him. Tell me what he looks like, and I will bring him to you at once.’

‘Well, he does not look like a chiromantist at all. I mean, he is not mysterious, secretive, or romantic-looking. He is a short, stout man with a funny bald head and large gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country lawyer. I am really sorry, but it is not my fault. People are so annoying. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. I remember last season inviting a terrible conspirator to dinner, a man who had blown up countless people, always wore a coat of mail, and carried a dagger up his sleeve. And do you know, when he arrived, he looked just like a pleasant old clergyman and told jokes all evening?’"}

{"request_id":"3bf8fc0a655dafad4d1e3af0","rewritten_text":"“I now examined the death’s-head carefully. Its outer edges—the edges of the drawing closest to the edge of the vellum—were much clearer than the rest. It was evident that the heat had acted imperfectly or unevenly. I immediately lit a fire and exposed every part of the parchment to the glowing heat. At first, the only result was that the faint lines of the skull grew stronger; but, after I continued the experiment, a figure appeared at the corner of the slip diagonally opposite the place where the death’s-head was drawn. At first I took it for a goat. Closer examination, however, convinced me that it was meant to be a kid.”

“Ha! ha!” I said. “Certainly, I have no right to laugh at you—a million and a half dollars is too serious a matter for amusement—but you are not going to establish a third link in your chain. You will not find any particular connection between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, you know, have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming interest.”

“But I have just said that the figure was not a goat.”

“Well, then, a kid—much the same thing.”

“Much the same, but not entirely,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately regarded the animal’s figure as a kind of punning or hieroglyphic signature. I say signature because its position on the vellum suggested that idea. The death’s-head at the diagonally opposite corner likewise had the appearance of a stamp or seal. But I was deeply troubled by the absence of everything else—of the body belonging to my imagined instrument, and of the text that would provide its context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something of that sort. The truth is, I felt irresistibly convinced that some immense good fortune was about to come to me. I can hardly say why. Perhaps, after all, it was more a desire than a genuine belief; but do you know that Jupiter’s foolish remark about the bug being made of solid gold had a remarkable effect on my imagination? And then there was the sequence of accidents and coincidences—they were extraordinarily strange. Do you see how slight an accident it was that these events should have occurred on the one day of the entire year when it was, or might be, cool enough for a fire, and that without the fire—or without the dog’s intervention at the exact moment he appeared—I would never have noticed the death’s-head, and therefore never possessed the treasure?”"}

{"request_id":"2a70b89797b0a67e12e0a936","rewritten_text":"I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then I remembered, with a shudder, that the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there, alive and moving about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. I begged him to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, then rushed toward my room. My hand was already on the lock before I stopped myself. A cold shiver passed over me. I threw the door open, as children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting on the other side, but nothing appeared. I stepped inside cautiously. The apartment was empty, and my bedroom was also free of its horrible guest. I could hardly believe such good fortune, but once I was certain that my enemy had fled, I clapped my hands with joy and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast. But I could not control myself. I felt more than joy; my whole body tingled with nervous excitement, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for even a moment. I jumped over the chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed loudly. At first Clerval thought my unusual excitement came from happiness at seeing him. But when he looked at me more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes that he could not explain. My loud, uncontrolled, empty laughter frightened and amazed him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “what on earth is wrong? Do not laugh like that. You are very ill! What has caused this?”

“Do not ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, because I thought I saw the dreaded spectre enter the room. “_He_ can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined that the monster had seized me. I struggled violently and fell unconscious.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had expected to be so joyful had turned so strangely bitter. But I did not witness his grief, for I lay senseless and did not regain consciousness for a very long time.

This was the beginning of a nervous fever that confined me for several months. Throughout that time, Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that, knowing my father was too old and unfit for such a long journey, and knowing how terribly my illness would distress Elizabeth, he spared them that suffering by hiding how serious my condition was."}

content.text: {"request_id":"fac4fc2fec4a2157b6ea8c7b","rewritten_text":"“They must matter to you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You don’t want people speaking of you as something vile and degraded. Of course, you have your position, your wealth, and all that. But position and wealth are not everything. Understand, I don’t believe these rumours at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin writes itself across a man’s face. It cannot be hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices. There are no such things. If a wretched man has a vice, it appears in the lines of his mouth, the droop of his eyelids, even in the shape of his hands. Someone—I won’t name him, but you know whom I mean—came to me last year to have his portrait painted. I had never seen him before and had heard nothing about him then, though I have heard a great deal since. He offered an extravagant price. I refused him. There was something in the shape of his fingers that repelled me. I know now that my instinct about him was entirely right. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian, with your pure, bright, innocent face and your wonderfully untroubled youth—I can’t believe anything against you. And yet I see you so rarely, and you never come to the studio now; when I am away from you and hear all these horrible things people whisper about you, I don’t know what to think. Why is it, Dorian, that a man like the Duke of Berwick leaves a club room when you enter? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse either to visit your house or invite you to theirs? You used to be friends with Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up in conversation, in connection with the miniatures you lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that you might have the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man no pure-minded girl should be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should sit in the same room with. I reminded him that I was your friend and asked what he meant. He told me. He said it openly, in front of everyone. It was horrible! Why is your friendship so disastrous for young men? There was that wretched boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were his closest friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with his name disgraced.”"}

{"request_id":"2a0cc0c307ab8f6dca18bef2","rewritten_text":"The insect’s weight was exceedingly remarkable, and, considering everything, I could scarcely blame Jupiter for his view of it; but, for the life of me, I could not understand Legrand’s agreement with that opinion.

“I sent for you,” he said in a pompous tone, after I had finished examining the beetle, “I sent for you so that I might have your advice and assistance in advancing the designs of Fate and the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I exclaimed, cutting him off, “you are plainly unwell, and ought to take a few precautions. You must go to bed, and I shall stay with you for several days, until you recover. You are feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did so, and, truthfully speaking, detected not the least sign of fever.

“But you may be sick without having a fever. Let me prescribe for you this once. First, go to bed. Then—”

“You are mistaken,” he interrupted. “I am as well as I can expect to be under the excitement I am enduring. If you truly wish me well, you will relieve that excitement.”

“And how can that be done?”

“Quite easily. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and for this expedition we shall require the help of someone we can trust. You are the only person available. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you now observe in me will be calmed just the same.”

“I am eager to oblige you in any way,” I answered; “but do you really mean that this infernal beetle is connected with your expedition into the hills?”

“It is.”

“Then, Legrand, I can take no part in such an absurd undertaking.”

“I am sorry—very sorry—for we shall have to attempt it alone.”

“Attempt it alone! The man must be mad!—but wait!—how long do you intend to remain away?”

“Probably the entire night. We shall leave at once and return, in any case, by sunrise.”

“And will you give me your word that, once this whim of yours is finished and the beetle affair (good God!) settled to your satisfaction, you will come home and follow my advice exactly, as you would that of your physician?”

“Yes, I promise; and now let us go, for we have no time to waste.”

With a troubled heart I accompanied my friend. We set out at about four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and myself. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, insisting on bearing them all—apparently more because he feared trusting either tool within his master’s reach than from any particular industry or willingness."}

{"request_id":"02d3ac6d2030cbc935c5fc36","rewritten_text":"A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from a citizen who was away and set off at once. When they were several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now you can see that this bluff looks the same all the way down from Cave Hollow—no houses, no woodpiles, and bushes that all look alike. But do you see that white spot up there where there’s been a landslide? Well, that’s one of my marks. We’ll go ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing, you could touch the hole I escaped from with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched all around but found nothing. Tom proudly walked into a thick clump of sumac bushes and said:

“Here it is! Look at it, Huck; it’s the best-hidden hole in the country. You must keep quiet about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I needed a place like this, and finding one was the hard part. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret—except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers join, because of course there has to be a Gang, or it wouldn’t be stylish. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“Well, it certainly does, Tom. And who will we rob?”

“Oh, almost anybody. Hide and ambush people—that’s mostly how it’s done.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not always. Keep them in the cave until they pay a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get as much as they can from their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if the money still hasn’t been raised, you kill them. That’s the usual way. But you don’t kill the women. You lock them up, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and terribly frightened. You take their watches and other things, but you always remove your hat and speak politely. Nobody is as polite as robbers—you’ll see that in any book. Then the women fall in love with you, and after they’ve been in the cave for a week or two, they stop crying. After that, you couldn’t make them leave. If you forced them out, they’d turn around and come back. That’s how it happens in all the books.”

“Why, it’s really great, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home, circuses, and everything else.”

By then everything was ready, and the boys entered the hole, with Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, tied their joined kite strings securely, and moved on."}

{"request_id":"a1d4d5474fb9c511cc440788","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. We could all come on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and me—with my caro sposo walking beside us. I really must speak to him about buying one. In country life, I consider it almost necessary; for however many resources a woman may have, she cannot always be confined at home. And there are such long walks, you know—in summer, dust, and in winter, mud.”

“You will find neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and now it is perfectly dry. Come on a donkey, if you prefer it. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I would like everything to suit you as much as possible.”

“That I am sure you would. Indeed, I do you justice, my good friend. Beneath that particular dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are a complete humorist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I am fully aware of your consideration for me throughout this whole plan. You have found exactly the thing to please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the party; and he knew that having any of them sit outdoors to eat would inevitably make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not be lured away to his misery under the plausible excuse of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell.

He was invited sincerely. No hidden dangers waited to reproach him for his trusting acceptance. He did agree. He had not been to Donwell for two years. “Some very fine morning, he, Emma, and Harriet could go perfectly well; and he could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked around the gardens. He did not suppose they could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would be extremely pleased to see the old house again, and very happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any other neighbors. He could see no objection at all to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there some very fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—much cleverer than dining out. He was not fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was fortunate in receiving everyone’s immediate agreement. The invitation was welcomed so warmly that it seemed, like Mrs. Elton, they all regarded the plan as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet expressed the highest expectations of pleasure from it; and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to bring Frank to join them if possible—a display of approval and gratitude that could have been spared. Mr. Knightley was therefore obliged to say that he would be glad to see him; and Mr. Weston promised to write at once and use every argument to persuade him to come."}

{"request_id":"2e8c5ba5d6654b86ce2d6aab","rewritten_text":"Matters having been settled so amicably and satisfactorily, the agreement was solemnly confirmed over another teacupful of peppermint mixture; rendered all the more necessary by the flutter and agitation of the lady’s spirits. While she drank it, she informed Mr. Bumble of the old woman’s death.

“Very good,” said that gentleman, sipping his peppermint; “I’ll call at Sowerberry’s on my way home, and tell him to send tomorrow morning. Was that what frightened you, love?”

“It wasn’t anything particular, dear,” replied the lady evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” insisted Mr. Bumble. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” returned the lady; “one of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” cried Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any impudence from one of those male paupers as—”

“No, no, love!” interrupted the lady quickly.

“If I thought it was,” continued Mr. Bumble; “if I thought any one of ’em had dared to raise his wulgar eyes to that lovely countenance—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” answered the lady.

“They had better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, porochial or extra-porochial, who would presume to do it; and I can tell him he wouldn’t do it a second time!”

Without any accompanying violence of gesture, this might have appeared a rather poor compliment to the lady’s charms; but as Mr. Bumble supported the threat with numerous warlike motions, she was deeply touched by this evidence of his devotion, and declared, with great admiration, that he was truly a dove.

The dove then turned up his coat-collar and put on his cocked hat; and, after exchanging a long and affectionate embrace with his future partner, once more faced the cold night wind: pausing only for a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward to abuse them somewhat, in order to assure himself that he could perform the duties of workhouse-master with the necessary harshness. Satisfied of his qualifications, Mr. Bumble departed the building with a light heart and glowing visions of future advancement, which occupied his thoughts until he arrived at the undertaker’s shop.

Now, Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out to tea and supper; and Noah Claypole was never inclined to undertake more physical exertion than was required for the convenient performance of eating and drinking. Consequently, the shop remained open, though the usual closing hour had passed. Mr. Bumble tapped several times upon the counter with his cane; but, receiving no answer, and seeing a light through the glass window of the small parlour at the rear of the shop, he ventured to peep inside and discover what was happening; and when he saw what was happening, he was considerably surprised."}

{"request_id":"38f7c6b1929b89365da18842","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had ventured so far across the ice in such an unusual vehicle.

His face immediately took on an expression of profound gloom, and he answered, “To find one who escaped from me.”

“And did the man you were following travel in the same manner?”

“Yes.”

“Then I believe we have seen him, for the day before we rescued you, we observed some dogs pulling a sledge, with a man seated in it, over the ice.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked many questions about the course which the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Shortly afterward, when he was alone with me, he said, “I have surely aroused your curiosity, as I have that of these good people; but you are too thoughtful to question me.”

“Certainly; it would be exceedingly impertinent and inhuman of me to trouble you with my curiosity.”

“And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation; you have kindly brought me back to life.”

Soon afterward he asked whether I believed the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied that I could not say with certainty, since the ice had not broken until nearly midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety before then; but I had no means of knowing.

From that moment, a renewed spirit of life seemed to animate the stranger’s failing body. He showed the greatest eagerness to go upon deck and watch for the sledge that had appeared before; but I persuaded him to stay in the cabin, as he is far too weak to endure the raw air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and immediately inform him if any new object came into view.

This is my journal, my dear Margaret, of everything connected with this strange event up to the present time. The stranger has gradually regained his health, but remains very quiet and seems uneasy whenever anyone besides myself enters his cabin. Still, his manner is so gentle and conciliating that all the sailors are interested in him, though they have spoken with him very little. For my part, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his continual, profound sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble being in happier days, for even now, amid his ruin, he is so attractive and amiable.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend upon the broad ocean; yet I have found a man whom, before misery had broken his spirit, I would gladly have embraced as the brother of my heart."}

content.text: {"request_id":"9d93e662f12dffc1700c6137","rewritten_text":"Weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something changed. I had painted you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis wearing a hunter’s cloak and carrying a polished boar spear. Crowned with heavy lotus blossoms, you had sat at the front of Adrian’s barge, looking across the green, muddy Nile. You had leaned over the still pool of a Greek woodland and seen, in its quiet silver surface, the wonder of your own face. And it had all been what art should be—unconscious, ideal, and distant. One day, a day I sometimes think was fatal, I decided to paint a wonderful portrait of you as you truly were, not in the clothing of ancient times, but in your own clothes and in your own age. I cannot say whether it was the realism of the method, or simply the power of your personality, shown to me directly and without mist or veil. But as I worked, every flake and layer of paint seemed to reveal my secret. I became afraid that others would discover my worship of you. I felt, Dorian, that I had said too much, that I had put too much of myself into the painting. So I decided never to let it be exhibited. You were a little annoyed, but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, whom I told about it, laughed at me. I did not mind. When the picture was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt that I had been right.... Well, after a few days it left my studio. Once I had escaped the unbearable fascination of its presence, I began to think I had been foolish to imagine I had seen anything in it beyond the fact that you were extremely handsome and that I could paint. Even now, I cannot help thinking it is a mistake to believe that the passion felt during creation is truly shown in the work created. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and color tell us about form and color—that is all. It often seems to me that art hides the artist far more completely than it reveals him. So when I received this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main work in my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The picture cannot be shown. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for telling you all this."}

{"request_id":"03ab895ed18612e9abaf3b41","rewritten_text":"But without me, he would never have escaped. Morgan le Fay detested him with all her heart, and nothing could have made her relent. Yet his offense sprang more from carelessness than intentional wickedness. He had said that she had red hair. She did, certainly; but that was not the proper way to describe it. When red-haired people belong to a certain social level, their hair is called auburn.

Think of it: among these forty-seven prisoners were five whose names, crimes, and dates of confinement had been forgotten! One woman and four men—all stooped, wrinkled, and mentally extinguished patriarchs. They themselves had forgotten those particulars long ago; at best they possessed only hazy notions, nothing certain, and nothing they told twice in the same fashion. The succession of priests whose duty had been to pray with the captives each day, remind them that God had placed them there for some wise purpose, and teach them that patience, humility, and submission to oppression were what He wished to see in people of an inferior station, possessed traditions concerning these wretched human remnants, but nothing beyond that. Those traditions went only a short distance, since they dealt merely with the duration of imprisonment, not with the names of the offenses. Even with tradition's aid, the sole fact that could be established was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years; how much longer they had endured the deprivation could not be guessed. The king and queen knew nothing of these poor beings except that they were heirlooms, assets inherited with the throne from the previous firm. No account of their past had accompanied them, and their inheriting owners had therefore judged them worthless and taken no interest in them. I said to the queen:

“Then why on earth didn’t you release them?”

The question baffled her. She did not know why she had not; the matter had simply never entered her mind. Thus, without realizing it, she was already forecasting the authentic history of future prisoners in the Castle d’If. It seemed clear to me now that, under her training, those inherited prisoners were merely property—nothing more and nothing less. After all, when we inherit property, we do not think of throwing it away, even if we place no value on it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open air and the harsh afternoon sunlight—having first blindfolded them, out of mercy for eyes so long unaccustomed to light—they were a sight to behold. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pitiful horrors, every one of them; the most legitimate children imaginable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"80ab970d339574bded3ac28b","rewritten_text":"The powerful voice—almost mechanical, we might call it, since we could not connect it with any pipe or keyboard—fell silent. The girl turned to help her aged companion and finally noticed us.

He was her father, and since childhood she had guided his blind steps. They were Germans from Saxony who had emigrated only a few years earlier and formed new friendships with the nearby villagers. Around the time the plague began, a young German student had joined them. Their simple story was easy to understand. He, a nobleman, loved the poor musician’s beautiful daughter and followed them while fleeing persecution from his family. But soon the great equalizer came, its sharp scythe cutting down the tall flowers of the field along with the grass. The young man was one of its first victims. She kept herself alive for her father’s sake. Because he was blind, she could continue a deception that had begun by accident. Now, as the only survivors in the country, he did not know what had happened. He was unaware that when he listened to his daughter’s music, the silent mountains, lifeless lake, and unfeeling trees were, apart from himself, her only listeners.

On the very day we arrived, she had been struck by the illness. She was horrified by the thought of leaving her old, blind father alone on the empty earth, but she could not bring herself to tell him the truth. The depth of her despair gave her extraordinary strength. At the usual evening hour, she led him to the chapel. Though she trembled and wept for him, she played without losing the rhythm or missing a note the hymn celebrating the creation of the beautiful earth, which would soon become her grave.

We came to her like visitors from heaven. Her carefully built courage and barely maintained strength vanished when she saw us. With a scream, she ran to Adrian, clasped his knees, and cried only, “O save my father!” Then, sobbing and shrieking hysterically, she released the grief she had held back for so long.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, the place she had shown us in her final moments. Her father eventually understood that she was in danger. Unable to see the changes in her beloved face, he stubbornly held her hand until death made it cold and stiff. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until kind death took him, twelve hours later, into his unbroken rest. They lie beneath the earth, with the tree as their monument. I still remember that sacred place, framed by the rugged Jura and the distant, endless Alps. The church spire they once visited still rises above the surrounding trees. And though her hand is cold, I still imagine the divine music they loved drifting around them and comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"79b9d7d1ae2c28406c23cb41","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father, of course, may spare you, if your mother can. Daughters never matter quite so much to a father. And if you stay one more complete _month_, I may be able to take one of you as far as London, since I am going there for a week early in June. Dawson does not object to the barouche-box, so there will be plenty of room for one of you—and, if the weather happens to be cool, I would not mind taking you both, since neither of you is large.”

“You are very kind, madam; but I believe we must follow our original plan.”

Lady Catherine appeared to accept this. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot bear the thought of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is highly improper. You must find a way to send someone. I have the greatest dislike of such things. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended, according to their position in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted that two male servants travel with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne, could not properly have appeared in any other way. I pay close attention to all such matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad I thought to mention it; it would truly be disgraceful to _you_ to let them go alone.”

“My uncle is sending a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a male servant, does he? I am very glad you have someone who considers such matters. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you give my name at the Bell, they will take good care of you.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey; and since she did not answer every one herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention—which she considered fortunate. Otherwise, with her mind so occupied, she might have forgotten where she was. She would have to save her thoughts for private hours. Whenever she was alone, she surrendered to them as her greatest relief; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, during which she could enjoy all the painful pleasure of unpleasant memories.

She was soon likely to know Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings toward its writer often changed greatly. When she remembered the manner in which he had addressed her, she was still filled with anger. But when she considered how unfairly she had judged and reproached him, her anger turned against herself, and she began to pity his disappointed feelings."}

content.text: {"request_id":"8bb4f57b33ac120aed96d82a","rewritten_text":"No imagination can picture the grandeur that a similar event might have shown if it had happened in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have seemed an appropriate image. Even in daylight, my hair stood on end as I gazed far down into the yawning depths, allowing my imagination to descend and wander through the strange vaulted halls, glowing gulfs, and red, terrible chasms of that dreadful, unfathomable fire. I had indeed escaped by a narrow margin. If the balloon had remained in the cloud only a little longer—that is, if the discomfort of getting wet had not led me to release the ballast—complete ruin would have followed. Such dangers, though rarely considered, may be the greatest that balloon travelers must face. By this time, however, I had risen too high to feel any further concern about that danger.\n\n“I was now rising quickly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of no less than nine and a half miles. I began to have great difficulty breathing. My head also hurt terribly; and after noticing moisture on my cheeks for some time, I finally discovered that it was blood, flowing fairly quickly from my eardrums. My eyes, too, caused me great discomfort. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to have pushed out from their sockets to a considerable degree; and everything in the car, even the balloon itself, looked distorted. These symptoms were worse than I had expected and alarmed me. At that moment, very foolishly and without thinking, I threw three five-pound pieces of ballast from the car. The faster ascent this caused carried me too quickly, without a gradual transition, into a layer of extremely thin air, and the result nearly ended both my expedition and my life. I was suddenly struck by a spasm that lasted more than five minutes. Even after it partly stopped, I could draw breath only at long intervals and in gasps, while blood poured from my nose and ears and trickled slightly from my eyes. The pigeons seemed terribly distressed and struggled to get free; the cat mewed miserably and, with her tongue hanging from her mouth, staggered back and forth in the car as if poisoned. Only then did I realize how reckless I had been to release the ballast, and I became extremely agitated. I expected nothing less than death—and death within a few minutes.”"}

{"request_id":"70a483451e0306d4e4395336","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” said the spy in the most contemptuous manner, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and benevolence to ask this other gentleman, so much your junior, whether he can under any circumstances reconcile it with his position to play that Ace of which he has spoken. I acknowledge that _I_ am a spy, and that it is regarded as a discreditable occupation—though someone must fill it; but this gentleman is no spy, and why should he lower himself by making himself one?”

“I play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, answering for himself and glancing at his watch, “without the slightest scruple, in a very few minutes.”

“I should have hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the conversation, “that your regard for my sister—”

“I could show no greater regard for your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You do not think so, sir?”

“I have made up my mind about it completely.”

The spy’s polished manner, strangely at odds with his deliberately coarse clothing, and likely with his ordinary behaviour as well, was so checked by Carton’s inscrutability—he was a mystery even to men wiser and more honest than the spy—that it faltered and failed him at this point. While he stood uncertain, Carton resumed his former appearance of studying the cards and said:

“And indeed, now that I think of it again, I have a strong feeling that I possess another good card not yet mentioned. That friend and fellow-Sheep who said he had been pasturing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You do not know him,” the spy replied quickly.

“French, eh?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, seeming not to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well, he may be.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy; “though it is not important.”

“Though it is not important,” Carton repeated in the same mechanical fashion—“though it is not important—No, it is not important. No. And yet I know the face.”

“I think not. I am certain not. It cannot be,” said the spy.

“‘It-cannot-be,’” Sydney Carton muttered retrospectively, idly swirling his glass again, which fortunately was a small one. “Cannot-be. Spoke good French. Yet I thought he seemed like a foreigner?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, striking his open hand upon the table as the truth became clear to him. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now you are hasty, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that tilted his aquiline nose still farther to one side; “there you truly give me an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"0a856d98fb42b4a2dcff2c19","rewritten_text":"“I hope I shall soon have the pleasure of presenting my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, quite ready to believe that such a hope contained a special compliment to herself, smiled with great graciousness.

“You have heard, I suppose, of a certain Frank Churchill,” he went on—“and know him to be my son, although he does not bear my name.”

“Oh! yes, and I shall be delighted to make his acquaintance. I am sure Mr. Elton will call on him without delay; and we shall both be very pleased to see him at the Vicarage.”

“You are extremely obliging.—Frank will, I am sure, be very happy.—He is expected in town next week, if not earlier. We have received notice of it in a letter to-day. I met the letters on my way this morning, and, seeing my son’s handwriting, took the liberty of opening it—though it was not addressed to me—it was for Mrs. Weston. She is his chief correspondent, I assure you. I scarcely ever receive a letter.”

“And so you actually opened one addressed to her! Oh! Mr. Weston—(laughing with affected surprise) I must object to that.—What a dangerous precedent!—I beg you will not encourage your neighbours to imitate you.—Upon my word, if this is what I am to expect, we married women must begin to defend ourselves!—Oh! Mr. Weston, I should never have thought it of you!”

“Aye, we men are sad creatures. You must look after yourself, Mrs. Elton.—This letter informs us—it is a short one—written in haste, merely to give notice—it tells us that they are all coming directly to town, on Mrs. Churchill’s account—she has been unwell throughout the winter, and considers Enscombe too cold for her—so they are all to move south without delay.”

“Indeed!—from Yorkshire, I believe. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, they are about one hundred and ninety miles from London, which is a considerable journey.”

“Yes, upon my word, very considerable. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of great fortune?—You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, sometimes travels about. You will scarcely believe me—but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and returned with four horses.”

“The disadvantage of the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, _as_ _we_ _understand_, has been unable to leave the sofa for a whole week. In Frank’s last letter, he said she complained of being too weak to reach her conservatory without the support of both his arm and his uncle’s!”"}

{"request_id":"be1711d58e31572a63c685d9","rewritten_text":"There would soon be other chances for Anne to observe them. She had spent enough time with all four together to form an opinion, though she was too sensible to admit it at home, knowing that neither husband nor wife would have been pleased. She thought Louisa was rather the favourite, but, judging as carefully as she could from memory and experience, she could not believe Captain Wentworth was in love with either of them. They were more in love with him; yet even that was not truly love. It was a brief fever of admiration, though it might, and probably would, end in love with someone. Charles Hayter seemed aware that he was being neglected, while Henrietta sometimes appeared torn between the two men. Anne longed to tell them all what they were doing and to warn them of the trouble they were bringing upon themselves. She suspected no one of deceit. It gave her the greatest satisfaction to believe that Captain Wentworth was completely unaware of the pain he was causing. There was no triumph, not even a mean kind of triumph, in his manner. He had probably never heard of, or even considered, any claim Charles Hayter might have. His only mistake was accepting the attentions—for accepting was the right word—of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to leave the field. Three days passed without his coming to Uppercross even once, a very clear change. He had also refused a regular invitation to dinner. On that occasion Mr Musgrove found him with several large books in front of him, and Mr and Mrs Musgrove became sure that something was wrong. With serious faces, they spoke of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had plainly rejected him, while her husband lived in constant expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only think that Charles Hayter was wise.

One morning around this time, Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth having gone shooting together, the sisters in the Cottage were sitting quietly at work when the sisters from the Mansion-house came to the window to visit them.

It was a very fine November day. The Miss Musgroves crossed the small grounds and stopped only to say that they were going for a _long_ walk, and therefore assumed Mary would not want to join them. Mary immediately replied, somewhat jealous that they did not consider her a good walker, “Oh, yes, I should very much like to come with you; I am very fond of a long walk.” From the looks of the two girls, Anne was convinced that this was exactly what they had not wanted. Once again, she was struck by the pressure created by the family’s habits: everything had to be shared, and everything had to be done together, however unwanted or inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"bafd1773deac3eacc055326f","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret lowering herself enough to visit the Coles. The visit gave her many pleasant memories the next day; and whatever she might have lost in dignified privacy would surely be more than repaid by the glory of being popular. She must have delighted the Coles—good people who deserved to be made happy!—and left behind a name that would not soon be forgotten.

Perfect happiness, even in memory, is uncommon; and there were two things that troubled her. She wondered whether she had broken the duty women owed one another by revealing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings to Frank Churchill. It had hardly been right; but the thought had been so strong that it had escaped her. And his acceptance of everything she said was such a compliment to her insight that she could not be completely sure she should have kept silent.

Her other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and about that she had no doubt. She sincerely and completely regretted that her own playing and singing were inferior. She deeply mourned the idleness of her childhood, then sat down and practised hard for an hour and a half.

Harriet’s arrival interrupted her; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she might soon have felt better.

“Oh! If only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t put us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh, dear—I think you play better than she does. I think you play quite as well as she does. I am sure I would much rather hear you. Everyone said last night how well you played.”

“Anyone who knew anything about music must have noticed the difference. The truth is, Harriet, that my playing is just good enough to be praised, but Jane Fairfax’s is far better.”

“Well, I shall always think you play quite as well as she does, or that, if there is a difference, no one would ever notice it. Mr. Cole said you had so much taste; and Mr. Frank Churchill spoke a great deal about your taste, saying he valued taste much more than technical skill.”

“Ah! But Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw that she had technical skill, but I did not know she had any taste. No one mentioned it. And I hate Italian singing—there is no understanding a word of it. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it is only what she must do, because she will have to teach.”"}

And then not to find him at home! I assure you, I am not at all pleased. And no apology left, no message for me. The housekeeper declared she knew nothing of my being expected.—Very extraordinary!—And nobody knew at all where he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods.—Miss Woodhouse, this is not like our friend Knightley!—Can you explain it?”

Emma amused herself by insisting that it was indeed very extraordinary, and that she had not a word to say in his defense.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, (feeling the insult as a wife ought to do,) “I cannot imagine how he could treat you so, of all people in the world! The very last person anyone would expect to be forgotten!—My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message for you, I am sure he must.—Even Knightley could not be so eccentric;—his servants must have forgotten it. Depend upon it, that was the case: and it is very likely with the Donwell servants, who, as I have often observed, are extremely awkward and negligent.—I am sure I would not have such a creature as his Harry standing at our sideboard for any consideration. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her indeed.—She promised Wright a receipt and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” continued Mr. Elton, “as I approached the house, and he told me I would not find his master at home, but I did not believe him.—William seemed rather out of sorts. He said he did not know what had come over his master lately, but he could hardly ever get to speak with him. I have nothing to do with William’s concerns, but it really is extremely important that _I_ should see Knightley today; and it therefore becomes a matter of very serious inconvenience that I should have taken that hot walk for nothing.”

{"request_id":"27c252568efac85f168bf685","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining-room, the clock tower began to strike midnight. With the final stroke came a crash and a sudden piercing cry; a terrible peal of thunder rattled the house, a line of unearthly music drifted through the air, and a panel at the head of the staircase sprang open with a loud report. Out on the landing stood Virginia, very pale and white, holding a small casket. At once they all hurried up to her. Mrs. Otis clasped her fervently in her arms, the Duke covered her with passionate kisses, and the twins danced a wild war-dance around them.

‘Good heavens, child, where have you been?’ asked Mr. Otis, somewhat angrily, supposing she had been playing another foolish trick. ‘Cecil and I have ridden all over the country searching for you, and your mother has been frightened nearly to death. You must never play such practical jokes again.’

‘Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!’ shrieked the twins, capering around.

‘My own darling, thank God we have found you; you must never leave my side again,’ murmured Mrs. Otis, kissing the trembling child and smoothing her tangled golden hair.

‘Papa,’ said Virginia calmly, ‘I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he had done, and before he died he gave me this box of lovely jewels.’

The entire family stared at her in silent astonishment, but she remained grave and earnest. Turning, she led them through the opening in the wainscoting and down a narrow hidden passage, while Washington followed with a lighted candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a large oak door covered with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung open on its heavy hinges, revealing a small, low chamber with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny barred window. Set into the wall was a massive iron ring, to which a gaunt skeleton was chained. It lay stretched full-length upon the stone floor, apparently trying to reach with its long, fleshless fingers an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just beyond its grasp. The jug had plainly once held water, for its inside was coated with green mould. The trencher held nothing but a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her little hands, and began to pray silently, while the others gazed in wonder at the dreadful tragedy whose secret had now been revealed."}

{"request_id":"2122af6cf691f37b28f99bfc","rewritten_text":"It was at this point that his eyes, and mine as well, lighted upon the scrap of parchment, which I had then taken for paper. It lay partly buried in the sand, with one corner protruding. Close to where we discovered it, I noticed the remains of what seemed to be the hull of a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have lain there for an immense length of time, since scarcely any likeness to boat timbers remained.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Shortly afterward we started homeward, and on the way encountered Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he asked me to allow him to carry it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately thrust it into his waistcoat pocket, leaving behind the parchment in which it had been wrapped, which I had kept in my hand while he examined it. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind and thought it prudent to secure the prize without delay—you know how ardent he is about everything relating to Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment into my own pocket.

“You recollect that, when I went to the table to make a sketch of the beetle, I found no paper in its usual place. I searched the drawer, but found none there either. I then felt through my pockets, hoping to discover an old letter, and my hand came upon the parchment. I describe exactly how it came into my possession because the circumstances affected me with unusual force.

“No doubt you will call me fanciful—but I had already formed a sort of connexion. I had joined two links in a great chain. There was a boat upon a sea-coast, and near the boat lay a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn upon it. You will naturally ask, ‘What is the connexion?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the familiar emblem of the pirate. The death’s-head flag is raised in every engagement.

“I have said that the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is lasting—almost imperishable. Things of little importance are seldom committed to parchment; for ordinary drawing or writing, it is far less suitable than paper. This thought suggested that the death’s-head must have some meaning—some relevance. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. Though one corner had been accidentally torn away, it was still evident that its original form had been oblong."}
