{"request_id":"0c4a0d71791f7e65f5a48497","rewritten_text":"Wake up after a while and look around to see what had caused the sound, and maybe spot a steamboat coughing its way upstream. It would be so far off, toward the opposite bank, that you couldn’t tell anything about it except whether it was a stern-wheel or side-wheel boat. Then, for about an hour, there would be nothing to hear or see—only complete loneliness. Next you might see a raft drifting by, far away, with perhaps some fellow chopping on it, since they were almost always doing that on a raft. You would see the axe flash and fall, but hear nothing. You would see it rise again, and by the time it was above the man’s head, you would hear the _k’chunk!_ It had taken all that time for the sound to cross the water. So we spent the day idling around and listening to the silence. Once there was a heavy fog, and the rafts and other things passing by beat on tin pans so the steamboats would not run them down. A scow or raft passed so close that we could hear the people talking, cursing, and laughing—hear them clearly—but we could not see any sign of them. It made you feel uneasy; it was like spirits carrying on in the air. Jim said he believed they were spirits, but I said:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

As soon as night came, we pushed off. When we reached about the middle of the river, we left the raft alone and let the current carry it wherever it wanted. Then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things. We were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes allowed it. The new clothes Buck’s family had made for me were too fine to be comfortable, and besides, I never cared much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we had the whole river to ourselves for a very long time. There were the banks and islands across the water, and perhaps a spark—which was a candle shining from a cabin window. Sometimes you could see one or two sparks on the water, from a raft or scow, you know. Maybe you could hear a fiddle or a song drifting over from one of those boats. It is lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky above us, covered with stars, and we would lie on our backs looking up at them and arguing about whether they had been made or had simply appeared. Jim believed they were made, but I believed they had just happened; I figured it would have taken too long to _make_ so many."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0c1b35008e7838f706290d7f","rewritten_text":"The mental qualities described as analytical are, in themselves, scarcely open to analysis. We recognize them only through their effects. Among other things, we know that, when possessed to an excessive degree, they are a source of the keenest pleasure to their possessor. As a strong man takes pride in his physical power, delighting in exercises that call his muscles into action, so the analyst rejoices in that mental activity which disentangles. He finds pleasure even in the most trivial occupations that bring his talent into play. He enjoys enigmas, conundrums, and hieroglyphics, displaying in solving each a degree of acumen that seems supernatural to ordinary understanding. His conclusions, reached through the very essence of method, have, in fact, the entire appearance of intuition.\n\nThe faculty of solving problems may be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, especially by its highest branch, which has been unjustly called analysis, merely because of its backward operations, as though it were analysis par excellence. Yet calculation is not, in itself, analysis. A chess player, for example, does one without attempting the other. It follows that chess is widely misunderstood in its effects on the mind. I am not writing a treatise now, but merely introducing a somewhat unusual narrative with observations made almost at random; I will therefore take this opportunity to assert that the higher and more useful powers of the reflective intellect are exercised more decisively by the quiet game of draughts than by all the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and bizarre ways and possess varied and shifting values, what is merely complicated is mistaken—a common error—for what is profound. Attention is called into forceful action. If it falters for even a moment, an oversight occurs, causing injury or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but intricate, the chances of such oversights increase; and in nine games out of ten, it is the more concentrated rather than the more perceptive player who wins. In draughts, by contrast, where the moves are unique and vary little, the likelihood of carelessness is reduced, and with mere attention left comparatively unoccupied, whatever advantages either side gains come from superior acumen. To be less abstract, suppose a game of draughts in which the pieces have been reduced to four kings, so that, naturally, no oversight need be expected. It is clear that the victory can then be decided—the players being otherwise equal—only by some recherché move resulting from a powerful exertion of intellect."}

{"request_id":"96a70f9b329869123ae776bf","rewritten_text":"His manner was extremely stubborn, and “that cursed bug” were the only words he spoke during the journey. I carried two dark lanterns, while Legrand kept the scarab, tied to the end of a piece of whipcord, and swung it back and forth like a magician as he walked. When I saw this final, clear sign of my friend’s madness, I could hardly hold back my tears. Still, I thought it best to indulge his fancy for the moment, until I could take stronger measures with some hope of success. Meanwhile, I tried in vain to learn the purpose of the expedition. After persuading me to come with him, he seemed unwilling to discuss anything of lesser importance, answering all my questions only with, “We shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s upper end in a skiff. Then we climbed the high ground on the mainland and traveled northwest through country so wild and desolate that there was no sign of a human footprint. Legrand led confidently, stopping only briefly from time to time to consult what seemed to be landmarks he had made earlier.

We traveled this way for about two hours, and the sun was setting when we entered a region even more gloomy than anything we had yet seen. It was a kind of plateau near the top of an almost impassable hill, thickly wooded from bottom to summit and scattered with huge rocks that seemed to rest loosely on the ground. In many places, they were kept from plunging into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines running in different directions made the scene seem even more severe and solemn.

The natural platform we had climbed was thick with brambles. We soon saw that it would have been impossible to get through them without a scythe. At his master’s direction, Jupiter cleared a path to the foot of an enormously tall tulip tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, towering above them all. Indeed, it surpassed every tree I had ever seen in the beauty of its leaves and shape, the broad spread of its branches, and the majestic appearance of the whole."}

{"request_id":"91c44374d1559b6ca734fe3e","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s affections had prevailed over her interest, and for the young man’s sake she had given up the chance of scheming longer for Sir Walter. Yet she possessed abilities as well as feelings; and it remained uncertain whether his cunning or hers would ultimately succeed—whether, after keeping her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he might not at last be coaxed and flattered into making her the wife of Sir William.

There could be no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and mortified by the loss of their companion, and by discovering her deception. They had their great cousins, certainly, to turn to for consolation; but they would long feel that flattering and following others, without receiving flattery and attention in return, amounted only to a state of incomplete enjoyment.

Anne, having been satisfied very early that Lady Russell intended to love Captain Wentworth as she ought, had no drawback to the happiness of her prospects except the awareness that she had no relations to offer him whom a sensible man could value. In that respect she felt her inferiority most painfully. The difference in their fortunes meant nothing; it caused her not a moment’s regret. But having no family able to receive and appreciate him properly, nothing respectable, harmonious, or kindly to give in return for all the worth and warm welcome she found in his brothers and sisters, was a source of pain as keen as her mind could feel amid otherwise profound happiness. She had only two friends in the world to add to his circle: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. To both, however, he was very willing to attach himself. Lady Russell, despite all her former offences, he could now value sincerely. Though he was not required to say that he believed her right to have separated them at first, he was prepared to say nearly everything else in her favour; and Mrs Smith possessed claims of several kinds that quickly and permanently recommended her.

The recent kindness Anne had shown her would have been sufficient by itself, and their marriage, rather than costing her one friend, gained her two. She was their first visitor once they were settled; and Captain Wentworth, by helping her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies—writing on her behalf, acting for her, and guiding her through every minor difficulty with the energy of a fearless man and steadfast friend—fully repaid the services she had given, or had ever intended to give, to his wife."}

{"request_id":"778d73e3a0f6c1d9945ca165","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced at him without success as he continued toward the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Show Monsieur my nephew to his chamber there!—And burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you like,” he added to himself, before ringing his little bell again and summoning his valet to his own bedroom.

After the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis paced back and forth in his loose chamber robe, gently preparing himself for sleep on that hot, still night. Rustling around the room, his softly slippered feet making no sound on the floor, he moved like a refined tiger—like some enchanted marquis of the irredeemably wicked kind in a story, whose periodic transformation into a tiger was either just ending or just beginning.

He crossed his luxurious bedroom from end to end, again reviewing the fragments of the day’s journey that had entered his mind unbidden: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the setting sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the little village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road mender in his blue cap pointing out the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain brought to mind the fountain in Paris, the small bundle lying on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, crying, “Dead!”

“I am cool now,” said Monsieur the Marquis, “and can go to bed.”

Leaving only one light burning on the broad hearth, he let his thin gauze curtains fall around him and heard the night break its silence with a long sigh as he settled himself to sleep.

The stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the black night for three heavy hours. For three heavy hours, the horses in the stables rattled at their racks, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound bearing little resemblance to the noise conventionally assigned to owls by men who write poetry. But such creatures stubbornly refuse, almost always, to say what men have prescribed for them.

For three heavy hours, the stone faces of the chateau, lion and human, stared blindly into the night. Dead darkness covered the entire landscape, and dead darkness added its own hush to the dust settling silently on every road. The burial ground had reached such a state that its small mounds of poor grass could no longer be distinguished from one another; for all that could be seen of it, the figure on the Cross might have come down. In the village, tax collectors and taxpayers slept soundly. Dreaming, perhaps, of banquets, as the starving commonly do, and of comfort and rest, as the driven slave and yoked ox may, its lean inhabitants slept deeply, fed and free."}

{"request_id":"bad4ea985d4a18c774412f5f","rewritten_text":"He said nothing about it, however, until their visitor had left for the night. As soon as the man was gone, he turned to his daughter and said,

“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”

Jane immediately went to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he replied, “and I am very pleased to think you will be so happily settled. I have no doubt that you will do very well together. Your tempers are not at all unlike. You are both so willing to give way that nothing will ever be decided; so trusting that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always spend more than you earn.”

“I hope not. Carelessness or thoughtlessness about money would be unforgivable in _me_.”

“Spend more than they earn! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what can you mean? He has four or five thousand a year, and probably more.” Then, turning to her daughter, she said, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I am sure I shall not sleep a moment tonight. I knew this would happen. I always said it must, in the end. I was certain you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember that as soon as I saw him, when he first came to Hertfordshire last year, I thought it very likely that you would come together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man anyone has ever seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were completely forgotten. Jane was now, beyond question, her favourite child. At that moment she cared about no one else. Her younger sisters soon began asking her for the happy things she might one day be able to provide.

Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield, while Kitty begged earnestly for a few balls there every winter.

From then on, Bingley naturally became a daily visitor at Longbourn. He often arrived before breakfast and always stayed until after supper, except when some hateful neighbour—someone he could not possibly dislike enough—had invited him to dinner, and he felt obliged to accept.

Elizabeth now had little time to talk with her sister. Whenever Bingley was there, Jane had no attention to give anyone else. But Elizabeth found herself very useful to both of them during the periods of separation that sometimes had to occur. When Jane was absent, Bingley always kept close to Elizabeth so that he could talk about her; and when Bingley had gone, Jane constantly sought the same comfort.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by telling me that he had no idea I was in town last spring!"}

content.text: {"request_id":"5e433ad4d445303c25ce7c57","rewritten_text":"No imagination can picture the sublimity that might have been displayed by a similar phenomenon occurring in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have served as an appropriate image. Even as it was, my hair rose on end as I gazed far down into the yawning abysses, allowing fancy, as it were, to descend and wander through the strange vaulted halls, ruddy gulfs, and red, ghastly chasms of that hideous, unfathomable fire. I had indeed escaped narrowly. Had the balloon remained only a little longer within the cloud—that is, had the discomfort of becoming wet not induced me to release the ballast—inevitable destruction would have followed. Such dangers, though seldom considered, are perhaps the greatest that balloons must face. By this time, however, I had reached too great an elevation to feel further anxiety on that account.\n\n“I was now ascending rapidly, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of no less than nine and a half miles. I began to experience great difficulty in breathing. My head was also exceedingly painful; and, after noticing moisture on my cheeks for some time, I finally discovered that it was blood, flowing rather quickly from my eardrums. My eyes, too, caused me considerable distress. When I passed my hand over them, they seemed to have protruded from their sockets to a remarkable degree; and every object in the car, even the balloon itself, appeared distorted. These symptoms exceeded my expectations and alarmed me. At this point, with great imprudence and no reflection, I cast from the car three five-pound portions of ballast. The increased speed of ascent thereby produced carried me too swiftly, and without adequate gradation, into a highly rarefied layer of atmosphere; the consequence nearly proved fatal both to my expedition and to me. I was suddenly overcome by a spasm lasting more than five minutes, and even after it had somewhat subsided, I could draw breath only at long intervals and with gasps—bleeding profusely all the while from my nose and ears, and slightly even from my eyes. The pigeons seemed extremely distressed and struggled to get free; while the cat mewed miserably and, her tongue hanging from her mouth, staggered back and forth in the car as though poisoned. Only now did I realize, too late, how reckless I had been in throwing out the ballast, and my agitation became intense. I expected nothing short of death, and death within a few minutes.”"}

{"request_id":"d2a18e27e7458f1a742dff9e","rewritten_text":"Their arrival had lit a kind of fire in the heart of Saint Antoine, spreading quickly as they came. It stirred and flickered in the faces seen at most doors and windows. Yet no one followed them, and no man spoke when they entered the wine-shop, though every eye turned toward them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

Perhaps this was a signal for everyone to speak. It brought back a chorus of “Good day!”

“It is bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.

At this, every man looked at his neighbour, then lowered his eyes and sat in silence. Except for one man, who rose and went out.

“My wife,” said Defarge aloud, speaking to Madame Defarge, “I travelled several leagues with this good road-mender, called Jacques. I met him by accident, a day and a half’s journey from Paris. He is a good fellow, this road-mender called Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender called Jacques. He removed his blue cap to the company and drank. He carried some coarse, dark bread inside his blouse; from time to time he ate it while sitting near Madame Defarge’s counter, munching and drinking. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge refreshed himself with a drink of wine, but took less than he had given the stranger, since wine was no rarity to him. He waited until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He looked at no one present, and no one now looked at him—not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and was working.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked after a suitable time.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come, then! You shall see the room I told you that you could occupy. It will suit you perfectly.”

From the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, and from the staircase into a garret—formerly the garret where a white-haired man had sat on a low bench, bent forward and deeply occupied in making shoes.

The white-haired man was gone now. But the three men who had left the wine-shop one by one were there. Between them and the white-haired man, far away, there was only one small connection: they had once looked in at him through the cracks in the wall.

Defarge carefully closed the door and spoke in a quiet voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness I met by arrangement, I, Jacques Four.”"}

Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent part of the morning with the invalid, who continued to recover, though slowly. In the evening, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room. The loo table did not appear, however. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley sat beside him, watching his letter and repeatedly interrupting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was watching their game.

Elizabeth took up some needlework and was entertained by what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady constantly praised either his handwriting, the evenness of his lines, or the length of his letter, while he received her compliments with complete indifference. Their exchange was amusing and perfectly matched Elizabeth’s opinion of them both.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!”

He made no reply.

“You write remarkably fast.”

“You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write during the year! Business letters, too! How unpleasant I should find them!”

“It is fortunate, then, that they are my responsibility rather than yours.”

“Please tell your sister that I am eager to see her.”

“I have already told her so once, at your request.”

“I am afraid you do not like your pen. Let me mend it for you. I mend pens extremely well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He remained silent.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear that she has improved on the harp, and please let her know that I am thrilled by her lovely little design for a table. I think it far better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to postpone your raptures until I write again? I have no room at present to do them justice.”

“Oh, it does not matter. I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charmingly long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long; but whether they are always charming is not for me to decide.”

“I believe that anyone who can easily write a long letter cannot write badly.”

“That is not much of a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” cried her brother, “because he does not write easily. He thinks too hard over four-syllable words. Do you not, Darcy?”

“My writing style is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cb9284bce06a745e4e8d1b8c","rewritten_text":"So the ringmaster made a little speech and said he hoped there would be no disturbance. If the man promised not to cause any more trouble, he would let him ride, provided he thought he could stay on the horse. Everybody laughed and said all right, and the man climbed aboard. The moment he was on, the horse began to buck, rear, and whirl, while two circus men clung to its bridle, trying to restrain it, and the drunk man hung onto its neck, his heels flying into the air with every leap. The whole crowd stood shouting and laughing until tears streamed down their faces. At last, despite everything the circus men could do, the horse broke free and tore around the ring like mad, with the drunk sprawled across him and clinging to his neck, one leg nearly dragging on one side, then the other on the other side, while the people went wild. It wasn’t funny to me; I was trembling at the danger he was in. But soon he struggled upright in the saddle and seized the bridle, reeling this way and that. Then, the next moment, he sprang to his feet, dropped the bridle, and stood there, while the horse raced like a house on fire. He stood sailing around as easily and comfortably as if he had never been drunk in his life—and then he began pulling off his clothes and throwing them away. He shed them so rapidly they seemed to clog the air, and altogether he removed seventeen suits. Then there he was, slim and handsome, dressed in the gaudiest, prettiest outfit you ever saw. He attacked that horse with his whip and made him fairly hum, then finally leaped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing room, while everybody howled with delight and astonishment.\n\nThen the ringmaster realized how completely he had been fooled, and he was the sickest-looking ringmaster you ever saw, I reckon. Why, it was one of his own men! He had invented the whole joke himself and never told a soul. I felt foolish enough to have been taken in that way, but I wouldn’t have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. I don’t know; there may be better circuses than that one, but I’ve never found them. Anyway, it was more than good enough for me, and wherever I come across it, it can have all my business every time."}

{"request_id":"baaf840829b8f38708ff7046","rewritten_text":"Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, met Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay in combat. All four knights fought fiercely and broke their spears against one another. Then Sir Pertolope came from the castle and met Sir Lionel. Sir Pertolope, the Green Knight, struck Sir Lionel, Sir Launcelot’s brother, from his horse. Noble heralds recorded all these deeds, noting who fought best and their names. Then Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth, but the force of the blow threw Sir Bleobaris to the ground. When Sir Galihodin saw this, he challenged Sir Gareth, and Sir Gareth struck him down. Sir Galihud then took up a spear to avenge his brother, but Sir Gareth treated him in the same way. He also knocked down Sir Dinadan and his brother, La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage—all with a single spear.

When King Aswisance of Ireland saw Sir Gareth fighting so well, he wondered who he could be. At one moment Gareth appeared green, and when he returned again he seemed blue. Each time he rode back and forth, his color changed, so that no king or knight could recognize him with certainty. Then King Agwisance of Ireland met Sir Gareth, who struck him from his horse, saddle and all. Next came King Carados of Scotland, and Sir Gareth knocked both horse and rider to the ground. He did the same to King Uriens of Gore. Then Sir Bagdemagus entered the fight, and Sir Gareth struck him down, horse and man. Bagdemagus’s son, Meliganus, broke a spear against Sir Gareth with great strength and skill.

Then Sir Galahault, the noble prince, called aloud, “Knight of the many colors, you have jousted well. Now prepare yourself, for I will joust with you.” Sir Gareth heard him and took up a great spear. They charged one another, and the prince’s spear broke. Sir Gareth struck him on the left side of his helmet, making him reel from side to side. He would have fallen if his men had not caught him.

“Truly,” said King Arthur, “that knight of the many colors is a good knight.” The king then called Sir Launcelot to him and asked him to fight that knight. “Sir,” said Launcelot, “I can easily find it in my heart to spare him for now, because he has worked hard enough today. When a good knight performs so well in a single day, it is not the part of a good knight to take away his honor, especially after seeing how much labor he has endured. Perhaps,” Sir Launcelot continued, “his cause is here today, and perhaps this lady loves him best of all who are here. I can see that he is straining himself to accomplish great deeds. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, he shall have the honor today. Though I had the power to take it from him, I would not.”"}

{"request_id":"8ff6eb42da0f647ed5aab894","rewritten_text":"His manner was stubborn in the extreme, and “that cursed bug” were the only words that escaped his lips during the journey. For my part, I carried a couple of dark lanterns, while Legrand contented himself with the scarab, which he had tied to the end of a piece of whipcord and twirled back and forth with the air of a conjurer as he walked. When I saw this final, unmistakable proof of my friend’s mental derangement, I could scarcely keep from tears. Still, I thought it best to indulge his fancy, at least for the moment, or until I could take some more forceful action with a reasonable chance of success. Meanwhile, I tried, entirely without success, to learn the purpose of the expedition. Having persuaded me to accompany him, he seemed unwilling to discuss any subject of lesser importance, and answered all my questions only with, “We shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s upper end in a skiff, then climbed the high ground along the mainland shore and proceeded northwest through a country so wild and desolate that there was no sign of a human footprint anywhere. Legrand led decisively, stopping only for an instant now and then to consult what seemed to be landmarks he had arranged on an earlier occasion.

We traveled in this way for about two hours, and the sun was just setting when we entered a region far drearier than anything we had yet seen. It was a kind of plateau near the summit of an almost inaccessible hill, thickly wooded from base to peak and scattered with enormous crags that seemed to rest loosely on the ground. In many places, they were kept from plunging into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines running in various directions gave the scene an even sterner solemnity.

The natural platform we had climbed was densely covered with brambles. We soon found that it would have been impossible to force our way through them without a scythe, so Jupiter, at his master’s direction, cleared a path for us to the foot of an enormously tall tulip tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, towered above them all, and surpassed every other tree I had ever seen in the beauty of its foliage and shape, the broad spread of its branches, and the majestic character of its appearance."}

{"request_id":"2027b576d767ef03e18efd77","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced angrily up and down the room. I stood prepared to receive and answer his reproaches. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is utterly ridiculous,” he cried. “If you were schoolboys, you could not behave more unreasonably.”

“You do not understand,” said Raymond. “This is only part of a system—a scheme of tyranny to which I will never submit. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in its empire? My privacy invaded, my actions censured, my friends insulted? But I will rid myself of the whole thing at once. Be my witnesses.” He removed the star, the insignia of office, from his breast and threw it onto the table. “I renounce my office; I abdicate my power—let whoever can assume it do so!”

“Let him assume it,” exclaimed Adrian, “who can declare himself, or whom the world will declare, your superior. There is no man in England with sufficient presumption. Know yourself, Raymond, and your indignation will end; your confidence will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country, or for our own, we also prayed for the Protector’s life and welfare, as inseparably bound to it. You devoted your hours to our benefit, and your ambition was to earn our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, established useful institutions for us, and made the soil abundantly fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your judgment seat, while the poor and oppressed rose like flowers awakened by morning beneath the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we are all horrified and mourn when this seems to have changed? But come, this fit of anger has already passed; resume your duties. Your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will be silenced, and our love, honor, and duty will once again be shown to you. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world is subject to you.”

“All this would be very sensible if it were addressed to someone else,” Raymond replied moodily. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first peer of the realm, may become its sovereign. You, the good, the wise, the just, may rule every heart. But I see—too soon for my own happiness, too late for England’s good—that I undertook a task beyond my abilities. I cannot rule myself. My passions are my masters; my smallest impulse is my tyrant. Do you think I renounced the Protectorate—and I have renounced it—in a fit of anger? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that bauble again; never again burden myself with the weight of care and misery of which it is the visible sign.”"}

{"request_id":"f005800fb8d00d67e857e2e1","rewritten_text":"She would live among people who loved her and had better judgment than she did, in a place private enough to keep her safe and busy enough to keep her cheerful. She would never be led into temptation, nor left for temptation to discover her. She would be respectable and happy; and Emma admitted that Harriet was the luckiest creature in the world, having inspired such a steady and lasting affection in such a man—or, if not quite the luckiest, second only to herself.

Harriet was necessarily drawn away by her commitments to the Martins and spent less and less time at Hartfield, which was no cause for regret. Her closeness with Emma had to fade; their friendship would become a quieter kind of goodwill. Fortunately, what ought to happen, and what had to happen, already seemed to be beginning in the most gradual and natural way.

Before the end of September, Emma went with Harriet to church and watched her marry Robert Martin with complete satisfaction. No memories, even those connected with Mr. Elton as he stood before them, could spoil it. Perhaps, indeed, Emma scarcely noticed Mr. Elton then, except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might soon be given to her. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Churchills were also in town, and they were only waiting for November.

The month between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley had chosen, as far as they dared, for their own marriage. They had decided that it should take place while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so that the couple could spend the planned fortnight away on a seaside tour. John and Isabella, along with every other friend, approved the plan. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could they persuade Mr. Woodhouse to agree? He had never spoken of their marriage except as something far in the future.

When they first raised the subject, he was so miserable that they nearly lost hope. A second mention caused less pain. He began to think that it would happen and that he could not stop it—a very encouraging step toward accepting it. Still, he was not happy. In fact, he seemed so distressed that his daughter lost courage. She could not bear to see him suffer or to know that he imagined himself neglected. Although she almost accepted the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys that, once the marriage was over, his distress would soon end as well, she hesitated. She could not go on."}

{"request_id":"7fb12c4ce1ab4676fa1bc6ac","rewritten_text":"I would pretend to die; my satisfied heirs would take possession of my fortune, and I would purchase my freedom. But my scheme must be carefully arranged; I could not be left penniless, and must secure some money. Alas! to what vile expedients was I compelled? Yet a whole lifetime of deceit was otherwise to be my lot: and whenever remorse at contriving any fraud made me recoil from my purpose, I was irresistibly drawn back and confirmed in it by the visit of some aunt or cousin, who would tell me that death was the fate of all men. They would then say that my father had certainly lost his reason since my mother’s death; that he was insane, and that I was fortunate, since in one of his fits he might have killed me rather than destroy his own deranged being. And all this, of course, was delicately expressed; not in plain words, lest my feelings should be wounded, but

Whispered so and so In dark hint soft and low

with lowered eyes and sympathetic smiles or whimpers; and I listened with a composed face while every nerve quivered; I, who dared not answer yes or no to all this blasphemy. Oh, what a delightful life, entirely free from guile! I with a dove’s expression and a fox’s heart: for I felt only the shame of falsehood, and none of that sacred sense of conscious innocence which might redeem it. I, who had formerly clothed myself in the radiant dress of sincerity, must now borrow one of many colours: it might fit awkwardly at first, but practice would teach me to arrange it in graceful folds, to lie with elegance. Yes, I might dye my soul in falsehood until I had wholly concealed its natural hue. Oh, beloved father! Receive the pure heart of your unhappy daughter; allow me to join you unblemished as I was, or you will not know my changed appearance. As sorrow might alter Constance, so deceit would alter me until, in heaven, you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy both now and when we meet again, I must flee from this life, which is mockery to one like me. Only in solitude shall I be myself; in solitude I shall be yours.

Alas! Even now I look back with disgust upon the devices and schemes by which, after many painful struggles, I accomplished my retreat. I could give a lengthy account of the means I employed, first to secure myself a modest support for the rest of my life, and afterward to establish the belief in my death: I could, but I will not."}

{"request_id":"84525c9dc6a29af331c7a1a6","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in amazement for a few moments. Then, seeing that he was completely serious, he wrote an address on a piece of paper, signed his initials, and passed it across the table.

‘Scotland Yard would pay a great deal to know this address, my dear fellow.’

‘They shan’t have it,’ cried Lord Arthur, laughing. After warmly shaking the young Russian’s hand, he ran downstairs, looked at the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

There he dismissed the coachman and walked down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court. He went beneath the archway and found himself in a strange dead-end passage, apparently occupied by a French laundry. Clothes-lines formed a complete network from house to house, and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked to the very end and knocked at a small green house. After some delay, during which every window in the court filled with blurred, watching faces, the door was opened by a rough-looking foreigner. In very poor English, he asked Lord Arthur what he wanted. Lord Arthur handed him the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. When the man saw it, he bowed and invited Lord Arthur into a shabby front parlour on the ground floor. A few moments later, Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, hurried into the room with a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

‘Count Rouvaloff has given me a letter of introduction to you,’ said Lord Arthur, bowing. ‘I would like a brief interview about a business matter. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I want you to supply me with an explosive clock.’

‘Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,’ said the cheerful little German, laughing. ‘Don’t look so worried. It is my duty to know everyone, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is quite well. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish breakfast? There is an excellent pâté, and my friends are kind enough to say that my Rhine wine is better than anything served at the German Embassy.’ Before Lord Arthur had recovered from his surprise at being recognised, he was seated in the back room, drinking the most delicious Marcobrünner from a pale-yellow hock glass marked with the Imperial monogram, and chatting as warmly as possible with the famous conspirator.

‘Explosive clocks,’ said Herr Winckelkopf, ‘are not very suitable for export abroad. Even when they get through Customs, the trains are so unreliable that they usually go off before reaching their proper destination.’"}

{"request_id":"c957a9877f02133281ec81d5","rewritten_text":"“Are you speaking of—Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I could never have meant anyone else—and so I thought you understood. When we spoke of him, it seemed perfectly clear.”

“Not entirely,” Emma replied, forcing herself to remain calm, “because everything you said then seemed to me to concern someone else. I could almost swear that you had _named_ Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain that you spoke of the service Mr. Frank Churchill had done you by protecting you from the gypsies.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly the substance of what I said at the time. I told you that I did not wonder at your attachment; that, considering the service he had done you, it was extremely natural. You agreed, speaking very warmly of your gratitude for that service, and even describing what you had felt when you saw him come forward to rescue you. The impression remains very strong in my memory.”

“Oh, dear,” cried Harriet, “now I remember what you mean; but I was thinking of something quite different then. It was not the gypsies—it was not Mr. Frank Churchill I meant. No!” she added with some emphasis. “I was thinking of something far more precious—of Mr. Knightley’s coming to ask me to dance when Mr. Elton would not dance with me, and when there was no other partner in the room. That was the kind action; that was the noble benevolence and generosity; that was the service that first made me feel how superior he was to every other person on earth.”

“Good God!” cried Emma. “This has been a most unfortunate—most dreadful mistake! What is to be done?”

“You would not have encouraged me, then, if you had understood me? At least, I cannot be worse off than I would have been if the other had been the person; and now—it _is_ possible—”

She paused for several moments. Emma could not speak.

“I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she continued, “that you should see a great difference between the two, whether in relation to me or to anyone else. You must think one five hundred million times above me compared with the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—that if—strange as it may seem—. You know they were your own words, that even more wonderful things had happened, and matches of greater inequality had taken place than one between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. Therefore, it seems possible that even such a thing as this may have happened before—and if I should be fortunate beyond expression—if Mr. Knightley should truly—if _he_ does not mind the difference, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, that you will not oppose it or try to place obstacles in the way.”"}

{"request_id":"b44855d4a02af6a768e49f09","rewritten_text":"He never tried a second time. The boys lay there, counting the dragging minutes until it seemed that time itself must be finished and eternity turning gray; then they were grateful to see that the sun was finally setting.

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, and smiled grimly at his companion, whose head was drooping onto his knees. He nudged him with his foot and said:

“Here! You’re supposed to be keeping watch, aren’t you? It’s all right, though—nothing’s happened.”

“My! Was I asleep?”

“Oh, partly, partly. It’s nearly time for us to move, partner. What’ll we do with the little loot we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here as we always have, I suppose. No point taking it away until we head south. Six hundred and fifty dollars in silver is something to carry.”

“Well—all right. It won’t hurt to come here one more time.”

“No—but I’d say come at night, like we used to. It’s better.”

“Yes, but listen; it may be a long time before I get the right chance for that job. Accidents could happen; it isn’t in such a good place. We’ll bury it properly—and bury it deep.”

“Good idea,” said his companion. He crossed the room, knelt down, lifted one of the hearthstones at the back, and took out a bag that jingled pleasantly. He removed twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same amount for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to Joe, who was now on his knees in the corner, digging with his bowie knife.

The boys forgot all their fears and misery in an instant. With greedy eyes, they watched every movement. Luck! The magnificence of it was beyond anything they could imagine. Six hundred dollars was enough money to make half a dozen boys rich! This was treasure hunting under the best possible circumstances—there would be no troublesome uncertainty about where to dig. They nudged each other constantly, eloquent nudges that were easy to understand, meaning simply: “Oh, but aren’t you glad now that we’re here!”

Joe’s knife struck something.

“Hello!” he said.

“What is it?” his companion asked.

“Half-rotten plank—no, I think it’s a box. Here—lend a hand and we’ll find out what it’s doing here. Never mind, I’ve made a hole.”

He reached inside and pulled out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as excited and delighted as the men themselves.

Joe’s companion said:

“We’ll make short work of this. There’s an old rusty pick among the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace—I saw it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"ae8fb3463bf1a26f0f0fec4f","rewritten_text":"The mighty voice—one might call it inorganic, since we could in no way connect it with the mechanism of pipe or key—ceased its sonorous utterance, and the girl, turning to help her aged companion, at last became aware of us.

It was her father; and from childhood she had guided his sightless steps. They were Germans from Saxony who, having emigrated there only a few years earlier, had formed new bonds with the neighboring villagers. Around the time the pestilence began, a young German student had joined them. Their simple story was easy to understand. He, a nobleman, loved the poor musician’s beautiful daughter and followed them in flight from the persecutions of his friends; but soon the great leveller came with his unblunted scythe, mowing down, along with the grass, the field’s tall flowers. The young man was among the first victims. She preserved herself for her father’s sake. His blindness allowed her to maintain a deception that had begun by accident—and now, as solitary beings and the only survivors in the land, he remained unaware of the change, not knowing that when he listened to his child’s music, the silent mountains, senseless lake, and unconscious trees were, except for himself, her only listeners.

On the very day we arrived, she had been seized by the symptomatic illness. She was paralyzed with terror at the thought of leaving her aged, blind father alone upon the empty earth; yet she lacked the courage to reveal the truth, and the extremity of her despair drove her to extraordinary exertions. At the usual vesper hour, she led him to the chapel; and, though trembling and weeping for his sake, played without a fault in time or a wrong note the hymn composed to celebrate the creation of the adorned earth, soon to become her tomb.

We came upon her like visitors from heaven itself; her exalted courage and barely maintained firmness vanished at the sight of relief. With a shriek she rushed toward us, clasped Adrian’s knees, and, saying only, “O save my father!” with sobs and hysterical cries, opened the long-sealed floodgates of her grief.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, and which she had indicated to us in her final moments. Her father, at last conscious of his daughter’s danger but unable to see the changes in her beloved face, stubbornly held her hand until death chilled and stiffened it. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until, twelve hours later, kindly death carried him to his unbroken rest. They lie beneath the sod, the tree their monument; the sacred place remains clear in my memory, shadowed by the craggy Jura and the distant, immeasurable Alps. The church spire they once attended still rises among the enclosing trees; and though her hand is cold, I seem still to hear the strains of divine music they loved drifting around them, comforting their gentle ghosts."}

{"request_id":"0ddbf2a8a0b4e504c83b0be9","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently placing his hand on the Doctor’s arm once more, after a brief silence on both sides, “to what would you attribute this attack?”

“I believe,” replied Doctor Manette, “that there had been a powerful and unusual revival of the chain of thought and memory that originally caused the malady. Some intense associations of an exceedingly painful nature were vividly brought back, I think. It is likely that a fear had long been hidden in his mind, that those associations might return—say, under certain circumstances—say, on a particular occasion. He tried vainly to prepare himself; perhaps the attempt to prepare himself left him less able to endure it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” asked Mr. Lorry, with understandable hesitation.

The Doctor gazed mournfully around the room, shook his head, and answered in a quiet voice, “Not at all.”

“Now, regarding the future,” suggested Mr. Lorry.

“As to the future,” said the Doctor, regaining his firmness, “I should have great hope. Since Heaven, in its mercy, restored him so quickly, I should have great hope. He yielded beneath the pressure of a complicated something, long feared, long dimly anticipated, and long resisted; and recovering after the cloud had broken and passed, I should hope that the worst was behind him.”

“Well, well! That is good comfort. I am thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am thankful!” repeated the Doctor, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other matters,” said Mr. Lorry, “about which I am anxious to be informed. May I continue?”

“You cannot render your friend a better service.” The Doctor extended his hand to him.

“To the first, then. He is studious by habit and unusually energetic; he applies himself with great enthusiasm to gaining professional knowledge, carrying out experiments, and many other things. Now, does he do too much?”

“I think not. It may be the nature of his mind to require occupation constantly and in an unusual degree. That may be partly natural to him, and partly the consequence of suffering. The less it was occupied with healthy matters, the more it would risk turning toward unhealthy ones. He may have watched himself and discovered this.”

“You are certain that he is not under too much strain?”

“I believe I am quite certain.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt whether that could readily happen. There has been a violent strain in one direction, and it requires a counterweight.”

“Forgive me, as a persistent man of business. Supposing for a moment that he were overworked; would it reveal itself through some recurrence of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"b0e54ecf3faaf2256a80274b","rewritten_text":"“‘We have been to your residence,’ said the first, ‘but were unfortunate enough not to find you there. We were told that you were probably walking this way, so we followed, hoping to catch up with you. Will you please enter the carriage?’

“The manner of both men was commanding, and as they spoke they moved to place me between themselves and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘forgive me, but I usually ask who has the honour of seeking my help, and what kind of case has brought me here.’

“The second speaker answered. ‘Doctor, your clients are people of rank. As for the nature of the case, our confidence in your skill assures us that you will discover it more accurately than we could explain it. Enough. Will you please enter the carriage?’

“I could do nothing but obey, and entered in silence. They followed me—the last one jumping in after raising the steps. The carriage turned around and continued at its former speed.

“I repeat this conversation exactly as it happened. I have no doubt that these are the precise words. I describe everything exactly as it occurred, forcing my mind not to stray from the task. Where I make the broken marks below, I stop for the moment and place my paper in its hiding place.

*****

“The carriage left the streets, passed through the North Barrier, and came out onto the country road. About two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier—I did not measure the distance then, but did so later when I traveled the route—it turned off the main road and soon stopped at a lonely house. All three of us got out and walked along a damp, soft path through a garden where an abandoned fountain had overflowed, to the house door. When the door did not open at once after the bell was rung, one of my two escorts struck the man who opened it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“This did not especially surprise me, since I had seen ordinary people struck more often than dogs. But the other man, also angry, struck him in the same way with his arm. The brothers’ expressions and manner were then so exactly alike that I realized for the first time that they were twins.

“From the moment we got out at the outer gate—which was locked, and which one brother opened to let us in before locking it again—I had heard cries coming from an upper room."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5896044c7fb185e906e04cb4","rewritten_text":"ABOUT ten minutes afterward, the tea bell rang, and, since Virginia had not come down, Mrs. Otis sent a footman upstairs to summon her. After a short while he returned, saying that he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. As she regularly went into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis was not initially alarmed; but when six o’clock struck and Virginia still had not appeared, she grew genuinely distressed. She sent the boys to search for her, while she and Mr. Otis examined every room in the house. At half-past six the boys returned, declaring that they had found no sign of their sister. Everyone was now in the utmost agitation and quite at a loss what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly recalled that a few days earlier he had allowed a band of gypsies to camp in the park. He immediately set out for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they had been staying, accompanied by his eldest son and two farm-servants. The little Duke of Cheshire, nearly frantic with worry, pleaded earnestly to be taken along, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be a struggle. When he reached the place, however, he discovered that the gypsies had departed, evidently in some haste, for the fire was still alight and several plates remained on the grass. After sending Washington and the two men to search the surrounding district, he hurried home and telegraphed every police inspector in the county, instructing them to watch for a little girl kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then had his horse brought round and, after making his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode away along the Ascot Road with a groom. He had scarcely gone two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Turning, he saw the little Duke approaching on his pony, his face flushed and his head bare. ‘I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy panted, ‘but I can’t eat dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry with me; if you had allowed us to become engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!’\n\nThe Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young scamp, and was deeply touched by his devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted the boy kindly on the shoulders and said, ‘Well, Cecil, if you refuse to go back, I suppose you must come with me—but I shall have to buy you a hat at Ascot.’"}

{"request_id":"e5e5c0c3d55f9581ec530527","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s feelings had overcome her self-interest, and for the young man’s sake she had given up the chance of scheming longer for Sir Walter. She has abilities, however, as well as feelings; and it is now uncertain whether his cunning or hers will ultimately prevail—whether, after keeping her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may not finally be coaxed and flattered into making her the wife of Sir William.

There can be no doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and humiliated by losing their companion and discovering her deception. They had their distinguished cousins, certainly, to turn to for comfort; but they must long feel that flattering and following others, without being flattered and followed in return, is only a form of incomplete enjoyment.

Anne, having been satisfied very early that Lady Russell intended to love Captain Wentworth as she ought, had no other shadow over the happiness of her prospects than the awareness that she had no relations to offer him whom a sensible man could value. In this respect she felt her own inferiority very deeply. The difference in their fortunes meant nothing; it caused her not a moment’s regret. But having no family who could receive him and appreciate him properly—nothing respectable, harmonious, or affectionate to offer in return for all the worth and warm welcome she had found in his brothers and sisters—was a source of pain as vivid as her mind could feel amid otherwise profound happiness. She had only two friends in the world to add to his circle: Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. To both, however, he was quite willing to attach himself. Lady Russell, despite all her former mistakes, he could now value sincerely. Though he was not required to say that he believed she had been right to separate them at first, he was ready to say almost everything else in her favour; and as for Mrs Smith, she had claims of many kinds that quickly and permanently recommended her.

The recent services she had performed for Anne would have been sufficient on their own, and their marriage, instead of taking one friend from her, gave her two. She was the first visitor to their established household; and Captain Wentworth, by helping her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies—writing on her behalf, acting for her, and guiding her through every minor difficulty with the energy of a fearless man and a determined friend—fully repaid the services she had rendered, or had ever intended to render, to his wife."}

{"request_id":"3c20118d0a367fabbf095191","rewritten_text":"“These were the events that weighed upon Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most wretched of his family. He could have borne poverty, and while this hardship was the reward of his virtue, he took pride in it; but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were sorrows more bitter and beyond repair. The Arabian’s arrival now breathed new life into his spirit.

“When word reached Leghorn that Felix had been stripped of his wealth and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to think no longer of her lover, but to prepare to return to her native land. Safie’s generous spirit was offended by this command; she tried to reason with her father, but he angrily left her, repeating his tyrannical order.

“A few days later, the Turk entered his daughter’s room and hurriedly told her that he had reason to believe his residence in Leghorn had been discovered, and that he would soon be surrendered to the French government; he had therefore hired a vessel to take him to Constantinople, where he would sail within a few hours. He meant to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant, who would follow at her convenience with most of his property, which had not yet reached Leghorn.

“When she was alone, Safie considered what course it would be proper for her to take in this crisis. Life in Turkey was hateful to her; both her religion and her feelings turned her against it. From some of her father’s papers that came into her possession, she learned of her lover’s exile and discovered the name of the place where he was then living. She wavered for some time, but at last made her decision. Taking several jewels that belonged to her, together with some money, she left Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who understood the common language of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

“She reached safely a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, where her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie cared for her with the greatest devotion, but the poor girl died, leaving the Arabian alone, unfamiliar with the country’s language and entirely ignorant of the ways of the world. Yet she came into kind hands. The Italian had named the place to which they were traveling, and after her death, the woman of the house where they had stayed took care that Safie should reach her lover’s cottage safely.”"}

No, I move far off to one side and work my way toward him little by little, so he never suspects I mean to strike him; then, all at once, he is flat on his back and cannot imagine how it happened. That was how I dealt with Brother Dowley. I began speaking in an easy, comfortable way, as if I were only talking to pass the time. “Boys, there are many strange things about law, custom, usage, and all the rest, when you stop to examine them; yes, and about the direction and progress of human opinion and action, too. There are written laws—they die; but there are also unwritten laws—they are eternal. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it says wages must rise, little by little, throughout the centuries. Notice how it works. We know what wages are now, in one place and another; we take an average and call that today’s wage. We know what wages were a hundred years ago and two hundred years ago. That is as far back as we can go, but it is enough to show us the law of progress—the size and speed of each increase. So, without any document, we can come fairly close to deciding what wages were three, four, or five hundred years ago. Good, so far. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking backward, turn around, and apply the law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what people’s wages will be at any future date you care to name, for hundreds and hundreds of years.”

“What, goodman, what?”

“Yes. In seven hundred years, wages will have risen to six times what they are now in this region, and farmhands will receive 3 cents a day, while mechanics will receive 6.”

“I wish I might die now and live then!” interrupted Smug, the wheelwright, with a greedy light in his eyes.

content.text: {"request_id":"70ed0ff9447925190d17eafe","rewritten_text":"Rising early, and once more managing to elude the watchfulness of my creditors, I hastened to the bookseller’s stall and spent the little ready money I had on several volumes concerning Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Having brought them safely home, I devoted every moment I could spare to reading them, and soon acquired, as I believed, enough proficiency in such studies to carry out my design. During this interval, I also made every effort to appease the three creditors who had caused me so much trouble. At length I succeeded—partly by selling sufficient household furniture to meet half their demand, and partly by promising to pay the remainder when a small project I claimed to have in hand was completed, for assistance with which I asked their services. By these means—for they were ignorant men—I had little trouble in winning them to my purpose.\n\n“Things being thus settled, I managed, with my wife’s help and with the utmost secrecy and caution, to dispose of the property still remaining to me, and to borrow, in small amounts and under various pretences, without considering how I should ever repay them, a considerable sum in ready money. With these funds I gradually obtained fine cambric muslin, in pieces of twelve yards each; twine; a quantity of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep wicker basket made to order; and various other articles required for constructing and fitting out a balloon of extraordinary size. I instructed my wife to assemble this as quickly as possible, giving her all the necessary directions concerning the particular method. Meanwhile, I fashioned the twine into a net of adequate dimensions, fitted it with a hoop and the requisite cords, and purchased a quadrant, a compass, a spy-glass, an ordinary barometer with several important alterations, and two astronomical instruments less commonly known. I then found opportunities to carry by night, to a secluded place east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks, each holding about fifty gallons, together with one larger cask; six tinned-ware tubes, three inches in diameter, properly shaped and ten feet long; a quantity of a certain metallic substance, or semi-metal, which I shall not identify; and twelve demijohns filled with a very common acid. The gas produced from these last materials is one that no person besides myself has ever generated—or, at least, ever employed for a similar purpose. I should have no objection to revealing the secret, except that it properly belongs to a citizen of Nantz, in France, who communicated it to me conditionally.”"}

{"request_id":"f1c5b569eb8b6dff133aab6b","rewritten_text":"And I summon you, spirits of the dead, and you wandering agents of vengeance, to assist and guide me in my task. Let the accursed, hellish monster drink deeply of suffering; let him know the despair that now torments me.”

I had begun my adjuration solemnly, with an awe that nearly convinced me the shades of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion; but as I finished, the furies took possession of me, and rage strangled my voice.

Through the silence of night, a loud and fiendish laugh answered me. It sounded long and heavily in my ears; the mountains echoed it back, and I felt as though all hell encircled me with mockery and laughter. Surely, at that instant, frenzy would have seized me and I would have ended my wretched life, had not my vow been heard and I been preserved for vengeance. The laughter faded, and then a familiar, hated voice, seemingly close beside my ear, spoke to me in a clear whisper: “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have resolved to live, and I am satisfied.”

I sprang toward the place from which the sound came, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly the moon’s broad disk rose and cast its full light upon his ghastly, distorted form as he fled with more than human speed.

I pursued him, and for many months this has been my occupation. Following a faint clue, I traced the windings of the Rhone, but without success. The blue Mediterranean came into view, and by a strange chance I saw the fiend enter it by night and conceal himself aboard a vessel bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same ship, but somehow he escaped me.

Through the wild regions of Tartary and Russia, though he continued to elude me, I have always followed his trail. At times the peasants, terrified by this dreadful apparition, told me where he had gone; at times he himself, fearing that if I lost every trace of him I would despair and die, left some sign to direct me. Snow fell upon my head, and I saw the mark of his enormous foot across the white plain. To you, just entering life, for whom care is unfamiliar and agony unknown, how can you comprehend what I have suffered and still suffer? Cold, hunger, and weariness were the smallest of the pains appointed for me; some devil had cursed me, and I carried an everlasting hell within me. Yet a benevolent spirit still followed and guided my steps, and whenever I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly free me from difficulties that seemed impossible to overcome. Sometimes, when hunger overcame nature and exhaustion brought me low, a meal had been prepared for me in the wilderness, restoring and strengthening me."}

{"request_id":"ec1ffd7c84fc95b3bf2f92ea","rewritten_text":"Why, we might build a very exciting superstition around this clue. I suppose you would call the bug _scarabæus caput hominis_, or something similar—there are many such names in natural histories. But where are the _antennæ_ you mentioned?”

“The _antennæ!_” said Legrand, who seemed to be growing strangely heated about the matter. “Surely you can see the _antennæ_. I made them as clear as they are on the real insect, and I assume that is enough.”

“Well, well,” I said, “perhaps you did—but I still cannot see them.” I handed him the paper without saying more, since I did not want to upset him. Yet I was greatly surprised by what had happened. His bad temper confused me—and, as for the beetle drawing, there were plainly _no antennæ_ visible, while the whole figure looked very much like the usual pictures of a death’s-head.

He took the paper irritably and was about to crumple it, apparently to throw it into the fire, when a passing glance at the drawing suddenly caught his attention. At once his face became intensely red, and then, just as quickly, extremely pale. For several minutes he sat examining the drawing closely. At last he stood, took a candle from the table, and went to sit on a sea-chest in the farthest corner of the room. There he studied the paper anxiously again, turning it every way. He said nothing, but his behavior astonished me. Still, I thought it wiser not to worsen his growing bad mood with any remarks. Soon he took a wallet from his coat pocket, placed the paper carefully inside it, and put both into a writing desk, which he locked. He now seemed calmer, but his earlier enthusiasm had completely vanished. He appeared less angry than lost in thought. As the evening passed, he became more deeply absorbed in his thoughts, and none of my attempts at conversation could draw him out. I had planned to spend the night at the hut, as I often had before, but seeing him in this state, I decided to leave. He did not ask me to stay; however, as I departed, he shook my hand with even greater warmth than usual.

About a month later—and during that time I had seen nothing of Legrand—I received a visit in Charleston from his servant, Jupiter. I had never seen the good old Black man look so discouraged, and I feared that some serious misfortune had happened to my friend."}

{"request_id":"df8eb1a8638a2787c001c87e","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining room, the clock tower began to strike midnight. When the final stroke sounded, they heard a crash and a sudden, piercing cry. A terrible roll of thunder shook the house, strange music drifted through the air, and a panel at the top of the staircase flew open with a loud bang. Virginia stepped onto the landing, looking very pale, with a small casket in her hand. At once they all rushed toward her. Mrs. Otis hugged her fiercely, the Duke covered her with excited kisses, and the twins danced wildly around them.

‘Good heavens, child, where have you been?’ Mr. Otis asked, somewhat angrily, thinking she had played another foolish trick. ‘Cecil and I have ridden all over the countryside looking for you, and your mother has been terrified. You must never play such practical jokes again.’

‘Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!’ the twins shouted as they danced around.

‘My darling, thank God we found you. You must never leave my side again,’ Mrs. Otis murmured, kissing the trembling girl and smoothing her tangled golden hair.

‘Papa,’ Virginia said calmly, ‘I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for everything he had done. Before he died, he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.’

The whole family stared at her in silent amazement. She remained completely serious, however, and led them through the opening in the wood paneling and down a narrow secret passage. Washington followed with a lighted candle he had picked up from the table. At last they reached a large oak door covered with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung open on its heavy hinges, revealing a small, low room with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny barred window. A huge iron ring was set into the wall, and chained to it was a thin skeleton stretched out on the stone floor. It seemed to be reaching with its long, bare fingers toward an old-fashioned wooden dish and water jug placed just beyond its grasp. The jug had clearly once held water, for its inside was coated with green mold. The dish held nothing but a heap of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her small hands, and began to pray silently. The others watched in wonder at the terrible tragedy whose secret had finally been revealed."}

{"request_id":"75f566d843515e95a238fb13","rewritten_text":"When we got back to the raft and he came to count everything up, he found he had collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also carried off a three-gallon jug of whisky, which he found beneath a wagon when he was starting home through the woods. The king said that, all things considered, it surpassed any day he had ever spent in the missionary business. There was no use arguing, he said; heathens were worthless compared with pirates when it came to working a camp meeting.

The duke had thought he was doing pretty well until the king came along to show him up, but afterward he did not think so highly of himself. He had set up and printed two small jobs for farmers in that printing office—horse bills—and collected four dollars. He had also secured ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper, which he said he would print for four dollars if they paid in advance, and they did. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he took three subscriptions at fifty cents each, provided they paid in advance. They had intended to pay in cordwood and onions as usual, but he said he had just bought the business, had reduced the price as far as he could afford, and would operate it for cash. He set up a short poem he had written himself, straight from his own head—three verses, rather sweet and sad—called “Yes, Crush, Cold World, This Breaking Heart,” and left it set and ready to print in the paper without charging anything. Altogether, he had taken in nine dollars and fifty cents, and said he had done a reasonably good day’s work.

Then he showed us another small job he had printed without charging us, since it was for our benefit. It showed a runaway Black man with a bundle tied to a stick over his shoulder, and “$200 Reward” beneath it. The text was all about Jim and described him exactly. It said he had run away from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, the previous winter, and had probably gone north; whoever caught him and returned him could claim the reward and expenses.

“Now,” said the duke, “after tonight we can travel in the daytime if we want. I awoke to a new life as one who dies in hope might awaken in Hell. I will not stain your imagination by describing my struggles, my anger at myself, and my despair. Let a veil cover the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father; the secrets of such an agonized heart must not be exposed. Everything was uproar, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet still the tenderest love. What first awakened my firm resolve to conquer my passion and restore your father to you was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic sorrow. That was what brought me here. I thought that if I could awaken again the grief I had felt at your mother’s death, and the many memories of her that had lain dormant for seventeen years, then all love for her child would die. In a moment of heroism I resolved to go alone, to leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But I could not. I had judged my strength too highly, or my love too lightly. I would certainly have died if you had not hurried to me. Would that I had truly been extinguished! “And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was terribly mistaken to think I could conquer my love for you; I never can. Seeing this house, these fields, and these woods, which my first love once inhabited, seems to have increased it. In my madness I dared tell myself: Diana died giving birth to her; her mother’s spirit passed into her body, and she should be Diana to me. With every attempt to cast it away, this love clings more tightly—this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which withers your hopes and destroys me forever. Better have loved despair, and safer kissed her. No time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since I arrived here, I have not for a moment ceased to feel the hell of passion planted in me, burning until everything is cold, stiff, and dead.”"}

{"request_id":"707b2a5afa03a198e52509ab","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently placing his hand on the Doctor’s arm again, after a brief silence from them both, “what do you think caused this attack?”

“I believe,” replied Doctor Manette, “that the thoughts and memories that first caused the illness returned with unusual force. I think some powerful and deeply painful associations were brought vividly back. He may have long feared that they would return—under certain circumstances, perhaps on a particular occasion. He tried to prepare himself, but in vain; perhaps that attempt left him less able to endure them.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked hesitantly.

The Doctor looked sadly around the room, shook his head, and answered in a low voice, “Not at all.”

“And what of the future?” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining his confidence, “I have great hope. Since Heaven, in its mercy, restored him so quickly, I have great hope. He gave way under the pressure of something complicated, long feared, dimly anticipated, and resisted for a long time. Now that the cloud has broken and passed, I hope the worst is over.”

“Well, well! That is comforting. I am thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am thankful!” repeated the Doctor, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other matters,” said Mr. Lorry, “about which I would like your advice. May I continue?”

“You could do your friend no better service.” The Doctor offered him his hand.

“Then, the first. He is very studious and unusually energetic. He works with great enthusiasm to gain professional knowledge, conduct experiments, and pursue many other interests. Now, does he work too hard?”

“I think not. His mind may naturally need constant occupation. That may be partly its nature and partly the result of his suffering. The less it was occupied with healthy matters, the more likely it was to turn in an unhealthy direction. He may have watched himself and discovered this.”

“You are certain he is not under too much strain?”

“I believe I am quite certain.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that would be easy. He has suffered violent pressure in one direction, and he needs an opposing weight.”

“Forgive me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose, for the moment, that he was overworked; would that appear as a return of this disorder?”"}

“Tell me what troubles you.”

“I have a cousin, my only relation and an orphan like me, whom I love very dearly. She is five years younger than I, and lives in a farmer’s house in the south country. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of my fate—for I cannot write—and if I could, how could I tell her? It is better so.”

“Yes, yes: better so.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”
