content.text: {"request_id":"854deb3de1c01a4ca16110ee","rewritten_text":"He chose Friday, the 17th of August, for his appearance, and spent most of the day examining his wardrobe, finally settling on a large slouch hat with a red feather, a winding-sheet frilled at wrists and neck, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening a fierce rainstorm broke, and the wind blew so strongly that every window and door in the old house shook and rattled. Indeed, it was precisely the sort of weather he adored. His plan was as follows. He would creep quietly to Washington Otis’s room, gibber at him from the foot of the bed, and stab himself three times in the throat to the accompaniment of slow music. He held Washington in particular dislike, knowing perfectly well that he was the one who regularly removed the celebrated Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. After reducing the rash and foolhardy youth to a state of utter terror, he would go on to the room occupied by the United States Minister and his wife, place a clammy hand upon Mrs. Otis’s forehead, and hiss the dreadful secrets of the charnel-house into her trembling husband’s ear. As for little Virginia, he had not entirely decided. She had never insulted him, and she was pretty and gentle. A few hollow groans from the wardrobe, he thought, ought to suffice; or, if that did not wake her, he could claw at the counterpane with fingers twitching as if palsied. Regarding the twins, however, he was firmly resolved to teach them a lesson. First, naturally, he would sit upon their chests, creating the suffocating sensation of nightmare. Then, since their beds stood very near one another, he would position himself between them as a green, ice-cold corpse until terror paralysed them; finally, he would cast off the winding-sheet and crawl around the room with bleached white bones and one rolling eyeball, in the guise of ‘Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton,’ a role in which he had more than once made a powerful impression, and which he considered fully equal to his celebrated part of ‘Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.’\n\nAt half-past ten he heard the family retiring. For a while he was distracted by the twins’ wild peals of laughter; with the carefree merriment of schoolboys, they were plainly entertaining themselves before going to bed. But at a quarter past eleven everything was quiet, and when midnight sounded, he ventured forth. The owl struck against the windowpanes, the raven croaked from the ancient yew, and the wind roamed mournfully around the house like a wandering soul. The Otis family, however, slept unaware of their fate, while high above the rain and tempest he could hear the United States Minister’s steady snoring."}

{"request_id":"02d6f1b6a7f9cc0c9bd1be89","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? It isn’t much! Many are under the Republic’s displeasure and must look out through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which is he?”

“I am he. Necessarily, since I am the last.”

It is Jarvis Lorry who has answered all the earlier questions. It is Jarvis Lorry who has climbed down and now stands with his hand on the coach door, replying to a group of officials. They stroll around the carriage and slowly climb onto the box to inspect the little luggage it carries on the roof; the country people lingering nearby press closer to the coach doors and stare greedily inside. A small child, carried by its mother, stretches out its short arm so that it may touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.”

“One may leave, citizen?”

“One may leave. Forward, my postilions! A good journey!”

“I salute you, citizens—and the first danger is past!”

These are again Jarvis Lorry’s words as he clasps his hands and looks upward. There is terror in the carriage, weeping, and the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveler.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can’t they be persuaded to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would look like flight, my darling. I must not urge them too strongly; it would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see whether we are being pursued!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, no one is pursuing us.”

Houses in twos and threes pass us, along with solitary farms, ruined buildings, dye-works, tanneries, and the like; then open country and avenues of leafless trees. The hard, uneven pavement lies beneath us, while soft, deep mud borders it on either side. At times we turn into the mud along the road to avoid stones that clatter against us and shake us; at others, we become stuck in ruts and bogs. Our impatience then becomes so agonizing that, in our wild alarm and haste, we want to get out and run—hide—do anything rather than stop.

From the open country, back again among ruined buildings, solitary farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like, cottages in twos and threes, and avenues of leafless trees. Have these men deceived us and taken us back by another road? Is this not the same place twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see whether we are being pursued! Hush! The posting-house.

Slowly, our four horses are taken out; slowly, the coach stands in the little street, stripped of horses and with no apparent chance of ever moving again; slowly, the new horses come into view, one by one; slowly, the new postilions follow, sucking and plaiting their whip lashes; slowly, the old postilions count their money, make incorrect additions, and reach dissatisfied conclusions."}

{"request_id":"7bbf54c8a3fd1fee598da015","rewritten_text":"Now that he had no work to occupy him, he placed the knuckles of his right hand in the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left hand in the hollow of his right. Then he passed a hand over his bearded chin, repeating these movements in a steady pattern without pause. Bringing him back from the wandering state he always fell into after speaking was like rousing a very weak person from a faint, or trying to hold back the spirit of a dying man in the hope of hearing some final revelation.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“Certainly I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was neither a sigh nor a groan, he bent over his work again, until the silence was broken once more.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, watching him closely.

His worn eyes turned toward Defarge, as though he wished to pass the question to him. But when no help came from that direction, he looked back at the questioner after first lowering his gaze to the ground.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away again, even for several minutes, all the while making those measured movements with his hands. At last his eyes slowly returned to the face from which they had wandered. When they settled on it, he started and continued like a sleeper suddenly awakened, returning to a subject from the night before.

“I asked permission to teach myself, and after a long time, with great difficulty, I received it. I have made shoes ever since.”

As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry continued to look steadily into his face.

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the ground, and he sat staring at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry placed his hand on Defarge’s arm—“do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no memory of former times rising in your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

As the prisoner of so many years sat staring by turns at Mr. Lorry and Defarge, faint traces of the alert intelligence once visible in the center of his forehead slowly pushed through the black mist that had covered him. They clouded over again, grew weaker, and disappeared; but they had been there."}

{"request_id":"692dceff85dc099e02fb30bb","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl replied.

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl answered firmly, “one reason the lady knows and will support me in—I know she will, because I have her promise. And for this other reason as well: bad a life as he has led, I have led a bad life too. There are many of us who have followed the same course together, and I will not turn against them—any of them—who might have turned against me, but did not, bad as they are.”

“Then,” said the gentleman quickly, as if this were the point he had been trying to reach, “put Monks in my hands and leave me to deal with him.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you that, in that case, if the truth is forced from him, the matter will end there. There must be circumstances in Oliver’s little history that it would be painful to expose publicly; and if the truth is once brought out, they shall go free.”

“And if it is not?” the girl suggested.

“Then,” the gentleman continued, “this Fagin shall not be brought to justice without your consent. In that event, I believe I could show you reasons that would persuade you to give it.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise for that?” the girl asked.

“You do,” Rose replied. “You have my true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never discover how you learned what you know?” the girl said after a brief pause.

“Never,” replied the gentleman. “The information would be used against him in such a way that he could never even guess its source.”

“I have been a liar, and among liars, since I was a little child,” the girl said after another silence, “but I will trust your word.”

After receiving assurances from both of them that she could safely do so, she began, in a voice so low that the listener often struggled to make out even the meaning of her words, to describe by name and location the public house from which she had been followed that night. From the way she occasionally paused, it seemed that the gentleman was making hurried notes of the information she gave him. When she had fully explained the place, the best position from which to watch it without attracting attention, and the night and hour when Monks most often visited it, she paused for a few moments, apparently trying to bring his features and appearance more clearly back to mind.

“He is tall,” said the girl, “and strongly built, but not stout. He walks furtively, and as he goes he constantly looks over his shoulder, first to one side and then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"b4285d23e42bd1a86711b3d8","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot, of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire, was a man who, for his own entertainment, never opened any book except the Baronetage; in it he found employment for an idle hour, and comfort in a troubled one. There his faculties were stirred to admiration and reverence as he considered the small surviving number of the earliest patents; there unpleasant feelings caused by domestic matters turned naturally into pity and disdain while he examined the nearly countless creations of the last century; and there, when every other page failed to interest him, he could read his own history with unfailing attention. This was the page to which the cherished volume always opened:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, in the county of Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

The paragraph had originally appeared from the printer’s hands exactly in that form; but Sir Walter had improved it by adding, for his own and his family’s information, these words after the date of Mary’s birth—“Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and by inserting with the greatest precision the day of the month on which he had lost his wife.

There followed, in the customary language, the history and advancement of the ancient and respectable family: how it had first settled in Cheshire; how it was mentioned by Dugdale; how its members had served as high sheriff, represented a borough in three successive parliaments, displayed loyalty, and received the dignity of baronet in the first year of Charles II, together with all the Marys and Elizabeths whom they had married. Altogether, it filled two handsome duodecimo pages, ending with the arms and motto—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,”—and Sir Walter’s handwriting once more in this conclusion:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity formed both the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity of person and of position. He had been remarkably handsome when young, and at fifty-four remained a very fine man. Few women could think more highly of their appearance than he did, nor could the valet of any newly made lord be more pleased with the station he occupied in society. He regarded the blessing of beauty as second only to that of a baronetcy; and Sir Walter Elliot, who possessed both advantages, was the continual object of his deepest respect and devotion.

His good looks and rank had one reasonable claim upon his attachment, since to them he must have owed a wife of far superior character to anything his own qualities deserved."}

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, pressing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical that he frightens me. But here is the orchestra. It is terrible, though it will last only about five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you will see the girl to whom I am going to give my whole life, and to whom I have given everything good in me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid a tremendous storm of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onto the stage. Yes, she was certainly beautiful—one of the loveliest creatures Lord Henry had ever seen. Her shy grace and startled eyes gave her something of a fawn’s look. A faint blush, like the reflection of a rose on silver, touched her cheeks as she looked at the crowded, excited audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat still, as if in a dream, staring at her. Lord Henry looked through his glasses and murmured, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of Capulet’s house, and Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, such as it was, played a few bars, and the dance began. Among the awkward, poorly dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a creature from a more beautiful world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant moving in water. The curves of her throat were like those of a white lily. Her hands seemed made of cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely lifeless. When her eyes fell on Romeo, she showed no joy. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much, Which mannerly devotion shows in this; For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch, And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

{"request_id":"882141724c3aea8093ac975a","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and vagabonds of every inferior sort were crowded together in one mass; the drovers’ whistling, the dogs’ barking, the oxen’s bellowing and plunging, the sheep’s bleating, the pigs’ grunting and squealing, the hawkers’ cries, and the shouts, oaths, and quarrels on every side; the ringing of bells and tumult of voices pouring from each public-house; the pressing, jostling, driving, beating, whooping, and yelling; the dreadful, discordant din echoing from every part of the market; and the unwashed, unshaven, ragged, and filthy figures continually darting to and fro, and bursting in and out of the crowd; made it a deafening and bewildering spectacle, which utterly confused the senses.

Mr. Sikes, pulling Oliver behind him, forced his way through the densest part of the throng, paying scarcely any heed to the many sights and sounds that so amazed the boy. He nodded two or three times to a friend who passed; and, declining just as many offers to take a morning dram, continued firmly onward until they had escaped the uproar and passed through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” said Sikes, glancing up at the clock of St. Andrew’s Church, “close upon seven! You must quicken your pace. Come, don’t begin lagging already, Lazy-legs!”

With these words, Mr. Sikes gave his little companion’s wrist a jerk; Oliver increased his pace to a sort of trot between a brisk walk and a run, and kept alongside the house-breaker’s rapid strides as best he could.

They continued at this speed until they had gone beyond Hyde Park Corner and were proceeding toward Kensington, when Sikes slackened his pace until an empty cart some distance behind them caught up. Noticing “Hounslow” painted upon it, he asked the driver, with all the civility he could muster, whether he would carry them as far as Isleworth.

“Jump up,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes; he’s my boy,” answered Sikes, staring hard at Oliver and absently placing his hand in the pocket containing the pistol.

“Your father walks a little too fast for you, doesn’t he, my lad?” asked the driver, observing that Oliver was breathless.

“Not at all,” Sikes cut in. “He’s accustomed to it. Here, take my hand, Ned. In with you!”

Speaking thus to Oliver, he helped him into the cart; and the driver, indicating a pile of sacks, told him to lie there and rest.

As they passed the successive milestones, Oliver grew increasingly curious about where his companion intended to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford were all left behind; yet they continued onward as steadily as though their journey had only just commenced."}

{"request_id":"28da8864fb56c4b65007002f","rewritten_text":"“But,” said I, handing the slip back to him, “I am no less bewildered than before. Had all the jewels of Golconda been promised me for solving this enigma, I am certain I could never have won them.”

“And yet,” said Legrand, “the solution is not nearly so difficult as a first hurried examination of the characters might lead you to believe. These characters, as anyone might readily surmise, constitute a cipher—that is, they carry a meaning; but, knowing what we do of Kidd, I could not imagine him capable of devising any of the more intricate cryptographs. I immediately concluded that this was a simple kind—one which, nevertheless, would seem to the sailor’s rough understanding utterly impossible to decipher without the key.”

“And you actually solved it?”

“Easily; I have solved others ten thousand times more obscure. Circumstances, together with a particular bent of mind, have made such puzzles interesting to me, and it may reasonably be questioned whether human ingenuity can create an enigma that human ingenuity, properly applied, cannot unravel. Indeed, once I had established that the characters were connected and legible, I scarcely considered the mere difficulty of discovering their meaning.

“In this instance—as in every case of secret writing—the first matter to determine is the cipher’s language; for the methods of solution, particularly with the simpler ciphers, depend upon and vary according to the character of the particular idiom. Usually, there is no choice but to test, guided by probability, every language known to the person attempting the solution, until the correct one is found. But with the cipher before us, the signature removed all uncertainty. The play upon the word ‘Kidd’ can be understood in no language except English. Without that clue, I should have begun with Spanish and French, the languages in which a secret of this sort would most naturally have been written by a pirate of the Spanish Main. As it was, I assumed the cryptograph was English.

“You will notice that there are no spaces between the words. Had spaces been present, the task would have been comparatively simple. I should then have begun by comparing and analyzing the shorter words; and if a one-letter word had appeared, as would most likely be the case—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for instance—I should have regarded the solution as certain. But since there are no divisions, my first step was to determine the letters occurring most often, as well as those appearing least frequently.”"}

{"request_id":"2e31b60c2527bebe393a07b3","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thank you for giving me the information I wanted. I always like to know everything about my new friends, and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I’ve invited myself and Mr. Gray. He’s her latest _protégé_.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, not to trouble me anymore with her charity appeals. I’m sick of them. Why, the good woman thinks I have nothing to do but write cheques for her silly causes.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, but it won’t make any difference. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity. That is their defining characteristic.”

The old gentleman growled approvingly and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low arcade into Burlington Street and headed toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parentage. Crude as the account had been, it had still moved him with the suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness cut short by a hideous, treacherous crime. Months of silent agony, followed by a child born in pain. The mother taken by death, the boy left to solitude and the tyranny of an old, loveless man. Yes; it was an interesting background. It gave the boy distinction, made him more perfect, so to speak. Behind every exquisite thing that existed, there was something tragic. Worlds had to be in labor so that the meanest flower might bloom.... And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, sitting opposite him at the club with startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure, the red candle shades deepening the rose in his awakening face. Talking to him was like playing an exquisite violin. He responded to every touch and tremor of the bow.... There was something terribly enthralling about exercising influence. No other activity was like it. To project one’s soul into some gracious form and let it remain there for a moment; to hear one’s own intellectual views echoed back with all the added music of passion and youth; to convey one’s temperament into another as though it were a subtle fluid or a strange perfume: there was genuine joy in that—perhaps the most satisfying joy left to us in an age as limited and vulgar as our own, an age grossly carnal in its pleasures and grossly common in its aims.... He was a marvelous type, too, this boy whom, by such a curious chance, he had met in Basil’s studio—or could be shaped into a marvelous type, at any rate."}

{"request_id":"f925527be2be79a38603aa77","rewritten_text":"When the wedding took place, about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a perfect crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester conducted the service with great solemnity, and everyone agreed that they had never seen a more handsome couple than the bride and groom. They were more than handsome, however—they were happy. Lord Arthur never once regretted all he had suffered for Sybil’s sake, while she, for her part, gave him the finest things a woman can give a man—devotion, tenderness, and love. For them, romance was not destroyed by reality. They always felt young.

Several years later, after two beautiful children had been born to them, Lady Windermere came to stay at Alton Priory, a lovely old house that had been the Duke’s wedding gift to his son. One afternoon, as she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl play up and down the rose walk like flickering sunbeams, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and asked, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, of course I’m happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I have no time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last person introduced to me; but usually, as soon as I get to know people, I grow tired of them.’

‘Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh, no! Lions are only good for one season. Once their manes are cut, they are the dullest creatures alive. Besides, they behave very badly if you are genuinely kind to them. Do you remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He was a terrible impostor. Of course, I didn’t mind that at all, and I even forgave him when he wanted to borrow money, but I couldn’t tolerate his making love to me. He has truly made me hate cheiromancy. I’m interested in telepathy now. It’s much more entertaining.’

‘You mustn’t say anything against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere; it is the only subject Arthur doesn’t like people to joke about. I assure you, he takes it quite seriously.’

‘You don’t mean to say he believes in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him, Lady Windermere—here he is.’ Lord Arthur came up the garden carrying a large bunch of yellow roses, with his two children dancing around him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You don’t mean to say that you believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Of course I do,’ said the young man with a smile.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe it all the happiness of my life,’ he murmured, lowering himself into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"ce6a6438791d2302e2643fa9","rewritten_text":"“April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction, and although I had fully anticipated it, it gave me the most unmistakable delight. After following its former course to about the twentieth parallel of southern latitude, it suddenly veered eastward at an acute angle and continued in that direction throughout the day, keeping nearly, if not entirely, in the exact plane of the lunar ellipse. Remarkably, this change of route caused a very noticeable swaying of the car—a motion that continued, to a greater or lesser degree, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was again greatly alarmed by a recurrence of the loud, crackling noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I reflected on it for a long time but could reach no satisfactory conclusion. The earth’s apparent diameter had greatly diminished and now subtended, from the balloon, an angle of scarcely more than twenty-five degrees. The moon was completely invisible, being almost directly overhead. I remained in the plane of the ellipse but made little eastward progress.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter was shrinking with extreme rapidity. Today I became firmly convinced that the balloon was actually ascending along the line of apsides toward the point of perigee—in other words, following the direct course that would carry it straight to the moon at the point in its orbit nearest the earth. The moon itself was directly overhead and therefore hidden from my sight. Great and prolonged effort was required to condense the atmosphere.

“April 15th. The outlines of continents and seas could no longer be distinguished on the earth with anything approaching clarity. Around noon, I became aware for the third time of that terrifying sound which had previously astonished me. This time, however, it continued for several moments, growing louder as it went on. At last, while I stood stupefied and terrified, expecting some dreadful destruction but not knowing what, the car shook with extraordinary violence, and a gigantic, flaming mass of material, which I could not identify, came roaring and booming past the balloon with the sound of a thousand thunders. When my fear and astonishment had somewhat subsided, I had little difficulty in supposing that it was some enormous volcanic fragment expelled from the world toward which I was rapidly approaching—most likely one of that strange class of substances sometimes found on earth and called meteoric stones for lack of a better name.

“April 16th. Today, looking upward as best I could through each side window in turn, I saw, to my great delight, a very small portion of the moon’s disk protruding on every side beyond the balloon’s enormous circumference.”"}

{"request_id":"52d888a4d73cf4f73061a7b7","rewritten_text":"The next day was chosen for the production, lest our honour should grow cold through delay, and Drummle appeared with a polite little statement in Estella’s handwriting, saying that she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. This left me no choice but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and, in general, to deny as impossible the idea that I was to be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove contradicted everything indiscriminately. At last, we declared that the cause of good feeling had advanced at an astonishing rate.

I speak of this lightly, but it was no light matter to me. I cannot fully express the pain it caused me to think that Estella should show favour to such a contemptible, clumsy, sulky fool, so far below even the average. To this day, I believe it was because of the pure generosity and selflessness of my love for her that I could not bear the thought of her lowering herself to that hound. No doubt I should have been miserable whoever had won her favour; but a more worthy object would have caused a different kind and degree of suffering.

It was easy to discover, and I soon did discover, that Drummle had begun following her closely, and that she allowed him to do so. Before long, he was always pursuing her, and he and I crossed paths every day. He continued in a dull, stubborn way, while Estella kept him going: sometimes encouraging him, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes almost flattering him, sometimes openly despising him, sometimes seeming to know him very well, and sometimes barely remembering who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had called him, was accustomed to waiting in ambush and had the patience of his kind. Besides this, he had a foolish confidence in his money and his family’s importance, which sometimes served him well, almost taking the place of focus and firm purpose. Thus the Spider, stubbornly watching Estella, outlasted many brighter insects, and would often uncoil himself and drop down at exactly the right moment.

At a certain Assembly Ball in Richmond—there were Assembly Balls in most places then—Estella had outshone all the other beauties. Drummle blundered around her so persistently, and with such tolerance from her, that I decided to speak to her about him. I took the next opportunity, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home and was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave."}

{"request_id":"234920719ba8bf03ee553c31","rewritten_text":"Not a word about it passed his lips until their visitor had left for the night; but as soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said—

“Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.”

Jane went to him at once, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are a good girl,” he replied, “and it gives me great pleasure to think that you will be so happily settled. I have no doubt that you will do very well together. Your tempers are not at all unlike. You are both so accommodating that nothing will ever be decided; so trusting that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always spend beyond your income.”

“I hope not. Carelessness or thoughtlessness in money matters would be unforgivable in _me_.”

“Spend beyond their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” cried his wife, “what can you mean? Why, he has four or five thousand a year, and very likely more.” Then, turning to her daughter, she continued, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I am sure I shall not sleep a wink tonight. I knew how it would end. I always said it must happen eventually. I was certain you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, as soon as I saw him, when he first came to Hertfordshire last year, I thought how likely it was that you would come together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man anyone has ever seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were completely forgotten. Jane was, beyond question, her favourite child. At that moment she cared about no one else. Her younger daughters soon began appealing to her for pleasures she might one day be able to provide.

Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield, and Kitty pleaded earnestly for a few balls there each winter.

From then on, Bingley was naturally a daily visitor at Longbourn, often arriving before breakfast and always staying until after supper—unless some barbarous neighbour, whom he could not possibly detest enough, had invited him to dinner, an invitation he felt obliged to accept.

Elizabeth now had little time to speak with her sister, because while Bingley was present Jane had no attention to give anyone else. But during the periods of separation that sometimes had to occur, Elizabeth found herself very useful to them both. When Jane was absent, Bingley always attached himself to Elizabeth for the pleasure of talking about her; and when Bingley had gone, Jane constantly sought the same comfort.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by telling me that he had been completely unaware that I was in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"5179191cccd74ca4f00e998d","rewritten_text":"And if he asked why I wanted it, or what claim I believed I had to it, I would tell him—though he cared little for such humble dreams—that I had loved Estella dearly and for a long time; and that, though I had lost her and must lead a life of bereavement, anything connected with her remained nearer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing that Mr. Jaggers stood perfectly still and silent, apparently unmoved by my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you have a tender heart. I have seen your agreeable home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful habits with which you renew yourself after business. I beg you to say something for me to Mr. Jaggers, and point out that, considering everything, he ought to be more frank with me!”

I have never seen two men regard each other more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this address. At first I feared that Wemmick would be dismissed from his employment on the spot; but that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers soften into something resembling a smile, while Wemmick grew more confident.

“What is all this?” said Mr. Jaggers. “You, with an old father, and you, with agreeable and playful habits?”

“Well!” returned Wemmick. “If I don’t bring them here, what difference does it make?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling frankly, “this man must be the most artful impostor in London.”

“Not at all,” replied Wemmick, becoming bolder still. “I think you’re another.”

Once more they exchanged their former peculiar looks, each apparently still suspicious that the other was making a fool of him.

“You, with an agreeable home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“Since it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick answered, “let it stand. Now, looking at you, sir, I shouldn’t be surprised if you were planning and arranging to have an agreeable home of your own someday, when you’ve grown weary of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t speak of ‘poor dreams’; you know more of such matters than I do, having much fresher experience in that direction. But now to this other business. I’ll put a case before you. Mind! I admit nothing.”

He waited until I had declared that I fully understood his explicit statement that he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “suppose this case. Suppose a woman, in circumstances such as you have described, kept her child hidden, and was compelled to tell the fact to her legal adviser, because he represented to her that, with regard to the scope of his defence, he had to know how matters stood concerning that child.”"}

{"request_id":"a6f948e6b01e9839c65adb2d","rewritten_text":"According to the latest reports from Rotterdam, that city appears to be in a remarkable state of philosophical agitation. Strange events have taken place there—so wholly unforeseen, so entirely new, so utterly opposed to established opinions—that I cannot doubt all Europe is by now in commotion, physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at open war.

It seems that on the—— day of—— (the exact date I cannot confidently state), an immense crowd had gathered, for reasons not clearly specified, in the great square of the Exchange in the well-kept city of Rotterdam. The weather was warm—uncommonly warm for the season—and scarcely a breath of wind moved; nor were the people displeased when, from time to time, brief friendly showers descended from broad white clouds that passed fitfully across the blue firmament. Yet around noon a slight but extraordinary disturbance arose among them: ten thousand voices began clattering; and immediately afterward ten thousand faces turned upward, ten thousand pipes dropped together from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a cry, comparable to nothing except the roar of Niagara, rolled long, loudly, and furiously through the whole neighborhood of Rotterdam.

The cause of this uproar soon became plain enough. From behind the enormous mass of one of the sharply outlined clouds already mentioned, there slowly appeared in an open patch of blue a strange, confused, yet seemingly solid object, so oddly formed and so whimsically assembled that the sturdy burghers below could neither understand it nor admire it sufficiently. What could it be? By all the vrows and devils in Rotterdam, what could it possibly signify? Nobody knew, nobody could guess; nobody—not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—possessed the least clue for solving the mystery. Thus, since nothing more sensible suggested itself, every man carefully put his pipe back into the corner of his mouth, raised his right eye toward the apparition, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and at last—puffed once more.

Meanwhile, the object that had aroused such curiosity and produced so much smoke descended lower and lower toward the pleasant city. Within a few minutes it had come near enough to be clearly examined. It seemed to be—yes! it was certainly a kind of balloon; but surely Rotterdam had never before witnessed such a balloon."}

{"request_id":"37f1a3d7b6b63d150179b782","rewritten_text":"But I wonder how long you _would_ have continued, had you been left to yourself. I wonder when you _would_ have spoken if I had not questioned you! My determination to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly produced a powerful effect. _Too powerful_, I fear; for what becomes of the moral, if our happiness arises from breaking a promise, since I ought not to have brought up the subject? This will never do.”

“You need not trouble yourself. The moral will remain entirely just. Lady Catherine’s unjustifiable attempts to part us were what dispelled all my doubts. I do not owe my present happiness to your eager wish to express your gratitude. I was in no mood to wait for you to begin. My aunt’s information had inspired me with hope, and I was resolved immediately to learn everything.”

“Lady Catherine has been of immeasurable service, which ought to please her, since she delights in being useful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and feel embarrassed? or had you planned consequences of a more serious nature?”

“My true object was to see _you_, and to determine, if possible, whether I could ever hope to make you love me. My declared object, or the one I admitted to myself, was to discover whether your sister still cared for Bingley, and, if she did, to make to him the confession I have since made.”

“Will you ever find the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is going to happen to her?”

“I am more likely to require time than courage, Elizabeth. But it must be done; and if you will give me a sheet of paper, it shall be done at once.”

“And if I had not a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire the steadiness of your handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt as well, who must not be neglected any longer.”

Because she was unwilling to admit how greatly she had exaggerated her intimacy with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s lengthy letter; but now, having _that_ to communicate which she knew would be most welcome, she was nearly ashamed to discover that her uncle and aunt had already been deprived of three days’ happiness, and at once wrote as follows:--

“I should have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, as I ought, for your long, kind, and satisfying account of everything; but, to tell the truth, I was too cross to write. You imagined more than truly existed. But _now_ imagine as much as you please; release your fancy, indulge your imagination in every flight the subject can possibly inspire, and unless you suppose me actually married, you cannot be very far wrong."}

content.text: {"request_id":"93fcd1f735069f6736145feb","rewritten_text":"Raymond was uplifted by the powerful sensations of restored health. As general of the Athenians, he felt he held a position worthy of his ambition. In hoping to conquer Constantinople, he looked toward an event that would stand out across the ages: an achievement unmatched in human history. A city rich in historic associations, whose beautiful setting was the wonder of the world, and which had been the Moslems’ stronghold for centuries, would be freed from slavery and barbarism and returned to a people famous for genius, civilization, and love of liberty. Perdita depended on his restored society, his love, hopes, and fame, as a Sybarite depends on a luxurious couch; every thought brought delight, and every feeling seemed immersed in a warm, welcoming atmosphere.\n\nWe reached Kishan on July 7. The weather throughout our journey had been calm. Each day, before dawn, we left our night’s camp and watched the shadows withdraw from hill and valley before the sun’s golden arrival. The soldiers traveling with us, with their usual liveliness, took enthusiastic pleasure in the beauty of nature. They greeted the rising sun with triumphant music, while birds, heard now and then, filled the pauses. At noon, we set up our tents in a shady valley or a wooded hollow among the mountains, while a stream murmuring over pebbles invited grateful sleep. Our evening march was calmer and even more delightful than the morning’s eager activity. When the band played, it instinctively chose music of restrained feeling: a lover’s farewell or a lament for absence, followed and ended by a solemn hymn that suited the peaceful beauty of evening and lifted the soul toward noble, religious thoughts. Often every sound stopped so that we could hear the nightingale, while fireflies danced brightly and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travelers. When we passed through a valley, gentle shadows surrounded us and rocks glowed with beautiful colors. When we crossed a mountain, Greece lay below like a living map, its famous peaks rising into the sky and its rivers tracing silver lines through the fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers gazed in wonder at this magnificent landscape, so unlike the sober colors and melancholy beauty of our native scenery. After we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer sights, though the journey remained interesting. An advance guard announced our approach, and the country people quickly began preparing to honor Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"86e4e3e5bf6de68014edfbf5","rewritten_text":"Knights and horses in heavy armor could not travel very fast. They would go as quickly as they could, and now that the ground was firm, without snow or mud, they could probably manage seven miles at a time. They would need to change horses twice and arrive around six, or shortly afterward. It would still be light enough for them to see the white cloth I would tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround the prison and have the king out in no time. All things considered, it would be quite a show, though I would have preferred noon, because the scene would have been more theatrical then.

Now, to add another string to my bow, I decided to look up some people I had known before and make myself known to them. That might get us out of our trouble without the knights. But I had to be careful, because it was risky. I needed to dress in splendid clothes, but I could not simply jump into them. I had to work up to it gradually, buying one suit after another in shops far apart, with each outfit a little finer than the last, until I reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I set out.

But the scheme fell through at once! At the first corner I turned, I came face-to-face with one of our slaves, prowling around with a watchman. I happened to cough, and he gave me a sudden look that seemed to pierce my bones. I guessed he thought he had heard that cough before. I immediately turned into a shop and moved along the counter, pricing things while watching from the corner of my eye. The two men had stopped and were talking together, looking in through the door. I decided to escape through the back, if there was one, and asked the shopwoman whether I could go out there to search for the escaped slave, who was believed to be hiding somewhere behind the shop. I told her I was an officer in disguise, and that my partner was at the door with one of the murderers under arrest. Would she kindly go out and tell him he need not wait, but should hurry to the far end of the back alley and be ready to stop the slave when I drove him out?

She was eager to see one of the already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand at once."}

{"request_id":"26df4b1e2bae63d6dd80ee6b","rewritten_text":"His understanding and temperament, though different from her own, would have fulfilled all her hopes. Their marriage must have benefited them both: her ease and liveliness might have softened his mind and improved his manners; while from his judgment, knowledge, and experience of the world, she would have gained advantages of far greater importance.

But no such happy marriage could now show the admiring multitude what true marital felicity was. A union of an entirely different kind, making the other impossible, was soon to be formed within their family.

How Wickham and Lydia were to be maintained in tolerable independence, she could not imagine. But how little lasting happiness could belong to a couple brought together only because their passions were stronger than their virtue, she could easily foresee.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. In response to Mr. Bennet’s thanks, he briefly assured him of his eagerness to promote the welfare of any member of his family, and ended by begging that the subject never be mentioned to him again. The chief purpose of his letter was to tell them that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

“It was very much my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree that leaving that corps is highly advisable, both for his sake and my niece’s. Mr. Wickham intends to join the Regulars; and among his former friends there are still some able and willing to help him in the army. He has been promised an ensigncy in General----’s regiment, now stationed in the north. It is an advantage that it should be so far from this part of the kingdom. He gives fair promise; and I hope that, among different people, where each will have a reputation to preserve, they will both behave more prudently. I have written to Colonel Forster, informing him of our present arrangements and asking him to reassure Mr. Wickham’s various creditors in and near Brighton that payment will be made shortly, for which I have pledged myself. Will you also take the trouble to give similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton, whose names I shall enclose according to his information? He has declared all his debts; I hope, at least, that he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be settled within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are invited first to Longbourn; and I understand from Mrs. Gardiner that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south."}

{"request_id":"36c325d05741b30d88abc132","rewritten_text":"Reading over his letter again while answering it had such a softening effect that it was especially necessary to strengthen her resolve with a few firm expressions; and she was so troubled by the thought of making him unhappy, thought so much about what his mother and sisters would think and say, and was so anxious that they should not consider her ungrateful, that Emma believed, if the young man had crossed her path at that moment, he would have been accepted after all.

The letter, however, was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She was rather downcast all evening, but Emma could make allowances for her kind-hearted regrets, sometimes easing them by speaking of her own affection, and sometimes by bringing Mr. Elton to mind.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” she said in a rather sorrowful tone.

“Nor, if you were, could I ever bear to part with you, my Harriet. You are far too necessary at Hartfield to be spared to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I am sure I should never want to go there; for I am never happy anywhere but at Hartfield.”

Some time later, she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. I am sure Miss Nash would be—for Miss Nash thinks her own sister very well married, and she is only married to a linen-draper.”

“One ought to regret seeing greater pride or refinement in a schoolteacher, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you such an opportunity to marry. Even this conquest would seem valuable in her eyes. As for anything better suited to you, I suppose she is completely unaware of it. The attentions of a certain person can hardly yet be part of Highbury gossip. So far, I believe you and I are the only people whose understanding has been enlightened by his looks and manners.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, and said something about being surprised that people should like her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton was certainly encouraging; but after a while she again felt tenderly toward the rejected Mr. Martin.

“Now he has received my letter,” she said softly. “I wonder what they are all doing—whether his sisters know—if he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he will not take it too badly.”

“Let us think of those absent friends who are more cheerfully occupied,” cried Emma. “At this moment, perhaps, Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters, telling them how much more beautiful the original is, and, after being asked for it five or six times, allowing them to hear your name—your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"e4b86bf5c002061bf450efc8","rewritten_text":"For years, Dorian Gray could not escape the influence of this book. Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say that he never tried to escape it. From Paris he obtained no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition and had them bound in different colours, so they would match his various moods and the shifting fancies of a nature over which he sometimes seemed to have almost completely lost control. The hero, that remarkable young Parisian in whom romantic and scientific temperaments were so strangely combined, became for him a kind of prophetic image of himself. Indeed, the entire book seemed to contain the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic hero. He never knew—never had any reason to know—that almost grotesque fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water which came over the young Parisian so early in life, caused by the sudden decay of a beauty that had once apparently been so extraordinary. With almost cruel delight—and perhaps cruelty has a place in nearly every joy, as surely as it does in every pleasure—he would read the latter part of the book, with its genuinely tragic, though somewhat exaggerated, account of the grief and despair of a man who had himself lost what he had valued most dearly in others and in the world.

For the extraordinary beauty that had so captivated Basil Hallward, and many others besides him, seemed never to leave Dorian. Even those who had heard the worst things about him—and from time to time strange rumours about his way of life spread through London and became the talk of the clubs—could not believe anything dishonourable of him when they saw him. He always looked like someone who had kept himself untouched by the world. Men who spoke crudely fell silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. There was something in the purity of his face that rebuked them. His mere presence seemed to remind them of the innocence they had stained. They wondered how someone as charming and graceful as he could have escaped the corruption of an age that was both sordid and sensual.

Often, after returning home from one of those mysterious, prolonged absences that provoked such strange speculation among those who were his friends, or believed themselves to be, he would creep upstairs to the locked room, open the door with the key that now never left him, and stand with a mirror before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him, looking first at the evil, aging face on the canvas and then at the beautiful young face smiling back at him from the polished glass."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0aebc51463a5a3a8d9402838","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner before them, though young in years, was old in the treasonable practices that demanded the forfeiture of his life. This correspondence with the public enemy was not a matter of to-day, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that the prisoner had, for longer than that, been accustomed to travel back and forth between France and England on secret business for which he could offer no honest explanation. If treasonable methods had been capable of prospering (which, happily, they never were), the true wickedness and guilt of his dealings might have remained concealed. Providence, however, had moved a person beyond fear and reproach to investigate the nature of the prisoner’s schemes and, horrified by what he found, reveal them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would be brought before them. His position and bearing were, altogether, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but, discovering his infamy at once in a fortunate and an evil hour, had determined to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer cherish in his bosom upon the sacred altar of his country. If Britain, like ancient Greece and Rome, awarded statues to public benefactors, this illustrious citizen would certainly have received one. Since Britain did not award them, he probably would not. Virtue, as the poets had remarked (in many passages which he knew the jury would have at their fingertips word for word; at which the jury’s faces showed the guilty awareness that they knew none of them), was in some degree contagious; particularly the radiant virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The exalted example of this spotless and unimpeachable witness for the Crown, to mention whom was an honour however unworthy the mention, had spread to the prisoner’s servant, inspiring him with a holy resolve to search his master’s table-drawers and pockets and conceal his papers. He (Mr. Attorney-General) expected that some attempt would be made to disparage this excellent servant; but, generally speaking, he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters, and respected him more than his own father and mother. He confidently called upon the jury to do the same. The testimony of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had discovered and which would be produced, would prove that the prisoner had been supplied with lists of His Majesty’s forces and their disposition and preparation, by sea and land, and would leave no doubt that he had habitually transmitted such intelligence to a hostile power."}

{"request_id":"35eb526d57ec2258a610516e","rewritten_text":"In the morning she was discovered dead in her bed, apparently without having suffered. Sir Mathew Reid had been summoned immediately, but naturally there was nothing to be done, and she was to be buried at Beauchamp Chalcote on the 22nd. A few days before her death she had made her will, leaving Lord Arthur her small house in Curzon Street, together with all its furniture, personal belongings, and pictures, except for her miniatures, which were to pass to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to receive. The estate was not particularly valuable; but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was most eager that Lord Arthur should return at once, if he could, since there were numerous bills to settle, and Lady Clementina had never maintained proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s affectionate remembrance of him, and felt that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Yet his love for Sybil outweighed every other feeling, and the knowledge that he had fulfilled his duty brought him peace and consolation. When he reached Charing Cross, he was entirely happy.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise never again to let anything separate them, and the wedding was arranged for the 7th of June. Life once more appeared bright and lovely to him, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, while he was inspecting the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of old letters and emptying drawers filled with miscellaneous rubbish, the young girl suddenly uttered a small cry of pleasure.

‘What have you discovered, Sybil?’ Lord Arthur asked, looking up from his task with a smile.

‘This beautiful little silver _bonbonnière_, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint, and so Dutch? Do give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.’

It was the box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a slight flush touched his cheek. He had almost completely forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whose sake he had endured all that dreadful anxiety, should be the first to recall it to him.

‘Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clementina myself.’

‘Oh, thank you, Arthur; and may I have the _bonbon_ as well? I had no idea Lady Clementina enjoyed sweets. I thought she was much too intellectual.’

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a terrible thought passed through his mind."}

{"request_id":"18fa17850ff4b6879b354bdc","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The neglect had come back upon the guilty party; when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no letter of condolence arrived at Kellynch. There was therefore too much reason to fear that the Dalrymples considered the family connection ended. How to put this troubling matter right and be accepted as cousins again was the question. In a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot thought it unimportant. “Family connections were always worth preserving, and good company always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple had taken a house in Laura Place for three months and would be living in style. She had been in Bath the year before, and Lady Russell had heard her described as a charming woman. It was very desirable to renew the connection, if it could be done without any loss of propriety on the Elliots’ part.”

Sir Walter, however, chose his own method. At last he wrote his right honourable cousin a very fine letter, full of explanation, regret, and entreaty. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot admired it, but it achieved what was needed: three lines of writing from the Dowager Viscountess. “She was very much honoured and would be happy to make their acquaintance.” The difficult part was over, and the rewards began. They paid a visit to Laura Place, received the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, and placed them wherever they would be most noticed. “Our cousins in Laura Place”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret”—were mentioned to everyone.

Anne was ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been very pleasant, she would still have been ashamed of the excitement they caused; but they were nothing special. They had no superiority in manner, accomplishments, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the name “a charming woman” because she smiled and gave a polite answer to everyone. Miss Carteret had even less to say and was so plain and awkward that she would never have been accepted in Camden Place except for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected something better, but still said, “It is an acquaintance worth having.” When Anne dared to give Mr Elliot her opinion of them, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but insisted that, as a family connection, as good company, and as people who would attract good company around them, they had value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people who have a great deal to talk about. That is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"d6e8a480e9fd2942625c11e0","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl replied.

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl answered firmly, “because the lady knows about it and will stand by me—I know she will, for I have her promise. And for this other reason too: bad a life as he has led, I have led a bad life as well. Many of us have followed the same path together, and I will not turn against them. Any of them might have turned against me, but they did not, bad as they are.”

“Then,” said the gentleman quickly, as if this were the point he had been trying to reach, “put Monks in my hands and leave me to deal with him.”

“What if he turns against the others?”

“I promise you that, if he does, and the truth is forced from him, the matter will end there. There must be parts of Oliver’s short history that would be painful to reveal publicly. If the truth is brought out, the others shall go free.”

“And if it is not?” the girl asked.

“Then,” continued the gentleman, “this Fagin shall not be brought to justice without your consent. In that case, I think I could show you reasons that would persuade you to give it.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise for that?” asked the girl.

“You do,” Rose replied. “You have my true and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never discover how you learned what you know?” the girl asked after a short pause.

“Never,” replied the gentleman. “The information would be used against him in such a way that he could never even guess its source.”

“I have been a liar, and lived among liars, since I was a little child,” said the girl after another silence, “but I will trust your word.”

After both assured her that she could safely do so, she began speaking so quietly that the listener often found it difficult to understand even the meaning of her words. She described, by name and location, the public house from which she had been followed that night. From the way she sometimes paused, it seemed that the gentleman was quickly writing down the information she gave him. When she had fully explained the place, the best position from which to watch it without being noticed, and the night and hour when Monks most often visited it, she paused for a few moments, trying to bring his face and appearance clearly back to mind.

“He is tall,” said the girl, “and strongly built, but not fat. He walks in a secretive way, and as he walks he constantly looks over his shoulder, first to one side and then to the other.”"}

{"request_id":"36edc8b769b1877370f96a43","rewritten_text":"“But,” said I, handing the slip back to him, “I am no less confused than before. Even if all the jewels of Golconda were promised to me for solving this riddle, I am certain I could not earn them.”

“And yet,” said Legrand, “the solution is not nearly as difficult as a first hurried look at the symbols might lead you to think. As anyone might guess, these symbols form a cipher—that is, they carry a meaning. But, knowing what I did of Kidd, I could not imagine him capable of creating one of the more complicated cryptographs. I immediately decided that it was a simple kind, though one that would seem completely impossible to the sailor’s rough mind without the key.”

“And you actually solved it?”

“Easily. I have solved others ten thousand times more difficult. Circumstances, along with a certain tendency in my mind, have made me interested in such puzzles, and it may well be that human ingenuity cannot create a riddle that human ingenuity cannot solve with proper effort. In fact, once I had found a sequence of connected, readable symbols, I hardly thought about the difficulty of discovering their meaning.

“In this case—as in every case of secret writing—the first question concerns the cipher’s language. The methods of solving it, especially in the simpler ciphers, depend on and change with the nature of the particular language. Usually, the solver has no choice but to test every language he knows, guided by probability, until he finds the right one. But with the cipher before us, the signature removed all difficulty. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ works in no language except English. Without that clue, I would have begun with Spanish and French, the languages in which a pirate of the Spanish Main would most naturally have written such a secret. As it was, I assumed the cryptograph was English.

“You will notice that there are no spaces between the words. If there had been spaces, the task would have been fairly easy. I would then have begun by comparing and studying the shorter words. If a one-letter word had appeared, as would most likely happen—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for example—I would have considered the solution certain. But since there were no spaces, my first step was to identify the most common letters, as well as the rarest ones.”"}

{"request_id":"6f4caf4cd891455698438fef","rewritten_text":"Wake up after a while and look around to see what had caused it, and maybe spot a steamboat coughing upstream, so far off toward the opposite bank that you couldn’t make out anything about her except whether she was stern-wheel or side-wheel; then for nearly an hour there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just complete loneliness. Next you might see a raft drifting by, far off yonder, and perhaps some fellow on it chopping, because they’re nearly always doing that on a raft; you’d see the axe flash and fall—you wouldn’t hear a thing; you’d watch it rise again, and when it was above the man’s head, then you’d hear the _k’chunk!_—it had taken all that time to cross the water. So we’d spend the day loafing around, listening to the quiet. Once there was a heavy fog, and the rafts and other things passing by were banging tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run them down. A scow or raft passed so near that we could hear them talking, cussing, and laughing—hear them clearly; but we couldn’t see the least sign of them; it made you feel creepy; it was like spirits carrying on in the air. Jim said he reckoned they were spirits; but I says:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

As soon as it was fully dark we pushed off; when we had reached about midstream we left her alone and let her drift wherever the current chose to take her; then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes allowed it—the new clothes Buck’s family had made for me were too fine to be comfortable, and besides, I never cared much for clothes, anyway.

Sometimes we’d have the whole river to ourselves for the longest while. There were the banks and islands over across the water; and perhaps a spark—which was a candle shining from a cabin window; and sometimes on the water you could see a spark or two—on a raft or scow, you know; and maybe hear a fiddle or a song drifting over from one of those boats. It’s wonderful living on a raft. We had the sky above us, thick with stars, and we’d lie on our backs looking up at them, arguing over whether they had been made or had simply happened. Jim said they were made, but I said they happened; I figured it would have taken too long to _make_ so many."}

{"request_id":"578c71efc4ab045bf94a3878","rewritten_text":"It was well past noon when he woke. His valet had crept into the room several times on tiptoe to see whether he was stirring, wondering what kept his young master asleep so long. At last the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sèvres china. He pulled back the olive-satin curtains, with their shimmering blue lining, covering the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, drank some tea, and looked through his letters. One was from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He paused, then set it aside. He opened the others without interest. They held the usual collection of cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private exhibitions, programmes for charity concerts, and similar things showered on fashionable young men each morning during the season. There was also a large bill for a chased silver Louis-Quinze toilet set, which he still had not dared send to his guardians. They were extremely old-fashioned and could not understand that we live in an age when unnecessary things are our only necessities. Several very polite letters came from money-lenders in Jermyn Street, offering to advance any amount at once and at the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes, he rose, put on an elaborate dressing gown of silk-embroidered cashmere, and went into the bathroom, whose floor was paved with onyx. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had endured. Once or twice, a faint feeling that he had taken part in some strange tragedy returned to him, but it seemed as unreal as a dream.

When he was dressed, he went to the library and sat down to the light French breakfast prepared on a small round table beside the open window. It was a beautiful day. The warm air seemed full of spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue dragon bowl before him, filled with sulphur-yellow roses. He felt completely happy.

Then his eyes fell on the screen he had placed before the portrait, and he started.

“Is it too cold for Monsieur?” his valet asked, setting an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"45de44d73d28b09e7bd73f16","rewritten_text":"According to the latest reports from Rotterdam, the city seems to be in a state of intense philosophical excitement. Strange events have occurred there—so unexpected, so new, and so completely opposed to accepted ideas—that I have no doubt all Europe is already in an uproar, all physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at war with each other.

It seems that on the—— day of—— (I am not certain of the date), a huge crowd had gathered, for reasons not clearly stated, in the great square of the Exchange in the prosperous city of Rotterdam. The day was warm—unusually warm for the season—and hardly a breath of wind was moving. The crowd did not mind being sprinkled now and then by brief, friendly showers falling from large white clouds that passed unevenly across the blue sky. Yet around noon, a slight but remarkable disturbance spread through the gathering. Ten thousand voices began chattering; then, in an instant, ten thousand faces turned toward the heavens, ten thousand pipes dropped from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout—like nothing so much as the roar of Niagara—rang out long, loudly, and fiercely across Rotterdam and its surroundings.

The cause of the uproar soon became clear. From behind the huge mass of one of the sharply outlined clouds already mentioned, a strange, mixed, but apparently solid object slowly emerged into an open patch of blue. It was shaped and assembled so oddly that the sturdy citizens below could neither understand it nor admire it enough. What could it be? In the name of every woman and devil in Rotterdam, what could it possibly mean? No one knew or could guess; no one—not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk—had the slightest clue to the mystery. Since nothing wiser could be done, everyone carefully put his pipe back into the corner of his mouth, raised his right eye toward the object, puffed, paused, waddled around, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and at last puffed again.

Meanwhile, the object that had caused so much curiosity and smoke came lower and lower toward the good city. Within a few minutes it was close enough to be seen clearly. It appeared to be—yes, it was certainly a kind of balloon; but Rotterdam had surely never seen such a balloon before."}

{"request_id":"c6af8b9d0e04572924cfe285","rewritten_text":"It was at Warwick Castle that I encountered the curious stranger I am about to describe. Three things drew me to him: his frank simplicity, his astonishing knowledge of ancient armor, and the ease of his company—for he did all the talking. We joined, as quiet people do, the rear of the group being led through the castle, and he immediately began saying things that interested me. As he continued, speaking softly, pleasantly, and smoothly, he seemed to drift imperceptibly out of the present world and age into some distant era and forgotten land. Gradually he cast such a spell over me that I seemed to move among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mold of a gray antiquity, conversing with one of its relics. Just as I might speak of my closest friends or enemies, or my most familiar neighbors, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table—and as he went on, he came to look incredibly, impossibly old: faded, dry, musty, and ancient. Presently he turned to me and said, as casually as one might discuss the weather or any other ordinary subject—

“You know about the transmigration of souls; do you know about the transposition of epochs—and bodies?”

I said I had never heard of it. He seemed so little interested—just as when people talk about the weather—that he did not notice whether I answered him or not. There was half a moment of silence, broken at once by the droning voice of the paid guide:

“Ancient hauberk, dating from the sixth century, the time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the round hole through the chain mail in the left breast; unaccounted for; believed to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not with a modern smile, but with one that must have fallen out of common use many centuries ago—and murmured, apparently to himself:

“Know this well: _I saw it done._” Then, after a pause, he added: “I did it myself.”

By the time I had recovered from the electric shock of this remark, he was gone.

That evening I sat beside my fire at the Warwick Arms, immersed in a dream of the olden days, while rain struck the windows and wind roared around the eaves and corners. From time to time I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, feasted on its rich abundance of marvels and adventures, breathed the fragrance of its obsolete names, and dreamed again."}

{"request_id":"d99016a6e70abb3b8305f1d3","rewritten_text":"Mrs Musgrove took the first opportunity to be alone with Anne and said, “Oh, Miss Anne, I cannot help wishing Mrs Charles had a little of your method with those children. They are quite different creatures with you! But, to be sure, they are generally so spoiled! It is a pity you cannot teach your sister how to manage them. They are as fine, healthy children as ever were seen, poor little dears—without partiality; but Mrs Charles knows no more how they ought to be treated—! Good heavens! How troublesome they sometimes are. I assure you, Miss Anne, it keeps me from wishing to have them at our house as often as I otherwise would. I believe Mrs Charles is not entirely pleased that I do not invite them more often; but you know it is very unpleasant to have children with one whom one must constantly be correcting: ‘Don’t do this,’ and ‘Don’t do that’; or whom one can keep in tolerable order only with more cake than is good for them.”

Mary, moreover, had this to say about her: “Mrs Musgrove thinks all her servants so dependable that it would be high treason to question it; but I am sure, without exaggeration, that her upper housemaid and laundrymaid, instead of attending to their work, are wandering about the village all day. I meet them wherever I go; and I declare, I never enter my nursery twice without seeing one of them. If Jemima were not the most trustworthy, steady creature in the world, it would be enough to corrupt her; for she tells me they are always trying to persuade her to take a walk with them.”

And from Mrs Musgrove’s side came this: “I make it a rule never to interfere in any of my daughter-in-law’s affairs, because I know it would not do; but I shall tell you, Miss Anne, since you may be able to put matters right, that I have no very high opinion of Mrs Charles’s nursery maid. I hear strange accounts of her; she is always out and about; and from my own knowledge I can say that she is such a smartly dressed woman that she is enough to ruin any servants she comes near. Mrs Charles quite swears by her, I know; but I give you this warning so that you may keep watch, because, if you notice anything wrong, you need not hesitate to mention it.”

Again, Mary complained that Mrs Musgrove was very likely not to give her the precedence due to her when they dined at the Great House with other families; and she could not see why she should be treated as so much at home that she lost her proper place."}
