{"request_id":"19b57f5d765c265ae6250b6c","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted that she was somewhat surprised by the match; but she spoke less of her astonishment than of her sincere wishes for their happiness, nor could Elizabeth persuade her to think it unlikely. Kitty and Lydia were very far from envying Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman; and the event affected them in no other respect than as news to circulate through Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not fail to feel triumphant at being able to return to Mrs. Bennet the consolation of having a daughter well married; and she visited Longbourn rather more frequently than before to declare how happy she was, though Mrs. Bennet’s sour countenance and unkind observations might have been sufficient to banish happiness altogether.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there was a reserve that kept them both silent on the matter; and Elizabeth was convinced that genuine confidence could never exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte led her to regard her sister with increased affection, certain that her opinion of Jane’s uprightness and delicacy could never be shaken, and becoming each day more concerned for her happiness, since Bingley had now been away a week and there was still no news of his return.

Jane had replied to Caroline’s letter without delay, and was counting the days until she might reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father, and composed with all the solemn gravity of gratitude that a year’s residence with the family might have inspired. Having relieved his conscience on that subject, he went on to tell them, in many delighted expressions, of his happiness at having secured the affection of their amiable neighbour, Miss Lucas. He then explained that his eagerness to accept their kind invitation to return to Longbourn had arisen solely from his wish to enjoy her company, and that he hoped to come back on the Monday fortnight. Lady Catherine, he added, approved his marriage so warmly that she wished it to occur as soon as possible; and he trusted this would prove an irresistible argument with his amiable Charlotte for fixing an early day on which to make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer welcome to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was as ready to complain of it as her husband. It was very odd that he should come to Longbourn rather than Lucas Lodge; it was inconvenient as well as extremely troublesome. She disliked having visitors in the house while her health was so poor, and lovers were the most disagreeable people of all."}

{"request_id":"e726e79c2cf24b10e0a2181d","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had taken him aboard, and ever since, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were suspected. I had seen none. We certainly had not been, and at that time we were just as certainly neither accompanied nor followed by any boat. If any boat had been waiting on us, I would have run ashore and forced her either to continue on or to make her purpose clear. But we held our course without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and looked, as I have said, like a natural part of the scene. It was remarkable—but perhaps the miserable life he had led explained it—that he was the least anxious of us all. He was not indifferent, for he told me that he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign country; nor, as I understood him, was he willing simply to submit or resign himself. But he had no intention of meeting danger halfway. When it came to him, he faced it; until then, he would not trouble himself.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here alongside my dear boy and have my smoke, after being shut up day after day between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the pleasures of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head gravely. “But you don’t know it as I do. You must have been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it as I do—but I’m not going to be downhearted.”

It seemed inconsistent to me that, for any ruling idea, he should have endangered his freedom and even his life. But I reflected that perhaps freedom without danger was so far removed from the whole habit of his existence that it could not mean to him what it would mean to another man. I was not far wrong, for after smoking a little he said:—

“You see, dear boy, when I was over there, on the other side of the world, I was always looking toward this side; and it became dull to be there, even though I was growing rich. Everybody knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody’s head would be troubled by him. They aren’t so easy about me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, at least, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you will be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he replied, drawing a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And think so?”"}

{"request_id":"756209e0d8885b72ec3ce22d","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” At that, he shook his head and tapped it, showing how inadequate he considered Joseph.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be exhausted. Sit down. Here is a chicken from the Boar, here is a tongue from the Boar, and here are one or two little things from the Boar, which I hope you will not despise. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again the instant after he had sat down, “see before me the boy I once played with in his happy infancy? And may I—_may_ I—?”

By this May I, he meant to ask whether he might shake hands. I agreed, and he did so fervently, then sat down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink to Fortune, and may she always choose her favourites with equal judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “see before me One—and also drink to One—without once more expressing—May I—_may_ I—?”

I said he might, and he shook hands with me again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more directly to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the liver wing and the best slice of tongue (none of those remote Pork No Thoroughfares now), while taking, comparatively speaking, no care of himself. “Ah! Poultry, poultry! You little knew,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl in the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what awaited you. You little knew you were destined to refresh beneath this humble roof one who—Call it weakness, if you will,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? _may_ I—?”

It was beginning to seem unnecessary to repeat that he might, so he did it immediately. How he managed to do it so often without injuring himself on my knife, I cannot say.

“And your sister,” he continued, after eating steadily for a while, “who had the honour of raising you by hand! It is a sad picture, to think that she is no longer capable of fully understanding the honour. May—”

I saw he was about to approach me again, and stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, completely limp with admiration, “that’s how you know them, sir!” (I do not know who Sir was, but he certainly was not me, and no third person was present); “that’s how you recognize the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"276cfc4e578ff95039eaefe9","rewritten_text":"Now that he had no work to occupy him, he placed the knuckles of his right hand in the hollow of his left, then those of his left in the hollow of his right, and next drew a hand over his bearded chin, continuing these regular changes without the least pause. To call him back from the wandering state into which he always fell after speaking was like rousing a very feeble person from a swoon, or trying, in hope of some revelation, to hold back the spirit of a man dying fast.

“Did you ask me my name?”

“Certainly I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was neither sigh nor groan, he bent once more to his work, until the silence was broken again.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” said Mr. Lorry, watching him intently.

His haggard eyes turned toward Defarge, as though he wished to leave the question for him to answer; but when no assistance came from that side, they returned to the questioner after first seeking the floor.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away again, for minutes at a time, all the while making those measured changes with his hands. At last his eyes slowly returned to the face from which they had strayed; when they settled upon it, he started and continued like a sleeper newly awakened, taking up a subject from the previous night.

“I asked permission to teach myself, and after a long time I obtained it with great difficulty, and I have made shoes ever since.”

As he extended his hand for the shoe that had been removed from him, Mr. Lorry said, still gazing steadily into his face:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the floor, and he sat staring fixedly at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry placed his hand on Defarge’s arm—“do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time, coming back into your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

As the captive of so many years sat staring in turn at Mr. Lorry and Defarge, faint traces of an intensely active intelligence in the center of his forehead gradually pressed through the black mist that had descended upon him. They clouded over once more, grew dimmer, and vanished; but they had appeared."}

{"request_id":"7922bba9b1664d13d10f6f03","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” said the spy in the most insulting way, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness to ask this other gentleman, so much younger than you, whether he can possibly justify playing the Ace he mentioned. I admit that I am a spy, and that spying is considered a disgraceful position—though someone must fill it. But this gentleman is no spy, so why should he lower himself by becoming one?”

“I play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, answering for himself and checking his watch, “without the slightest hesitation, in a few minutes.”

“I should have hoped, gentlemen,” said the spy, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the discussion, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I could show no greater respect for your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I have made up my mind completely.”

The spy’s smooth manner, strangely at odds with his deliberately rough clothes and probably with his usual behavior, was stopped by Carton’s unreadable expression. Carton was a mystery even to wiser and more honest men than Barsad. The spy faltered and could say no more. While he hesitated, Carton resumed his earlier pose of studying the cards and said:

“And now that I think of it, I strongly suspect I have another good card here, one I have not yet mentioned. That friend and fellow-Sheep who said he was pasturing in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” the spy replied quickly.

“French, eh?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, seeming not to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well, he may be.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy, “though it isn’t important.”

“Though it isn’t important,” Carton repeated mechanically. “Though it isn’t important—No, it isn’t important. No. And yet I know the face.”

“I don’t think so. I’m sure you don’t. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“‘It can’t be,’” Sydney Carton muttered, thinking back, and idly moving his glass—which was fortunately a small one—again. “Can’t be. He spoke good French. Yet I thought he seemed foreign?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, striking his open hand on the table as the truth suddenly became clear. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now you are being hasty, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that tilted his aquiline nose even farther to one side. “There you have really given me an advantage over you.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"170d93948abda8cb8a0bcb6c","rewritten_text":"“How long I remained in this condition, it is impossible to say. It must, however, have been a considerable time, for when I partly recovered my senses, dawn was breaking. The balloon was at an enormous height above a wilderness of ocean, and no land could be seen anywhere within the vast horizon. Yet my feelings, when I came to myself, were not nearly as painful as might have been expected. Indeed, there was something almost mad in the calm way I began to examine my situation. I raised each hand to my eyes in turn and wondered what could have caused the veins to swell and the fingernails to become horribly black. Then I carefully examined my head, shaking it again and again and feeling it closely, until I convinced myself that it was not, as I had half suspected, larger than my balloon. Next, with a knowing air, I felt in both my trouser pockets. Finding that my tablets and toothpick case were missing, I tried to explain their disappearance. Unable to do so, I felt deeply annoyed. I then noticed a severe discomfort in the joint of my left ankle, and a faint awareness of my situation began to return. But, strangely enough, I was neither surprised nor terrified. If I felt anything, it was a sort of amused satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to show in escaping this difficulty; and I never once doubted that I would ultimately be safe. For several minutes I remained lost in deep thought. I clearly remember often pressing my lips together, placing my forefinger beside my nose, and making other gestures and grimaces typical of men who, comfortably seated in their armchairs, think over complicated or important matters. Once I believed I had gathered my thoughts sufficiently, I carefully and slowly put my hands behind my back and unfastened the large iron buckle on the waistband of my trousers. The buckle had three teeth, which were somewhat rusty and turned only with great difficulty. After some effort, I brought them to right angles with the body of the buckle, and was pleased to find that they stayed firmly in place. Holding this tool between my teeth, I began to untie my cravat. I had to stop several times before I could complete the task, but at last I succeeded.”"}

{"request_id":"859d2e8bf506a1d9d28f0120","rewritten_text":"‘Good heavens!’ the Duchess said to herself. ‘So he really is some kind of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I hope he is a foreigner, at least. It wouldn’t seem quite so bad then.’

‘I must certainly introduce him to you.’

‘Introduce him!’ cried the Duchess. ‘You don’t mean to say he is here?’ She began looking around for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very tattered lace shawl, so that she would be ready to leave at a moment’s notice.

‘Of course he is here; I would never dream of giving a party without him. He tells me I have a purely psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been even slightly shorter, I would have become a confirmed pessimist and entered a convent.’

‘Oh, I see!’ said the Duchess, greatly relieved. ‘He tells fortunes, I suppose?’

‘And misfortunes too,’ Lady Windermere replied, ‘in unlimited quantities. Next year, for example, I am in great danger both on land and at sea, so I am going to live in a balloon and have my dinner hauled up in a basket every evening. It is all written on my little finger, or in the palm of my hand—I forget which.’

‘But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.’

‘My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their hands read once a month, so they will know what not to do. Naturally, one does it anyway, but it is so pleasant to be warned. Now, if someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I shall have to go myself.’

‘Let me go, Lady Windermere,’ said a tall, handsome young man who stood nearby, listening to the conversation with an amused smile.

‘Thank you so much, Lord Arthur; but I am afraid you would not recognise him.’

‘If he is as wonderful as you say, Lady Windermere, I could hardly miss him. Tell me what he looks like, and I will bring him to you at once.’

‘Well, he does not look like a chiromantist at all. I mean, he is not mysterious, esoteric, or romantic-looking. He is a short, stout man with a funny bald head and large gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country solicitor. I am truly sorry, but it is not my fault. People are so irritating. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. I remember last season inviting a most dreadful conspirator to dinner, a man who had blown up countless people and always wore a coat of mail and carried a dagger up his sleeve. And do you know, when he arrived, he looked exactly like a pleasant old clergyman and spent the whole evening telling jokes?’"}

{"request_id":"eb3b038d737c0037f86cfeb4","rewritten_text":"“And so I’m owner of a few knights,” said I, as we rode away. “Who would ever have thought I should live to enter assets of that kind. I shan’t know what to do with them, unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, if you please, sir, with their squires.”

“That’s a handsome haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I understood thee not. That will I tell thee presently.” Then she said thoughtfully and softly, turning the words delicately upon her tongue: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; eh, even so; where do they hang out. Truly the phrase hath a pleasant and winning grace, and is prettily fashioned besides. I will repeat it anon and anon in mine idleness, whereby I may perhaps learn it. Where do they hang out. Even so! already it trips readily from my tongue, and inasmuch as—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. You remember, a while ago. Figuratively speaking, the game’s called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Go to bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t use so much kindling getting your fire going. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will indeed, and shall begin lightly. So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I knew my mistake immediately. I had set her machinery in motion; it was my own fault, and she would take thirty days to reach those facts. She usually began without a preface and ended without a conclusion. If you interrupted her, she would either continue without noticing, or answer in a few words and then return to repeat the sentence. Thus interruptions only made matters worse; yet I had to interrupt, and often, too, to preserve my life. A man would die if he allowed her monotony to drip over him all day long.

“Great Scott!” I said in my distress. She went straight back and began again:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“_Which_ two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, where they were well lodged. On the morrow they heard their masses in the abbey, and then rode forth until they came to a great forest; there Sir Gawaine became aware, in a valley by a turret, of twelve fair damsels and two knights armed upon great horses, while the damsels went to and fro beside a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"4164844b66599d5f2012e5b3","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was more crowded than ever. Six Cabinet Ministers had come straight from the Speaker’s Levée, wearing their stars and ribands; all the pretty women were in their finest gowns; and at the far end of the picture-gallery stood the Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a massive, Tartar-like woman with minute black eyes and magnificent emeralds, speaking atrocious French at the top of her voice and laughing extravagantly at everything said to her. It was truly a remarkable mixture of people. Splendid peeresses conversed pleasantly with fierce Radicals, fashionable preachers rubbed shoulders with distinguished sceptics, a whole flock of bishops followed a stout prima-donna from room to room, several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, occupied the staircase, and it was rumoured that the supper-room had at one point been packed with geniuses. Indeed, it was one of Lady Windermere’s most successful evenings, and the Princess remained until nearly half-past eleven.

When she had departed, Lady Windermere went back to the picture-gallery, where a famous political economist was gravely expounding the scientific theory of music to an outraged Hungarian virtuoso, and began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. She looked extraordinarily beautiful, with her noble ivory throat, her great blue forget-me-not eyes, and her thick coils of golden hair. _Or pur_ they were—not that pale straw shade which in modern times usurps the gracious title of gold, but gold such as is woven through sunbeams or concealed in curious amber; and they gave her face something of a saint’s setting, with more than a little of a sinner’s allure. She was an intriguing psychological study. In early life she had learned the significant truth that nothing resembles innocence so closely as an indiscretion; and through a succession of reckless adventures, half of them entirely harmless, she had won all the privileges of a personality. She had changed husbands more than once; indeed, Debrett assigned her three marriages; but since she had never changed her lover, society had long since stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, without children, and possessed of that excessive passion for pleasure which is the secret of staying young.

Suddenly she glanced eagerly about the room and said, in her clear contralto, ‘Where is my cheiromantist?’

‘Your what, Gladys?’ cried the Duchess, starting involuntarily.

‘My cheiromantist, Duchess; I cannot do without him just now.’

‘Dear Gladys! you are always so original,’ murmured the Duchess, trying to recall exactly what a cheiromantist was, and hoping it was not the same thing as a cheiropodist.

‘He comes to read my hand twice every week without fail,’ Lady Windermere continued, ‘and is most fascinating about it.’"}

{"request_id":"cf153105069a54afe299e9b4","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced the room in anger. I remained prepared to hear and answer his reproaches. Adrian stood leaning against the wall. “This is utterly absurd,” he exclaimed; “if you were schoolboys, you could not behave with greater unreasonableness.”

“You do not comprehend,” said Raymond. “This is merely one part of a system—a plan of tyranny to which I will never yield. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the sole slave in its empire? My privacy violated, my conduct condemned, my friends insulted? But I will cast off the whole of it at once. Be witnesses,” and he removed from his breast the star, the badge of office, and flung it upon the table. “I renounce my office; I abdicate my power—let whoever can take it assume it!”

“Let him assume it,” cried Adrian, “who can declare himself, or whom the world will declare, your superior. There is no man in England possessed of sufficient presumption. Know your own worth, Raymond, and your anger will fade; your confidence return. A few months since, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country, or for our own, we prayed at the same time for the Protector’s life and welfare, so closely were they bound together. Your hours were spent for our advantage, and your ambition was to win our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, founded useful institutions for us, and made the soil richly fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your judgment-seat, while the poor and oppressed rose like flowers awakened by morning beneath the sunshine of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we are all dismayed and grieving when this seems altered? But come, this fit of spleen has already passed; take up your duties again. Your supporters will welcome you, your enemies will be silenced, and our love, honour, and duty will once more be shown to you. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world is subject to your will.”

“All this would be excellent sense if it were spoken to someone else,” Raymond replied gloomily. “Apply the lesson to yourself, and you, the first peer of the realm, might become its sovereign. You, being good, wise, and just, might govern every heart. But I see, too soon for my happiness and too late for England’s welfare, that I accepted a task beyond my powers. I cannot govern myself. My passions rule me; my slightest impulse is my tyrant. Do you suppose I renounced the Protectorate—and renounced it I have—in a moment of irritation? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that bauble again; never again burden myself with the care and misery whose visible emblem it is.”"}

{"request_id":"914b912a15f4b2c4f4900b92","rewritten_text":"The winters at Sullivan’s Island’s latitude are rarely harsh, and in autumn it is an unusual thing for a fire to be thought necessary. About mid-October, 18—, there came, however, a day of extraordinary cold. Shortly before sunset I made my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, which I had not visited for several weeks—my home then being in Charleston, nine miles from the island, while travel to and from it was far less convenient than in the present day. When I reached the hut, I knocked as usual, and receiving no answer, looked for the key in its accustomed hiding place, opened the door, and entered. A bright fire burned upon the hearth. It was a novelty, and certainly not an unwelcome one. I removed my overcoat, settled into an arm-chair beside the snapping logs, and patiently awaited my hosts’ arrival.

They came soon after dark and welcomed me most warmly. Jupiter, grinning broadly, hurried about getting some marsh-hens ready for supper. Legrand was in one of his fits—what else can I call them?—of excitement. He had discovered an unknown bivalve, belonging to a new genus, and, beyond that, had tracked down and captured, with Jupiter’s help, a _scarabæus_ he believed entirely new, though he wanted my judgment on it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, warming my hands over the fire and wishing the entire tribe of _scarabæi_ elsewhere.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” said Legrand. “But it has been so long since I saw you; how could I have guessed that you would visit me on this particular night? On my way home I met Lieutenant G——, from the fort, and foolishly lent him the insect; so you cannot see it until morning. Remain here tonight, and I will send Jup for it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in creation!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Foolishness! No—the bug. It is a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory-nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back, and another, rather longer, at the other. The _antennæ_ are—”

“Dey aint no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep a tellin on you,” interrupted Jupiter; “de bug is a goole bug, solid, ebery bit of him, inside and all, sep him wing—neber feel half so hebby a bug in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"4725443f6fe704f2b8433970","rewritten_text":"After joining in general lamentation over the dreadful outcome of this event, which Elizabeth regarded as almost certain, and Miss Bennet could not claim was entirely impossible, the former continued, “But tell me everything about it that I have not already heard. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they no suspicion of anything before the elopement? They must have seen them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted that he had often suspected some partiality, especially on Lydia’s side, but nothing that caused him any alarm. I am so sorry for him. His conduct was as attentive and kind as possible. He was coming to us to assure us of his concern before he had any idea that they had not gone to Scotland; when that fear first became known, it hastened his journey.”

“And was Denny convinced that Wickham would not marry? Did he know they intended to run away? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything about their plan and would not state his true opinion. He did not repeat his belief that they would not marry, and from that I am inclined to hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster came himself, not one of you, I suppose, doubted that they were truly married?”

“How could such an idea have entered our minds? I felt somewhat uneasy—a little afraid for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his conduct had not always been entirely proper. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only understood how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then admitted, with very natural satisfaction at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had prepared her for such a step. It seems she had known for many weeks that they were in love with each other.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I believe not.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think poorly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit that he did not speak of Wickham as favorably as he once had. He believed him imprudent and extravagant; and since this sad affair occurred, it is said that he left Meryton deeply in debt. But I hope that may be untrue.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secretive, if we had told what we knew of him, this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But exposing anyone’s former faults without knowing what their present feelings were seemed unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"ca4bb2b46738d97991093c58","rewritten_text":"‘Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,’ cried the old lady as he entered the room, ‘why haven’t you come to see me all this time?’

‘My dear Lady Clem, I never have a moment to myself,’ said Lord Arthur, smiling.

‘I suppose you mean that you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense? I cannot understand why people make such a fuss about being married. In my day, we never dreamed of billing and cooing in public—or in private, for that matter.’

‘I assure you I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.’

‘Of course; that is the only reason you come to visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder you men never take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am, a poor rheumatic creature with a false front and a bad temper. Why, if it were not for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can find, I do not think I could get through the day. Doctors are no use at all, except for taking one’s money. They cannot even cure my heartburn.’

‘I have brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,’ said Lord Arthur gravely. ‘It is a wonderful thing, invented by an American.’

‘I do not think I like American inventions, Arthur. I am quite sure I do not. I read some American novels recently, and they were complete nonsense.’

‘Oh, but there is nothing nonsensical about this, Lady Clem! I assure you it is a perfect cure. You must promise to try it’; and Lord Arthur took the little box from his pocket and handed it to her.

‘Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a present? That is very sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I will take it at once.’

‘Good heavens, Lady Clem!’ cried Lord Arthur, seizing her hand. ‘You must not do anything of the kind. It is a homoeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it might do you an immense amount of harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You will be astonished by the result.’

‘I should like to take it now,’ said Lady Clementina, holding up to the light the little transparent capsule, with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine. ‘I am sure it is delicious. The fact is, although I hate doctors, I love medicines. However, I will keep it until my next attack.’

‘And when will that be?’ Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"7c3baec65f5952b37847d16d","rewritten_text":"‘Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my case. Would you care for it?’

‘No, thank you. I never eat anything now; but it is very kind of you nevertheless, and you are far nicer than the rest of your horrid, impolite, vulgar, dishonest family.’

‘Stop!’ cried Virginia, stamping her foot. ‘You are the rude, horrid, vulgar one, and as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to touch up that absurd bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, vermilion included, so I could paint no more sunsets; then you took the emerald-green and chrome-yellow, and at last I had nothing but indigo and Chinese white, so I could only paint moonlight scenes, which are always depressing to see and not easy to paint at all. I never told on you, though I was extremely annoyed, and the whole affair was ridiculous; for who ever heard of emerald-green blood?’

‘Well, really,’ said the Ghost, rather meekly, ‘what could I do? Real blood is very difficult to obtain nowadays, and since your brother started the whole business with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason why I should not use your paints. As for colour, that is always a question of taste: the Cantervilles have blue blood, for example—the bluest in England; but I know you Americans do not care for such things.’

‘You know nothing about it, and the best thing for you would be to emigrate and improve your mind. My father will be delighted to provide you with a free passage, and although there is a heavy duty on spirits of every sort, the Custom House will cause no trouble, since all the officers are Democrats. Once you reach New York, you are bound to be a great success. I know many people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather, and considerably more for a family Ghost.’

‘I do not think I should like America.’

‘I suppose that is because we have no ruins or curiosities,’ said Virginia sarcastically.

‘No ruins! No curiosities!’ replied the Ghost. ‘You have your navy and your manners.’

‘Good evening. I will go and ask papa to give the twins an extra week’s holiday.’

‘Please do not go, Miss Virginia,’ he cried. ‘I am so lonely and unhappy, and I truly do not know what to do. I want to go to sleep, but I cannot.’

‘That is quite absurd! You have only to go to bed and blow out the candle.’"}

{"request_id":"7e353f95834ab7c8589cb38f","rewritten_text":"At the stairs where we had taken him aboard, and ever since, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were suspected. I had seen none. We certainly had not been followed then, and no boat was following us now. If any boat had been waiting for us, I would have turned toward shore and forced her either to continue on or to show her purpose. But we continued without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and looked, as I have said, like a natural part of the scene. It was remarkable—though perhaps the miserable life he had led explained it—that he was the least anxious of us all. He was not indifferent. He told me he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign country. Nor, as I understood him, was he willing simply to submit or give up. But he had no intention of going out to meet danger. When danger came to him, he faced it; until then, he would not trouble himself about it.

“If you knowed, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here alonger my dear boy and have my smoke, arter being day by day betwixt four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the pleasures of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head seriously. “But you don’t know it equal to me. You must have been under lock and key, dear boy, to know it equal to me—but I ain’t a-going to be low.”

It seemed inconsistent to me that, for any ruling idea, he should have risked his freedom and even his life. But I reflected that freedom without danger might be so unlike everything he had known that it could not mean to him what it would mean to another man. I was not far wrong, for after smoking a little he said:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, t’other side the world, I was always looking toward this side; and it got flat to be there, though I was growing rich. Everybody knowed Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody’s head would be troubled about him. They ain’t so easy concerning me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, leastwise, if they knowed where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you will be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he replied, drawing a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And think so?”"}

{"request_id":"731f498b284e270d856a096f","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He seemed deliberately to misunderstand the word she had repeated. He quickly added, “Yes, customers; in banking, we usually call the people connected with us our customers. He was a French gentleman; a learned man; a man of great knowledge—a doctor.”

“From Beauvais?”

“Yes, from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, he was from Beauvais. Like your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our relationship was business, but confidential. At that time I was working in our French branch, and had been there—oh, twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask when that was, sir?”

“I mean, miss, twenty years ago. He married an English lady, and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen and families, were entirely handled by Tellson’s. In the same way, I am, or have been, trustee for dozens of our customers. These are only business relationships, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing sentimental. During my working life, I have moved from one to another just as I move from one customer to another during my business day. In short, I have no feelings; I am only a machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I am beginning to think”—her strangely furrowed forehead was fixed intently on him—“that when I was left an orphan, because my mother lived only two years longer than my father, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the small, trusting hand that reached toward his and kissed it with some ceremony. Then he led the young woman back to her chair. Holding the back with his left hand, and using his right at different times to rub his chin, tug at his wig near the ears, or point as he spoke, he looked down at her while she looked up at him.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how honestly I described myself just now, when I said I had no feelings and that all my relationships with other people were merely business, if you consider that I have never seen you since. No; you have been under Tellson’s care ever since, and I have been occupied with Tellson’s other business. Feelings! I have no time for them, and no opportunity for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an enormous money-making machine.”"}

{"request_id":"3ab162cf99f4364ce3b1b89e","rewritten_text":"She studied me closely for a while, then said quietly,

“What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I replied, “that you would not treat them as you do the others. They may share the same blood, but believe me, they are not the same in nature.”

Still watching me closely, Miss Havisham repeated,

“What do you want for them?”

“You see, I am not clever enough,” I said, aware that I was beginning to blush, “to hide from you, even if I wished to, that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would spend the money to give my friend Herbert lasting help in life—help that, because of the circumstances, must be given without his knowing—I could show you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowledge?” she asked, resting both hands on her stick so she could study me more closely.

“Because,” I said, “I began helping him myself more than two years ago, without his knowledge, and I do not want to be exposed. I cannot explain why I am unable to finish what I began. That is part of a secret belonging to someone else, not to me.”

She slowly turned her eyes away from me and fixed them on the fire. She watched it for what seemed, in the silence and the light of the slowly burning-down candles, a long time. Then the collapse of some red coals brought her back, and she looked at me again—first blankly, then with steadily growing attention. Throughout this, Estella continued knitting. When Miss Havisham had focused on me, she spoke as though our conversation had not been interrupted:

“What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her and trying to control my trembling voice, “you know that I love you. You know I have loved you for a long time, and deeply.”

Hearing herself addressed, she lifted her eyes to my face. Her fingers continued their work, and her expression did not change. I saw Miss Havisham look from me to her, and then from her back to me.

“I should have said this earlier, if I had not been mistaken for so long. That mistake made me hope Miss Havisham intended us for each other. While I believed you could not help yourself, in a way, I held back from saying it. But now I must say it.”

Keeping the same expression, and still moving her fingers, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said, responding to that gesture. “I know. I do not hope ever to call you mine, Estella."}

{"request_id":"330eaa524d3d67ea035af278","rewritten_text":"During dinner, Mr. Bennet hardly spoke at all. But once the servants had left, he decided it was time to talk with his guest. He chose a subject on which he expected Mr. Collins to speak well, remarking that he seemed very fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort seemed remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen a better topic. Mr. Collins praised her at length. The subject made him more solemn than usual, and with a very serious expression he declared that he had never seen such conduct in a person of rank—such friendliness and kindness as he had experienced from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both sermons he had already had the honour of preaching before her. She had also invited him to dine at Rosings twice, and had sent for him only the previous Saturday to complete her evening quadrille party. He knew that many people considered Lady Catherine proud, but he had never seen anything in her except friendliness. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman. She had not objected in the least to his joining the society of the neighbourhood, or to his leaving his parish for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even advised him to marry as soon as possible, provided he chose carefully. Once, she had visited him at his modest parsonage, approved all the changes he had been making, and even suggested some improvements herself—such as shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and polite, I am sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very pleasant woman. It is a pity that great ladies in general are not more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden surrounding my humble home is separated from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s residence, by only a lane.”

“I think you said she was a widow, sir. Has she any children?”

“She has one daughter only, the heiress of Rosings and of a very large fortune.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better provided for than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is a most charming young lady, indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest women, because there is something in her features that shows the young woman of distinguished birth."}

{"request_id":"b55356efe64665bb33375b4b","rewritten_text":"“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” He shook his head and tapped it, showing how little he thought of Joseph.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry and exhausted. Sit down. Here is a chicken from the Boar, here is a tongue from the Boar, and here are one or two little things from the Boar, which I hope you will not despise. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again the moment after sitting down, “see before me the boy I once played with in his happy infancy? And may I—_may_ I—?”

By this, he meant to ask whether he might shake hands. I agreed, and he did so warmly before sitting down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink: Thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favourites with equal judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “see before me One—and drink to One—without once more expressing—May I—_may_ I—?”

I said he might. He shook hands with me again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could not have gone more quickly to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook helped me to the liver wing and the best slice of tongue—none of those remote Pork No Thoroughfares now—and took almost no care of himself. “Ah! Poultry, poultry! You little knew,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the fowl on the dish, “when you were a young fledgling, what was waiting for you. You little knew you were to provide refreshment beneath this humble roof for one who—Call it weakness, if you like,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? _may_ I—?”

It was no longer necessary to repeat that he might, so he did it at once. How he managed to do it so often without cutting himself on my knife, I do not know.

“And your sister,” he continued after eating steadily for a while, “who had the honour of raising you by hand! It is sad to think that she is no longer able to understand that honour fully. May—”

I saw he was about to come at me again, and stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, limp with admiration, “that’s how you recognize them, sir!” (I do not know who Sir was, but he certainly was not me, and no third person was present); “that’s how you recognize the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"b06ee9212787d4979ae4be97","rewritten_text":"In my youth, discontent never entered my mind. If I was ever overcome by boredom, the sight of nature’s beauty or the study of what was excellent and sublime in human creations could always engage my heart and lift my spirits. But I am like a blasted tree; the bolt has struck my soul. I felt then that I would live only to display what I would soon become—a miserable ruin of humanity, pitied by others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a long time at Oxford, walking through its surroundings and trying to identify every place connected with the most inspiring period of English history. Our small journeys of discovery were often extended by the new sights that appeared before us. We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the field where that patriot died. For a moment, my soul rose above its degrading and miserable fears as I considered the noble ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice that these places preserved and recalled. For an instant, I dared to throw off my chains and look around me with a free and proud spirit. But the iron had cut into my flesh, and I sank once more, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford reluctantly and went on to Matlock, our next place of rest. The countryside around this village resembled Switzerland more closely, though everything was smaller, and the green hills lacked the distant white Alps that always crown the pine-covered mountains of my native land. We visited the marvelous cave and the small natural-history rooms, where the curiosities were arranged much as they were in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name made me tremble whenever Henry spoke it, and I hurried to leave Matlock, since that terrible scene had become linked with the place.

From Derby, still traveling north, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow still clinging to the northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all familiar and dear to me. We also made several acquaintances there, who nearly managed to trick me into happiness. Clerval’s pleasure was much greater than mine; among talented people, his mind opened, and he discovered in himself abilities and inner resources greater than he had imagined while keeping company with those beneath him."}

{"request_id":"9a154b2eebdfe980da9821c4","rewritten_text":"When I returned, I found the following letter from my father:

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter confirming the date of your return to us; at first, I was tempted to write only a few lines, simply naming the day on which I should expect you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I dare not do it. What would your surprise be, my son, when, expecting a joyful welcome, you instead found tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you of our misfortune? Absence cannot have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows; and how can I inflict pain upon my son, absent for so long? I wish to prepare you for the terrible news, but I know it is impossible; even now, your eyes are racing over the page, searching for the words that will bring you the dreadful tidings.

“William is dead!—that sweet child, whose smiles delighted and warmed my heart, who was so gentle and yet so cheerful! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you; I will simply relate what happened.

“Last Thursday, May 7th, my niece, your two brothers, and I went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, and we continued farther than usual. It was already dusk before we thought of returning; then we discovered that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be found. We therefore sat on a bench until they returned. Soon Ernest came and asked whether we had seen his brother. He said he had been playing with him, that William had run away to hide, and that he had searched for him in vain and then waited a long time, but William had not returned.

“This account alarmed us, and we continued searching until night fell, when Elizabeth suggested that he might have gone back to the house. He was not there. We returned once more with torches; I could not rest while thinking that my sweet boy might be lost and exposed to the damp and dew of night, and Elizabeth was suffering terribly as well. At about five in the morning, I found my lovely boy, whom I had seen the previous evening healthy, lively, and blooming, lying on the grass, pale and motionless; the mark of the murderer’s fingers was on his neck.

“He was carried home, and the anguish on my face revealed the secret to Elizabeth. She was desperate to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she persisted and entered the room where it lay. She quickly examined the victim’s neck, then clasped her hands and cried, ‘O God!"}

{"request_id":"ff0334eb65c9d1fcc58b9972","rewritten_text":"“Git up! What you ’bout?”

I opened my eyes and looked about, trying to figure where I was. The sun was already up, and I’d been sleeping soundly. Pap stood over me, looking sour and sickly besides. He says:

“What you doing with this gun?”

I reckoned he didn’t know a thing about what he’d been up to, so I says:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Well, I tried, but I couldn’t; I couldn’t move you.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there talking all day, but get out and see whether there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along directly.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried up the river-bank. I saw bits of limbs and suchlike drifting down, with a sprinkling of bark; so I knowed the river had started rising. I reckoned I’d have a fine time now if I was over in town. The June rise had always been lucky for me; for as soon as it began, cordwood came floating down, along with pieces of log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs together; and all you had to do was catch them and sell them to the wood-yards and sawmill.

I went on up the bank, keeping one eye open for pap and the other for whatever the rise might bring along. Then, all at once, here came a canoe; a real beauty, too, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high as a duck. I plunged head-first from the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and struck out for the canoe. I expected somebody would be lying in it, because folks often did that to fool people, and when a fellow had pulled a skiff nearly up to them, they’d sit up and laugh. But it wasn’t so this time. It was a drift-canoe sure enough, and I climbed in and paddled her ashore. I thought, the old man will be pleased when he sees this—she’s worth ten dollars. But when I reached shore pap still wasn’t in sight, and as I was running her into a little creek like a gully, all covered over with vines and willows, another notion struck me: I figured I’d hide her well, and then, instead of taking to the woods when I ran off, I’d go downriver about fifty miles and camp in one spot for good, so I wouldn’t have such a hard time tramping on foot.

It was pretty near the shanty, and I thought I heard the old man coming every minute; but I got her hidden. Then I stepped out and looked around a clump of willows, and there was the old man a little way down the path, drawing a bead on a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"dba2f818de5b14d8901c5fe2","rewritten_text":"Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.

His face immediately took on an expression of the deepest gloom, and he replied, “To seek someone who fled from me.”

“And did the man you pursued travel in the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I believe we have seen him, for the day before we picked you up, we saw some dogs pulling a sledge, with a man in it, across the ice.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked many questions about the route the dæmon, as he called him, had taken. Soon afterward, when he was alone with me, he said, “I have surely aroused your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you are too considerate to ask questions.”

“Certainly; it would indeed be very impertinent and inhuman of me to trouble you with my curiosity.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and perilous situation; you have kindly restored me to life.”

Soon afterward he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied that I could not say with any certainty, since the ice had not broken until near midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety before then; but I had no way of knowing.

From that moment, a new spirit of life animated the stranger’s failing body. He showed the greatest eagerness to go on deck and watch for the sledge that had appeared before; but I persuaded him to remain in the cabin, for he is far too weak to endure the raw air. I promised that someone would watch for him and immediately inform him if any new object came into view.

This is my journal of everything connected with this strange event up to the present day. The stranger has gradually recovered some health, but he is very quiet and seems uneasy whenever anyone except me enters his cabin. Yet his manner is so gentle and conciliatory that all the sailors are interested in him, although they have spoken with him very little. For my part, I am beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant, profound sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in better days, since even now, amid his ruin, he remains so attractive and kind.

I said in one of my letters, my dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the open ocean; yet I have found a man whom, before misery broke his spirit, I would have been happy to call the brother of my heart."}

{"request_id":"f2d9548d5b354db83a11826c","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, the force of gravitation would be continually decreasing in proportion to the squares of the distances; and thus, with a velocity increasing to an extraordinary degree, I should eventually reach those remote regions where the earth’s attraction would be replaced by that of the moon. In keeping with this reasoning, I did not consider it worthwhile to burden myself with provisions for more than forty days.

“There remained, however, another difficulty, which caused me some slight concern. It has been remarked that, in balloon ascents to any considerable elevation, apart from the pain involved in breathing, great discomfort is felt in the head and body, frequently accompanied by bleeding from the nose and other alarming symptoms, all becoming increasingly troublesome as the altitude rises. This was a somewhat startling consideration. Was it not likely that these symptoms would continue increasing without limit, or at least until death brought them to an end? In the end, I decided that they would not. Their cause was to be sought in the gradual withdrawal of the ordinary atmospheric pressure from the body’s surface, and the resulting expansion of the superficial blood-vessels—not in any actual derangement of the animal system, as occurs in difficulty of breathing, when the atmosphere is chemically too thin to renew properly the blood in one of the heart’s ventricles. Except through failure of this renewal, I could see no reason why life might not be maintained even in a vacuum; for the expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is purely muscular action, and the cause rather than the consequence of respiration. In short, I believed that, as the body grew accustomed to the absence of atmospheric pressure, the painful sensations would gradually lessen—and, while they lasted, I trusted confidently to the iron strength of my constitution to endure them.

“Thus, may it please your Excellencies, I have set forth some, though certainly not all, of the considerations that led me to conceive the plan of a voyage to the moon. I shall now proceed to present the outcome of an attempt so seemingly audacious in conception, and, in any event, so entirely without precedent in the history of mankind.

“After reaching the altitude previously stated, namely three miles and three-quarters, I cast a quantity of feathers from the car and discovered that I was still rising at a sufficient speed; consequently, there was no need to release any ballast. I was pleased by this, since I wished to keep with me as much weight as I could carry, for reasons that will be explained later.”"}

{"request_id":"e5770304bc06b6e16daacf04","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ so I assumed ‘anybody’ included—well, anybody; that is, everybody.”

“It does—anybody of noble birth, and preferably royal.”

“That seems reasonable,” said the abbot, who saw a chance to smooth matters and prevent disaster. “Surely so remarkable a gift would not be granted to reveal the affairs of lesser people, but only those born near the heights of greatness. Our King Arthur—”

“Would you like to know about him?” the enchanter interrupted.

“Most gladly, and with thanks.”

Everyone was immediately filled with awe and interest again, the hopeless idiots. They watched the spells with great attention and looked at me as if to say, “Well, what can you say to that?” when the announcement came:

“The king is tired from the hunt and has been lying in his palace for two hours, sleeping soundly.”

“God bless him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep restore both his body and his soul.”

“And it might, if he were asleep,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping. The king is riding.”

There was trouble again—a clash of authority. No one knew which of us to believe, though I still had some reputation left. The magician’s pride was offended, and he said:

“Behold, I have seen many wonderful fortune-tellers, prophets, and magicians in my lifetime, but never one who could sit idle and see into the heart of things without a single spell to help him.”

“You have lived in the woods and lost much because of it. I use spells myself, as this good brotherhood knows—but only when the matter is important.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I believe I know how to hold my own. That remark made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and received this answer:

“They are all asleep, overcome by weariness, just as the king is.”

I said:

“That is simply another lie. Half of them are enjoying themselves; the queen and the other half are not asleep—they are riding. Now perhaps you can show us what you can do and tell us where the king, queen, and everyone riding with them are going at this moment.”

“They are sleeping now, as I said; but tomorrow they will ride, for they are traveling toward the sea.”

“And where will they be at vespers the day after tomorrow?”

“Far north of Camelot, with half their journey completed.”

“That is another lie, by a distance of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"abf2f25df93856f81e10cd47","rewritten_text":"“How long I continued in this condition I cannot possibly say. It must, nevertheless, have been a considerable while, since, when I partly regained a sense of existence, I saw dawn breaking, the balloon at an immense height above a wilderness of ocean, and no sign of land anywhere within the bounds of the enormous horizon. My sensations, however, on recovering were by no means as agonizing as might have been expected. Indeed, there was something almost incipiently mad in the composed inspection I began to make of my circumstances. I raised each of my hands to my eyes in turn, wondering what event could have caused the veins to swell and the fingernails to become horribly black. I then examined my head with care, shaking it again and again and feeling it minutely, until I managed to convince myself that it was not, as I had half suspected, larger than my balloon. Next, with an air of understanding, I felt in both breeches pockets, and, finding a set of tablets and a toothpick case missing, tried to explain their disappearance; failing to do so, I was deeply chagrined. It now came to me that I was suffering considerable discomfort in the joint of my left ankle, and a faint awareness of my situation began to dawn upon me. But, strange to say! I was neither amazed nor filled with horror. If I experienced any emotion, it was a sort of chuckling satisfaction at the ingenuity I was about to show in freeing myself from this predicament; and never for an instant did I regard my eventual safety as doubtful. For several minutes I remained absorbed in the deepest meditation. I distinctly remember repeatedly pressing my lips together, placing my forefinger beside my nose, and employing other gestures and grimaces familiar to men who, comfortably settled in armchairs, ponder over matters of difficulty or importance. Having, as I believed, sufficiently gathered my thoughts, I now, with great care and deliberation, reached my hands behind me and unfastened the large iron buckle attached to the waistband of my inexpressibles. The buckle had three teeth, which, being somewhat rusty, rotated only with great difficulty upon their axis. After some effort, however, I brought them to right angles with the buckle’s body, and was pleased to find that they held firmly in that position. Keeping the instrument thus formed between my teeth, I then set about loosening the knot of my cravat. I was obliged to pause several times before completing this manoeuvre, but at last it was done.”"}

{"request_id":"2b481d826a59838f61b41bfa","rewritten_text":"His account was that, traveling from his home and passing through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke rising from the inn’s chimney. Assuming he would find fellow travelers gathered there, he knocked and was admitted. No one was in the house except Lucy and her mother. The older woman had lost the use of her limbs after an attack of rheumatism, and so, one by one, all the remaining inhabitants of the country had set out, leaving them alone. Lucy begged the man to stay with her; her mother would be better in a week or two, and they could then depart, but they would perish if left so helpless and abandoned. The man said that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, and therefore, as he saw it, he could not remain. As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to deliver wherever he might meet us. At least he carried out this commission, and Idris received the following letter with deep emotion:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I am certain you will remember and pity me, and I dare hope that you will help me; what other hope have I? Forgive the way I write—I am so confused. A month ago my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already improving, and in another month, I am sure, she would be able to travel, in the manner you were kind enough to say you would arrange for us. But now everyone is gone—everyone—as they left, each one said that perhaps my mother would recover before we were completely deserted. But three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who, because of his newborn child, had remained until the last; since they were a large family, I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us, but I found the house deserted. I have not seen a soul since, until this good man arrived. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation; she is so ill that I have concealed it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we must perish miserably if we remain here. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road; and if, when she improves, I were somehow able to discover the roads and travel so many miles to the sea, you would all be in France, with the vast ocean between us—an ocean terrible even to sailors.”"}

{"request_id":"27f45eb2cbc898efe24f5c2e","rewritten_text":"“Do you understand me? I have learned the language of despair; I know it by heart, because I am Despair—and a strange being I am: joyful, triumphant Despair. Yet those words are false, for the wave may be dark, but it is not bitter. We lie down and close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we wake, we are free. Come, then, no more delay, you who linger! Behold the pleasant potion! Look, I am a spirit of goodness, not a human maiden inviting you; and in winning tones—oh, if only they could win you!—I say, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my eyes fixed on his face. His exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, and his gentle yet earnest expression of concern and wonder, even before he spoke, changed my strained emotions. They took away all the harshness of despair and filled me only with the softest grief. I saw that his eyes were moist as he took both my hands in his. Sitting down beside me, he said:

“This is a sad act you would lead me toward, dearest friend, and your sorrow must be very deep to fill you with such unhappy thoughts. You long for death, yet fear it, and wish me to be your companion. But I have less courage than you, and even with you beside me, I dare not die. Listen to me, then consider whether you should persuade me to your plan, even if the forceful eloquence of despair could make black death seem so inviting that bright heaven appeared dark. Listen, I beg you, to one who has himself encouraged desperate thoughts and longed impatiently for death, but who at last has trampled that phantom underfoot and crushed its sting. Come: since you have played Despair with me, I will play Una with you and lead you safely from his dark cavern. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by words untouched by selfish desire.

“We do not know what this wide world means, with its strange mixture of good and evil. But we have been placed here and told to live and hope. I do not know what we are meant to hope for; yet some good lies beyond us, and we must seek it. That is our earthly task. If misfortune comes against us, we must fight it; we must push it aside and continue searching for what it is our nature to desire. I do not know whether this hope of future good prepares us for another existence, or whether we are simply workers in God’s vineyard, helping to smooth the way for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"ed39889c03dc458e6dc182ed","rewritten_text":"They know what a sharp lad he is; he’ll be a lifer. They’ll make the Artful nothing short of a lifer.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What’s the use of talking that way to me; why don’t yer speak so I can understand yer?”

Fagin was just about to translate these puzzling expressions into plain language; and, once interpreted, Mr. Bolter would have learned that they meant the words “transportation for life,” when the conversation was interrupted by the entrance of Master Bates, his hands in his breeches-pockets and his face twisted into a half-comical expression of misery.

“It’s all up, Fagin,” said Charley, after he and his new companion had been introduced to one another.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to ’dentify him; and the Artful’s booked for a passage out,” replied Master Bates. “I must have a complete suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband, to wisit him in before he starts on his travels. To think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—going abroad for a common twopenny-halfpenny sneeze-box! I never thought he’d have done it for less than a gold watch, chain, and seals. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his walables, and go out like a gentleman, instead of as a common prig, without any honour or glory!”

Having thus expressed his feelings for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates seated himself on the nearest chair, looking chagrined and despondent.

“What do you mean by saying he has neither honour nor glory!” exclaimed Fagin, casting an angry glance at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the top-sawyer among you all! Is there one of you who could touch him, or come near him on any scent! Eh?”

“Not one,” replied Master Bates, his voice made husky by regret; “not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin answered angrily; “what are you blubbering for?”

“’Cause it isn’t on the rec-ord, is it?” said Charley, driven into complete defiance of his venerable friend by the force of his sorrow; “’cause it can’t appear in the ’dictment; ’cause nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he stand in the Newgate Calendar? P’raps he won’t be there at all. Oh, my eye, my eye, what a blow it is!”

“Ha! ha!” cried Fagin, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter in a fit of chuckling that shook him as if he had the palsy; “see what pride they take in their profession, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"594d66eae0bf51174ef18eef","rewritten_text":"On the morning appointed for Admiral and Mrs. Croft to see Kellynch Hall, Anne found it most natural to take her almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s and stay out of the way until everything was over; then she found it most natural to regret having missed the opportunity of seeing them.

The meeting between the two parties proved highly satisfactory and settled the entire business at once. Each lady was already well disposed toward an agreement and therefore saw nothing but good manners in the other; and as for the gentlemen, there was such hearty good humour and such open, trusting generosity on the Admiral’s side that it could not fail to influence Sir Walter, who had also been flattered into his finest and most polished behaviour by Mr. Shepherd’s assurances that the Admiral knew him by reputation as a model of good breeding.

The house, grounds, and furniture were approved; the Crofts were approved; the terms, timing, everything, and everyone were right. Mr. Shepherd’s clerks were set to work, without a single preliminary disagreement needing adjustment in all that “This indenture showeth.”

Sir Walter declared without hesitation that the Admiral was the best-looking sailor he had ever met, and went so far as to say that, if his own man had been allowed to arrange the Admiral’s hair, he would not have been ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. And the Admiral, with sympathetic warmth, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we should soon reach an agreement, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—mutual compliments that would have been considered nearly equal.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas; and since Sir Walter proposed moving to Bath during the preceding month, there was no time to lose in making all the necessary arrangements.

Lady Russell, convinced that Anne would not be permitted to have any use or importance in choosing the house they were about to secure, was very unwilling to have her hurried away so soon. She wanted to make it possible for Anne to remain until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas; but, having engagements of her own that would keep her away from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not extend the full invitation she wished to offer. And Anne, though she dreaded the possible September heat amid all the white glare of Bath and grieved to surrender all the influence—so sweet and so sad—of the autumn months in the country, did not feel that, all things considered, she wished to stay."}

{"request_id":"16c812d6bdd9577954cc1211","rewritten_text":"You must adopt a little of my philosophy. Think only of the past when remembering it gives you pleasure.”

“I cannot credit you with philosophy of that sort. _Your_ recollections must be entirely free from reproach, so that the satisfaction they bring comes not from philosophy, but, what is far better, from ignorance. With _me_, it is different. Painful memories will intrude, and they cannot, nor ought they, be driven away. I have been selfish all my life in practice, though not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was _right_, but not how to govern my temper. I was given sound principles, yet left to follow them with pride and conceit. Unhappily, as an only son (and for many years an only _child_), I was spoiled by my parents, who, though good themselves—my father especially, being all benevolence and kindness—allowed, encouraged, and almost taught me to be selfish and domineering; to care for no one beyond my own family; to think poorly of the rest of the world; and at least to _wish_ to think their understanding and worth inferior to my own. Such was I from eight to eight-and-twenty, and such I might still have remained but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you? You taught me a lesson, difficult indeed at first, but of the greatest benefit. Through you, I was properly humbled. I came to you without doubting that I would be accepted. You showed me how inadequate all my claims were to please a woman deserving of being pleased.”

“Had you then convinced yourself that I would?”

“Indeed I had. What will you think of my vanity? I believed you wished for, and expected, my addresses.”

“My manner must have been at fault, though I assure you it was not intentional. I never meant to mislead you, but my spirits may often have carried me astray. How you must have hated me after _that_ evening!”

“Hated you! I was angry, perhaps, at first, but my anger soon found a more proper object.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, indeed; I felt nothing but surprise.”

“Your surprise could not have exceeded _mine_ at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no unusual politeness, and I confess I did not expect to receive _more_ than was my due.”

“My purpose _then_,” replied Darcy, “was to show you, through every civility within my power, that I was not so mean as to resent the past; and I hoped to gain your forgiveness and lessen your poor opinion by allowing you to see that I had heeded your reproofs.”"}

{"request_id":"71387eff4b249c1e04190ce4","rewritten_text":"I know she would!”

Widow Douglas’s generous hospitality was a tempting offer, and Tom’s arguments soon won. They decided not to tell anyone about their plans for the night. Then Tom thought that Huck might come that very night and give the signal. The idea took much of the excitement out of his expectations. Still, he could not bear to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’s. And why should he, he reasoned? The signal had not come the night before, so why was it more likely to come tonight? The certain pleasure of the evening outweighed the uncertain treasure. Like a boy, he chose what he wanted most and decided not to think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town, the ferryboat stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the distant forest and rocky heights echoed with shouts and laughter. Everyone tried every possible way to get hot and tired. After a while, the explorers wandered back to camp with hearty appetites, and then they began destroying the feast. When they had eaten, they rested and talked in the shade of broad oak trees. Before long, someone shouted:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. They gathered bundles of candles and immediately raced up the hill. The cave entrance was partway up the slope, shaped like the letter A. Its huge oak door stood open. Inside was a small chamber, cold as an icehouse, with solid limestone walls covered in a chilly, dewy sweat. It was romantic and mysterious to stand there in the deep darkness and look out at the green valley shining in the sun. But the feeling soon faded, and the rough play began again. Whenever someone lit a candle, everyone rushed at its owner. A struggle and brave defense followed, but the candle was soon knocked down or blown out, bringing delighted laughter and another chase. Yet everything eventually ends. After a while, the group filed down the steep slope of the main passage. Their flickering lights faintly showed the tall rock walls, which nearly met sixty feet above them. The main passage was only eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps, other tall, narrower cracks branched off on both sides. McDougal’s cave was a huge maze of twisting passages that joined one another, separated again, and led nowhere."}
