{"request_id":"ee194f66173a17bdac3e3495","rewritten_text":"During dinner, Mr. Bennet scarcely spoke at all; but once the servants had withdrawn, he decided it was time to converse with his guest. He therefore introduced a subject on which he expected Mr. Collins to shine, remarking that he seemed very fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort appeared remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have chosen better. Mr. Collins praised her eloquently. The subject raised him to an even greater solemnity than usual; and, with an extremely important expression, he declared that he had never in his life witnessed such conduct in a person of rank—such affability and condescension as he had experienced from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both sermons he had already had the honour of preaching before her. She had also invited him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the previous Saturday to complete her quadrille party that evening. Lady Catherine was considered proud by many people, he knew, but he had never seen anything in her except affability. She had always spoken to him as she would to any other gentleman; she had not objected in the least to his joining the society of the neighbourhood, or to his leaving his parish occasionally for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as possible, provided he chose wisely; and had once visited him in his humble parsonage, where she had entirely approved the alterations he had been making, and had even been kind enough to suggest some herself—shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and civil, I am sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very agreeable woman. It is a pity that great ladies in general are not more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden where my humble home stands is separated from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s residence, only by a lane.”

“I think you said she was a widow, sir? Does she have any family?”

“She has only one daughter, the heiress of Rosings and of a very extensive estate.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better provided for than many girls. And what sort of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is a most charming young lady, indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in true beauty, Miss de Bourgh is far superior to the handsomest women of her sex; because there is something in her features that marks a young woman of distinguished birth.”"}

{"request_id":"28a96b5a25b3f20548504c99","rewritten_text":"Of course, he was very entertaining and all that, but I was terribly disappointed; and when I questioned him about the coat of mail, he merely laughed and said it was much too cold to wear in England. Ah, here is Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you must remove your glove. No, not the left hand, the other.’

‘Dear Gladys, I really don’t think it is quite proper,’ said the Duchess, feebly undoing a rather dirty kid glove.

‘Nothing interesting ever is,’ said Lady Windermere: ‘_on a fait le monde ainsi_. But I must present you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favourite cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley, and if you say she has a larger mountain of the moon than I do, I shall never believe in you again.’

‘I am certain, Gladys, there is nothing of that sort in my hand,’ said the Duchess solemnly.

‘Your Grace is perfectly right,’ said Mr. Podgers, examining the small fat hand with its short square fingers, ‘the mountain of the moon is undeveloped. The line of life, however, is excellent. Please bend the wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines on the _rascette_! You will live to a very advanced age, Duchess, and be exceedingly happy. Ambition—quite moderate, line of intellect not excessive, line of heart—’

‘Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Nothing would delight me more,’ said Mr. Podgers, bowing, ‘if the Duchess had ever been so, but I regret to say that I see great constancy of affection, joined to a powerful sense of duty.’

‘Please continue, Mr. Podgers,’ said the Duchess, looking thoroughly pleased.

‘Economy is certainly among your Grace’s virtues,’ continued Mr. Podgers, and Lady Windermere burst into peals of laughter.

‘Economy is an excellent thing,’ remarked the Duchess complacently; ‘when I married Paisley he possessed eleven castles, and not one house fit for habitation.’

‘And now he has twelve houses, and not one castle,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Well, my dear,’ said the Duchess, ‘I like—’

‘Comfort,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘and modern conveniences, and hot water supplied to every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the sole thing our civilisation can provide us.

‘You have described the Duchess’s character admirably, Mr. Podgers, and now you must read Lady Flora’s’; and at a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl, with sandy Scotch hair and prominent shoulder-blades, stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa and extended a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

‘Ah, a pianist! I see,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘an excellent pianist, though perhaps scarcely a musician.’"}

{"request_id":"f5ab7cb6e7c0068d547fd96b","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, his face pale with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile rushed out of Bentinck House. He pushed through the crowd of fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, seeming neither to see nor hear them. The night was bitterly cold, and the gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind. Yet his hands were feverishly hot, and his forehead burned like fire. He walked on and on, almost like a drunken man. A policeman watched him curiously as he passed. A beggar, who came out from an archway to ask for money, grew frightened when he saw someone whose misery seemed greater than his own. Once Lord Arthur stopped beneath a lamp and looked at his hands. He thought he could already see bloodstains on them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had seen there. Murder! The very night seemed to know it, and the lonely wind seemed to howl the word in his ear. The dark corners of the streets were filled with it. It grinned at him from the rooftops.

First he reached the Park, whose dark, solemn trees seemed to draw him in. Weary, he leaned against the railings, cooling his forehead on the wet metal and listening to the trembling silence of the trees. “Murder! Murder!” he kept repeating, as if saying the word again and again might lessen its horror. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he almost hoped Echo would hear him and wake the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a wild urge to stop some passer-by and tell him everything.

Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, disgraceful alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came curses and the sounds of blows, followed by sharp screams. Huddled on a damp doorstep, he saw the bent forms of poverty and old age. A strange pity came over him. Were these children of sin and misery destined for their fate, just as he was destined for his? Were they, like him, only puppets in some monstrous show?

Yet it was not the mystery of suffering that struck him, but its comedy: its complete uselessness and absurd lack of meaning. How confused everything seemed! How little harmony there was in the world! He was astonished by the contrast between the shallow optimism of the age and the real facts of life. He was still very young.

After some time, he found himself standing before Marylebone Church. The silent road looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there by the dark, twisting patterns of moving shadows."}

{"request_id":"0de8153518dbbff8b4651ff1","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. We could all come on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and me—with my caro sposo walking beside us. I really must speak to him about buying one. In the country, I think a donkey is almost necessary; for no matter how many resources a woman has, she cannot always stay shut up at home. And long walks, you know—in summer there is dust, and in winter there is mud.”

“You will find neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and now it is perfectly dry. Still, come on a donkey if you prefer it. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I would like everything to suit you as much as possible.”

“I am sure you would. Indeed, I give you full credit, my good friend. Beneath that unusually dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are a complete humorist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I fully understand how thoughtful you have been toward me in arranging all this. You have chosen exactly what would please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the party, and he knew that having any of them sit outside to eat would certainly make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not be lured away from his misery under the false promise of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell.

He was invited sincerely. There were no hidden dangers waiting to punish his easy trust. He agreed. He had not been to Donwell for two years. “On some very fine morning, he, Emma, and Harriet could go quite comfortably; and he could sit with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked around the gardens. He did not suppose the gardens could be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would be extremely pleased to see the old house again, and happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any other neighbors. He could see no objection at all to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there on some very fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible, and much better than dining out. He was not fond of dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was lucky that everyone agreed so readily. The invitation was received so warmly everywhere that it seemed, like Mrs. Elton, they all considered the plan a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet declared that they expected great pleasure from it; and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to bring Frank if possible—a sign of approval and gratitude that was unnecessary. Mr. Knightley was therefore obliged to say that he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston promised to write at once and use every argument to persuade him to come."}

{"request_id":"0fad09b94592466266b4c7b2","rewritten_text":"But I must warn you first that I shall tell Sybil everything. She is coming to lunch with me tomorrow to talk about bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a bad temper, a tendency toward gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I shall certainly tell her all about it.’

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. ‘I am not afraid,’ he replied. ‘Sybil knows me as well as I know her.’

‘Ah! I am a little sorry to hear you say that. The proper foundation for marriage is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical at all; I have simply gained experience, which is much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is eager to have his palm read. Do not tell him that he is engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that appeared in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.

‘Dear Lady Windermere,’ cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please let Mr. Podgers stay a little longer. He has just told me I should go on the stage, and I am extremely interested.’

‘If he has told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly take him away. Come here at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.’

‘Well,’ said Lady Jedburgh, making a small grimace as she rose from the sofa, ‘if I am not allowed to go on the stage, I must at least be allowed to join the audience.’

‘Of course; we are all going to be in the audience,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘And now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my particular favourites.’

But when Mr. Podgers looked at Lord Arthur’s hand, he became strangely pale and said nothing. A shudder seemed to pass through him, and his thick, bushy eyebrows twitched violently, in the odd, irritating way they did when he was puzzled. Then large drops of sweat appeared on his yellow forehead, like poisonous dew, and his fat fingers became cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur noticed these strange signs of distress, and for the first time in his life, he felt afraid. His first impulse was to run from the room, but he held himself back. It was better to know the worst, whatever it might be, than to remain in this terrible uncertainty.

‘I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We are all waiting,’ cried Lady Windermere in her quick, impatient manner, but the palm reader made no answer.

‘I believe Arthur is going on the stage,’ said Lady Jedburgh, ‘and that after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him so.’"}

{"request_id":"abdb5070f69823ea6bb4e6d7","rewritten_text":"“And so I’m the owner of some knights,” I said as we rode away. “Who would ever have thought I’d live to list assets like that? I won’t know what to do with them, unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, if you please, sir, and their squires.”

“That’s a good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I did not understand you. I shall tell you at once.” Then she said thoughtfully and softly, turning the words carefully over in her mouth: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; yes, that is it; where do they hang out. Truly, the phrase has a pleasant and charming grace, and is nicely worded too. I will repeat it again and again in my spare time, so that perhaps I may learn it. Where do they hang out. Just so! Already it comes easily from my tongue, and since—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. You remember, a while ago. Figuratively speaking, the game has begun.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Go to bat. I mean, get to work on your statistics, and don’t waste so much kindling getting your fire started. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will, and I shall begin at once. So the two of them left and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I realized my mistake immediately. I had started her going; it was my own fault, and she would take thirty days to reach those facts. She usually began without an introduction and ended without a conclusion. If you interrupted her, she either continued without noticing or answered in a few words and then went back to repeat the sentence. So interruptions only made things worse; yet I had to interrupt, and often, to save my life. Anyone would die if he let her monotony drip over him all day.

“Great Scott!” I said in distress. She simply went back and began again:

“So the two of them left and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, where they were well lodged. In the morning they heard mass in the abbey, and then rode on until they came to a great forest. There Sir Gawaine saw, in a valley beside a turret, twelve fair damsels and two knights armed and mounted on great horses, while the damsels moved back and forth by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"86396239a97610a0d9954392","rewritten_text":"On the morning fixed for Admiral and Mrs Croft to inspect Kellynch Hall, Anne thought it most natural to take her nearly daily walk to Lady Russell’s, and remain out of the way until everything was finished; after which she thought it equally natural to regret having missed the chance of seeing them.

The meeting between the two parties proved extremely satisfactory, and settled the entire matter at once. Both ladies were already favourably inclined towards an agreement, and consequently saw nothing but good manners in one another; while, as for the gentlemen, there was such hearty good humour and such frank, trusting generosity on the Admiral’s part that it could not fail to affect Sir Walter, who had also been flattered into his finest and most polished conduct by Mr Shepherd’s assurances that, by reputation, he was known to the Admiral as a model of good breeding.

The house, grounds, and furniture were approved; the Crofts were approved; terms, timing, everything, and everybody, were satisfactory; and Mr Shepherd’s clerks began their work without a single preliminary disagreement requiring alteration in all that “This indenture sheweth.”

Sir Walter declared without hesitation that the Admiral was the best-looking sailor he had ever encountered, and even went so far as to say that, if his own man had been permitted to arrange the Admiral’s hair, he would not have been ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. The Admiral, with equal cordiality, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we should soon come to terms, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—mutual compliments that might have been considered fairly balanced.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas; and since Sir Walter intended to move to Bath during the previous month, there was no time to waste in arranging all the necessary dependent matters.

Lady Russell, certain that Anne would not be permitted to have either use or influence in choosing the house they were about to secure, was very reluctant to see her hurried away so soon, and wished to make it possible for Anne to remain until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. But, having engagements of her own that would keep her away from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not extend the full invitation she desired; and Anne, though she dreaded the possible September heat amid all Bath’s white glare, and mourned the loss of the autumn months in the country, with all their gentle and melancholy influence, did not feel that, on the whole, she wished to stay."}

{"request_id":"e20f38c5dde280bde2ecc307","rewritten_text":"It should be said in the young lady’s favor that she did not plainly say she would not go. She only expressed an emphatic and earnest wish to be “blessed” if she did. This was a polite and delicate way of avoiding the request, showing that she possessed the natural good manners that cannot bear to cause another person the pain of a direct refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned from the young lady, who was dressed brightly, almost extravagantly, in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” said the Jew soothingly, “what do _you_ say?”

“That it won’t do, so there’s no use trying it on, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” asked Mr. Sikes, looking up angrily.

“What I say, Bill,” the woman answered calmly.

“Why, you’re exactly the person for it,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody around here knows anything about you.”

“And since I don’t want them to, either,” Nancy replied in the same calm voice, “it’s more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes was right. Through a mixture of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman was finally persuaded to accept the task. She was not held back by the same concerns as her agreeable friend. She had recently moved to the neighborhood of Field Lane from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, and therefore did not fear being recognized by her many acquaintances.

So, with a clean white apron tied over her gown and her curl-papers tucked beneath a straw bonnet—both supplied from the Jew’s endless stock—Miss Nancy prepared to set out on her errand.

“Wait a moment, my dear,” said the Jew, producing a small covered basket. “Carry that in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key to carry in the other, Fagin,” said Sikes. “It makes the whole thing look real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, so it does,” said the Jew, hanging a large street-door key from the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There! Very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears and twisting the little basket and street-door key in desperate distress. “What has happened to him? Where have they taken him? Oh, have pity, and tell me what they’ve done with the dear boy, gentlemen; please do, gentlemen, if you please!”"}

{"request_id":"f33d83ff90086d55a734c4af","rewritten_text":"“Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” said Joe.

“Is there another Miss Havisham down town?” my sister replied.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. And of course he’s going. He had better play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me to encourage me to be very light and playful, “or I’ll work him.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham up town—everyone for miles around had heard of her—as an extremely rich and grim woman who lived in a large, gloomy house protected against robbers and who lived in seclusion.

“Well, to be sure!” said Joe, amazed. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Fool!” cried my sister. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Someone,” Joe politely suggested again, “said that she wanted him to go and play there.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy who could go and play there? Isn’t it just possible that Uncle Pumblechook might be one of her tenants, and that he might sometimes—we won’t say quarterly or half-yearly, since that would demand too much of you—but sometimes—go there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy who could go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, always thoughtful and considerate toward us—though you may not think so, Joseph,” she added in a deeply reproachful tone, as if he were the most heartless of nephews, “then mention this boy, standing and Prancing here”—though I solemnly swear I was not—“to whom I have always been a willing slave?”

“Good again!” cried Uncle Pumblechook. “Well said! Nicely put! Very good! Now, Joseph, you understand the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” said my sister, still reproachful, while Joe apologetically rubbed the back of his hand again and again across his nose, “you do not yet—though you may not think so—understand the situation. You may believe that you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that, for all we know, this boy’s fortune may be made by his going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, keep him there tonight, and take him himself to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And mercy me!” cried my sister, suddenly throwing off her bonnet in despair, “here I am talking to mere Mooncalfs, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the mare is getting cold at the door, and the boy is covered in soot and dirt from the top of his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"6c7380bc17359e487a223b5d","rewritten_text":"This marriage is entirely right. I did not think so at first, but I admit it now. The gods made Sibyl Vane for you. Without her, you would have been incomplete.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, pressing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical that he frightens me. But here is the orchestra. It is dreadful, but it lasts only about five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you will see the girl to whom I am going to give my whole life, to whom I have given everything good in me.”

A quarter of an hour later, amid an extraordinary storm of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onto the stage. Yes, she was certainly beautiful—one of the loveliest creatures Lord Henry had ever seen. There was something fawnlike in her shy grace and startled eyes. A faint blush, like the shadow of a rose reflected in silver, touched her cheeks as she glanced at the crowded, enthusiastic audience. She stepped back a few paces, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat motionless, as if in a dream, gazing at her. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, murmuring, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of Capulet’s house, and Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, such as it was, played a few bars, and the dance began. Among the crowd of ungainly, shabbily dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a creature from a finer world. As she danced, her body swayed like a plant moving in water. The curves of her throat were the curves of a white lily. Her hands seemed made of cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely listless. She showed no joy when her eyes rested on Romeo. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

along with the brief dialogue that followed, were delivered in a thoroughly artificial manner. Her voice was exquisite, but its tone was completely false. Its color was wrong. It drained all life from the verse. It made the passion unreal.

Dorian Gray grew pale as he watched her. He was confused and anxious. Neither of his friends dared say anything to him. To them, she seemed utterly incompetent."}

{"request_id":"f7f804c5af89815d21ab3117","rewritten_text":"The day passed much as the previous one had. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent part of the morning with the invalid, who continued, though slowly, to recover; and in the evening Elizabeth joined them in the drawing room. The loo table did not appear, however. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley, seated beside him, watched his letter take shape and repeatedly interrupted him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was watching their game.

Elizabeth took up some needlework and was sufficiently entertained by what passed between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praise—of his handwriting, the evenness of his lines, or the length of his letter—together with the complete indifference with which he received it, made a curious dialogue and perfectly matched Elizabeth’s opinion of both.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!”

He did not answer.

“You write remarkably fast.”

“You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write over the course of a year! Business letters, too! How hateful I should find them!”

“Then it is fortunate that they fall to me rather than to you.”

“Please tell your sister that I long to see her.”

“I have already told her so once, at your request.”

“I am afraid you do not like your pen. Let me mend it for you. I mend pens extremely well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He remained silent.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her improvement on the harp, and please let her know that I am absolutely enchanted by her beautiful little design for a table. I think it infinitely better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to postpone your raptures until I write again? At present I have no room to do them justice.”

“Oh, it does not matter. I shall see her in January. But do you always write such charmingly long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are generally long; but whether they are always charming is not for me to decide.”

“It is my rule that anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write badly.”

“That will not serve as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” cried her brother, “because he does not write with ease. He thinks too carefully over four-syllable words. Do you not, Darcy?”

“My writing style is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless manner imaginable."}

content.text: {"request_id":"213176a496961e46ce566602","rewritten_text":"The storm raged violently throughout the night, but nothing noteworthy happened. The next morning, however, when they came down to breakfast, they found the dreadful bloodstain once again on the floor. “I don’t think the Paragon Detergent can be to blame,” said Washington, “because I’ve tried it on everything. It must be the ghost.” He therefore scrubbed away the stain a second time, but it reappeared the following morning. It was there on the third morning as well, although Mr. Otis himself had locked the library that night and taken the key upstairs. The entire family was now deeply interested; Mr. Otis began to suspect that he had been too absolute in denying the existence of ghosts, Mrs. Otis announced that she intended to join the Psychical Society, and Washington drafted a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore concerning the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains when Associated with Crime. That night, all doubt about the objective existence of phantoms was removed forever.\n\nThe day had been warm and sunny, and in the cool of the evening the whole family went out for a drive. They did not return until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. The conversation did not turn toward ghosts, so there were not even those basic conditions of receptive expectation that so often precede the appearance of psychic phenomena. The topics discussed, as I later learned from Mr. Otis, were simply the usual subjects of cultivated Americans of the better class: the enormous superiority of Miss Fanny Davenport to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of obtaining green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the finest English houses; the importance of Boston in the development of the world-soul; the advantages of the baggage-check system in railway travel; and the sweetness of the New York accent compared with the London drawl. The supernatural was not mentioned at all, nor was Sir Simon de Canterville referred to in any way. At eleven o’clock the family went to bed, and by half-past, all the lights were out. Some time later, Mr. Otis was awakened by a strange noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like metal clanking and seemed to draw nearer with every moment. He rose immediately, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He remained perfectly calm and felt his pulse, which was not at all feverish. The strange noise continued, and with it he clearly heard footsteps. He put on his slippers, took a small, oblong phial from his dressing case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"64d6598a468939b494b793a0","rewritten_text":"After I had sent them in, I could not stay away from the places where they were, and I felt that they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near. In this unreasonable restlessness and distress, I would wander the streets in the evening, passing the offices and houses where I had left the petitions. Even now, the tired western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their rows of stern, closed mansions and long lines of lamps, seem melancholy to me because of this connection.

The daily visits I was allowed to make him were shorter now, and he was watched more closely. Thinking, or imagining, that I was suspected of planning to bring him poison, I asked to be searched before sitting beside his bed. I told the officer who was always there that I was willing to do anything to prove that my intentions were sincere. No one was harsh with either of us. There was a duty to perform, and it was performed, but not cruelly. The officer always assured me that he was worse, and some of the other sick prisoners in the room, along with prisoners who cared for them as nurses—criminals, but thankfully not without kindness—always gave me the same report.

As the days passed, I noticed more and more that he would lie calmly staring at the white ceiling, with no light in his face until one of my words brightened it for a moment; then the light would fade again. Sometimes he was almost, or completely, unable to speak. Then he would answer me by gently pressing my hand, and I came to understand him very well.

The days had reached ten when I saw a greater change in him than ever before. His eyes were turned toward the door, and they brightened when I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said as I sat beside his bed, “I thought you was late. But I knowed you couldn’t be.”

“It is exactly the right time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So I won’t lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand in silence, for I could not forget that I had once intended to desert him.

“And the best thing of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable alonger me since I was under a dark cloud than when the sun shone.”"}

{"request_id":"85b9760f1885835b93daa0a7","rewritten_text":"She now felt strongly inclined to go to the outer door; she wished to see whether it rained. Why should she suspect herself of any other motive? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight. She rose from her seat and would go; one half of her should not always be so much wiser than the other, or forever suspecting the other of being worse than it was. She would see if it rained. In an instant, however, she was driven back by the entrance of Captain Wentworth himself, with a party of ladies and gentlemen, evidently his acquaintances, whom he must have joined a little below Milsom Street. The sight of her struck and confused him more plainly than she had ever seen before; he looked quite red. For the first time since their renewed acquaintance, she felt that she was betraying less sensibility than he. She had the advantage of him, having been prepared during the last few moments. All the overpowering, blinding, bewildering first effects of strong surprise had passed for her. Still, she had felt enough! It was agitation, pain, pleasure, something between delight and misery.

He spoke to her, then turned away. His manner was marked by embarrassment. She could not have called it cold or friendly, nor anything so definite as embarrassed.

After a brief interval, however, he approached her and spoke again. Mutual enquiries on ordinary subjects followed: neither of them, probably, much enlightened by what they heard, while Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than formerly. By having been so constantly together, they had learned to speak to each other with considerable apparent indifference and composure; but he could not do so now. Time had altered him, or Louisa had altered him. There was some kind of consciousness. He looked very well, not as though his health or spirits had suffered, and he spoke of Uppercross, the Musgroves, even of Louisa, with a momentary return of his own arch significance as he mentioned her; yet Captain Wentworth was not comfortable, not easy, and unable to pretend that he was.

It did not surprise Anne, but it grieved her, to see that Elizabeth would not acknowledge him. She saw that he saw Elizabeth, and that Elizabeth saw him; there was complete inward recognition on both sides. She was convinced that he was ready and expecting to be recognized as an acquaintance, and she suffered the pain of watching her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was becoming very impatient, now drew up; the servant entered to announce it."}

{"request_id":"8c134ee0174488e798aca7f4","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I said, “I think you could tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, _I_ don’t know. But he has to have one. All the nobility does.”

That was simply his way. If he didn’t feel like explaining something to you, he wouldn’t. You could question him for a week, and it wouldn’t make any difference.

He had finished all that coat-of-arms business, so now he began completing the rest of that part of the work, which was to plan a mournful inscription—Jim had to have one, just as they all did. He composed a lot of them, wrote them on a sheet of paper, and read them aloud:

1. _Here a captive heart broke._

2. _Here a poor prisoner, forsaken by the world and friends, wore out his sorrowful life._

3. _Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity._

4. _Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice trembled as he read them, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he couldn’t decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall, because they were all so good; but finally he said he would let him scratch them all on. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch so much writing onto the logs with a nail, and besides, he didn’t know how to form letters; but Tom said he would outline them for him, and then Jim would only have to follow the lines. Then, after a moment, he said:

“Come to think of it, the logs won’t do. They don’t have log walls in a dungeon; we have to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll bring in a rock.”

Jim said the rock would be worse than the logs; he said it would take him such an awfully long time to carve them into a rock that he would never get out. But Tom said he would let me help him. Then he looked over to see how Jim and I were doing with the pens. It was terribly tedious, difficult, slow work, gave my hands no chance to heal from the sores, and we hardly seemed to be making any progress; so Tom said:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"2de87c81a22650af8daa96ce","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were delighted to see their dear friend again, declared that it had been ages since they had met, and repeatedly asked what she had been doing since they parted. They paid little attention to the rest of the family: avoiding Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, saying little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. They soon left, rising with such energy that their brother was surprised, and hurrying away as though eager to escape Mrs. Bennet’s polite attentions.

The prospect of the Netherfield ball was extremely pleasing to every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to regard it as a compliment to her eldest daughter, and was especially flattered to receive the invitation from Mr. Bingley himself rather than a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening in the company of her two friends and their brother’s attentions; Elizabeth looked forward to dancing often with Mr. Wickham and seeing confirmation of everything in Mr. Darcy’s expression and conduct. Catherine and Lydia’s anticipated happiness depended less on any one event or particular person; for although each of them, like Elizabeth, intended to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was far from the only partner who could satisfy them, and a ball was, in any case, a ball. Even Mary could assure her family that she had no objection to it.

“As long as I can have my mornings to myself,” she said, “that is sufficient. I do not think it a sacrifice to take part occasionally in evening engagements. Society makes demands upon us all; and I consider intervals of recreation and amusement desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so high that, although she did not often speak unnecessarily to Mr. Collins, she could not help asking whether he intended to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation and, if so, whether he thought it proper to join in the evening’s amusement. She was rather surprised to discover that he had no hesitation on that point and was far from fearing a reprimand, either from the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh, for venturing to dance.

“I am certainly not of the opinion,” he said, “that a ball of this kind, given by a young man of good character for respectable people, can have any harmful tendency; and I am so far from objecting to dancing myself that I hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins during the evening. I take this opportunity of requesting yours, Miss Elizabeth, especially for the first two dances—a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to its proper cause, and not to any disrespect toward her.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cb84c76ee96fd27bb9353a42","rewritten_text":"Weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something new happened. I had drawn you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis wearing a huntsman’s cloak and carrying a polished boar spear. Crowned with heavy lotus blossoms, you had sat on the prow of Adrian’s barge, gazing across the green, muddy Nile. You had leaned over the still pool of some Greek woodland and seen in its silent silver the wonder of your own face. And it had all been what art should be—unconscious, ideal, and distant. One day, a fatal day, I sometimes think, I decided to paint a magnificent portrait of you as you truly are, not in the costume of vanished ages, but in your own clothes and your own time. Whether it was the realism of the method, or simply the force of your personality, presented to me so directly, without mist or veil, I cannot say. But I know that as I worked, every flake and film of color seemed to reveal my secret. I became afraid that others would discover my idolatry. I felt, Dorian, that I had said too much, that I had put too much of myself into it. Then I resolved never to let the picture be exhibited. You were somewhat annoyed, but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, whom I spoke to about it, laughed at me. But I did not care. When the picture was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt that I had been right.... Well, after a few days it left my studio, and once I had escaped the unbearable fascination of its presence, I thought I had been foolish to imagine I had seen anything in it beyond the fact that you were extraordinarily handsome and that I could paint. Even now I cannot help thinking it is a mistake to believe that the passion felt in creation is ever truly visible in the work created. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and color tell us of form and color—that is all. It often seems to me that art conceals the artist far more completely than it reveals him. And so, when I received this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the central work in my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The picture cannot be shown. You must not be angry with me, Dorian, for telling you this."}

{"request_id":"d816c54f023906389604deca","rewritten_text":"There was a pleasant feeling in our village on Saturday nights: everything seemed to be tidied up, and there was a quiet pause before beginning life again. This encouraged Joe to stay out half an hour later on Saturdays than at other times. When the half-hour ended and the rum and water ran out together, Joe stood up to leave and took me by the hand.

“Wait half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I have a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if I do, the boy shall have it.”

He found it among a handful of small coins, wrapped it in some crumpled paper, and gave it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Mind! It’s your own.”

I thanked him, staring at him much longer than good manners allowed and holding tightly to Joe. He said good-night to Joe and to Mr. Wopsle, who left with us. To me he gave only a look with his aiming eye—or rather, not a look, since he closed it. Still, strange things can be done with an eye by hiding it.

On the way home, if I had felt like talking, I would have done all the talking, because Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen. Joe walked the whole way home with his mouth wide open, trying to rinse the rum out with as much air as possible. But I was almost stunned by the return of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

My sister was not in a very bad mood when we entered the kitchen, and Joe took advantage of this unusual event to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll be bound,” said Mrs. Joe triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.”

I took it from the paper, and it turned out to be genuine. “But what’s this?” said Mrs. Joe, dropping the shilling and picking up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

They were two large, sweaty one-pound notes that seemed to have spent a great deal of time among all the cattle markets in the county. Joe immediately grabbed his hat and ran back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, fairly sure that the man would not be there.

After a while, Joe returned and said the man had gone, but that he had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"72b06a25ea70f49639050653","rewritten_text":"Biddy wept; the garden growing dark, the lane, and the emerging stars all swam before my eyes.

“Was nothing ever found out, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what has become of Orlick?”

“Judging by the colour of his clothes, I should say he is working in the quarries.”

“Then you have seen him, of course?—Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there on the night she died.”

“That was not the last time, Biddy?”

“No; I have seen him there since we began walking here.—There is no use,” said Biddy, putting her hand on my arm as I was about to rush out, “you know I would not deceive you; he was there less than a minute, and then he was gone.”

My indignation was renewed by discovering that this man still haunted her, and I felt an enduring hatred for him. I told her so, and said I would spend whatever money or endure whatever trouble was necessary to drive him from that country. Gradually she drew me into calmer conversation, and told me how Joe loved me, and how Joe never complained of anything—not, she did not say, of me; there was no need, for I understood her meaning—but always performed his duty in his station, with a firm hand, a quiet tongue, and a tender heart.

“Indeed, it would be difficult to say too much in his praise,” I said; “and Biddy, we must often talk of these matters, since naturally I shall be coming down here frequently now. I am not going to leave poor Joe by himself.”

Biddy did not say a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Leaving aside your calling me Mr. Pip—which seems to me in poor taste, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, with a self-righteous air of assertion, “I must ask you to explain what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Now, don’t repeat my words,” I answered. “You never used to echo, Biddy.”

“Never used to!” said Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Never used to!”

Well, I rather thought I would abandon that point as well. After another quiet circuit of the garden, I returned to my principal argument.

“Biddy,” I said, “I remarked that I intended to come down here often to see Joe, and you answered with conspicuous silence. Be so good, Biddy, as to tell me why.”

“Are you quite certain, then, that you WILL come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping on the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with a frank and truthful eye."}

{"request_id":"905df9b799cd399e84d8b7c1","rewritten_text":"A little after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from an absent citizen and set off immediately. When they were several miles below “Cave Hollow,” Tom said:

“Now you can see this bluff looks the same all the way down from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood-yards, and bushes everywhere alike. But do you see that white spot up there where there’s been a landslide? Well, that’s one of my marks. We’ll go ashore now.”

They landed.

“Now, Huck, from where we’re standing you could touch the hole I escaped from with a fishing-pole. See if you can find it.”

Huck searched all around, but discovered nothing. Tom proudly pushed into a thick patch of sumach bushes and said:

“Here it is! Look at it, Huck; it’s the snugest hole in the country. You just keep quiet about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I’d need a place like this, and finding one was the trouble. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers join—because naturally there has to be a Gang, or there wouldn’t be any style to it. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds splendid, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“Well, it certainly does, Tom. And who will we rob?”

“Oh, nearly anybody. Waylay people—that’s generally how it’s done.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not always. Keep them in the cave until they raise a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them get all they can from their friends; and after you’ve held them a year, if it still hasn’t been raised, then you kill them. That’s the usual way. Only you don’t kill the women. You lock up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich, and terribly frightened. You take their watches and things, but you always remove your hat and speak politely. Nobody is as polite as robbers—you’ll find that in every book. Then the women fall in love with you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two, they stop crying, and afterward you couldn’t make them leave. If you forced them out, they’d turn around and come back. That’s how it is in all the books.”

“Why, it’s really splendid, Tom. I believe it’s better than being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s near home and circuses and everything.”

By then everything was prepared, and the boys entered the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, secured their spliced kite-strings, and continued on."}

{"request_id":"218f89ebca26e38f72e65506","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in astonishment for several moments. Then, seeing that he was entirely serious, he wrote an address on a sheet of paper, initialled it, and passed it across the table.

‘Scotland Yard would pay a great deal to know this address, my dear fellow.’

‘They won’t get it,’ cried Lord Arthur, laughing. After warmly shaking the young Russian’s hand, he ran downstairs, looked at the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square.

There he dismissed him and wandered down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court. He went beneath the archway and found himself in a strange cul-de-sac, apparently occupied by a French laundry: an elaborate web of clothes-lines stretched from house to house, and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked to the very end and knocked at a small green house. After some delay, during which every window in the court filled with blurred, watching faces, the door was opened by a rather rough-looking foreigner, who asked him in very poor English what he wanted. Lord Arthur handed him the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. On seeing it, the man bowed and ushered Lord Arthur into a shabby front parlour on the ground floor. A few moments later Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in, a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

‘Count Rouvaloff has given me a letter of introduction to you,’ said Lord Arthur, bowing. ‘I would like a brief interview concerning a business matter. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I want you to provide me with an explosive clock.’

‘Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,’ said the cheerful little German, laughing. ‘Please don’t look so alarmed. It is my duty to know everyone, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope her ladyship is quite well. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish breakfast? There is an excellent pâté, and my friends are kind enough to say that my Rhine wine is better than anything served at the German Embassy.’ Before Lord Arthur had recovered from his surprise at being recognised, he found himself seated in the back room, sipping the most delicious Marcobrünner from a pale-yellow Hock glass bearing the Imperial monogram, and chatting as amicably as possible with the famous conspirator.

‘Explosive clocks,’ said Herr Winckelkopf, ‘are not very suitable for export abroad. Even when they manage to pass through Customs, the train service is so unreliable that they generally go off before reaching their intended destination.’"}

{"request_id":"acd482270140e171f4d840b8","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and courtyards finally opened into a large space. Pens for animals and other signs of a cattle market stood scattered around it. Sikes slowed when they reached the place, because the girl could no longer keep up the fast pace they had maintained. Turning to Oliver, he roughly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“Do you hear?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and looked around.

They stood in a dark corner, well away from the path used by passers-by.

Oliver saw clearly that resisting would do no good. He held out his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly.

“Give me the other,” said Sikes, taking Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog looked up and growled.

“Listen, boy!” said Sikes, placing his other hand around Oliver’s throat. “If he says even the softest word, hold him! Do you understand?”

The dog growled again. Licking his lips, he watched Oliver as though eager to fasten onto his throat at once.

“He’s as willing as a Christian, I swear he is!” said Sikes, looking at the animal with grim, fierce approval. “Now you know what to expect, master, so call out as quickly as you like; the dog will soon stop you. Move on, boy!”

Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail as if pleased by this unusually affectionate speech. Then, giving Oliver another warning growl, he led the way forward.

They were crossing Smithfield, though Oliver might have thought it was Grosvenor Square, for all he knew. The night was dark and foggy. The shop lights could barely shine through the thick mist, which grew heavier by the moment and covered the streets and houses in gloom. The strange place seemed even stranger to Oliver, and his uncertainty became more miserable and depressing.

They had gone only a few hurried steps when a deep church bell struck the hour. At its first stroke, both his guides stopped and turned toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” said Nancy when the bell stopped.

“What’s the point of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes replied.

“I wonder whether they can hear it,” said Nancy.

“Of course they can,” Sikes answered. “It was fair time when I was locked up, and there wasn’t a penny trumpet at the fair whose squeaking I couldn’t hear. After they shut me in for the night, the noise outside made that huge old jail so quiet that I could almost have smashed my brains against the iron door.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"37b3206aff759f9352822726","rewritten_text":"In my time, in my own country, this money was raised through duties, and the citizen imagined that the foreign importer paid them; it comforted him to think so. In reality, the American people paid them, distributed so evenly and precisely among everyone that the annual cost to the multimillionaire and the annual cost to the day laborer’s nursing infant were exactly the same—each paid six dollars. Nothing could be fairer than that, I suppose. Scotland and Ireland were tributary to Arthur, and the combined population of the British Isles was somewhat under a million. A mechanic’s average wage was three cents a day when he paid for his own keep. By this calculation, the national government’s expenses came to ninety thousand dollars a year, or about two hundred and fifty dollars a day. Thus, by replacing gold with nickels on a king’s-evil day, I not only harmed no one and displeased no one, but pleased everyone involved and saved four-fifths of that day’s national expense as well—a saving equivalent to eight hundred thousand dollars in my time in America. In making this substitution, I had drawn on wisdom from a very distant source—my boyhood—for a true statesman despises no wisdom, however humble its origin. As a boy, I had always saved my pennies and contributed buttons to the foreign missionary cause. Buttons would serve the ignorant savage as well as coins, while coins would serve me better than buttons; everyone was satisfied and no one was harmed.\n\nMarinel received the patients as they arrived. He examined each candidate; if the person failed to qualify, he was turned away; if he qualified, he was sent on to the king. A priest recited the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king stroked the ulcers while the reading continued. At last, the patient completed the ceremony and received his nickel—the king himself hanging it around his neck—and was dismissed. Would you believe that this could cure anyone? It certainly did. Any ritual will cure if the patient’s faith in it is strong enough. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who used to herd geese there—the girl said so herself. They built the chapel on that spot and hung inside it a picture depicting the event, a picture you might think dangerous for a sick person even to approach. Yet thousands of the lame and sick came to pray before it every year and went away healed and sound; even the healthy could look upon it and live."}

{"request_id":"762e8ce874665fc86e2add1e","rewritten_text":"It was the start of February; and Anne, who had been a month in Bath, was becoming very impatient for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wished to hear far more than Mary had told her. It was three weeks since she had received any news at all. She knew only that Henrietta had returned home; and that Louisa, though thought to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. She was thinking of them all very earnestly one evening, when a letter from Mary, thicker than usual, was brought to her; and, to increase the pleasure and surprise, it came with Admiral and Mrs Croft’s compliments.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was an interesting circumstance. They were people toward whom her heart naturally turned.

“What is this?” cried Sir Walter. “The Crofts have arrived in Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they sent you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.”

“Oh! Such letters are useful passports. They obtain an introduction. I should have called on Admiral Croft in any case. I know what is owed to my tenant.”

Anne could listen no longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion escaped notice; her letter had completely absorbed her. It had been started several days before.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

I offer no excuse for my silence, because I know how little people care for letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to concern yourself with Uppercross, which, as you know very well, gives one little to write about. We have had a very dull Christmas; Mr and Mrs Musgrove have not held a single dinner party throughout the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anybody. The holidays are finally over: I believe no children ever had such a long one. I am certain I never did. The house was emptied yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear that they have not gone home. Mrs Harville must be a strange mother to keep them away so long. I cannot understand it. They are not at all agreeable children, in my opinion; yet Mrs Musgrove appears to like them quite as much, if not more, than her grandchildren. What terrible weather we have had! It may not matter in Bath, with your excellent pavements; but in the country it is a serious concern. No one has called on me since the second week of January, except Charles Hayter, who had been coming much more often than was welcome. Between ourselves, I think it a great pity Henrietta did not stay in Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her somewhat out of his way."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7601553324471608ba102c75","rewritten_text":"Dawn had come when I set the Manuscript aside. The rain had nearly stopped. The world was gray and sorrowful, and the spent storm sighed and sobbed as it settled into rest. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his slightly open door. I could hear his voice, so I knocked. There was no answer, though the voice continued. I looked inside. The man lay on his back in bed, speaking in broken phrases but with energy, waving his arms restlessly as sick people do in delirium. I slipped in quietly and leaned over him. His muttering and cries continued. I spoke—only a word, to get his attention. At once, his glassy eyes and ashen face brightened with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome:\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you have come at last—how I have longed for you! Sit beside me—do not leave me—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand? Give it to me, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is well, everything is peaceful, and I am happy again—we are happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You are so dim, so unclear, only a mist, a cloud, but you are here, and that is blessing enough; and I have your hand. Do not take it away—it will be only for a little while. I shall not need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello, Central!... She does not answer. Perhaps she is asleep? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say good-bye.... Sandy! Yes, you are there. I lost myself for a moment and thought you were gone.... Have I been ill long? It must be so; it seems like months to me. And such dreams! Such strange and terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality—delirium, of course, but so real! Why, I thought the king was dead. I thought you were in Gaul and could not get home. I thought there had been a revolution. In the wild madness of those dreams, I thought Clarence and I and a handful of my cadets fought and destroyed all the chivalry of England! But even that was not the strangest thing. I seemed to be a creature from a distant age that had not yet been born, centuries in the future, and even that seemed as real as everything else! Yes, I seemed to have flown back from that age into our own, then forward to it again, and to have been left, a stranger and alone, in that strange England, with an abyss of thirteen centuries opening between you and me! Between me and my home and my friends! Between me and everything dear to me, everything that could make life worth living!”"}

{"request_id":"e66dfc31d47cb3fd55d8eb17","rewritten_text":"“But when I saw you become the object of another man’s love; when I imagined that you might be loved in any way other than as a sacred type and image of beauty and excellence; or that you might love another more ardently than you loved me, then the fiend awoke within me. I sent your lover away, and from that moment I have known no peace. In vain I sought sleep and rest; my eyes would not close, and my blood was perpetually in turmoil. I awoke to a new existence as one who dies in hope might awaken in Hell. I will not stain your imagination by describing my struggles, my anger against myself, and my despair. Let a veil cover the unimaginable sensations of a guilty father; the secrets of a heart so tortured must not be made common. All was tumult, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet still the most tender love; and what first roused me to the firm determination of mastering my passion and restoring her father to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic grief. This brought me here: I thought that if I could awaken once more in my heart the sorrow I had felt at your mother’s death, together with the many memories connected with her which had slept for seventeen years, then all love for her child would die away. In a moment of heroism I resolved to go alone; to leave you, the life of my life, and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it was impossible: I had overestimated my strength, or undervalued my love. I should surely have died had you not hastened to me. Would that I had truly been extinguished!

“And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I have been wretchedly deceived in thinking that I could conquer my love for you; I never shall. The sight of this house, these fields, and woods, which my first love once inhabited, seems only to have increased it. In my madness I dared tell myself—Diana died to give you birth; her mother’s spirit passed into your body, and you ought to be Diana to me. With every attempt to cast it away, this love fastens itself more tightly, this guilty love, more unnatural than hatred, which withers your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better have loved despair, & safer kissed her.

No time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since arriving here I have not for one instant ceased to feel the hell of passion implanted within me, burning until everything is cold, rigid, and dead.”"}

{"request_id":"b68defb299d29519e6a5385c","rewritten_text":"“What is it?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honour told me to wake you.”

“Oh! I remember. Very well, very well.”

After several dull attempts to fall asleep again—which the man skillfully thwarted by constantly stirring the fire for five minutes—he got up, put on his hat, and went out. He turned into the Temple and, having revived himself by walking twice along the pavements of King’s Bench Walk and Paper Buildings, turned into Stryver’s chambers.

The Stryver clerk, who never took part in these conferences, had gone home, and Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing gown, and his throat was bare for greater comfort. Around his eyes was that somewhat wild, strained, weathered look seen in all hard drinkers of his kind, from the portrait of Jeffries onward, and traceable, beneath various artistic disguises, through the portraits of every age of drinking.

“You are a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time; perhaps a quarter of an hour later.”

They entered a dingy room lined with books and covered with papers, where a fire blazed. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the disorder of papers a table gleamed, set with plenty of wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

“You have had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I was dining with the day’s client—or watching him dine; it amounts to the same thing!”

“That was an excellent point, Sydney, the one you used to establish the identification. How did you think of it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was rather a handsome fellow, and I thought I would have been much the same sort of fellow if I had had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his prematurely developed belly shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

The jackal, sullen enough, loosened his clothes, went into an adjoining room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. He soaked the towels in the water, partly wrung them out, folded them around his head in a hideous fashion, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down to do tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, as he looked through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“There they are, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion then settled himself on his back on a sofa at one side of the drinking table, while the jackal sat at his own proper, paper-covered table on the other side, with the bottles and glasses within easy reach."}

content.text: {"request_id":"52b32ff07cf6bd1d3e4ca292","rewritten_text":"The storm raged fiercely all night, but nothing unusual happened. The next morning, however, when they came down to breakfast, they found the terrible bloodstain once again on the floor. “I don’t think the Paragon Detergent is to blame,” said Washington, “because I’ve tried it on everything. It must be the ghost.” He rubbed out the stain again, but it returned the following morning. It was there on the third morning too, although Mr. Otis himself had locked the library that night and taken the key upstairs. The whole family was now very interested. Mr. Otis began to suspect that he had been too certain in denying the existence of ghosts, Mrs. Otis said she intended to join the Psychical Society, and Washington prepared a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the Permanence of Bloodstains Connected with Crime. That night, all doubt about the ghost’s real existence disappeared forever.\n\nThe day had been warm and sunny, and in the cool evening the whole family went out for a drive. They did not return until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. Their conversation did not turn to ghosts, so there were not even the basic conditions of expectant belief that so often come before psychic phenomena. As I later learned from Mr. Otis, they discussed only the usual subjects of cultured, upper-class Americans: the great superiority of Miss Fanny Davenport to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of getting green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy, even in the finest English houses; Boston’s importance in developing the world-soul; the benefits of the railway baggage-check system; and the sweetness of the New York accent compared with the London drawl. They did not mention the supernatural at all, nor did they refer to Sir Simon de Canterville. At eleven o’clock the family went to bed, and by half-past eleven all the lights were out. Some time later, Mr. Otis woke to a strange noise in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like metal clanking and seemed to come closer every moment. He got up immediately, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He was perfectly calm and felt his pulse, which was not at all feverish. The strange noise continued, and he could clearly hear footsteps with it. He put on his slippers, took a small, oblong bottle from his dressing case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"6f609b187cacbade0c321317","rewritten_text":"Reading over his letter again while replying to it had such a softening effect that Emma found it especially necessary to strengthen Harriet with a few firm words. Harriet was so troubled by the thought of making him unhappy, cared so much about what his mother and sisters would think and say, and was so anxious that they should not consider her ungrateful, that Emma believed the young man would have been accepted after all if he had appeared before her at that moment.

The letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She was rather downcast all evening, but Emma understood her kind-hearted regret. At times she eased it by speaking of her own affection, and at others by mentioning Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” Harriet said sadly.

“And even if you were, I could never bear to part with you, my Harriet. You are far too necessary at Hartfield to be spared to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I am sure I should never want to go there; I am never happy anywhere but at Hartfield.”

Some time later, Harriet said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. I am sure Miss Nash would be—for Miss Nash thinks her own sister very well married, and she is only married to a linen-draper.”

“One ought to be sorry to see greater pride or refinement in a schoolteacher, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you such a chance to marry. Even this achievement would seem valuable to her. As for anything better for you, I suppose she has no idea of it. The attentions of a certain person can hardly yet be part of Highbury gossip. So far, I believe you and I are the only people who have understood his looks and manners.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, and said something about being surprised that people should like her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton certainly cheered her; but after a while she again felt tenderly toward the rejected Mr. Martin.

“Now he has received my letter,” she said softly. “I wonder what they are all doing—whether his sisters know. If he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he will not take it too badly.”

“Let us think of those absent friends who are more happily occupied,” cried Emma. “At this moment, perhaps, Mr. Elton is showing your picture to his mother and sisters, telling them how much more beautiful the original is, and, after they have asked for it five or six times, allowing them to hear your name—your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"8cd295bfdf37f60891481bbc","rewritten_text":"“I now come quickly to the most moving part of my story. I shall describe events that filled me with feelings which, changing me from what I had been, made me what I am.

“Spring came on quickly; the weather grew pleasant, and the skies were clear. I was amazed that the land which had once seemed barren and gloomy could now be covered with beautiful flowers and green plants. My senses were delighted and refreshed by countless pleasant scents and lovely sights.

“It was on one of these days, when my cottagers were taking their regular rest from work—the old man playing his guitar while the children listened—that I noticed Felix looked deeply sad. He sighed often. Once, his father stopped playing, and from his manner I guessed that he asked his son why he was unhappy. Felix answered cheerfully, and the old man was beginning to play again when someone knocked at the door.

“It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman acting as her guide. She wore a dark riding suit and a thick black veil. Agatha asked her a question, but the stranger answered only by saying, in a sweet voice, the name Felix. Her voice was musical, but unlike either of my friends’ voices. At hearing his name, Felix hurried toward her. When she saw him, she lifted her veil, and I saw a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was shining raven-black and carefully braided; her eyes were dark but gentle and lively; her features were perfectly formed, and her remarkably fair complexion was touched with a lovely pink in each cheek.

“Felix seemed overwhelmed with joy when he saw her. All his sadness disappeared, and his face immediately showed such ecstatic happiness that I could hardly believe it possible. His eyes sparkled, and pleasure colored his cheeks. At that moment, I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed moved by other feelings; wiping a few tears from her lovely eyes, she held out her hand to Felix. He kissed it eagerly and called her, as far as I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him, but smiled. He helped her dismount and, sending away her guide, led her into the cottage. He spoke for a while with his father, and the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet and tried to kiss his hand. He lifted her up and embraced her warmly.

“I soon realized that although the stranger made clear sounds and seemed to have a language of her own, neither she nor the cottagers understood one another.”"}

{"request_id":"ded9c817ab34743d13cc6ec3","rewritten_text":"“Shall I ask them? Or Miss Bates? She is closer by.—And I am not sure that Miss Bates may not understand everyone’s wishes as well as anyone. I think we need a larger council. Suppose I go and invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you like,” said Mrs. Weston, hesitating a little, “if you think she will be useful.”

“You will get nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and thanks, but she will tell you nothing. She will not even listen to your questions. I see no benefit in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so entertaining, so very entertaining! I am very fond of hearing Miss Bates talk. And I need not bring the whole family, you know.”

Mr. Weston now joined them, and when he heard the proposal, gave it his firm approval.

“Yes, do, Frank.—Go and fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle the matter at once. She will enjoy the plan, I am sure; and I do not know a better person to show us how to overcome difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming a little too particular. She is a constant lesson in how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady—?”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I did not remember at once. Certainly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And away he ran.

Long before he returned with the short, neat, quick-moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston, being a kind-hearted woman and a good wife, had looked over the passage again and found its problems much less serious than she had first thought—indeed, very slight. With that, the decision was made. Everything else, at least in theory, was perfectly easy. The smaller arrangements of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper, seemed to arrange themselves; or could be left as minor matters to settle later between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes.—Everyone invited was certainly coming; Frank had already written to Enscombe asking to stay a few days beyond his fortnight, and this could not possibly be refused. It was to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed most warmly that it must be. She was not needed as an adviser; but as an approver, a much safer role, she was very welcome. Her approval, both general and detailed, warm and endless, could not fail to please; and for another half-hour they all walked back and forth between the different rooms, some making suggestions, some listening, and everyone happily enjoying the plans for the future."}
