{"request_id":"c973f819bbaba26655dae4d5","rewritten_text":"Yet despite all this, the boy became increasingly melancholy, pale, and dejected. She added hot baths, sitz baths, shower baths, and plunges. The boy stayed as gloomy as a hearse. She began supporting the water treatment with a thin oatmeal diet and blister-plasters. She reckoned his capacity as she might a jug’s, and filled him daily with patent cure-alls.

By this time Tom had grown indifferent to persecution. This stage filled the old lady’s heart with alarm. That indifference had to be broken at any cost. Then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a large supply immediately. She tasted it and felt profoundly grateful. It was nothing less than fire in liquid form. She abandoned the water treatment and everything else, placing all her faith in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched anxiously for the effect. Her troubles vanished at once, and her soul was peaceful again, because the “indifference” had been shattered. The boy could not have displayed a livelier, heartier interest if she had set a fire beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to wake up; this kind of existence might be romantic enough in his ruined condition, but it was acquiring too little sentiment and too much distracting variety. He considered several ways of obtaining relief, and at last settled on pretending to be fond of Pain-killer. He requested it so frequently that he became a nuisance, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop troubling her. Had it been Sid, she would have enjoyed the matter without a doubt; but because it was Tom, she secretly kept watch on the bottle. She saw that the medicine truly was being used up, but never suspected that the boy was repairing a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One day Tom was dosing the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat approached, purring, eyeing the teaspoon greedily, and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter made it clear that he did want it.

“You’d better be certain.”

Peter was certain.

“Now that you’ve asked for it, I’ll give it to you, because there’s nothing mean about me; but if you discover you don’t like it, you must blame nobody but yourself.”

Peter agreed. So Tom pried open his mouth and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped a couple of yards into the air, then gave a war-whoop and raced around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flower-pots, and creating general havoc."}

{"request_id":"36afbc4f3bb90b12c8a69bb2","rewritten_text":"“Nothing but a tick.”

“Where did you get it?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What will you take for it?”

“I don’t know. I don’t want to sell it.”

“All right. It’s a very small tick, anyway.”

“Oh, anyone can catch a tick that doesn’t belong to them. I’m satisfied with this one. It’s good enough for me.”

“Sure, there are plenty of ticks. I could have a thousand if I wanted them.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know perfectly well you can’t. This is an early tick, I reckon. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for it.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom took out a piece of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry looked at it longingly. The temptation was very strong. At last he said:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the empty space.

“Well, all right,” said Huckleberry, “it’s a trade.”

Tom put the tick into the percussion-cap box that had recently been the pinchbug’s prison, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom reached the small, isolated frame schoolhouse, he walked in briskly, looking like someone who had hurried there as fast as he could. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike speed. The master, sitting high in his large splint-bottom armchair, had been dozing to the sleepy hum of study. The interruption woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew that hearing his full name meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to hide behind a lie when he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized through the powerful sympathy of love. Beside that figure was the only empty place on the girls’ side of the schoolhouse. He immediately said:

“_I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!_”

The master’s pulse seemed to stop, and he stared helplessly. The hum of study ended. The pupils wondered whether this reckless boy had lost his mind. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no misunderstanding the words.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astonishing confession I have ever heard. A simple whipping will not be enough for this offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm kept moving until it was tired, and the supply of switches had been greatly reduced. Then came the order:

“Now, sir, go and sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.”

The laughter that moved around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth he was affected more by his deep awe of his unknown idol and by the thrilling pleasure of his great good fortune."}

{"request_id":"f52d6859577b4748ee79745b","rewritten_text":"Those old and feeble men were always seen by the public bowing, and people commonly believed that after bowing one customer out, they continued bowing in the empty office until they bowed another customer in.

The barrister was perceptive enough to understand that the banker would not have expressed such a strong opinion without something close to moral certainty behind it. Though unprepared for the large pill he had to swallow, he forced it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, shaking his lawyerly forefinger at the Temple in general once he had done so, “my way out of this is to prove that you are all in the wrong.”

This was a piece of Old Bailey courtroom strategy, and it brought him great relief. “You shall not prove me wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver. “I’ll do that for you.”

So, when Mr. Lorry called that night at ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver appeared, amid books and papers spread out for the purpose, to have nothing on his mind but the morning’s subject. He even seemed surprised to see Mr. Lorry and was completely absent-minded and preoccupied.

“Well!” said the good-natured messenger, after half an hour of unsuccessful attempts to bring him back to the matter. “I have been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” Mr. Stryver repeated coldly. “Oh, of course! What was I thinking?”

“And I have no doubt,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was right in our conversation. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” replied Mr. Stryver in the friendliest manner, “that I am sorry for it on your account, and on the poor father’s account. I know this must always be a painful subject for the family; let us say no more about it.”

“I don’t understand you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I dare say you don’t,” Stryver replied, nodding in a calming, final way. “Never mind, never mind.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No, it doesn’t; I assure you it doesn’t. I had imagined there was good sense where there is none, and worthy ambition where there is none. I am glad to have discovered my mistake, and no harm has been done. Young women have made similar foolish choices before, and have often regretted them in poverty and obscurity. From an unselfish point of view, I am sorry the matter has been abandoned, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms; from a selfish point of view, I am glad it has been abandoned, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms—it is hardly necessary to say that I could have gained nothing from it."}

{"request_id":"17a6188b8b0633a7991daef4","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton halted in the street, still uncertain where to go. “At Tellson’s banking-house at nine,” he said thoughtfully. “Would it be wise, meanwhile, to show myself? I think so. It is best that these people should know there is such a man as I here; it is a prudent precaution, and may be a needful preparation. But care, care, care! Let me reason it out!”

Checking the steps that had begun to carry him towards a purpose, he turned once or twice through the street, now growing dark, and followed the thought in his mind to its possible results. His first impression was strengthened. “It is best,” he said at last, having made up his mind, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” And he turned towards Saint Antoine.

Defarge had that day described himself as the keeper of a wine-shop in the suburb of Saint Antoine. Anyone well acquainted with the city could find his house without making inquiries. Having learned where it stood, Carton came out again from the narrower streets, dined at a place of refreshment, and fell into a deep sleep after dinner. For the first time in many years, he took no strong drink. Since the previous night he had consumed nothing but a little light, thin wine, and on that night he had let the brandy trickle slowly onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth, like a man who had finished with it.

It was as late as seven o’clock when he awoke refreshed and went out once more into the streets. As he proceeded towards Saint Antoine, he paused at a shop-window containing a mirror, and slightly rearranged his loose cravat, his coat-collar, and his wild hair. This done, he went straight to Defarge’s and entered.

There was, by chance, no customer in the shop except Jacques Three, with the restless fingers and croaking voice. This man, whom he had seen on the Jury, stood drinking at the little counter and talking with the Defarges, husband and wife. The Vengeance joined in the conversation like a regular member of the establishment.

When Carton came in, sat down, and asked, in very indifferent French, for a small measure of wine, Madame Defarge gave him a careless glance, then a sharper one, and then another sharper still, before approaching him herself to ask what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” asked Madame Defarge, raising her dark eyebrows with curiosity.

After looking at her as though even the sound of a single French word took time to reach him, he replied in the same pronounced foreign accent."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e68a2d04c2bab211d68b2b20","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the dead man's luxury was astonishing.\n\nThen he turned his attention to embroidery and to the tapestries that served as frescoes in the cold rooms of northern Europe. As he studied the subject—and he always possessed an extraordinary ability to become completely absorbed, for the moment, in whatever he undertook—he was almost saddened by the thought of the ruin time brought upon beautiful and marvelous things. He, at least, had escaped that fate. Summer followed summer, the yellow jonquils bloomed and died many times, and nights of horror repeated the story of their shame, but he remained unchanged. No winter damaged his face or dulled his flowerlike bloom. How different it was with material things! Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe, on which the gods battled the giants, woven by brown girls for Athena's pleasure? Where was the enormous velarium Nero had stretched across Rome's Colosseum, that purple Titan's sail depicting the starry sky, with Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white horses with gilded reins? He longed to see the curious table napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, displaying every delicacy and dish that might be desired at a feast; the funeral cloth of King Chilperic, with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastic robes that outraged the Bishop of Pontus and were decorated with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—all, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, whose sleeves bore the verses of a song beginning “_Madame, je suis tout joyeux_,” with the words' musical accompaniment worked in gold thread, each note—square-shaped in those days—formed from four pearls. He read about the room prepared at the palace in Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in embroidery and emblazoned with the king's arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings were similarly ornamented with the queen's arms, the whole worked in gold.” Catherine de Medici had a mourning bed made of black velvet scattered with crescents and suns. Its damask curtains bore leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold-and-silver ground and were edged with pearl embroidery; it stood in a room hung with rows of the queen's devices, cut from black velvet and set against cloth of silver. Louis XIV had gold-embroidered caryatids fifteen feet high in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"1ec2ada581728ccae717ed6c","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how mysterious they were! The soul contained something animal, while the body had moments of spirituality. The senses could become refined, and the intellect could deteriorate. Who could say where the physical impulse ended, or the psychological impulse began? How shallow were the arbitrary definitions of ordinary psychologists! And yet how difficult it was to choose between the claims of the various schools! Was the soul a shadow sitting in the house of sin? Or was the body truly within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? The separation of spirit from matter was a mystery, and the union of spirit with matter was a mystery as well.

He began to wonder whether psychology could ever become such an exact science that every small source of life would be revealed to us. As things stood, we always misunderstood ourselves and seldom understood others. Experience had no ethical value. It was merely the name people gave to their mistakes. Moralists had generally treated it as a form of warning, claimed that it had some ethical power in shaping character, praised it as something that taught us what to pursue and showed us what to avoid. But experience had no driving force. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly proved was that our future would resemble our past, and that the sin we had committed once, with disgust, we would commit many times, with pleasure.

It was clear to him that the experimental method was the only way to reach any scientific analysis of the passions; and certainly Dorian Gray was a subject ready to hand, promising rich and fruitful results. His sudden, mad love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon of considerable interest. There was no doubt that curiosity had much to do with it, along with the desire for new experiences, yet it was not a simple passion but a highly complex one. Whatever it contained of the purely sensual instinct of boyhood had been transformed by the workings of imagination, changed into something that seemed to the boy himself far removed from the senses, and was therefore all the more dangerous. It was the passions whose origins we misunderstood that ruled us most powerfully. Our weakest motives were those whose nature we understood. It often happened that when we thought we were experimenting on others, we were actually experimenting on ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat dreaming about these things, there was a knock at the door. His valet entered and reminded him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"2244d35a9c5fe07999fe393e","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted that she was somewhat surprised by the match; but she spoke less of her astonishment than of her sincere wish for their happiness, and Elizabeth could not persuade her to think it unlikely. Kitty and Lydia were not at all jealous of Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman; to them, the marriage was simply news to pass around Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant that she could now return Mrs. Bennet’s comfort of having a daughter well married. She visited Longbourn more often than usual to say how happy she was, though Mrs. Bennet’s sour expressions and unkind remarks might have been enough to destroy anyone’s happiness.

Elizabeth and Charlotte were both restrained by an awkwardness that kept them silent on the subject, and Elizabeth became convinced that they could never again share real confidence. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her value her sister more warmly. She was certain that Jane’s honesty and delicacy could never lose her respect, and she grew more anxious for Jane’s happiness each day, since Bingley had now been gone a week and there was still no news of his return.

Jane had sent Caroline an early reply to her letter and was counting the days until she could reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father and written with all the solemn gratitude that a year’s stay with the family might have inspired. Having satisfied his conscience on that matter, he went on to tell them, with many delighted expressions, how happy he was to have won the affection of their pleasant neighbour, Miss Lucas. He then explained that he had agreed so readily to their kind invitation to return to Longbourn only because he wished to enjoy her company. He hoped to come back on the Monday two weeks from then. Lady Catherine, he added, approved of his marriage so warmly that she wanted it to happen as soon as possible. He trusted this would be an irresistible reason for his dear Charlotte to choose an early date and make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer welcome to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was just as ready to complain about it as her husband. It was very strange that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge, and it was also inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She hated having visitors in the house while her health was so poor, and lovers were the most unpleasant visitors of all."}

{"request_id":"792ba3cca1d1be43e2795dc1","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said when we reached its base, “come here! Was the skull nailed to the branch with its face turned outward, or toward the branch?”

“The face was out, massa, so the crows could reach the eyes easily, without any trouble.”

“Well, then, was it through this eye or that one that you dropped the beetle?” Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes in turn.

“It was this eye, massa—the left eye—just as you told me,” he said, pointing to his right eye.

“That will do—we must try it again.”

My friend, whose madness now seemed to me—or I fancied it did—to show certain signs of method, moved the peg marking the spot where the beetle had fallen to a point about three inches west of its former position. He then took the tape from the nearest point of the trunk to the peg, as before, and extended it in a straight line for fifty feet. This indicated a spot several yards away from where we had been digging.

We drew a circle around the new position, somewhat larger than the first, and set to work again with our spades. I was terribly tired, but, scarcely knowing what had changed in my thoughts, I no longer felt much resistance to the labor before me. I had become inexplicably interested—even excited. Perhaps there was something in Legrand’s extravagant behavior—some air of foresight or deliberation—that affected me. I dug eagerly, and from time to time caught myself looking with something very like expectation for the imagined treasure whose vision had driven my unfortunate companion mad. When these strange thoughts had taken their strongest hold on me, and after we had worked for perhaps an hour and a half, the dog’s violent howling interrupted us again. At first his uneasiness had clearly been only playfulness or caprice, but now his cries became harsh and serious. When Jupiter tried once more to muzzle him, the dog resisted furiously, leaped into the hole, and began tearing at the soil with his claws. Within seconds he had uncovered a mass of human bones, forming two complete skeletons, mixed with several metal buttons and what seemed to be the dust of decayed wool. One or two strokes of a spade turned up the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug farther, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin appeared."}

{"request_id":"12650a10144a2f58734ce29a","rewritten_text":"Not everyone would have behaved so kindly as she did, or refused to accept Jane’s answer; but she firmly declared that she would _not_ write the refusal Jane had asked of her yesterday. She would wait—and, sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was settled: Jane was to go. What a surprise to me! I had not the slightest idea! Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her immediately that, after considering the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had decided to accept it. I did not know a thing until it was all settled.”

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us; Mrs. Elton insisted that we come. It was arranged on the hill, while we were walking with Mr. Knightley. ‘You _must_ _all_ spend your evening with us,’ she said—‘I absolutely must have you _all_ come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he declined from the beginning. Although I thought he would come, because Mrs. Elton declared she would not excuse him, he did not—but my mother, Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very pleasant evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, must always seem agreeable, though everyone appeared rather exhausted after the morning’s party. Even pleasure, you know, is tiring—and I cannot say that any of them seemed to have enjoyed it very much. Still, _I_ shall always consider it a very pleasant party, and feel extremely grateful to the kind friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you did not know it, had been making up her mind throughout the day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time comes, it must be unwelcome to her and all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every possible advantage—I mean, in the character and manners of the family.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, it has everything in the world that could make her happy. Except for the Sucklings and Bragges, there is no other nursery establishment in all Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance so generous and elegant. Mrs. Smallridge is a most delightful woman! Her way of living is almost equal to Maple Grove—and as for the children, except the little Sucklings and little Bragges, there are nowhere such elegant, sweet children. Jane will be treated with such respect and kindness! It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary! I really cannot bring myself to tell you her salary, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"4fffd30166d66bcc7cefd1cb","rewritten_text":"It seemed to me that this quaint lie had been told in the simplest and most beautiful way. But I had heard it only once, and that makes a difference; no doubt it had pleased the others when it was still fresh.

Sir Dinadan the Humorist was the first to wake, and he soon roused the others with a rather poor practical joke. He tied some metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let it loose. The dog raced around the place in terror, while the other dogs chased it, barking and crashing into everything in their path. The result was complete confusion, with a deafening uproar. Every man and woman in the crowd laughed until tears ran down their faces; some even fell from their chairs and rolled on the floor in delight. They were just like children. Sir Dinadan was so proud of his trick that he kept explaining, again and again, how his brilliant idea had come to him, until everyone was tired of hearing it. Like humorists of his kind, he was still laughing at it after everyone else had stopped.

He was so pleased with himself that he decided to give a speech—naturally, a humorous one. I do not think I had ever heard so many worn-out jokes strung together. He was worse than the minstrels, worse than a circus clown. It was especially sad to sit there, thirteen hundred years before my birth, and hear once more the stale, worm-eaten jokes that had given me indigestion when I was a boy, thirteen hundred years later. It nearly convinced me that no new joke could ever be invented. Everyone laughed at these ancient jokes—but people always do; I had noticed that centuries afterward. The scoffer did not laugh, of course—I mean the boy. He scoffed instead; there was nothing he would not mock. He said most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes were rotten, and the rest were petrified. I said “petrified” was a good word. I myself believed that the only proper way to classify the great ages of some jokes was by geological periods. But the idea meant nothing to the boy, since geology had not yet been invented. Still, I made a note of the remark and planned to educate the whole country up to it if I survived. There was no reason to throw away a good idea merely because the market was not ready for it.

Then Sir Kay rose and began to run his history machine, using me as fuel."}
